Noble seats, cathedral, archives · the great houses and their households · cold air, incense and coin

The topmost plateau and the cliffs above it: the Duke's palace, the Zayida's Aegistower over the walls, the Merca's Vaulted Court built into the Mithril Reserve, the Virellarion's Crucible Spire carved into the mountainside with lightning rods humming at its top, the Citadel Cathedral, the Citadel Archives, and the Molten Crucible, where Vulkrim metal and Virellarion alchemy meet for the upper streets. The Gilded Imperator Casino stands where the Helm drops to the Middle City: brass and marble on wall-stone, dice where the battle-roar used to be.

Ties: House Caerthain; House Merca; House Zayida; the Crucible Spire.

The Geomantic Forge Existing · Upper Streets

Specialised foundries · smiths and geomancers · sulphur, wind and hot stone

Not a single grand forge but a string of smaller foundries arrayed across the citadel's plateaus, each harnessing a different natural force: geothermal vents, arid wind-tunnels, sun-traps, a cold spring. They belong mostly to House Vulkrim, whose mother-forge, the Geomanthic Foundries, burns in a volcanic ridge at the citadel's base.

Ties: House Vulkrim; the Forge of Vulcan.

The Marketplace Existing · Middle City

Covered market · every class · cool shade and spice

Roofed lanes running four ways from a central well, each lane a trade, dim, cool and permanently crowded, lit by shafts from vents in the vaulting. Everything the citadel eats, wears or builds with passes through. Stalls are heritable and change hands for sums that scandalise outsiders. The Gilded Vault and the Mithril Reserve keep counters at the market end. Once a year, at the Sweeping, the stallholders clear and rewhiten the whole market before dawn.

Ties: Clan Ironhand; Ember and Anvil and the Gilded Crucible nearby.

The Ju Colliseum Existing · Middle City

Arena · fighters, gamblers, priests · sand, blood and ash-oil

No actors, no scripts, no enchantments: only the pit, the blade and the crowd. Death matches for criminals and bond-debtors, yield duels, chain fights and mass pits; bonded fighters with the obsidian chain-mark, freemen gladiators, judgment champions. Nobles bet land and marriage pacts in the House Ring, commoners bet coin in the Circle of Bone. Five sanctioned wins earn a petition to House Zayida for pardon, bounty or a retainer's contract. Every fighter passes the Ember Gate and the Bowl of Judgment.

Ties: Marcia Ferox; the Sanctum of Hoplodamus; House Zayida.

Drakkur's Expeditionary Existing · Middle City

Outfitter · prospectors, mine crews, caravan guards · rope, lamp oil and dust

Racks and hooks of rope, lamps, water-skins, dust masks and rock hammers, and by the door a ledger larger than any of the stock. Every party signs out and signs back in; the entries never closed stay open on the page. Once a year, at the Reading of the Open Lines, they are read aloud, name and date and destination, and the shop does no trade that day.

Ties: the Dune Mines; the ruins past Zaruk'thal Spine.

The Parched Ox Existing · Lower City

Drinking hall, hiring hall, courthouse · gang masters and crews · beer and chalk

A long vaulted room with a stone counter, benches worn to a shine, and a slate by the door where work and grievances are chalked. Gang masters hire crews here; disputes nobody wants before the Duke's officers are settled at the back table by whoever the room agrees is impartial. The rulings have no force and are obeyed, because a man who ignores one does not get hired. At midwinter the slate is wiped clean.

Ties: Gavin Caesar drinks here; the Quarrymen.

The Quarrymen District Existing · Lower City

Stoneworkers' quarter · cutting gangs · grey dust on everything

Terraced housing on the cut face, hoists and sledways past the doors. The district supplies the building stone and the crews for the deep galleries. Gangs are family-based and a gang's name for a clean face is its living; pay is good and lives are short. The year's last block is carved with the year and set into the district wall, now a calendar four centuries long.

Ties: Overseer Tarnak; the Dune Mines.

The Rockpools Existing · Lower City

Cisterns and bath-houses · water-keepers · the only district never dry or quiet

Stepped cisterns cut into the rock, open and vaulted, taking the mountain channels' flow and sending it upward to every district above. The keepers are lower-city people with power over the whole citadel, a mismatch nobody has resolved. The cistern levels are read publicly at the year's turn; in a poor year the reading behaves like an omen.

Ties: the Terraces; Water.

Terraces Farms Existing · Lower and Middle City

Inner-slope fields · every household · wet earth in a dry mountain

Stepped fields on the inner slope, watered from the Rockpools: vegetables, fruit and fodder, not enough to feed the citadel but enough to matter. They are why two sieges failed. Plots are allotted by household and redistributed by lot every seventh year, at the Allotment, which is fiercely watched, occasionally violent, and has never been abolished.

Ties: the Rockpools.

The Furnace Ring Lower City · inside the outer wall

Blast-houses · armourer families · smoke day and night

A ring of squat blast-houses inside the outer wall, working in shifts around the clock. The Iron Furnaces smelt iron, temper steel by methods the families do not discuss, and forge a few ingots of cold iron a year. A buyer is received in the front hall by armourers wearing their best work; admire a blade and you are offered a price. Lately one family's blades have stopped ringing.

Ties: House Vulkrim; Mavelon's arsenal.

Rule

Duke Roderick Caesar rules, and his authority is not constitutional: it rests on the household, on marriages, obligations and the fact that the citadel's other families are all, in some degree, his clients. The Duke governs the citadel; Duchess Kivia Elea Caesar governs the house, its keys, stores, marriages and accounts, and the Argentar ask for her when the debt needs revisiting. Day-to-day administration and the forces belong to House Zayida from the Aegistower under Count Faris Zayida, the Duke's right hand. The Adamantine Line, the citadel's ancient legion, holds the Iron Parade Grounds under Commander Daud, the Royal Protector, whose nickname says whose person he keeps, with Vice-Commander Meagan Foster actually running the legion; Gavin Caesar commands the standing garrison.

Who checks him: the Pact, signed in enchanted water, binds the allied houses to the citadel's defence and its secrets; the Mithril Reserve holds the debt; the Rockpools' keepers hold the water; and the Imperium, to which the citadel is allied but not subject, holds the road north. Roderick sends levies when asked and accepts no Dux.

Houses and families

House Caerthain, "the Caesars" Duke

Crest: a silver-winged helm atop a black mountain, flanked by twin golden sunbursts · Motto: "We held the peaks. We hold the skies." · Seat: the ducal palace on the Helm

Guardians of the south, stoic and occasionally treated as divine; their word is law and their silence means more than their decrees. Pioneers of the Skyward Bastions, the Serathian Fleet and a prototype airship called the Sovereign Star.

  • Duke Roderick Caesar — a war-made ruler in a peace he did not want; not cruel, not sentimental, and spending on temples rather than admit the ore is failing.
  • Duchess Kivia Elea Caesar — has held the keys and accounts for twenty-six years; the reason Merca and Vulkrim have not fallen out openly in a decade.
  • Roland Caesar, the Heir — capable, impatient, has read the assay reports; on good terms with the Reserve and contemptuous of Tristan.
  • Gavin Caesar, second son — commands the garrison, drinks in the Parched Ox, twice paid a mine crew from his own purse; the lower city adores him.
  • Helena Caesar — married at seventeen into a marquis house, widowed at twenty-four, now the house's sharpest negotiator; close to Isolde Merca.
  • Tristan Caesar — the acknowledged natural son, barred from succession, sent where a legitimate son cannot go; keeps rooms in the Middle City by choice.
  • Scribonia Caesar — carries the name, manages much of the correspondence, appears on no genealogy; the Duchess's silence protects her.
  • Lady Isolde Merca, resident guest — hostage, ally and the Reserve's eyes on its largest debtor.

Ties: Persemenid and Xerastri (The Cloudspine Feud with House Mihran).

House Merca Marquis · founders of the Mithril Reserve

Crest: a silver stag on a pile of coins, antlers tipped with scales · Motto: "Trust, like gold, is forged over fire." · Seat: the Vaulted Court

Calculating, clever, feared by debtors, and dangerous in rooms with contracts. Inventors of Runes of Trust and Ledgerlocks; rumoured to mint a private currency and to hold a ledger of every secret debt, the Duke's included. Lady Isolde's letters go to Deiperduem and to every branch master on the continent (The Mithril Ledger).

  • Marquis Edran Merca, head — has not left the Vaulted Court in nine years and runs the Reserve by letter.
  • Lady Isolde Merca — his daughter, in the Duke's household.
  • Lord Selvane Merca — her brother, Treasurer of the Vaulted Court, often at Deiperduem.

Ties: Deiperduem; Banking; Clan Ironhand.

Clan Ironhand Dwarven line · keepers of the Reserve's vaults

Crest: an iron gauntlet holding a key · Motto: "What is given to stone is kept" · Seat: the vault levels under the Vaulted Court

Dwarves who have kept the Mithril Reserve's vaults for as long as there have been vaults, and who supply its branches with masters: a Dominus Argentar called Ironhand sits in Aeterna, Aepistra and Mavelon. Sworn on a shard of the original Mithril Lode; loyal to the Reserve first and the Merca second.

  • Haldor Ironhand, Dominus Argentar of Duneforged and Master of the Vaults — knows the Duke's debt to the coin and the Duke's ore to the ton.
  • Sigrun Ironhand, Captain of the Custodes — has doubled the vault watch since the hum began.
  • Quellan Fennick, Arcanist-Securitas, a gnome — keeps the wards and the bound guardian, and is not an Ironhand, which the clan never lets him forget.

Ties: House Merca; Aeterna, Aepistra, Mavelon branches.

House Vulkrim Marquis · smiths

Crest: a molten hammer over crossed tongs, ringed by a crown of fire · Motto: "From fire, we rise." · Seat: the Geomanthic Foundries

Common blacksmiths raised to nobility by friendship with a duke; one of the Three Great Smithing Houses. The Embersteel Line, living anvils, and a forbidden design for soulbound forge armour in their archive.

  • Ferratus Vulkrim, Marquis of Vulkrim, Forge-Lord of the Southern Ridges — renounced politics for the forge; his left hand is fused into an iron gauntlet; the Order of Ember, a secret brotherhood of warrior-smiths, treats him as near-divine.
  • Lady Ottilde Vulkrim, his niece and heir — runs Ember and Anvil and the house's politics, since her uncle will not.
  • Quartermaster Thestun Vulkrim — furious about stolen goods and a bandit called the Jackal at the Broken Gate.

Ties: the Geomantic Forge; House Virellarion (the Molten Crucible).

House Virellarion Count · alchemy and artifice

Crest: a silver serpent eating its tail around a glowing gear and a crystal vial · Motto: "Minds of metal, hearts of fire." · Seat: the Crucible Spire

Philosopher-smiths who refuse to separate alchemy from artifice; every member must transmute as easily as construct. Aetherblood Elixirs, Soulcoil Engines, Memorysteel, and the Stillflame Vault deep in the Spire.

  • Countess Aurelie Virellarion, Mistress of the Crucible Spire.
  • Lord Ambrose Virellarion, her brother — keeps the Gilded Crucible, the atelier in the Middle District.

Ties: House Vulkrim.

House Zayida Count · stewards and generals

Crest: a golden falcon clutching a scroll and a sword over a blue mountain · Motto: "Loyalty is the highest command." · Seat: the Aegistower

The Duke's right hand: administration and command. Strict, fair, and feared by the corrupt. Keepers of the Codex of Rule, the living ledger of every citizen, soldier and sack in the citadel; their elite Silent Warden Order is rumoured to be alchemically enhanced.

  • Count Faris Zayida, Steward of the Aegistower — arena fighters still call him "the Marquis" from an old courtesy he has never corrected.
  • Lady Nadira Zayida, Warden of the Silent Warden Order.
  • Idris Zayida, keeper of the Codex of Rule — has noticed that the Codex now counts fewer miners than the payroll does.

Ties: the Ju Colliseum.

Notable figures

  • Marcia Ferox, the Unbought champion of the Ju Colliseum — the arena's greatest freeman fighter; no house has managed to back her.
  • Commander Daud, the Royal Protector Commander of the Adamantine Line — guards the Duke's person; the court gave him his nickname.
  • Vice-Commander Meagan Foster Adamantine Line — the officer who actually keeps the legion running.
  • Overseer Tarnak Foreman of the Lower Mines — needs the hum explained quietly, because a shut mine pays no wages.
  • Elira junior scholar, Citadel Archives — bright, under-supervised, currently set on going out to the shifting plains herself.
  • Drakkur outfitter — keeps the ledger of the missing and reads it once a year.

Connections

  • Mavelon and Aeterna — north up the Via Ferraria; ore by Gilded Horizon contract to the arsenal, levies to the capital when asked.
  • Persemenid and Xerastri — House Mihran's strongholds; The Cloudspine Feud.
  • Deiperduem — the Reserve's largest branch outside the citadel; Isolde Merca's letters (The Mithril Ledger).
  • Romulo — where the citadel's export contracts are sealed against the master weights.

The towns

Road town · Imperium Invicta · Via Septentrionalis

Anticata

One long street that is also the northern highway: a mansio, a market and a remount station, and a town that has made a living out of being passed through.

Codex now: An Invictian road town on the northern highway — mansio, market and remount station, and used to being passed through.

Governor
Titus Lollius Varro
Title
Praefectus of the Mansio (appointed)
Population
c. 2,400 residents, and nearly as many again on any given night
Built on
A day's march from the capital and a guaranteed bed
Patron
Mercury of the roads; Janus at the milestones
Trouble
Fewer patrols, more drifting veterans, a watch nobody wanted to need

The town

Anticata (some milestones still say Anticasta) exists because a day's march out of Aeterna ends here. The highway is the high street and every door faces it. The official waystation of the Cursus Legionis keeps fresh horses, a register of every courier and officer who changes mounts, and a clientele the state is obliged to send. Stabling, lodging, farriers and food take the rest. The farmland behind is decent and goes to the Annona like everything else in the province; the inns keep what is left.

Half the people in Anticata on any night do not live there, and the permanent population has organised itself entirely around that fact. A bed costs two asses in the loft of the Milestone, a denarius for a room with a door, and an officer's diploma for the upstairs suite, which is kept empty for officers and let to merchants when none arrive. Every trade serves travellers: cobblers who re-nail a legionary's caligae while he eats, a cookshop that sells a day's bread and cheese wrapped in a cloth for the road, a shrine to Mercury where carters pour the last of their cup.

New lore

The road used to be patrolled every second day. Since the Great Concord it is patrolled when a cohort happens to be going that way. Demobilised legionaries walk through in both directions, looking for land that was promised and pensions that are late, and two years ago Anticata hired its own watch for the first time in its history. The older residents regard it as an admission of something. Gossip still arrives before news, which makes the town unusually well informed and unusually wrong.

At the Milestone each spring the road's two markers are cleaned and repainted, with a procession to each. At the Long Table each midsummer a single table runs down the middle of the highway and the road is closed for a day: the only day Anticata makes travellers wait. Two years ago a courier of the northern Legate tried to ride through the Long Table and was pulled off his horse by the Innkeepers' wives. The Legate's office complained; the town framed the complaint and hung it in the Milestone.

The road has a new traffic. Recruiters in good boots buy wine for veterans at the back tables and ask who served under whom. Some pay in pre-debasement silver, which is how the town knows they are not the state.

Quarters

The Street Existing · the highway itself

Inns, cookshops, farriers · innkeepers and touts · horse, woodsmoke and fried fish

A mile of frontage on both sides of the paving, painted with prices. The Milestone inn stands at the middle; the two cleaned and repainted markers stand at either end. Touts meet every rider at the south marker and walk beside him, reciting the menu, until he chooses a door. The paving is the Imperium's and nobody here has the right to mend it, so the town fills the potholes with gravel at night and denies it in the morning.

Ties: the Pollii; the Collegium of Innkeepers; the Stabularia.

The Stabularia Existing · remount yards

Cursus stables and the register-house · grooms and clerks · hay and liniment

The state's yards behind the north end of the street: forty stalls, a smithy, and the register in which every official rider signs. The register is the most valuable object in town. It is kept in a bronze-bound chest with two locks; the Praefectus holds one key and the chief clerk the other, and in practice the chief clerk holds both.

Ties: the Cursus Legionis; Information; the Street.

The Veterans' Field Beyond the north milestone

Tents, lean-tos and cookfires · discharged legionaries and their women · damp wool and boiled barley

A strip of common grazing past the north marker where walking veterans have camped since the Concord. It began as a night's stop and has become a village nobody chartered: a smith who was a cohort armourer, a barber who was a medicus, a latrine trench dug to regulation depth. The Collegium wants it cleared; Captain Duro keeps finding reasons why tomorrow would be better.

Ties: the Watchers of the Eternal Rest; the town watch; Aepistra, where most claim their land is.

Who governs

Praefectus Titus Lollius Varro, appointed from Aeterna to run the mansio, holds the town by virtue of holding the horses. He answers to the Cursus Legionis office in the capital. His check is the Collegium of Innkeepers, which pays for the new watch and therefore decides whom it watches. Varro is of the gens Lollia, cousin at three removes to Legatus Sextus Lollius Calvus of the south, which on the northern Legate's road makes every courier treat him as a spy whether he is one or not. His chief clerk of the register, Atilius Nepos, is the man who actually runs the Stabularia.

Families

The Pollii Innkeepers · collegium masters

Crest: a milestone with a lamp on it · Motto: "Everyone passes. We remain." · Seat: the Milestone inn

Owners of the largest inn and three smaller ones, masters of the Collegium of Innkeepers for four generations, and quiet lenders to half the street.

  • Pollia Secunda, head of the family — knows every regular's debts and every officer's preferred room.
  • Gaius Pollius Rufus, her son, paymaster of the town watch — enjoys the post more than he should.
  • Pollia Minor, her granddaughter, who keeps the Milestone's books — counts the old silver separately and has started to wonder where it comes from.

Ties: the Collegium of Innkeepers; the Street; rivals of the Equitii.

The Equitii Horse-breeders · the remount contract

Crest: a bay mare under a lamp-post · Motto: "Fresh horses, honest legs." · Seat: the paddocks behind the Stabularia

Breeders who have sold the Cursus its remounts for three generations, paid by the state on a schedule that has slipped from quarterly to "in due course". They hate the Pollii for lending them money at the Collegium rate and need them for the same reason.

  • Gnaeus Equitius Faber, head of the family — has sold six horses to a buyer who paid in old silver and asked for no brand.
  • Equitia Rufa, his wife, who rides the courier stage to Aepistra when the state is short of riders — knows the road better than any cohort.

Ties: the Stabularia; the Cursus Legionis; the Pollii (debt).

Notable figures

  • Titus Lollius Varro Praefectus of the Mansio — a decent administrator with the wrong surname, writing careful letters to Aeterna that nobody answers.
  • Sextus Duro captain of the town watch · ex-centurion — twenty-six years in the legions, a pension in arrears, and a soft spot for men who are walking the road he walked.
  • Old Faustina farrier — shoes the Cursus horses and reads the register upside down while she works.
  • Mennas the Teller gossip-seller — sells news by the cup at the Milestone; is right about one time in three, and charges the same either way.
  • Atilius Nepos chief clerk of the register — dry, precise and underpaid; can tell from the ink which day an entry was made.

Connections

  • Aeterna City — a day south on the Via Septentrionalis; every rumour from the capital stops here first.
  • Aepistra — the provincial capital further north on the same road; its couriers change horses here.
  • Information — the Cursus register is a list of who went where, and several people would pay for it.
  • Military (Invicta) — the veterans in the Field are the unpaid end of the demobilisation.

Hill town · Imperium Invicta · the hills above the capital

Falecosa

Stone houses stacked on a south-facing slope above terraced vines: a small, old town whose wine the capital buys at prices the growers find funny.

Codex now: An Invictian hill town of terraced vineyards — small, old, and producing wine the capital pays absurdly for.

Governor
Marcus Helvius Tappo and Gaius Sallustius Pictor
Title
Duumviri (two annual magistrates)
Population
c. 1,800
Built on
A south slope and eight hundred years of dry walls
Patron
Liber Pater of the vine; Ceres for the bread grown between rows
Trouble
Absentee landlords, ancient tenants, and walls that one bad season could ruin

The town

The vines grow on terraces held up by dry-stone walls that have needed rebuilding every generation for eight hundred years. Falecosa makes wine and very little else: one named, aged vintage sold to Aeterna. A clay amphora of a good year fetches forty denarii in the capital; the grower who trod it is paid four. The estates are owned from the capital now, worked by tenants whose families were on the same terraces long before the owners' families bought them. The wall round the town is in poor repair and there is no garrison; there is nothing here to take but wine, and wine is easier to buy.

Life is slow, hierarchical and intensely local. Everyone is related, everyone knows which terrace belongs to whom, and boundary disputes run for generations. The Treading, the nine-day harvest, is when the whole town works and the whole town drinks, in that order.

New lore

The vineyards are the real weak point. A season's vandalism would ruin the town for a decade, and landlords' bailiffs mention this whenever a rent dispute turns sharp. Since the coin went bad the capital owners have started paying for the harvest in new silver and demanding rents in old, and the tenants have noticed. At the Naming each spring the year's vintage is opened, judged and named. A bad name is remembered for decades: the vintage of eleven years ago is still called "the Senator's Bladder". The College of the Starlit Lute collects harvest songs here; they are among the oldest attested, and they vary by terrace.

Peace brought buyers, not tenants. Two capital houses have bought terraces since the Concord, House Lucretia among them, and both talk of working them with bought labour from the Farshore markets at Romulo. The slope has heard. New verses have appeared in the treading songs, and they are not about grapes.

Quarters

The Terraces Existing · below the town

Vines and dry walls · tenant families · dust, sun and crushed grapes in autumn

Forty-one numbered terraces, each with its own family, its own songs and its own grudges. At the Walling in early spring everyone repairs everyone's walls. Attendance is not optional in any sense that matters. Terrace Seven, the Helvii's, is the best; Terraces Thirty to Forty-one, on the steep western end, are where new owners buy first because they are cheapest.

Ties: the Helvii; the College of the Starlit Lute; the Cellae.

The Cellae Existing · upper town

Cellars under the houses · bailiffs and coopers · cold stone and old wine

The stacked houses at the top of the slope, with the ageing cellars cut beneath them. The landlords' bailiffs keep offices here, next to the coopers and the tasting hall where the Naming is held. The cellars connect, unofficially, by passages older than any deed; a cask can travel the length of the town without seeing daylight.

Ties: the Sallustii; the capital estates; Romulo, where the vintage contracts are sealed.

The Press Yard Mid-slope, by the old gate

Beam presses, the treading floors and the market · everyone, at harvest · must, wasps and lamp smoke

The communal treading floors and the four great beam presses owned in common by the town, the one thing in Falecosa no capital house has managed to buy. In the off-season it is the market and the place where disputes are argued in front of everyone. The ruined town gate stands at one corner, propped up by a press beam.

Ties: the Duumviri; the Terraces; Nemibano, whose offering wine is pressed here.

Who governs

Two Duumviri are elected each year by the citizens. Custom gives one seat to the growers and one to the owners: this year Marcus Helvius Tappo speaks for the terraces and Gaius Sallustius Pictor, chief bailiff to three capital estates, speaks for the money. Their check is the Walling: if the tenant families do not turn out, the walls fall, and both Duumviri know it. The presses are kept by an elected Master of the Presses, at present Cornelia Vinitrix, who decides whose grapes go under the beam first and is therefore the most courted woman in town every autumn.

Families

The Helvii Tenant growers · Terrace Seven

Crest: a vine-knife over a stone · Motto: "The wall outlives the owner." · Seat: the house at the head of Terrace Seven

Tenants of the best terrace for thirty generations, owners of nothing, and the family the rest of the slope follows in any dispute.

  • Marcus Helvius Tappo, Duumvir — patient, stubborn, and keeping a ledger of every rent paid in bad coin.
  • Helvia Prima, his mother, the Namer — has named the vintage nineteen times; two of the names are still insults.
  • Lucius Helvius, his nephew — wants to break the walls of an absentee landlord's terrace and has said so in a tavern.

Ties: the Terraces; the Sallustii (opponents).

The Sallustii Bailiffs to the capital estates

Crest: a sealed amphora · Motto: "Measured, sealed, delivered." · Seat: the bailiffs' house in the Cellae

A family of freedmen's descendants who have been stewards to absentee owners for four generations and have quietly bought six terraces of their own through nominees. Hated on the slope, needed in the capital, and richer than either side suspects.

  • Gaius Sallustius Pictor, Duumvir and chief bailiff — sends rents to the capital and threats down the slope.
  • Sallustia Paulla, his sister, who keeps the estate ledgers — wants her brother out of the feud before it costs them the terraces they secretly own.

Ties: House Lucretia; the Cellae; Romulo.

Notable figures

  • Gaius Sallustius Pictor Duumvir · chief bailiff — sends rents to the capital and threats down the slope; sincerely believes he is the reasonable one.
  • Ione of the Lute bard of the College of the Starlit Lute — collecting terrace songs, and noticing that the newest verses are about burning.
  • Old Statius master waller — knows which walls hold up which terraces, and which single stone would bring three of them down.
  • Cornelia Vinitrix Master of the Presses — incorruptible in public and fond of gifts in private; the order of pressing is the town's real calendar.
  • Aulus Lucretius Primus's factor, Hermeros capital buyer · freedman — walking the western terraces with a measuring rope and a purse of new silver.

Connections

  • Aeterna City — a day or two down to the capital, where the owners live and the vintage is drunk.
  • Romulo — every great vintage contract is registered and sealed there against the master measures.
  • Nemibano — the next hill town over; Falecosa sends its offering wine to the grove each Torchlight.
  • The purse (Invicta) — rents in old coin, wages in new: the debasement in one slope.

River port · Imperium Invicta · mouth of the River Tiberius

Fucostia

Wharves, cranes and granaries where sea hulls hand over to river barges: the bottleneck through which every sack of the capital's grain must pass.

Codex now: An Invictian river port at the mouth of the Tiberius — grain wharves, warehouses, and the bottleneck the capital cannot afford to lose.

Governor
Quintus Annaeus Brocchus
Title
Praefectus of the Port, answering to the Prefect of the Annona
Population
c. 9,000, swelling to 15,000 in the shipping season
Built on
The river mouth, where sea hulls give way to barges
Patron
Ceres of the Annona; Portunus of the harbour
Trouble
Falling throughput and porters who can count to three weeks

The town

Warehouses, and more warehouses. All the grain of the Annona passes through Fucostia, and its warehousemen, lightermen and porters know exactly what that means. The town smells permanently of grain dust and tar. A sea hull anchors in the roads; lighters take its cargo to the Lighter Steps; saccarii carry it up on their backs, a modius at a time, to the horrea; mensores measure it in and out; and barges hauled by oxen take it up the River Tiberius, a day up to Aeterna and two back. Every hand in that chain is paid by the sack and counts the sacks.

The Aurum Pact runs the isolation warehouses outside the walls, and their certificate is what lets a suspect cargo up the Tiberius at all. A harbour watch and the fleet's anchorage are the only defence: a serious enemy at Fucostia means the war is already lost. Life is rough, wet and organised by guild, and the town swells and shrinks with the shipping.

New lore

The real danger is internal. A strike on these wharves empties Aeterna's granaries in about three weeks, and since the coin went bad the porters' guilds have started saying so out loud. Farshore grain from Khemaret now comes coastwise from Mavelon to make up the shortfall, at prices the Annona cannot sustain. At the First Hull the season's first grain ship is met, blessed and unloaded free by the guilds; at the Weighing each autumn the year's throughput is read out against the last: it has fallen three years running and the reading has become tense. At the Lantern Tide lamps are floated downriver for men lost on the wharves. The mood on the wharves is the best forecast of trouble in the capital, and the people who count the dole understand its arithmetic better than anyone in Aeterna does.

Fucostia has a new trade: grain theft. The town calls the thieves the Weevils. They are not one gang but a habit: a sack split on the steps, a false floor in a lighter, a measurer's thumb on the modius. Prefect Macer's office prosecutes porters for a handful of spilt wheat while barge-loads go missing on paper, and the porters have noticed which end of the scale is being watched.

Quarters

The Horrea Existing · granary rows

State granaries in brick ranks · clerks, measurers and rat-catchers · dust that gets into everything

Twenty-two numbered granaries on raised floors, each with a measurer's office at the door. Grain comes in by the sack, goes out by the barge-load, and is counted twice in between. Horreum Nine has been "under repair" for two years and is always full. Cats are on the state payroll at an as a month each; the rat-catchers' collegium claims the cats are frauds.

Ties: the Prefect of the Annona; the Annona; the Emporium at Aeterna.

The Lighter Steps Existing · wharves

Quays, cranes and guild halls · porters and lightermen · tar, river mud and sweat

The stone stairs where sea hulls unload into flat lighters. The guild halls stand at the top of the steps, and the Lantern Tide starts here when lamps are floated for men lost on the wharves. Six treadwheel cranes, each worked by eight men walking inside the wheel, are rented by the hour from the Mamilii.

Ties: the Mamilii; the Collegium of Saccarii; the Towpath.

The Towpath Barge basin and the up-river road

Barge basin, ox-sheds, rope-sellers · bargemen, drovers, Weevil fences · dung, wet rope and fried eel

The basin where loaded barges are made up into strings and the oxen are yoked for the haul to Aeterna. Taverns along the path sell to bargemen at all hours, and some buy as well: a sack of Annona wheat fetches three denarii here, no questions, which is more than the dole is worth to the man who carried it. Half the barges belong on charter to House Ovinia.

Ties: House Ovinia; the Annaei; the River Tiberius to Aeterna.

Who governs

Praefectus Quintus Annaeus Brocchus runs the port for the Prefect of the Annona, Sextus Naevius Macer, in Aeterna, and is judged by one number. His check is the porters' collegia, chief among them the Collegium of Saccarii, who can stop the town by sitting down. The Aurum Pact's certificate is a second check he cannot overrule. The harbour watch answers to his Tribune of the Watch, Gnaea Tullia Rufa, and the fleet anchorage to the Praefectus Classis at Mavelon, which means to nobody here. The Saccarii are led by their elected Magister, Burrus the Ox.

Families

The Mamilii Lightermen · guild masters

Crest: crossed boat-hooks over a grain measure · Motto: "We carry the city." · Seat: the Lightermen's Hall on the Steps

Masters of the lightermen's guild for five generations. They own forty lighters, rent the cranes, and decide which hulls unload first.

  • Mamilia Tertia, guild mistress — has never raised her voice, and has never needed to.
  • Decimus Mamilius, her brother — speaks for strike in the guild hall, loudly, and is useful to her because of it.
  • Mamilius Parvus, her son, a crane-master — has seen lighters come in lighter than their tallies and has said nothing yet.

Ties: the Lighter Steps; the Collegium of Saccarii; the Annaei.

The Annaei Port officials · the Praefectus's kin

Crest: a balance over a wave · Motto: "Weighed and found." · Seat: the Praefectus's house above the Horrea

An equestrian family of clerks and measurers who have held lesser offices of the port for a century and the Praefecture for the last six years. Honest by habit, poor by the standards of their office, and therefore regarded in Aeterna as either saints or incompetents.

  • Quintus Annaeus Brocchus, Praefectus — see below.
  • Annaea Severa, his wife, who runs the Towpath charity kitchen — feeds the porters' children and hears what their fathers say at night.

Ties: the Prefect of the Annona; the Horrea; the Towpath.

Notable figures

  • Quintus Annaeus Brocchus Praefectus — honest, overworked, and frightened of the next Weighing.
  • Ysolde Varn Aurum Pact inspector — signs the certificates; has refused two cargoes this season and been offered money for both.
  • Pannonius the Measurer chief mensor of the Horrea — reads the Weighing aloud each year, and knows his figures do not add up.
  • Burrus the Ox Magister of the Saccarii — carries two sacks up the Steps at once to prove a point; can call a strike with one word and is being paid by two people to say it.
  • Lucius Ovinius Balbus House Ovinia's barge-charterer — down from Aeterna, knows the Annona's shortfall to the sack, and knows which of his barges carry more than their manifests.

Connections

  • Aeterna City — up the River Tiberius; its granaries are three weeks from empty without Fucostia.
  • The Annona — the grain dole that passes, in its entirety, through these warehouses.
  • Mavelon — the great southern port, three days by sea; Farshore grain comes coastwise from its harbours.
  • Napplesia — down the coast; the grain escorts' officers retire there.

Bay town · Imperium Invicta · end of the Via Litoranea

Napplesia

A warm southern bay of springs and shore villas, full of retired officers with pensions, opinions and time, and of moralists from the capital on holiday.

Codex now: A southern Invictian bay town — hot springs, retired officers, and a leisure economy the capital pretends to disapprove of.

Governor
Spurius Nautius Crassipes and Lucius Arruntius Stella
Title
Duumviri (two annual magistrates)
Population
c. 6,000, half again in the villa season
Built on
A warm bay and six centuries of paid admission to hot springs
Patron
Venus of the bay; Apollo of the healing springs
Trouble
Pension arrears, and the men angry about them once commanded cohorts

The town

A curved bay, a warm sea, and villas along the shore built by people who could have built somewhere better and chose here. The town proper sits behind them, older and much less pretty. Napplesia sells sea air, fish, rented villas and the mineral springs, to which the Radiant Heartwardens send patients and for which the town has charged admission for six hundred years. The capital's moralists have condemned it for eight hundred, and holidayed here throughout.

It sits at the end of the Via Litoranea and on the sea lane to Mavelon, two days' sail south. Coasters from the caldera call every few days with oysters, wine, Farshore cloth and Farshore company. A villa on the Ripa rents for two hundred denarii a season; admission to the Great Bath is a quadrans, the same for a senator as for a fishwife, which is the town's oldest joke and its proudest law.

New lore

Since the Great Concord retired officers have taken their discharge here in numbers. The Discharge, when the year's new arrivals are welcomed by those already settled, has grown very large in five years. When the Watchers of the Eternal Rest publish pension arrears, Napplesia is where the loudest answer comes from. Social life is villa-based, evening-heavy and famously indiscreet; more Invictian politics is settled at dinner tables here than anyone admits, and Information treats the town as a listening post. The Opening of the Baths, after the winter cleaning, is decided by lot, not rank, and is genuinely popular.

The newest money is the pleasure-trade. Farshore houses that sell at Mavelon have learned that Napplesia buys: Tyrsan purple, Sabaian myrrh for the baths, Keftaran bull-leapers hired for dinners, and dancers and hetaira-companions from Qart-Hadeth's ships, who keep a whole lane of the old town. The capital's moralists now have something new to condemn, and they come down in greater numbers to do it.

Quarters

The Ripa Existing · shore of villas

Colonnaded villas and private jetties · capital money and pensioned officers · jasmine, salt and lamp-oil

The crescent of villas along the beach. At the Sea Table each villa feeds whoever arrives, and for one night a fisherman may eat beside a retired tribune. The eastern end, nearest the springs, is old senatorial money; the western end, with the newer, squarer villas, is called the Castra by the old money, because that is where the officers bought.

Ties: the Veterans' Table; the Arruntii of Napplesia; Information.

The Thermae Existing · old town and springs

Bath-houses and narrow lanes · bath-keepers, physicians, fishmongers · sulphur and steam

The older town around the springs: three bath-houses, a Heartwarden infirmary, and lanes too narrow for a litter, which the residents consider a defence. The hottest spring, the Cauldron, boils an egg in the time it takes to say a prayer to Apollo; the infirmary uses it for cleaning instruments, and the cookshops for eggs.

Ties: the Nautii; the Radiant Heartwardens.

Lantern Lane The Farshore quarter by the fish quay

Wine-shops, dancing-houses, a Tyrsan shrine · Farshore sailors, companions and their clients · cedar oil, myrrh and grilled octopus

Three alleys behind the fish quay where the coasters from Mavelon tie up, lit by red lamps from Tyrsa that give the lane its name. Companions from Qart-Hadeth and Keftara keep houses here under Farshore law, which the Duumviri tolerate because the lane pays a third of the town's harbour dues. Every dinner on the Ripa ends, sooner or later, with someone sending a slave down here.

Ties: Mavelon's south harbour; Romulo, where the Farshore houses are registered; Information.

Who governs

Two Duumviri, elected yearly: Spurius Nautius Crassipes, of the old bath-keeping family, and Lucius Arruntius Stella, a retired tribune and the first veteran ever elected here. Their check is the Veterans' Table, a dining club of former officers that now outvotes the old town in every assembly. The harbour and its dues are kept by the Aedile of the Quay, Publilia Merula, who knows to the as what Lantern Lane earns. Behind them all is the town's informal fourth power, the hostesses of the Ripa, whose invitations decide who is heard.

Families

The Nautii Bath-keepers · old town

Crest: a steaming spring in a ring of stones · Motto: "Everyone undresses the same." · Seat: the Great Bath

Keepers of the largest spring for six centuries. They take the admission money, hear the gossip of every naked senator, and sell neither.

  • Spurius Nautius Crassipes, Duumvir — fat, cheerful and much sharper than he lets visitors see.
  • Nautia Lepida, his daughter, keeper of the bath ledgers — knows who bathes with whom, and when.

Ties: the Thermae; the Radiant Heartwardens; uneasy allies of the Arruntii.

The Arruntii of Napplesia Officer family · cadet branch of gens Arruntia

Crest: an oar crossed with a vine-staff · Motto: "We served. We remember." · Seat: the Villa Stella at the western end of the Ripa

A cadet branch of the Mavelon gens Arruntia that has sent sons to the legions for six generations and brought them home to the bay. Their villa is the Veterans' Table's dining room, and their cousin is the Dux of Mavelon, which makes them the town's channel south.

  • Lucius Arruntius Stella, Duumvir, retired tribune — elected to keep the veterans calm.
  • Arruntia Vesta, his wife — hostess of the Ripa's most important table and keeper of the Discharge roll.
  • Marcus Arruntius Stella, his son, a serving centurion under Legatus Sextus Lollius Calvus — home on leave, too often.

Ties: gens Arruntia of Mavelon; the Veterans' Table; the Council of Legates.

Notable figures

  • Lucius Arruntius Stella Duumvir · retired tribune — elected to keep the veterans calm; increasingly elected to lead them.
  • Sister Aurelia Lenis Radiant Heartwarden physician — treats old wounds at the springs and hears more confessions than a priest.
  • Felix the Fishmonger Information agent — sells the best mullet on the bay and reports every dinner guest list to Aeterna.
  • Imilce of Qart-Hadeth mistress of the House of the Red Lamp, Lantern Lane — hosts the dinners after the dinners; keeps her own ledger of officers' debts and pays her harbour dues in Farshore gold.
  • Gaius Fabricius Durus retired primus pilus · president of the Veterans' Table — sixty-eight, one eye, the loudest voice at the Discharge; reads the arrears figures aloud at every dinner like a casualty list.

Connections

  • Aeterna City — north by the Via Litoranea; senators come down to disapprove of the town in person.
  • Mavelon — further along the coast road and two days by the sea lane; Napplesia's villas buy Farshore luxuries from its quays.
  • Information — the town is treated as a listening post, and knows it.
  • Fucostia — up the coast; grain escorts' officers retire here, retired admirals compare notes.

Grove town · Imperium Invicta · the hills above the capital

Nemibano

A town on the rim of a wooded crater lake, serving the sacred grove below, where the wardenship is still held by whoever takes it in single combat.

Codex now: An Invictian grove town under the Verdant Sentinels — the sacred wood is the town, and the wardenship is held by combat.

Governor
Aulus Vettius Lento and Marcia Ocrea
Title
Duumviri (civil); the grove has its own warden
Population
c. 1,500, more at the Torchlight
Built on
A crater lake and a priesthood held by the sword
Patron
Diana of the grove
Trouble
The capital wants the custom abolished; strangers keep asking about it

The town

A lake in a wooded crater and a town on its rim that exists to serve the grove of Diana below. The trees are old, the path down is stepped, and nobody goes below the treeline after dark without a reason. Nemibano lives on pilgrims, offerings, lodging and guides, and on farmland worked under restrictions the Verdant Sentinel Order enforces: no iron plough within sight of the lake, no fire on the slope, no hunting of deer at all. The timber is never cut. It is not a rich town and has refused, repeatedly, to become one. A pilgrim's lamp costs an as; a votive clay stag, two; a guide to the treeline at dusk, a denarius, paid to the Ocreae and to no one else.

New lore

The Order garrisons the grove lightly, but the wardenship follows the old custom: the warden holds the post until another takes it from him in single combat, at the grove. Gnaeus Ferrus has held it nineteen years. The capital has tried four times to abolish the arrangement and the town has declined four times. This is the only Invictian town where the local rite outranks the imperial one, and the townspeople are quietly certain that the arrangement below the treeline is not symbolic. Strangers are treated courteously and watched closely, particularly strangers who are fit, armed and asking about the custom. At the Torchlight the lake is ringed with torches and the women lead the procession round the grove; the warden does not attend. At the Asking, petitions are left at the treeline.

The Challenge Day. Once a year, at the dark of the moon after the Torchlight, a challenge may lawfully be made, and on no other day. The rite is precise. The challenger must come down the Steps alone, unarmed, before dawn, and break a bough from the one oak in the grove that has mistletoe on it, the Golden Bough. The warden must then meet him at the lake's edge with whatever weapon the challenger names. The fight ends when one man cannot rise. Nobody may help; the Sentinels form a ring and face outward. Most years the day passes quietly: nobody comes, and the town drinks to the warden that night without him. In nineteen years Ferrus has been challenged seven times. Seven graves stand under the yews at the bottom step, unmarked except by the weapon each man chose.

Since the Concord, the challengers have changed. Before the war they were runaways and desperate men, for whom the wardenship was sanctuary. Now they are veterans with nothing to go home to, and they have started to come with backers.

Quarters

The Rim Existing · the town

Lodges, shrines and offering-sellers · townsfolk and pilgrims · pine resin and lamp smoke

One ring of houses around the crater edge, all facing inward towards the lake. The basilica of the Duumviri is the smallest public building in the province, and the town is proud of it. Lodges let beds to pilgrims; the offering-sellers make clay stags, little bronze hands, and wax wombs for women asking Diana for children.

Ties: the Vettii of Nemibano; the Duumviri; Falecosa's wine-carts.

The Steps Existing · the way down

Stone stairs through old trees · guides and Sentinels · damp moss and silence

Six hundred steps from the Rim to the treeline. At the Asking, petitions are left at the bottom step; what is left is gone by morning, and no one claims to remove it. Every hundredth step has a niche with a lamp the Ocreae refill at dusk, so a pilgrim can count his way down in the dark.

Ties: the Ocreae; the Verdant Sentinel Order.

The Grove Below the treeline, on the lake shore

Oaks, yews and the warden's ground · the Sentinels, the Mother, the warden · leaf-mould, cold water and smoke from no visible fire

The sacred wood itself: the temple of Diana, a roofless ring of columns open to the lake; the Golden Bough's oak; the seven yews over the challengers' graves; and the warden's ground, which has no house, because Ferrus does not sleep under a roof. The Sentinels keep a post at the treeline and turn back anyone after dusk. Players see the grove by day, with a guide, or not at all.

Ties: Gnaeus Ferrus; Sylvia Nemorina; Faith (Invicta).

Who governs

The town is a municipium with two Duumviri, Aulus Vettius Lento and Marcia Ocrea, who collect taxes, keep the roads and answer letters from the capital. Below the treeline they have no authority. Their check is the grove itself: the warden, Gnaeus Ferrus, the Rex Nemorensis, and the Mother of the Grove, Sylvia Nemorina, whose word the town follows before theirs. Both are champions in their own right. The Verdant Sentinel post at the treeline is commanded by Ranger-Captain Silvanus Arbo, who obeys the Mother, salutes the warden, and reports to his Order, in that order.

Families

The Ocreae Guides of the Steps

Crest: a torch over a stag's antler · Motto: "We show the way down. Not back." · Seat: the Guides' Lodge at the top of the Steps

Hereditary guides of the stepped path, the only family allowed to lead pilgrims to the treeline at dusk.

  • Marcia Ocrea, Duumvir — first woman of the family to hold office, and the one who wrote the town's fourth refusal to the capital.
  • Titus Ocreus, her son, chief guide — counts every stranger who walks the Steps, and remembers them.
  • Ocrea Minor, her daughter, sixteen — walks the Torchlight beside the Mother and is said to be her chosen successor.

Ties: the Steps; the Mother of the Grove.

The Vettii of Nemibano Lodge-keepers · kin of the Vettii of Romulo

Crest: a lamp in a niche · Motto: "A bed for every pilgrim." · Seat: the Lodge of the Stag on the Rim

The largest pilgrim lodge on the Rim and two smaller ones. A poor branch of the Vettii of Romulo, and the family that would profit most if the custom ended and the grove became an ordinary sanctuary with an ordinary priest and many more visitors.

  • Aulus Vettius Lento, Duumvir — a careful man in a town that frightens him.
  • Vettia Calla, his sister, who runs the lodges — lodges every challenger free, and asks who sent them.

Ties: House Vettia of Romulo; the Rim.

Notable figures

  • Gnaeus Ferrus Rex Nemorensis, warden of the grove · champion — nineteen years unbeaten; sleeps lightly and never below the same tree twice.
  • Sylvia Nemorina Mother of the Grove · champion — leads the Torchlight, speaks for the wood, and knows what happens to the petitions.
  • Aulus Vettius Lento Duumvir — a careful man in a town that frightens him, keeping letters from Aeterna in a locked box.
  • Silvanus Arbo Ranger-Captain of the Verdant Sentinels — has stood in the ring facing outward seven times, and has heard every fight without seeing one.
  • Caeso Rufinus ex-legionary · would-be challenger — twenty-four, a veteran of the last campaign, training on the Rim and paying in new imperial silver.

Connections

  • Aeterna City — a day or two away; it has tried four times to end the custom.
  • Falecosa — the neighbouring hill town, which sends offering wine for the Torchlight.
  • Nemorus — the grove-carvers' village; Nemibano's shrine doors were made there.
  • Romulo — the Verdant Sentinels walk Romulo's Boundary; the Vettii there have cousins on the Rim.

The villages

Forest village · Imperium Invicta · Araucaria, on the old forest road

Alderpool

Stilt houses around a black, still pool under closing conifers: charcoal, coppice timber, and a rule about which trees may be cut that has never once been broken.

Codex now: An Araucarian forest village around a black pool — charcoal, timber and a strict rule about which trees may be cut.

Head
Magister Vici Septimus Carbo
Population
c. 140
Patron
Vulcan, whose forges eat the charcoal; Silvanus of the wood
Trouble
The arsenal wants more charcoal than the rotation allows

Timber houses on stilts stand around a still, dark pool under conifer that closes over the paths. Alderpool burns charcoal and sells it, with coppice poles, down to the arsenal forges at Mavelon by the old forest road to the Iron Landing. A cartload fetches eight denarii at the Landing, and the village sends sixty carts a year. It cuts on a rotation agreed generations ago with the Circle of the Eternal Grove, and the stacks smoke at the clearing's edge most of the year. Magister Vici Septimus Carbo keeps the rotation tally on a notched post by the pool.

The Fumii, the oldest burning family, light the year's first stack at the Kindling. By custom the youngest burner of the family puts the torch in, and the fire is not allowed out until the season's last stack is drawn; there is a Fumius awake beside a live stack every night of the season. This year the youngest is Fumia Parva, nine. Her uncle Quintus Fumius is the one who has been talking to the arsenal men. The pool itself is not used, and Alderpool does not explain why: nobody drinks from it, washes in it, or fishes it, and children are taught to walk round it on the side away from the uncut trees.

An arsenal factor, Tullus Naso, from the Praefectus Fabrum's office at Mavelon, now visits each month. He brings new silver, figures for warship hulls, and news that the forges are short.

Grove village · Imperium Invicta · Araucaria, on the old forest road

Nemorus

A shrine in a clearing ringed by houses whose every doorpost is carved: a small, devout village of woodcarvers whose temple fittings stand across the Imperium.

Codex now: An Araucarian grove village of woodcarvers — small, devout, and supplying temple fittings across the Imperium.

Head
Magister Vici Lucilla Dolabra
Population
c. 200
Patron
Diana of the grove; Minerva of craftsmen
Trouble
Temples ordering more than the managed wood can give, and paying in bad coin

A clearing with a shrine at its centre and houses around it, every doorpost, lintel and shutter carved by the household that lives behind it. Nemorus carves temple doors, screens and altar fittings for Invictian sanctuaries, and its work is recognised at a glance across the province: deep-cut vine scrolls, and a small hidden owl somewhere in every piece, which is the village's signature. A pair of temple doors takes a household two years and costs a temple six hundred denarii. The grove may not be cut; timber comes from managed woodland an hour's walk out, which the villagers consider an important and obvious distinction.

Magister Vici Lucilla Dolabra takes the commissions and sets the order of work. Her family, the Dolabrae, carved the doors of the Temple of Juno in Aeterna, and the village has not let anyone forget it. Nemibano's shrine doors were also made here. At the Setting of the Door the whole village escorts one household's door to the road, singing, and the household's eldest touches the owl for luck before the cart moves.

The order book is full for six years. Since the Concord every Legate wants a temple to his victory, and every temple wants Nemorus doors. The temples pay in debased silver; the timber does not grow faster for it. The Lignarii, the household that tends the managed wood, say quietly that it has perhaps four years left.

Forest village · Imperium Invicta · Araucaria, on the old forest road

Silva Caminia

A clearing astride a paved road the forest is taking back, with a long low inn on one side, the village on the other, and guides who know where the road still goes.

Codex now: An Araucarian forest village on the old road — a waystation in deep woodland where travellers pay for a roof and a guide.

Head
Magister Vici Gaius Semita
Population
c. 160
Patron
Silvanus of the wood; Janus of the way
Trouble
The road is failing faster than the village can clear it

A clearing straddling a paved road the forest is slowly taking back, with a long low inn on one side and the village on the other. Silva Caminia lives on guiding, lodging and forage. The road beyond is unreliable and the villagers know where it is passable, which is the whole of their trade; Invictian columns that hire them arrive where they intended. A guide costs a denarius a day and his keep; a cohort pays fifty for the stretch to the far edge of the forest and gets there in four days instead of nine.

Magister Vici Gaius Semita keeps the inn and assigns the guides. His family, the Semitae, have walked the road for so long that their name now means "path". Every Semita guide carries a knotted cord, one knot for each bad stretch, and can walk it blind. The Silent Stalkers of the Glade recruit here, and take the best guides with them; the village is proud of this and resents it in equal measure. The Clearing of the Road, a week's communal cutting, ends with the last stretch walked by torchlight.

Since the Concord the road carries a new kind of column: small, well-paid escorts moving silver and men between Legates' estates without the Dominus Militum's knowledge. They pay well and ask for discretion. The Semitae have always given both. Lately Semita Aurelia, the Magister's daughter and best guide, has started asking what is in the carts.

Part III · The north

Hellenoria

A league of harbour cities under an emperor nobody has seen. Hellarchon first, then the city-states, each with its own word for the man in charge, then the towns.

The capital

Capital · Hellenoria · Hellenorian coast

Hellarchon City

The League's capital and naval hegemon: a temple rock and a war harbour two miles apart, walled into one fortress, paid for in silver, and governed by an Assembly that votes, loudly and in the open, on what the shipowners settled over dinner.

Codex now: Capital of Hellenoria and its naval hegemon — a harbour city of colonnades and shipsheds whose fleet the rest of the League has begun to fear.

Ruler
The Assembly, in theory; in practice Hegemon Kleandros Nikandrides and the shipowners who fill the Council's agenda
Title
Hegemon of the League's common fleet (first of the ten strategoi); the Archon Eponymous, drawn by lot each year, is Aristeas Melanthiou
Population
c. 300,000, perhaps 60,000 of them citizens
Built on
A sacred rock, a harbour two miles below, walls between them, and silver in the hills behind
Patron
Athena, the Maiden of the Rock; Poseidon at the harbour; Hestia at the civic hearth
Trouble
A fleet the League pays for, Hellarchon crews, and nobody else trusts

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Hellarchon was built twice: the old town on its rock, and the harbour two miles below, joined by walls that run the whole distance, so that the two are one fortress with a port inside it. The natives' poetic name is Aetherion. Nobody uses it at the fish market. The upper city is temple and assembly, white stone and colonnades, its sacred rock visible a day out at sea. The harbour is tar, timber, noise, and the long roofed shipsheds where the fleet sits out of the weather, each shed numbered and each berth accounted for. Between them, along the walls, is where most people live: the wealth is on the hill and the population is on the road. The Arcane Academy keeps its grove inside the walls, and at dusk the sky turns violet, which the court scribes call ancient magic and footnote to a vault record nobody may read.

The harbour is the economy. Hellarchon grows almost nothing and imports its bread through the Golden Scythe Accord, the standing vulnerability of every League city and of this one most of all. It sells carriage, silver struck into the owl coinage, and finished work: pottery, bronze, and the products of the Geolith Artisan Covenant and the Forgeflame Artisans. Harbour dues fund the state; the Theoric Fund takes the surplus first, by law, to pay citizens to attend the festivals. This is popular, untouchable, and the reason the fleet is undermanned while the temples are magnificent.

The fleet is the largest in the world: the League's common defence in name and Hellarchon's hegemony in fact, crewed by its citizens and answerable to its Assembly. The other cities have spent five years noticing. Rival alliances have formed inside the League, and the fire-signal chain that once warned of Acheaorian raiders now mostly reports the movement of Hellenorian ships. On land Hellarchon is weak and knows it, and hires the Sunward Valiants for anything that needs speed rather than a line.

Life is argumentative, public and outdoors. The courts are enormous and staffed by lot, and a citizen expects to speak, serve and vote in a way no Invictian would recognise. The ideal is democracy; the reality is shipowners and merchants who manage the process, and the gap is complained about loudly, which is part of the culture. Metics and slaves do most of the harbour work and vote on nothing. The Hearthfire Sanctum keeps the civic hearth; the Ivory Chorus sings at every wedding that matters and hears everything. The year turns on the Greater Panegyris (a paid procession from harbour to Rock behind a new robe for the goddess), the spring Launching (the fleet rowed out before invited allied delegates: nominally a rite, unmistakably a demonstration), the four-day Dionysia (plays that mock the powerful under a licence that expires with the festival, the Obsidian Masquerade masked in the seats) and the autumn Naming of the Dead, when the year's lost crews are read out by ship. During the war it took a full day.

New lore

The League Chest. In the war the allies' contributions to the common fleet were moved from a neutral island to the back room of the Maiden's temple, "for safety", and never went back. The allies still pay, assessed by a Hellarchon board, and their delegates meet on the Rock under a ceiling gilded, they suspect, with their own money. Corinth says so every session. Thebesieas has stopped attending.

The count. The Treaty of Myrianth fixed the League's war fleet at two hundred and forty hulls. Hellarchon's sheds are numbered to two hundred and forty. There are three hundred and twelve sheds; the rest hold "hulls under construction", which by the Hellenorian text of the Treaty are not ships until launched. The Invictian inspectors at each Launching write the number down, and the Imperium goes on holding Ephelanum's harbour as a pledge.

The silver. A day's walk into the hills, the Silver Drifts are tunnels and washing-floors where slave gangs and their free overseers dig lead with a thin vein of silver. The floors run white. The state owns the hills and leases galleries for a fee and a share; the richest leases are House Euxenidai's. The fleet is paid for by the silver, the miners are paid in less, and nobody is allowed to count the miners.

The Sherd. Once a year the Assembly may exile any citizen for ten years, without charge, by scratching his name on six thousand potsherds. Two years ago Antiphates Euxenides organised a Sherd against the Hegemon and fell four hundred short. The Clay Gate has noticed unusual orders for broken pottery since.

Rumours. That the shed with no number holds the state's secret fire. That the Emperor's letters are written by whoever reads them. That the Academy will pay four thousand drachmas for a sleeper who wakes speaking a language nobody taught her, because the Dream Dormitory at Delphara and the Enchanted Muse at Persevalis hunt the same quarry: the last Nethranan dream-walker.

Districts

The Akra Sacred rock · temple precinct · theatre

Holy and gilded · priests, guides, allied envoys · marble dust, incense, sea wind

The Rock is the city's walled temenos: one gate, a marble stair, and on the summit the Maiden's temple, whose cult image wears the robe woven new for each Panegyris. Every open space is crowded with dedications from citizens who want the goddess and their neighbours to know what they gave. Behind the cult room is the strongroom of the League Chest. The Theatre of Hellarchon is cut into the south slope, home of the Dionysia and of the Assembly when weather drives it off its hill. Guides charge an obol to point out the Mirrored House on the north spur, which has no windows facing the city.

Ties: House Thalorid; the League synedrion; the Geolith Artisan Covenant; the Agora.

The Agora Market · courts · civic hearth

Loud from dawn · stallholders, jurors, philosophers · fish, figs, hot bronze from the mint

An open square framed by stoas beneath the Rock: market in the mornings, courts in the colonnades, and the rule that anyone may speak and everyone will answer. The Courts of the Lot pick juries with slotted allotment stones and bronze tickets, five hundred and one jurors to a case at three obols a day. The round Tholos houses the councillors on duty; the Prytaneion keeps the Hearthfire Sanctum's civic fire. The Mint strikes the owls. Philosophers argue in the Stoa of the Ships, under paintings of sea battles the city won and one it pretends it did.

Ties: the Speakers' Hill; the Hearthfire Sanctum; the Ivory Chorus.

The Speakers' Hill and the Court-Hill Assembly ground · old council · censors

Windy and bare · citizens on Assembly days, nobody otherwise · thyme, rock, red ochre

The Assembly meets on the Speakers' Hill, six thousand citizens on a rock-cut slope facing a stone platform. On Assembly mornings public slaves sweep the Agora with a rope dipped in red ochre; a citizen caught with red on his cloak loses his attendance pay. Across a saddle of rock, the Old Council of former archons tries homicide and sacrilege by lamplight on the Court-Hill, where the Truth-Flame has kept its seats since the war. A cleft at the hill's foot shelters the shrine of the Kindly Ones, where acquitted men sacrifice.

Ties: the Assembly and Council (see Rule); Inquisitor Vireon; the Sherd.

The Clay Gate Potters' quarter · double gate · cemetery

Smoky and sombre · potters, painters, mourners · wet clay, kiln smoke, cypress

The potters work by the great double gate, and the dead lie just beyond it: grave monuments line the road for half a mile, and the war dead have their own ground, one stone per ship, where the Naming of the Dead ends. The Sacred Way to Delphara starts here, so pilgrims buy lamps and votive cups from the workshops that sell grave vases. The kilns also sell broken pottery by the basket, which the quarter swears is for paving and everyone knows is for the Sherd.

Ties: Delphara; Araavyna, whose painted ware the quarter calls provincial and copies; Ione Kael.

The Academy Grove Arcane Academy · gymnasion

Quiet and watched · magi, students, athletes · olive leaves, ozone, scorched stone

A walled olive grove that stood outside the city until the war, when the wall was moved out two hundred yards to take it in; Selenarion's "heart of Hellarchon" is true by about that margin. The Arcane Academy holds the centre: lecture halls, warded vaults and three slender observatories that do not float, though from the harbour at dusk they appear to. The Gymnasion of Hellarchon shares the grove, and young magi train bodies and arguments in the same colonnades. The Academy denies that its cellars have a second level.

Ties: Kallisto Pyrphoros; the Ecliptica Arcanum; the Dreamers' Hunt; Asteria Erebide.

The Road The Long Walls · where the people live

Packed and proud · rowers, metics, refugees' grandchildren · bread ovens, tanning pits, too many people

Two walls run parallel from the Rock to the harbour, a long bowshot apart, and the road between them became a town. In the war the countryside came inside and never left: tenements four storeys high lean on the wall faces, rope-walks run along their feet, and every courtyard is a workshop. The fleet's rowers live here, which is why the Road votes as one on anything touching the ships. Half its houses are mortgaged to the Daryavand table. The Sunward Valiants keep a muster-yard by the halfway tower and will not garrison it.

Ties: the Shipsheds; House Daryavand; the Sunward Valiants.

The Shipsheds Existing · War harbour

Tar, timber and noise · shipwrights, caulkers, trierarchs · hot pitch, sawdust, bilge

The harbour below Hellarchon is tar, timber and noise, and its long roofed shipsheds, ranged around two round basins called the Moon and the Cup, hold the largest fleet in the world. Each shed is numbered and each berth accounted for. The triremes are the League's common defence in name and Hellarchon's hegemony in fact. Rich citizens fund and command a ship each year as a public duty, and boast of it for life. In spring, at the Launching, the fleet is drawn from the sheds and rowed out in formation: nominally a rite and unmistakably a demonstration.

Ties: House Nikandridai; House Erebides's pitch-yard; Treaty inspectors; Ephelanum.

The Emporion Merchant harbour · the Spice Wharf

Commercial and thieving · factors, tax-clerks, foreign crews · cassia, pepper, wet grain

The merchant harbour lies east of the war basins. Grain ships unload at the Accord quays. Along the Spice Wharf, warehouses sealed at night with three locks receive sacks from the farthest east, some brought by monsoon captains from Maurash and Sabaian traders in sewn-plank ships, and every pinch of cassia, pepper and root of warmth is weighed in front of the buyer and the tax-clerk. A pickpockets' guild works the crowd with tidy discipline. The Long Stoa holds the sample market, the money tables and the windowless block of the Mithril Reserve.

Ties: the Table of Daryavand; the Golden Scythe Accord; Corinth by the Long Lane.

Rule

In theory the Assembly of all citizens governs. It meets forty times a year, needs six thousand present for the great votes, and may decide anything the Council of Five Hundred has tabled, and nothing it has not. The Council, the courts and the annual archons are all drawn by lot; this year's Archon Eponymous, who names the year and presides at the Panegyris, is Aristeas Melanthiou, a retired steersman.

In practice the ten strategoi are the only great officers elected by show of hands, because the Assembly will gamble with its courts but not with its ships, and they may be re-elected without limit. Kleandros Nikandrides has been first strategos eleven years running, and the first strategos commands the common fleet as Hegemon. The shipowners' dining clubs decide in the evening what the Council tables in the morning; the Hegemon's club, the Oarsmen's Table, decides most of it. Strategos Eukrates Nausimachou commands the war harbour; Glaukos Timonos, harbour-master of the Emporion, collects the dues.

The checks are real, and slow. Every officer faces a year-end audit (the chief auditor, Sophrona Damonidou, has passed Kleandros eleven times, with a shrug). The Sherd can exile anyone; the courts can fine a strategos into poverty; proposing to spend theoric money on war is a capital offence; allies can withhold contributions. Above it all the Imperial Family reigns without governing: the Emperor's letters are read to the Assembly by his Voice, Archigrammateus Orestes Phylarchides, and the Truth-Flame on the Court-Hill decides what may be written about any of it.

Houses and families

House Nikandridai Shipowners · Eupatrid · the Hegemon's house

Crest: a bronze ram-prow on sea-blue, an owl perched on it · Motto: "The sea keeps the shore." · Seat: the Rock's north slope, and the Nikandrid sheds at the Emporion

Forty merchant hulls, the Long Lane grain contract with the Golden Scythe Accord, and six warships funded each year as a public duty, which is how a shipowner buys the love of rowers. They want the hegemony kept, the Theoric Fund opened to the fleet, and their heir home alive.

  • Kleandros Nikandrides, Hegemon, 58 — speaks rarely and always last; lost his only son with the Swift Owl in the war's last year, and stands through every Naming of the Dead.
  • Eurydike Nikandride, his wife — keeps the ledgers and the marriages; dines monthly with the senior singer of the Ivory Chorus.
  • Thrasyboulos Nikandrides, nephew and heir, 26 — the Treaty Guest in the Invictian compound at Deiperduem; his letters are read by three parties before they arrive, and he writes for all three.
  • Myrrhine Nikandride, Kleandros's daughter — runs the merchant fleet better than anyone, and would be heir if the house counted daughters.

Ties: Deiperduem (Thread 3); House Euxenidai; sponsors of House Daryavand.

House Thalorid Imperial Family · the unseen Emperor's household

Crest: a round mirror ringed with seven stars · Motto: "Wisdom and will, we are one." · Seat: the Mirrored House, on the Rock's north spur

The Imperial Family does not govern Hellarchon; it reigns, and its presence is a household, a scriptorium and a voice. The Mirrored House shelters the Circles of Mirrors, the court scribes who write Hellenoria's account of itself, and receives the Emperor's letters. Thalorion IV has not been seen in public for ten years; the Truth-Flame's instruction is that he is ever-present. Read by Orestes, his voice is a dry tenor with a harbour accent. Delegates from other cities say it does not sound like that at home.

  • Emperor Thalorion IV — unseen for ten years "for security and metaphysical preservation".
  • Lady Kassiane Thaloris, his cousin, keeper of the Mirrored House — the only Thalorid seen at the Panegyris, where she lays the robe on the goddess in his name.
  • Archigrammateus Orestes Phylarchides, First Scribe of the Circles and the Emperor's Voice — the only man in the city who claims to receive the Emperor's words directly.

Ties: the Truth-Flame; Thessalonika's Epistates; the Hellenorian compound at Deiperduem, which hosts Princess Roshanak under the imperial seal.

House Euxenidai Oligarch shipowners · Eupatrid

Crest: a silver ingot crossed by an oar · Motto: "Let the best row the ship." · Seat: a walled house at the top of the Road

The second fleet in the city and the richest galleries in the Silver Drifts. The Euxenidai want the hegemony as much as the Nikandridai; they want it without the Assembly. Their dining club, the Few, argues for votes limited to the five thousand who can arm themselves, and a council of four hundred chosen by "merit", meaning ships.

  • Antiphates Euxenides, head, 64 — fell four hundred sherds short of exiling the Hegemon, and has been buying pottery since.
  • Kleito Euxenide, his daughter — funds choruses at the Dionysia; the comedies she pays for mock her father, and sell out.
  • Hagnodoros Euxenides, grandson — trierarch of the sacred galley Halia, which carries the League's dispatches and so hears them first.

Ties: the Silver Drifts; quiet friends in Corinth; borrowers of House Daryavand.

House Daryavand Metic bankers · the Table at the Emporion

Crest: a balance with a lamp on each pan · Motto: "Count twice, lend once." · Seat: the third arch of the Long Stoa

Four generations ago an Acheaorian money-changer came in on a spice ship and stayed. His descendants are metics: twelve drachmas a head in metic tax, a citizen sponsor (the Nikandridai), and no right to own land. So they hold mortgages on half the Road and cannot foreclose on a brick of it; they sell the debts to citizens and rent their own house from a debtor. They change Acheaorian darics and correspond with the Vaults of Equilibrium; the Mithril Reserve sees them as a competitor it could crush and a barometer it would rather keep.

  • Nanaia Daryavand, matriarch, 71 — counts in four scripts; has lent to both Kleandros and Antiphates and will not say whose debt is larger.
  • Bagadata Daryavand, her son — weighs pepper for the tax-clerk at the Spice Wharf, and notices more than he is paid to.
  • Anahid Daryavand, granddaughter, 24 — has petitioned for citizenship by decree, which needs six thousand votes; both oligarch houses have promised them, so neither will deliver.

Ties: the Emporion; the Vaults of Equilibrium; kin in Persemenid.

House Erebides Voidfolk (tiefling) · citizens by the Accord

Crest: a black pitch-pot under a crescent horn · Motto: "We keep what burns." · Seat: the pitch-yard on the war harbour's north mole

The tiefling families absorbed under the Voidfolk Accord were enrolled in a new deme, the Deme of the Accord, which has no land, no village and no shrine, and votes like any other. The Erebides are its largest family: pitch-boilers, caulkers and rope-makers to the fleet. Nobody else is admitted to their yard, and the Truth-Flame visits it monthly.

  • Melantho Erebide, head, horn-tips capped in silver — drawn by lot to the Council this year, the first of the Voidfolk to sit on it; she has not yet spoken.
  • Iason Erebides, her son, master of the pitch-yard — has applied eleven times for leave to travel; every answer has been "pending".
  • Asteria Erebide, granddaughter — an evoker at the Academy, "the girl who doesn't flinch at fire"; means to be the first Voidfolk Scholarch.

Ties: the Shipsheds; the Academy Grove; Inquisitor Vireon.

Notable figures

  • Kallisto Pyrphoros Scholarch of the Arcane Academy · wizard (evocation) — runs the Academy like a ship, refuses the Truth-Flame the cellars, and does not intend to lose the dream-walker to Delphara.
  • Inquisitor Vireon Third Seat of the Truth-Flame · censor — strikes passages from Temple copies with a reed dipped in lamp-black; annotated Selenarion's tribute himself. Wants the Academy's lower cellars opened.
  • Selenarion of Hellarchon Court Scribe of the Fourth Circle of Mirrors · missing — listed by the Circles as "on leave of the mirrors"; his last known writing location is redacted. A copy of his tribute with margin notes in two hands sells for more than he earned in a year.
  • Ione Kael potter at the Clay Gate — daughter of Deremios Kael, the dissident scholar executed seventeen years ago; paints cups of the Naming of the Dead, and has never asked for her father's body.
  • Aristeas Melanthiou Archon Eponymous, by lot — finds the office brings a dining-right in the Prytaneion and little else, and has begun inviting guests the Council would rather not feed.
  • Theron Oneirokrites the Academy's Reader of Dreams — runs the Academy's share of the Dreamers' Hunt for Vesperine Ilaro, paying sleep-readers on the Road for strange dreamers.
  • Dorgrim Ironhand Dominus Argentar of the Mithril Reserve · dwarf, Clan Ironhand — holds the city's four-hundred-talent bond on the harbour dues, reads Lady Isolde Merca's monthly letter twice, and chalks the day's discount on Invictian silver by the door.

Connections

  • Corinth — two days by the Long Lane; the rival money market, which has funded alliances against the hegemon for two centuries.
  • Thessalonika — north by the Long Lane; its Epistates holds the last imperial letter-patent still in force.
  • Helionyx and Ephelanum — by the Southern Run; Hellarchon claims to speak for the Hellenorian half of the Ephelanum Condominium (Thread 4).
  • Delphara — by the Sacred Way; the Dreamers' Hunt (Thread 10) sets the Academy against the Dream Dormitory and the Enchanted Muse of Persevalis, all with eyes on Eronis.
  • Deiperduem — by the Treaty Road; Thrasyboulos is the guest in the Invictian compound, and Hellarchon's compound hosts Princess Roshanak of House Zindar (Persemenid) (Thread 3).
  • Aeterna — the Dominus Militum's office (gens Valeria) reads Thrasyboulos's letters before his uncle does.
  • Duneforged Citadel — the Mithril Reserve; Lady Isolde Merca (House Merca) writes to Dorgrim monthly (Thread 9).
