  • Carianea — and every small port like it, which supplies crews and resents where the ships are berthed.

The cities

City · Hellenoria · Hellenorian isthmus

Corinth City

The isthmus city with a harbour on each sea and a stone road between them: whole ships are dragged overland, everything that crosses pays, and a clan of two hundred cousins has kept the money and the rock for longer than Hellarchon has had a fleet.

Codex now: Hellenoria's crossroads port — two harbours on two seas, a haulway between them, and tolls on everything that passes.

Ruler
Telestes Bacchiades, for the Bacchiad clan
Title
Prytanis (Archon rank), chosen each year by and from House Bacchiadai
Population
c. 90,000
Built on
A neck of land, two harbours, and a rock that has never fallen
Patron
Poseidon of the Isthmus; Aphrodite on the Upper Fortress
Trouble
Selling forbidden iron to one rival of Hellarchon while Hellarchon watches the toll-houses

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Corinth stands on a neck of land with a harbour on either side, under a fortified rock that dominates both. Between the two ports runs its defining feature: a paved haulway with grooves cut for wheeled cradles, on which whole ships are dragged overland from one sea to the other. The city is loud in a particular way: ox teams, capstans, and the shriek of a hull winched across stone. It never stops, because the tolls never stop. The Upper Fortress is the strongest position in Hellenoria and has never been taken by assault.

A cargo that crosses here saves several days and a dangerous cape, and Corinth charges accordingly. It has no need to produce and produces anyway: its bronze is famous, its potters supply half the League, and the Luminastra Alchemists keep their largest workshop here because every ingredient on the continent passes through the warehouses. After Hellarchon it is the League's chief money market, and the Mithril Reserve and the Vaults of Equilibrium keep branches on the same street, watching each other. Corinth has declined to build an army and never needed one: it has the rock, a modest fleet and a great deal of money with which to hire other people, and the Order of Morning's Rise holds a standing contract here, the nearest thing to an endorsement a mercenary company can earn. For two centuries its foreign policy has been to make sure Hellarchon never has a free hand, and it funds rival alliances inside the League as routine.

The city is commercial, mixed and frankly disreputable by League standards. Every people on the continent is represented in the harbour quarters, and Corinthian tolerance is a business decision rather than a virtue. Wealth is new and visible; the rich build ostentatiously, sponsor lavishly, and are looked down on by Thessalonika and Hellarchon for it, which Corinth finds funny and profitable. Its temples are well endowed, busy, and cater to sailors, which is to say they run on the money of men who may not come back. The calendar holds the Isthmian Games every two years, the League's second-greatest, under a truce even tyrants keep; the Hauling, when the season's first ship is crewed across by the magistrates, who are notoriously bad at it; and the Two Tides, a rite performed at both harbours at once by two halves of one priesthood, who then race back to the centre.

New lore

The clan. Corinth is ruled by the Bacchiadai, some two hundred adult cousins who form the Council, choose a Prytanis from among themselves each year, and marry only one another. The rule kept the money in the family through the whole war. Five years ago Lykon Bacchiades, the Prytanis's brother, married Calpurnia Secunda of House Calpurnia, an Invictian patrician, after the Council voted 104 to 97 to enrol her as a "daughter of the clan". The Lechaion Marriage was the first match outside the clan in three hundred years. Every Bacchiad with a foreign sweetheart has cited it since.

The terminus. Atarabad's silk caravans now come west on the Treaty Road through Deiperduem, and the shortest way to every sea beyond is Corinth's Haulway. House Suren-Pahlav keeps a factor on the Street of Counting-Houses, and bolts of silk cross the isthmus on mules while the hulls cross on cradles. Farshore ships call too: Qart-Hadeth tin-traders at the western harbour, Tyrsan pilots hiring themselves out at the eastern one at a price that makes local pilots spit.

The iron. Invictian law forbids the export of iron from the Imperium. Corinthian ironmongers have a great deal of it, the ships from Mavelon's sea harbour unload a remarkable tonnage of "founders' scrap" at Lechaion, and Thebesieas's soldiers are better equipped every spring. Nobody on the Street will discuss it, which is the Street's way of discussing it.

Districts

The Street of Counting-Houses Existing · Banking quarter and the Agora

Quiet money beside loud money · bankers, toll-farmers, factors · ink, wax seals, the Agora's fish

After Hellarchon, Corinth is the League's chief money market, and its bankers keep to one street off the Agora's north stoa. The branches of the Mithril Reserve and the Vaults of Equilibrium sit on it side by side, watching each other; their doormen have not exchanged a word in eleven years. The Luminastra Alchemists keep their largest workshop at the street's end, because every ingredient on the continent passes through Corinth's warehouses. The Agora beyond is the busiest and least decorous in the League, crowded with shippers, toll-farmers and every people on the continent.

Ties: House Euphranoridai; the Mithril Reserve; the Vaults of Equilibrium; Suren-Pahlav factors from Atarabad.

The Haulway Ship road · toll-houses

Never silent · haulers, ox-drivers, capstan gangs · dung, tallow, hot stone

A paved track across the neck with grooves cut for wheeled cradles, on which whole ships are dragged from sea to sea. Tolls are charged by the length of keel, measured against a bronze rod at the toll-house at each end. A light galley crosses in half a day; a laden merchantman takes two and a great deal of shouting. The toll-farm is auctioned each year, and this year House Larnakidai holds it. The season's first ship is decorated, blessed and crewed by the magistrates, and the haulers bet on how many of them fall off.

Ties: House Larnakidai; Nerissa Thalassine; the Silk Terminus.

Lechaion and the Copper Smelts Western harbour · founders

Grimy and rich · founders, ore-crews, foreign tin-traders · metal on the tongue, green water

The western harbour, long moles and deep water, and beside it the Copper Smelts: furnaces, casting-pits and the sheds of founders who have worked the same alloys for six generations. Ore comes in from the islands, tin from Qart-Hadeth, and bronze and brass go out the same way. The air tastes of metal and the harbour has a green sheen. The founders' guild keeps a hall and a hostel for buyers; strangers are not let near the furnaces. Above the harbour, Lykon Bacchiades's villa is built in the Invictian style around an atrium, and the dockers call it the Bride's House.

Ties: House Glaukotidai; Lykon and Calpurnia Secunda; ships from Mavelon.

The Lebes Eastern harbour · sailors' temples

Pious and drunk · sailors, pilots, priests · incense, tar, spilled wine

The eastern harbour is round as a cauldron, which gives it its name. The Temple Precinct of Corinth crowds its slope, unusually well endowed and unusually busy, running on the vows of men about to sail. The Two Tides race ends here half the time. Against the old city wall stands the Wise Owl Inn, three storeys dark with smoke, where a little owl lives in the rafters and is treated by the regulars as the house's conscience. On the quay, Ixion Keraunios sells winds in knotted cords.

Ties: Ixion Keraunios; the Wise Owl; Tyrsan pilots; the Long Lane to Hellarchon.

The Upper Fortress Citadel · Aphrodite's temple · clan treasury

High, cold and guarded · garrison, priestesses, clan treasurers · wind, myrtle, wet stone

The fortified rock rises above the isthmus and commands both harbours. It has never been taken by assault and has a spring inside the walls that has never run dry, which is why nobody has seriously tried. Aphrodite's temple stands on the summit, rich in sailors' offerings. Below it, in vaults cut into the rock, is the Bacchiad treasury. The Order of Morning's Rise garrisons the gates, and the Polemarch of the Rock, Deinias Bacchiades, holds the keys.

Ties: House Bacchiadai; the Order of Morning's Rise.

The Isthmian Quarter Games · gymnasion · theatre

Athletic and showy · trainers, luthiers, sponsors · olive oil, sawn shell, laurel

The stadium and its gymnasion train the athletes of the Isthmian Games. Beside the stadium, the Laurel Court is a cloistered garden where victors are crowned with laurel cut that morning by the priest, and living acanthus grows between columns carved with acanthus until stone and plant are hard to tell apart. Along the Lyre-Makers' Row, luthiers cure tortoise shells for a year before stringing them; a musician knows a row-made lyre by the first note. The Theatre of Corinth is new money's favourite gift to the city.

Ties: the Isthmian Games; Delphara's truce-heralds; sponsors from every rich house.

Rule

Prytanis Telestes Bacchiades presides over the Council of the Bacchiadai, which is the whole adult clan sitting in the Prytaneion by the Agora. The Prytanis is chosen each year "by rotation"; Telestes has rotated into the office five times in nine years. Non-Bacchiad citizens meet in the theatre twice a year to acclaim what the Council has decided. The Polemarch of the Rock, Deinias Bacchiades, holds the citadel; the Haulmaster, Archelaos Bacchiades, oversees the toll-farmers; the hired companies answer to a non-Bacchiad paymaster, Phaidon Larnakides.

The checks are commercial. The clan borrows from the Street, so the Street is heard. The toll-farm goes to the highest bidder, which put the Larnakidai's money and popularity next to the clan's. The Order of Morning's Rise is loyal to whoever pays on time. The Golden Scythe Accord can short the city's grain. Hellarchon's fleet sits two days away, and the Isthmian truce binds everyone, including the Prytanis.

Houses and families

House Bacchiadai Ruling clan · Eupatrid

Crest: two dolphins, tail to tail, across a paved road · Motto: "Between two seas, one purse." · Seat: the Prytaneion, and the treasury on the Upper Fortress

City · Hellenoria · Hellenorian north coast

Thessalonika City

The League's great northern port and market: a gridded city on a curved bay where the steppe's horses, hides, amber and grain meet the sea, the books are audited to the last jar, and the riders outside the walls are always paid on the day.

Codex now: The League's northern port and its scholarly capital — cold, orderly, and quietly the best-administered city in Hellenoria.

Ruler
Eudoros Anaxilaou
Title
Epistates (Archon rank), holding an imperial letter-patent "pending instructions"
Population
c. 110,000 within the walls; up to 20,000 more at the Horse Gate in the trading season
Built on
A planned grid on a curved bay, a sea wall, and a citadel on the slope
Patron
Hermes of the Gate and of eloquence; Athena in the academies
Trouble
An appointment from an Emperor nobody has seen, a steppe that has grown crowded since the peace, and one line in the audit nobody reads aloud

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

A gridded city on a curved bay, built to a plan and still following it, with a long sea wall and a citadel on the slope above. Thessalonika is the tidiest large city on the continent, and the tidiness is old: the street-lines were pegged out by a surveyor whose bronze rod is still kept in the citadel and still used to settle boundary suits. It is the League's second port by tonnage and its first by grain. The waterfront is warehouses, ropewalks and fish-sheds; behind it the grid fills with markets, guild halls, bath-houses, temples and tenements in neat blocks; the upper town holds the academies and the long porticoes where teaching is done in public and interrupting is expected. It is colder than the rest of Hellenoria, and the buildings show it: enclosed courtyards, glazed windows, roofs pitched for snow, and braziers in the stoas from the First Frost to the spring.

Trade. Thessalonika is the gateway to the northern interior. Everything moving between the League and the Malaunian Steppe passes through it: grain from the river plain, horses and hides from the steppe, amber from the northern rivers, salt fish from the bay, timber from the Olympus foothills, and mercenaries from everywhere. Ships load grain at the Sea Wall for Hellarchon and Corinth; caravans unload felts and furs at the Horse Gate; and the Grid Agora in between is the busiest market north of the Long Lane, where a horse, a slave, a cask of pickled tunny and a copy of any book on the continent can be bought before noon. The academies are an industry too: they draw fee-paying students from all three empires, and the copying trade around them is the largest outside the great Sanctum library, a rivalry conducted through catalogues.

Defence. Its small standing force is better funded than most of the League's, which the other cities call extravagant and Thessalonika calls obvious. The walls are modern, the citadel maintained, and the grain reserve fixed by statute and actually audited. The city has never been taken. The steppe horsemen are hired, paid promptly, and never let inside the walls in numbers. Every spring the Council of Auditors votes the "steppe retainer", the single largest line in the city's accounts, and the Assembly passes it without debate: the riders are paid whether or not the city needs them, because a rider who has been paid does not need to be fought.

Way of life. Citizens are sober, literate, punctual and a little smug. Public argument is conducted with citations, contracts are kept, and the city is kind to foreigners with skills and cold to foreigners without them. Debts are recorded at the Agora and called on the day. A scholar's correspondence is one of the few things that crosses imperial borders uninspected, which is not lost on anyone. Thessalonikans are fond of saying that nothing in their city happens by accident, and they are more right than they know.

Festivals. The Disputation: five days of public argument in the porticoes, positions assigned by lot, enormously popular and heavily bet on. The First Frost: the harbour is blessed on the day ice first appears in the upper town's fountains, and the date is entered in a series four hundred years long. The Reading: new works are read aloud before publication and heckled; several careers have ended here. To these the market city adds the Horse Fair at midsummer, when the steppe camps double and a thousand horses change hands in nine days; and the Exchange of Cups on the last day of the fair, when the Epistates and the eldest of the steppe camp drink from each other's cup at the Horse Gate, a custom so old that both sides describe it as "hospitality".

New lore

The letter-patent. Thessalonika's Epistates is formally an imperial appointee. Eudoros Anaxilaou's letter-patent was the last one Thalorion IV sealed before he stopped appearing, and no successor has been named in ten years, so Eudoros governs "pending instructions". He keeps the city audited to the last jar so that nobody can call him illegitimate, and he publishes the audit on whitened boards in the Agora every quarter. Hellarchon would like to replace him with an elected archon who owes it a favour.

The peace. Five years without war have been good to Thessalonika's trade and hard on its arithmetic. The steppe trade doubled once the frontier forts stood down; the Horse Gate camp is now a town of felt tents for half the year. The steppe clans that once raided Acheaoria's northern frontier now have nowhere to ride, and more of them arrive every spring asking for contracts. The retainer has risen by a third in five years. The auditors have signed every increase, and Sosipatra Lysimachou has begun asking, in writing, what exactly the city buys with it.

The circle. The Illuminated Scholars and the Seekers of Eternal Truth keep correspondents here, and the Whispering Eyes are understood to as well. Since the peace the Porticoes have joined the Aeterna Lexicon and Persemenid's Sage's Archive in a quiet copying circle comparing the three empires' histories; the shared Old Empires chronicle came out of it. A chest of copies leaves the Sea Wall twice a year on a Boreadai grain ship.

The wards. Thessalonika's leading houses have an old habit of sending a younger child "to be fostered with friends in the north" for a few years; the children come back speaking good steppe tongue and riding well, and nobody asks which friends. In return the city has always hosted a few steppe children at the Porticoes, enrolled as the sons and daughters of horse-dealers. Phila Anaxilaou was fostered north from her eighth year to her fifteenth; so was Basileios Akrites.

Rumours. That the Epistates' seal is not quite the Emperor's. That the granaries hold more jars than grain. That the city "has never been taken" because it was never worth the trouble. That a steppe chieftain's daughter is enrolled in the Porticoes under a false name, and her father wants her home.

Districts

The Porticoes Existing · Academic quarter

Learned and rude · scholars, students, copyists · lamp oil, wet wool, argument

The upper town's long colonnades, where teaching is done in public and interrupting is expected, with the gymnasia and libraries behind them. Courtyards are enclosed and windows glazed, for this is the coldest city in Hellenoria. A master rents a bay between two columns by the year; the best bays face south and are auctioned. The gymnasia here are as much academies as exercise grounds, and the old men who wrestle at dawn lecture at noon. The Porticoes host the Disputation, in which a scholar may have to defend the opposite of everything he has written. Krates the Dog sleeps in a storage jar at the east end and heckles everyone.

Ties: Krates the Dog; House Pinakidai; the Three Libraries; Ink Row in the Lower Grid.

The Sea Wall and the Granaries Waterfront · audited grain

Orderly and cold · stevedores, auditors, ship-masters · grain dust, salt, frost

A long wall along the bay guards a waterfront of numbered warehouses, each with its tally-board by the door. Ships tie up in the order they were sighted, and the harbour clerks will tell you so before you ask. The statutory reserve sits in the granaries behind the harbour gate, sealed by the auditors each quarter with a lead tag on a cord; breaking a tag is a capital charge. Steppe grain comes in on carts and goes out by sea to Hellarchon and Corinth. The First Frost blessing begins here at the harbour gate; a late frost is an omen, and a frost that never comes has happened twice.

Ties: the Golden Scythe Accord; House Boreadai; Sosipatra Lysimachou.

The Grid Agora Market · theatre · temple

Tidy and glazed · traders, jurors, playgoers · baked bread, ink, braziers

The tidiest agora in the League, a planned square on the grid, its stoas glazed against the cold. Market in the mornings, courts in the colonnades, and the League's rule that anyone may speak and everyone will answer, though here the answer usually comes with a reference. The quarterly audit hangs on whitened boards by the speakers' step. Above the square the sanctuary of Hermes of the Gate stands among the academies, and its priests bless the harbour at the First Frost. The theatre holds the Reading, where several careers have ended on stage, and the monthly Assembly.

Ties: the Epistates; the Reading; the Council of Auditors.

The Horse Gate Steppe market · outside the walls

Loud and transient · horse-dealers, hide-merchants, steppe riders · dung, amber, smoke

Outside the landward gate, the steppe trade camps on a fenced field: horses, hides, amber, and riders for hire. Since the peace the field has grown into a seasonal town of felt tents with its own wells, a fermented-mare's-milk tavern and a court of three elders who settle disputes by steppe custom. The riders may enter the city ten at a time, wearing a bronze token issued at the gate and returned on leaving; a token not returned by dusk brings out the watch. The Boreadai exchange stands at the gate itself, half inside the wall and half out, and on the first day of spring the steppe retainer is counted out there in silver, in sight of both sides, before the camps have asked for it. At midsummer the Exchange of Cups is drunk under the gate arch, and the eldest of the camp sits on the Epistates' right.

Ties: the Malaunian Steppe; Xerastri's horse trade; House Boreadai.

The Citadel Slope Fortress · Epistates' house · standing force

Stern and swept · officers, clerks, the better families · pine smoke, oiled leather, snow

The citadel commands the bay from the slope above the grid, and the better families live on the terraces below it, where the view is good and the wind is worse. The barracks of the standing force are inside: two thousand foot and four hundred horse, paid on the first of every month, with a waiting list of applicants from other League cities. The surveyor's bronze rod lies in the citadel's record room beside the city's charter and Eudoros's letter-patent, framed, under glass, and checked every morning by a clerk who signs to say it is still there. A second, older chest in the same room has three locks; the keys are held by the Epistates, the Strategos and the head of House Boreadai, and the record-room clerks say it is opened once a year, in spring.

Ties: House Anaxilaidai; House Akritai; the northern passes.

The Lower Grid Trade quarter · guild halls · Ink Row · tenements

Crowded and punctual · tanners, fish-salters, ropemakers, copyists, couriers · brine, tan-bark, oak-gall ink

Forty blocks between the Sea Wall and the Agora, every one the same size, where most of the city lives and works. Each block has a fountain, a bakehouse and a guild: the tanners by the river channel, the fish-salters by the harbour gate with their tunny jars, the ropemakers on a walk four hundred paces long, the felt-fullers who turn steppe wool into the League's winter cloaks. Six streets in the upper corner are Ink Row: copying-shops, binders and booksellers who will sell any work on the continent within a month. The scholars' post leaves from the courier-house at its foot, and letters sealed with an academy's mark travel uninspected, by long custom.

Ties: the Sea Wall; the Porticoes; the Three Libraries; the Whispering Eyes.

Rule

Epistates Eudoros Anaxilaou governs with a Council of Auditors, ten citizens elected for three years, which must sign every disbursement. The Assembly meets in the theatre monthly and can refuse a levy, and does about once a year to prove it still can. Strategos Demetrios Akrites commands the standing force and the northern passes; the chief auditor, Sosipatra Lysimachou, has refused the Epistates' signature twice and kept her post both times. The harbour-master, Nikanor Chrysou, is elected by the shippers and answers to the auditors, not the Epistates. The academies check everyone, publicly and with footnotes.

The weak point is the title itself. An Epistates rules by imperial appointment; this one's appointment is ten years old and its author unseen. Hellarchon's Hegemon has asked, politely and twice, whether the city would like to elect an archon "to regularise matters". Eudoros answered both times that he awaits his Emperor's instructions, and copied the answer to the Mirrored House.

Houses and families

House Anaxilaidai Administrators · Eupatrid

Crest: a set square on grey · Motto: "Measure, then build." · Seat: the Epistates' house on the citadel slope

Three generations of city officials who have never owned a ship or a mine and are proud of it. Eudoros Anaxilaou, Epistates, keeps his letter-patent framed and his accounts open. His daughter Phila clerks for the auditors and reports to nobody.

History. The founder, Anaxilas, was a land-surveyor brought from the south to re-peg the grid after the great fire of three centuries ago; his rod is the one in the citadel. His descendants became the city's clerks, then its auditors, then its Epistates. They have held the office four times in a hundred years, always by imperial letter, never by election, and the city considers them dull, honest and indispensable, in that order. The house's income is land on the river plain and a reputation it cannot afford to lose. It keeps a custom of fostering one child of each generation "with friends in the north"; the family tomb has a horse carved on every third stone.

  • Eudoros Anaxilaou, Epistates, 61 — walks to the citadel every morning by the same streets, knows which of them need paving, and drinks mare's milk at the Exchange of Cups without a grimace.
  • Phila Anaxilaou, his daughter, 30 — fostered in the north from eight to fifteen; clerks for the auditors and speaks steppe tongue better than her father's Hellenorian; has noticed the extra granary jars, and has not told him.
  • Theano Anaxilaou, his late brother's widow — keeps the house's correspondence with the Mirrored House, and writes a better hand than the Emperor's Voice.
  • Little Anaxilas, Phila's son, 7 — the next to be fostered north, next spring; Phila has not agreed.

Ties: House Thalorid; the Citadel Slope; the steppe camps.

House Boreadai Horse and grain traders · Eupatrid

Crest: a running horse under a north wind · Motto: "Paid on the day." · Seat: the Horse Gate exchange

The steppe trade's middlemen. Kallisthenes Boreades pays the hired riders and is the only citizen they trust; his sister Aglaia buys amber for three empires.

History. The family claims descent from the north wind, and from a horse-coper who married a steppe chieftain's daughter two hundred years ago and opened the first exchange at the Horse Gate. The wall was later built around the exchange rather than through it, which is why the building stands half in and half out. They hold the contract to pay the steppe retainer, which has made them the richest house in the city without ever owning more than six ships. Their dead are buried facing north, and their weddings include a race on horseback that the bride is expected to win.

  • Kallisthenes Boreades, head, 47 — rides out to the camps alone, holds one of the three keys to the spring chest, and has never missed a pay-day in twenty years.
  • Aglaia Boreade, his sister — buys amber by the sack and sorts it by what is trapped inside; an amber with a wasp sells to Persemenid for its weight in gold.
  • Leontiskos Boreades, Kallisthenes's son, 19 — wants to ride with the steppe companies, and is in love with a student who claims to be a horse-dealer's daughter.

Ties: the Horse Gate; the Sea Wall; Xerastri.

House Pinakidai Cataloguers · scholars

Crest: a stack of tablets · Motto: "Found is kept." · Seat: the Library of the Porticoes

Keepers of the Porticoes' library for four generations. Melitta Pinakis, Archivist, runs the Thessalonikan end of the Three Libraries circle; her nephew Zenon copies for it and talks too much at the Reading.

History. The first Pinakides was a slave cataloguer who was freed for finding a lost will, which settled the largest inheritance suit in the city's history; he was paid in citizenship and a shelf. The house still charges a fee to every scholar who wants a work found, compiles the catalogues that conduct the city's war with the Sanctum library, and keeps the city's oldest records, including the founding treaties with the steppe that nobody has asked to read in a century.

  • Melitta Pinakis, Archivist, 66 — reads Acheaorian and old Invictian court script, and keeps the circle's correspondence in her head.
  • Zenon Pinakides, her nephew, 28 — a fast, careless copyist; boasts at the Reading of "certain correspondents abroad".
  • Hypatia Pinakis, Melitta's granddaughter, 15 — catalogues faster than Zenon, and has found a shelf-mark in the old registers that points to a box that is not there.

House Akritai Frontier soldiers · Eupatrid

Crest: a watchtower on a bare ridge · Motto: "The pass is the city." · Seat: the tower-house at the head of the northern road

The family that has held the northern passes for Thessalonika for seven generations, elected strategos so often the city has stopped pretending to look elsewhere. They own hill pasture and the toll on the pass road, and they want the peace to last long enough to stop paying for it in sons.

History. The Akritai built the watchtowers on the passes and have manned them since; their family saga is a list of raids turned back, recited at every funeral. It is a short list for seven generations. The towers are excellent, the garrisons small, and the tower-captains on good terms with the camps below them; one of the house's proudest relics is a steppe saddle given "in friendship" by a chieftain whose name the family will not say.

  • Demetrios Akrites, Strategos, 52 — pays his men before himself, holds the second key to the spring chest, and distrusts the steppe companies he has never had to fight.

  • Basileios Akrites, their son, 24 — fostered north as a boy; commands the citadel's horse; lost two fingers to frostbite on the passes and writes poetry about it, badly.

City · Condominium of Hellenoria and Imperium Invicta · Hellenorian coast

Ephelanum City

The breadbasket of the southern coast and its festival city: a goddess's sanctuary at the end of a marble street, a red-earth plain of grain, vines and olives behind it, a calendar crowded with harvest rites that draw the whole coast, and two governments by treaty who agree on the date of almost none of them.

Codex now: A Hellenorian temple-port whose sanctuary draws more money than its harbour — pilgrims, silversmiths, and a permanent argument about who owns the goddess.

Ruler
Archon Philostratos Melanippou and Hierarchis Melissa Aristarchis (city and sanctuary); Dux Marcus Vettius Calvo (harbour, garrison, estates)
Title
Archon (Hellenorian) · Dux (Invictian) — a condominium
Population
c. 85,000 in the city; perhaps 60,000 more on the plain; roughly double in festival season
Built on
A marble street from a silting harbour to a temple, and a red plain that feeds the coast
Patron
Artemis, the Lady of Ephelanum (Diana, in the Invictian text), Lady of the Plain and of the first sheaf; Demeter at the threshing-floors
Trouble
Two governments, one goddess, two harvest calendars, and a harbour neither will pay to dredge

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

A harbour silting up, a marble street running from it, and at the end of the street a temple large enough to be seen well out at sea. Behind the temple, as far as a man can ride in a day, lies the Red Plain: a wide alluvial country of red earth, watered by the river whose silt is choking the harbour, and the richest farmland on the Hellenorian coast. Wheat and barley on the flats, vines on the first slopes, olives above them, and the red earth itself dug, washed and sold as pigment. The plain fed the southern League for a thousand years, and since the Treaty of Myrianth it has fed the Imperium's southern garrisons too.

The sanctuary is the city's reason to exist; its colonnade alone took a century. The Lady of Ephelanum is a huntress in the hills and a mother of harvests on the plain, and her year is the farming year: she is woken with the first furrow, carried through the fields at the barley harvest, and thanked with the first sheaf, the first must and the first oil. Around the temple, packed close, is the trade her festivals generate: lodging, sacrificial animals, and street after street of silversmiths selling votive models of the temple and silver sheaves. The temple is also a bank, holding deposits under sanctuary protection and lending, mostly against next year's harvest; by some measures it is the largest single holder of coin in Hellenoria, a role the Vaults of Equilibrium would recognise and the Mithril Reserve calls amateurish but substantial.

Defence is weak, and relies on sanctuary status: Ephelanum has walls and a small force, and sacking a great sanctuary is a thing even tyrants think twice about. The temple guard answers to the priesthood, not the city, the city's oldest quarrel. The Amphictyony of Delphara has no jurisdiction here, which Ephelanum insists on loudly. The Ivory Chorus and the Hearthfire Sanctum keep houses here, and the Luminastra Alchemists supply the temple's medicines.

Way of life. Devout, agricultural, commercial and quarrelsome. Everybody in Ephelanum either owns land, works it, sells its produce, or sells something to the people who come to celebrate it. The city's year has two halves: the working half, when the plain empties the taverns, and the festival half, from the barley harvest to the olive pressing, when the population roughly doubles, prices triple, and the permanent residents make most of their annual income while complaining continuously.

The festival year

The codex festivals are the city's oldest; the rest have accreted around the harvest, and every one draws visitors from the whole coast.

The First Furrow (early spring) — the Archon and the Dux plough one furrow together across the sanctuary's sacred field, behind two white oxen, one from each zone. Each government argues annually about whose ox walks on the right. The furrow's straightness is read as an omen for the harvest.

The Procession of the Image (late spring) — the goddess's statue is carried from the temple down the marble street to the harbour and back, a full day, with the whole city and every pilgrim in attendance; since the treaty the route also loops through the nearest barley fields, so that the Lady can see the crop.

The Barley Games (early summer, at the barley harvest) — four days of races, wrestling, and the reaping contest, in which teams from each estate cut a measured field against each other; the winners carry the first sheaf to the altar. The coast's athletes come for the races; the plain comes for the reaping, and bets on it with a seriousness the races never see.

The Two Feasts (midsummer) — the Lady's great feast, held twice: in the month of Artemision by the Hellenorian text and on the Ides of Sextilis by the Invictian, eleven days apart. Each government closes its offices for its own feast and works through the other's. Since first-fruits are due to the sanctuary "at the feast", every estate on the plain argues which feast it owes them at.

The Fair of the Lady (late summer, eighteen days) — the coast's great market, held on the Festival Meadow outside the walls under the sanctuary's truce. Grain contracts for next year are struck here, slaves and oxen sold, wine of last year's vintage opened, and Farshore merchants set up stalls that the Dux's customs men tax on the way in.

The Smiths' Offering (at the Fair's close) — the silversmiths' guild presents a model of the temple worked over the whole preceding year, displayed inside after a competition between workshops that is bitter even by guild standards.

The Treading (autumn) — the vintage. The estates tread their grapes on the same three nights; the sanctuary's own vineyard is trodden by the novice priestesses, and its first must is poured on the altar. The city drinks the rest of last year's wine to make room.

The Dredging (autumn) — nominally a rite for the harbour's health, in practice a yearly reminder of the silt. Attendance has been falling.

The Olive Night (early winter) — the first oil of the year is pressed by torchlight and carried up to the temple's lamps, which are relit from it. The plain's pickers come into town for the one night of the year they are paid in advance.

The Condominium

At the Treaty of Myrianth, Hellenoria ceded Ephelanum to the Imperium as a pledge for the Treaty's naval clauses, and the result is a condominium. The Invictians call it the Great Concord's pledge and file it at Aepistra; the Hellenorians call it a lease and refuse to say "ceded" in public. The Dux holds the harbour, the garrison and the red-earth estates inland; the Archon and the priesthood hold the city and the sanctuary. The line is drawn in the treaty's annex street by street, and in the forum it is drawn in the paving: a bronze strip two fingers wide, which a stall may not straddle without paying two taxes.

Who owns the land. This is the condominium's real question, and it is older than the treaty. Before the war the plain was owned by the city's old families, the Melanippidai first among them, in middling estates worked by tenants and slaves, and the sanctuary owned the best third outright as the goddess's land. The war ruined the families; the treaty gave the plain outside the sanctuary's boundary-stones to the Dux "for the support of the garrison". The Dux leased it, on long terms, to Invictian buyers who could pay in silver: the gens Rubria took the red-earth hills and the great grain flats as latifundia, worked by slave gangs from the Imperium's wars; the old Hellenorian owners kept what they could prove by deed, mostly vineyards on the slopes. So the plain is now a patchwork: Invictian grain estates on the flats, Hellenorian vineyards and olives above, the goddess's land in a ring around her temple, and the boundary-stones between them moved at night.

Who works it. Invictian slave gangs on the latifundia, under overseers who answer to the Rubrii; Hellenorian tenant families on the slopes, paying a sixth of the crop; free day-labourers by the thousand at harvest, hired at dawn in the forum; and, since the peace, demobilised legionaries, promised land by the Imperium and given none, who have drifted to the plain and work for wages on the estates that were supposed to be theirs.

The joint board. The Archon, the Hierarchis and the Dux meet monthly in the warm room of the Baths, the one building the treaty assigns to both governments. Minutes are kept in two languages and signed in the order the three entered the room, which is why all three arrive at the same moment through three different doors. The board has agreed unanimously on six matters in five years. Four concerned the drains, one the date of the First Furrow, and one the price of bread in festival season.

Incidents. The Legionary at the Altar: in the second year a soldier who had struck his centurion fled up the marble street and claimed asylum, which runs a bowshot from the altar; the board spent a month arguing whose bow defined a bowshot, settled on a neutral archer from Delphara, and the soldier is still in the precinct, now the temple's best gardener. The Weighing: the Dux's customs men weighed a Smiths' Offering model at the quay as taxable silver; the guild filled the theatre and chanted "Great is the Lady" for two hours, and the model was declared sacred by a board vote of two to one. The Night of the Two Feasts: four years ago legionaries celebrating Diana's Ides were pelted with roof-tiles by Hellenorians who were working; an optio lost an eye. The Moving Stones: every winter boundary-stones between the latifundia and the sanctuary's land walk a few paces one way or the other, and every spring the board walks the line with surveyors from both zones and a priestess with a measuring-cord.

Customs at the harbour. The quays are Invictian, and every cargo landed pays the portorium, one fortieth of value, at the Dux's stone customs shed. Every cargo that then passes the city gate pays the Hellenorian pentekoste, one fiftieth, forty yards up the same street. Goods consigned to the sanctuary pay neither. Grain going out pays the Dux an export fortieth unless it is bound for an Invictian garrison, which most of it now is. Pilgrims are exempt from both duties if they wear the red-and-white festival ribbon sold at the temple; two years ago nine hundred forged ribbons turned up in one bale of Khemaret linen.

The Farshore traders. The Fair of the Lady draws ships from beyond Asetheria that the great harbours tax too high. Tyrsan dyers taught the far-shore vats their purple and still sell their own cheaper, which is why the Tyrian Vats are named for a rival; Khemaret linen comes in for the festival robes and Khemaret grain-factors come to watch the harvest, because Ephelanum's price sets theirs; Sabaian incense arrives by the shipload in sewn-plank hulls and burns on the altar all festival season. The Hierarchis has argued for three years that incense bought for the goddess is hers from the moment it leaves Sabaia, and should pay no portorium.

The silversmiths. Some four hundred masters with two thousand journeymen, the city's largest single body of free men, who cast votive temples, silver sheaves and little silver oxen for the First Furrow in two moulds now: the Lady with her stag and Diana with her hounds and crescent, priced the same and sold from the same stalls. They will take Invictian silver only by weight, since the Assays began; the last magistrate who proposed regulating them saw the guild fill the theatre.

New lore

The silt and the plain. The river that makes the plain red also makes the harbour shallow. Dredging costs some forty talents and lasts a dozen years. Under the treaty the harbour is the Dux's, so the Archon says the Imperium must pay; the silt comes from the estates' ploughed hills, so the Dux says the landowners must pay; the sanctuary, which has the money, says the goddess does not dredge. The estates have cleared more hillside every year since the peace to grow grain for the garrisons, and the harbour silts faster.

The bank and the harvest. The sanctuary lends to every farmer on the plain against the coming crop, at one in ten for citizens and one in eight for everyone else. Its loans fall due at the Fair. A bad year on the plain is a good year for the goddess, who takes the land of defaulters into her ring; the Melanippidai's last estates went that way.

Rumours. That the Dux borrows from the temple to pay his garrison. That the Hierarchis keeps a third treaty text in which the goddess is named in neither language. That the Rubrii ship more than red earth in their ochre jars. That the ruins on the plain beyond the estates are older than the temple and the goddess came from there.

Districts

The Silting Harbour Existing · Invictian-held

Muddy and anxious · customs men, grain-factors, dredgers · silt, salt, wet grain

The harbour is silting up. It has been dredged four times and the sea retreats anyway, leaving the waterfront further from the water every generation; the oldest mooring-rings hang over reed-beds. Grain barges come down the river to the inner quay, and seagoing ships load from lighters across the bar. The Dredging is nominally a rite for its health; in practice it is a yearly reminder. The Dux's customs shed stands at the harbour gate. The Baths of Ephelanum stand at the harbour end, first stop for pilgrims arriving by sea before they climb to the goddess, and the joint board meets in their warm room.

Ties: the Dux's customs; Aepistra; Farshore ships; the Red Plain's grain.

The Forum Line Forum · basilica · the treaty strip

Divided and bustling · silversmiths, grain-brokers, day-labourers, two sets of tax-men · hot silver, chaff, argument

The forum is the commercial end of the marble street, given over to the silversmiths' votive trade and, at dawn in harvest season, to the hiring of day-labourers, who stand on the Hellenorian side of the bronze strip to be hired for Invictian estates. A stall that straddles the strip pays two taxes. The basilica hears the temple's lending cases and the boundary suits of the plain, and both governments dispute whose law applies; a case may be heard twice, once in each language, with two verdicts.

Ties: House Argyrides; the temple bank; the Festival Meadow.

The Great Sanctuary Temple · bank · asylum · the goddess's ring

Vast and holy · priestesses, depositors, suppliants, sacred herdsmen · incense, beeswax, red earth

The temple at the end of the marble street, visible far out to sea, its deposit vaults under the cult image. The priestesses are called the Bees, and keep the sanctuary's hives as well as its ledgers. Around the temple lies the goddess's ring: the sacred field ploughed at the First Furrow, her vineyard, her olive groves, her herds of white cattle, and the boundary-stones that walk in winter. Asylum runs a bowshot from the altar. Behind it, the Red-Earth Sheds wash and seal Sinopic red in jars stamped by the sanctuary, and the workers have red hands and red hair.

Ties: House Hagnotheidai; the Mithril Reserve; the festival year.

The Festival Meadow Fairground · stadium · theatre

Empty half the year, heaving the other half · stallholders, athletes, actors, pickpockets · trampled grass, roasting meat, new wine

Outside the walls on the Hellenorian side, a flat meadow between the theatre hill and the sanctuary's ring, kept unploughed by sacred law. For eighteen days of the Fair it holds a city of booths; at the Barley Games, a stadium of turf banks and a reaping-field marked with stakes. The theatre is cut into the hill above, large enough for twenty-four thousand, which is roughly the number the silversmiths can bring out in an hour. The silversmiths' workshops ring the hill behind it.

Ties: the Fair of the Lady; the Barley Games; House Argyrides.

The Red Plain Latifundia · vineyards · olive terraces · Invictian-held

Wide and sweating · slave gangs, tenants, overseers, legionary day-men · dust, cut barley, crushed grapes

A day's ride of red earth inland. On the flats, the Rubrian latifundia: wheat to the horizon, worked by slave gangs from barracks called the Pens, under overseers on horseback. On the slopes, the vineyards and olive terraces of the Hellenorian families who kept their deeds, with the tenants' villages among them. Threshing-floors of beaten earth sit at every crossroads, each with its shrine of Demeter. The plain is the Dux's by treaty, the goddess's in part by older right, and its boundary-stones are the most argued-over objects in the condominium.

Ties: gens Rubria; House Melanippidai; House Kallikratidai.

The Far Shore and the Garrison Road Dye-works · legionary camp · granaries

Reeking and martial · dyers, legionaries, granary clerks · rotting shellfish, leather, grain dust

Downwind on the far shore, the Tyrian Vats crush purple-snail into the colour of rulers beside shell-heaps taller than the sheds. Inland, the Ephelanum Garrison stands outside the sacred line as Invictian law requires, a rectangular camp with one under-strength cohort, and beside it the military granaries where the plain's tithe for the southern garrisons is stored. The road beyond runs into the Red Plain.

Ties: gens Rubria; the Dux's household; Tyrsan dyers.

Rule

Archon Philostratos Melanippou, elected by the city and confirmed by Hellarchon, holds the walls, markets, courts and the festival calendar of the city. Hierarchis Melissa Aristarchis, high priestess of the Lady, holds the sanctuary, its bank, its guard, its land and the rites. Dux Marcus Vettius Calvo, appointed by the Dominus Militum and reporting through Aepistra, holds the harbour, the garrison and the estates. The joint board of all three meets monthly in the Baths. Each checks the others with the treaty text that suits them; the silversmiths' guild checks all three with the theatre, and the plain checks them with the harvest.

The officials. Under the Dux, Praefectus Portus Titus Opsius Naso runs the customs shed and the quays, Tribune Gnaea Laelia Rufa the garrison cohort, and the Procurator of the Estates, Sextus Afranius Bassus, the leases and the grain tithe. Under the Archon, the Agoranomos Lysikles Thrasonos runs the markets, the bread price and the Fair. Under the Hierarchis, the Neokoros Megabyxos, a eunuch priest by ancient custom, keeps the temple guard, the asylum and the boundary-cord. Appeals from the Invictian zone go to Aepistra, where Procurator Decimus Veturius Scaurus keeps the Ephelanum files; appeals from the Hellenorian zone go to Hellarchon, which hears them slowly to show it can.

Houses and families

House Hagnotheidai Priestly house · Eupatrid

Crest: a bee on a crescent · Motto: "The Lady keeps." · Seat: the priests' houses behind the sanctuary

The family that supplies the Lady's high priestesses. Melissa Aristarchis, Hierarchis, plays one treaty text against the other; her brother Kleon keeps the deposit ledgers.

History. The house traces itself to the first Bee, a herdswoman who found the goddess's image in a hollow oak on the plain, and every Hierarchis for nine hundred years has been born or married into it. It has outlived two conquests and a tyranny by the same method: the goddess owns the land, the house manages it, and every ruler finds it cheaper to borrow from the Lady than to rob her. Its wealth is the sanctuary's ring of land and its harvest loans, and it has quietly enlarged the ring by a field or two every bad year for centuries.

  • Melissa Aristarchis, Hierarchis, 54 — addresses the Dux in flawless Invictian and the Archon in temple Hellenorian, and never in the same room; walks the boundary-cord herself every spring.
  • Kleon Aristarchou, her brother — keeps the deposit and harvest-loan ledgers in a cipher of his own; knows exactly how much the Dux owes and which estates will default this year.
  • Daphne Aristarchis, her niece, 20 — a novice Bee who treads the sanctuary's grapes and carries the Image's veil, courted by a tribune of the garrison.

Ties: the Great Sanctuary; the Mithril Reserve; the Vettii.

House Argyrides Silversmiths' guild dynasty

Crest: a silver temple model · Motto: "Great is the Lady." · Seat: the guild hall on the Forum Line

Hermias Argyrides, guildmaster, can fill the theatre in an hour; his niece Thalia is making this year's Offering model, and three workshops want it to fail.

History. The Argyrides cast the first silver sheaf sold at a Barley Games, and have held the guild's mastership for five generations by marrying their daughters to rival workshops. The house's great day was the riot that ended a magistrate's career over a tax on votives; its motto is the chant. It owns forty workshops and the guild's assay furnace, so every bar of silver in the city passes its touchstone, and it supplies the silver oxen, sheaves and vine-leaves that every festival needs by the thousand.

  • Hermias Argyrides, guildmaster, 59 — led the chant over the Weighing; has a seat at no board and a veto over all of them.
  • Thalia Argyris, his niece, 27 — working the Offering model in silver she refined herself from debased Invictian coin, to make a point.
  • Demetrios Argyrides, his son — runs the Diana moulds and sells to the garrison, which his father pretends not to know.

Ties: the Forum Line; the Festival Meadow.

Gens Rubria Invictian estate-holders · Comes

Crest: a red ochre jar · Motto: "Terra rubra, terra nostra." · Seat: the villa on the red-earth estates

Owners of the inland latifundia and of the hill across the bay where the sanctuary's red earth is dug. Gaius Rubrius Fenestella wants the sanctuary to pay rent for its clay.

History. A patrician-adjacent family of Aepistra that made its money supplying the legions in the war, and was first in line with silver when the Dux put the plain's leases up in the first year of the peace. They took the grain flats and the red-earth hills on ninety-nine-year terms, bought slave gangs cheap from the last campaigns, and cleared hillside the old owners had left in scrub for centuries. Their wheat feeds the southern garrisons on contract; their red earth sells everywhere; their villa has a bath-house larger than the Archon's. The Hellenorian families call them "the lessees", never "the owners".

  • Gaius Rubrius Fenestella, Comes, 50 — has sued the sanctuary for clay-rent in both courts and won in one; his reaping teams have won the Barley Games three years running.
  • Rubria Paulla, his wife — corresponds with patrician houses in Aeterna who want their silver kept out of the Assay's reach.
  • Gaius Rubrius Minor, their son, 22 — runs the Pens with a whip and a ledger, and is hated on the plain in a way his father has never quite managed.

Ties: Aepistra; the Dux; the Red Plain; rivals of the Melanippidai.

House Melanippidai Old landowners · Eupatrid · the Archon's house

Crest: a black mare under a crescent · Motto: "We were here before the temple." · Seat: the old council-hall on the theatre hill

The oldest civic family, whose estates were the best of the plain until the war ruined them and the treaty gave the rest to the Dux to lease. They kept the Archonship and one vineyard, and they want the land back without paying for the harbour.

History. The Melanippidai claim to have farmed the plain before the goddess's image was found, and their black mare is said to be older than her bee. They led the city's cavalry for centuries, lost their horses and their sons in the war, mortgaged their land to the goddess to pay their war-levy, and lost half of it to her in two bad harvests. The treaty took most of the rest. They have held the Archonship four times since, partly from sentiment, mostly because no other family can afford to be seen to want it.

  • Philostratos Melanippou, Archon, 57 — wants Hellarchon to pay for the dredging, Hellarchon to stay away, and the Rubrian leases declared void on a point of Hellenorian law.
  • Hipparete Melanippe, his sister — a widow who leases the family's last vineyard to the garrison's officers and hears their complaints for free.
  • Kallias Melanippou, his nephew, 25 — captains the Hellenorian reaping team at the Barley Games and has lost to the Rubrii three years running; next year he means to win, by any method.

Ties: the theatre hill; Hellarchon; rivals of gens Rubria.

House Kallikratidai Vintners and olive-growers · Eupatrid

Crest: a vine-leaf and an olive-sprig crossed · Motto: "The slope remembers." · Seat: the press-house above the vineyards

The one Hellenorian estate family that came out of the war richer. They grow the plain's best wine and oil on the slopes, kept every deed in a sealed jar through the war, and proved title to every vine in the treaty commission. They sell to both sides, sit on neither, and host the Treading.

History. Kallikrates the elder planted the "Lady's Red" vine three generations ago from a cutting he swore came from the sanctuary's vineyard; the Hagnotheidai have never contradicted him. In the war the house sold wine to the Hellenorian fleet and oil to the Invictian legions, through different cousins. Since the peace they have bought the deeds of ruined neighbours at low prices, and the Melanippidai, whose vineyards some of those were, do not forgive it.

  • Kallikrates Kallikratidou, head, 68 — tastes every vat himself, and knows the vintage of every amphora in the city by the clay.
  • Chrysis Kallikratis, his daughter-in-law — runs the presses and the sales; supplies the Dux's table and the Archon's at the same price.
  • Nikias Kallikratidou, his grandson, 17 — wants to marry Kallias Melanippou's sister, which both houses forbid.

Ties: the Red Plain; the Treading; House Melanippidai.

The Vettii at Ephelanum Invictian equestrian household · the Dux's house

Crest: a legion's eagle over a ploughshare · Motto: "Serve, and be paid." · Seat: the praetorium of the garrison

A provincial equestrian family risen through the legions, not the Senate. The Dux has a soldier's pension owed, a garrison unpaid in good coin, and a household that lives better than either should allow.

History. Vettius Calvo's grandfather was a centurion given a farm for service; the ploughshare on the crest is that farm. His father rose to the equestrian order on the war's profits; he himself commanded a legion's cavalry in the last campaigns and was given Ephelanum by the Dominus Militum as a reward that looked like a promotion and is turning out to be a debt. He ploughs the First Furrow with real skill, which the Hellenorians did not expect.

  • Marcus Vettius Calvo, Dux, 55 — holds the harbour with an unpaid garrison and a straight face.
  • Vettia Prisca, his wife — bathes daily at the Baths, has learnt Hellenorian, and gives to the goddess under both names.
  • Lucius Vettius Calvo, their son, 23 — tribune of the garrison, in love with a novice of the Bees.

Ties: gens Valeria, who appointed him; Aepistra; House Hagnotheidai.

Sanctuary City · Hellenoria · Hellenorian highlands

Delphara

A mountain sanctuary of switchback terraces where twelve cities share one oracle, and where the League still does as it is told, because Delphara can decline to answer.

Codex now: The sanctuary city — home of the oracle, governed jointly by twelve cities, and the one place in Hellenoria where the League still obeys.

Ruler
Eudoros Pythokles, presiding delegate of the Amphictyony
Title
Hieromnemon of Delphara (Archon rank)
Population
c. 25,000; nearer 60,000 in a Games year
Built on
A sacred road of switchbacks, a purifying spring, and a crack in the mountain that breathes
Patron
Apollo, the Radiant One; older rites to Phoebe the Visionary are still kept at the spring
Trouble
Two tyrants' delegates, a neutrality that has been paid for, and a dream-priest gone missing

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Terraces climb a mountainside above a valley of olives, switchback by switchback, to the temple at the top. Treasuries line the whole ascent: small, exquisite buildings put up by individual cities to hold their dedications, each trying to outdo its neighbour in stone. The climb is eight centuries of Hellenorian rivalry told in architecture, and it ends at a temple where people put questions to the god. The town below exists to serve the sanctuary, with lodging, sacrificial animals, and guides who explain what you are looking at.

Delphara produces nothing and is extremely rich, which the Scales of Eternal Justice have pointed out in writing more than once. Consultation is not free. The petitioner pays for the sacrifice, the attendance and the interpretation, and the fee scales with who is asking: cities pay more than men. The Amphictyony of Delphara audits the treasuries and lends them to nobody. The olives of the sacred plain may not be farmed for profit, a rule enforced by sacred war three times. The town has a ceremonial guard and the Amphictyony's oath. It has been sacked twice in fifteen centuries, both times by parties who then found out what the oath obliges the other eleven cities to do, and it has never needed a wall worth the name.

Life follows the calendar of consultation days, because the god does not answer on demand. Delpharans are hosts by profession: what is asked at the temple is not repeated in the town, and a guide who repeats it is finished. The priesthood is local and serves for life. The interpreters, who turn the response into verse a petitioner can carry home, hold the real influence. The festivals are the Pythian Games every four years, with music before athletics (the reverse of everywhere else, and a point of pride); the Silence, the winter months when the god is absent, the temple shuts and the Amphictyony audits; and the Boundary Rite, a tedious annual walk round the plain's markers that has triggered every sacred war ever declared.

New lore

How the god answers. The oracle speaks on the seventh day of each of the nine warm months, so there are nine consultation days a year and several hundred questions waiting for each. The speaker is the Pythia, a Delpharan woman over fifty who wears a girl's white dress for the work. She washes at the spring, goes down beneath the temple floor, and sits on a bronze tripod over a crack that breathes a faint, sweetish air, chewing a leaf of sleep-poppy the priests give her. What she says is rarely verse and sometimes not Hellenorian. On the other days of the year, anyone can draw the bean-lot in the porch for an obol: white for yes, black for no.

The first-asking. On consultation days the order of asking is everything. The sanctuary has granted the right to ask first in perpetuity to exactly one petitioner: the Acheaorian throne. The grant came with the Golden Tripod, which Shahanshah Ariyamna the Generous dedicated during the Barley Truce, three hundred and forty years ago. The League has moved to revoke it nineteen times and failed nineteen times, usually by two votes.

The twelve. The members include Hellarchon, Corinth, Thebesieas, Thessalonika, Helionyx and Delphara itself. They also include Argotiko, Atticenea and Kirimitsana, which are cities only in the old sense of having a hearth and a vote; Kirimitsana has not sent a delegate in living memory. Three coast and island cities complete the twelve. Ephelanum is not a member and says so loudly.

Five years of peace. Pilgrim numbers have trebled, and most of the new questions are about the war dead. In the first spring after the Treaty of Myrianth, an Invictian embassy in civilian cloaks asked one sealed question, and the answer went to Aeterna unread by anyone here except the Exegete who wrote it. The Arcane Academy has twice asked to copy the oracle's records and twice been refused. The Hegemon has let it be known that he would welcome a response blessing theoric money for the fleet. Nobody has yet dared to put that question to the god.

Districts

The Sacred Way Existing · Processional way

Treasuries and guides · treasury-keepers, pilgrims, touts · incense, hot marble, goat dung

The switchback road from the valley to the temple is lined with twenty-three treasuries, each raised by one city to hold its dedications and outdo its neighbours. Eleven are still kept up by the cities that built them, and the rest belong to cities that no longer exist. The Thebesian treasury is plain and full of captured shields. Helionyx's gilded sun-disc blinds the switchback above it at noon. The Acheaorian Treasury, called the House of the Tripod, stands at the sixth turn. It is the richest building on the mountain.

Ties: House Vashtiri; guides of the Labyadai; Persemenid, Thebesieas, Helionyx.

The Temenos Temple terrace

The sacred ground · priests, Exegetes, the sick · laurel smoke, wet stone, the sweet breath of the crack

The walled precinct at the head of the Way holds the oracle temple, the great altar and a forest of dedications, all within two hundred paces. Here is the Dream Dormitory, a long, cool hall where the sick sleep among olive-coloured Healer's Serpents and report their dreams at dawn. Behind the temple is the Herbalists' Lodge, a courtyard of drying bunches where physicians and herb-wives trade as equals.

Ties: House Pythokleidai; Lysandra Anthemis; herb-wives from Kirimitsana.

The Phoibad Terrace Spring and gymnasion

Purification · athletes, bathers, old women at the shrine · cold water, olive oil, crushed thyme

Every petitioner washes their hair at the Phoibad Spring before going up. Beside it stands a round shrine older than the temple, kept by local women for the Titan Phoebe, who held the oracle before the god did. The priests tolerate it and do not discuss it. Below lies the Gymnasion of Delphara, with its track and the music-schools that train for the Pythian contests.

Ties: the Pythia purifies here; the High Seats.

The High Seats Theatre and stadium

The Games ground · musicians, judges, the council in session · pine resin, dust, rehearsing pipes

The Theatre of Delphara is cut into the mountain above the temple, and its view down the valley counts as part of the performance. The Pythian musical contests are held here, and so are the Amphictyony's spring and autumn sessions, with the twenty-four delegates in the front row and the town watching from above. The stadium is higher still, with nothing above it but a stand of Thunder-Oak.

Ties: runners from Thebesieas and riders from Argotiko dominate the Games.

The Lower Town Agora and hostels

Hospitality as an industry · innkeepers, animal-sellers, money-changers · roasting meat, wet wool, donkey

The Agora of Delphara serves pilgrims: lodging brokers, sellers of goats and cockerels, and guides who explain the treasuries for a fee. A goat certified fit for sacrifice costs 2 gp in spring and 6 gp in a Games year. Under the north stoa is the stone vault of the Mithril Reserve branch. It handles pilgrims' letters of credit, the only banking allowed on the mountain.

Ties: House Labyadai; the Mithril Reserve; pilgrims from Corinth.

The Sacred Plain Valley, vines and markers

Holy land that may not pay · temple dependents, vintners · cut grass, wine-lees, wild fennel

The valley floor belongs to the god. Its olives may light the sanctuary's lamps but may not be sold, and its hundred and four boundary stones have each been the subject of a lawsuit. On the lower slopes, the Oracle's Vineyards are harvested on the day the oracle names. A vintner who picks a day early or late loses the year's wine to the god. A muddy track runs down to the pilgrim harbour.

Ties: House Kastalidai; the Boundary Rite.

Rule

Each member city sends two delegates, the hieromnemones. Delphara's senior delegate presides over all twenty-four and governs the town between sessions: Hieromnemon Eudoros Pythokles, now in his ninth year. His remit is the calendar, the audits, the boundaries and the right to consult. Drains, inns and the price of goats go to the town's own small assembly. The temple has three parts. The Pythia speaks. The five Hosioi, life priests from the old houses, decide which questions reach her and in what order. The five Exegetes render her answers, under Lysandra Anthemis. Kleobule Pythokleia, Epimelete of the Treasuries, keeps the inventories. Captain Hagnon's Tripod Guard, a hundred and twenty men with bronze-shod staves, keeps order on the Way.

The council audits the Hieromnemon every winter in the Silence, and the Scales of Eternal Justice audit everyone uninvited. The deepest check is the oath: no city can afford to be the one Delphara refuses to answer. The weakness is that the council cannot command the full twelve until it decides whether a tyrant's delegate counts as a delegate. Eudoros has put that vote off for three sessions, because he is not sure how it would go.

Houses and families

House Pythokleidai Priestly house · Eupatrid

Crest: a tripod between laurel sprigs · Motto: "We keep the order of asking" · Seat: the priest-house by the temple wall

The oldest Delpharan family, with more Hieromnemons and Hosioi to its name than any other. It lives on a small share of every consultation fee, under a decree nobody has read in four hundred years. The house wants the sanctuary neutral and itself in charge, and has stopped asking whether those aims conflict.

  • Eudoros Pythokles, Hieromnemon, 71. Reads every inventory twice and votes last.
  • Kleobule Pythokleia, his daughter, Epimelete. Has found a chest in the House of the Tripod that is on no list.
  • Damon Pythokleides, his brother, one of the Hosioi. Wears new rings.
  • Lykos Pythokleides, grandson, a guide of 19. Talks too much in wine-shops.

Ties: rivals of the Labyadai; uneasy hosts of the Vashtiri.

House Labyadai Hosts and guides · Eupatrid

Crest: an open door and a lamp · Motto: "The guest's word is the god's" · Seat: the Hostel of the Seven Turns

The Labyadai hold a third of the town's beds, license every guide and enforce the oath of silence with exile. They are rich, popular and shut out of the priesthood. They want the town assembly to have a council seat, and they would accept a tyrant's delegate as the price.

  • Aristomache Labyadis, Master of Guides. Remembers every face that has slept under her roof.
  • Euthymos Labyadas, her son, runs the lodging brokers. Owes money in Corinth.
  • Hagnon, a cousin, Captain of the Tripod Guard. Has never drawn a blade in anger.

Ties: courted by the tyrant of Atticenea.

House Kastalidai Vintners and boundary-keepers · Eupatrid

Crest: a vine bound to a boundary stone · Motto: "Here, and not one foot further" · Seat: the press-house below the vineyards

Hereditary keepers of the boundary stones, and owners of the best private vines just outside the plain. Their wine reaches pilgrims a fortnight before the temple's, labelled "from the oracle's slopes", which is strictly true.

  • Philoxenos Kastalides, head of house. Pays the priest of the vines a "gift of first must" each spring.
  • Moschion, a cousin, priest of the vines. Names the harvest day "as the god directs".
  • Eirene Kastalis, keeper of the stones. Has found one moved.

Ties: the Sacred Plain.

House Vashtiri Resident Acheaorian zarate · keepers of the Tripod

Crest: a winged disc over a tripod · Motto: "The King's gift does not tarnish" · Seat: the House of the Tripod

A cadet line of an Acheaorian zarate, hereditary custodians of the Acheaorian Treasury for eleven generations. They speak unaccented Hellenorian, marry Delpharans, and send their sons to Persemenid at fifteen to be reminded whose they are. They are paid a stipend "for the lamps of the Tripod" that is far more than lamps could burn.

  • Mehrdad Vashtir, ganzabara (treasurer). Courteous, unhurried, and generous to every priest's widow on the mountain.
  • Mahsa Ruzbehan, "almanac clerk". In fact a dream-reader of the Enchanted Muse.

Ties: Persemenid; the House of Zindar.

Notable figures

  • Lysandra Anthemis the Exegete · diviner — Writes down what the Pythia actually says and decides what it means. Suspects the oracle is no longer honest.
  • Theano the Pythia · vintner's widow, 58 — Cannot read. Remembers every word she has spoken on the tripod and has noticed that the verses sent home do not always match.
  • Durgan Ironhand Dominus Argentar, Mithril Reserve · dwarf — Offended by gold that is never lent. Lady Isolde Merca's letters keep asking what the House of the Tripod holds.
  • Iphianassa Oneiropolos, keeper of the Dream Dormitory — Frightened for the first time in her life. Her junior priest Philokles vanished after reading one pilgrim's dream.
  • Myrrhine of Kirimitsana keeper of the Herbalists' Lodge — Suspects the new physician Zopyros of poisoning villagers so he can sell them the cure.
  • Phaidimos "student of winds" · Arcane Academy — Copies the Aeolus Reach wind chart by day. By night, asks guides about pilgrims who dream strangely.

Connections

  • Persemenid — The Golden Tripod: the throne's right to ask first, and a stipend that buys more than lamp oil.
  • Hellarchon — By sea to the pilgrim landing, then up the Sacred Way. The Hegemon wants a blessing; the Arcane Academy wants the records and the last dream-walker.
  • Persevalis and Eronis — The Enchanted Muse and the drowned dream-capital: the other two ends of the hunt for Vesperine Ilaro.
  • Corinth — A day's sail from the western harbour. Most pilgrims and most of the wine pass through Corinthian hands.
  • Helionyx — The consultation days are reckoned from its solar tables, and the oracle forbade it to raise its fallen colossus.
  • Aeterna — The sealed Invictian question, and an answer filed in the Dominus Militum's house.
  • Deiperduem — The Reserve's great branch, where Durgan's reports go.

City · Hellenoria · Hellenorian south

Helionyx

A lime-white harbour city under a sun that does not relent, whose priests read a gnomon every clear day and so own the League's calendar. Its bronze colossus fell two centuries ago; its sea-law is still standing.

Codex now: The sun-city of the Hellenorian south — white, blinding, and built around a solar cult that keeps the continent's best astronomical records.

Ruler
Philinna Halikis, senior of the five prytaneis
Title
Prytanis of Helionyx (Archon rank)
Population
c. 70,000
Built on
A white hill, a gnomon, and the feet of a fallen bronze giant
Patron
Helios of the Aetherian Ancients, the Titan who is the sun; Apollo is kept as a guest in the lower shrine
Trouble
The almonds came early and the storks did not come; foreign purple undercuts the dye

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Lime-washed white everywhere, by ordinance. Helionyx sits on a dry southern coast under a sun that does not relent, and the city's answer has been to reflect all of it: white walls, white roofs, and narrow shaded streets between them. Visitors wear smoked glass. Residents squint and are amused. At the high point stands the solar precinct, an open court with a gnomon at its centre and a graduated arc cut into the pavement, read and recorded every clear day for six hundred years.

The city lives on salt, dye and knowledge. The flats to the south yield salt in quantity and a shellfish purple that is the most expensive substance in Hellenoria by weight. The precinct's records are the third export. Every serious calendar in the League is calibrated against them, and so, quietly, is that of the Celestial Astromancers of the Imperium. The Ecliptica Arcanum keeps a house here, and each institution suspects the other of wanting the records. The city's defence is modest and naval. The coast is poor for landing and the harbour is small, and that has done more for its security than any garrison. Twice it has been blockaded for its salt rather than attacked, and twice it settled. When it needs soldiers it hires, which means the Sunward Valiants, who can come quickly along the coast.

The day starts early and then stops. Work runs from before dawn to mid-morning and halts completely through midday; a visitor who tries to do business at noon is simply not attended to. The solar priesthood is the civic authority here, unusually for Hellenoria, because it keeps the calendar and therefore the schedule of everything. Night is social. The evening streets are the liveliest in the League, and the city sleeps late and briefly. The festivals are the Standing, the summer solstice, when the exact moment is announced and the whole city falls silent and then very much does not; the Reading of the Arc, the year's tables published before scholars from three empires; and the Dyeing, the public opening of the first vat, whose smell is famous and whose attendance is compulsory for guild members.

New lore

The Charioteer. For two centuries a bronze Helios seventy cubits high stood over the harbour mouth. It was cast from the rams of a corsair fleet the city's navy burned four hundred years ago. An earthquake brought it down two hundred and twelve years ago. The city asked Delphara whether to raise it again, and the answer was "Do not move what has fallen." So the pieces lie where they fell, across what is now the Fallen Quarter, with a thumb no man can get his arms around. Children climb inside the hollow forearm, and scrap merchants from three empires have offered sums that would rebuild the harbour twice over.

The Law of the Jettison. When a crew throws cargo overboard to save a ship, everyone with goods aboard shares the loss in proportion. Helionyx wrote that rule down first. Its Court of the Jettison, which sits at dawn under the agora awnings, is cited by every maritime court in the League and, without acknowledgement, by the Invictian harbour court at Fucostia. Helionyx exports judges as other cities export oil.

The year has a name. Each year is named after the Sun-Priest, a rich citizen elected to pay for the Standing, wear the gold crown, and have his name cut into every contract. This is the Year of Hegesias. The real priesthood is the College of the Arc, thirty life-sworn gnomonists who read the shadow. The city's emblem is the Ash Phoenix, and the College logs every sighting of the bird.

Five years of peace. Invictian Astromancers now attend the Reading of the Arc openly, and Magi from Atarabad come to compare the arc with their fire-calendar. The Acheaorian court is buying purple again. That revival has drawn Tyrsian dye-ships from the Farshore Realms into the harbour, selling a cheaper purple and the best charts afloat. This winter the Almond Slope blossomed three weeks early, and nobody agrees what the omen means.

Districts

The Dye-Works Existing · Industrial quarter

The purple · dyers stained to the elbow, shell-crushers · rotting shellfish, urine, wealth

The dye-works lie on the edge of the white city, downwind. Rows of lead vats steep crushed shellfish in brine for ten days. A cloak's purple border costs twelve thousand shells, and the shell middens behind the works stand taller than the city wall. The season opens with the Dyeing, a festival of appalling smell and compulsory attendance. The colours made here are worn across the League, and the white city's wealth lies in them.

Ties: House Kochlidai; buyers from Persemenid.

Temple Hill Solar precinct and sun-temple

The calendar · gnomonists, pupils, stork-watchers · hot stone, cedar presses, bird lime

The Solar Precinct crowns the hill: gnomon, arc, and the cedar presses where six centuries of tables are kept. The Temple Precinct beside it holds the sun-temple. Its gold dome blinds ships at sea, and its flat roof is the Stork Roof, where a dozen cartwheel-sized nests sit among the chimneys and a priest records the first arrival each spring for the farmers. Apollo's guest-shrine is down a side stair.

Ties: House Phaethontidai; the College of the Arc.

The Awning Agora Market and courts

Shade as a public good · brokers, jurists, salt factors · canvas, wet stone, ink

Awnings strung between the white walls shade the Agora of Helionyx. In this city people gather in the shade, not the sun. The Court of the Jettison sits at dawn. By mid-morning the sea-loan brokers have written the day's bottomry, a loan on a ship that is repaid only if the ship comes home. The Mithril Reserve branch is the only building on the square that is not white. It is grey basalt, and nobody has dared to report it.

Ties: House Halikidai; Hellenorian law; the Reserve.

The Fallen Quarter Harbour and colossus

Sailors and ruins · rowers, Valiants, Tyrsian pilots · tar, fish, sun-hot bronze

The small harbour, its two shipsheds and the salt warehouses are built in and around the Charioteer's pieces. A tavern uses the bronze knee as a wall. The Sunward Valiants' hiring-house sits under the fallen torso. The Tyrsian ships moor at the outer mole, where their pilots sell charts of waters no Hellenorian has sailed.

Ties: Hellarchon and Ephelanum by the Southern Run.

The Salt Flats Pans south of the city

White on white · pan-workers in veils, carters · brine, heat, nothing growing

Square pans stretch for miles south of the walls, flooded in spring and raked in summer. The glare is worse than the city's, and the workers wear linen veils with slits. Salt goes out by the cart to the harbour and by the shipload to the League. It is the city's real strategic asset, and both blockades were aimed at it.

Ties: House Halikidai owns most pans; salt to Fucostia.

The Evening Terraces Theatre, gymnasion, orchard

Where the city wakes · everyone, after dusk · lamp oil, grilled octopus, almond blossom

The Theatre of Helionyx faces away from the afternoon sun, and its performances begin at dusk. The Gymnasion keeps the sun's hours: exercise at dawn, lectures in the shade at noon, the astronomers' pupils at the arc by evening. Above them rises the Almond Slope, which flowers in midwinter. The sun-priests walk up on the first day of blossom and proclaim the end of the cold, whatever the weather.

Ties: the Ecliptica Arcanum's house; Temple Hill.

Rule

Five prytaneis govern, each for six months, and the senior of them is the city's Archon: Prytanis Philinna Halikis, who has held the senior seat for three terms by an arrangement the council renews without discussion.
