The boule of one hundred and fifty is drawn from shipowners and the salt and dye houses. The assembly meets in the theatre after dusk. Navarch Timokles Aigeides commands eleven warships and a coast patrol.

The College of the Arc, under Gnomonarch Asterope Kleidemou, is the hidden check. No market, court day or assembly can be held on a day the College has not reckoned, and the College can declare a day "unreckoned". It has done so four times in a century, and each time the business in question quietly died. The other checks are the dye guild, which can close the vats; the Golden Scythe Accord, because Helionyx imports its bread; and the Hegemon's fleet, whose squadron calls every month on the Southern Run.

Houses and families

House Halikidai Salt house · Eupatrid

Crest: a white salt-cone on blue · Motto: "Everything keeps in salt" · Seat: the Pan House above the flats

Owners of two-thirds of the pans and the ruling house in all but name. They want the salt price held, the blockades never repeated, and the Phaethontid colossus nonsense kept out of the council.

  • Philinna Halikis, Prytanis, 63. Negotiated the last blockade's end and kept the terms secret.
  • Menekrates Halikos, her brother, salt factor at Fucostia. Speaks better Invictian than Hellenorian.
  • Theron Halikos, her son, a jurist of the Jettison court. Ambitious and bored.

Ties: Fucostia; the Salt Flats.

House Kochlidai Dye house · Eupatrid

Crest: a murex shell, purple on white · Motto: "We do not fade" · Seat: the Purple Hall

Masters of the dye guild for six generations. They grew rich on the Acheaorian court's orders and are now frightened of the Tyrsian ships. They want the harbour closed to foreign purple, which the shipowners will never allow.

  • Eumelos Kochlides, guild master. Smells faintly of his trade at all times and is proud of it.
  • Iole Kochlis, his daughter. Holds the Persemenid contracts and has been to the Court of Vipers twice.

Ties: the Dye-Works; Persemenid.

House Phaethontidai Sun-priest house · Eupatrid

Crest: a four-horse chariot in gold · Motto: "Raise what fell" · Seat: the house on the precinct steps

They have held the Sun-Priest's crown more often than any other family and claim descent from the Charioteer's sculptor. They want the colossus raised, the oracle reinterpreted, and the early almonds read as permission.

  • Hegesias Phaethontides, Sun-Priest of the year. Has hired a Corinthian engineer.
  • Asterope Kleidemou, his great-aunt, Gnomonarch. Half-blind from sixty years of reading shadows, and against the plan.

Ties: Temple Hill; the oracle of Delphara.

Notable figures

  • Hrefna Ironhand Dominus Argentar, Mithril Reserve · dwarf — Buys next season's purple on forward contracts and discounts the debased Invictian silver the Astromancers pay in. Writes to Lady Isolde Merca every new moon.
  • Pelagon keeper of the Stork Roof — No stork has returned this spring. He has told nobody and is leaving offerings.
  • Quintia Caelestina factor of the Celestial Astromancers · Invictian — Pays the gnomonists' pupils for the tables a week before the Reading.
  • Hipponoe housemistress of the Ecliptica Arcanum — Wants the cedar presses copied before "somebody careless" burns them.
  • Magus Tirdad observer from the Fire-Temple of Atarabad — Compares the arc with the Magi's fire-calendar and has found a one-day difference he is too polite to mention.
  • Abdmelqart Tyrsian dye-merchant · Farshore — Sells purple at two-thirds of the Kochlidai price and charts at any price.

Connections

  • Hellarchon — North by the Southern Run. The Hegemon's squadron calls monthly, and every visit is counted.
  • Ephelanum — South on the same run. The Invictian Dux there buys salt for the garrison.
  • Delphara — Its consultation days are reckoned from the arc, and it forbade the colossus.
  • Aeterna — The Celestial Astromancers calibrate the Imperium's calendar here and never say so.
  • Persemenid — The King of Kings' robes are bordered in Helionyx purple; the Court of Vipers issues the permits.
  • Atarabad — The Magi send observers to the Reading of the Arc.
  • Thebesieas — Bread through the Golden Scythe Accord, paid for in salt.

City · Hellenoria · Hellenorian interior

Thebesieas

A squat, walled farm-city on the League's best wet plain, with seven real gates, the only real army in Hellenoria, and a Sacred Band at full strength for the first time since the Treaty.

Codex now: The League's inland military power — agricultural, conservative, and the only Hellenorian city that fields a serious army.

Ruler
Melanthios Sparton, of House Spartidai
Title
Polemarch of Thebesieas (Archon rank)
Population
c. 80,000 (also written Thebeseieas in older lists)
Built on
Seven gates, a citadel with its own spring, and men sown from dragon's teeth
Patron
Hercules the Champion, born here, the city says; Demeter of the furrow; an altar of Ares at the citadel gate, kept up and never thanked
Trouble
An army nobody else wants it to have, armed with iron nobody was allowed to sell it

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Inland, walled and squat. Thebesieas has no harbour and no interest in one, and it is built like a city that expects to be attacked by land: heavy walls, a citadel with its own water, and gates that are real gates rather than ceremonial arches. The country around it is the best farmland in Hellenoria, flat, wet and worked in large holdings, which explains both its wealth and its reputation for being slow. By League standards the city is unadorned, and the other cities never let it forget that.

Grain and horses, in a league that imports both. Thebesieas is the only Hellenorian city that feeds itself, and its surplus supplies the Golden Scythe Accord's allocations. That gives it a stronger position in the Accord than its diplomacy would suggest, and leverage it has historically been too clumsy to use. Its wealth is in land, not trade, so the elite are conservative, cash-poor, land-rich, and increasingly in debt to lenders in Corinth and Hellarchon. Its heavy infantry are the best in Hellenoria and the whole of the city's identity. The citizen phalanx drills to a standard the maritime cities cannot match, and twice in its history it has broken armies that had no business losing. The Sacred Band is the League's most decorated formation. The other cities find all this alarming and say so at the League. Thebesieas replies, accurately, that it has never once used its army offensively outside its own borders.

Life is rural, communal and unfashionable. Thebesieas values land, family and service, distrusts cleverness, and produces almost no philosophy, a fact Thessalonika mentions constantly. The assemblies are dominated by landholders, and politics are stable to the point of stagnation. The tyrants have made no headway here, because there is no disenfranchised urban poor to promise anything to. The Circle of the Eternal Grove is strong in the countryside, and the city defers to it on land as no maritime city would. The festivals are the Muster, when every citizen of military age presents himself and his equipment for public inspection; the Ploughing, when the Polemarch cuts the year's first furrow in the presence of the Circle; and the Naming of the Band, when the Sacred Band's roll is read, living and dead together, and the living answer for the dead.

New lore

Seven gates, seven generals. Each gate has its own ward, and each ward elects a gate-general for one year. Together, the Seven and the Polemarch make up the war council. A gate-general who keeps his command one day past his year is liable to death. The city has twice tried a victorious general under that law and acquitted both, after a very long day.

The Band. The Sacred Band is three hundred men in a hundred and fifty pairs: lovers, brothers or sworn friends. The Band has never asked which. Each pair swears at the tomb of Hercules's shield-bearer outside the Spring Gate, on the principle that no man runs while the one he loves is watching. The war's last decade cost the Band a hundred and twelve men. It took five years to refill the roll, and this spring's Naming read three hundred living names for the first time since the Treaty of Myrianth. Epameinon Kleitarchos commands it.

The Barley Truce. Three hundred and forty years ago, an Acheaorian army marched through the interior under a truce. Thebesieas sold it grain and stood aside. That was the same truce in which the Golden Tripod went up the Sacred Way. In Hellarchon, any Thebesian compromise is still called "barleying", and the Hellarchene envoys brought the word up again at Deiperduem.

What lies underneath. The citadel stands on Mycairan walls. In the war's last years, diggers deepening the citadel cistern broke into a Mycairan hall full of fire-baked clay tablets in the old runes, and the phrase "the gift beneath stone" appears on six of them. The plain itself was drained by Mycairan engineers, and their dikes still carry the water. If they are neglected, the fields go back to marsh within three winters. In the middle of the plain, a limestone island carries a Mycairan fortress called the Hollow Rock. Farmers will not plough within bowshot of it, and the Circle forbids anyone to try.

Districts

The Sown Hill The citadel

Fortress and archive · garrison, keepers, the Seven in council · cold water, oiled bronze, old stone

The Citadel of Thebesieas has walls of its own, a spring that has never failed, and granaries for a year, so that it can hold out after the lower city falls. It keeps the roll of the Sacred Band, a bronze tablet that is re-cut at every Naming. The new arsenal sits behind the council hall, and its storemen are forbidden to discuss what is in it. Below the cistern, the Mycairan hall has been bricked up again.

Ties: House Dirkaidai; the roll; the Pairs' Ground.

The Muster Ground Agora and courts

Market that doubles as parade ground · farmers, factors, magistrates · trampled earth, barley, horse

The Agora of Thebesieas is a parade ground first. At the Muster, every citizen of military age presents himself and his kit here, and inspectors from other wards check his greaves. The magistrates' court stands on the east side. Behind it is the walled Garden of Quiet Death, where the state grows the poisons it uses on the condemned. The Mithril Reserve branch and the Corinthian factors' counting-rooms face the court across the square.

Ties: the Reserve; factors from Corinth.

The Pairs' Ground Gymnasion and Band quarters

Where the phalanx is made · ephebes, drill-masters, the Band · sweat, sand, olive oil

The Gymnasion of Thebesieas is where boys become hoplites, drilled in eight-deep files until they can wheel without looking. The Sacred Band lives here in the long barracks called the Pairs' Hall, two cots to a bay, and is fed at public cost. Old men watch the drill from the colonnade and argue about the oblique advance as other cities' old men argue about philosophy.

Ties: Epameinon Kleitarchos; House Spartidai.

The Temple Ward Sanctuary and theatre

Plain worship · priests, widows, veterans · cold incense, rust, cut grass

The Temple Precinct is plain by League standards, and its dedications are captured arms, some so old that nobody remembers whose they were. Hercules's temple is squat and enormous. The Theatre of Thebesieas was built late and reluctantly, and it is used more for reading the Band's roll than for plays. A visiting Thessalonikan company once performed a comedy here. The audience was polite.

Ties: the Naming of the Band; Thessalonika's scorn.

The Seven Gates Gate wards

Neighbourhood as regiment · tenant farmers, smiths, carters · woodsmoke, dung, bread

Each gate is a ward, a voting district and a file of the phalanx. The Grain Gate faces the barns. The Isthmus Gate opens on the Inland Road to Corinth, and the Horse Gate on the road to Argotiko. The Spring Gate leads to the Band's oath-tomb, the Mothers' Gate to Demeter's fields, and the Hollow Gate looks toward the Rock. The Dead Gate is used only for funerals. Families hold their gate's keys by inheritance and lend them to nobody.

Ties: House Ismenidai holds the Grain Gate; Argotiko.

The Wet Plain Estates, dikes and the Rock

The city's real body · tenants, dike-wardens, druids · black mud, reeds, frogs at dusk

Large estates of barley and wheat sit between straight Mycairan channels, and the dike-wardens are paid by the city and feared by the landholders. The Circle of the Eternal Grove keeps groves at the field corners that no plough may enter. The Hollow Rock rises from the middle of the plain. Its walls are cyclopean, and its gate faces inward.

Ties: the Spartidai estates; the Ploughing.

Rule

Polemarch Melanthios Sparton was elected by the Shield Assembly, in which only men who can afford a full panoply vote, for a term of three years. He is in his second term. He presides over the war council, holds the key to the Garden of Quiet Death as chief magistrate, and cuts the first furrow at the Ploughing. The council sits in four quarters, each serving three months of the year, and a measure becomes law only when all four have passed it. That is slow by design. The Seven gate-generals command the phalanx. Hipparch Philon Kentauridas commands the city's own six hundred horse, landholders' sons who resent hiring the Argotiko squadrons.

The checks are the death-law, the four-quarter council, the Muster (citizens inspecting each other, which no faction can fix), the Circle of the Eternal Grove on any question of land, and the creditors in Corinth and Hellarchon, who check everything else.

Houses and families

House Spartidai The Sown · Eupatrid

Crest: a dragon's tooth sprouting a spear · Motto: "We came up out of this ground" · Seat: the Old Tower by the Mothers' Gate

The house claims descent from the warriors who sprang from the dragon's teeth. It is the largest landholder on the plain, the leader of the war party, and heavily mortgaged.

  • Melanthios Sparton, Polemarch, 58. Believes the Hegemon will move on the inland cities within five years.
  • Kleonike Spartis, his wife. Runs the estates and keeps the debt ledgers, and knows exactly what the iron cost.
  • Chthonios Spartides, their son, 24, of the Sacred Band. Quiet since his pair-partner was crippled in drill.

Ties: the Wet Plain; lenders in Corinth.

House Ismenidai Grain sellers · Eupatrid

Crest: a river reed · Motto: "Bread before bronze" · Seat: the Reed House, Grain Gate

The house sells the city's surplus and holds its seat in the Golden Scythe Accord. It leads the faction that wants half the phalanx stood down and the debts paid off instead. The Spartidai call them barleyers.

  • Hippolochos Ismenias, gate-general of the Grain Gate. Dines with Hellarchon's proxenos more often than he admits.
  • Myrto Ismenis, his sister, delegate to the Accord. Sells grain privately to the tyrant of Atticenea.

Ties: Atticenea; Hellarchon.

House Dirkaidai Keepers of the spring · Eupatrid

Crest: a spring beneath a shield · Motto: "The hill drinks last" · Seat: the Spring House, Sown Hill

Hereditary keepers of the citadel spring and the Band's roll, and the city's delegates to the Amphictyony. They are poorer than the Spartidai and older than anyone, and whoever leads the city has to court them.

  • Agathon Dirkaios, Keeper of the Spring and the Roll. Reads the names at the Naming without notes.
  • Antiope Dirkaia, his niece, hieromnemon at Delphara. Will vote that a tyrant's delegate is no delegate.

Ties: Delphara; the Sown Hill.

Notable figures

  • Epameinon Kleitarchos Lochagos of the Sacred Band — A smallholder's son from the Mothers' Gate, poor and unmarried. Swore the Band would never march for conquest. He knows where the iron came from and objects to the lie, not the iron.
  • Bergthor Ironhand Dominus Argentar, Mithril Reserve · dwarf — Holds mortgages on a third of the plain's great estates. Lady Isolde Merca's last letter asked how many harvests Thebesieas has already sold.
  • Archias the Weigher Corinthian factor — Weighs grain for a living, and other things for a better one.
  • Sosipatros keeper of the Garden of Quiet Death — A gentle old man with gloved hands. Answers any question, offers nothing, and has never lied.
  • Kallirhoe Thesmia elder of the Circle of the Eternal Grove — Speaks at the Ploughing, and has warned the council about "the channels" three times this year.
  • Lykophron Ktesiou Hellarchon's proxenos — Counts spearheads at the Muster for the Hegemon's office.
  • Dexippe of the Porticoes Thessalonikan scholar — Has been trying for two years to buy rubbings of the Mycairan tablets.

Connections

  • Corinth — Down the Inland Road to the isthmus: lenders, factors, and the quay where the iron lands.
  • Mavelon — The Imperium's arsenal port. Its iron goes out by sea to Corinth against Invictian export law (the Mavelon Contract).
  • Argotiko — A day's ride on the Inland Road. Thebesieas has the infantry and Argotiko has the horse, and neither will serve under the other.
  • Hellarchon — The naval hegemon, and a creditor that dislikes the Band.
  • Delphara — The treasury of captured shields on the Sacred Way, and a council seat.
  • Persemenid — The Barley Truce, which the Hellarchenes never let anyone forget.
  • Thessalonika — Mockery, and a scholar who wants the Mycairan tablets.

The towns

Town · Hellenoria · western coast

Carianea

A town of sponge divers and shipwrights, old at forty, where the widows own the property and a returned trierarch now owns the harbour.

Codex now: A Hellenorian coastal town of sponge divers and shipwrights — hard work, short lives, and the best small hulls in the League.

Ruler
Mnasilochos son of Pyrrhias
Title
Tyrannos (seized power two years ago)
Population
c. 4,500
Built on
A small harbour, a beach of boat sheds, and racks of drying sponges
Patron
Poseidon of the harbour mouth; the Nereids, placated
Trouble
The League wants its crews; the tyrant has stopped sending them

A harbour too small for anything large, boat sheds along the shore, and drying racks of sponges that give the town its smell: low tide, salt, and something like bread gone wrong. Carianean sponges are the League's finest, and the divers who take them are why the town's men are old at forty. A diver goes down naked on a breath, holding a flat stone to sink him and a knife on a cord, to forty fathoms at the best beds; he comes up with a net of sponges, bleeding from the ears in his first season and deaf in one by his tenth. The yards build small: fishing hulls, coasters and the fast light craft the Sunward Valiants favour. Nothing here can build a trireme, and the town has never wanted to.

Carianea has crewed the League fleet for centuries, which is its entire contribution and its entire claim, and it resents that the ships sit at Hellarchon and the crews are drawn from places like this. Half the smaller ports share the grievance, and since the peace they have started writing to each other about it. Diving families intermarry, and the loss rate means widows hold more property here than anywhere in the League; the Widows' Council, which meets under the protection of the Matriarch's Loom of Bonds, owns most of the racks, the sheds and the houses, and has run the town in everything but name for three generations. Its pilots are among the few who will enter Nereid's Veil, a day's sail west, and they charge accordingly.

The year turns on three days. The First Descent: the diving season opens with a rite at the harbour mouth, and the first sponge of the year is dedicated, not sold. The Counting: at the season's end, divers who came back are counted aloud, and so are those who did not; last year it was eleven. The Launching: every hull finished that year is put in the water on the same morning.

Two years ago Mnasilochos son of Pyrrhias came home from the League fleet with forty oarsmen whose pay was eighteen months in arrears, took the harbour mole one night, and stopped the levy. Nobody died. The demarch went to his sister's in the hills and stayed there. The widows' council tolerates the tyrant because he keeps their sons at home, and he tolerates the council because it owns everything he would need to tax. Hellarchon has written three times; the third letter was nailed to the mole.

Quarters

The Sponge Racks Harbour

Salt and rot · divers, sorters, the tyrant's oarsmen · drying sponge, low tide, tar

Divers, drying racks and the tyrant's forty oarsmen on the mole. Sponges are beaten, trodden, rinsed and dried on racks in tiers down to the water, sorted by the widows' girls into seven grades, and sold to Corinthian buyers who arrive with the first south wind. The forty live in the old customs house at the mole's end and fish when they are not guarding anything.

Ties: House Kymothoidai; Corinth's buyers.

The Widows' Terraces Upper town

Whitewashed and watchful · widows, daughters, old divers · bread, basil, lime-wash

Where the property-holding widows meet, under the Matriarch's Loom of Bonds: a long white house with a loom on which a thread is woven for every diving family and cut for every death. Marriages are arranged here, debts are settled here, and the council's decision on whether a boy may dive is final.

Ties: the Matriarch's Loom of Bonds; House Kymothoidai.

The Boat Sheds Shipyards · the beach

Busy and sawdusted · shipwrights, caulkers, apprentices · pine resin, wet oak, pitch

The beach east of the harbour, lined with open sheds where a hull goes from keel to launch in a season. The yards build to the eye from patterns kept in no book, and a Carianean coaster is known anywhere by its rising stern. Sunward Valiants officers come here to order dispatch boats, and pay in advance.

Ties: House Naupegidai; the Sunward Valiants.

Families

House Kymothoidai Diving family · the widows' house

Crest: a sponge and a knife on a cord · Motto: "One breath." · Seat: the head of the Widows' Terraces

The oldest diving family and the richest in racks, with more widows than any other. They have produced the council's eldest for four generations and lost a man at every Counting for longer than anyone can remember.

  • Kallirhoe Kymothois, eldest of the Widows' Council, 63 — buried a husband and three sons; keeps the Loom and the ledgers, and decides who may dive.
  • Glaukos Kymothoides, her last son, 26 — the best diver on the coast, forbidden by his mother to go below twenty fathoms; goes to forty.
House Naupegidai Shipwrights

Crest: an adze over a rising stern · Motto: "Built to come back." · Seat: the largest shed on the beach

Master shipwrights for six generations, and Mnasilochos's mother's people; the house sheltered him the night he took the harbour and has done well from the Valiants' orders since.

  • Pyrrhias Naupegides, master of the sheds, 58 — the tyrant's uncle, not his father; builds without drawings and has trained half the coast.
  • Eirene Naupegis, his daughter — the town's best pilot into Nereid's Veil, and the only woman in the yards.

Notable figures

  • Mnasilochos son of Pyrrhias Tyrannos · former trierarch's mate — keeps forty oarsmen, the harbour and the levy; wants recognition from the League, or failing that from someone with money.
  • Kallirhoe Kymothois eldest of the Widows' Council — tolerates the tyrant exactly as long as no son of hers is levied.
  • Eirene Naupegis pilot of Nereid's Veil — will take anyone into the fog for a price, and brings back most of them.
  • Sotades sponge-buyer from Corinth — buys the whole season every year, pays well, and delivers a sealed letter to the tyrant with each payment.
  • Thrasyllos captain of the forty — eighteen months unpaid in the fleet and two years paid in fish here; thinks the arrangement fair, for now.

Town · Hellenoria · inland hills

Araavyna

A hill town of kilns whose clay is held in common, whose glazes are family secrets, and whose lawsuits are the main entertainment.

Codex now: A Hellenorian hill town of potters — the League's everyday tableware comes from here, and so does its best painted ware.

Ruler
Theodosia Pelopidou
Title
Demarch, elected by the workshops
Population
c. 6,000
Built on
Common clay beds, a terraced hillside, and kiln smoke
Patron
Hephaestus of the kiln; Athena of the potter's wheel
Trouble
A huge order of heavy jars nobody will explain

Kilns. Araavyna is built above good clay beds, and the hillside is terraced with workshops, drying yards and firing kilns whose smoke hangs over the town most of the year; visitors smell it a mile off and leave with it in their cloaks. The bulk trade is amphorae and plain ware shipped through Corinth, and the oil town of Atticenea buys its jars nowhere else; the prestige trade is painted work signed by named hands and collected across three empires, where a cup by a famous painter costs more than the house it was made in.

The clay is the whole basis, and the beds are held communally, dug by allotment and guarded by everyone, which has kept any one family from dominating and kept the town argumentative. Status is craft status: a painter who develops a recognisable hand becomes a public figure, and is followed through the market by apprentices. Workshops take apprentices at eight and guard techniques jealously; glaze recipes are family property, and lawsuits over them, heard in the open before the whole town, are the main entertainment. A good suit draws more people than a festival. The demarch is elected by the workshops, one vote per kiln.

A wall and a militia that drills without enthusiasm. Araavyna's defence has always been that it is inland, poor in coin and awkward to reach. It sends neither ships nor cavalry to the League and is criticised for it, which the potters answer by pointing out who makes the jars an army marches on. Festivals: the Firing, the year's great communal kiln, loaded by every workshop and opened in public, with losses borne in common; the Signing, when new painters may sign their work for the first time; and the Breaking, when flawed prestige pieces are smashed in public rather than sold. The pile is enormous and the practice fiercely defended.

Since the peace, orders have doubled. This spring a Corinthian banker ordered four thousand double-walled jars "for oil", paid half in advance in good silver, and asked that they be marked with Atticenea's oil stamp. The workshops are delighted, the clay beds are being dug faster than the allotment allows, and Theodosia Pelopidou has started asking why oil needs a double wall.

Quarters

The Clay Beds Common ground

Red and wet · diggers, allotment-wardens, children · wet earth, crushed thyme

Dug by allotment and guarded by everyone. Each kiln draws a lot at the new year for its share of the face; the wardens mark it with painted stakes, and moving a stake is the one crime the town punishes with exile. This year's double-walled order has the beds dug past their marks for the first time in living memory.

Ties: House Pelopidai.

The Kiln Terraces Workshops · drying yards · the communal kiln

Hot and secretive · potters, painters, apprentices · smoke, slip, hot iron oxide

Terrace after terrace of workshops, each with its wheel-room, painting-room and kiln, and walls high enough that no rival can see a glaze being mixed. The communal kiln stands at the top, a dome the size of a temple, opened at the Firing before the whole town. The court of suits sits on the terrace below it on market days.

Ties: House Euthymidai; House Pelopidai.

The Breaking Ground The pile

Crunching underfoot · sherd-sellers, collectors, thieves · dust, broken glaze

An enormous heap of smashed masterpieces, sold off by the basket to Hellarchon's Clay Gate as sherds. Collectors pay boys to search it for pieces of famous hands, and a forger in Corinth is said to glue them back together.

Ties: Hellarchon's Clay Gate.

Families

House Pelopidai Plain-ware potters · the demarch's house

Crest: an amphora with two handles · Motto: "Every jar counts." · Seat: the biggest workshop on the lower terrace

Amphora-makers with eleven kilns, the most in town, and a reputation for honest weight and dull pots. They elect the demarch more often than not because they employ more voters than anyone.

  • Theodosia Pelopidou, Demarch, 49 — throws a perfect amphora in the time it takes to describe one; took the Corinthian order and now regrets asking questions.
  • Lykos Pelopides, her son — negotiated the order, has been to Corinth twice this year, and came back with a new cloak.
House Euthymidai Painters · prestige ware

Crest: a painted cup · Motto: "As never the others." · Seat: the walled workshop on the top terrace

The town's most famous painters, whose great-grandfather signed a cup "as never my rival could" and started a suit that lasted forty years. They own the black glaze recipe the League calls Araavynan, and have been in court about it for three generations.

  • Euthymides the Younger, head, 55 — his cups sell in Persemenid; he has not painted one in two years, and nobody knows why.
  • Korinna Euthymis, his niece, 22 — signs this year at the Signing, and paints better than her uncle ever did.

Notable figures

  • Theodosia Pelopidou Demarch — wants the order filled, the beds respected, and an answer about the double walls.
  • Damon Euphranorides Corinthian banker, of House Euphranoridai — placed the order "for oil", pays on time, and visits the kilns more often than a banker should.
  • Euthymides the Younger master painter — has stopped painting; his hand is losing its shake, not gaining one.
  • Antiope advocate of the court of suits — has argued every glaze suit for twenty years on one side or the other, sometimes both.

Town · Hellenoria · hot-spring hills

Loutrokleion

A spa town on hot springs, neutral by a convention no tyrant has tested, where the League's quietest business is done in the middle pools.

Codex now: A Hellenorian spa town built on hot springs — a place of cures, consultations, and conversations that could not be had at home.

Ruler
Sostrate Iamenou
Title
Demarch, a physician chosen by the Physicians' Assembly
Population
c. 3,000 residents; as many patients again in season
Built on
Seven hot springs and an unwritten truce
Patron
Apollo the Healer and Asclepius; the nymphs of the springs
Trouble
A tyrant has booked a six-week cure

Colonnaded bath-houses over natural hot springs, steam standing over the roofs in cold weather, and a town of lodgings arranged around them in strict order of price: the dearest nearest the springs, the cheapest at the bottom of the valley where the water arrives lukewarm. Loutrokleion sells baths, treatment, lodging and diet to the sick and the merely wealthy, and has done so long enough to have a specialist trade in every complaint: the sulphur spring for skin, the iron spring for blood, the warm pool for joints, and the hot spring, which nobody can bear for long, for "conditions of the spirit". The Radiant Heartwardens and the Healer's Sanctuary send patients, and its physicians are good, expensive and unusually well documented: every case is written up and filed in the Physicians' Hall.

It has a watch and a convention of neutrality older than the war: the sick of every city come here, and even during the war it was not attacked. The convention is unwritten and has never been tested by a tyrant. Patients stay for weeks, which makes the town's social life unlike anywhere else in Hellenoria: leisured, mixed by origin, and organised around the bathing schedule. It is consequently a superb place to meet someone quietly, and a great deal of League business is done in the middle pools, where nobody carries a weapon or a tablet, and nobody is admitted with either.

Festivals: the Clearing of the Springs, when the pools are drained, scoured and refilled and the town is briefly and unpleasantly ordinary; the Physicians' Assembly, at which cases are presented and argued and reputations made and destroyed; and the Grateful, when dedications from the cured, clay legs, bronze eyes, tablets of thanks, are hung in the colonnade. There are thousands, and they are read.

Mnasilochos of Carianea has booked a six-week cure in the best lodging, for himself and twelve companions. The Hegemon's harbour-master has booked the same weeks. The Demarch has booked nothing, and has asked the watch to count weapons at the gate.

Quarters

The Middle Pools Baths

Steaming and discreet · patients, attendants, envoys · sulphur, oil, wet marble

Where League business is done wet and unrecorded. Three linked pools at blood heat under a vaulted roof, with niches along the walls where two men can talk without being heard over the water. Bathers enter naked through a changing-room where the attendants take everything; the rule is older than the war and is the convention's only written part.

Ties: House Hydriadai.

The Colonnade of the Grateful Shrine walk

Pious and crowded · pilgrims, priests, readers · incense, clay dust

Thousands of thank-offerings, read aloud each year. The colonnade runs from the Physicians' Hall to the shrine of Asclepius, and the older offerings are moved into storerooms to make space; some date from before the Continental War.

Ties: House Iamidai; the Radiant Heartwardens.

The Lodging Terraces Inns · diet-kitchens · the lower valley

Graded by price · innkeepers, cooks, servants · barley gruel, mint, wood smoke

From the colonnaded guest-houses beside the springs to the dormitories in the valley bottom, every bed is graded and priced on a board at the town gate. The diet-kitchens cook to the physicians' orders, and a patient's menu tells the town how ill, and how rich, he is.

Ties: House Hydriadai.

Families

House Iamidai Physicians · the Demarch's house

Crest: a serpent on a staff over a spring · Motto: "Write it down." · Seat: the Physicians' Hall

A physicians' dynasty that has supplied a third of the town's demarchs and kept its case archive for two centuries.

  • Sostrate Iamenou, Demarch, 56 — the best diagnostician in the League; keeps a ledger of who met whom in the pools.
  • Iamos Iamenou, her son — a surgeon; trained among the Radiant Heartwardens in the Imperium, and came back with opinions.
House Hydriadai Bath-lessees · innkeepers

Crest: a water-jar pouring · Motto: "Hot, and quiet." · Seat: the guest-house by the first spring

The family that leases the bath-houses from the town and owns the best lodgings. Their attendants staff the changing-rooms, which means they hold every weapon and every tablet that enters the middle pools.

  • Kleoboulos Hydriades, head, 61 — has never been inside the middle pools, and knows everything said there.
  • Myrto Hydrias, his granddaughter — chief attendant of the changing-rooms; has been offered a great deal for one tablet.

Notable figures

  • Sostrate Iamenou Demarch · physician — wants the convention kept and the tyrant cured and gone, in that order.
  • Mnasilochos of Carianea Tyrannos, patient — says his lungs are bad from the oar; has come to be seen talking to someone.
  • Glaukos Timonos harbour-master of Hellarchon's Emporion, patient — has booked the same six weeks, "for his liver".
  • Myrto Hydrias chief attendant — holds the weapons, the tablets and the secrets, and is underpaid for all three.

Town · Hellenoria · the Argotiko horse plain

Argotiko

A sprawl of paddocks and wide streets on the inland plain, where the League's only real cavalry is bred, registered and rented out, and where the town still enjoys reminding the sailors.

Codex now: A Hellenorian horse town on the inland plain — the League's cavalry comes from here, and it never lets the sailors forget it.

Governor
Demarch Androkles Xanthippides
Population
c. 6,000 people; more horses
Trouble
The sacred bloodline registry is not what it claims to be

Argotiko is low and spread out, with more stabling than housing and streets wide enough to ride four abreast, because people ride them that way. It breeds, trains and sells horses, and has kept a bloodline registry for four centuries that it treats as sacred. Buyers come from all three empires: Acheaorian remount officers, agents of Invictian legates, and Thebesian landholders' sons. That makes Argotiko cosmopolitan for an inland town and rich for one without a port. Its leading families hire out cavalry squadrons, not an army. The town's relationship with Thebesieas is close and slightly resentful, and neither will serve under the other. Standing here is measured in bloodlines, disputes are settled by racing, and children are put on horses before they can properly walk. Every breeder carries a seal-jasper carved with his line's mount. The festivals are the Running, three days of races that update the registry and are then disputed for months; the Judging of Foals; and the Riding of the Bounds.

The Demarch is chosen by race. In every fourth year, the family whose rider wins the Long Course names him. Androkles Xanthippides won the post through his granddaughter Kallisto's mare and governs mostly by deciding which disputes are worth a race.

Quarters

The Registry and the Course Civic heart

Pedigrees and racing · registrars, jockeys, gamblers · ink, liniment, dust

The Registry Hall holds four centuries of bloodlines, in ledgers chained to lecterns. Beside it, the oval Course is used for the Running and for settling lawsuits.

Ties: runners at Delphara's Games.

Buyers' Street Inns and paddocks

Foreign money · factors from three empires · hay, roast lamb, Acheaorian tea

Inns for foreign buyers back onto the sale paddocks. Hoopoes forage the garden terraces behind them. An Acheaorian and an Invictian buyer once bid against each other for three hours, and the auctioneer retired on his share.

Ties: Persemenid; Aeterna.

Notable figures

  • Androkles Xanthippides Demarch — Wants the Thebesian Hipparch to hire his squadrons on equal terms, or not at all.
  • Eupraxia the Registrar Keeper of the Book of Dams — The only person who has read the oldest ledger. Has stopped sleeping well.

Town · Hellenoria · the olive hills

Atticenea

A poor white town above ancient olive terraces that exports oil and philosophers. For three years it has been ruled by a tyrant who pays its teachers.

Codex now: A Hellenorian olive town on thin soil — poor in everything but oil, and exporting philosophers because it cannot feed them.

Governor
Aristeas Kotinos, "the Oil-Lender"
Title
Tyrannos (in place of a Demarch)
Population
c. 5,000
Trouble
A tyrant's seat at Delphara, and grain bought round the Accord

Grey-green olive terraces climb stony ground to a small white town, and the soil is visibly bad while the trees are visibly ancient. The ground will not carry grain, so Atticenea makes oil and nothing else, pressing it into amphorae bought from Araavyna. The oil pays for the grain, until shipping stops. The town musters a few dozen men and relies on the League, which it finds humiliating. Its leverage is reputation: an unusual number of the League's magistrates, teachers and envoys were born here, and Atticenea calls in favours shamelessly. It is argumentative, literate and poor, producing more educated men than it can employ, and the surplus leave for Thessalonika and the academies. The schools are excellent and the buildings are falling down. The festivals are the Pressing, whose grade sets the year's prices; the Leaving, when the whole town walks its students to the road; and the Old Tree, the ceremony for an olive so old it has its own guardian family.

The tyrant. In the second winter of peace the grain ships failed. Aristeas Kotinos, the largest press-owner, fed the town from his own credit. The assembly voted him a guard of fifty club-bearers and never got them back. He lends seed money to smallholders, pays teachers' salaries for the first time in a century, and exiles anyone who writes against him. Through his delegate, he holds Atticenea's seat on the Amphictyony, one of the two tyrant seats that paralyse it.

Quarters

The Press Quarter Lower town

Oil and debt · pressmen, carters, club-bearers · crushed olive, lamp smoke

The beam-presses and amphora yards, with the tyrant's own press-house in the middle and his club-bearers at its door.

Ties: Araavyna's potters.

The School Steps Upper town

Argument as industry · teachers, students · dust, cicadas, cheap wine

Schools in cracked porticoes along a stair to the Old Tree's terrace, loud with Tree-Singer cicadas all summer.

Ties: Thessalonika's Porticoes.

Notable figures

  • Aristeas Kotinos tyrannos — Wants legitimacy, meaning a vote at Delphara declaring his delegate a delegate.
  • Charmion of the Old Tree guardian of the oldest olive — Refused the tyrant's gift of a new terrace wall, publicly.

Town · Hellenoria · the high mountains

Kirimitsana

A dozen cold hamlets on one mountain, counted together for tax and never quite taxed, whose dark honey and unwritten herb-lore supply half the League's remedies.

Codex now: A Hellenorian mountain town of beekeepers and herbalists — remote, medicinal, and the source of half the League's remedies.

Governor
Demarch Panaretos Kerinos (on paper); the Grandmothers of the Dozen (in practice)
Population
c. 3,000 across twelve hamlets
Trouble
The Luminastra want the knowledge, and the honey has a darker use

Kirimitsana is high, cold and scattered: less a town than a dozen hamlets on one mountain, joined by paths and counted together for tax. Its honey and herbs come from the mountain's thyme, which gives a dark, medicinal, expensive honey. The same slopes supply wild ingredients that the Luminastra Alchemists buy in bulk. Families gather by season, at some risk, and guard their gathering grounds as property, though nothing is written down. The town has no defences and needs none. An armed party can reach Kirimitsana, but not quickly, and not without being watched all the way. The town has never been taxed to its full assessment and considers that a tradition rather than an offence. Lowlanders find the place uneasy: the dialect is difficult, and the rites, to the Titan Melisseus of the bees, are older than the League's. The herb-lore is deep, unwritten and passed down within families, and the Luminastra have spent two centuries failing to buy it. The festivals are the Smoking, when the hives are worked together; the Gathering Days, set by the oldest women of each hamlet and obeyed absolutely; and the Winter Door, the night the paths shut until spring.

Who rules. Demarch Panaretos Kerinos is the name on the League's lists. His real duty is to be politely absent when the assessor comes. The twelve Grandmothers decide everything that matters.

Quarters

The Beekeepers' Hall Upper hamlet

Hives in a long row · beekeepers, Grandmothers · wax, smoke, thyme

The one stone hall on the mountain, where the honey is graded at the Smoking and the Grandmothers sit in council.

Ties: the Herbalists' Lodge at Delphara.

The Plane Wells Lower hamlets

Where outsiders are received · traders, Luminastra factors · cold water, drying herbs

Ancient plane trees shade the wells where lowland buyers are received politely and not encouraged to stay.

Ties: Luminastra factors.

Notable figures

  • Grandmother Thymo eldest of the Dozen — Sets the Gathering Days, and once sent her niece Myrrhine to keep the Lodge at Delphara.
  • Kleitos Pharmakeus Luminastra factor — Has lived at the wells for nine years and still has not been told a single recipe.

Part IV · The east

Acheaoria

The plateau empire of the King of Kings. Persemenid first, then the four great satrapal cities, then the qanat towns and the island villages.

The capital

Capital · Acheaoria · Acheaorian plateau

Persemenid City

The seat of the King of Kings: a stone terrace of columned halls above a mud-brick garden town, built so the whole empire climbs to it bearing gifts, and slowly learning that it no longer has to.

Codex now: Seat of the King of Kings — a terraced palace-city of columned halls and tribute processions, magnificent, ceremonial, and increasingly ignored by its own provinces.

Ruler
Shahanshah Vishtaspa III, "the Magnificent", of the House of Zindar
Title
Shahanshah, King of Kings; the town below the terrace and its home satrapy are held by Satrap Prince Tiridat
Population
c. 150,000 with the court, perhaps 30,000 of them in its pay
Built on
A terrace cut from the mountain's foot, a stair of all peoples, and a walled paradise
Patron
The undying fire of the Magi; Hajama for the throne's valour, Zann for its rolls
Trouble
Tribute that no longer climbs the stair, and a court spending what it has not collected

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

A platform cut into the rock of the plateau, forty feet above the plain, and on it a city of halls. Persemenid is approached by a stair wide enough for ten horsemen to ride up abreast, and it is meant to be climbed slowly. The columned audience hall on the terrace is the largest roofed space on the continent. Along the stair runs a relief of tribute-bearers, every subject people in procession, each in its own dress, each carrying what it owes, so that a visitor climbs alongside the entire empire bringing gifts.

Below the platform lies an ordinary Acheaorian town of mud-brick, gardens and water channels, watered by the Zheret-al-Nur and by the qanats. Above it, nothing is ordinary and nothing is accidental.

Persemenid consumes tribute and produces ceremony. It is not a market city; the great trading is done at Atarabad, and what arrives here arrives as obligation. That obligation is failing. The ledgers of the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger carry a lengthening column of provinces marked "not presented", and the court spends against expected collection rather than collection. The Vaults of Equilibrium lend against the shortfall at rates the Mithril Reserve will not match, which keeps the halls gilded and makes the arithmetic worse each year.

The Ten Thousand hold the platform and have, by their own count, never been fewer. Their first regiment quarters inside the precinct and is drawn from the old nobility, which makes it a guard and a hostage-house at once. Field strength is another matter. The heavy cavalry of the Lion's Mane Vanguard is raised and paid by the satraps, two of whom have quietly grown their squadrons past the permitted establishment. The Ironclad Oath swears to the throne directly and is the one force the court can rely on, and its oath forbids war on the empire's own subjects, which is most of what the court currently needs done.

Access is the whole currency: who may approach, how closely, and whether one may speak or must be spoken for. The household staff run the palace and rather more than the palace. The Magi hold the calendar and the rites, and remain the one check on the throne that has never been removed. Life below the terrace is comfortable: gardens, running water, ice in summer, and a court economy that employs thousands. Nobody down there speaks about the platform casually.

The year turns on four rites. The Bringing opens it: every satrapy that still acknowledges the throne sends a delegation up the stair in the order the relief shows, and the absences are the empire's real annual audit. The Royal Hunt follows in the Paradise, where the King of Kings kills a lion before the court under arrangements everyone understands and nobody mentions. The Fire Watch is the Magi's rite, signalled from temple to temple along the hilltop chain; it is sacred, unsupervised, and increasingly used for other messages. The Naming of the Rolls counts the guard aloud at full strength. It is always at full strength.

New lore

Twenty-three peoples walk the relief. At the last Bringing, sixteen climbed the stair. Three sent gifts by courier, which protocol counts as present and everyone else counts as absent; four sent nothing at all. The hazarapat had the empty panels hung with cloth of gold "to honour delegations delayed upon the roads", and the cloth is now the most discussed object in the empire. House Karin, hereditary Masters of the Stair, walked the procession with the gaps left open, as the old protocol requires. Nobody has thanked them.

Five years into what Acheaorians call the Peace of the Signing, the court's own chroniclers write of "a decade of peace". The Sandglass Circle counts the war's last years as peace on the grounds that the King of Kings had already decided to grant it. Outside the court, the arithmetic is simpler: the Peace is five years old, the tribute is smaller each year, and the King of Kings is sixty-one. The lion at the last Royal Hunt was older, and slower, and the Ten Thousand's spearman stood closer than usual.

Succession is the real business of the Inner House. Crown Prince Ariaramna is careful, well-read and unloved; his younger brother Prince Tiridat, Satrap of the Throne Plain, is popular below the terrace and keeps a household that grows every season. Princess Roshanak, the King's youngest daughter, lives at Deiperduem as the empire's Treaty Guest in the Hellenorian compound; her letters come up the Royal Road in nine days and are opened twice before her guardian, Lady Andia, reads them.

The court still pays. Four reigns ago a King of Kings dedicated a golden tripod at Delphara, and the Acheaorian treasury on the Sacred Way is the richest of them all; its "lamp-oil", a yearly sum, still leaves the Treasury of Hours on schedule, though it is now borrowed from the Vaults to send. The Treasury's keeper resigned last spring and will not say why. The westernmost channel of the Paradise has been failing for two years, and the dying trees on that side are cut at night by order.

Rumours below the terrace: that the ground under the platform rings hollow when the Ten Thousand drill in step; that a well-digger in the garden town brought up a brick stamped with a king nobody can name, and was paid to forget it; that Archivist Hashmet, executed for treason on the second day of Peaceful in the first year of the Peace, was not the only clerk who saw what he saw.

Districts

The Royal Stair and the Gate of All Peoples Ceremonial approach

Processional · delegations, guards, guides for hire · dust, horse, cold stone

A double flight of shallow steps, each low enough for a horse in procession, climbing forty feet beside the tribute relief. At the top stands the Gate of All Peoples: four columns, two pairs of winged bull-guardians with bearded human faces, and an inscription in the empire's scripts claiming every road for the King of Kings. Delegations wait at the foot in the order the relief gives them. Children of the garden town sell water and corrections; a good guide can tell you which carved people you are standing beside and whether they came this year.

Ties: House Karin keeps the order of approach; the Caravanserai in the Quarter of Tongues lodges delegations before the Bringing.

The Terrace of Columns Throne halls

Court · courtiers, petitioners, the first regiment · cedar, incense, polished limestone

The Audience Hall stands on its own raised floor, the largest roofed space on the continent, its roof carried on columns crowned with paired bull-heads; beside it the Hall of a Hundred Columns holds the throne-room proper, where satraps kneel and envoys are seated by rank. Here the King of Kings receives, and here nothing is accidental, from the height of the step to the hour of the light. The first regiment of the Ten Thousand quarters along the terrace's north edge, noble sons on guard duty and in quiet custody at once.

Ties: the hazarapat's house commands the gate-guard; petitions pass the Inner House first.

The Inner House Palace and treasury

Household · eunuchs, women of the royal house, scribes · rosewater, lamp-smoke, whispers

Behind the halls, the residence: courts within courts, the women's apartments, the eunuchs' offices, and the corridors where the Court of Vipers does its work. Beneath it lies the Treasury of Hours, a columned vault whose pillars are carved with the hours of the day and whose doors open only at the hour the king chooses. It holds the tribute in bullion, ingots of orichalcum, white platinum no smith in the empire can melt, a single plate of adamantium older than the dynasty, and a room the keepers do not enter after dark. Visitors see the great door and nothing else.

Ties: House Spandiyad keeps the Treasury; the royal House of Zindar lives here.

The Hill of Fires Citadel, temples and royal tombs

Sacred and fortified · Magi, garrison, tomb-wardens · ash, juniper, wind

The mountain behind the terrace carries the old citadel, the royal tombs cut high in the cliff face, and a chain of fire-temples along its spine, from which the Magi mark the Fire Watch. The chief of them, the Fire-Temple of Persemenid, is heavy and plain, its sacred flame visible through a screen and never allowed to die; the oldest, the Temple of Breath, burns on a draught that rises from the rock itself. Outside the walls, on the north spur, stand the Silent Towers, where the dead are laid out for the birds so that they do not defile earth or fire.

Ties: Magus Rashnu-Vahram keeps rooms below the Temple of Breath; signals run to Atarabad's fire.

The Bazaar of Persemenid Existing · roofed market and the Square

Trade · guildsmen, court buyers, porters · cassia, copper, hot bread

An Acheaorian bazaar is a district, not a square: roofed lanes laid out by trade, coppersmiths in one, spice-sellers in another, each lane with its own gate, warden and guild. Prices are bargained, never posted, and a stranger is expected to fail at it. Persemenid's bazaar lies in the town below the platform and supplies the court above; it is the only door through which cassia enters the continent. At its western mouth opens the Square, a long dusty ground for polo, executions and proclamations, in that order of popularity.

Ties: House Nahid'zar buys for the court here; the Vaults of Equilibrium keep a temple-bank off the Square.

The Garden Town Lower city

Residential · clerks, cooks, grooms, gardeners · wet clay, mint, cut grass

Mud-brick houses turned inward around courtyard pools, streets shaded by plane trees, and water in every gutter. The Water-Court of Persemenid is here, a cool vaulted chamber where the qanat surfaces and its flow is divided into shares, each measured by a timed bowl and owned by deed; it feeds both the town and the Paradise. Beside it stand the ice-houses, domed pits where winter ice is stored to chill the court's sherbet in high summer, and the great cisterns that would carry the town through a siege of eighty days.

Ties: the Bountiful Harvesters hold the shares (water); House Nahid'zar holds the ice.

The Quarter of Tongues Foreign merchants' quarter

Mixed · envoys, factors, interpreters, the Reserve's dwarves · tallow, ink, strange cooking

Where the Royal Road enters the town, the royal Caravanserai receives every delegation before the Bringing: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Around it has grown a district of interpreters, factors and foreigners. Invictian traders keep a chapel to Mercury behind a cloth merchant's; Hellenorians argue in a wine-shop that pretends not to be one; steppe horse-dealers camp in the yards. The stone branch of the Mithril Reserve stands here, windowless, the most trusted building in the city and the least loved.

Ties: the Treaty Road to Deiperduem; the Mithril Reserve (banking).

The Paradise of Persemenid Royal hunting garden

Walled wilderness · wardens, huntsmen, royal grooms · cedar, dung, standing water

A wall of fired brick eleven miles around enclosing watered woodland in a country that has none: cedar, plane and fruit trees in ranks, streams led from three qanat channels, and deer, boar, onager and lion kept at numbers the land could never support. The royal stud of heavenly horses grazes its eastern meadows. Here the King of Kings hunts before the court once a year. The beasts are driven, the ground is chosen, and a man of the Ten Thousand stands within a spear's throw throughout. Every satrap keeps a lesser paradise; the size of a man's garden is understood to be the size of his claim.

Ties: the Predator's Guild culls the surplus; House Mihran keeps its horses beside the eastern wall.

Rule

In theory, everything belongs to the King of Kings. In practice Shahanshah Vishtaspa III rules the terrace, the ceremony and the appointments, and the empire increasingly arranges itself around him rather than under him. His chief of the court is the hazarapat, Aspachana Farnaka, commander of the first thousand of the Ten Thousand and master of access: no petition, satrap or son reaches the throne without passing him. The Chief Eunuch Sparamiz, Master of the Inner House, runs the household, the harem and the King's daily calendar, and is the hazarapat's rival in everything but public.

The town below and the home satrapy of the Throne Plain are governed by Satrap Prince Tiridat, the King's second son, who collects the plain's tribute, keeps the roads and appoints its Frataraka. Watching him, as a King's Eye watches every satrap, is Bagapana, the King's Eye of the Throne Plain, a soft-spoken eunuch whose reports go to the hazarapat and, by a second route, to the Chief Eunuch. The arashshara run what the court actually eats and wears: Queen Mother Irdabama oversees the royal workshops and estates by right, and Arashshara Mandana Nahid'zar holds the provisioning of the Bringing. The Magi of the Hill of Fires, under Herbad Tansar, keep the calendar and crown the king; no coronation, war or execution is lawful on a day they have not declared fit. The Scribes of the Infinite Ledger audit the tribute; the Lanterns of Justice may not ride within sight of the terrace, by a privilege older than anyone can document. See Political and Tax.

Houses and families

The House of Zindar Royal house · Shahanshah

Crest: a winged sun-disc above a lion and a knotted cord · Motto: "Together We Rise, Together We Conquer" · Seat: the Inner House

The dynasty of Zindar Rashan al-Khavari, who united the desert tribes and whose name the court hopes will outlive the stars. The house owns, in law, all the land in the empire, and in practice the terrace, the Paradise and the royal estates. Its income is tribute, which is falling, and the Queen Mother's workshops, which are not.

  • Shahanshah Vishtaspa III, the Magnificent, King of Kings — sixty-one, still splendid in procession, and tired of hearing numbers.
  • Queen Mother Irdabama, eighty, arashshara of the royal estates — signs her own sealed tablets and has never once been audited.
  • Crown Prince Ariaramna, the heir — reads the Sage's Archive's readings in private and agrees with too many of them.
  • Prince Tiridat, Satrap of the Throne Plain — generous, loud, owed by half the garden town.
  • Princess Roshanak, Treaty Guest in the Hellenorian compound at Deiperduem — writes home weekly, in a hand her tutors did not teach her.

Ties: Farnaka backs the Crown Prince; Mihran courts Tiridat; R'eyshar sends the royal table its quinces.

House Mihran Zarate · Azata

Crest: a white horse on red, with an empty saddle · Motto: "The debt rides with us" · Seat: the Mihran house by the Paradise's east wall

The proudest horse-lords of the plateau and the largest private contributors to the Lion's Mane Vanguard. In the war, the Mihran heir Mihrdat rode into the Cloudspine pass behind the Acheaorian advance and died when Kaelen Caerthain brought the mountain down on it. The house has carried a blood-feud with House Caerthain ever since: each new head swears it at accession, an empty saddle is led in every Mihran procession, and every generation names a son Mihrdat. The Mihran count the debt in generations; the Caerthain count it as history. Strong here and at Xerastri, where a cadet line holds the march.

  • Azata Narsai Mihran, head of the house — seventy, blind in one eye, and still the first man at the Bringing.
  • Spahbed Artabazos Mihran, commander of the house's Vanguard squadrons — the best lance in the empire and the feud's sharpest edge.
  • Lady Gordiya Mihran, arashshara of the Mihran studs — sells remounts to both sides of every quarrel and keeps the house solvent.
  • Mihrdat Mihran, nine — named for the dead heir, already taught to hate a family he has never met.

Ties: the Cloudspine Feud with House Caerthain of Duneforged; the cadet line, Mihran of Xerastri.

House Farnaka Zarate · Azata · the hazarapat's house

Crest: a golden apple on a spear-butt · Motto: "None pass unannounced" · Seat: the Gate Court on the terrace

An old guard family that has held the hazarapat's office three times in a century by making itself the throne's door. The first thousand of the Ten Thousand, the Golden Apples, carry spears with golden apple-weights at the butt, and a Farnaka has commanded them for forty years. The house earns from the gate: audiences are free, but the order in which they happen is not.

  • Hazarapat Aspachana Farnaka, chief of the court — patient, sleepless, and convinced the empire can be saved by protocol.
  • Lady Rodaba Farnaka, his wife — keeps the list of who has been refused and when, which is the more dangerous list.
  • Bagabukhsha Farnaka, captain of the Golden Apples — has never seen a battle and drills his men twice a day to hide it.

Ties: backs Crown Prince Ariaramna; rival of Chief Eunuch Sparamiz in the Inner House.

House Karin Zarate · Azata · Masters of the Stair

Crest: a stair of seven steps · Motto: "Each in his place" · Seat: the Karin house at the foot of the Royal Stair

Hereditary keepers of the order of approach: who climbs the stair in what sequence, who may stand at which column, how far a satrap's knee must bend. Their great book, the Register of Approaches, is the empire's protocol and its family history at once. The Karin are old, poor in coin and rich in precedent, and the shrinking Bringing is shrinking them with it.

  • Azata Sukhra Karin, Master of the Stair — walks the gaps in the procession because the book says so.
  • Sudabeh Karin, his granddaughter, keeper of the Register — has started recording who stood beside whom, and why.
  • Varaz Karin, a cousin — sells better places in the order to delegations that can pay.

Ties: the Royal Stair; quietly owed by Shir'abad D'ar, whose satrap paid for a better place.

House Spandiyad Zarate · Azata · Treasurers of the Hours

Crest: a key across a sundial · Motto: "At the hour appointed" · Seat: a narrow house in the shadow of the terrace

The family that keeps the Treasury of Hours, by appointment renewed every reign for eleven reigns. They are paid well, watched constantly and forbidden to own land, horses or jewels beyond a schedule. Last spring the treasurer, Bagapata Spandiyad, resigned his keys, and the house has been in a state of polite terror since.

  • Bagapata Spandiyad, former treasurer — lives in his garden, will not speak of the vault, and sleeps with the lamps lit.
  • Mazdayar Spandiyad, acting treasurer, twenty-six — holds keys he was never trained for and asks too many people for advice.
  • Ispitamu Spandiyad, the house's clerk — the only person living who knows the full inventory, including what is missing.

Ties: the Treasury of Hours; the Golden Tripod account at Delphara.

House Nahid'zar Arashshara trading house

Crest: a dome of ice over running water · Motto: "Cold in summer, paid in spring" · Seat: the Ice Court in the Garden Town

A house of women who hold the ice-house concession, the wool for the royal workshops and the contract to feed and lodge every delegation at the Bringing. They buy from Atarabad and Persevalis, sell to the court on credit, and collect from the Vaults of Equilibrium when the court cannot pay, which is now always. They are the most solvent family in Persemenid and the most exposed.

  • Arashshara Mandana Nahid'zar, head of the house — can price a banquet for four thousand in her head and knows to the cup what the court owes her.
  • Pari Nahid'zar, her daughter — keeps the ice-houses, and the court's secrets that are told over sherbet.
  • Taraneh Nahid'zar, at Atarabad — buys silk and saffron and sends home the prices before anyone else knows them.

Ties: Suren-Pahlav of Atarabad; House Golab of Persevalis; creditor of the throne.

Notable figures

  • Magus Rashnu-Vahram Keeper of the Rite of Return · Magus — keeps the oldest rites of the Hill of Fires and attends every Immortal's funeral, which are rarer than they should be.
  • Bagoas the Nameless the Court of Vipers · the creed — a quiet man in household grey whom every faction believes belongs to another.
  • Spahbed Artabazos Mihran House Mihran · Lion's Mane Vanguard — wants a war with Duneforged before the King dies and the chance goes with him.
  • High Scribe Ivenzu al-Mirazid Chronicler of the Sandglass Circle — writes the official history, believes most of it, and knows exactly which parts he does not.
  • Master-Reader Vidarna Kaus head of the Sage's Archive at Persemenid — reads the cliff inscriptions and copies her notes to correspondents abroad whom she has never met.
  • Dominus Argentar Hulda Ironhand Mithril Reserve, Persemenid branch · dwarf — discounts debased Invictian silver at the door, will not lend to satrapies at any rate, and answers Lady Isolde Merca's letters within the day.
  • Master of Scales Jahanbakht Zarrin Vaults of Equilibrium, high temple-bank — holds most of the court's debt and has begun to wonder who, exactly, he can collect it from.
  • Chief Eunuch Sparamiz Master of the Inner House — plump, pleasant and indispensable; has outlived three hazarapats and means to outlive a fourth.

Connections

  • Atarabad — the first great stage of the Royal Road, with post-stations every day's ride; the court's money comes from there even when its tribute does not.
  • Persevalis — by the Garden Road; fruit, wine and rosewater for the court's best tables, and the satrapy the court can least afford to lose.
  • Mithratal and Xerastri — north on the Royal Road; the King's covenants are registered at the first and his frontier is held at the second.
  • Deiperduem — by the Treaty Road; Princess Roshanak lives in the Hellenorian compound there, as Lucius Valerius Maximus lives in the Acheaorian one (the Treaty Guests).
  • Hellarchon — the Hegemon's people host the princess, and the court reads every Hellenorian courtesy to her as a message.
  • Delphara — the Golden Tripod: the Acheaorian treasury on the Sacred Way, richest of them all, and an oracle whose answers to Persemenid are always favourable.
  • Aeterna and Thessalonika — the Sage's Archive exchanges copies with the Aeterna Lexicon and the Porticoes (the Three Libraries).
  • Duneforged Citadel — the Cloudspine Feud; House Mihran will not let the court forget the pass.
  • De'rakhtak Bon and R'eyshar — the throne plain's cold stores, and the old town whose archive the Sandglass Circle keeps asking to borrow.

The cities

City · Acheaoria · Acheaorian plateau

Atarabad City

Acheaoria's caravan city and its real treasury: an undying fire on the high ground, a caravanserai at the end of every road, and more money moving through its gates than the throne collects in a year.

Codex now: Acheaoria's great caravan city — a fire-temple at its heart, gates on every road east, and the place where the empire's trade actually happens.

Ruler
Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad
Title
Satrap (xšaçapāvan, "protector of the realm") of Atarabad
Population
c. 200,000, and twice that in the caravan season
Built on
A fire that has never gone out, and a gate on every road
Patron
The sacred fire of the Magi; Jauhar the Gilded for the merchants
Trouble
Fortunes leaving the empire in saddlebags, and a satrap with more lances than he is allowed

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Mud-brick and shade. Atarabad is built to exclude the sun: streets roofed with matting, courtyards turned inward, and wind-towers on every roof of consequence pulling cool air down into the rooms below. At the centre, on the highest ground, stands the fire-temple, a squat, heavy building where the Magi keep a flame they hold has never been extinguished. The city is oriented on it; every street that is not a lane climbs towards it. Around the edge stand the caravanserais, great walled courtyards with stabling below and rooms above, one for each major road and each a small foreign quarter of its own.

This is the commercial capital of Acheaoria in every way that Persemenid is not. Everything moving east or west crosses here, and the city takes a share of all of it. The Gilded Vault and the Wheelwalkers both keep their headquarters here, which means gems, bullion and the movement of portable wealth, a trade grown alarming in volume as the satrapies grow restless and nobles convert estates into things that fit in a saddlebag. Water comes by qanat, and the shares are held by the Bountiful Harvesters, which makes the guild one of the city's powers despite a seat on nothing.

A satrapal garrison holds the walls, and a great many private guards hold everything else; the total considerably exceeds the official force. The satrap's squadrons of the Lion's Mane Vanguard are one of the two establishments in the empire that have quietly outgrown their permitted size. The city's real defence has always been that everyone needs it working. Sacking Atarabad would impoverish whoever did it.

Mercantile, multilingual and formal: bargaining is a protracted social ritual, and treating it as a transaction marks a man as a foreigner. The Magi are strong here, conservative, suspicious of foreign practice, and unusually powerful because the fire at the city's centre is theirs. Beneath them the caravanserais bring Invictians, Hellenorians and steppe riders, and the city is more cosmopolitan than the Magi would like. The year runs on the Tending, when the fire is formally fed at intervals the public may watch but not approach; the Opening of the Roads, when every caravanserai sends out its first convoy on the same morning amid a great deal of unofficial racing; and the Long Bargain, a market week in which prices are fixed by public negotiation, theatrical, exhausting and taken seriously.

New lore

The Peace of the Signing turned Atarabad's face west. Before it, the Western Caravanserai was the smallest of the ring, a yard for spies and smugglers; now it sends out three convoys for every one that leaves by the eastern gates, down the Treaty Road to Deiperduem and on to Aepistra and Corinth's Haulway. House Suren-Pahlav saw it first and keeps factors at both ends. Silk, saffron, carpets and cassia go west; Invictian silver comes back, lighter every quarter, and the bazaar has learned to weigh it rather than count it.

The east is quieter, and not because it is safer. Two caravans on the deep eastern road were lost last year beyond the Zaruk'thal notches, and the Wheelwalkers now charge a "far cousin" premium for anything going past Qa'zshahrv'in. Meanwhile the Gilded Vault's back rooms have never been busier. A stone sewn into a coat cannot be confiscated, and three satrapal families have left the city in the past year with less luggage than they arrived with.

Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad filed the correct returns when he raised his squadrons past the establishment, and received no reply. He has taken the silence as permission. At the last Opening of the Roads his new lancers escorted the convoys out of the city in full parade order, which nobody had asked them to do and everyone understood.

Rumours in the bazaar: that the saffron sold in the third lane is cut with the cheap kind and the warden knows; that the charmers on the Cobra Heaps have found a snake no one can name and have locked their gate; that the Magi once let the fire go out and will flog anyone who says so.

Districts

The Fire Hill Temple precinct and water-court

Sacred · Magi, temple servants, water-clerks · sandalwood smoke, wet stone

The Fire-Temple of Atarabad crowns the highest ground: heavy, plain, built around an inner chamber where the sacred flame burns behind a screen the public may look through but not approach. The Magi's houses, schools and wood-stores climb the slope around it, and every load of fuel is weighed, blessed and logged. At the hill's foot the qanat surfaces in the Water-Court, where the flow is divided into shares by timed bowls and the Bountiful Harvesters' clerks keep the rota. Fire above, water below: the city's two oldest authorities share a hill and not much else.

Ties: Mobad Atar-Farnbag keeps the flame; signals reach Persemenid's Hill of Fires.

The Bazaar of Atarabad Existing · the largest bazaar on the continent

Trade · every guild, every tongue · saffron, hot copper, camel

Roofed lanes laid out by trade, each with its own gate, warden and guild, and prices bargained, never posted. Atarabad's is the largest bazaar on the continent: forty-one lanes, a carpet hall with a dome like a temple's, and a weigh-house where Invictian coin is now weighed rather than counted. During the Long Bargain prices are fixed by public negotiation in the central court, and the merchants who win are toasted for a year. Strangers are expected to lose; the polite ones lose gracefully and are remembered for it.

Ties: the lanes' arashshara answer to Shahdokht Abrisham; carpets from Tabrishi'ir.

The Wind-Tower Quarter Existing · great houses

Wealthy residential · merchant houses and their guards · cool air, jasmine, oiled steel

Inward-turned houses under roofed streets, with wind-towers on every roof of consequence pulling the breeze down into rooms where the water-jars sweat. The great houses of the merchant city sit here, each with its own armed guard. The Gilded Vault and the Wheelwalkers both keep their headquarters in this quarter, the first behind a door with no sign and the second in a courtyard full of carts, because a Wheelwalker headquarters may not be a house. The gems and bullion moving through it have grown alarming in volume as the satrapies turn restless.

Ties: seat of House Suren-Pahlav and House Tir'dad.

The Caravanserai Ring The road-gates

Foreign quarters · drovers, factors, envoys, guards · dung, tea, tallow

The Caravanserai of Atarabad is not one building but a ring of them, one at each road: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Each is a foreign quarter of whoever travels its road. The Western Caravanserai on the Treaty Road houses Invictian and Hellenorian factors, with the stone branch of the Mithril Reserve beside it; the Royal Caravanserai serves the road to Persemenid; the eastern yards speak languages the city scribes cannot write. On the Opening of the Roads they all send their first convoy out on the same morning.

Ties: the Treaty Road to Deiperduem; the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon books its eastern legs here.

The Silk Quarter and the Saffron Terraces Workshops and fields

Industrious · women breeders, dyers, pickers · warm leaves, steam, crocus

Behind the quarter's dye-yards stand the Mulberry Sheds: long wooden buildings, warm and humid, loud with ten thousand silkworms chewing like rain. The women who feed them sleep in the sheds in season, and the cocoons are stifled in steam before the moths break out; buyers are received in the front room and offered tea. Above the city, the Saffron Terraces lie bare for fifty weeks and lilac for ten days, when every household picks the crocus before dawn and plucks the threads at the kitchen table by night. Poor man's saffron grows in a lower field and is sold, occasionally, as the real thing.

Ties: House Abrisham owns the sheds; the silkmoth line came from Tabrishi'ir.

The East Gate and the Cobra Heaps Gate ward and rubble mounds

Rough · charmers, drovers, rubble-pickers · dust, hot stone, snake-musk

Outside the east gate lie the Cobra Heaps, old rubble mounds left by the demolition of a dozen forgotten buildings, whose cracks the snakes were happy to move into. A guild of charmers holds rights to the ground and keeps the mongoose called the Snake-Warden as a working partner against the Hood-Asp. A charmer will give a demonstration for a few coins; the guild does not let strangers handle the snakes, and locals give the heaps a wide berth. Inside the gate, the drovers' ward is cheap, loud, and the last place to buy water before the eastern road.

Ties: the eastern road to Qa'zshahrv'in; Wheelwalker convoys muster here.

Rule

Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad governs the city and its satrapy from a palace in the Wind-Tower Quarter, collects the caravan tolls and the tribute, and forwards to Persemenid a share that is still, by any standard, honest. He raises and pays his own Vanguard squadrons and appoints the Frataraka of the outlying towns and the wardens of the gates. The throne's watcher is Tahmineh of the Seal, the King's Eye of Atarabad, widow of a Royal Road post-master, who reads every courier's bag that passes the Royal Caravanserai and sends her reports up the road in nine days. The satrap knows exactly what she sees and arranges for her to see it.

The bazaar is governed by its lanes, and the lanes by their arashshara, the senior of whom is Arashshara Shahdokht Abrisham, keeper of the city weights; a false scale in Atarabad is her business before it is the satrap's. The Magi, under Mobad Atar-Farnbag, hold the calendar, the guild oaths and the fire, and can close the bazaar for a day by declaring it impure. The Bountiful Harvesters hold the water and the Gilded Vault holds the portable wealth, and neither has ever needed a seat on anything. See Economic.

Houses and families

House Tir'dad Zarate · the Satrap's house

Crest: an arrow through a crown of wind-towers · Motto: "The road pays the lance" · Seat: the Satrap's Palace, Wind-Tower Quarter

A zarate of the eastern plateau that has held the satrapy of Atarabad for three generations by being useful to every King of Kings and dependent on none. Its income is tolls, and its pride is cavalry. The house has not decided what it will do if the throne falls; it has decided to have the lances ready when it does.

  • Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad — courteous, frugal and patient; counts his squadrons every evening the way other men count coins.
  • Lady Azadokht Tir'dad, his wife, arashshara of the satrapal granaries — feeds the garrison and knows to the sack how long it could hold.
  • Captain Volagash Tir'dad, his nephew — commands the new squadrons and wants a reason to use them.

Ties: watched by the King's Eye; owes the Vaults of Equilibrium nothing, which the Vaults find suspicious.

House Suren-Pahlav Zarate · Azata · caravan house

Crest: a camel's head above nine road-stones · Motto: "Every road ends at our gate" · Seat: the Suren-Pahlav house, Wind-Tower Quarter

The greatest caravan house in Acheaoria, an old zarate that turned itself into a trading company two centuries ago and has never apologised for it. Suren-Pahlav convoys run the Royal Road, the eastern routes and, since the Peace, the Treaty Road west, where the house keeps factors at Deiperduem, at Aepistra and on Corinth's Haulway. This is the Silk Terminus, and Suren-Pahlav is its spine.

  • Azata Gondophar Suren-Pahlav, head of the house — rode his first caravan at nine and still sleeps better on a camel.
  • Pakor Suren-Pahlav, factor at Deiperduem — dines with all three embassies and pays for none of the dinners.
  • Sanatruk Suren-Pahlav, factor at Aepistra — sells silk to Invictian officers' wives and buys their husbands' gossip.
  • Arashshara Delbar Suren-Pahlav, factor on the Haulway at Corinth — the only Acheaorian with a standing berth on the slipway, and furious at what it cost.
