Ties: sells to House Nahid'zar of Persemenid; carries for the Wheelwalkers when they need a name on the paperwork.

House Abrisham Arashshara silk house

Crest: a white cocoon on green · Motto: "Thread before gold" · Seat: the Mulberry Sheds, Silk Quarter

A house of women breeders and reelers who own the Mulberry Sheds and the pale, strong silkmoth line that no one may export raw. They sell thread, never eggs, and the old penalty for selling eggs to a rival is the loss of both hands. The head of the house is also the senior arashshara of the bazaar, which gives a silk family the keeping of the city's weights.

  • Arashshara Shahdokht Abrisham, head of the house and keeper of the weights — once threw a satrap's cousin out of the weigh-house for leaning on the scale.
  • Nushin Abrisham, the best breeder in the sheds — and, the house fears, the one selling eggs.
  • Golbanu Abrisham, Shahdokht's granddaughter — wants to sell silk direct to Corinth and cut out Suren-Pahlav.

Ties: the Silk Quarter; rivals of Tabrishi'ir in the dye trade.

Notable figures

  • Mobad Atar-Farnbag First Flame of the Magi — keeps the undying fire, and the Magi's whole calendar with it; wants foreign shrines out of the caravanserais.
  • Dominus Argentar Brokk Ironhand Mithril Reserve, Atarabad branch · dwarf — the busiest branch master outside Deiperduem; his Custodes escort Suren-Pahlav silver to the Western Caravanserai and not one step further.
  • Master of Scales Pouran Dastvar Vaults of Equilibrium, Atarabad temple-bank — lends to satrapies the Reserve will not touch, and has started asking for collateral that fits in a strongbox.
  • Gem-Master Laal Firuzan Gilded Vault — keeps no ledger linking stone to seller, and remembers every face anyway.
  • Javid of the Wheels Wheelwalkers, the senior uncle — related to everyone; knows which convoys will go east this year, and which will not come back.
  • Margir Shahrokh master of the charmers' guild, the Cobra Heaps — locked the guild's gate last month and will not tell the satrap why.
  • Kamran Zafarani saffron merchant, third lane — sells the best saffron in the city, and some of the worst, at the same price.

Connections

  • Persemenid — by the Royal Road; the court's provisioners buy here, and the King's Eye's reports go there.
  • Mithratal — north on the Royal Road; every great caravan contract worth its seal is sworn there.
  • Deiperduem — by the Treaty Road, the Silk Terminus's first great market; Suren-Pahlav keeps a warehouse inside the neutral walls.
  • Aepistra and Corinth — the western ends of the Silk Terminus; Atarabad silk crosses the Haulway between two seas.
  • Tabrishi'ir — carpets come to the bazaar by Wheelwalker cart, and dye-stuff goes back.
  • Qa'zshahrv'in — the last certain water on the eastern caravan road, four days out.
  • Persevalis — dried fruit and rosewater for the caravans, silk for the satrap's pavilion.

City · Acheaoria · Acheaorian plateau

Mithratal City

The oath-city: a quiet walled town around an empty stone court, where a bargain sworn before the fire binds anywhere on the plateau, and where people have learned to choose their words.

Codex now: A city built around a covenant — the Acheaorian centre of oath and contract, where a bargain sworn here is enforceable anywhere on the plateau.

Ruler
Satrap Zariadres Vohuman
Title
Satrap of Mithratal
Population
c. 80,000, and some 6,000 parties waiting out their intervals
Built on
An empty court of dressed stone where every road ends
Patron
The sacred fire as witness; Hakiyah the Just Scales; Vatagatal the Dutiful
Trouble
Satraps swearing covenants with each other instead of with the throne

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

A walled city of straight streets around a central precinct that is not a palace and not a market but a court. Every road runs to the place where oaths are sworn: an open precinct, roofless, floored in one expanse of dressed stone and empty of decoration. The city's wealth went into the buildings around it, the archives, the chambers where terms are drafted, and the lodgings where parties wait out the required intervals. It is a strikingly quiet city for its size.

Its product is enforcement. A covenant sworn at Mithratal is recognised across Acheaoria and, by long custom, by the Mithril Reserve and most Hellenorian courts. Parties travel weeks to swear here; the city houses, feeds and bills them, and the archivists hold the record in perpetuity for a fee paid annually, forever. The Oathbound Sanctum keeps a correspondence with Mithratal's registrars, the two verifying each other's documents: the only formal Invictian–Acheaorian legal link that survived the war.

The garrison is small, and deliberately so; no party to a covenant can afford the city to fall. The Lanterns of Justice ride circuit from here, and a judgement made at Mithratal is carried outward by riders whose approach is visible for an hour. The archives are the only thing seriously fortified, and they are fortified absurdly.

Legalistic, patient and precise, Mithratal's people speak carefully because careless speech here has been held binding, and there is case law. Certain covenants require intervals of days or a season between agreement and swearing, so that no oath is taken in heat, and the inns, gardens and teahouses that fill those intervals have bred a fine local tradition of poetry and board games. The Melodic Circle is strong, and its licensed criticism is taken as seriously as the courts. The calendar has three fixed points: the Renewal, eleven days in which every standing covenant is read out by class and any party wishing to dispute must appear; the Silent Day, on which nothing said is binding and people say what they have been holding; and the Setting of the Stone, when each decade a new slab is laid in the precinct floor and the old one broken and shared out.

New lore

The Peace of the Signing is registered here. The Acheaorian copy of the treaty lies in the Covenant Archives under the class of covenants between sovereigns, and is read aloud on the eleventh day of every Renewal. In five years no one has appeared to dispute it, though an Invictian notary of the Oathbound Sanctum stands in the precinct each year, says nothing, and asks for a fair copy afterwards.

The city's new trade is less comfortable. Satraps have begun swearing "covenants of neighbourhood" with one another: mutual aid against raiders, shared qanat maintenance, the return of runaways, all perfectly lawful and none of them involving the throne. Satrap Vohuman registers them at the standard fee. The Scribes of the Infinite Ledger have noted that three of them describe, in careful language, what each party will do "should the roads to the west be closed", and the only road to the west is the one that runs to Persemenid.

The last Setting of the Stone, four years ago, was the first since the war cut by the Geolith Artisan Covenant's own masons, who crossed from Hellenoria under a safe-conduct sworn in this same precinct. The chips of the old slab, shared among the city's families, now sell to foreigners as luck-stones. The finest go for a gold piece; most are gravel from the quarry road.

Districts

The Precinct of Oaths Covenant court and fire-temple

Sacred and legal · parties, witnesses, Magi · cold stone, smoke, silence

The open court at the city's heart, roofless and bare, laid in dressed slabs, one renewed each decade. Here parties stand barefoot on the stone and swear before the Fire-Temple of Mithratal, whose flame burns at the precinct's eastern edge behind its screen; the Magi witness every covenant and put their seal beside the parties'. On the Silent Day the precinct fills with people who come simply to say things aloud where it does not count.

Ties: the Magi under the Witness of the Fire; the old slab's chips are prized in Persemenid.

The Archive Ward Covenant Archives

Fortified · registrars, drafters, archive guard · ink, wax, dry sand

The Covenant Archives of Mithratal, where every covenant sworn in the city is drafted, registered and kept. Three walls, each higher than the last; a moat of raked sand that shows every footprint; doors that open only to two keys held by different families. The registrars swear never to sleep outside the ward more than one night in seven. At the Renewal the readers work in shifts from dawn to dusk, and the class of the covenant decides the day it is read.

Ties: House Dadvar holds the registry; documents checked against the Oathbound Sanctum's.

The Waiting Lodges Caravanserai ward

Hospitable and idle · parties, their servants, poets · cardamom, tea, tile-dust

The Caravanserai of Mithratal began as a caravan inn and multiplied into a ward of walled lodges, each with one gate, where parties to a covenant wait out their intervals. Rival parties are lodged at opposite ends by custom and meet only in the teahouses, where the boards are always out and the poets always in. A season's interval is long enough to lose a fortune at the dice-board, which is why several covenants have been renegotiated between moves.

Ties: run by House Golnar; the Melodic Circle sings here nightly.

The Bazaar of Mithratal Existing · the scribes' market

Trade · seal-cutters, paper-sellers, notaries · lamp-black, wax, cut stone

Roofed lanes by trade, each with its own gate, warden and guild, prices bargained, never posted. Mithratal's bazaar is quiet for its size, like the rest of the city, and its busiest stalls sell writing materials and seals. A whole lane cuts cylinder seals in carnelian and agate; another sells paper by the weight of its promises. Forging a seal is punished as perjury, and the seal-cutters' guild keeps impressions of everything it has ever cut.

Ties: carnelian from the desert washings; ink from Atarabad.

The Garden Ward Covenant Garden and Water-Court

Shaded · oath-priests, water-clerks, wealthy parties · wet roots, hyssop, plane leaves

The Covenant Garden is a square court shaded by one enormous plane tree, the Plane of the Wells, whose roots have drunk a channel of clean water for six hundred years. Contracts of consequence are sworn beneath it with the parties' hands in the channel; a bargain broken after such an oath is said to dry the offender's wells. Swearing is charged by the hour and by the stake. Nearby, in the Water-Court, the city's water shares are themselves covenants, registered and read at the Renewal with the rest.

Ties: Temple Hyssop cut by the oath-priests; the Bountiful Harvesters keep the rota (water).

The Grove Gate Ordeal Grove and the Lantern House

Outside the wall · the accused, their families, Lantern riders · bitter bark, horse, lamp-oil

Beyond the south gate, within a low wall, stands the Ordeal Grove, a circle of grey, gnarled trees ringed by tall King's Candle stalks. Those accused of lying under covenant may choose the ordeal: a cup of water in which the bark has soaked. The innocent are sick and recover; the guilty die. The priests hold that the gods decide; the survivors hold that the dose does. The crowds on ordeal days are large and quiet. By the gate stands the Lantern House, from which the Lanterns of Justice ride.

Ties: the Lanterns' circuit to Shir'abad D'ar; the law.

Rule

Satrap Zariadres Vohuman governs the city and a modest satrapy of grain-plain around it, collects the archive fees, which are the richest tax in the empire per head, and forwards his tribute in full and on time; Mithratal is the one satrapy the Scribes have never marked "not presented". He keeps the garrison small and the courts open, and the city's real sovereign is its record. Watching him is Mardak the Listener, the King's Eye of Mithratal, who attends every swearing between satraps and copies the terms to the hazarapat; he is the most hated man in the city because he is the only one who may write during the Silent Day.

The Covenant Archives answer to the Chief Registrar, Azata Yazdin Dadvar, whose family has drafted the empire's bargains for three hundred years. The Witness of the Fire, Magus Frawardin, leads the Magi of the precinct and seals every covenant; without his seal an oath is merely a promise. The arashshara of the city is Simin Golnar, whose house runs the Waiting Lodges, the city's largest employer. The Lanterns of Justice, under Lantern-Captain Zarir Roshanpur, answer to no satrap and carry Mithratal's judgements across the plateau.

Houses and families

House Vohuman Zarate · the Satrap's house

Crest: two hands clasped over a flame · Motto: "Kept" · Seat: the Satrap's Residence by the north gate

A careful, legal-minded zarate that has held the satrapy for four generations by never once being late with tribute and never once being interesting. Its fortune is the archive fee and the registry of land titles across the northern plain. Lately it has been very busy registering other satraps' covenants, at the standard fee, and asking no questions.

  • Satrap Zariadres Vohuman — dry, exact, and privately terrified of being the satrap under whom the record failed.
  • Lady Mahin Vohuman, his daughter — married by covenant into House Tir'dad of Atarabad, and the conduit for its letters.
  • Arsham Vohuman, his brother, commander of the garrison — four hundred men, and he knows every one of them by name.

Ties: House Tir'dad by marriage; the King's Eye in the next street.

House Dadvar Zarate · Azata · the Hands of Terms

Crest: a reed pen across a key · Motto: "As written" · Seat: inside the Archive Ward

Hereditary drafters and registrars who have written the terms of most great Acheaorian bargains for three centuries. A Dadvar drafter is hired for a covenant the way a mercenary is hired for a war: expensively, and with an eye to the other side's choice. The house lives inside the Archive Ward, marries inside it, and is buried, it is said, in the stacks.

  • Azata Yazdin Dadvar, Chief Registrar — can recite the class and date of any covenant in the archives and will not recite its terms without a fee.
  • Shirindokht Dadvar, senior drafter — has never lost a dispute at the Renewal, and has drafted terms for both sides of four of them.
  • Kavus Dadvar, a young drafter — wrote a clause last year that nobody has yet read closely enough.

Ties: the Archive Ward; correspondents of the Oathbound Sanctum.

House Golnar Arashshara house · the Waiting Lodges

Crest: a split pomegranate · Motto: "All things in their season" · Seat: the Great Lodge, Waiting Lodges

A house of women who own or manage most of the Waiting Lodges, the teahouses and the board-game halls, and so feed, house and entertain every party that comes to swear. They know who is waiting for whom, how long, and how impatiently, which in Mithratal is worth more than gold.

  • Arashshara Simin Golnar, head of the house — seats rival parties at opposite ends of every room and has prevented more feuds than the Lanterns.
  • Laleh Golnar, her niece — the finest board-game player on the plateau, who plays only for information.
  • Zhaleh Golnar, keeper of the Teahouse of Intervals — hears everything said on the Silent Day, and writes nothing down.

Ties: the Melodic Circle's local hall; supplies from Persevalis.

Notable figures

  • Dominus Argentar Odila Stonebrow Mithril Reserve, Mithratal branch · dwarf — decides which Mithratal covenants the Reserve will honour, and has quietly stopped honouring covenants of neighbourhood; reports to Lady Isolde Merca by every courier.
  • Master of Scales Bahar Navabi Vaults of Equilibrium, Mithratal — lends against registered covenants, and holds more satrapal promises than any man alive.
  • Lantern-Captain Zarir Roshanpur Lanterns of Justice — rides with his lamp lit at noon, and has never yet had to use his sword on a man who saw him coming.
  • Brother Septimus Auctor Oathbound Sanctum · Invictian notary in residence — the only Invictian in the city by right of covenant; appears every Renewal, says nothing, and takes notes.
  • Kersasp priest of the Ordeal Grove — his verdicts are famously consistent, and his house is famously new.
  • Ruzbeh the Unhurried poet of the Melodic Circle — writes one couplet for every day of a party's interval; his latest cycle, about a satrap who swore to his neighbour, is being sung in four cities.

Connections

  • Atarabad and Persemenid — south on the Royal Road; caravan contracts and court marriages come here to be sworn.
  • Xerastri — north on the Royal Road; the frontier's pension rolls are sworn and registered here, and argued over here.
  • Deiperduem — the Mithril Reserve's great branch honours Mithratal covenants, and Treaty Hall's clerks ask for certified copies.
  • Duneforged Citadel — Lady Isolde Merca reads Dominus Stonebrow's reports on which covenants the Reserve should trust.
  • Aeterna — the Oathbound Sanctum's correspondence, the one legal thread between the empires the war never cut.
  • Corinth — the Prytanis's courts accept Mithratal covenants for Acheaorian merchants on the Haulway.
  • Shir'abad D'ar — its satrap swore a covenant of neighbourhood here last year, and the King's Eye copied every word.

City · Acheaoria · Acheaorian plateau, the Garden Road

Persevalis City

The garden satrapy: a hillside of walled gardens with water led along every terrace, which feeds the court's best tables and cannot be defended by anything except its own usefulness.

Codex now: The Acheaorian garden city — terraces, water and orchards on the plateau's edge, and the satrapy that feeds the court.

Ruler
Satrap Farrokh Bagh'dar
Title
Satrap of Persevalis
Population
c. 70,000
Built on
A terraced slope, a deed for every channel, and mother wells a day's ride out
Patron
The sacred fire; Shajar at the channel heads; Selan for the dreamers
Trouble
Water running the wrong way, and a court that borrows against the harvest

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Green, in country that is not. Persevalis is terraced down a long slope with water led along every level, so that the city is a series of gardens with buildings in them rather than the reverse. Every house of consequence has a walled garden with a channel through it, and the right to that channel is written into the deed. The public spaces are orchards. From below, the city reads as a hillside of trees with roofs showing through, which is exactly the impression it was built to give. From above, from the Channel Head, it reads as what it is: a staircase of water, each landing owned by somebody.

It grows fruit, wine and the supply of the court, an old, protected and lucrative trade. Persemenid eats Persevalis at its best tables: the white mulberries, the seedless grapes, the long pears wrapped one by one in vine leaves, the damask rosewater in the King's sherbet. Channel maintenance is a civic duty shared by deed-holders, and neglecting one's section is a genuine scandal; a house whose stretch silts up is struck off the guest-lists for a season, which in Persevalis is a kind of exile. Grafted cultivars are kept by cutting over centuries, and the registry of named trees lives in the city archive. A good tree has a name, a lineage and a price; a famous one has a song.

The city is indefensible, since a terraced city cannot be walled usefully, and its real security is its water: the channels run underground, the mother wells lie a day's ride out, so whoever wants the gardens alive must hold a great deal of empty country. Three armies have taken Persevalis in its history and none has kept it, because none could keep the water running. The satrap keeps cavalry for show and the hunt; the Predator's Guild holds culling rights in the parks.

Leisured at the top, intensely skilled below: the ease rests on generations of gardeners, grafters and channel-men whose craft is inherited and not written down. An invitation to sit in another man's garden is a real event with rules: the guest washes his hands in the channel, praises one tree by name, eats what is cut for him and does not ask the price of anything. Refusing it is an insult. The River's Embrace keeps shrines at the channel heads; the Enchanted Muse is well established, and Persevalis plans by its almanac, so that a betrothal, a sowing or a lawsuit may wait a month for a better dream. The year turns on the Opening of the Channels in spring, when the water walks down the city in a day with a procession behind it; the Grafting in late winter, when new cuttings are registered by name; and the Night Gardens in high summer, when every gate stands open and the city walks through each other's houses until dawn. It is the one night of the year the walls do not mean anything.

New lore

The court pays for its fruit later every year. Before the Peace the bills were settled at the Bringing; now they are settled, in part, eighteen months on, in court silver of a weight Arashshara Golab weighs twice. The Vaults of Equilibrium have lent the court money secured, it is whispered, on the Persevalis harvest itself, which would mean the satrap is growing fruit he no longer owns. Farrokh Bagh'dar has not been told, and the people who know are all careful to be at his table.

Meanwhile the channel-keepers report that water in the eastern channels now flows faster than the slope allows, as if something downhill were drawing it. Two terraces on the east side have gone dry at the lower ends; their owners have sued the owners above them, who have sued the Water-Court, which has sued nobody yet and is measuring.

And the dreams. The Enchanted Muse's almanac marked last summer's Night Gardens as a "spring tide of dreams", and half the city dreamed of the same woman in grey walking the terraces, opening gates that were already open. Children drew her. A rose-presser swore she asked him the way to the sea. The Muse has sent to Delphara and the Arcane Academy, carefully, to ask whether anyone else saw her too, and both have answered by sending people. This is the Persevalis end of what the scholars of three empires now call, among themselves, the Dreamers' Hunt: the search for the last Nethranan dream-walker, Vesperine Ilaro. The gardens have never had so many polite foreign guests who do not care about trees.

Districts

The Terraced Gardens Existing · the hillside

Residential · deed-holders and their gardeners · roses, wet earth, quince

The paradise garden at the scale of a city: walled gardens on every level, a channel through each, the public orchards between. The higher the garden, the older the deed and the earlier the water; the lowest terraces drink what the upper ones have washed their feet in, and their families say so at every lawsuit. Gardeners live in the wall-houses of the gardens they tend and are inherited with them, like the trees. On the Night Gardens every gate stands open, and one garden's lamps always burn low and blue. Nobody owns that garden on paper. Everybody knows where it is.

Ties: House Peyvand's registry of trees; the channel deeds at the Channel Head.

The Channel Head Fire-temple, Water-Court and Qanat Pools

Sacred and hydraulic · Magi, channel-keepers · wet stone, moss, smoke

At the top of the terraces the Fire-Temple of Persevalis stands where the water enters the city, and its Magi bless the Opening of the Channels. Below it the Water-Court divides the flow by deed, each share measured by a timed bowl of perforated copper; the Bountiful Harvesters hold most of the shares and all of the bowls. Beside it the Qanat Pools, stone-lined reservoirs at the tunnel mouths, hold pale blind newts in cold clear water while nightingales sing in the garden above. A channel-keeper will take a visitor to the first pool; beyond it the way is not for the casual.

Ties: the hereditary channel-keepers of House Kariz; water; faith.

The Pomegranate Walk The satrap's avenue

Courtly · guests, servants, rose-pressers · pomegranate, damask rose

A long avenue of pomegranate trees on one side and damask roses on the other, ending in the pavilion where the satrap entertains. The fruit is cut at table and guests are told that every seed eaten is a promise, and that the promise is remembered. Petitioners wait under the trees in the mornings, when the walk is public; the pavilion is by invitation only, and the invitations are written on rose petals pressed into paper, which fade in a week, so that nobody can show an old one.

Ties: House Bagh'dar; rosewater from House Golab's stills.

The Bazaar of Persevalis Existing · the orchard market

Trade · growers, court buyers · ripe fruit, cut stems, seed-dust

Roofed lanes by trade, each with its gate, warden and guild, prices bargained, never posted; but here they are mostly fruit, cuttings and seed, sold under the trees of the public orchards. A registered cutting sells with its name and pedigree, like a horse, and a forged pedigree is prosecuted like horse-theft. The Lane of Knives sells grafting blades and nothing else. Court buyers arrive before dawn and take the best of everything at prices fixed last year, and the growers sell to them first because refusing the court is not a thing one does twice.

Ties: court buyers of House Nahid'zar; economy.

The Foot of the Slope Caravanserai and the Green-Nut Orchards

Working · carters, pickers, drovers · dust, dry leaves, mule

The Caravanserai of Persevalis sits where the green ends and the plateau's ordinary dust begins, and the Garden Road convoys load there for Persemenid, fruit packed in snow-straw and sealed baskets. Beyond it, on the plateau's edge, the Green-Nut Orchards run in long grey rows watered by qanat, with old emmer sown in the fallow strips. The nuts are picked before dawn, and a good year buys the satrapy a bridge. The pickers live here, in mud-brick rows below the first terrace, and walk up into the gardens only to work.

Ties: the Garden Road to Persemenid; cold stores at De'rakhtak Bon.

The Still-Houses The rose quarter

Industry · arashshara, pressers, coppersmiths · steam, rose, hot copper

A terrace given over to rose-fields and the copper stills that turn them into rosewater and attar, owned almost entirely by women and run on the arashshara's books. In picking season the petals are taken before the sun touches them, and the whole east side of the city smells of roses for three weeks, which visitors find charming for one. The attar is sold by the drop in glass vials sealed with the Golab rose; forty thousand blooms make a vial. The still-masters' guild meets here and sets the season's price, which the court then ignores.

Ties: House Golab; buyers from Atarabad and Deiperduem.

Rule

Satrap Farrokh Bagh'dar governs from his pavilion at the end of the Pomegranate Walk, collects the fruit-tribute and forwards it in kind, and is owed by the court more than he is owed by anyone else. Persevalis forwards its tribute in full, on time and frequently early, because fruit does not wait; it is the only satrapy that pays the throne in something the throne cannot defer. Parvaneh, the King's Eye of Persevalis, sits at his table so often that guests assume she is his wife. She writes to Persemenid every ten days and has nothing bad to say about him, which worries her more than it should.

The channel deeds are kept by the Bountiful Harvesters; the court supply is run by Arashshara Golrokh Golab; the Magi of the Channel Head, under Herbad Shirzad, open the water each spring and can refuse to. The satrap's steward of the satrapy, the Frataraka Dariush Baghban, runs the plateau villages and the nut orchards and reports to the satrap at breakfast. In practice four powers rule Persevalis: the satrap who hosts, the Magi who open the water, the Harvesters who measure it and the arashshara who sell what it grows. The satrap is the only one of the four who is not paid.

Houses and families

House Bagh'dar Zarate · the Satrap's house

Crest: a cypress inside a walled garden · Motto: "What is tended endures" · Seat: the Pavilion of the Pomegranate Walk

Hospitable, cultivated, and owed a fortune by the throne. The Bagh'dar have held the satrapy for five generations by being the most agreeable hosts in the empire and the least threatening; no King of Kings has ever feared a Bagh'dar, and several have dined with one. Their wealth is in the oldest deeds on the slope and in court debts that look less like wealth every year.

  • Satrap Farrokh Bagh'dar — a gracious host who has started counting the seeds his guests eat.
  • Lady Shahrzad Bagh'dar, his mother — remembers when the court paid on time, and says so at dinner.
  • Kamran Bagh'dar, his heir, twenty — rides with the satrap's show cavalry, borrows from the Vaults in his own name, and believes no one has noticed.
  • Lady Laleh Bagh'dar, the satrap's wife — a Peyvand by birth, who keeps the house's grafting knives and her family's silence.

Ties: married into House Peyvand; creditor of the court at Persemenid.

House Peyvand Zarate · Azata · the grafters

Crest: two branches bound as one · Motto: "Cut, bind, wait" · Seat: the Registry Garden

Keepers of the registry of named trees and the oldest grafted lines on the plateau. Every registered tree in Persevalis is entered in the Peyvand books with its parents, its grafting date and its grafter; a registered cutting is worth ten unregistered, and the Peyvand take a fee on every one. They are the city's memory and its notaries, and nobody marries on the slope without asking them whose trees the bride's family really owns.

  • Azata Kiyan Peyvand, keeper of the Registry — can name the grandparent of any tree in the city.
  • Mina Peyvand — has grafted a quince that fruits at midwinter and will not say how.
  • Sohrab Peyvand, Kiyan's brother — keeps the archive's back rooms, where the oldest registers name trees that grew before the qanats did.

Ties: the registry in the Terraced Gardens; cuttings sold to R'eyshar at its Grafting.

House Golab Arashshara trading house

Crest: a copper still under a rose · Motto: "The scent outlasts the flower" · Seat: the Still-Houses

Women who own the copper rose-stills and hold the contract to supply the court with fruit, wine and rosewater. The contract was signed by a King of Kings four reigns ago and is renewed by silence; the Golab have never once missed a delivery, and the court has missed a great many payments. They carry the debt on their books at its face value and in their heads at about a third.

  • Arashshara Golrokh Golab — knows exactly what the court owes and has stopped extending credit.
  • Nasrin Golab — sells rosewater to Hellenorian buyers at Deiperduem, against her mother's wishes.
  • Azar Golab, the still-mistress — can tell a field's year by the smell of its attar and a forger's by the colour.

Ties: the Still-Houses; court buyers of House Nahid'zar; the Silk Terminus buyers of House Suren-Pahlav.

House Kariz Hereditary channel-keepers · no title, and no need of one

Crest: a lamp in a well-shaft · Motto: "Down first, up last" · Seat: the keepers' houses beside the Qanat Pools

Not a zarate and not interested in being one: the family of master channel-keepers who have walked the Persevalis qanats for longer than the Bagh'dar have held the satrapy. They are paid by the deed-holders, fed at every Opening, and excused all tax. Their knowledge of the channels is not written down anywhere, by deliberate policy, which is why no satrap has ever been able to replace them.

  • Ustad Babak Kariz, master channel-keeper — says the water is being pulled, and is the only one who has walked far enough to know.
  • Golnar Kariz, his daughter — the first woman to go down past the first pool, last year, and she came back with a brick stamped with a mark no one could read.
  • Old Hormoz Kariz — blind, ninety, and able to tell by ear which channel is running low.

Ties: the Channel Head; the muqanni of Qa'zshahrv'in are cousins by marriage.

Notable figures

  • Shirin Navaz First Voice of the Melodic Circle — sings the satrap's failings in his own hall, to applause; lately her songs are about the court, and lately the court has been sending people to hear them. She sang at the last Night Gardens until dawn and says she does not remember the last song.
  • Almanac-Mistress Mahtab The Enchanted Muse, Persevalis chapter — keeps the dream-almanac and is hunting the woman in grey everyone dreamed of; she wants to find her first, before the foreigners, and is not sure what she would do then.
  • Parvaneh the King's Eye of Persevalis — fond of the satrap, loyal to the throne, and slowly realising that the throne is what is robbing him.
  • Herbad Shirzad Magus of the Channel Head — opens the water each spring; has let it be known he will not open the east channels this year until someone explains where the water goes.
  • Dominus Argentar Ewald Ironhand Mithril Reserve, Persevalis branch · dwarf — wants to retire to a garden here; refuses to lend against fruit not yet grown, and holds Lady Isolde Merca's letter asking him exactly how much of the harvest the Vaults have taken.
  • Master of Scales Navid Tahmasp Vaults of Equilibrium — holds the court's paper on the Persevalis harvest and hopes the satrap never asks.
  • Ustad Babak Kariz master channel-keeper — wants hired hands who can fight and do not talk, to go further down the east qanat than anyone has gone.
  • Theodora Hypnaia envoy of Delphara's Dream Dormitory — a soft-spoken incubation-priestess who sleeps in a different garden every night, by invitation, and writes down what she dreams.
  • Magister Phaidon Lykides Arcane Academy, Hellarchon · tiefling — a Voidfolk scholar travelling as a buyer of rose-cuttings, who knows nothing about roses and a great deal about Nethranan illusion.
  • Huntmaster Bahram Tir The Predator's Guild — holds the culling rights in the satrap's parks; his hounds will not go near the blue-lamped garden.

Connections

  • Persemenid — by the Garden Road, two days for a laden convoy; the court's table, and its unpaid bills.
  • Delphara, Hellarchon and Eronis — the Dreamers' Hunt: the Muse, the Dream Dormitory and the Arcane Academy all seek the last dream-walker, Vesperine Ilaro.
  • Atarabad — dried fruit and rosewater out, silk in.
  • De'rakhtak Bon — the cold stores where Persevalis fruit waits for the court.
  • Deiperduem — Nasrin Golab's rosewater, and the Mithril Reserve's main branch, where Lady Isolde Merca reads Ewald Ironhand's letters.

City · Acheaoria · Northern frontier

Xerastri City

The shield against the steppe: two walls, a ditch, the empire's largest garrison outside the capital, and a city that rides and shoots like the enemy it was built to stop.

Codex now: Acheaoria's frontier fortress-city — the shield against the steppe, garrisoned, walled twice, and the most heavily armed place in the empire.

Ruler
Satrap Vindarna Sarvand; the march held by Marzban Piruz Mihran
Title
Satrap of Xerastri; Marzban of the Northern March
Population
c. 55,000, most of them the garrison and its families
Built on
Two walls and a ditch, with the city between them
Patron
The sacred fire; Vatagatal the Dutiful; Hajama for the cavalry
Trouble
A subsidy cut twice since the Peace, and a garrison taxing the trade it is meant to stop

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Two walls and a ditch, and between them the city. Xerastri (Xerastir on older maps) is built for one purpose and does not pretend otherwise: everything is low, thick and sited to be defended. The outer wall faces the Malaunian Steppe and is the taller; the inner wall is older and encloses the citadel, the granaries and the wells. The space between is where people live, and everyone understands that in a serious assault that space is expendable. Houses between the walls are built of mud-brick on purpose, because mud-brick is cheap to lose. There are no gardens. A Persevalis fruit-buyer who once planted a rose by the Horse-Fair gate found it pulled up the next morning, with a note pinned to it in garrison script: "Cover."

The garrison is the economy: armour, tack, dried provisions and horses, against an imperial subsidy that has arrived late for three years and been cut twice since the Peace. Trade with the steppe is constant and officially discouraged, hides, horses and remounts in, grain and worked metal out; the Predator's Guild and the Savage Pack both do business here, and the customs officers are famously easy to satisfy. The garrison has answered the cuts by taxing the steppe trade it is supposed to suppress. Every Malaunian horse that passes the gate now pays a silver piece to a wall that is meant to keep it out.

The largest permanent force in Acheaoria outside the capital: heavy infantry hold the walls, light horse patrol, and the empire's best siege engineers maintain engines with nothing to besiege. The Ironclad Oath keeps a chapter here, one of the few places its oath to the throne is an operational advantage, since the satrap cannot order it against the empire's own subjects and the steppe is full of nominal subjects. Relations with the Lion's Mane Vanguard are poor, because Xerastri's professionals have watched the satraps' noble cavalry arrive late.

Hard, disciplined and unsentimental, the city rides like the Malaunians, shoots like them and has absorbed their customs: felt caps in winter, fermented mare's milk at weddings, a habit of naming horses before children. Officers from the capital find it barbarous, and the garrison finds officers from the capital useless. The Acheaorian counterpart of the Watchers of the Eternal Rest keeps the pension rolls, and the rolls are the chief grievance: a wall-soldier who survives thirty years is owed a pension the rolls say exists and the treasury says it will pay next quarter. The year has the Counting of the Wall, when each family reports its stretch sound or otherwise in public; the Horse Fair, a truce week when steppe clans trade in the outer city, the closest thing the frontier has to diplomacy; and the Riding, a full muster in view of the steppe that everyone understands is a message.

New lore

The Peace did not reach the steppe, which signed nothing. Raids have not increased; contracts have. Malaunian riders now hire out to all three empires in the same season, and the Horse Fair has become a hiring fair as much as a horse market: Invictian recruiters from the Council of Legates' private legions, Hellenorian tyrants' agents, satraps' stewards, all bidding in the same yard for the same archers. The garrison's pay is four months behind. The Satrap has begun paying it from the steppe tolls directly, without forwarding them, and the Scribes have recorded this as "presented in kind".

Beyond the wall the steppe has its own news. Tomyra of the Lion Grass, the Malaunian war-leader who takes coin from everyone and orders from no one, has wintered two days' ride from the outer gate for the second year running, closer than any clan has camped since the war. She has not raided. She sends a rider to the Horse Fair every month with a single question: who in Xerastri speaks for the city? Nobody has given the same answer twice.

And the feud. The Mihran cadet line holds the Northern March and carries the Cloudspine Feud against House Caerthain of Duneforged, whose son Kaelen brought the mountain down on the Mihran heir at the pass. The senior line in Persemenid wants a war; the cadet line at Xerastri has a war, of a sort, every day, and would rather have its back pay. Squadrons of the Lion's Mane Vanguard sent north "to strengthen the march" have begun asking the Marzban for maps of the southern roads instead.

Districts

The Inner Citadel Citadel, granaries, wells

Military · officers, Magi, engineers · grain-dust, oil, cold water

The older inner wall encloses what the city keeps if it loses everything else: the citadel, the granaries and the wells and the Water-Court, where in a siege water is the citadel's argument. The Fire-Temple of Xerastri stands here too; the fire is one of the things Xerastri will not give up, and the Magi keep a coal of it in a sealed brass pot ready to be carried out if the citadel falls. The siege engineers' yards fill the north corner, with engines oiled, tensioned and tested on the first of each month by throwing stones at a hill that has never done anything to anyone.

Ties: the Ironclad Oath's chapter house; House Sarvand's residence; military.

The Outer Wall The steppe face

Fortified · wall-families, sentries · wind, horse, wet mortar

The taller wall, facing the steppe, every stretch owned by a family responsible for its upkeep and named in the Counting each spring. A failed stretch shames a family for a generation; a sound one for nine generations makes a family close to noble. The wall-families live in the towers of their own stretch and marry along the wall, so that a wedding is often between neighbours a hundred yards apart. The gate-towers carry the garrison's horn-signals: one blast, riders seen; two, riders coming; three, nobody laughs.

Ties: House Dezhban holds the longest section.

The Bazaar of Xerastri Existing · between the walls

Trade · smiths, saddlers, steppe traders · leather, smoke, mare's milk

Roofed lanes by trade, prices bargained, never posted, in the ward everyone knows would be given up in a serious assault. Bowyers and saddlers outnumber spice-sellers ten to one, and half the stalls take payment in horses. The Lane of Arrows sells shafts by the sheaf of thirty and heads by weight; the Lane of Felt sells steppe goods the customs officers have not seen. Prices drop on the day the subsidy is announced late, and rise on the day it is announced cut.

Ties: the Predator's Guild and the Savage Pack trade here.

The Horse-Fair Ground Caravanserai and the truce yards

Mixed · steppe clans, remount buyers, recruiters · dung, dust, roasting mutton

Inside the outer gate, the Caravanserai of Xerastri and its great yards receive the steppe clans during the Horse Fair, under truce, heavily policed and very profitable. The rest of the year the yards hold remounts and recruiters. Since the Peace a corner of the yards has been chalked off as "the Hiring Ground", and foreign agents bid there openly for Malaunian archers by the hundred. The truce-stone by the gate bears the clan-marks of every chief who has sworn the Fair peace; Tomyra's is the newest and the deepest-cut.

Ties: House Asbdar runs the remount trade.

The Married Lines The garrison families' ward

Residential · soldiers' wives, widows, pensioners · bread ovens, wet wool, tallow

Long barrack-rows between the walls on the citadel side, where the garrison's families live in numbered houses and the widows keep the houses when the husbands do not come back. The Married Lines run on credit until the subsidy arrives and on rage after it does not. The pension office stands at the end of the lines with a barred window; the queue outside it is the city's real forum, and more than one officer has learned his posting from what was said in it. The women of the lines hold the ration tallies, and the quartermasters fear them more than the steppe.

Ties: the pension rolls; Lady Banu Mihran's grain.

The Hunting Park Outside the walls

Officers' sport · huntsmen, falconers · scrub, feathers, cat-musk

A walled reserve of scrub and meadow where huntsmen run trained cheetahs at hares from horseback, fly falcons, and keep tufted lynxes caged for display. Officers' guests are welcome; a commoner who wants to see a cheetah run must befriend a huntsman. The huntsmen are half Malaunian, and the park is the only place in Xerastri where garrison officers and steppe men sit together without a truce being needed.

Ties: the garrison's officers; Malaunian falconers.

Rule

Satrap Vindarna Sarvand governs the city, the subsidy and the customs. Marzban Piruz Mihran, warden of the Northern March, commands the frontier garrisons beyond the walls and answers to the throne directly, which the satrap resents. The two men split Xerastri along its walls: the satrap rules what is inside them, the Marzban what is outside, and the gates are argued over weekly. Bagadata the Lame, the King's Eye of Xerastri, a retired engineer, watches both. Arashshara Nasrin Asbdar runs the remount trade and the Horse Fair; Herbad Burzin keeps the fire and the oaths of the wall-families.

Beneath them the garrison is run by the Commander of the Walls, Thousand-Commander Datis Kamboj, a thousand-commander promoted from the ranks who reports to the satrap for pay and to the Marzban for war, and has lately found that only one of them pays. The siege engineers answer to Chief Engineer Ustad Mehran Zarrinkamar. Beyond the city, in the Parthian Ravine, Roxana Surena holds the gorge as a warden of the march, on the Marzban's commission and nobody's payroll.

Houses and families

House Mihran of Xerastri Cadet line of House Mihran · Marzban

Crest: the white horse and empty saddle, on black · Motto: "The debt rides with us" · Seat: the March House by the north gate

The frontier branch of House Mihran, holding the march for three generations and the Cloudspine Feud as fiercely as the senior line. The black field is the cadet difference; the Xerastri Mihran say it is because they have been in mourning longer. The march is theirs by royal commission, renewed each reign, and every renewal has come with fewer men and the same frontier. Mihrdat, the heir who died at the pass, was raised partly here, and his saddle hangs empty in the March House hall.

  • Marzban Piruz Mihran — a hard, competent soldier who would trade the feud for a paid garrison, and cannot say so.
  • Lady Banu Mihran, his wife — runs the march's grain and writes weekly to Persemenid.
  • Arsham Mihran, their son, nineteen — rides with Roxana Surena in the Ravine and has come back speaking like a Malaunian.
  • Spahbed Vahriz Mihran, Piruz's uncle — retired, crippled at the Cloudspine, and the loudest voice for the feud in the north.

Ties: the Cloudspine Feud with House Caerthain; cousin Artabazos Mihran in Persemenid.

House Dezhban Zarate · senior wall-family

Crest: a tower on a ditch · Motto: "Sound" · Seat: the Long Stretch, outer wall

Professionals who have held the longest stretch of the outer wall for nine generations. They were raised to a zarate for it four reigns ago and have never behaved like nobility: they still mix their own mortar, and every Dezhban child lays a course of brick on the Long Stretch before they are allowed to marry.

  • Azata Rostam Dezhban — reports his stretch sound every spring and has never been wrong.
  • Mahsa Dezhban, his granddaughter — keeps the family's tally of every stretch in the wall, not just their own, and knows which ones are lying.

Ties: the Outer Wall; the Counting of the Wall.

House Asbdar Arashshara trading house

Crest: a mare and foal · Motto: "Every rider needs two" · Seat: the Horse-Fair Ground

Women who buy steppe horses, sell remounts to the garrison, and quietly broker Malaunian contracts. The garrison owes them for four years of remounts; they hold the debt as leverage rather than as money, and nobody in Xerastri gets a horse without an Asbdar knowing why.

  • Arashshara Nasrin Asbdar — speaks four steppe dialects and holds the garrison's horse-debt.
  • Yasaman Asbdar, her niece — keeps the Hiring Ground's books and takes a tenth of every Malaunian contract signed there.

Ties: the Horse-Fair Ground; the Mihran studs of Lady Gordiya Mihran.

House Sarvand Zarate · the Satrap's house

Crest: a cypress-spear and a key · Motto: "Hold what is given" · Seat: the Satrap's Residence, inner citadel

A plateau zarate given Xerastri by the present King of Kings as a reward for a loyalty no one now remembers. They are not frontier people and do not pretend to be; they are administrators, and Vindarna Sarvand has administered the garrison into his own pocket with great care and complete legality, so far.

  • Satrap Vindarna Sarvand — pays the soldiers when the throne will not, and is quietly collecting their gratitude.
  • Lady Atossa Sarvand, his sister — keeps the customs ledgers, two sets, both accurate.
  • Farhad Sarvand, his nephew — commands the satrap's new stables and the hundred riders in them.

Ties: the Inner Citadel; correspondence with Shir'abad D'ar.

Notable figures

  • Roxana Surena Warden of the Parthian Ravine — holds the gorge three days from the city with horse-archers the subsidy does not pay for. She comes into Xerastri twice a year, for arrows and for an argument with the satrap, and has lately been seen talking to Tomyra's riders at the Fair.
  • Tomyra of the Lion Grass Malaunian · hired by all, ruled by none — comes to the Horse Fair each year to hear offers, and has taken all three empires' coin. This year she is asking who speaks for Xerastri, and listening to the answers.
  • Bagadata the Lame the King's Eye of Xerastri · retired engineer — limps the walls daily, counts the bricks, and has three letters to Persemenid written and unsent.
  • Herbad Burzin Magus of the Fire-Temple — keeps the fire and the oaths of the wall-families; has been asked by Tomyra's rider whether a Malaunian may swear on the fire.
  • Thousand-Commander Datis Kamboj Commander of the Walls — a ranker who loves the garrison, owes the satrap and is beginning to wonder what happens when those two are different.
  • Dominus Argentar Gunnvor Ironhand Mithril Reserve, Xerastri branch · dwarf — the smallest branch on the continent, which holds the garrison's back pay in escrow until the subsidy arrives; she reports to Lady Isolde Merca that the escrow is now the largest deposit in the north.
  • Oath-Captain Arya Kardar The Ironclad Oath, Xerastri chapter — will fight the steppe, will not fight subjects, and is not sure which the clans are this year.
  • Ustad Mehran Zarrinkamar Chief Engineer — maintains engines with nothing to besiege and has drawn, privately, the plans to besiege Xerastri, because someone should know how.
  • Qutlugh the Hooded Malaunian huntsman of the Hunting Park — runs the satrap's cheetahs and his own clan's messages.

Connections

  • Mithratal and Persemenid — south by the Royal Road, the subsidy's road, with a post-station every day's ride; it arrives late.
  • Duneforged Citadel — the Cloudspine Feud: the Mihran here keep it alive.
  • Shir'abad D'ar — the next frontier seat; its satrap's swelling squadrons ride the same roads.
  • Deiperduem — where the Mithril Reserve's main branch reads Gunnvor Ironhand's reports, and where Malaunian contracts end up in front of the Treaty Hall's lawyers.
  • The Malaunian Steppe and the Parthian Ravine — horse country beyond the wall, and the gorge no army has forced.

The towns

Underground town · Acheaoria · off the Garden Road

De'rakhtak Bon

A town cut into the rock around a living taproot: the region's cold store, and a place where the root is read like a clock.

Codex now: An Acheaorian underground town cut around a taproot — houses in the rock, and a tree above whose roots are the town's calendar.

Ruler
Frataraka Behzad Zirak
Title
Frataraka, under the Satrap of the Throne Plain
Population
c. 3,000
Trouble
A prince's grain filling the deep chambers

From outside: one enormous tree on a bare rise, and a few chimneys. Below, chambers cut into soft rock on several levels, the taproot running down through the heart of them, dressed and exposed. The chambers keep one temperature all year, so the town is the region's warehouse for anything that spoils: fruit, oil, medicine and the seed stock of a dozen villages. Persevalis fruit waits here for the court; a Persevalis pear picked in autumn comes out of De'rakhtak Bon in spring tasting of autumn, and the court pays for the difference. The Bountiful Harvesters keep their reserve here; so, quietly, does the satrapy.

Attackers take the surface in an afternoon; nobody has taken the lower levels, which are narrow, dark and known. The plan has not changed in centuries: give up the top, hold the third level, wait. Sound carries oddly, so the town speaks softly by habit, and outsiders find the hush unnerving before they find it restful. Lamps burn sesame oil, which smokes least; a family's wealth is measured in lamp-hours. The root is the town's clock and its shrine. Its condition, sap, colour and the wet on it, is read for the season, and the readings have been cut into the chamber wall for six hundred years. The town reads the root four times a year at the Reading of the Root, and planting above ground follows it; shows new households the lowest levels at the Descent; and fills up on the Cool Night of high summer, when the whole district comes down to sleep in the chambers.

Since the Peace, carts with the seal of Prince Tiridat, Satrap of the Throne Plain, have filled two whole levels with grain and arrow-shafts, and the Frataraka has been told not to count them. He has counted them anyway, in his head, and does not like the number. Storage fees from the prince's rooms have not been paid; the order not to count them came with an order not to bill them either.

Quarters

The Root Hall Shrine and calendar

Sacred · the Root-Reader, pilgrims, farmers waiting · damp wood, sap, lamp-smoke

The chamber where the taproot is dressed and read, its readings cut into the wall for six hundred years: a column of marks running from floor to ceiling and round the corner. Farmers from the plain wait here on Reading days for the season to be declared. The sap is caught in a silver dish and kept; the oldest dishes are black.

The Cold Levels Storage

Commercial · store-keepers, Harvesters' clerks, guards · cold stone, apples, grain-dust

Third level down and below: the stores, the Harvesters' seed, and the prince's sealed rooms. Each chamber has a keeper and a tally-stick; a missing tally is a hanging matter. The fourth level is the seed vault, where the stock of a dozen villages is kept against famine and handed back only on the Frataraka's seal.

The Lamp Galleries The living levels

Residential · families, oil-sellers, lamp-trimmers · sesame oil, bread, warm wool

First and second levels, where people live in rooms cut off a long gallery, with light-wells to the surface and a common oven at each end. Doors are curtains; privacy is a matter of tact. The Zirak and Sarvi families have galleries of their own, and the lamp-trimmers who keep every corridor lit are paid by the town.

Rule

Frataraka Behzad Zirak keeps the stores and the keys; the Root-Reader, Old Mother Sarv, declares the seasons, and planting above ground follows her, not him. The Harvesters' reserve is under Clerk-Warden Simin Daneh, who answers to her guild in Persemenid. The prince's rooms are watched by a dozen of his household riders under Captain Shapur Varaz, who sleep in the chambers and pay for nothing.

Houses and families

The Zirak family Frataraka's house · store-keepers

Mark: a key over a root · Seat: the Key Gallery, second level

Keepers of the cold stores for seven generations and Frataraka for four. They own no land; they own the keys, and the knowledge of which chamber stays coldest in which year.

  • Frataraka Behzad Zirak — honest, frightened, and keeping a second tally of the prince's rooms in his head.
  • Nushin Zirak, his wife — runs the fee-books, and has sent the unpaid storage bill to Persemenid anyway, in her own name.
The Sarvi family Root-Readers

Mark: a cypress with roots showing · Seat: the Root Hall

The line that reads the root, mother to daughter, since the first marks on the wall. They take no fee and accept every gift; the gifts are larger in bad years.

  • Old Mother Sarv, the Root-Reader — eighty, sharp, and refusing to declare a season she does not understand.
  • Tahmineh Sarvi, her granddaughter and heir — wants to read the root by the old marks alone, and has found marks older than the wall.

Notable figures

  • Frataraka Behzad Zirak governor — wants someone to take the prince's rooms off his hands without anyone noticing.
  • Old Mother Sarv Root-Reader — wants to know why the root bleeds before she speaks.
  • Captain Shapur Varaz Prince Tiridat's household rider — polite, bored, and under orders to let no one past the sealed doors, including the Frataraka.
  • Clerk-Warden Simin Daneh Bountiful Harvesters — has noticed her seed vault is a degree warmer every month.
  • Kaveh the Trimmer lamp-trimmer — walks every corridor nightly and has seen light below the third level where no lamp is kept.

Connections

  • Persemenid — the prince's stores; Persevalis — fruit waiting for the court; Zi'rzamin Dar'a — shares the storage trade.

Caravan town · Acheaoria · the eastern caravan road

Qa'zshahrv'in

A walled square of mud-brick around a pool, and the last certain water for four days: it sells that water by the head and by the beast, as it has for eight hundred years.

Codex now: An Acheaorian caravan town at a qanat head — walled, watered, and the last certain water for four days in any direction.

Ruler
Frataraka Mahrokh Qazi
Title
Frataraka, under the Satrap of Atarabad
Population
c. 2,500, and as many travellers
Trouble
The pool's marks are lower every year

A walled square of mud-brick around a pool (Qa'zshahr'in on Wheelwalker maps). The caravanserai takes a third of the interior; the town crowds into the rest. Outside, nothing: gravel to the horizon in every direction, and the line of qanat shafts marching off to the hills like the holes of a giant flute. The town sits at the outfall of a major channel of the Qanat Network and is the last reliable water on a four-day stretch of the caravan road.

Water is charged per head and per beast, and has been for eight hundred years: a copper a man, three a camel, five a horse, because horses are a luxury out here and should be charged like one. Fodder, repairs and lodging follow. A wall, a gate and about forty men suffice, because destroying the town would close the road for everyone including the destroyer. The real threat is the channel: the muqanni who maintain it are the most protected residents, their families effectively hostages to the town's survival. They are paid double, fed first, and not allowed to leave.

Transactional, multilingual and tightly controlled: water is rationed by household under a rota older than the dynasty, and water-theft is the one crime punished without mercy, by exile into the gravel with a single skin. The caravanserai is a separate world within the walls, and townspeople and travellers mix commercially and almost not at all otherwise. The year has the Clearing, when the muqanni go down feasted and come up feasted, if they come up; the Measuring, when the pool's level is marked publicly on the same day each year (the marks are the town's history, and the recent ones are lower); and Gate Night, when the gate stays open and town and caravanserai eat together.

Since the Peace, caravans have doubled; water has not. Mahrokh Qazi has raised the price twice and been called a thief in four languages. The Wheelwalkers have begun carrying their own water past the town, which costs them a third of their cargo space and the town a third of its income.

Quarters

The Caravanserai A world within the walls

Foreign · caravan-masters, drovers, factors · camel, spice, wet canvas

Travellers' third of the town, run by Arashshara Soheila Ab'kesh, who sets the water price each morning. Stabling below, lodging above, one gate shut at sunset. Suren-Pahlav factors keep a permanent room; so does a Chyrsus Syndicate toll-clerk, unofficially.

The Pool Ward The town proper

Residential · households, water-wardens · cool stone, mint, clay jars

Houses around the pool and its marking-stone; the muqanni's houses nearest the outfall. The marking-stone carries eight hundred years of lines; children learn to count on it, and to notice that the numbers go down.

Muqanni Row The channel-diggers' street

Guarded · muqanni families, rope-makers · lamp-oil, wet rope, fear

A short lane by the outfall with its own gate, where the muqanni live under the town's protection and its watch. Their windows face the channel mouth. Every door has a rope hung beside it, one for each man who went down and did not come up.

Rule

Frataraka Mahrokh Qazi, the "Pool-Mistress", keeps the rota and the gate; Ustad Gav, master of the muqanni, keeps the channel and can stop the town by refusing to go down. Arashshara Soheila Ab'kesh runs the caravanserai and its prices. The forty watchmen answer to Gate-Captain Bijan Sorkh.

Houses and families

The Qazi family Frataraka's house · keepers of the rota

Mark: a bowl with eight lines · Seat: the Rota House on the pool

The family that keeps the water rota and the measuring-stone. They hold no water shares themselves, by ancient rule, so that nobody can accuse them of pouring for their own cups.

  • Frataraka Mahrokh Qazi — the Pool-Mistress, hated by every caravan-master and trusted by every household.
  • Darius Qazi, her son — keeps the old rota scrolls and has found the eight-hundred-year price was once a third of today's.
The Gav family Master muqanni

Mark: a lamp on a rope · Seat: Muqanni Row

Masters of the channel for as long as there has been a channel. They know every shaft by name and every collapse by the year.

  • Ustad Gav, master of the muqanni — broad, silent, and grieving.
  • Roshan Gav, his daughter — reads the channel's air with a candle and wants to go down in her brother's place.

Notable figures

  • Frataraka Mahrokh Qazi the Pool-Mistress — wants the falling water explained before the next Measuring.
  • Arashshara Soheila Ab'kesh mistress of the caravanserai — sets the water price at dawn, and has started selling forward water contracts to caravans not yet arrived.
  • Ustad Gav master of the muqanni — will not go down again without someone to go first.
  • Gate-Captain Bijan Sorkh captain of the forty — a former Immortals sergeant who left the ranks and will not say why.
  • Hamid the Eel Wheelwalker water-carrier — runs water past the town in sealed skins and knows a spring the town does not.

Connections

  • Atarabad — four days west by the caravan road; the Wheelwalkers' far-cousin premium starts here. The Silk Terminus caravans of House Suren-Pahlav water here.

Old town · Acheaoria · the Throne Plain

R'eyshar

An old town living in one corner of its own walls, among orchards, rubble and street names read aloud for streets that are gone.

Codex now: An old Acheaorian town outlived by its own ruins — the living quarter is a fraction of what the walls enclose.

Ruler
Frataraka Nowzar Kuhan
Title
Frataraka, under the Satrap of the Throne Plain
Population
c. 4,000
Trouble
The court wants its archive, and will not say why

Walls enclosing far more ground than is lived in: the living town is a knot of streets in one corner, and the rest of the circuit is orchard, rubble and the outlines of streets nobody has walked in centuries. Walk from the inner quarter to the far gate and you cross five dynasties, each identifiable by its brick: square and yellow, long and red, glazed blue, plain mud, and the oldest, small and grey, stamped with a cord-knot.

It lives on fruit, tiles and salvage. The orchards inside the walls are excellent, watered by channels that predate the current town and kept by families with hereditary rights; its quinces go to the royal table. The tile-kilns turn out glazed work for every satrap's residence on the plain. Salvage, dressed stone, brick and worked metal from the old quarters, is officially forbidden and actually the town's second income; every new house in Persemenid's lower town has a little R'eyshar in it.

The walls are too long to hold, and the town knows it. The written and rehearsed plan is to abandon the circuit and hold the inner quarter, which has worked four times in recorded history. Its people are long-memoried and a little haunted: they know which dynasty built which quarter and will tell you at length, and the town's sense of itself is of something in a late chapter. The Cult of Whispering Roots, outlawed, recruits here successfully, to the satrap's irritation. The year has the Walking of the Circuit, when the full wall is walked and each stretch's condition called out; the Naming of the Streets, when the old streets' names are read aloud from the archive, including those with nothing left on them; and the Grafting, when the orchard families exchange cuttings, which doubles as the marriage market.

Twice since the Peace the Sandglass Circle has asked to borrow the street archive; twice the town has said it is being recopied. The second time, the Circle's clerk asked which streets were being recopied first, and named one.

Quarters

The Inner Quarter The living town

Residential · townsfolk, archivists · kiln-smoke, quince, old paper

Houses, the archive and the tile-kilns, in the corner the town has never lost. The archive is a domed brick room with one door and the Frataraka's key; the street rolls are kept in clay jars by dynasty.

The Empty Quarters Orchard and rubble

Abandoned · orchard families, salvagers, cultists · quince blossom, dust, cut stone

Hereditary orchards on old channels, and the salvagers' paths through what is left of the servants' lanes. Orchard walls are built of salvaged brick in five colours. At night lamps move in the oldest quarter, and nobody asks whose.

The Kiln Yards Tiles and salvage

Industry · tile-makers, stone-dressers, carters · wet clay, glaze, hot brick

By the inner gate, where the kilns fire blue and green tiles and where, behind the kilns, salvaged stone is re-dressed so that no one can tell which quarter it came from. The Kuhan family owns both businesses, which saves argument.

Rule

Frataraka Nowzar Kuhan governs, tolerates the salvage and keeps the archive key; the orchard families' eldest, Arashshara Pari Behi, governs the water and the Grafting. The street archive is kept by Archivist Ferdows, who reads the Naming each year and has read it for forty.

Houses and families

The Kuhan family Frataraka's house · kilns and salvage

Mark: a blue tile with a crack · Seat: the Kiln House, inner gate

The town's richest family, from glazed tiles and from not asking where the stone came from.

  • Frataraka Nowzar Kuhan — tolerant, practical, and frightened of the Sandglass Circle without knowing why.
  • Roya Kuhan, his daughter — runs the salvage crews and has stopped them working the grey-brick quarter.
The Behi family Eldest orchard family

Mark: a quince on a branch · Seat: the Old Orchard by the far gate

Holders of the oldest water rights inside the walls and the court's quince contract.

  • Arashshara Pari Behi — governs the water and the Grafting; arranges marriages with a grafting knife in her hand.
  • Esfandyar Behi, her grandson — a quiet young man the Cult of Whispering Roots has recruited, and who has told her so.

Notable figures

  • Frataraka Nowzar Kuhan governor — wants the archive out of his hands before the court takes it.
  • Archivist Ferdows keeper of the street rolls — has read the Naming for forty years and has always skipped one line.
  • Arashshara Pari Behi orchard eldest — wants her grandson out of the cult and alive.
  • Clerk Haxamanish Sandglass Circle, Persemenid — patient, courteous, and back for a third time.

Connections

  • Persemenid — quinces for the court and a Sandglass Circle that keeps asking; the House of Zindar. Tabrishi'ir — buys salvaged carpet fragments. Persevalis — the Peyvand sell cuttings at the Grafting.

Satrapal seat · Acheaoria · the frontier

Shir'abad D'ar

A lesser satrap's seat behind a lion-carved gate, collecting the full tribute of a wide district and forwarding less of it every year.

Codex now: An Acheaorian frontier town under a lion-carved gate — a satrap's seat, a garrison, and the collection point for tribute nobody wants to forward.

Ruler
Satrap Vaumisa Shir'vand
Title
Satrap of Shir'abad D'ar (a lesser satrapy)
Population
c. 9,000
Trouble
Tribute withheld and squadrons growing

A double gate cut with facing lions, and behind it a town that is mostly administration: the satrap's residence, the treasury, barracks, and the walled yard where tribute is assembled. The lions are re-cut on every satrap's accession at the Lion Gate Rite, so that they are both very old and very sharp; the present pair have Vaumisa Shir'vand's own heavy jaw, which the masons insist is coincidence.

Tribute, and the skimming of it. The town collects from a wide district and forwards a portion to Persemenid, a portion that has shrunk for five years while collection has not. The difference pays for the satrap's household, his expanded squadrons of the Lion's Mane Vanguard, raised locally and paid locally, which is precisely the arrangement the throne has cause to worry about, and a building programme the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger have recorded in unhelpful detail: a new residence wing, a covered riding school, and stables for six hundred horses in a town that officially needs two hundred.

An Ironclad Oath chapter is stationed here too, sworn directly to the throne, and relations are correct and cold. Formal, watchful and factional: everyone of consequence is attached to the satrap's household or to the garrison, and the two do not mix socially. Ordinary townspeople keep clear of both. The Lanterns of Justice ride through twice a year, visible for an hour, which is generally long enough. At the Assembling, the tribute laid out and the tribute that departs are counted by different people; the Riding Out, the squadrons' parade, has grown larger three years running.

The satrap has also sworn a covenant of neighbourhood at Mithratal, which binds him to nothing much except to be seen to be bound. He reads Mithratal's covenant law with great attention, the way a man reads a lock.

Quarters

The Tribute Yard Treasury and residence

Official · clerks, porters, the satrap's household · grain, wool bales, sealing wax

Where the district's goods are laid out, counted twice, and diminished between counts. The residence wing overlooks it, so that the satrap can watch his tribute from breakfast. The treasury vault below has two doors; the Scribe has a key to one.

The Barracks Ward Two forces, one town

Military · Vanguard riders, Oath soldiers · horse, leather, rivalry

Vanguard stables on one side of the street, the Oath's hall on the other; neither drinks in the other's taverns. The new stables run the whole length of the street now, and the Oath's hall looks small beside them, as intended.

The Lion Gate Quarter The town that is not the satrap's

Civic · masons, innkeepers, petitioners · stone-dust, bread, waiting

Inside the double gate, the only part of town with ordinary people in it: masons who re-cut the lions, inns for petitioners, and the market. Everyone here knows the size of the Riding Out to the horse, and talks about it only in whispers.

Rule

Satrap Vaumisa Shir'vand rules; Oath-Captain Zhubin Arzan commands the Ironclad Oath chapter; Scribe Farnaz Daftari of the Infinite Ledger records every refusal; the King's Eye was recalled last year and has not been replaced. The squadrons answer to the satrap's brother-in-law, Spahbed Arshak Karin, of the Persemenid house that paid for a better place on the stair.

Houses and families

House Shir'vand Zarate · the Satrap's house

Crest: two lions facing across a gate · Motto: "The gate is ours" · Seat: the Residence over the Tribute Yard

A frontier zarate that has held this lesser satrapy for three generations and has begun to think of it as a greater one.

  • Satrap Vaumisa Shir'vand — heavy-jawed, patient, and building for something.
  • Lady Apama Shir'vand, born Karin — the link to Persemenid, and the one who reads the court letters first.

Ties: married into House Karin.

The Daftari family Scribal line

Mark: an open ledger · Seat: the Scribes' house by the treasury

A family of Infinite Ledger scribes posted across the empire; Farnaz is the third Daftari to keep this town's books.

  • Scribe Farnaz Daftari — records everything, and has begun to fear for her life.
  • Kurosh Daftari, her young brother and copyist — makes a second copy of every page and hides it.

Notable figures

  • Satrap Vaumisa Shir'vand satrap — wants the ledgers delayed and the throne distracted.
  • Oath-Captain Zhubin Arzan The Ironclad Oath — two hundred men against six hundred horse, and an oath to a throne that has not written in a year.
  • Scribe Farnaz Daftari Scribes of the Infinite Ledger — wants an escort to Persemenid and does not trust the Oath to provide it unseen.
  • Spahbed Arshak Karin commander of the squadrons — ambitious, likeable, and counting horses.

Connections

  • Mithratal — where the satrap swore a covenant of neighbourhood; Xerastri — the next frontier seat, whose satrap writes often; House Karin — paid for a better place on the stair.

Weaving town · Acheaoria · Acheaorian plateau

Tabrishi'ir

Courtyard looms and dyed wool on every roof: carpets knotted over years and sold across three empires, by a town whose real authority is the women who hold the pattern-books.

Codex now: An Acheaorian weaving town — carpets knotted over years, sold across three empires, and the only Acheaorian export the Imperium admits admiring.

Ruler
Frataraka Esfandiar Tarh
Title
Frataraka, under the Satrap of Atarabad
Population
c. 7,000
Trouble
Invictian buyers paying in silver that weighs less every quarter

Courtyard workshops with looms standing full height, and dyed wool drying on every flat roof, so that from above the town is a grid of colour: madder red, indigo, pomegranate-rind yellow, and the walnut brown nobody admits is the most expensive. A court-grade carpet takes years, a dozen hands and the price of a farm; ordinary work goes out in quantity, mostly by Wheelwalker cart. It is the only Acheaorian export the Imperium admits admiring, and Invictian officers' wives buy through Suren-Pahlav factors at Aepistra, at prices that would buy the officers.

Designs are family property in coded pattern-books, kept in the town strongroom and withdrawn only by two members together; stealing one is the town's worst crime. A watch and a low wall are all the defence there is, because the product is wanted by everyone, including everyone who might take it. The workshops are worked largely by women, who hold the designs, the keys and much of the town's real authority. Its people are famously unhurried and exact; a Tabrishi'iri asked to hurry will ask, politely, which part of the carpet you would like to be wrong.

The year has the Cutting, when a finished court piece is cut from the loom in public and seen whole for the first time, even by its weavers; the Dye Days, when the vats are opened and the season's colours fixed (the smell is dreadful and the results decide the year's work); and the Reading of the Books, when apprentices learn to read the coded patterns and a girl becomes a weaver.

Since the Peace, Invictian demand has trebled and Invictian silver has lightened. The town now weighs every Imperial coin twice and accepts Mithril Reserve notes from Deiperduem at a discount the Reserve calls insulting and the weavers call arithmetic.

Quarters

The Loom Courts Workshops

Craft · weaving families · wool, lanolin, tea

Family courtyards with full-height looms, run by the senior weaver of each house. The knotters sing to keep count; each family has its own counting-songs, and a weaver who hums another family's song is assumed to be a spy.

The Dye Yards Vats and roofs

Industry · dyers, mordant-sellers · urine, madder, alum

Where the season's colours are fixed; the smell reaches the next post-station. The dye-masters are men, by tradition, and the only men in Tabrishi'ir whose opinion on colour anyone takes.

The Strongroom Square Books, tolls and buyers

Civic · the arashshara, the Frataraka's clerks, foreign buyers · ink, coin, dust

The square around the vaulted strongroom where the pattern-books lie, with the toll-house on one side and the buyers' inn on the other. Every withdrawal of a book is announced from the strongroom step, with both names.

Rule

The Frataraka governs the gate; the arashshara governs the strongroom. Frataraka Esfandiar Tarh collects tolls and signs what Arashshara Mehri Gereh, keeper of the strongroom keys, has already agreed. The senior weavers meet as the Council of Looms each new moon; the Frataraka attends by invitation.

Houses and families

The Gereh family Arashshara · keepers of the keys

Mark: a knot inside a square · Seat: the Strongroom House

Weavers of court pieces for six reigns and holders of the strongroom keys for four.

  • Arashshara Mehri Gereh — keeper of the keys, who has never let a book out alone.
  • Golbanu Gereh, her daughter — reads old patterns better than anyone alive, and has seen the disputed border before.
The Tarh family Frataraka's house · dye-masters

Mark: a vat with three colours · Seat: the Dye Yards

Masters of the Dye Days and of the town's dealings with buyers, who make their money from colour and their influence from tolls.

  • Frataraka Esfandiar Tarh — signs what is agreed, and is quietly building an export house of his own.
  • Navid Tarh, his son — sells to Invictian buyers at Aepistra and wants to be paid in iron.

Notable figures

  • Arashshara Mehri Gereh keeper of the strongroom keys — wants the border dispute settled before it becomes a feud.
  • Frataraka Esfandiar Tarh governor — wants better silver and more say.
  • Factor Ardashir Suren House Suren-Pahlav buyer — buys court pieces for Aepistra and pays in Invictian silver he knows is light.
  • Golbanu Gereh pattern-reader — believes the disputed pattern is not a pattern at all.

Connections

  • Atarabad — carpets to the bazaar, dyes back; Aepistra — Invictian officers' wives buy through Suren-Pahlav; R'eyshar — salvaged carpet fragments.

Underground town · Acheaoria · a dry valley

Zi'rzamin Dar'a

Eight levels dug under an empty valley, invisible until you touch the door: a refuge that has sheltered whole villages and keeps no lists of anyone, ever.

Codex now: An Acheaorian underground town in a dry valley — dug rather than built, and invisible until you are inside it.

Ruler
Frataraka Pashang Tarik
Title
Frataraka (nominally under the Satrap of the Throne Plain)
Population
c. 2,000, and however many guests
Trouble
Satraps demanding lists that do not exist

A dry valley with nothing in it. The town is entirely below the floor: chambers, stairs and ventilation shafts on eight levels, entered by doorways cut in the valley sides that cannot be seen until you are close enough to touch them. A goatherd on the slope, a few cairns, a smell of bread from nowhere: that is all a traveller will notice, and a wise traveller will not mention the bread.

Refuge, and the fee for it. For centuries the town has taken in people who need not to be found (during the war, whole villages) and it charges fairly and without comment: a fee by the head and the month, payable in coin, goats or labour on the shafts. Otherwise it herds goats above and shares the storage trade with De'rakhtak Bon. Nothing is grown in the valley, which would give it away.

The design is the defence. Passages narrow at each level, doors are round stones rolled across from inside, and the ventilation is deliberately confusing. Two forces have tried to clear it and lost men in the dark; the town's account of both is notably matter-of-fact. Ordered, communal and strict about air: every household serves on the shaft rota, and neglect is treated as attempted murder, because it is. It keeps no written records of guests, ever, which is the whole basis of its trade; satraps have demanded the lists repeatedly and been told, politely, that there are none.
