The year has the Opening of the Shafts, when the ventilation is cleared and tested level by level with the whole town counting off; the Sealing, when the stone doors are rolled shut and the town lives closed for a day and a night; and the Guest Table, where those sheltering are fed once before terms are discussed. The order matters.

Since the Peace the guests have changed. During the war they were villagers; now they are clerks, deserters, a eunuch from the Court of Vipers, and once a Hellenorian who paid in gold and spoke to no one. The fees are up. So is the traffic of polite men on the valley road asking for goat cheese.

Quarters

The Upper Levels The town

Residential · households, herders · goat, bread, cold air

Households, the shaft-rota hall and the goat pens at the valley doors. The rota board is a wall of pegs, one for each household; a missing peg is noticed within the hour.

The Guest Levels Below the fifth door

Hidden · the sheltered, their hosts · lamp-oil, damp, fear

Where the sheltered live, unasked and uncounted. Guests are given a room, a lamp and a name for the town's use, which is never their own.

The Air Galleries The shafts and their keepers

Vital · rota-keepers, the Master of Air · wind, dust, candle-smoke

The maze of vents, baffles and false shafts that keeps eight levels breathing and confuses any enemy. Only the Master of Air knows the whole of it; each rota-keeper knows her own stretch and no more.

Rule

Frataraka Pashang Tarik answers the satraps' demands politely and in person; Master of Air Roudabeh runs the shaft rota, and in a sealing her word overrides his. Terms with guests are set by the Table-Keeper, Old Khorshid, who serves the Guest Table and remembers faces but never names.

Houses and families

The Tarik family Frataraka's house · the door-keepers

Mark: a round stone in a doorway · Seat: the First Door

The family that answers the door, in every sense: they meet satraps' officers on the valley floor so that no officer ever comes inside.

  • Frataraka Pashang Tarik — courteous, immovable, and very good at saying "none".
  • Ilnaz Tarik, his sister — collects the fees and has never written a figure down.
The Havaei family Masters of Air

Mark: three lines rising · Seat: the Air Galleries

Keepers of the ventilation since the first shaft was dug; the Master of Air is always of their blood.

  • Master of Air Roudabeh — can tell a blocked shaft three levels away by the candle-flame.
  • Farzin Havaei, her apprentice son — has been mapping the shafts on paper, which is forbidden.

Notable figures

  • Frataraka Pashang Tarik governor — wants the Lantern gone without a fight.
  • Master of Air Roudabeh keeper of the shafts — wants her son's map found and burned.
  • Old Khorshid Table-Keeper — has fed two clerks the creed believes dead and does not know who they are.
  • "Bird" a guest · eunuch of the Court of Vipers — pays well, talks less, and is waiting for news from Persemenid.

Connections

  • De'rakhtak Bon — storage partners; Persemenid — whose courtiers sometimes need to vanish.

The villages

Island village · Acheaoria (in name) · the inland sea

Azadeh Atoll

A ring of sand and palm around a farmed lagoon, which has never paid tribute to anyone and celebrates the fact annually.

Codex now: An island village of free divers and fishers — a ring of coral with a lagoon inside and no lord over it.

Head
Kadkhuda Marjan Dalir, chosen by the boats
Population
c. 300

A low ring of sand and palm around a pale lagoon, the village on the sheltered side and boats drawn up before every house. Fish, pearls and salt: the lagoon is farmed rather than merely fished, stock moved between stone-walled pens for generations, and the salt-pans on the windward side are worked by the children. Pearls go to the mainland twice a year in one boat, sold through a single broker the village has used for three generations and trusts for exactly that long.

Azadeh pays no tribute to any satrapy and never has, because it is far out, poor-looking and hard to reach in the season when anyone might bother. The villagers cultivate the poor look carefully: the best pearls are never worn on the atoll. The Kadkhuda is chosen by the boats, one vote per hull, on the beach. On the Free Day the last tax-collector's boat is re-enacted, badly, and sunk. The Dalir family, divers for six generations, provide the Kadkhuda more often than not, and Marjan Dalir has held the post through two attempted surveys, both of which ended with the surveyors fed, charmed and sent home with the wrong map.

The Peace has brought more ships to the inland sea, and more ships means more people who might bother.

Island village · Acheaoria · the inland sea lanes

Bahrami Rock

Forty families on a stone stack with a light at the top, paid by both the League and Acheaorian shipping and asked by neither to choose.

Codex now: An island village on a bare stack — a lighthouse, a fishing fleet, and forty families who have not left in four generations.

Head
Kadkhuda Esfand Bahrami, Keeper of the Light
Population
c. 200

A stone stack rising out of open water, houses cut into the landward face, and a stair to the light that is frightening in weather: four hundred and twelve steps, no rail, worn into hollows by eleven generations of feet. The light burns oil and driftwood behind a polished bronze mirror older than anyone can date.

The keepers were paid by the League of the Hellenes and by Acheaorian shipping alike right through the war, without anyone discussing it. Everything not caught is landed from the mainland, and in a bad winter the Rock is alone for weeks; the cisterns are the village's real wealth, and stealing water is the only crime. Forty families have not left in four generations, and marry each other with the help of a very long genealogy painted on the cistern wall. At the Lighting, the first night of the season, every household sends someone up the stair regardless of age or weather. The Bahrami family has kept the light for eleven generations; Esfand Bahrami keeps both sets of pay-books and shows each paymaster only his own.

Since the Peace both paymasters have started asking for receipts.

Island village · Acheaoria · the inland sea, on the flyway

Parvaz Cay

A flat cay under a forest of net-poles, living on two great bird passages a year and idle in between.

Codex now: An island village on the migration path — bird-catchers, feather traders, and a calendar set entirely by what is overhead.

Head
Kadkhuda Parastu Torbaz
Population
c. 250

A flat sandy cay with nets on tall poles over the whole of it and low houses beneath, so that from the water it looks like a wood of bare masts. Twice a year enormous flocks pass over, cranes, geese, quail in clouds, and the village takes, salts and sells meat, down and the long feathers Acheaorian courts pay foolishly for: a heron's crest-plume buys a goat, a matched pair of crane primaries a boat. The catch is salted in clay pits and shipped in casks.

Between passages there is very little to do, and the village fishes, mends nets and is famously idle; the cay's proverb is that a man who works between flights has not understood the arrangement. Watchers sit on platforms at the top of the poles through the passage months and call the flocks in a whistled language. At the First Flight the season's first flock is watched and counted and none of it taken. The count is recorded, and the recent counts are smaller. The Torbaz family keep the count-book, and Kadkhuda Parastu Torbaz has started to fear what it says. The white cranes have never been taken, by a rule older than the count-book.

Part V

Free Lands and Ruins

The neutral treaty city, the dead capital of the dream-walkers, and the villages that belong to nobody.

Neutral city · Held by no empire · Continental interior

Deiperduem City

The city where the war was signed away: walled embassies, the best notaries on the continent, and sixty thousand people who make their living from three empires not trusting each other.

Codex now: Where the Treaty was signed — a neutral city held by no empire, thick with envoys, and living entirely on the peace it hosts.

Ruler
Arbiter Hesper of the Brass Scales, over the Council of Thirty
Title
Arbiter (chosen by lot every three years from three nominees, one per empire)
Population
c. 60,000, of whom perhaps 22,000 are Deiperdene citizens
Built on
A small market town where three road systems meet
Patron
None by law; Concordia, Mercury and Jauhar all have shrines, none has a temple
Trouble
Peace is so stable nobody needs to negotiate, or about to fail

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Deiperduem sits where the territories of the three empires come nearest to meeting, and for most of the Continental War that made it a place armies passed through on the way to somewhere worth burning. Five years ago it became the place they signed. Since then it has rebuilt itself as embassies: walled compounds, each flying its own colours and keeping its own guard, each pretending the others are not watching.

In the middle is the old town, small and unremarkable, and now the most expensive ground on the continent. On its square stands the Treaty Hall, deliberately plain and kept exactly as it was on the day of signing, because no empire could be seen to have built it. The roads in carry constant traffic, almost all of it people with credentials.

Diplomacy is the industry. Deiperduem sells lodging, security, discretion and paper; everything else is imported and marked up. The Caravan of the Gilded Horizon runs three services a week on the Treaty Road, the Mithril Reserve keeps its largest branch outside the Duneforged Citadel here, and the Chyrsus Syndicate holds the city's tolls on a long contract signed when the peace looked fragile.

New lore

Why the lot. The Treaty's drafters could agree that the city must belong to nobody and could not agree on anybody to run it. The compromise was the Arbiter: every three years each empire nominates one Deiperdene citizen, never one of its own subjects, and a child drawn from the Foundlings' House pulls one of three sealed tokens from an urn in the Treaty Hall. Each empire has therefore spent five years cultivating Deiperdene families it can nominate, and every family of note in the city is quietly understood to be "Invictian", "Hellenorian" or "Acheaorian" in the way a horse is understood to belong to a stable.

House-signs, not surnames. Old Deiperdene families take their names from the signs over their doors (the Brass Scales, the Green Lamp, the Seven Quills, the Iron Cup), a habit from the war years when a surname that sounded Invictian or Acheaorian could get a family killed by whichever army arrived next. The custom has hardened into law: a citizen standing for the Council of Thirty must use a house-sign.

The second terror. The codex says the city's fear is that the Treaty holds so well nobody needs to negotiate. In the last year the opposite fear has grown. The guards in the compounds, all described as household staff, now number a little over 1,900 by the Council's count. The Ironclad Legion has 600 men under contract. Every innkeeper can name the three compounds' best swordsmen.

The Treaty Guests. Each empire keeps a high-born guest in a rival's compound, the old hostage custom polished until nobody uses the word. Lucius Valerius Maximus, grand-nephew of the Dominus Militum, lives in the Acheaorian compound and has learned excellent court Acheaorian. Princess Roshanak, a daughter of the King of Kings, lives in the Hellenorian compound and attends lectures by correspondence with the Arcane Academy. Thrasyboulos Nikandrides, nephew of the Hegemon of Hellarchon, lives in the Invictian compound and gambles. All three are allowed the city, never the roads.

Districts

The Old Town Existing · Centre

Notaries, copyists, translators · ink, wax and expensive coffee-substitute

Narrow streets of three-storey houses, each with its sign, and rents that would buy a farm in any province. The notaries, translators and copyists here are the best on the continent and charge accordingly: a sworn translation in all three tongues costs 25 gp a page, and a certified copy of a contract with the seals of two embassies 100 gp. In high summer the Market of Nations fills every lane, each empire's goods in its own quarter. It is nominally a trade fair and in practice the year's most productive week of unofficial negotiation.

Ties: the House of the Seven Quills; the Three Libraries circle copies its comparisons here (Thessalonika, Aeterna, Persemenid).

Treaty Square Old town

The Treaty Hall, the Assayers' Tower, the urn of the lot

The plain hall where the Treaty of Deiperduem was signed, unchanged down to the scuffed table and the chair whose leg the Acheaorian delegation insisted on shortening. Across the square stands the Assayers' Tower, built by a pact of the three powers to settle what is worth what: its stamp on Mithril, Embersteel, Nullstone or Shattergleam is accepted at every court. The wards on the Hall are kept by Aulus Severinus Custos, who has rooms above the archive and is rarely seen leaving them.

Ties: Aulus Severinus Custos; the Assay at the Temple of Juno in Aeterna sends its trial pieces here for a second opinion.

The Embassy Compounds Existing · Ring

Three walled worlds and several smaller ones

The Invictian Legation is a square fort in everything but name, with a parade ground called a garden. The Hellenorian Proxeny is a colonnaded house around a courtyard with a fountain nobody is allowed to drink from. The Acheaorian House of the King's Word is the largest, a walled paradise-garden with a gatehouse painted in tribute processions. Between them sit lodges for the Duneforged Citadel, the Mithril Reserve's guest-house and two Farshore factors who arrived last year and have been watched ever since.

Ties: the Treaty Guests (Lucius Valerius Maximus, Princess Roshanak, Thrasyboulos Nikandrides); Tristan Caesar keeps the Caerthain lodge (Duneforged).

The Caravan Fields Outer city

Where the three road systems end · dust, camels, mules, axle-grease

The flat ground outside the east gate where the Via Septentrionalis spur, the Hellenorian Inland Road and the Acheaorian caravan track all finish at the same row of toll-booths. Caravanserais for the Acheaorian trains, Invictian road-inns with stabling, and the painted wagons of the Wheelwalkers, who camp here more or less permanently and are related to half the drovers in the yard. The Silk Terminus runs through here: House Suren-Pahlav keeps a factor in the largest caravanserai.

Ties: Atarabad, Aepistra, Corinth; Caravan of the Gilded Horizon; the Chyrsus toll-house.

The Counting Ward North of the square

Stone banks, money-changers, the city's richest silence

The Mithril Reserve's great branch, cut from grey stone with no windows below the third storey, faces the Chyrsus Syndicate's toll-house across a street the locals call Interest Lane. The Vaults of Equilibrium keep a smaller office that is losing customers, and a dozen money-changers sit at tables outside weighing debased Invictian silver against the Reserve's published discount, which is chalked on a board each morning and is the most-read text in the city.

Ties: House Ironhand (the branch); Lady Isolde Merca's letters arrive here from Duneforged.

The Quiet Ground West of the walls

A field with three stones and no names

A mown field with three plain stones, one for each empire, each cut with a single number: that empire's war dead as it agreed to report them. At the Quiet Hour on the evening of the Signing, the three numbers are read aloud and the city stops. It is the only occasion on which nobody argues, which is why a great deal of quiet business is done by people standing next to each other in the dark afterwards.

Ties: the Watchers of the Eternal Rest and the Cycle of the Eternal Bloom keep it jointly.

Rule

Arbiter Hesper of the Brass Scales was Hellenoria's nominee and was drawn by lot two years ago. She is a notary by trade, sixty-one, and has made herself acceptable to everyone by being precisely as useful to each empire as to the others. She chairs the Council of Thirty, citizens elected by the city's ten wards, which sets tolls, licenses notaries and publishes the guard count.

Order is kept by the city watch, the Lamplighters, under Captain Brannoc Ise, a half-orc who was a sergeant in no army anyone can name, and by the Ironclad Legion on contract under Prefect Vibius Strabo, whose terms forbid his men to take any other work in the city. The Treaty Hall's wards and the Assayers' Tower answer to nobody, which the Council finds restful.

The envoys: Servius Annaeus Calvus for the Imperium (a patrician the Council of Legates sent here to keep him out of Aeterna); Proxenos Dion Makarios for the League of the Hellenes (a Corinthian, and therefore suspected by Hellarchon); and Ambassador Mehrdad Kāren-Tabar for the King of Kings (old, courteous, and the best-informed man in the city, because the King's Eyes and Ears report to him before they report home).

Houses and families

The House of the Brass Scales Notaries · Arbiter's house

Sign: a brass balance over the door · Motto: "Weighed, not judged" · Seat: a narrow house on Treaty Square

Four generations of notaries who drew up surrender terms for all three empires during the war, often in the same month. Counted "Hellenorian" because Hellenoria nominated Hesper; the family considers this an accident and is careful to keep it one.

  • Hesper of the Brass Scales, the Arbiter — reads every document twice and every envoy once.
  • Corvin of the Brass Scales, her son, senior notary — drafts the annual Signing speeches for two of the three embassies, which neither knows.
  • Little Ana, her granddaughter, eleven — wants to be the Foundlings' House child who draws the lot, and has been told that is impossible.

Ties: the Proxeny of Hellarchon; the Corinthian counting-houses (Corinth).

The House of the Green Lamp Innkeepers

Sign: a green glass lamp, lit day and night · Motto: "No opinions on the premises" · Seat: the Green Lamp inn, Old Town

Keepers of the most famous neutral inn on the continent, where the three delegations drank, separately and at the same time, through the last month of negotiations. An innkeeper who has an opinion loses half a clientele; the Green Lamp has not had an opinion in ninety years and is rich.

  • Mother Ottla of the Green Lamp, proprietor — seats rivals back to back, never face to face.
  • Jory of the Green Lamp, cellarman — sells to the Whispering Eyes what is said in the snug, and believes nobody knows.

Ties: the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon lodges its drivers here; Thrasyboulos Nikandrides owes the house 340 gp.

House Ironhand of Deiperduem Mithril Reserve · Clan Ironhand

Crest: an iron gauntlet closed on a silver bar · Motto: "Fides in Metallo" · Seat: the great branch, Counting Ward

The dwarven line that runs the Reserve's largest branch outside the Duneforged Citadel. Their basalt ledgers record every Permutatio letter between the empires, which makes this branch the best picture anywhere of who is paying whom.

  • Dominus Argentar Hildra Ironhand, branch master — has refused two embassies' requests to "consult" the ledgers and accepted the third's, for a fee, in front of the other two.
  • Brokk Ironhand, her nephew, captain of the Custodes — has never lost a coin and is bored.
  • Seren Vaal, Arcanist-Securitas — a gnome abjurer trained by Aulus Severinus Custos, and his only regular visitor.

Ties: House Merca (Duneforged); every city's Dominus Argentar reports discounts here.

The House of the Seven Quills Copyists

Sign: seven quills in a jar · Motto: "Every word, no more" · Seat: a scriptorium on Notaries' Row

The copying house that holds the contract for the Treaty's official copies. Counted "Acheaorian", because the House of the King's Word has used it for twenty years. Its master copyist is one of three people living who has handled the original Treaty.

  • Master Ilkin of the Seven Quills — can reproduce any hand in the three empires and has sworn never to.
  • Tamsa of the Seven Quills, his daughter — runs the Three Libraries' copying in secret on the top floor.

Ties: the Sage's Archive (Persemenid); the Porticoes (Thessalonika).

Notable figures

  • Lucius Valerius Maximus Treaty Guest · Invictian, 23 — the Dominus Militum's grand-nephew, living among Acheaorians; affable, bored, and writing letters home that the Acheaorian compound reads with great interest and that say exactly what he wants them to read.
  • Princess Roshanak Treaty Guest · Acheaorian, 19 — a daughter of Shahanshah Vishtaspa III, lodged with the Hellenorians; studying evocation by letter, and asking pointed questions about the violet sky over Hellarchon.
  • Thrasyboulos Nikandrides Treaty Guest · Hellenorian, 26 — the Hegemon's nephew, lodged with the Invictians; a gambler with real debts, which every embassy knows and two have offered to pay.
  • Captain Brannoc Ise Lamplighters · half-orc — runs a watch of 300 that is outnumbered by every compound's "household staff"; keeps a private tally of every guard he has seen drill.
  • Prefect Vibius Strabo Ironclad Legion — six hundred professionals on a contract that ends next spring; he has been approached about renewal by all three embassies and by somebody who will not give a name.
  • Factor Oribasios Kell Chyrsus Syndicate — holds the tolls, knows every caravan's cargo, and is lobbying to have the contract extended before anyone reads it again.
  • Aulus Severinus Custos Warden of the Treaty Wards — the Invictian-born abjurer who keeps the Hall unbreakable and the Treaty unstolen.

Connections

  • Aepistra — the Invictian end of the Treaty Road and the Silk Terminus; the Legation's couriers ride this way.
  • Corinth and Thebesieas — the Hellenorian Inland Road; Corinthian bankers handle most Hellenorian Permutatio letters here.
  • Atarabad — the Acheaorian caravan track; House Suren-Pahlav's trains arrive weekly.
  • Duneforged Citadel — the Mithril Reserve's headquarters; Lady Isolde Merca's letters; Tristan Caesar's lodge.
  • Aeterna, Hellarchon, Persemenid — the three capitals' envoys and the Treaty Guests.
  • Zandar Isle — what the Counting Ward will not carry, Zandar will.

Ruined capital · Nethrana, the Kingdom of Mirrors and Mist · Velothis

Eronis

The dead capital of the dream-walkers: a city nobody has lived in for centuries that has not stopped working.

Codex now: Capital city of Nethrana, seat of the dream-walkers.

Ruler
None; once the Council of Eronis
Status
Ruin, uninhabited, visited by expeditions and salvagers
Population
None resident; perhaps 200 visitors in a season
Built on
An island whose shape is not agreed to be natural
Patron
Unknown; the murals show gods nobody can name
Trouble
The ruins still function, and someone has opened a door from below

Faith: The temples, shrines and cults of this city

The city

Eronis was the capital of Nethrana and the seat of the Council of Eronis, dream-walkers and illusionists whose reach is said to have run well past their own borders. What stands now is walls lined with shimmering murals that change if you look at them too long, an avenue of black-green cypresses still alive among the rubble, and at the centre the Palace of Eronis, a labyrinth of enchanted glass and stone whose corridors defeated its own architects and do not stay where they are put.

Ruins do not usually keep working. Eronis appears to be an exception. Lamps that have no oil light at dusk; fountains run in a city with no aqueduct; and visitors agree that the shadows on the Mourning Cypress Walk fall the wrong way.

New lore

Velothis, the island. Eronis stands on Velothis, an island one account calls a god's gift and another an accident of magic that reshaped the land and left an empire standing on the result. It is also where the fall of Mycairos stopped: their armies stood poised to take it, and then their own cities were empty and the campaign was simply over. The bronze siege camp they left on the eastern shore is still there, the tent-pegs green with age and the cook-pots full of sand.

Irelas, the port. A day's walk from the capital, Irelas was where a kingdom of mirrors and mist sold things: enchanted textiles, illusions frozen in glass, ships that sailed without flapping sails. Its quays are intact. Salvagers from Zandar Isle work them in the calm months and leave before the autumn fogs, because the fog in Irelas harbour shows ships that are not there and hides ones that are.

Who comes now. Since the Treaty, expeditions have returned: the Arcane Academy of Hellarchon under Kallisto Pyrphoros's seal, the Sage's Archive of Persemenid, the Enchanted Muse's dream-readers, the Sanctuary of the Silver Veil (who would like everything found here buried again), and the Whispering Eyes (who would like to sell it). All of them are also looking for the same woman: Vesperine Ilaro, who is said to be the last Nethranan dream-walker and to have been seen on the Cypress Walk in daylight.

Districts

The Palace of Eronis Centre · labyrinth

Glass, stone and corridors that move

The seat of the Council and the heart of every legend about portals into dreamscapes. The corridors rearrange when nobody is watching them; expeditions mark walls with chalk and come back to find the chalk on the ceiling. A dungeon that rearranges is only frightening if the party can tell that it has, so the Palace has landmarks: a hall of thirteen empty thrones, a mirror that shows the room one minute ago, and a door of black glass that no expedition has opened.

Ties: Vesperine Ilaro; the Arcane Academy (Hellarchon).

The Mourning Cypress Walk Existing site · north avenue

Black-green trees that never shed · the royal necropolis

A long avenue of cypresses planted by a dynasty that planned its own funeral. The trees have outlived the dynasty and the city; the burial-gardens at the end are planted with Vital Mauveroot, which the dream-walkers claimed could keep the dead from decay. The trees all lean the same way, as though listening, and at the avenue's end a door has been opened from below.

Ties: herbalists from Willowheart pay well for Mauveroot cuttings and ask no questions.

The Mural Streets Residential ruins

Rubble houses and walls that keep painting themselves

The old residential city, mostly rubble, except the walls, which are lined with murals in Nethrana's pictorial script. Each symbol changes meaning with the light, and the scenes change if watched for longer than a slow count of a hundred. Scholars copy them at dawn, noon and dusk and get three different texts. One mural, near the old water-court, shows three suns in the sky.

Ties: the Three Libraries circle compares copies (Thessalonika, Persemenid).

The Quays of Irelas Port ruin · a day's walk

Magnificent docks, empty slipways, the wrong ships in the fog

Nethrana's trade port, its stone quays still sound, its warehouses roofless. Salvagers dive for the glass cargoes of ships that sank at their moorings; an unbroken "frozen illusion" sells in Romulo for the price of a house. The salvagers' camp is the only place on Velothis with a fire at night.

Ties: Zandar Isle; foreign buyers in Romulo and Mavelon.

The Bronze Camp Eastern shore

Where the Mycairos army stopped

The siege camp of the army that came to take Velothis and found nobody to fight. It was abandoned when the soldiers' own cities fell silent: tents rotted to their pegs, bronze weapons still racked, and a field altar carved with a phrase in Mycairos runes that scholars render "the gift beneath stone". Nobody takes the bronze home. The salvagers say it is because it is cursed; the truth is that it is heavy and the curse is a useful rumour.

Ties: the Mycairos ruins in the Hellenorian hills (Thebesieas).

Rule

Nobody rules Eronis. No empire claims Velothis, because no empire can say what it would be claiming. Expeditions agree among themselves, at the salvagers' fire, which halls each will work; the agreements are honoured about as well as the Palace corridors stay put.

Notable figures

  • Vesperine Ilaro the Last Dreamwalker — hunted by three powers, seen on the Cypress Walk in daylight, and apparently looking for something herself.
  • Dagny Saltfinger salvage-boss · Zandar Isle — runs the Irelas diving crews; has a list of the cargoes still on the harbour floor and of which buyers in Romulo pay in coin rather than promises.
  • Exetastes Philon Damaskenos Arcane Academy expedition leader — careful, frightened and correct to be; carries orders under seal that he is not to open until he reaches the black glass door.
  • Haftvad of the Sage's Archive Acheaorian epigrapher — copying the three-suns mural; has begun to believe that "the Third Sun" is not a prophecy but a date.

Connections

  • Zandar Isle — the nearest working anchorage and the salvagers' home port.
  • Hellarchon, Persemenid, Persevalis, Delphara — the Dreamers' Hunt for Vesperine Ilaro.
  • Romulo — where Nethranan glass is registered and sold to Farshore buyers, legally or nearly.
  • Marshroot Grove — the reed-cutters' nets bring up pale carved stone that matches the Palace walls.

Island village · Free · between three jurisdictions

Zandar Isle

A fishing station on paper and the quiet route between three empires in fact, with more boat-sheds than boats and more boats than fishermen.

Codex now: An island village of boatwrights and smugglers — officially a fishing station, actually the quiet route between three empires.

Head
Hull-Reeve Abelard Tunny, chosen yearly by the boat-owners
Population
c. 260, double in the smuggling season
Trouble
Everyone wants Zandar to stay unimportant

A wooded island with a hidden anchorage on the lee side, a handful of houses and a great many boat-sheds. Zandar lives on fishing, boatbuilding and moving things that would be taxed elsewhere. It sits where three jurisdictions almost meet and none quite reaches. The Veilborn Syndicate uses the anchorage, carefully and within its ceiling; the Aurum Pact certifies cargo here that would fail anywhere else; and since the Treaty the salvage crews who work the quays of Irelas on Velothis winter here and sell their glass through the island's middlemen to buyers in Romulo and Mavelon.

Who runs it. The boat-owners choose a Hull-Reeve each spring. The present one, Abelard Tunny, is a boatwright with a talent for forgetting what he has seen. The family that matters is the Saltfingers: Dagny Saltfinger runs the Irelas salvage, her brother Orm keeps the best pilot's charts of the three coasts, and their mother, Old Hild, has been paid by all three empires' customs officers, and remembers which ones.

The Counting of Hulls. Every boat on the island is drawn up and counted on the same day. The count is always exactly what was declared, which has made it a joke. Nobody mentions the boat-sheds that are never opened on that day.

Swamp village · Free · Maeotis Helos

Marshroot Grove

Reed-cutters on stilts who have paid tribute to three empires, sometimes at once, and have changed nothing in a thousand years.

Codex now: A swamp village on stilts in the Maeotis — reed-cutters who pay tribute to whoever asks and change nothing.

Head
Pile-Elder Wenna Reedmother
Population
c. 180
Trouble
The nets keep bringing up carved stone

Platforms and walkways on piles above black water, roofed in reed, the whole village shifting a little every year as the channels move beneath it. Marshroot cuts, bundles and sells reed for roofing and matting across the region and moves its walkways when the water decides. No army has ever profitably come further into the Helos: a column enters, the guides prove unreliable, the water rises, and a smaller column comes out somewhere unintended.

Who runs it. The oldest person who can still walk the piles is the Pile-Elder. Wenna Reedmother is seventy-four and walks them daily. Her rule on tribute is simple: pay whoever asks, in reed, promptly, and never let a tax-collector stay the night. The tribute receipts nailed to the meeting-house wall come from all three empires and from two that no longer exist.

The Moving. When a walkway must be shifted the whole village does it in a day, and the old piles are left standing as a record of where the village used to be. The oldest piles are stone, not wood, and nobody remembers sinking them.

Swamp village · Free · Maeotis Helos

Willowheart Enclave

Herbalists and midwives living in one enormous willow, whose bark-medicine is sold across three empires and whose recipe is sold to nobody.

Codex now: A swamp village around a single vast willow — herbalists and midwives whose reputation reaches well beyond the marsh.

Head
Mother of the Bark, Isaura Fenwick
Population
c. 120
Trouble
The Luminastra Alchemists want the method, not the medicine

One enormous willow stands out of the water, and the village is built into and around it on platforms among the roots, so that the tree is structure and shelter at once. Willowheart's bark preparations for pain and fever are the best in the region and its midwives are sent for from towns three days away. The Luminastra Alchemists buy here and have never persuaded the enclave to sell the method, only the preparation.

Who runs it. The Mother of the Bark allots which sections of the tree may be stripped each year, and her word on the tree is final. Isaura Fenwick has held the office for twenty years. Her deputy, the Midwife-Warden Tovah Brightwater, keeps the register of every child the enclave has delivered across three empires, a list that would interest several noble houses a great deal.

The Stripping. Bark is taken from allotted sections under supervision so strict it is effectively a rite. Taking unallotted bark is the one offence that gets a person expelled. Two were expelled last year, and one of them now works for the Luminastra Alchemists in Ephelanum.

Faith

Temples, Shrines and Hidden Faiths

Every city’s house of many gods, its own temples, the forgotten ones, the hidden ones, and the cult in the cellar, with the priestly families who run them.

The faith of the Imperium: a contract, kept in writing

Invictians do not ask whether the gods are listening. They ask whether the rite was done correctly. Religion in the Imperium is a contract between the state and its gods: the state sacrifices on the right day, in the right words and with an unblemished animal, and the gods keep the state. A temple is a public institution with a roof, a treasury and a staff, and a priest is a magistrate with an altar. Belief is permitted. Nobody checks for it. The gods could not come to collect in person if they wished: since the Recessio Deorum the grey fog has kept them in the Capitol Above, and only their grace comes down, thinnest-filtered at the greatest altars.

The College of Pontiffs. Fifteen pontiffs keep the calendar, the lists of lucky and unlucky days, the rules of every rite and the register of every temple. The augurs read the birds before any public act. The Imperator was always Pontifex Maximus, and the chair is empty, so the college governs itself by seniority. Its senior member, Manius Furius Aquila, is ninety-one and hard of hearing, and he sits in the Pantheum at Aeterna. The correct versions of the rites are kept at Romulo, where the Rex Sacrorum and the Virgo Maxima of Vesta rule on practice. Their rulings bind every temple in the Imperium, Aeterna's included, which Aeterna dislikes. Without a chief pontiff nobody can declare a new festival, so the Legates pay for "games of thanksgiving" and build victory temples instead. Every one of those temples wants carved doors from Nemorus.

Licences. No temple may stand inside a sacred line without a dedicatio by a pontiff and a lex templi filed at Romulo. The lex is cut on a stone by the door and fixes the god, the tariff of sacrifices, the days of opening and what may not be brought inside. Unlicensed gods may be worshipped outside the line, which is why every Invictian city has a far bank, a canabae or a quay where the foreign altars stand. Farshore gods are licensed as hospites, guests, for one sailing season at a time, and must leave with their ships. A licensed god's priests may own land, take deposits and sue. An unlicensed god's priests may do none of these things, and in a city may be fined or chained for public rites.

Money. A temple lives on five purses. It has its sacred estates, worked by tenants and managed by the priests. It has its fees, the tariff on the door: a lamb at the Temple of Juno costs a denarius, and an oath witnessed by the Oathbound Sanctum costs ten. It has the state stipend, paid each quarter through the college, now in debased coin. It has deposits, because temples are the oldest banks in the Imperium and a god is a better guard than a strongroom. And it has the votives, which are melted down every fifty years in a rite called the Renewal. Every temple sends a tenth of its fees to its mother-temple, the decima matris. Daughter-temples copy their mother's cult statue, rites and calendar, and a priest ordained at a mother may serve at any of her daughters.

The Iter Sacrum. The pilgrim road ties the cities together. A pilgrim starts at Vesta's hearth in Romulo, lights a lamp there and buys a lead token stamped with the hearth. Each great temple on the way punches it. The route runs up the Via Sacra Aeterna to the Arx and the Pantheum, out to the grove at Nemibano and the wine-altar at Falecosa, down the Tiberius past Portunus at Fucostia, by sea to the Keelhall at Mavelon, and down the Via Ferraria to the Citadel Cathedral at Duneforged. A northern branch runs through Anticata to the Capitolium of Aepistra. A pilgrim with all eleven punches may be buried by the Cycle of the Eternal Bloom at no charge. Since the Concord the road has filled with veterans walking it for exactly that reason.

What is spreading. The state cult is old and orderly, and it is losing customers. Discharged legionaries brought home gods they met on campaign. The Mithradaic brotherhood holds oath-feasts in caves under legion fortresses. The continental dark cults have found the peace congenial. The Mother of Corruption needs only a repair left undone, and the Imperium is now made of those. Shaking Rest sits with dying veterans in the Tent Rows and tells them, kindly, that rest is not what waits. The Mending Needle opens accounts in Romulo, where people have a great deal they want mended. The Masque of Eternal Revelry has gone back to the wine country, and something under Mavelon's caldera has begun to be prayed to again.

Temples · Aeterna

The Temples of Aeterna

A capital of four hundred altars, a college of pontiffs with no head, and a domed hall built exactly on the line no soldier may cross under arms.

Pantheon building
The Pantheum, the House of All Gods, on the sacred line at the Campus gate
Chief priest
Pontifex Manius Furius Aquila, senior of the College of Pontiffs, aged ninety-one
Patron gods
Jupiter and Juno on the Arx; Ceres on the commons' hill; Mars and Bellona outside the line
Banned here
Unlicensed rites inside the sacred line; weapons in any temple except the outer half of the Pantheum
Trouble
A headless college that alone can declare the chair empty, and a spear somebody wants thrown

The Pantheon

The Pantheum. At the foot of the Campus Hastarum, where the Via Triumphalis leaves the city, stands a drum of brick-faced concrete a hundred and fifty feet across. It is roofed with an unsupported dome and lit by a single round opening at the top, the Eye. A portico of sixteen grey Oros columns faces the city. The sacred line runs through the building. The surveyors who laid it out four centuries ago put the boundary stones where the augurs told them to, and the augurs put them through the middle of the floor. A strip of bronze, polished by feet, crosses the marble from wall to wall under the Eye. The portico and the eastern half of the rotunda are inside the line. The western half is not.

That accident gives the building its use. It is the one roof in Aeterna under which the gods of the city and the gods of war can stand together, so it is where the Imperium makes its public vows. A Legate coming home lays down his command on the outer half, steps over the bronze and is a citizen again. The Senate receives enemy envoys here now that Bellona's temple is full of soldiers. When rain falls through the Eye it drains through twenty-two holes in the floor, and Aeternans say the city is the only place where the gods get wet.

The order of the gods. Thirteen niches ring the drum, and their order is fixed by the college. Facing the door, in the great apse, stands Jupiter Optimus, a seated goliath in gilt bronze with the thunderbolt across his knees. On his right is Juno, holding the scales of the Standard, and on his left Minerva with her stylus. These three are the Capitoline triad, copied from the Arx. Clockwise after Juno come Vesta, who has no image and is a lamp that is never allowed to go out, then Ceres, Mercury, Neptune and Diana. Anticlockwise after Minerva come Vulcan, Janus and Venus. On the outer half, beyond the bronze, stand Mars and Bellona, the only statues in Aeterna holding drawn weapons, because they are the only ones standing outside the line. Janus has a niche of his own and also a second, two-faced statue in the doorway, so that every visitor passes him twice.

The thirteenth niche. Between Venus and Mars one niche is empty, hung with a purple cloth that is changed on the first of every month, the same day as the cushion on the empty chair. Twenty years ago, in the flush of a victory, the Senate voted a statue of Iovianus Sandarion "to stand among the gods when the time comes". The statue was carved and is in a crate in the crypt. A statue in a niche makes a man a god, and in the Imperium the only way to become a god is to die first. Every month the purple cloth is lifted, the empty niche is shown to the college, and the cloth goes back. It is the most closely watched liturgy in the city.

Its priests. The Pantheum is the seat of the College of Pontiffs, which meets in the Regia, a low annex behind the apse, and keeps the calendar there on bronze tablets. Its senior, Pontifex Manius Furius Aquila, is ninety-one and hears only what is shouted. He was ordained under the last Imperator who held the chief pontificate, he has outlived nine colleagues, and he presides at every new moon from a chair carried in by four freedmen. His grand-niece Furia Sabina is the college's secretary. She sets his agenda, writes his rulings, and speaks into his good ear. The Furii have held a pontifical seat for eleven generations; see gens Furia.

Temples

The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Jupiter · the northern summit of the Arx

Head priest: the Flamen Dialis, Titus Fabricius Vatia · state treasury of oaths · thunder-stones and burnt fat

The oldest and largest temple in the capital, raised on a podium of tufa blocks the size of carts. Its three cellae are kept for the triad, but the god of the house is Jupiter. A Legate swears his command here and leaves his first spoils here. The roof is gilded bronze and is regilded whenever a war is won, which means it has not been regilded in five years and has begun to show green. The Flamen Dialis, Titus Fabricius Vatia, is the most restricted man in the Imperium. He may not touch iron, ride a horse, look on an army in arms, take an oath, or spend a night outside Aeterna. He is therefore the one man in the capital who has never seen the legions camped at the boundary. He finds this restful.

Rites and festivals: the Ides sacrifice of a white ox each month; the Feast of the Thunder in high summer, when the Senate dines with the god's statue; and the Oath of Command, now rare. Money: the spoils treasury, which no living person has audited, and a fee of a hundred denarii for every oath of command. Politics: the Stormlord Vanguard keeps an honour guard on the temple steps, swore to the Treaty here, and does not like what it swore.

Ties: mother-temple to Jupiter of the Standards at Aepistra; daughter of Jupiter Lapis at Romulo; gens Fabricia; the Arx.

The Temple of Juno of the Warning Juno · the southern summit of the Arx

Head priest: Junia Tertulla, Keeper of the Standard · mint, geese and the Assay · incense, hot metal and goose

The temple where the Assay is held. Juno's precinct contains the Imperial Mint, the Geese Court and the strongroom of the Standard, so the goddess of oaths is also the goddess of money. Every Invictian coin is struck within her walls and weighed on her steps. The temple has seven priestesses and a male staff of forty, most of them assayers. Junia Tertulla presides at the quarterly Assay and reads the figures aloud whatever they are. She was ordained at the mother-temple in Romulo, writes daily and unhappily to the Oathbound Sanctum, and is the only priest in Aeterna who checks the geese herself before dawn.

Rites and festivals: the quarterly Assay; the Matronalia, when the wives of Aeterna bring gifts and the Mint closes; and the Feeding of the Geese, done each morning at public expense. Money: a fortieth of every bar struck, plus deposits from half the patrician remnant. Politics: the Seekers of Eternal Truth have petitioned to watch the Assay from inside the strongroom. Quaestor Asellus opposes the petition on grounds of sanctity.

Ties: daughter of Juno of the Weights at Romulo; sister to the Temple of Juno in the Citadel Cathedral; sends trial pieces to the Assayers' Tower at Deiperduem.

The Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera Ceres · the crown of the Mons Cerealis

Head priest: Sacerdos Cerialis Plautia Rufina · the commons' temple · flour, wax and queue

The plebeians' temple, built when the commons' hill was outside the city and the patricians would not share the Arx. It has an archaic portico of painted terracotta and a cella crowded with ex-votos in the shape of wheat-ears, loaves and ploughs. The dole office sits in its portico, so every citizen's tessera is checked under the goddess's eye. The temple also keeps the archive of the plebeian aediles and the copies of every law the commons ever forced through. Plautia Rufina is a miller's widow, the first plebeian in thirty years elected priestess by the hill's collegia, and she has said from the steps what the granaries hold. The Prefect of the Annona has asked her twice not to.

Rites and festivals: the Cerealia in spring, with foxes loosed in the Circus carrying torches; the Opening of the Mundus is not hers, whatever the hill says. Money: the Golden Harvest Covenant pays a tithe in grain, which is now worth more than silver. Politics: whoever controls this portico controls the queue, and the queue is where riots start.

Ties: mother of Ceres of the Annona at Fucostia and the estate-temple at Aepistra; the Mons Cerealis; Falecosa sends its first must here.

The Temple of Bellona and the War Column Bellona · the Campus Hastarum, outside the line

Head priest: the Bellonarius Lucius Atilius Serranus · armed priests · blood, oiled leather and smoke

A dark, narrow temple with no windows and a black marble floor, dedicated in a war nobody now remembers to win. Before it stands the war column, a short pillar over which the fetial priest throws a spear into "enemy ground" to declare war. Nobody has thrown one in five years. The Obsidian Phalanx is sworn to Bellona, not to the state, and quarters beside her. Lucius Atilius Serranus leads the Bellonarii, priests who cut their own arms on the Day of Blood and offer what runs. He keeps the spear, a plain ash shaft with an iron head, in a case beside the altar. He has had three offers for it this year.

Rites and festivals: the Day of Blood in spring; the Spear Rite, unperformed; and the monthly Lustration of the Phalanx, now held at night by torchlight. Money: a share of every legion's spoils by ancient right, so nothing at all since the Concord, and gifts from the Legates, which are plentiful. Politics: the most dangerous building in Aeterna, because a priest can start a war here without asking anyone.

Ties: the Campus Hastarum; gens Atilia; Decimus Aurelianus Corvus sacrifices here monthly; the Obsidian Phalanx.

The forgotten temple

The Temple of Cronus, under the Forum. At the Forum's west end, behind the Basilica of Aeterna, eight grey columns stand on a podium with no roof, and most Aeternans think they are part of the basilica. They are the front of the oldest temple in the city, dedicated to Cronus, the Titan of Time and Harvest, from the days when the Titans had not yet been put down and the Imperium was a hill town that counted its grain in a god's cellar. The vaults under the podium were the state treasury for three centuries, the Aerarium Vetus, until the treasury moved to Juno's Arx and the Titan was struck from the calendar.

His festival survives without him. At midwinter, in the Insulae, masters serve their slaves at table for one night and a mock-king rules each tenement block until dawn. The pontiffs have banned it four times. The vaults still hold the Republic's war-chest: forty bronze-bound chests that the last free Senate sealed and swore would be opened only "when the Republic is restored". The Calpurnii have the oath by heart. The Basilica's clerks use the podium steps to eat lunch.

Priestly houses

gens Furia Patrician · pontifical house

Crest: a bronze tablet under a crescent · Motto: "Dies fasti, dies nefasti" (Days for business, days for none) · Seat: a cramped old house behind the Regia

Pontiffs for eleven generations and keepers, by custom, of the calendar tablets. The Furii decide which days are lucky, which means they decide when the Senate may meet, when a Legate may march and when a debt falls due. They have used this sparingly for three hundred years, and everyone knows they could stop. They are poor, proud, and courted by every faction now that the college alone can declare the chair empty.

  • Pontifex Manius Furius Aquila, senior of the college — ninety-one; hears only shouting, and has therefore heard every argument in the college at its loudest and least sincere.
  • Furia Sabina, his grand-niece, secretary of the college — forty; writes his rulings and has started deciding, very slightly, what he hears.
  • Publius Furius Philus, pontiff — Sabina's brother; gentle, melancholy and a swing vote; pays for the Tent Rows' funerals and attends a reading in the Gullet.
  • Furia Minor, nine — already reciting the unlucky days; the Vestals have asked for her.

History and lore: a Furius was the pontiff who fixed the boundary through the Pantheum's floor, and the family keeps his augur's staff. Family lore says that whenever a Furius dies the Eye of the dome drops one drop of water out of a clear sky. The college clerks have recorded it seven times.

Ties: the Pantheum; the Rex Sacrorum at Romulo, whose rulings they enforce and resent.

gens Fabricia Patrician · Flamines Diales

Crest: a white peaked cap with an olive twig · Motto: "Non tango" (I do not touch) · Seat: the Flamen's house on the Arx, which may have no knot tied anywhere in it

The family from which the Flamen Dialis has been chosen for nine generations, because the office requires a man married by the oldest rite to a woman also married by it, and almost nobody else still marries that way. The Fabricii marry cousins to keep the qualification, live under the Flamen's taboos, and are the most ceremonially pure household in the Imperium. They are also the most bored.

  • Titus Fabricius Vatia, Flamen Dialis — has never seen a soldier under arms and believes the Imperium is basically at peace with itself.
  • Fabricia Vera, his wife, the Flaminica — must also not be widowed; if she dies he must resign, so the household guards her more closely than the Mint.
  • Gaius Fabricius, their son — heir to the cap; a quiet student of the augural books.
  • Aemilia Tertia, Gaius's wife — restless, clever, and a visitor to the Castellum of the Gullet.

History and lore: the first Fabricius Flamen was struck by lightning on the Arx steps and walked away with his cap smoking, which the family takes as a contract. Every Flamen's cut hair and nails are buried under a fruit tree in the temple precinct; the tree is three hundred years old and bears every year.

Ties: the Temple of Jupiter; Jupiter Lapis at Romulo.

gens Atilia Plebeian · Bellonarii and fetials

Crest: a spear over a broken cup · Motto: "Hasta loquitur" (The spear speaks) · Seat: a fortified house on the Campus Hastarum

Plebeian war-priests who have held Bellona's cult and the fetial office together for two centuries. The fetial is the priest who declares war, so the Atilii can start one. They are scarred, devout and well connected to the officer class, and since the Concord they have been the most visited family on the Campus.

  • Lucius Atilius Serranus, Bellonarius and fetial — keeps the spear; has refused three offers and has not reported any of them.
  • Atilia Calva, his sister — runs the temple's treasury and the Phalanx's victualling contracts.
  • Marcus Atilius Regulus, his nephew — a centurion of the Obsidian Phalanx; drills at night and says nothing at dinner.

History and lore: the family claims a fetial who threw the spear so hard that it went through the war column, and the hole is still there. The spear in the case is said to be the same spear. It is not; it is the fourth.

Ties: the Temple of Bellona; the Obsidian Phalanx; gens Valeria, who watch them.

Temples · Romulo

The Temples of Romulo

The senior altars of the Imperium: a first fire that has not gone out in nine centuries, a god who is a flint, and a long low house that keeps the true face of every god as the city keeps its ancestors.

Pantheon building
The Atrium of the First Gods, on the Hearth beside Vesta's round temple
Chief priest
The Rex Sacrorum, Aulus Pinarius Natta, with the Virgo Maxima Tarquitia Lucilla
Patron gods
Vesta of the first hearth, Janus of the gates, Juno of the weights; Mercury on the Guild Square
Banned here
Any rite not in the Romulan books; new gods inside the old wall; bronze tools at the hut
Trouble
Everyone needs a priest's seal, and Farshore gods are paying rent on the Square

The Pantheon

The Atrium of the First Gods. Romulo has no dome and wants none. Its house of all gods is a long, low hall of dressed stone, two hundred feet by forty, under a roof of old clay tiles. It was built on the plan of a founding family's house, because that is what it is: the house of the city's oldest family, which is the gods. An open court runs down the middle, with a rain-pool under a square opening in the roof. Along both walls stand cupboards of black cedar with painted doors, exactly like the cupboards on the Ancestors' Row where the patricians keep their wax masks. Each cupboard holds a god.

What they hold are the exemplaria, the first images: the oldest likeness of each god the Imperium possesses. Romulo keeps the copy that counts of every institution, and that includes the gods. Every cult statue in every licensed temple must be measured against its exemplar before it is dedicated, by the same rule that tests a pound against the master weight. The proportions are taken with a knotted cord. A statue that fails is not consecrated, and its temple cannot open. Since the Concord the Legates have commissioned victory temples by the dozen, and every one of their statues has come up the Via Sacra on an ox-cart to be measured. The Atrium charges sixty denarii a measuring and has a waiting list of nine months.

The order of the gods. The cupboards are arranged by the order in which each god was received into the city, oldest nearest the door. On the right: Janus, a doubled face of blackened oak no bigger than a fist; Jupiter Lapis, who is a flint, the stone on which the oldest oaths were sworn; the shields of Mars, twelve bronze figure-of-eight shields of which one is said to have fallen from the sky and the other eleven were made so that no thief could tell which; and Juno, an olive-wood figure holding a pair of scales. On the left: Vesta, who has no image, and whose cupboard holds a bronze dish into which a live coal is carried from the hearth each morning; then Ceres, a sheaf bound in red wool and renewed each harvest; Faunus, a horned mask; Pomona, a basket; Mercury, a squared pillar with a head. At the far end, in newer cupboards, come Minerva, an owl, Neptune, a trident head found in a field, and Vulcan, an anvil. The last cupboard is kept empty and unpainted for the next god the city receives. It has been empty for two hundred years.

Its priests. The Atrium belongs to the Rex Sacrorum, the one man in the Imperium still called king, and only of sacred things. Aulus Pinarius Natta lives in two rooms behind the rain-pool, owns almost nothing, and rules on correct practice for every temple in the empire. His rulings bind the Dux, and in law they bind the College of Pontiffs at Aeterna, which disputes it. His wife, the Regina Sacrorum Sergia Paulla, performs the queen's rites at each new moon and keeps the waiting list for measurings, which makes her the most courted woman in Romulo. Their only son died in the war. Natta's heir to the office is therefore a cousin, and the Pinarii (gens Pinaria) are giving a great deal of thought to which cousin.

Temples

The Temple of Vesta Vesta · the Hearth

Head priest: the Virgo Maxima, Tarquitia Lucilla · six Vestals · woodsmoke and laurel

A small round temple of white stone with a conical bronze roof and a smoke-hole, and inside it a fire that has not gone out in nine centuries. There is no statue. Six Vestal Virgins serve thirty years each, chosen as girls from patrician families. They keep the fire, the sacred salt-cake and the wills of anyone rich enough to deposit one. Tarquitia Lucilla holds the master standards' second key. When she walks in the street a lictor clears her way, and a condemned man who meets her by chance is freed.

Rites and festivals: the Vestalia in early summer, when the inner shrine is opened to barefoot matrons; the Vigiles' Night, when the flame is carried by runners to Aeterna; and the Renewal of the Fire on the first of the year, struck with a board and a drill, never with iron. Money: a fee for every will deposited. The Vestals never reveal what the wills say, and never forget it. Politics: every city's public hearth is lit from this one. A Vestal ruling that a city's fire was polluted forces that city to fetch a new flame from Romulo, at a price.

Ties: mother of every civic hearth, including the Pantheum lamp at Aeterna; the Vigiles' Night; the Hearth.

The Temple of Juno of the Weights Juno · over the Hall of Weights

Head priest: Antistita Gavia Prisca · the master standards · beeswax and cold bronze

A small, very old temple built over the strongroom of the master standards, so that the standards sit under the goddess's floor. It is the mother of every Juno temple in the Imperium, the Arx temple at Aeterna included, and every priestess of Juno is ordained here. At the spring Weighing the standards are carried up from the strongroom and set on the altar, and the copies from every city are tested against them in public. Gavia Prisca is sixty, short-sighted and exact. She holds the first key and the right to refuse any copy. She has recently refused to discuss Aeterna's.

Rites and festivals: the Weighing of the Standards; the Kalends sacrifice of a white heifer; and the Oath of the Even Scale, sworn by every weigher in the Imperium on taking office. Money: a share of the seal-fee on every Farshore cargo, which makes this the richest small temple in the empire. Politics: the Oathbound Sanctum keeps its register in the next lane and witnesses every Weighing. Gavia Prisca and Junia Tertulla of Aeterna were ordained together and have not spoken in two years.

Ties: mother of Juno at Aeterna and in the Citadel Cathedral; House Vettia; the Guild Square.

The Gate of Janus Janus · the entrance to the Hearth

Head priest: Ianitor Aulus Sempronius Atratinus · a temple that is a doorway · draughts and bronze hinges

Not a building but a passage: a double archway roofed in bronze, with a two-faced statue of the god between the arches and great doors at each end. By law the doors stand open in war and are shut in peace. They have stood open for as long as anyone can remember, and five years after the Concord nobody has dared to shut them. The Ianitor, Aulus Sempronius Atratinus, has asked the College of Pontiffs for leave to perform the Closing. The college cannot rule on it without a chief pontiff, and the Dominus Militum has let it be known that he would regard the Closing as premature.

Rites and festivals: the first sacrifice of every rite in the Imperium is to Janus, so his priest is paid a copper by every other temple; the Agonium in winter; and the yearly greasing of the hinges, which draws a hopeful crowd. Money: very little. Politics: a door that every faction wants left open, for its own reasons.

Ties: the milestone shrines of Anticata; the threshold shrine at the Gate of Mavelon; the Gatekeepers of the Eternal Threshold, who visit unannounced.

The Temple of Mercury of the Square Mercury · the end of the Guild Square

Head priest: the Mercurialis Tiberius Claudius Hermeros, a freedman · merchants' temple and guest-house of foreign gods · pepper, wax and wet ink

Built outside the old wall when Romulo was a market town, and swallowed by the Guild Square when the Square grew. Its priests have always been merchants, and its altar is where great contracts are sworn once they are sealed. Behind the cella is a colonnaded yard, the Hospitium, where licensed Farshore gods lodge as guests for the sailing season. The Tyrsan Lord of the City has a cedar shrine there; Khemaret's ibis-headed scribe has a niche; there is a Sabaian incense-altar, and a Maurashi pepper-vine trained up a column. Each pays rent. Hermeros was born a slave in a Tyrsan counting-house, was freed, and is the richest man ever elected Mercurialis.

Rites and festivals: the Mercuralia in late spring, when merchants sprinkle their goods with water from the temple well to wash away the year's lies; the Licensing of the Guests at the start of each season. Money: the guests' rent, a fee for every contract oath, and the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon's tithe. Politics: the Rex Sacrorum regards the Hospitium as an abomination with excellent accounts.

Ties: mother of Mercury of the Terminus at Aepistra and of the Vault of Mercury at Duneforged; the House of Guest Gods at Mavelon; the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon.

The forgotten temple

The Temple of Spes, under the caravan yard. Romulo keeps the copy that counts of everything except Hope. The temple of Spes, the Embodiment of Aspiration, stood outside the old wall where the Caravan Suburb now is. It burned in a siege three hundred years ago and was never rebuilt; the pontiffs ruled at the time that hope was a private matter and not an affair of state. Its cupboard in the Atrium was given to Neptune. Its foundations lie under the largest caravan yard in the Suburb, and the Gilded Horizon's camels are stabled on the podium. The drovers call it Hope's Yard without knowing why. Every spring someone leaves a garland of green barley on a stump of column by the water-trough. The yard-master thinks it is a drovers' custom and has never asked whose.

Priestly houses

gens Potitia Patrician · Custodians of the Images

Crest: a knotted measuring cord in a circle · Motto: "Ad exemplar" (To the pattern) · Seat: the Custodians' house at the far end of the Atrium

Keepers of the exemplaria and the knotted cords, by grant of the first Rex Sacrorum. The Potitii measure every cult statue in the Imperium, which gives a poor family the power to keep a Legate's temple shut. They are meticulous, slow and proud of it, and they are the only people allowed to open the cupboards.

  • Gnaea Potitia, Chief Custodian — seventy; can tell an image cut from bad timber by its smell; has failed four Legates' statues this year.
  • Marcus Potitius Pulcher, her son — would like to pass the statues faster and charge more; she will not let him.
  • Lucius Potitius Scaurus, her grandson — junior custodian; owes the Mending Needle for a mended hand.

History and lore: a Potitius once refused an Imperator's statue of himself as Jupiter because the head was a finger's breadth too large, and kept his post. Family lore says the empty cupboard at the end of the Atrium is not empty, and that a dying Potitia is told what is in it.

Ties: the Atrium; Nemorus, whose woodcarving they examine; every Legate's victory temple.

gens Quinctia Patrician · Salii, the leaping priests of Mars

Crest: a figure-of-eight shield on a red ground · Motto: "Saltamus" (We dance) · Seat: the Curia Saliorum by the Founder's Forum

The Salii are twelve young patricians who take Mars's shields from the Atrium twice a year and dance them through the streets, striking them with staves and singing a hymn so old that nobody understands the words. The Quinctii have provided the master of the dance for five generations and keep the hymn, which is not written down.

  • Kaeso Quinctius Flamininus, master of the Salii — fifty and still leaps; his knees can be heard from the next street.
  • Quinctia Secunda, his daughter — knows the hymn, which no woman is supposed to, and has written it down.
  • Titus Quinctius, his nephew — a dancer this year, on leave from Corvus's legion.

History and lore: the shields are danced out in spring to open the campaigning season and danced home in autumn to close it. Since the Concord the autumn dance has been held every year and the spring dance has been argued over. The Dominus Militum has ruled it a matter for the priests, and the priests have ruled it a matter for the Dominus Militum.

Ties: the shields in the Atrium; the Temple of Bellona at Aeterna; Corvus.

Temples · Aepistra

The Temples of Aepistra

Imported gods in a standard plan, a temple that is a copy of a copy, and under the forum paving the stumps of a grove whose god nobody wrote down.

Pantheon building
The Capitolium, on its podium at the north end of the forum, with the Portico of the Old Gods
Chief priest
Gaius Flavius Verecundus, Flamen of the Province and the provinces' one pontiff in the college
Patron gods
Jupiter of the standards; Ceres of the estates; the White Mare and the Mothers at home
Banned here
Native rites inside the old camp walls, except under an Invictian name; private oaths to a commander
Trouble
The Legate's legion has its own god, and the city's pontiff has a price

The Pantheon

The Capitolium. Every colonia gets one, built to the Romulan measure, and Aepistra's is the most correct in the provinces. It stands on a podium twelve feet high at the north end of the forum, where the surveyors' plan put it, and has three cellae side by side behind a deep portico: Jupiter in the middle, Juno on the right, Minerva on the left. The cult statues are copies of the Arx statues at Aeterna, which are themselves measured against the exemplaria at Romulo. The city is proud of being a copy of a copy, and says so on the dedication stone.

The provincials added something the plan did not provide. Along the east flank of the podium runs a colonnade, the Portico of the Old Gods, built eighty years ago by the first enfranchised Duumvir to house the region's own gods under Invictian names, which is the only lawful way to keep them inside the old camp walls. There the white mare of the plains stands as "Diana Equestris"; the river of the valley is "Neptune of the Fords"; and three seated stone women with baskets in their laps, whom every grandmother in the city calls the Mothers, are labelled "the Junones" in letters that are a little too large. The pontiffs at Aeterna have never inspected the Portico. The grandmothers do not light lamps in the Capitolium. They light them in the Portico.

The order of the gods. Jupiter, Juno, Minerva in the cellae; then, along the Portico from the forum end, Ceres, Mercury, Diana Equestris, Neptune of the Fords and the Mothers. A ninth niche at the end holds the Genius of the Province, a bronze youth with a cornucopia, put up by the Legate's father. Every year at the Games of the Province the Genius is crowned with laurel. This year the laurel was paid for by Quintus Herennius Strabo, and the crown was cut in the shape of a legion's mural crown. Several people noticed.

Its priests. The Capitolium is served by the Flamen of the Province, chosen by the provincial council for five years. Gaius Flavius Verecundus, a cousin of the Duumvir from a cadet branch of House Flavia Brannoca, is in his fourth year and holds something no provincial has held in a century: a seat in the College of Pontiffs, bought for the province by his family's gifts to the Pantheum. He gilded the Capitolium's roof at his own cost. He is fifty, courteous and anxious, and he has more debts than gilding. His wife Matugena Verecunda keeps the Portico's lamps herself and was born under another name (the Verecundi).

Temples

The Shrine of the Standards Jupiter · the Castra Nova

Head priest: the legion's haruspex, Sextus Tettius Ligur · the eagle and the pay-chest · leather, oil and wet stone

In every legionary fortress the standards stand in a shrine at the heart of the headquarters building, over the strongroom that holds the pay-chest. At the Castra Nova the shrine is larger than the plan allows. Its marble came from the Capitolium's own quarry, and Strabo dedicated it to "Jupiter of the Standards and the Fortune of the Legion". Before the eagle the legion swears its annual oath to the Imperator. Sextus Tettius Ligur reads the livers before every parade and has never found a bad one.

Rites and festivals: the Oath on the Kalends of the year; the Rose Day, when the standards are garlanded; the Birthday of the Eagle. Money: the soldiers' compulsory savings, held in the strongroom under the god, and now the land-grant registers of the Legate's Mile. Politics: this year, for the first time, the oath named the Legate before the Imperator. The haruspex called it a slip of the tongue.

Ties: daughter of Jupiter Optimus at Aeterna; the Castra Nova; gens Herennia; the Stormlord Vanguard, which has asked to send an observer.

The Temple of Ceres of the Estates Ceres · outside the south gate

Head priest: Sacerdos Arria Fadilla · the bailiffs' temple · chaff and wet sacking

A square brick temple among threshing floors on the road south, where the estate bailiffs swear their harvest returns and the Golden Harvest Covenant keeps its northern chapter. Its walls carry the grain levy of every estate in the province, painted fresh each year. Arria Fadilla is a bailiff's daughter and has read out, at three harvests running, what the Covenant thinks of being paid in light coin. The Legate's quartermasters now take a share of the threshing before it reaches the levy, and the painted figures have stopped adding up.

Rites and festivals: the First Sheaf, carried to the Capitolium; the Ambarvalia, when the estates' boundaries are walked with a pig, a sheep and a bull. Money: a fee on every sworn return. Politics: Arria Fadilla's figures are the only honest record of how much grain the Legate keeps back.

Ties: daughter of Ceres at Aeterna; the Golden Harvest Covenant; the Annona.

Mercury of the Terminus and the Guest-Fire Mercury · the Terminus Yards, east gate

Head priest: the Mercurialis Lucius Calidius Merops · couriers' god and caravan altar · camel, saffron and naphtha

A small temple of Mercury, god of roads and messages, beside the relay station, where couriers of the Cursus Legionis touch the god's foot before they ride. Since the Treaty Road opened it has grown a yard at the back, licensed as a hospitium on the model of the Guild Square at Romulo. There, in a brass fire-bowl under a roof with no walls, burns the Guest-Fire: a flame carried from the Fire-Temple of Atarabad and tended by a Magus, Herbad Farrokh, for the caravans of House Suren-Pahlav. Calidius Merops collects its rent and does not pretend to understand it.

Rites and festivals: the courier's touch; the Arrival, when a caravan that has crossed the whole Treaty Road sacrifices a kid to Mercury and pours oil on the Guest-Fire, both at once. Money: the caravans' gifts, and the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon's tithe. Politics: the Magus may not let the fire touch a corpse; the relay station's horses die here often. There have been words.

Ties: daughter of Mercury of the Square at Romulo; the Fire-Temple of Atarabad; the Terminus Yards; Deiperduem, the next fire on the road.

The Yard of the White Mare the White Mare, licensed as Diana Equestris · the horse-fair, the Canabae

Head priest: Senna Ollovica, matriarch of the Ollovici · a horse-yard with an altar · hay, dung and juniper smoke

Behind the Ollovici's stables in the Canabae is a paddock with a single white mare in it, never ridden, and a wooden shrine at the paddock gate. This is the old rite the Ollovici keep in their yard. Every horse sold at the fair is led past the shrine; every foal is named there. The mare is replaced from her own line when she dies, and the old one is buried standing. The licence calls the goddess Diana Equestris. Senna Ollovica calls her by a name she will say only in the old tongue, and the Cursus Legionis buys its remounts here because no rider wants a horse that has not been past the gate.

Rites and festivals: the Foaling, in spring; the Horse-Run at midsummer, when the Canabae's young race bareback round the old camp walls. Money: a penny on every horse sold. Politics: the Legate wants his own herd blessed here. Senna has said the mare does not bless brands.

Ties: the Ollovici; the Canabae; the Cursus stables at Anticata.

The forgotten temple

The grove under the forum. When the first legion of the northern conquest surveyed its camp, the crossing of the two main streets fell in the middle of a grove of very old oaks. The surveyors felled it, because the plan is the plan. The headquarters were built on the stumps, and later the forum was paved over the headquarters. Nobody wrote down whose grove it was. The grandmothers of the Canabae say it belonged to "the Lord of the Oaks", and the oldest of them say he is still there, under the paving, and is patient. Each Founding Day, when the chief magistrate ploughs the boundary, the ceremonial plough is drawn once across the forum. It snags every year on the same flagstone, the third from the speakers' platform. The flagstone has been relaid four times.

Priestly houses

The Verecundi Enfranchised provincials · cadet line of House Flavia Brannoca · flamens of the province

Crest: a boar under a laurel, with a priest's cap above · Motto: "Pietate cives" (Citizens by piety) · Seat: a new house in the Old Lines with a private chapel bigger than its dining room

The younger branch of the family that opened its gates to the first legion. Where the Brannoci bought their way into the council with baths, the Verecundi bought theirs into the priesthood with gilding. They have held the provincial flaminate for two generations and a seat in the college for four years, and are deeply in debt to the Mithril Reserve and, more recently, to someone more patient.

  • Gaius Flavius Verecundus, Flamen of the Province and pontiff — a swing vote in the college on the question of the chair; his debts were quietly bought last winter.
  • Matugena Verecunda, his wife — born a Matugena of the Canabae; lights the Mothers' lamps and is the reason the Portico has never been inspected.
  • Marcus Flavius Verecundus, elder son — tribune in Strabo's legion, initiate of the Cave of Brothers.
  • Lucius Flavius Verecundus, younger son — rehearses with the horns.

History and lore: the first Verecundus Flamen dreamed, the night before his election, that the Mothers took his cap and gave it back full of barley. The family keeps a cap full of barley in its chapel and replaces the grain each harvest.

Ties: the Capitolium; the College of Pontiffs at Aeterna; the Old Lines.

The Matugeni Native seers · unenfranchised · keepers of the Mothers

Crest: three seated women with baskets · Motto: in the old tongue, "We were here before the plan" · Seat: a long house at the edge of the Canabae

A native family of seers and midwives, cousins of the Ollovici, who never took an Invictian name and never asked for citizenship. They keep the knowledge of the Mothers: the right words for a birth, a burial and a new house. Half the enfranchised families of the Old Lines call a Matugena to their childbeds and pay her by the back door.

  • Old Matugena, the grandmother — blind; knows where the grove's stumps are, and which one was the god's.
  • Riganta Matugena, her daughter — midwife to the Herennii; delivered the Legate's grandson and keeps quiet about what she saw at the birth.
  • Esunertos, her grandson — a horse-boy for the Cursus; carries messages for the Ollovici.

History and lore: the family says the Mothers' statues in the Portico were carved from the grove's last oak, and that the three faces are the faces of three Matugena women who watched it felled.

Ties: the Ollovici; the Verecundi by marriage; the Canabae.

Temples · Mavelon

The Temples of Mavelon

Two peoples' sea-gods under one roof built over a burned warship, two forge-proud priesthoods who hate each other, and a caldera that some people have started praying to.

Pantheon building
The Keelhall (Mavari: the Kielhof; Invictian: the Aedes Carinae), in the burned slip under the Gate
Chief priest
Two, alternating yearly: this year the Gudja Thrasamund of the Kielings; next year the Sacerdos Aulus Vibius Nauta
Patron gods
Neptune and Vulcan in the south; Saiwar the Sea-Father and Kiliga the Ship-Mother in the north; Juno over the Oath
Banned here
Blessing a keel without the Abyssal Tideguard; shedding blood in the Keelhall; Farshore gods after the season closes
Trouble
Fewer launches means less keel-silver for the Mavari gods, and the volcano is warm again

The Pantheon

The Keelhall. On the Burning of the Slips, ninety-one years ago, the Mavari crews fired the warship slips of the south harbour. Eight were rebuilt. The ninth, the one cut deepest into the cliff under the Gate, was not. When the Oath at the Gate was sworn, it was sworn in that slip, among the ashes, over the burned keel of the quinquereme Pietas, because it was the one place on the island that both sides agreed was nobody's. The treaty made the slip a sanctuary of both peoples, and it has been one ever since.

It is a long cave of a building, three hundred feet from the water to the back wall, roofed with the original arched vault of the slip and floored with the slip's own slope, so the whole temple runs gently downhill to the caldera. The Pietas's keel lies down the middle where it burned, a black spine of oak, fenced with a low bronze rail. For the Invictians it is the relic of a betrayal forgiven. For the Mavari it is the relic of a victory paid for. Both sides touch the rail on the way in, for opposite reasons, and both sides know it.

The order of the gods. The south aisle, on the left as you come down from the cliff, belongs to the Imperium: Neptune with his trident nearest the water, then Vulcan, then Mercury, then Venus of the Harbour, whom sailors' wives pray to. The north aisle belongs to the Mavari.
