Their gods have no statues but carved posts of ship-timber: Saiwar the Sea-Father, a post carved with waves and a bearded face, nearest the water; Kiliga the Ship-Mother, a post shaped like a keel standing on end, whose belly the women touch before a launch; and beyond them a forest of old oars hung from the vault, each carved with the name of a Mavari drowned at sea. At the top of the slope, against the back wall, stands the Oath-Stone, a block of black basalt cut with Juno's seal on one face and nine Mavari spear-ring marks on the other. The Imperial priests hold that Saiwar is Neptune under a northern name. The Mavari hold that Neptune is Saiwar with a southern haircut. Neither side has asked the gods.

Its priests. Like the Gate Court, the Keelhall has two heads and they rule together or not at all. They take the presidency in alternate years. This year it is the Mavari gudja, Thrasamund of the Kielings, sixty, bald, with a voice like a rope taking strain. He is the cousin of the Lawspeaker Gisla Thurwinsdottir and the first gudja to speak Invictian at the altar, which the Skeldings hold against him. His colleague, Aulus Vibius Nauta, priest of Neptune and Master of the Abyssal Tideguard's chapter, takes the chair next midsummer. The two men have run the Keelhall together for eleven years, dislike each other's gods, and trust each other completely. See the Kielings and gens Vibia.

Rites. At the Midsummer Thing the Lawspeaker recites the Oath at the Gate from the Oath-Stone, and the Oathbound Sanctum's witness reads the Invictian text after her. At every launch, the hull is blessed in the Keelhall before it goes into the water: the Tideguard sprinkles it for Neptune, the gudja cuts a lock of the shipwright's hair for Kiliga, and the keel-silver is weighed out on the Oath-Stone. Fewer launches have meant fewer blessings. The Keelhall's treasury has fallen by half in five years, and the north aisle's lamps are now bought from the gudja's own purse.

Temples

The Temple of Neptune Neptune · the High Crescent forum

Head priest: Aulus Vibius Nauta, Master of the Abyssal Tideguard at Mavelon · keel-blessings and wreck-rights · salt, tar and sacrificial horse

A blue-painted temple on the south rim's little forum, facing Vulcan's across the paving and looking down the cliff at the Mouth. Neptune here is the Sovereign of the Deep, lord of the fleet, and his priests are the Abyssal Tideguard: harbour defence, salvage rights, and the only body in the Imperium permitted to bless a keel. Every Invictian warship carries a bronze plaque from this temple nailed to its stem. Vibius Nauta is a former trierarch, sixty-four, who still swims the Mouth every Neptunalia to show he can.

Rites and festivals: the Neptunalia at high summer, when the south side builds leaf-huts on the quays; the Drowning of the Horse, every fifth year, at the Mouth; and every keel-blessing. Money: the blessing fee, and a share of every wreck in the Imperium's waters. Politics: the Praefectus Classis wants the Mavari steersmen cut; Nauta has told him from the altar that Neptune does not want them cut.

Ties: mother of Neptune's shrines at Fucostia and Napplesia; the High Crescent; the South Harbour.

The Temple of Vulcan of the Arsenal Vulcan · the High Crescent forum

Head priest: the Flamen Volcanalis, Gnaeus Gellius Faber · the arsenal fires · coal smoke and hot iron

Its doors face Neptune's, and its priests have not crossed the forum to speak to Neptune's in a generation. Vulcan was once worshipped outside the walls for fear of his flame; here he is worshipped above the arsenal whose forges are his. Every new forge on the Mill Banks is lit from the temple's own fire, and every guild master swears on the temple's anvil. The quarrel with Neptune is over water: the arsenal outfall stains the caldera for a mile. Neptune's priests call it pollution of the god's house. Vulcan's call it evidence of prosperity. Gnaeus Gellius Faber is the brother of the Praefectus Fabrum, Titus Gellius Naso.

Rites and festivals: the Quenching at midwinter, when the Flamen gives the signal; the Volcanalia in late summer, when small fish are thrown into the forge-fire on the god's behalf. Money: a tithe from every forge on the Banks and the guilds' oath-fees. Politics: the Emberforge Collective's Hellenorian-descended masters worship here and call him by another name in private.

Ties: sister to the Forge of Vulcan in the Citadel Cathedral; the Mill Banks; House Demetria.

The Hof of the Thingstead Saiwar and Kiliga · beside the standing stones, north rim

Head priest: the hof-wife Audofleda of the Kielings · keel-silver and spear-rings · peat smoke and sheep fat

The Mavari gods' own house, on the flat ground at the top of the Hollows beside the Thing's ring of stones: a long timber hall with a roof of turf, posts carved with ships, and a hearth down the middle. Here the keel-silver is kept, counted and blessed before it is shared among the clans. Here the spear-rings are kept on which the Oath was sworn, one for each clan that swore. The hof-wife Audofleda keeps the hall, the silver chest and the ring-board. She is the gudja's sister and the only person on the north side who can stop the Reiks's key-bearer at the hall door.

Rites and festivals: the Midsummer Thing's opening sacrifice of a ram; the Keel-Silver, when the year's silver is shared; and the Night of the Oars in autumn, when the names of the drowned are read and their oars carried down to the Keelhall. Money: the keel-silver, and nothing else. Politics: the Skeldings' ring was nearly taken down this spring. Audofleda refused to let it be touched.

Ties: the Hollows and the Thingstead; the Hrodnings; the Skeldings.

The House of Guest Gods Farshore gods, licensed as hospites · the eastern mole, Farshore Quays

Head priest: Procurator of Guests Marcus Sentius Hospes, a freedman of House Sentia · altars by the season · cedar, myrrh and rope

A long colonnaded shed at the mole's root, beside the Aurum Pact's isolation sheds, where Farshore gods are lodged for the sailing season. A ship's god may not go ashore until it has a licence, and the licence is issued here, after the Aurum Pact has certified the ship. The Tyrsan Lord of the City has a cedar shrine. Qart-Hadeth's sailors keep a stone for their sky-lady. Khemaret's grain-crews bring a small gilded boat with a god in it. A Maurashi pepper-boat has left a stone that is never to be moved. When the season closes the gods must leave with their ships, and the Procurator walks the shed with a list.

Rites and festivals: the Licensing at the season's opening; the Clearing at its close. Money: licence fees, split with the Temple of Mercury at Romulo, which licenses the gods again when their cargoes arrive there. Politics: the Seric envoy's ship carried an altar no one could license because no one could say what it was for.

Ties: Mercury of the Square at Romulo; House Sentia; the Aurum Pact; Lantern Lane's Tyrsan shrine at Napplesia.

The forgotten temple

The Sunken Hof. Twice a year, at the lowest spring tides, the tops of eleven columns break the surface of the caldera a cable's length inside the Race. They are white marble, fluted, and older than anything on the island. The Mavari call the place the Sunken Hof and say it belonged to the people who were here before them, who sank with it when the mountain broke. The Invictian antiquaries say it is a temple of Tethys, the Titan of rivers and navigation, from when the crater was a lake. Fishermen of both halves will not drop a net within a stone's throw of it. Mavari steersmen still touch their foreheads as they pass, and their Invictian masters have learned to do the same without asking why. At dead low water on the darkest night of winter, those who have dived there say, a lamp can be seen burning at the bottom.

Priestly houses

The Kielings Mavari clan · gudjas and hof-wives

Crest: a keel standing upright between two oars · Motto: "The keel remembers" · Seat: the Hof of the Thingstead

The Mavari priestly clan. Before the conquest a Kieling blessed every keel on Mavaholm; after it the Imperium gave that right to the Tideguard and the clan kept only the hof and the oars of the drowned. The Oath at the Gate gave them half the Keelhall, and they have spent ninety years learning the Invictian rites well enough to argue with them.

  • Gudja Thrasamund, head and this year's president of the Keelhall — speaks Invictian at the altar and Mavari everywhere else.
  • Audofleda, his sister, hof-wife — keeps the keel-silver, the spear-rings and the clan's memory of every insult.
  • Gaiso Thrasamundsson, his son — a steersman laid off when the fleet cut crews; angry, and spending time with the Skeldings.
  • Wiliarit, Audofleda's daughter — fourteen; can carve a drowned man's oar from a description and has never been wrong about the face.

History and lore: on the Burning of the Slips it was a Kieling gudja who walked into the burning ninth slip and cut the first lock of hair from the dying ship, claiming the keel for Kiliga before it was ash. That is why the Keelhall's north aisle exists. His oar hangs nearest the Oath-Stone.

Ties: the Hrodnings by marriage; the Lawspeaker, a cousin; gens Vibia, their partners at the altar.

gens Vibia Equestrian · priests of Neptune and masters of the Tideguard

Crest: a silver trident over a ship's stem · Motto: "Mare dat, mare aufert" (The sea gives, the sea takes) · Seat: a villa on the High Crescent with its own stair to the water

A naval family whose men retire from command into Neptune's priesthood, so that the god's temple is run by former captains. They hold the Tideguard chapter by habit rather than law, and with it the wreck-rights of the coast, which have made them richer than their rank.

  • Aulus Vibius Nauta, priest of Neptune — swims the Mouth every year; distrusts every Mavari god and every Mavari he has served with.
  • Vibia Salvia, his wife — Mavari-born, from a Kieling cousin-line; their marriage is older than the Gate Marriage and quieter.
  • Gaius Vibius Pansa, his son — salvage-master of the Tideguard; has found something on the caldera floor near the Sunken Hof and filed no report.

History and lore: a Vibius commanded the fleet that forced the Mouth in the conquest, and his son commanded the ship that burned in the ninth slip. The family is the only Invictian house that owes both the conquest and the revolt a death.

Ties: the Temple of Neptune; the Abyssal Tideguard; gens Arruntia.

Temples · Duneforged Citadel

The Temples of Duneforged

Five temples under one mountain roof, where Titans stand beside the Imperium's gods, the Duke pays for gold leaf instead of answers, and the oldest chapel in the citadel hums.

Pantheon building
The Citadel Cathedral, cut into the Helm: the Forge of Vulcan, the Temple of Juno, the Vault of Mercury, the Shrine of Anchiale and the Sanctum of Hoplodamus
Chief priest
Archpriest Edmund Corvane, Warden of the Five Doors
Patron gods
Vulcan, Juno and Mercury, beside the Titans Anchiale and Hoplodamus
Banned here
Oaths sworn anywhere but Juno's font; a weapon past Hoplodamus's door unless it is to be judged; going below the eighth gallery to pray
Trouble
A duke spending on the cathedral to avoid spending on the truth, and a chapel nobody visits that has started to sing

The Pantheon

The Citadel Cathedral. It is not built; it is dug. The cathedral stands on the Helm between the ducal palace and the Citadel Archives, and its only outside wall is a façade of dressed mountain stone with five doors in it. Behind the façade the mountain has been hollowed into a round central hall, the Crossing, sixty feet across, lit from far above by a shaft cut through the rock to the sky. At noon a column of sunlight stands in the middle of the floor for the length of a prayer. From the Crossing five passages run into the mountain like the fingers of a hand, and at the end of each is a temple with its own priests, its own treasury and its own door to the street. The codex is right that they are held separately. They share the Crossing, the sunlight and the Archpriest, and nothing else.

The order of the gods. The order is the order of a citizen's life, and the Archpriest recites it at every great feast. The visitor comes in under the Sanctum of Hoplodamus, which is built into the gatehouse, because the Titan of Guardianship stands at every threshold and judges who comes in. On the right is the Temple of Juno, where the oath is sworn. On the left is the Vault of Mercury, where the bargain is kept, and its passage slopes down into the rock towards the Merca's Vaulted Court. Straight ahead, largest and brightest, is the Forge of Vulcan, where the work is blessed. Set into the back wall of the Forge, behind the god's altar, is a small hot niche: the Shrine of Anchiale, Titaness of the warmth a forge holds after the flame dies. You reach her only by walking past Vulcan, which is the point. Duneforged honours Titans beside the Imperium's gods. Aeterna's pontiffs have never approved it, have never been asked, and have never been in a position to object.

The Duke's gifts. In the last three years Duke Roderick has paid for a new bronze door on the Forge of Vulcan, a gilded ceiling in the Crossing and an anvil for Vulcan's altar cast from four tons of Embersteel. The anvil cost as much as a year's wages in the Dune Mines. The Archpriest accepted each gift with a speech. The quarrymen, whose wages are late, have learned the speeches by heart and recite them at the Parched Ox.

Its priests. The cathedral is governed by the Archpriest, the Warden of the Five Doors, who holds the keys of the Crossing, presides at the great feasts and settles disputes between the five priesthoods. Edmund Corvane is sixty-six, a Count's grandson with a smith's forearms, and he has held the office for twenty years. He sleeps in a cell off the Crossing and eats at the Duke's table twice a week. He is the one man in the citadel who can tell the Duke something unwelcome during grace. He has not yet done so. The Corvanes have kept the Crossing since the Pact; see House Corvane. The cathedral's purse is held by the Duchess, Kivia Elea Caesar, who approves its budget each quarter. She has begun to approve it more slowly.

Temples

The Forge of Vulcan Vulcan · the end of the great passage

Head priest: High Smith-Priest Hadrian Voss · where the work is blessed · coal, hot stone and new bronze

A vaulted hall with a working forge for an altar, fed by a geothermal vent through the rock, and the new Embersteel anvil before it. Every apprentice's first piece in the citadel is struck here, and every airship's first keel-plate is blessed here before it goes to the Skyward Bastions. Hadrian Voss is a master smith who took the priesthood after losing an eye to a bursting crucible. He beats out a nail for every child born in the citadel and hangs it from the vault, and the vault is now heavy with forty thousand nails.

Rites and festivals: the First Strike at the year's turn; the Blessing of the Keel-Plate; the Quenching, held on the same night as Mavelon's. Money: the Duke's gifts and a tithe from the Three Great Smithing Houses. Politics: the Order of Ember, House Vulkrim's secret brotherhood of warrior-smiths, meets in the forge after midnight, with the High Smith-Priest's knowledge.

Ties: sister to Vulcan of the Arsenal at Mavelon; House Vulkrim; the Geomantic Forge.

The Temple of Juno Juno · the right-hand passage

Head priest: Prioress Elspeth Marrow · where oaths bind and coin is assayed · cold water and wax

A white chamber with a font of black stone in the centre, filled from a spring that rises in the rock. This is the enchanted water in which the Pact was signed, and every oath of the allied houses is still sworn with a hand in it. The temple also assays the citadel's coin and the Reserve's ingots on Juno's scales, so it is both court and mint. Elspeth Marrow was ordained at Romulo, which she mentions, and she keeps the Pact's original, written on vellum that has never dried, in a case under the font.

Rites and festivals: the Renewal of the Pact every seventh year, when each allied house dips its seal; the quarterly Assay, held a day after Aeterna's so the figures can be compared. Money: oath-fees and an assay fee on every Reserve ingot. Politics: Juno's Duneforged figures differ from Aeterna's by one part in forty. The Prioress has written to Junia Tertulla about it and been asked not to again.

Ties: daughter of Juno of the Weights at Romulo; sister to Juno at Aeterna; the Oathbound Sanctum; House Caerthain.

The Vault of Mercury Mercury · the left-hand passage, descending

Head priest: Vault-Priest Corwin Hale · where the bargain is kept · dry stone and lamp oil

A god of trade and trickery, kept in a vault: either an act of devotion or a precaution. The passage slopes down a hundred steps into rock, through two doors locked with Merca Ledgerlocks, to a chamber whose walls are lined with small sealed niches. Each niche holds a contract sworn before the god, and a contract kept here is enforced by Mercury as well as by the Reserve. Every Dominus Argentar in Asetheria swears his oath on a shard of the original Mithril Lode in this room. Corwin Hale is a former Reserve clerk, smiling and patient, who knows the contents of every niche and has been known to forget them for the right people.

Rites and festivals: the Oath of the Argentar; the Day of Settling at midwinter, when debts sworn here fall due. Money: a fee per niche per year, paid by the Reserve. Politics: a door at the bottom opens into the Merca's Vaulted Court, and nobody is sure which side keeps the key.

Ties: daughter of Mercury of the Square at Romulo; House Merca; Clan Ironhand; the Mithril Reserve at Deiperduem.

The Shrine of Anchiale the Titaness Anchiale · behind Vulcan's altar

Head priest: Ember-Keeper Isaura Quell · the warmth that stays · ash and hot clay

A niche in the rock behind the Forge, kept hot by the same vent and never lit. The Titaness of the heat a forge holds after the flame dies has no statue, only a bed of grey ash that is always warm, and her offerings are pressed into it: a failed casting, a cracked tool, a letter. Her faithful are smiths who work at night, alchemists, and fighters of the Ju Colliseum, who name her for adaptability and cunning. Isaura Quell tends the ash, speaks to almost no one, and has been seen in the arena's underground training pits after midnight. Vulcan's priests consider her shrine their back room. She considers the Forge her front porch.

Rites and festivals: none on the calendar. She is honoured by being given room, so the shrine is shut on every feast day and open on the days in between. Money: whatever is left in the ash. Politics: the Virellarions send their failed experiments here, and some of them still move.

Ties: House Virellarion; Countess Aurelie Virellarion; the Ju Colliseum.

The Sanctum of Hoplodamus the Titan Hoplodamus · the gatehouse

Head priest: Warden-Priest Garrick Ashgrove · the guardian's judgement and the fast, clean death · sand, oil and iron

A square stone chamber in the cathedral's gatehouse, holding a seated figure of the Titan twice life-size, a shield across his knees and his eyes on the door. Every fighter of the Ju Colliseum comes here before a trial. The Ember Gate and the Bowl of Judgment, through which every arena fighter passes, are consecrated here. The divine mercy the Titan grants is a fast, clean death. His priests are trained to give it, and they stand at the arena's edge in grey with a short blade each. Garrick Ashgrove has given mercy two hundred and eleven times. He has never been asked to give it to someone who had won.

Rites and festivals: the Watch before every trial; the Great Martial Festival, which the Sanctum opens and closes. Money: a share of the House Ring's stakes. Politics: the Mihran fighter at this year's Festival has asked for the Titan's blessing. By rule it cannot be refused.

Ties: House Ashgrove; Marcia Ferox; House Zayida.

The forgotten temple

The Chapel of Mylinus, in the eighth gallery. Before the Caerthain were nobles and before the cathedral was cut, the first miners of the mountain had a chapel in the deep galleries. It was dedicated to Mylinus, the Titan of Endurance and Stone. It is a small rough cave at the end of the eighth gallery, with a bench, a niche and a wall into which every gang drove a chip from every new face it opened. When the cathedral was built, the Titans of fire and guardianship were taken up to the Helm. The miners' Titan was left behind, because a god of endurance does not need to be moved, and in two generations nobody went down to him. The Quarrymen still set the year's last block into their district wall, and nobody remembers that the custom started in the eighth gallery. The hum in the lower shafts is loudest at this chapel. Overseer Tarnak's men say that if you sit on the bench it stops, and you hear something like breathing.

Priestly houses

House Corvane Lesser noble · Wardens of the Five Doors

Crest: five keys on a ring over a black mountain · Motto: "Every door, one key-holder" · Seat: the Warden's lodgings off the Crossing

A minor house raised with the Caerthain in the war, when a Corvane chaplain held the cathedral's doors against looters during a siege. They received the wardenship of the Crossing under the Pact and have held it since. They marry into the counts' families, keep no estates, and live on the cathedral, which means they live on the Duke.

  • Archpriest Edmund Corvane, Warden of the Five Doors — has rehearsed telling the Duke the truth about the ore for two years.
  • Lady Rowena Corvane, his sister — secretary of the cathedral; reads the Duchess's marginal notes on the budget better than anyone.
  • Oswin Corvane, his nephew and heir — a novice in the Forge of Vulcan who has been down to the eighth gallery and will not say what he heard.
  • Mother Agatha Corvane, his aunt — ninety; remembers when the Duke's father first visited the Oratory.

History and lore: the first Corvane Warden swore that every door of the cathedral would have one key and one holder. The family has kept that oath with one exception, the door at the bottom of the Vault of Mercury, which has two keys and, they suspect, three holders.

Ties: House Caerthain; House Zayida by marriage.

House Ashgrove Common-born · the Grey Mercy of Hoplodamus

Crest: a grey shield over a short blade · Motto: "Swift, and kind" · Seat: the Sanctum's gatehouse and a narrow house above the Ju Colliseum

A family of former arena fighters who took the Titan's grey after winning their pardons, and who have provided the mercy-givers of the Ju Colliseum for six generations. They are trained surgeons as well as killers, and the lower city trusts them as it trusts nobody on the Helm.

  • Garrick Ashgrove, Warden-Priest — has never given mercy to a winner and fears this year's Festival will ask him to.
  • Brenna Ashgrove, his daughter — a mercy-giver at the arena and Marcia Ferox's oldest friend; refuses to bet.
  • Tobin Ashgrove, his son — an arena surgeon who stitches bond-debtors for free and keeps their names.

History and lore: the first Ashgrove was a bond-fighter who refused the killing stroke in the pit and was granted mercy, then lived when the stroke missed. The Sanctum took it as the Titan's judgement and made him its priest. Every Ashgrove's blade is forged from the head of that first stroke, melted and reforged each generation.

Ties: the Sanctum of Hoplodamus; the Ju Colliseum; the Parched Ox.

Temples · Deiperduem

The Temples of Deiperduem

A city where temples are illegal, so the gods lodge at an inn: three doors, three empires, one courtyard, and a plinth kept empty on purpose.

Pantheon building
The House of Three Doors, registered as a lodging-house, on Lantern Row off Treaty Square
Chief priest
None by law; the House is kept by Mother Wenna of the Iron Cup, a lay innkeeper
Patron gods
None by law; Concordia, Mercury and Jauhar have shrines, and so, less officially, do several others
Banned here
Temples; any priest in office for an empire's state cult; any rite on Treaty Square except at the Quiet Hour
Trouble
Every embassy wants its own god given a roof, and the only roof is shared

The Pantheon

The House of Three Doors. The Treaty that made Deiperduem neutral forbids any empire to build in it what it could not be seen to have built: no fortress, no garrison and no temple. The drafters were thinking of a great marble sanctuary to some imperial god at the foot of the Treaty Hall. The effect has been that the gods of a city of sixty thousand have nowhere to live. The Deiperdene solved it the way they solve everything, with a lease. On Lantern Row, a lane off the north side of Treaty Square, stands a square, plain building of three storeys round a courtyard, registered with the Council of Thirty as a lodging-house. Its guests are gods.

It has three street doors on three sides. The western door, painted red, opens on the Invictian wing, where Concordia and Mercury have shrines. The northern door, painted blue, opens on the Hellenorian wing, where Hermes has a shrine. The Hellenorians insist he is not Mercury, and the House charges them separately. Hestia's hearth stands beside him, lit from the Proxeny's own fire. The eastern door, painted saffron, opens on the Acheaorian wing, where Jauhar the Gilded has his shrine and a fire is kept in a brass bowl for travellers who will not pray without one. Each wing has its own stair, its own cistern and its own night-porter. The three wings meet only in the courtyard, where a fountain runs and nobody prays, and all three doors open on it from inside.

The order of the gods. There is no order, which is the point. The shrines are rented by the season, and the rent fixes everything: Concordia's lease is the oldest and Jauhar's the most expensive, and Mercury's has been in arrears since the debasement. In the centre of the courtyard stands a plinth of grey stone, bare. The House calls it the Fourth Shrine. It is kept for no god, by a clause in the original lease drafted by the Brass Scales, so that no empire can ever say the House has a centre and that its god is in it. Pilgrims of all three empires leave coins on the plinth anyway. The House gives them to the Foundlings' House.

Its keeper. There is no chief priest, because a priest of an empire's state cult may not hold office in the city. The House is kept by Mother Wenna of the Iron Cup, an innkeeper of the old Deiperdene kind, sixty, broad, and unshockable. She collects the rents, settles the disputes between the wings, and keeps the night-porters from arguing. She was "Invictian" until her son married an Acheaorian caravan-mistress, and the city is still deciding what that makes her. See the House of the Iron Cup.

Temples

The Shrine of Concordia Concordia · the west wing of the House, and an altar on Treaty Square

Head: Mediator Quintus Laelius Mitis of the Accord of Infinite Wisdom · treaties and reconciliations · beeswax and new parchment

Concordia has two shrines: a room in the House of Three Doors, and a waist-high altar set against the outer wall of the Treaty Hall, which the Council of Thirty licensed as "a fixture" so that nobody had to call it a temple. Couples reconcile at the altar; rival merchants swear a truce there; at the Signing each year the three envoys each lay a sprig of olive on it, in an order fixed by lot. Quintus Laelius Mitis is a mediator of the Accord of Infinite Wisdom, Invictian by birth and citizen of nowhere by choice. He drafted two clauses of the Treaty that are still argued over. The Order of the Silver Flame keeps a single knight at the altar day and night.

Rites and festivals: the Signing; the monthly Reconciliation, when feuds may be laid down without loss of face. Money: mediation fees, charged on a sliding scale that rises with the number of embassies involved. Politics: the Accord would like the Fourth Shrine for Concordia. Mother Wenna has said no.

Ties: Treaty Square; Aulus Severinus Custos, who warded the altar; the Pantheum at Aeterna.

The Shrine of Mercury of the Fields Mercury · the Caravan Fields, by the toll-booths

Head: Drover-Priest Stellan Marr of the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon · road and contract · axle-grease and camel

Mercury's shrine in the House is a formality. His real shrine is a roofed pillar among the toll-booths in the Caravan Fields, where the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon's drivers touch his head before every run and leave a copper in the box. Stellan Marr has driven the Treaty Road for thirty years and is licensed by the Gilded Horizon, not by any empire, which is how he can serve here. He blesses wagons, witnesses drovers' contracts, and settles disputes with the Wheelwalkers over grazing.

Rites and festivals: the blessing of the first caravan of the year; the Run of Lamps, when the Fields light every lantern for drivers lost on the road. Money: the box, and a fee on every contract sworn at the pillar. Politics: the Chyrsus Syndicate wants the pillar moved off its toll-ground. Every driver on the road has said what will happen if it is.

Ties: daughter of Mercury of the Square at Romulo; Mercury of the Terminus at Aepistra; the Caravan Fields.

The Shrine of Jauhar the Gilded Jauhar · the east wing of the House, and a niche in the Counting Ward

Head: Herbad Ardashir Gilan · prosperity and fortune · rosewater and warm brass

Jauhar, the Acheaorian god of prosperity and fortune, has the most expensive room in the House and a gilded niche on Interest Lane, between the Mithril Reserve and the Chyrsus toll-house, where money-changers of all three empires touch the god's gilt hand before they open their tables. Ardashir Gilan is a lay herbad, licensed by no Magus, who came west with a caravan of House Suren-Pahlav and stayed. He reads the morning's discount board as a kind of augury and is wrong less often than the bankers.

Rites and festivals: the Gilding at the Acheaorian new year, when the god's hand is regilded by whoever had the best year; the Weighing of Hearts at the year's end, when merchants burn a list of debts they will forgive. Money: the Gilding, which the bankers compete to pay for. This year Hildra Ironhand paid. Politics: the Vaults of Equilibrium consider Jauhar theirs and Gilan a poacher.

Ties: the Counting Ward; House Ironhand; the Fire-Temple of Atarabad by caravan.

The Three Stones Senectus and Proserpina, unnamed · the Quiet Ground, west of the walls

Head: Keepers Halvard of the Watchers and Sister Ione of the Cycle · the war dead of three empires · cut grass and cold stone

The three plain stones on the Quiet Ground are not a temple, and the Council has never licensed them as anything. They are kept jointly by the Watchers of the Eternal Rest, who keep the dead's pensions, and the Cycle of the Eternal Bloom, who keep their burials. Neither order names its god on the stones, which is the condition of the arrangement. Halvard is a one-armed Invictian veteran. Ione is a Hellenorian-born sister of the Cycle. Between them they mow the grass, read the numbers at the Quiet Hour, and turn away anyone who tries to add a name.

Rites and festivals: the Quiet Hour on the evening of the Signing. Money: a grant from each embassy, paid late by all three. Politics: every year someone tries to correct one of the numbers with a chisel.

Ties: the Quiet Ground; the Watchers' rolls at Romulo.

The forgotten temple

The Temple of the Lost One, under the Treaty Hall. Long before the war came near it, the market town was a caravan halt of the Acheaorian conquest, when Acheaoria held most of the continent. Its people built a temple there to the Lost One, the Acheaorian god of exile and longing, whom caravaneers far from home pray to. When the Acheaorian tide went out, the Invictians used the temple as a stable. Then a Hellenorian column burned it, and the town carted its stones away for building. Many went into the foundations of a plain hall on the square, the hall in which, centuries later, the Treaty was signed. The Treaty Hall's own masons' marks show it. No empire could be seen to have built the hall, and none did. It stands on the house of a god of exiles. Old Deiperdene say the city's name comes from the soldiers' slang of some forgotten army, "the place where the god was lost". The scholars of three empires have three other explanations.

Priestly houses

The House of the Iron Cup Innkeepers · keepers of the House of Three Doors

Sign: an iron drinking-cup on a chain · Motto: "Any guest, one price" · Seat: the House of Three Doors, Lantern Row

An old innkeeping family whose sign survived the war when their surname did not. They took the House of Three Doors on a ninety-nine-year lease when the Treaty made temples illegal, on the theory that gods are only guests who stay longer. They are counted "Invictian" by habit and are spending a great deal of effort becoming uncountable.

  • Mother Wenna of the Iron Cup, keeper — collects rent from three empires' gods; has never been inside any of the wings during a rite.
  • Dace of the Iron Cup, her son — night-porter of the saffron door; married to Golnar Parvaneh, an Acheaorian caravan-mistress.
  • Parvaneh of the Iron Cup, as Golnar is now styled — keeps the Acheaorian wing's fire and the House's accounts, and is the best bookkeeper on Lantern Row.
  • Little Tamsin, Wenna's granddaughter, seven — has been told not to leave things on the Fourth Shrine, and does.

History and lore: in the war the family hid priests of all three empires in the same cellar, on successive nights, and swore each set that the others had never been there. The Iron Cup on the sign is the one they passed round among the fugitives.

Ties: the Green Lamp, rivals in neutrality; the Brass Scales, who drafted their lease.

The House of the Blue Kettle Apothecaries · suppliers to every altar

Sign: a blue copper kettle · Motto: "Measured, then mixed" · Seat: a shop and still-room on Notaries' Row

Apothecaries who sell incense, holy oils and lamp-wicks to every shrine in the city and medicine to every embassy. Their incense is the only kind all three wings of the House will burn, because they make three blends, each to the correct rite. They are counted "Acheaorian", and are in fact nobody's.

  • Master Corwen of the Blue Kettle — mixes the three incenses and the Gallienain Cult's reagents in the same still-room.
  • Hesta of the Blue Kettle, his wife — keeps the cellar, and the missing assayer in it.
  • Pell of the Blue Kettle, their son — delivers to the embassies and knows which envoy takes what for sleep.

History and lore: a Blue Kettle apothecary embalmed the war dead of all three empires in the last campaign before the Treaty and was paid by none of them. The family has been collecting the debt in its own way ever since.

Ties: the House of Three Doors; the Old Town; the Assayers' Tower.

Temples · Eronis

The Temples of Eronis

A dead city's gods, still keeping their hours: a ring of black mirrors that show the sleeping what the waking cannot see, and a priesthood whose last heir is being hunted by three empires.

Pantheon building
The House of the Sleeping Gods, a ring of seven mirrors on the crown of the Mural Streets
Chief priest
None living; the last name on the roll is the Hierophant Aurelis Ilaro
Patron gods
The gods of the murals, whom the dream-readers call the Dreaming Gods
Banned here
By salvagers' custom: sleeping inside the ring, taking glass from a shrine, lighting a fire on the Cypress Walk
Trouble
The temples still work, and every expedition wants to be the one that wakes them

The Pantheon

The House of the Sleeping Gods. On the highest ground of the Mural Streets, above the rubble, is an open circular court a hundred feet across, paved in pale stone worn smooth. It has no roof and never had one. Around its rim stand seven mirrors of black glass, each twice a man's height, set in frames of grey stone carved with the shifting Nethranan script, all facing inward. In the centre is a low stone couch long enough for a body. That is all of it. Expeditions have measured it, sketched it and slept beside it, and they agree on one thing. A visitor awake who looks into the mirrors sees only the court and himself, a little darker. A visitor who dozes, even for a moment, sees a figure standing in each mirror where his own reflection should be.

These are the gods of Eronis. The murals show them everywhere and name them nowhere, because Nethranan glyphs change meaning with the light. The scholars of the Three Libraries have matched seven of the mirror-figures to gods the Enchanted Muse's dream-readers know as the Dreaming Gods. The match is plausible and unprovable, and every expedition uses it.

The order of the gods. The mirrors are arranged by the hours of the night, and the couch's head points to the first. At dusk stands the mirror the scholars give to Horthonel, God of Fleeting Moments, and it is the only one whose frame is chipped by hands, because it was touched most. Then, round the ring, come the Pale Guardian, Tzarash, keeper of oaths and of time's borders; the Burning Whisper, Kaelrath, god of forbidden illumination; a mirror whose figure every sleeper describes differently and none wishes to describe at all, which the scholars leave unassigned; Vaedoris, the Spear of Verdance, at the deep of night; the Waiting Hunger, Urakh-Rynis, whose mirror is cracked across, perhaps on purpose; and at the hour before dawn Velkora, the Flame Beyond Dawn, whose frame is carved with three suns. The couch is for the Hierophant, who slept in the ring and spoke for whichever god appeared.

Its priests. The priesthood of the House was the Council of Eronis's spiritual arm. Its hierophants were dream-walkers who entered the gods' dreams on the couch and came back with law. A roll of their names is cut into the inner face of the dusk mirror's frame, and the glyphs, unusually, do not shift. The last name on it is Aurelis Ilaro. The murals near the court show a woman with that name's glyph on her breast standing before the mirrors while the figures in them turn their faces away. The Ilaro line held the couch for nine generations. The expeditions know of one living Ilaro; see the House of Ilaro.

Temples

The Hour-Court of Horthonel Horthonel, God of Fleeting Moments · the Mural Streets

Last head priest: Keeper of Hours Ilaro Saveth · a sundial with no gnomon · dust and warm stone

A small square court below the House of the Sleeping Gods with a great sundial on its floor and no gnomon to cast the shadow. At certain moments, never the same two days running, a shadow falls across it anyway, from nothing, and marks an hour that is not the hour. Nethranans came here to ask for a moment back. The god of ephemera, inspiration and lost time takes his offering in moments: the custom, recorded on the court's walls, was to stand on the dial and give up the memory of one ordinary hour. Vesperine Ilaro's pact is with Horthonel, and she has been seen on the dial.

Rites: the Giving of the Hour; the Night Without Minutes, once a generation. Now: the Enchanted Muse's dream-readers want the dial; the Arcane Academy has a sealed instruction about it; Delphara's Dream Dormitory has sent a letter of claim to nobody in particular.

Ties: Vesperine Ilaro; the Dream Dormitory at Delphara; the Enchanted Muse at Persevalis; the Mural Streets.

The Pale Gate of Tzarash Tzarash, the Pale Guardian · the head of the Mourning Cypress Walk

Last head priest: the Warden of the Dead, Corvael Sethra · the necropolis gate · cypress resin and cold

A gatehouse of white stone at the head of the Mourning Cypress Walk, through which the royal dead were carried to the burial-gardens. The Pale Guardian keeps curses, sacred oaths and the borders of time, and the gate's carvings show a tall pale figure barring the way with a staff, facing outward, towards the living. The inscriptions are oaths sworn by the dynasty's heirs never to disturb the dead their Mauveroot was keeping from decay. The Warden of the Dead held the gate's key; the key is carved into the figure's hand, and the hand is empty.

Rites: the Sealing at each royal burial; the Oath of Heirs. Now: the door at the walk's end has been opened from below, which by the gate's own inscriptions should not be possible while the Guardian stands. The figure's staff is broken.

Ties: the Mourning Cypress Walk; the Sethra; herbalists of Willowheart.

The Terrace of Velkora Velkora, the Flame Beyond Dawn · the Palace's eastern terrace

Last head priest: Dawn-Singer Iseult Ilaro · three discs and a fire-bowl · ash and sea wind

An open terrace on the Palace's eastern side, facing the sea, where three discs of polished bronze stand on pillars. Two are bright. The third is blackened, as if by heat, though nothing on the terrace is burned. A great fire-bowl, cold for centuries, sits before them. The god of rebirth through fire, twilight revelation and destruction was greeted here at dawn, and the murals show the Dawn-Singers lifting their arms to three suns in the sky. Haftvad of the Sage's Archive has copied the terrace's inscription and will not let anyone see his translation.

Rites: the Greeting of the Dawn; the Burning, of which the murals show only the before and the after. Now: the Arcane Academy's expedition camps closest to this terrace, and its leader carries sealed orders.

Ties: the three-suns mural; Kallisto Pyrphoros's Academy at Hellarchon; the Palace of Eronis.

The Green Spear of Vaedoris Vaedoris, the Spear of Verdance · the Quays of Irelas

Last head priest: the Harbour-Mother Lyss of Irelas · a living tree in a stone ship · salt and green sap

On the end of Irelas's longest quay is a stone ship, a full-size hull carved from a single outcrop, and growing from the place where its mast should be is a cypress, green and alive, though nobody has watered it in centuries. The god of flourishing, renewal and wild instinct was the sailors' god at Irelas. The tree was the mast of every Nethranan ship in spirit, and its cuttings went to sea in every hull that sailed without wind. The salvagers of Zandar Isle hang their first find of each season in its branches and take it down when they leave.

Rites: the Hanging of the First Find; the Launching, when a cutting was given to a new hull. Now: Dagny Saltfinger's crews keep a lamp at its foot through the calm months. The tree has put out new growth since the expeditions returned.

Ties: the Quays of Irelas; Zandar Isle; the wind-less ships; Lake Serathal at Duneforged.

The forgotten temple

The Field Altar of the Bronze Camp. The Mycairos army that came to take Velothis and found nobody to fight raised a field altar in the middle of its siege camp: a block of dark stone carried all the way across the sea, carved with the phrase scholars render "the gift beneath stone". The army's priests made sacrifice there every morning of the siege. Then their own cities fell silent, and the camp was abandoned with its weapons still racked. Nobody prays at the altar now. Nobody knows what it was raised to, beyond that phrase. The salvagers say the bronze is cursed and leave it. They also say that the altar's top is never dusty and is always faintly greasy to the touch, as if something has been laid on it recently.

Priestly houses

The House of Ilaro Nethranan · hierophants of the Sleeping Gods

Crest: a closed eye under seven points · Motto (from the dusk mirror): "We go in so that you need not" · Seat: once, the couch in the House of the Sleeping Gods

The line of dream-walkers who held the hierophant's couch for nine generations and spoke for the gods of the mirrors. The murals show them as tall, pale-eyed people with the closed-eye glyph on their breasts. Their last head, Aurelis Ilaro, was hierophant when the Council made its bargain.

  • Aurelis Ilaro, last Hierophant — shown on the murals standing before mirrors whose gods turn away from her.
  • Iseult Ilaro, Dawn-Singer of Velkora — Aurelis's sister; her name is the last carved on the eastern terrace.
  • Ilaro Saveth, Keeper of Hours — a cousin; the Hour-Court's last keeper, recorded as having "given up all his hours".
  • Vesperine Ilaro, the Last Dreamwalker — living; pact-bound to Horthonel; hunted by three powers; looking for something in the mirrors.

History and lore: the house's custom was that a hierophant who went into a god's dream and did not come out was not mourned, because she was not dead, only elsewhere. The Ilaros of the murals are all shown with their eyes closed except one, and the scholars cannot agree whether that one is Aurelis or Vesperine.

Ties: Vesperine Ilaro; the Dreamers' Hunt (Delphara, Hellarchon, Persevalis).

The Sethra Nethranan · mirror-wrights and Wardens of the Dead

Crest: a hand holding a pane of glass · Motto: "What is seen is kept" · Seat: once, the glass-houses of Irelas and the Pale Gate

The house that made the mirrors of the House of the Sleeping Gods, the frozen illusions of Irelas and the gate-key of the Cypress Walk. They were craftsmen rather than priests, but the Wardens of the Dead were always Sethra, because a family that made the glass could tell when something was looking out of it.

  • Corvael Sethra, last Warden of the Dead — his key is the one carved in the Pale Guardian's empty hand.
  • Lyss of Irelas, Harbour-Mother of Vaedoris — a Sethra by marriage; she cut the last cutting from the stone ship's tree.
  • Dagny Saltfinger, salvage-boss of Zandar Isle — living; claims a Sethra great-grandmother, and can read which Irelas glass is safe to lift better than any scholar.

History and lore: the Sethra are said to have set a little of themselves into every mirror they made, so that the glass would remember its maker. Salvagers say a frozen illusion handled by a Sethra hand does not crack. Dagny has never let anyone test it.

Ties: Zandar Isle; Nethranan glass sold at Romulo.

Temples · Towns of the Imperium

The Temples of the Invictian Towns

Smaller altars on the pilgrim road: a god of travellers at a milestone, wine-presses that belong to a god, a harbour god with a key, a bay where a Hellenorian god is licensed by special law, and a grove where the priest is whoever won the last fight.

Anticata The Shrine of the Milestones · Mercury and Janus

Head priest: Marcus Caecina Viator, priest of the Collegium of Innkeepers · road-god and threshold-god · horse, dust and lamp oil

Anticata's temple is a crossroads shrine-house at the north milestone. It is a square room with four open arches, so the road runs straight through it, and a bench for travellers on each side. Mercury of the roads stands in the north arch, facing Aepistra, holding a purse and a staff. Janus stands in the south arch with one face to the capital and one to the road. Between them, in small niches, are the road-spirits, little bronze figures every innkeeper on the street has paid for, each holding a cup. Couriers of the Cursus Legionis touch Mercury's foot on the way north and Janus's on the way home. Marcus Caecina Viator is elected by the innkeepers, keeps the shrine, punches pilgrims' tokens on the Iter Sacrum, and sells lamps at a mark-up the collegium sets.

Festivals: the Compitalia at midwinter, when every inn hangs a woollen doll for each free person and a ball for each slave; the Long Table. Trouble: the veterans camped at the milestone sleep in the shrine's arches. Calm, unpaid people in grey have begun sitting with the sick among them, and two old soldiers have died smiling in a way that frightened the innkeepers. Hidden: behind Janus's niche is a loose stone where couriers leave copies of what they carry, for a fee, for someone who collects at night.

Ties: daughter of Mercury of the Square at Romulo; the Gate of Janus at Romulo; Anticata; Aepistra.

Falecosa The Temple of Liber Pater · the Press Yard

Head priest: Helvia Marcella, Sacerdos of Liber, aunt of the Duumvir Marcus Helvius Tappo · the vine-god's presses · must, wasps and pine pitch

The four great beam presses in the Press Yard are the one thing in Falecosa no capital house has managed to buy, and the reason is religious. They are consecrated to Liber Pater, as the hill people call Bacchus, the Bountiful Spirit, and a god's property cannot be sold. His temple is the old gatehouse beside them, a single vaulted room painted with vines, holding a bearded wooden god with a cup and a mask. Each spring the first must is poured over his feet, and a jar is sent to Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Mons Cerealis in Aeterna. Helvia Marcella was elected priestess by the tenant families, holds the presses' keys, and has said that any owner who tries to use bought labour on the terraces will find the presses consecrated to a very long feast.

Festivals: the Treading; the Liberalia, when boys of the terraces take the man's toga; the Naming; and the Torchlight wine for Nemibano. Hidden: the cellars under the Cellae connect, and in the deepest one, at the Treading, masked people dance who are not all from Falecosa. The new verses in the treading songs come from there. Forgotten: Liber's consort Libera once had her own shrine on Terrace One. It is now a bailiff's tool-shed.

Ties: the Helvii; the Temple of Ceres at Aeterna; the grove at Nemibano; the Press Yard.

Fucostia The Temple of Portunus and Ceres of the Annona · the Lighter Steps

Head priest: the Flamen Portunalis, Gnaeus Annaeus Pollio, uncle of the Praefectus · the harbour god's key · tar, river mud and wet incense

Portunus is the god of harbours and of keys. His temple stands at the top of the Lighter Steps, a round building with a portico facing the river, and his statue holds a great bronze key. By custom it is the key of the Horrea: on the first day of each shipping season the Flamen Portunalis unlocks the granary gates with it and the season can begin. In a side chapel Ceres of the Annona, a daughter of the Mons Cerealis, receives the First Hull's first sack. Behind the temple, by Mavelon's gift, is a little shrine of Neptune where coastwise grain crews pray. Gnaeus Annaeus Pollio is honest like the rest of his family and very old, and he has started asking why Horreum Nine, which is always full, is never opened with Portunus's key.

Festivals: the Portunalia in late summer, when keys are thrown into the fire for luck; the First Hull; the Lantern Tide. Outside the walls: the Aurum Pact's isolation sheds keep a shrine to Febris, the fever goddess, and nothing leaves them uncertified. The cult: the dredging of the river mouth has not been done in three years. Each time it is scheduled, a requisition goes to the wrong store. Aeterna's Castellum of the Gullet has a daughter cell here.

Ties: the Annaei; the Temple of Ceres at Aeterna; Neptune at Mavelon; the Horrea.

Napplesia The Temple of Venus of the Bay and the Spring of Apollo

Head priest: Nautia Galla, priestess of Venus, sister of the Duumvir Spurius Nautius Crassipes · a goddess for the villas, a god for the baths · jasmine, sulphur and steam

Venus of the Bay has a white temple on the headland at the east end of the Ripa, where brides of the villa families are married and retired officers' widows remarry. Nautia Galla runs it with her brother's charm and none of his patience. The town's stranger god is in the Thermae: the Cauldron spring was dedicated to Apollo of the healing springs by Hellenorian settlers before the Imperium came. The Imperium was not willing to anger a god who heats water for nothing, so it licensed him by a special law that has been renewed every fifty years for six centuries. The bath-keepers keep his altar, and the Radiant Heartwardens pray to him beside their own god.

Festivals: the Veneralia in spring, when the women of the town wash the goddess's statue in the sea; the Opening of the Baths, by lot. Lantern Lane: a Tyrsan guest-god keeps a cedar shrine for the season, licensed through Mavelon. The cult: a quiet craftsman in the Thermae mends old wounds that no Heartwarden can, for veterans of the Ripa, and opens accounts. Several officers of the Veterans' Table now owe him favours to be named later.

Ties: the Nautii; the House of Guest Gods at Mavelon; the Mending Needle at Romulo; the Thermae.

Nemibano The Grove of Diana · below the treeline, on the lake shore

Head priest: none by appointment; the warden Gnaeus Ferrus, Rex Nemorensis, and the Mother of the Grove, Sylvia Nemorina · a priesthood held by the sword · pine resin and lake water

Diana's temple is a roofless ring of columns open to the lake, with the Golden Bough's oak nearby and seven yews over the graves of failed challengers. It is the only Invictian sanctuary where the local rite outranks the imperial one. Its priest is whoever holds the grove in single combat, and has been Gnaeus Ferrus for nineteen years. The rites of the wood are led by Sylvia Nemorina, whose word the town follows before the Duumviri's. The Verdant Sentinel Order guards the treeline and is sworn to Diana. Women ask for children with wax wombs; huntsmen with clay stags; the sick with little bronze hands. The capital has tried four times to replace the warden with an ordinary priest.

Festivals: the Torchlight, when the town carries torches round the lake and Falecosa's wine is poured; the Challenge Day at the dark of the moon after. Forgotten: above the lake, in a cave choked with ivy, is an older shrine to Cybele, the Earthen Mother, whose grove this was before Diana came. Sylvia Nemorina keeps it clear and says nothing about it. Hidden: one of the seven yews has no grave under it. It is kept for the present warden.

Ties: the shrine doors from Nemorus; the Vettii of Nemibano; the Iter Sacrum from Aeterna; the Grove.

The Roll and the Twelve: faith in Hellenoria

Ask a Hellenorian which gods his city worships and he will name twelve, and the twelve will not match the next city's. The League has no church. It has a roll, a court and a great many arguments. Every city keeps its favourite gods in a Synnaos, a "shared house": a pantheon hall with a chapel or a plinth for each god, arranged in an order the city fixed centuries ago and fights about every year. The order is the procession order at the city's great festival, so it is also the order in which priests, guilds and families walk, and who walks third instead of fourth is the kind of question that ends friendships and occasionally starts tyrannies. Hellarchon puts the Maiden first; Corinth puts whoever took most in vows last season first; Thessalonika's order was fixed by audit; Ephelanum's runs round the year like a calendar. None of the gods so ranked has set foot in a Synnaos since the Closing of the Bright Court; the grey fog keeps them in their halls, and a temple matters because it is where the fog is thinnest and prayer goes up fastest.

The gods and their families. The Hellenorian stories are family stories, told differently in every port. The Storm Lord Zeus and Hera, Matron of Families, sit at the head of the house and quarrel there. Zeus's brothers are Poseidon, the Earth Shaker, who took the sea, and Hades, who took what lies under the earth, the dead and the silver alike; his sisters are Demeter of the grain and Hestia of the hearth, who gave up her seat to keep the fire. All six are children of the Titans Cronus and Rhea, which every priest admits and none dwells on. The next generation is the working pantheon: Athena, born armoured from her father's head; the twins Apollo and Artemis, born to the Titaness Leto on a floating island; Hermes the messenger, who stole his brother's cattle on the day he was born; Hephaestus the smith, lame, married to Aphrodite and cuckolded by Ares; Dionysus, twice-born, the youngest and the loudest; Hercules, the mortal son who climbed. Around them stand powers with no seat at the table: Hecate of the crossroads, Nyx the primordial night whom even Zeus would not cross, Tyche of fortune, Nike of victory (a daughter of the Titaness Styx, by whom the gods swear), Pan of the pastures and Terra the Earthshaper, whose masons cut every temple in the League.

The Tribunal and the Truth-Flame. Which gods are gods is decided in Hellarchon. The Tribunal of the gods sits in the Synnaos below the Rock and keeps the Roll: twenty-one recognised powers. A god on the Roll is protected; its temples have asylum, its priests immunity, its treasuries the sacrilege laws. A god off the Roll is not banned, merely unprotected (see the Academy, the Lexicon and the Tribunal), which in practice means anyone may rob its shrine. The Titans are not on the Roll. They were "put down, not killed", their temples still stand, and the Tribunal's position is that one does not need to recognise one's grandparents. Helionyx, which worships the sun Titan as its patron, is the standing exception and the standing embarrassment (the temples of Helionyx). Behind the Tribunal stands the imperial Truth-Flame, which does not judge gods but words: every hymn, oracle-book and temple copy in the League must pass its readers, and Inquisitor Vireon, Third Seat, strikes verses with a reed dipped in lamp-black. A struck verse is struck in every temple. Priests learn to sing the gaps.

The Voidfolk and their gods. The tiefling families absorbed under the classified Voidfolk Accord brought their own powers with them: the old pact-holders their ancestors bargained with, whose names appear in no sanctioned text. The Accord's public clause enrolled them under Hades, whose Asetherian image already wears horns, and under Hecate; its classified clause, the Truth-Flame says, deals with the rest. So in every Synnaos the Voidfolk worship at Hades's chapel, which is nearly always the lowest step and the last in procession, and in every city the Truth-Flame visits that chapel monthly. What the Voidfolk say at home is their own business, until it is not.

The games and the circuit. Hellenorian piety is athletic. The League keeps three crowned festivals, the Periodos: Hellarchon's Greater Panegyris, Corinth's Isthmian Games every two years, and Delphara's Pythian Games every four, music before athletics. A victor at all three is a "circuit-man" and dines at public cost for life in his own city, which several cities can no longer afford. The games carry a truce even tyrants keep; heralds from Delphara announce it in every Synnaos. Pilgrims walk the same circuit: up the Long Lane, across Corinth's isthmus, along the Southern Run to Ephelanum's harvest and back, and always, in the end, up the Sacred Way to Delphara. Delphara is the circuit's hinge and the Tribunal's conscience. No god may be added to the Roll without an oracle from the god at Delphara, so every petition for recognition goes up the Sacred Way, and every pilgrim token, a lead disc stamped by each sanctuary he visits, is countersigned at Delphara's gate. The Amphictyony can close the oracle; a city whose petitions are closed loses its gods' standing one by one. Every Hellenorian city therefore pays Delphara, and Delphara remembers which ones paid late (Thebesieas has opinions).

Temples · Hellarchon

The Temples of Hellarchon

The city that decides which gods exist keeps them in a round hall below the Rock, pays for their festivals before it pays for its fleet, and has a Titan under its goddess's floor that nobody mentions in front of the Truth-Flame.

Pantheon building
The Synnaos of the Tribunal, at the head of the Agora under the Rock
Chief priest
Archiereus Theodektes Eteoboutades, President of the Tribunal
Patron gods
Athena, the Maiden of the Rock; Poseidon of the Sheds; Hestia of the civic hearth
Banned here
The Eclipsed Mirror's crossroads rites inside the walls; any hymn the Truth-Flame has struck; altars to Titans on public ground
Trouble
The Theoric Fund keeps the temples magnificent while the fleet goes short, and the Tribunal's Roll has been closed for ten years

The Pantheon

The Synnaos of the Tribunal stands where the Agora meets the foot of the Rock: a round hall of grey Oros marble, cut by the Geolith Artisan Covenant over sixty years, roofed with a shallow dome of bronze tiles that turn green in the sea air and are scrubbed back to gold before every Panegyris. Twelve columns carry the dome, and between each pair stands a god's chapel, each with its own altar outside on the ring-walk and its own door, so that the building looks from the Agora like twelve temples that have agreed to share a roof. In the centre, under the open eye of the dome, is the Table of the Roll: a slab of black stone on which the names of the twenty-one recognised powers are cut, with space below for more. The space has been empty for ten years. Nine more plinths stand outside the ring, under the eaves, for the gods of the Roll who have no chapel here; their priests pay rent for the shade.

The order of the twelve, walking sunwise from the east door, is the Panegyris order: Athena the Maiden; Poseidon; Hestia, whose chapel has no image, only a lamp lit from the Prytaneion hearth; Zeus; Hera; Apollo; Artemis; Demeter; Hephaestus; Hermes; Dionysus; and last, on the lowest step by the west door, Hades, where the Voidfolk of the Deme of the Accord make their offerings because they have no shrine of their own. Aphrodite, Ares, Hecate, Nike, Tyche, Pan, Terra, Hercules and Nyx have the plinths outside. Every few years someone proposes moving Hermes above Hephaestus, the merchants and the smiths fill the Agora, and the motion is tabled.

The Tribunal sits at the Table on the first day of each month: nine judges, the high priests of the first nine chapels, presided over by the Archiereus. It hears petitions for recognition, disputes over procession order between cities, and charges of impiety against priests; the Truth-Flame sends a reader who sits behind the president and says nothing until he does. The present Archiereus is Theodektes Eteoboutades, seventy-two, high priest of Poseidon and head of the oldest priestly house in the city. He has presided for nineteen years, has never added a god to the Roll, and has turned away forty-one petitions, most recently one for Astraphael the Destructive Star, whose hero-shrine the Circles of Mirrors wanted made a temple. His cousin Hagne Eteoboutadou is the Maiden's priestess, and his grandson Kallias keeps the Table's ledgers and lets the Truth-Flame's reader see them a day early. The family has held both great priesthoods of the Rock for longer than the Rock has had walls (House Eteoboutadai).

Temples

The Maiden's Temple Athena · the summit of the Rock

Gilded and crowded · priestesses, robe-weavers, allied delegates · olive oil, marble dust, new wool

The great temple on the Akra, its cult image of ivory and gold three men high, its strongroom holding the League Chest. The priestess is Hagne Eteoboutadou, sixty, who has served thirty-one years and speaks to the goddess in the old dialect the Lexicon has stopped sanctioning. Her rites: the daily feeding of the sacred snake that lives under the porch and has not been seen in four years (a honey-cake is left, and taken); the Washing in early summer, when the robe-washers of House Praxiergidai strip the image, wash its robe in the sea and leave the city's business suspended for a day as "unlucky"; and the Greater Panegyris, when the new robe is carried up from the harbour behind six hundred maidens and laid on the goddess by Lady Kassiane Thaloris in the Emperor's name. The temple's money is the allies' money: the League Chest pays the priestesses a "guardian's fee" of one part in sixty, which Corinth calls embezzlement and the Tribunal calls custom.

Ties: the Akra; House Thalorid; the Ecliptica Arcanum, Athena's magicians, keep a reading-room in the porch; Thessalonika's Athena of the Porticoes sends a scroll each year (see Thessalonika).

Poseidon of the Sheds Poseidon · between the Moon and the Cup

Salt and tar · trierarchs, rowers, widows · pitch, wet rope, burnt fat

A long low temple on the mole between the two war basins, built like a shipshed and roofed with old ships' timbers, each beam carved with the name of the hull it came from. The Archiereus himself is its priest, though the daily work is done by his deputy, Nausikrates Ktesiou, a former steersman who lost a hand at the oar-port and blesses rams with the stump. Rites: the Launching in spring, when every hull leaving the sheds is touched with seawater from the god's basin; a black bull drowned off the mole before any war vote; and the autumn Naming of the Dead, which ends here after the Clay Gate, the year's lost crews read out by ship. The temple is rich in ram-prows taken in war, and poor in coin since the peace. It keeps the crew-rolls of the fleet in a chest behind the altar, which makes Nausikrates the only man who knows how many rowers the city really has. The Poseidon of the Isthmus at Corinth claims seniority; Theodektes refuses to say the two are the same god's house.

Ties: the Shipsheds; House Nikandridai, who fund six ships' sacrifices a year; the crews that never come ashore.

The Common Hearth Hestia · the Prytaneion

Warm and official · councillors, ambassadors, victors at dinner · olive wood smoke, barley bread

The civic hearth in the Prytaneion on the Agora, kept by the Hearthfire Sanctum, Hestia's order, whose fire has never gone out. Its keeper is Mother Eirene Hestiaia, a widow chosen by the Sanctum for life, who has outlived three Hegemons and feeds the fire with olive wood from the sacred trees only. The rites are plain: a pinch of everything eaten at the public table goes into the flame first; every colony and every allied city lights its own hearth from here, and a city that lets its fire go out must send to Hellarchon for a new one and pay. The circuit-men and the Archon Eponymous dine here at public cost. The Hearth's real power is the Lending of the Coal: Hellarchon's fire is carried to every new Synnaos in the League, so the Sanctum can say, truthfully, that every civic hearth from Thessalonika to Ephelanum is a daughter of this one, and can also say, less truthfully, that a daughter owes her mother rent.

Ties: the Agora; the Hearthfire Sanctum's houses at Ephelanum and Thessalonika; Aristeas Melanthiou's unwelcome guests.

The Smith's House Hephaestus and the Maiden Worker · above the Clay Gate

Sooty and proud · potters, bronze-casters, kiln-masters · kiln smoke, hot bronze, wet clay

A Doric temple on the knoll above the potters' quarter, shared by Hephaestus and the Maiden in her working aspect, the only temple in the city where Athena takes second place. The priest is Lampon Kerameus, a kiln-master elected by the guilds, who runs the temple like a workshop: dues by the kiln, a strike fund in the treasury, and a bronze-cast image of the lame god that the Forgeflame Artisans recast every fifty years under the Invictian name they are not allowed to say inside. Rites: the Torch-Race from the Academy Grove to the altar, relay teams of apprentices carrying fire that must not go out; the blessing of the first firing of every new kiln; the Feast of the Bellows, when the smiths eat in the street and the potters complain about the noise. The temple banks the guilds' strike fund, which is why the Council treats Lampon with care, and it sells the Clay Gate's broken pottery by the basket, which is why the Euxenidai do.

Ties: the Clay Gate; Corinth's founders' altar at Lechaion (see Corinth); Araavyna's kiln-shrine (see the towns).

Dionysus of the Theatre Dionysus · the south slope of the Rock

Loud and licensed · actors, chorus-masters, sponsors · spilled wine, pine resin, greasepaint

A small old temple at the foot of the Theatre of Hellarchon, holding the wooden image of the god that is carried into the theatre each Dionysia and set in the front row, where he watches the plays mock everyone. The priest has the best seat in the theatre by law; this year it is Pyrrhias Komodou, a retired comic actor whose grandfather wrote the play that got the last Hegemon but three exiled by the Sherd. Rites: the Bringing-In of the image by torchlight, the four-day Dionysia under a licence that lets the stage say anything until it expires at the fourth sunset, and the Opening of the Jars in early spring, when the new wine is tasted and the dead are thought to walk for a day, so doors are smeared with pitch. The Obsidian Masquerade sits masked in the seats; Pyrrhias pretends not to know which masks are new. Kleito Euxenide pays for the choruses; Pyrrhias pays for nothing and is owed by everyone.

Ties: the Theatre; the Obsidian Masquerade; House Euxenidai; Ephelanum's Vintage, where the same masks reappear.

The forgotten temple

The Old House of Pallas. Under the floor of the Maiden's temple, reached by a stair behind the strongroom that the priestesses use as a store for broken lamps, are the foundations of an older temple: rough blocks the size of carts, laid without mortar, with bronze clamps gone green. The guides on the Akra call it "the first Maiden's house". The priestesses know better and say nothing. The old house belonged to Pallas, the Titan of Defence, whose name the goddess still wears as an epithet on the oldest dedications and whom the city's founding story says she killed in single combat on this rock and wore as a shield. A fragment of the Titan's image, a bronze foot as long as a man, lies in the store under sacking. At the back of the foundation a doorway has been filled with later masonry; the fill has the Maiden's owl cut into every block, as if someone wanted very much to make the point. Nobody has worshipped Pallas here for a thousand years, and every Panegyris, before dawn, the oldest priestess goes down the stair alone with a cup of unmixed wine and pours it at the filled door. She says it is housekeeping.

Priestly houses

House Eteoboutadai Priestly house · Eupatrid · the Rock's two priesthoods

Crest: an olive tree and a trident crossed above a snake · Motto: "We were here first." · Seat: the old house below the Rock's north slope, next to the Mirrored House and on worse terms with it every year

The oldest family in the city, descended (they say) from the king who judged between the Maiden and the Earth Shaker when both wanted the Rock. The judgment went to the Maiden, and the family has kept both gods ever since: the women hold the Maiden's priesthood, the men Poseidon's, by right of blood, not lot. They own no ships and want none. Their income is temple perquisites, a share of the sacrificial meat, and land in the hills that the silver-leases have not reached.

  • Theodektes Eteoboutades, Archiereus and priest of Poseidon, 72 — has said no to forty-one gods; keeps the Table's key on a chain and his opinions to himself.
  • Hagne Eteoboutadou, the Maiden's priestess, 60 — his cousin; feeds a snake nobody has seen and pours wine at a door nobody uses.
  • Kallias Eteoboutades, his grandson, 25 — keeps the Table's ledgers and shows them to the Truth-Flame's reader early, out of fear or ambition; his family suspects both.
  • Phanostrate Eteoboutadou, Hagne's niece, 19 — the next priestess by blood; has taken a lover in the Academy Grove and asks him questions about the second cellar.

History. The family held both priesthoods before the city had an Assembly, kept them through the tyrants, and kept them through the war by never once preaching for or against it. When the Truth-Flame arrived on the Court-Hill after the war, Theodektes handed it the temple copies of the hymns himself, so that the striking would be done by the family's hand. Each struck verse is copied into a book the family keeps in its own house, and the book is now thicker than the hymnal.

Ties: the Maiden's Temple; Poseidon of the Sheds; the Tribunal; the Isthmiadai of Corinth, with whom they disagree about Poseidon in letters going back two hundred years (see Corinth).

House Praxiergidai Robe-washers of the Maiden · hereditary office

Crest: a folded robe on a wave · Motto: "Clean hands, closed mouths." · Seat: the Washers' House on the Road, by the halfway tower

A family of fullers who hold one sacred office: once a year they strip the Maiden's image, wash her robe in the sea and dress her again, behind screens, unseen by anyone else. For that day and its eve they are the only people permitted to touch the goddess. They have done it for six hundred years and been paid for it in bread and a front seat at the Panegyris. They are Road people, not Rock people, and the Road is proud of them.

  • Mnesarete Praxiergidou, eldest washer, 58 — has seen the image undressed thirty times and says only that "the goddess is in good repair".
  • Euthymos Praxiergides, her son, 33 — a rower, the first of the family to sit in the war fleet; his crew calls him "the Maiden's laundryman" and fights anyone else who does.
  • Korinna Praxiergidou, his daughter, 12 — will wash the robe in eight years; has started sneaking up the store stair to look at the bronze foot.

History. The family's founder was a fuller who rescued the robe from a fire during a tyranny and was given the washing as a reward. The office has made them untouchable and poor; a Praxiergid cannot be prosecuted during the Washing month, and three of them have timed their debts accordingly. They know one thing nobody else knows: what is under the image's robe. They have never said, and the Eteoboutadai have never asked.

Ties: the Maiden's Temple; the Road; the Ivory Chorus, who sing at the Washing.

Temples · Corinth

The Temples of Corinth

The most profitable gods in the League live on the slope above the round harbour, ranked each year by takings, served by a priesthood split down the middle, and paid for by men who may not come back.

Pantheon building
The House of Vows in the Temple Precinct of the Lebes
Chief priest
Archiereia Pherenike Isthmiadou of the Eastern Tide
Patron gods
Poseidon of the Isthmus; Aphrodite of the Upper Fortress; Tyche of the Street
Banned here
Ares and his priests inside the walls during the Isthmian truce; the Truth-Flame's readers in the Precinct on vow-days
Trouble
The two halves of the Isthmian priesthood are racing for more than the Two Tides this year

The Pantheon

The House of Vows stands at the top of the Temple Precinct on the Lebes slope, where every sailor leaving the round harbour can see it over his shoulder. It is a long colonnaded hall of yellow limestone faced in Corinthian bronze at every capital, the acanthus leaves cast so fine they tremble in a strong wind, which the priests say is the gods breathing and the founders say is a casting defect they could not afford to fix. Inside, twelve bays open off a central aisle, each with a god's image, an offering-table and a strongbox. At the far end, where another pantheon would put its chief god, hangs the Board: a great painted tablet listing the twelve, re-lettered every spring.

The Board is the Corinthian order. Every god in the House is ranked by the value of the vows paid at its table over the last sailing season: a sailor promises a god a share of a voyage's profit if he comes home, and when he comes home, he pays, publicly, and the priests enter it. Whoever took most stands first in the next year's procession. This year's order is Poseidon, Aphrodite, Tyche, Hermes, Nike, Hephaestus, Apollo, Demeter, Dionysus, Zeus, Hera and Hades, who takes vows from the families of the drowned and has never risen above eleventh. Zeus's priests think tenth is an insult. Corinth thinks it is arithmetic. Hellarchon's Tribunal has twice ruled that the Board is impious and twice been told that Corinth will pay its Delphara dues when Hellarchon returns the League Chest.

The House is run by the Archiereia, the high priestess of the Isthmian priesthood, and this year that is Pherenike Isthmiadou of the Eastern Tide, fifty-four. The Isthmian priesthood is one family in two halves: the Eastern Tide keeps Poseidon's altar at the Lebes, the Western Tide keeps his altar at Lechaion, and at the Two Tides each half sacrifices at its own harbour at the same moment and runs for the god's temple at the Haulway's midpoint. The half that arrives first holds the House of Vows for a year. Pherenike's half has won six of the last eight races; her cousin Agasikles Isthmiades of the Western Tide has started training runners from the stadium, which Pherenike calls cheating and the Bacchiadai call competition (House Isthmiadai).

Temples

Poseidon of the Isthmus Poseidon · the Haulway's midpoint

Shaken and wet · haulers, captains, athletes · tallow, brine, pine

The god's own temple stands in a grove of pines at the midpoint of the Haulway, where the ship road tops the neck of land and both seas are visible at once. Every hull dragged across stops at the temple steps while its captain pours seawater from one sea onto the altar and takes a jar of the other sea away. The keeper is whichever Tide won the last race; the god's chief priest by blood is Agasikles Isthmiades, sixty, who presides at the Isthmian Games every two years and crowns the victors with pine (the Laurel Court crowns them again, with laurel, for a fee). Rites: the Two Tides race; a horse driven into the sea at each harbour before the Games; and the earthquake-vigil, when the ground shakes and the priests sit up all night outside to show the god they are not afraid. The temple takes a tithe of the Haulway toll by ancient right, which makes it richer than most cities, and lends to the clan at a rate the clan sets.

Ties: the Haulway; House Bacchiadai; Hellarchon's Poseidon of the Sheds, whose priests will not admit the Isthmus is senior; Delphara's truce-heralds at the Games (see Delphara).

Aphrodite of the Rock Aphrodite · the summit of the Upper Fortress

Windy and scented · priestesses, sailors' wives, singers · myrtle, rose oil, wet stone

The goddess's temple crowns the Upper Fortress, small, old and so rich in offerings that the porch is closed with a bronze grille. Its high priestess is Lysidike, called the Rose, a former singer of the Ivory Chorus, who keeps the chorus's Corinthian house in the temple's lower court and its gossip in her head. Rites: the Bathing, when the image is carried down to the spring inside the fortress walls and washed; the doves released at the start of every sailing season, one for each ship, and counted when they come home; and weddings, many of them, because a marriage vowed on the Rock is said to hold through any voyage. Sailors' wives dedicate a lock of hair when the ship leaves and a mirror when it returns. The temple's money comes from the sailors' offerings and from the Ivory Chorus's wedding contracts, a share of every dowry sung over. Lysidike knows every marriage the clan has made for thirty years, including the one it voted 104 to 97 to allow.

Ties: the Upper Fortress; the Ivory Chorus; Calpurnia Secunda, who was married here and lit a lamp to Venus in the Invictian manner, which Lysidike allowed and the priestesses still discuss.

Tyche of the Street Tyche · the sea end of the Street of Counting-Houses

Quiet and expensive · bankers, factors, gamblers · sealing wax, incense, counted coin

A round shrine at the Street's sea end, its image a woman holding a ship's rudder and a horn of plenty, blindfolded by order of a priest three centuries ago after a run of bad harvests. The priestess is Archippe Kybeia, who is also a member of Fate's Spindle Circle, the philosophical society that argues destiny on her steps every evening.
