Rites: every sea-loan written on the Street is sworn before the image, and the lender drops a coin in the goddess's urn so that she has a stake; the Turning, at the new year, when the image's wheel is spun and the Street's interest rates are, by custom, set by where it stops (the bankers have agreed the result in advance for ninety years); and a lot-oracle of knucklebones for merchants who cannot afford Delphara. The shrine is the Street's neutral ground: the doormen of the Mithril Reserve and the Vaults of Equilibrium, who do not speak to each other, both leave a coin in the urn on the same morning each week.

Ties: the Street; House Euphranoridai, whose loans are all sworn here; Fate's Spindle Circle.

Nike of the Laurel Court Nike · beside the stadium

Green and anxious · victors, trainers, mercenaries · cut laurel, olive oil, sweat

The cloistered garden in the Isthmian Quarter is Nike's precinct: the winged goddess stands at its centre on a column carved with acanthus, among living acanthus, holding out a wreath. Her priest is Euagoras, nervous, honest and frightened, who cuts the victors' laurel each morning of the Games from trees grown from cuttings taken at Delphara. Rites: the second crowning of every Isthmian victor, the Oath of the Order, sworn here by every new officer of the Order of Morning's Rise, who are Nike's own mercenaries and garrison the Upper Fortress; and the hanging of captured shields along the cloister. The precinct is paid for by the Order's dedications and by victors' families, who pay the priest to cut a wreath for every grandchild. Someone is cutting the laurel at night and selling wreaths to men who did not win.

Ties: the Isthmian Quarter; the Order of Morning's Rise; the laurel of Delphara; Thebesieas's runners, who win too often for Euagoras's comfort.

The Founders' Altar Hephaestus · Lechaion, among the Copper Smelts

Green-sheened and hot · founders, tin-traders, smelt-crews · metal on the tongue, charcoal

No temple, only an altar in a walled yard between the furnaces, with a bronze image of the lame god cast by the first Glaukotid and recast by every one since. The priest is the head of the founders' guild for the year, at present Kyra Glaukotis, the first woman to hold it, who took it the week her husband died and has not been challenged. Rites: the first pour of every new alloy is offered here before it is sold; the founders eat a meal of bread baked in a cooling mould on the god's day; and every apprentice's first casting, however bad, is buried under the altar, so that the yard is floored with three hundred years of failures. The altar keeps the guild's strongbox, which held the recipe for Corinthian bronze until last month. The Forgeflame Artisans send a delegate every year to argue about whose god this is.

Ties: Lechaion; House Glaukotidai; Hellarchon's Smith's House; Qart-Hadeth tin-traders, who bring their own god and leave him in the hostel.

The forgotten temple

The Sun's Seat on the Rock. Before the goddess took the summit of the Upper Fortress, the Rock belonged to Helios. The Corinthian story, told by old haulers and nobody else, is that Poseidon and the Sun both claimed the isthmus, and the judge gave the sea to Poseidon and the Rock to the Sun, who later gave it to Aphrodite as a wedding gift and went home. The Sun's temple is the ruin on the Rock's eastern shoulder that the garrison uses as a goat pen: a platform facing exactly due east, a broken altar with a disc cut into it, and the remains of a channel that once carried water from the spring inside the walls to a basin where the sunrise would strike it. The spring that has never run dry is the Sun's gift, the old story says, and he will take it back if he is forgotten. He has been. The Order of Morning's Rise, which keeps its goats there, greets the sunrise every day from the platform out of military habit and does not know it is the last rite still kept in the ruin. Helionyx, where the Sun is patron, sends a priest once a generation to ask for the altar stone back (see Helionyx). The clan has always said it will consider the matter.

Priestly houses

House Isthmiadai Priestly house · the two Tides of Poseidon

Crest: a trident with one prong broken off · Motto: "Both seas, one god." · Seat: two houses, one above each harbour, and the god's temple at the midpoint

The family that keeps Poseidon's priesthood at Corinth, split into two branches two centuries ago when brothers quarrelled over an inheritance and the god's oracle at Delphara ruled that both should serve. The Eastern Tide lives above the Lebes and marries sailors' daughters; the Western Tide lives above Lechaion and marries founders' daughters. They meet at the Two Tides, the Games, and funerals, and run against each other at the first two. Their income is the Haulway tithe, divided by a formula nobody else understands.

  • Pherenike Isthmiadou, Archiereia, of the Eastern Tide, 54 — runs the House of Vows like a counting-house and the Two Tides like a war; has won six of eight races with her own sons.
  • Agasikles Isthmiades, of the Western Tide, 60 — chief priest of the Isthmus by blood, president of the Games; has hired stadium runners and called them "nephews".
  • Melanthios Isthmiades, Pherenike's eldest, 30 — her fastest runner, in love with Agasikles's daughter, and thinking of losing the race on purpose.
  • Hermione Isthmiadou, Agasikles's daughter, 24 — keeps the Western Tide's books and has found the Haulway tithe short by a twelfth for six years.

History. The split is older than the Bacchiad monopoly of office and the clan has used it ever since: a priesthood that races itself has no time to race the clan. The family corresponds with Hellarchon's Eteoboutadai about whose Poseidon is senior, two hundred years of letters, every one polite and none conceding.

Ties: Poseidon of the Isthmus; House Eteoboutadai of Hellarchon; House Bacchiadai.

House Kybeidai Diviners and lot-keepers · citizens, not clan

Crest: three knucklebones on a blue field · Motto: "The throw is honest." · Seat: the house behind Tyche's shrine

Keepers of Tyche's shrine and of the knucklebone oracle for nine generations, and the Street's quiet referees: when two bankers disagree on a contract, the Kybeidai throw the bones, and both have agreed in advance to abide. They make their money from the urn, from the lot-oracle, and from knowing everyone's loans.

  • Archippe Kybeia, priestess, 47 — blindfolds the goddess every morning and herself every evening for the Spindle Circle's debates.
  • Glaukippos Kybeides, her brother — throws the bones for the Street; has never been accused of a weighted throw, and has never thrown against the clan.
  • Nikeso Kybeia, her daughter, 17 — has worked out how the Turning is fixed, and is deciding whom to tell.

History. The first Kybeides was a dice-cheat sentenced to serve the goddess for life as penance, and served her so well his descendants inherited the job. The family has the best records on the Street: every vow and every loan sworn before Tyche since the war, in the shrine's books.

Ties: Tyche of the Street; the Mithril Reserve; Fate's Spindle Circle.

Temples · Thessalonika

The Temples of Thessalonika

The tidiest gods in the League: ranked by the date on their foundation deeds, housed in a glazed stoa with braziers, blessed with frost, audited every quarter, and honoured with a hospitality nobody in the city examines too closely.

Pantheon building
The Stoa of the Twelve, on the upper side of the Grid Agora
Chief priest
Hiereus Aristokles Kerykides, priest of Hermes of the Gate
Patron gods
Hermes of the Gate; Athena of the Porticoes; Zeus of Guests at the Horse Gate
Banned here
Any rite that keeps no record, which in practice means the Obsidian Veins and Dionysian night-rites outside the theatre
Trouble
The Truth-Flame wants the scholars' post opened, and the priests of the Gate have always carried it sealed

The Pantheon

The Stoa of the Twelve closes the upper side of the Grid Agora: a two-storeyed colonnade two hundred paces long, its intercolumns glazed with thick greenish panes against the north wind, its floor warmed by braziers from the First Frost to the spring, so that in winter the gods of Thessalonika are the only ones in the League who are never cold. Twelve chambers open off the colonnade, one per god, each with its altar on the Agora side so that sacrifice is public and smoke is not. Over each door hangs a bronze tablet giving the god's name, the date its altar was founded, and the deed by which the founding was proved. That is the order.

After the great fire three centuries ago, when the surveyor Anaxilas re-pegged the grid, every priesthood in the city claimed seniority for the new Stoa. The Assembly referred the matter to the auditors, who asked for documents. The order of the Twelve has followed the documents ever since: Hermes of the Gate, whose altar stood at the original landward gate before there was a city; Athena; Zeus of Guests; Demeter; Poseidon; Hestia, whose lamp was lit from Hellarchon's hearth and whose receipt survives; Apollo; Artemis; Hera; Hephaestus; Dionysus, admitted a hundred and forty years ago "on probation" and still on it; and Hades, last, by League custom, whose chamber the city's few Voidfolk families keep. Aphrodite has a plinth in the colonnade and a petition pending with the auditors; her priestess has been told to find a deed.

The Stoa is governed by the priest of the first god, who is Hiereus Aristokles Kerykides, sixty-three, head of the herald family that has served Hermes of the Gate since the first deed was written (House Kerykidai). His office makes him president of the Twelve, keeper of the harbour blessing at the First Frost, and, by a custom older than the Porticoes, warden of the scholars' post: letters sealed with an academy's mark are blessed at the god's altar and carried by the Kerykidai's couriers uninspected, under Hermes's protection, to every border. His wife Theodote keeps the Stoa's accounts and submits them to the auditors before they are asked. His nephew Philon rides the courier routes himself, which is how the family knows where every letter in the city goes and has never once said.

Temples

Hermes of the Gate Hermes · the sanctuary among the academies

Brisk and cold · couriers, merchants, students · pine smoke, wet wool, sealing wax

The old sanctuary above the Agora, among the academies, where the god stands as a square pillar with a head and a phallus, rubbed bright by every traveller who leaves the city. Its priest is Aristokles Kerykides. Rites: the First Frost, when ice first appears in the upper town's fountains and the priests carry the god's staff down to the harbour gate to bless the bay, the date entered in a register four hundred years long; the Sealing, each morning, when the day's scholars' post is laid on the altar and blessed; and the Boundary-Rubbing, when every boundary pillar on the grid is anointed with oil and checked against the surveyor's rod. The sanctuary is paid by the merchants' guild and the courier fees, and it lends to nobody, which the Kerykidai call piety and the bankers call a missed opportunity. Since the Three Libraries circle began, the Sealing has been the busiest rite in the city.

Ties: the Grid Agora; the courier-house on Ink Row; the Sunward Valiants, Hermes's mercenaries, who pray here before northern contracts; Corinth's Hermes, fourth on the Corinthian Board and resentful of it.

Athena of the Porticoes Athena · the east end of the colonnades

Learned and draughty · scholars, Ecliptica magicians, students in debt · lamp oil, parchment, cold stone

A temple built into the Porticoes' east end, its cult image an armoured Athena with an open scroll instead of a shield. Its priestess is Hypsipyle Glaukopis, a mathematician elected by the masters, who lectures from the temple steps. The Ecliptica Arcanum, Athena's magicians, hold their northern chapter in its back rooms and plan workings on slates before casting them. Rites: the Disputation opens and closes with sacrifice here, and the losing side of each debate pays for the cake; new masters swear to "teach in public and be answered"; and every new book is laid before the goddess for a night before the Reading. The temple's money is fees from the Disputation's betting, which the priestess takes a twentieth of. Each year it sends a fair copy of the year's best work to the Maiden on Hellarchon's Rock, and each year the Truth-Flame's readers send back a list of passages struck.

Ties: the Porticoes; Krates the Dog, who sleeps in a jar fifty paces away and heckles the sacrifices; Hellarchon's Maiden's Temple; House Pinakidai.

Demeter of the Granaries Demeter · behind the harbour gate

Dusty and sealed · grain clerks, auditors, ship-masters · grain dust, lead, salt

A plain temple built into the granary wall, so that the goddess literally sits among the statutory reserve. The priestess is Sitone Sitonidou, of the family that has kept Demeter's altar and co-sealed the granaries for two centuries (House Sitonidai). Each quarter the auditors' lead tags are blessed at her altar before they are tied, and breaking one is sacrilege as well as a capital charge, which doubles the penalty without changing it. Rites: the First Loaf, baked from the year's first steppe grain and broken by the Epistates; the Counting of the Jars, when the priestess walks the reserve with the chief auditor; and the women-only Seed-Night before the autumn sowing. The temple is a member shrine of the Golden Scythe Accord, Demeter's farmers' guild that decides which cities eat in a bad year, and Thessalonika's vote in the Accord is cast by its priestess.

Ties: the Sea Wall; the Golden Scythe Accord; Ephelanum's threshing-floor shrines (see Ephelanum); Thebesieas's Demeter of the furrow.

Zeus of Guests Zeus Xenios · under the Horse Gate arch

Smoky and solemn · steppe riders, horse-dealers, the Boreadai · dung, fermented milk, burning fat

An altar and a small roofed shrine built into the Horse Gate itself, half inside the wall and half out like the Boreadai exchange beside it. The god of hospitality protects the guest and the host alike, and here he protects the steppe trade. The priest is Kallisthenes Boreades by hereditary right, since his ancestors built the altar, and the daily rites are kept by a steppe-born under-priest, Tarkan, who wears the god's fillet over a felt cap. Rites: every rider who enters the city receives his bronze token at the altar; every contract between citizen and steppe is sworn here with salt and a cup; and at midsummer the Exchange of Cups is drunk before the god, the Epistates on the left of the altar, the eldest of the steppe camp on the right. The shrine is paid from the steppe retainer, a line in the audit labelled "hospitality", and it is the only shrine in the city whose accounts the auditors have never asked to see.

Ties: the Horse Gate; House Boreadai; Xerastri, whose Magi call this altar "the place the horse-lords drink with Hellenes".

The forgotten temple

The House of Memory. Before the great fire, the city's library was a temple: the Mouseion of Mnemosyne, the Titaness of memory, mother of the Muses, whose priests kept the city's records on the principle that a city which remembers accurately need not fight about the past. It burned with half the city three hundred years ago, and the surveyor Anaxilas pegged the new grid straight across its foundations. The Lower Grid's third block from the Agora stands on it now. The tenement cellars on that block have walls of fine dressed marble; one cellar has a floor mosaic of nine women holding nine instruments, under a layer of fish-salters' brine, and a bakehouse oven is built into what was the altar. The Pinakidai, who inherited the library's duties, keep no shrine to its goddess, because a Titaness is not on the Roll and the Stoa admits no god without a deed. Old copyists on Ink Row still touch the corner-stone of the block when they pass, for luck with names and dates, and the bakehouse's bread is said to make a child remember its lessons.

Priestly houses

House Kerykidai Heralds of Hermes · Eupatrid

Crest: a herald's staff with two snakes on frost-white · Motto: "Sealed is sacred." · Seat: the courier-house at the foot of Ink Row

The herald family of Hermes of the Gate, and the city's couriers. They run the scholars' post, the harbour blessing and the Stoa of the Twelve, and they make their money from courier fees, which are modest, and from being the only people who know where everything goes, which is priceless and never sold.

  • Aristokles Kerykides, Hiereus, 63 — president of the Twelve; blesses every sealed letter in the city and has opened none, he says, in forty years.
  • Theodote Kerykis, his wife — keeps the Stoa's accounts and submits them before the auditors ask, which the auditors find suspicious.
  • Philon Kerykides, his nephew, 31 — rides the courier routes to Hellarchon, Corinth and the passes; has a sweetheart in every post-house and a memory for seals.
  • Eudokia Kerykis, Aristokles's granddaughter, 14 — fostered north last spring; writes home in a hand that gets better every letter.

History. The first Kerykides was the herald who carried the city's first treaty, and the family has carried its correspondence since. When the Truth-Flame demanded the scholars' post be opened for inspection after the war, Aristokles answered that the letters were Hermes's until delivered, and that the Truth-Flame was welcome to take the matter to the Tribunal. It did. The Tribunal, which has Hermes in its tenth chapel, has not yet ruled.

Ties: Hermes of the Gate; the Three Libraries; House Anaxilaidai.

House Sitonidai Grain-priests of Demeter · citizens

Crest: a sheaf bound with a lead tag · Motto: "Counted is kept." · Seat: the priests' house in the granary wall

Keepers of Demeter's altar at the granaries and co-sealers of the statutory reserve. Their women hold the priesthood; their men are grain-measurers to the harbour. They are poor, exact and indispensable, and they vote in the Golden Scythe Accord on behalf of the city.

  • Sitone Sitonidou, priestess, 52 — blesses every lead tag, walks the reserve with the chief auditor, and knows how many jars hold grain.
  • Agathon Sitonides, her husband, harbour measurer — has measured every grain ship for twenty years with a bronze measure checked against the surveyor's rod.
  • Myrto Sitonidou, her daughter, 22 — next priestess; befriended Phila Anaxilaou at the auditors' office, and asks her a great many questions about the north.

History. The family was appointed to co-seal the granaries after a famine two centuries ago, when an archon sold the reserve and fled; the city decided the goddess should hold a key. The Sitonidai have never broken a seal and never missed a count, and they are the only family in the city who have walked every row of the reserve.

Ties: Demeter of the Granaries; the Golden Scythe Accord; Sosipatra Lysimachou, the chief auditor.

Temples · Ephelanum

The Temples of Ephelanum

A city whose gods keep the farming year: twelve chapels in a ring, one for each month's festival, around the altar of a Lady who is huntress in the hills and mother of the harvest on the plain, and who has two names, two feast-days and a third text nobody has read.

Pantheon building
The Menaion, the House of the Months, inside the goddess's ring before the Great Sanctuary
Chief priest
Hierarchis Melissa Aristarchis, high priestess of the Lady
Patron gods
Artemis, the Lady of Ephelanum (Diana in the Invictian text); Demeter at the threshing-floors; Dionysus at the Treading
Banned here
Iron on the first sheaf (it is cut with a bronze sickle); hunting in the Lady's hills in the festival half of the year; the Eclipsed Mirror
Trouble
Two governments keep two harvest calendars, and the gods' first-fruits are owed "at the feast", of which there are two

The Pantheon

The Menaion stands at the top of the marble street, just inside the boundary-stones of the goddess's ring, so that every procession bound for the Great Sanctuary passes through it. It is a round court open to the sky, ringed by twelve small temples of red-veined stone, each with a porch facing inward and a door facing out to the plain. Each temple is the house of the god who keeps one month of the festival year, and its door faces the fields or the hills where that month's work is done. In the centre of the court stands the Lady's Altar of the Year, a block of white marble carved with the twelve labours of the months and worn smooth on top by nine hundred years of first-fruits. The Lady is not one of the twelve. She is the year itself, the priestesses say, and the twelve are her household.

The order is the calendar, beginning with the plough: Demeter for the First Furrow; Apollo, the Lady's twin, who walks before his sister at the Procession of the Image; Hercules for the Barley Games; Zeus, by whom the Two Feasts' oaths are sworn; Hermes for the Fair of the Lady; Hephaestus for the Smiths' Offering; Dionysus for the Treading; Poseidon for the Dredging, whose temple door faces the silting harbour and has been stuck half-open by drifted earth for a decade; Athena for the Olive Night; Hestia for the midwinter hearth; Hades for the dead months when the seed lies under the earth; and Pan for the lambing, which closes the year. Each month the procession of that month's festival walks once round the court, stops at its god's porch, and goes out by his door to the fields. The gods' order cannot be argued, which in Ephelanum means it is argued about the dates instead.

The Menaion is the Hierarchis's, as everything in the ring is. Melissa Aristarchis, fifty-four, high priestess of the Lady and head of the Bees, presides over the twelve priesthoods, appoints eight of them, and lends to the other four (House Hagnotheidai). Her brother Kleon keeps the first-fruits ledger, in which every estate's offering to every month's god is entered, with the estate's harvest loan beside it. Her niece Daphne carries the Image's veil and treads the goddess's grapes. Every month the Hierarchis receives the first-fruits on the Altar of the Year with her own hands: barley, must, oil, a lamb. When the Dux's estates bring theirs on the Invictian feast-day instead of the Hellenorian, she receives them anyway, and dates the receipt by neither calendar.

Temples

Demeter of the Threshing-Floors Demeter · the first chapel and a hundred crossroads

Dusty and practical · tenants, reapers, gleaners · chaff, sweat, baking bread

Demeter has the first chapel in the Menaion and a hundred more on the Red Plain: a little shrine at every threshing-floor, a niche with a clay goddess, a bundle of last year's ears and a bowl for the first handful. Her priestess is Thesmo Thesmophoridou, a tenant farmer's widow from the slopes, of the family that has served the goddess on the plain since before the condominium (House Thesmophoridai). Rites: the First Furrow, where her priestess walks behind the Archon's and the Dux's oxen scattering seed from a basket; the blessing of every threshing-floor before the barley is trodden; the women's Seed-Days in autumn, three days on which no man may enter the chapel. Money: a handful from every floor, and the Golden Scythe Accord's dues, since the plain's vote in the Accord is the largest in the south. The Rubrian latifundia keep the floor-shrines because their slaves will not thresh without them, and the overseers have learnt not to argue.

Ties: the Red Plain; the Golden Scythe Accord; Thessalonika's Demeter of the Granaries; Thebesieas's Demeter of the furrow, whose Polemarch ploughs the same day.

Dionysus of the Treading Dionysus · the seventh chapel and the press-houses on the slopes

Sticky and loud · vintners, pickers, masked revellers · crushed grapes, pine resin, wine lees

The god's chapel in the Menaion holds a wooden mask the size of a cart-wheel hung on a pillar, which is taken down at the Treading and carried to the slopes. His priest is Lykourgos Bakchiou, a vintner on the Kallikratid estate, who has kept the mask for twenty years and the Kallikratidai's cellars for longer. Rites: the Treading, three nights when every estate treads at once and the mask visits each press-house by torchlight; the Opening of Last Year's Jars, when the city drinks to make room; and the Swinging, when girls swing from the vine-arbours to make the next year's vines climb. The Treading draws masked revellers from the whole coast, and some of the masks are not revellers: the Obsidian Masquerade, Dionysus's secret society, holds one of its few open gatherings in the Kallikratid press-house, and the same masks sit in Hellarchon's theatre at the Dionysia.

Ties: House Kallikratidai; Hellarchon's Dionysus of the Theatre; the Obsidian Masquerade.

Diana and Ceres of the Camp Diana and Ceres · the Garrison Road, Invictian zone

Square and dutiful · legionaries, officers' wives, overseers · leather, incense, cheap wine

Invictian law forbids the garrison inside the sacred line, so the garrison brought its own gods. Outside the camp gate stands a small square temple with a pediment, shared by Diana of the grove, the Invictian name of the Lady, and Ceres, the Invictian Harvest Mother. Its priest is the camp's chaplain-augur, Quintus Paccius Felix, who reads the birds for the Dux and keeps the Invictian festival calendar. Rites: the Ides of Sextilis, Diana's feast, eleven days after the Hellenorian one, with a procession from the camp to the bronze strip in the forum and no further; the dedication of the first sheaf from the latifundia to Ceres, which the Hierarchis claims is owed to the Lady; and a lamp for the dead of the Night of the Two Feasts. Money: the Procurator of the Estates pays from the grain tithe. Vettia Prisca, the Dux's wife, gives at this temple and at the Great Sanctuary on the same morning, under both names.

Ties: the Garrison Road; the Vettii; Aepistra, which sends the camp its calendar.

Pan of the White Herds Pan · the twelfth chapel and the goddess's pastures

Wild and smelly · sacred herdsmen, shepherds from the hills · goat, wild thyme, wet fleece

Pan's chapel in the Menaion faces the hills, and he is honoured where the goddess's herds of white cattle and her flocks graze, in the ring's upper pastures. His priests are the sacred herdsmen, a fraternity of shepherds led by Aigon, a weathered old man who has never slept under a roof and sleeps in the chapel porch when he comes to town. Rites: the Lambing, which closes the year, when the first lamb born in the goddess's flocks is carried round the Menaion; the choosing of the white heifer for the Two Feasts; the noon silence on the hill pastures, when nobody may shout or play a pipe in case the god is sleeping. The herdsmen pay the god in cheese and keep the boundary-stones of the upper ring, which is why the stones up there never walk.

Ties: the goddess's ring; the Primalhorn Kin, Pan's hill-folk, who trade lambs at the Fair.

The forgotten temple

The Hive of Melisseus. Among the sanctuary's hives on the slope behind the Great Sanctuary stands a round stone building shaped like a beehive, corbelled to a point, with a door so low a grown woman must kneel. The Bees use it as a honey store, and the honey kept in it does not spoil. It is the temple of Melisseus, the Abundant Guardian, the Titan who kept the bees that fed the infant Zeus, and it is older than the Great Sanctuary by any measure the masons can apply. The priestesses are called the Bees because his were; the Hagnotheidai's crest is his bee before it was the Lady's; the "first Bee" who found the Lady's image in a hollow oak was, by the oldest version of the story, his priestess, and the oak stood by this door. The Titan is not on the Roll. Nobody sacrifices to him. But every novice Bee spends her first night in the sanctuary kneeling inside the Hive in the dark with the honey jars, and none of them will say what she hears there.

Priestly houses

House Thesmophoridai Demeter's priestesses of the plain · tenant family

Crest: a basket of seed and a torch · Motto: "What goes down comes up." · Seat: the oldest threshing-floor on the slopes

A tenant family on the slopes that has supplied Demeter's priestesses on the plain for longer than any landlord has held their land: they have served the Melanippidai, the goddess, and now pay a sixth to the Kallikratidai, and the priesthood has stayed with them through every change of owner. The women keep the threshing-floor shrines and the Daughter's Floor; the men farm. They are poor, revered on the plain and ignored in the city.

  • Thesmo Thesmophoridou, priestess, 61 — scatters the seed at the First Furrow and has walked behind both oxen; says the Dux's ox walks straighter.
  • Kallichore Thesmophoridou, her daughter, 36 — leads the women down on the Seed-Days; has started teaching the officers' wives the hymn, which her mother thinks unwise.
  • Euboulos Thesmophorides, Thesmo's grandson, 19 — a reaper on the Hellenorian team at the Barley Games; owes the temple bank for his father's debts and the Rubrian overseers for his own.

History. The family's founder was the first tenant to refuse to thresh until the goddess had been given her handful, and the story is that the year he refused, the whole plain's harvest rotted except his. They have never owned the floor they keep. In the treaty commission's survey the oldest threshing-floor was entered as "Kallikratid land, with a shrine", and the Thesmophoridai have spent five years explaining that it is the other way round.

Ties: Demeter of the Threshing-Floors; House Kallikratidai; the Golden Scythe Accord.

The Megabyzoi Adoptive house of the Neokoros · temple guard

Crest: a key and a measuring-cord · Motto: "A bowshot, no more." · Seat: the gatehouse of the goddess's ring

The Lady's Neokoros, the keeper of her temple guard, asylum and boundary-cord, is by ancient custom a eunuch priest, and so cannot found a family. He adopts one instead. Each Neokoros takes the name Megabyxos and adopts his successor from among the temple guard, and the line of adopted sons, nephews and brothers-in-office forms a house of its own, with a crest, a tomb and a long memory.

  • Megabyxos, Neokoros, 48 — the present holder; keeps the asylum, the boundary-cord and a legionary deserter who gardens in the precinct.
  • Arsames, his adopted son, 26 — captain of the temple guard, born on the far shore to a Tyrsan dyer; will be the next Megabyxos.
  • Old Megabyxos, his predecessor, 80 — retired to the gatehouse; remembers the last time the boundary-cord was cut, and who cut it.

History. The office is older than the city's walls, and its holders came from every people that ever sailed into the harbour, which the Megabyzoi count as the goddess's proof that she belongs to nobody. They have refused asylum to no suppliant in nine hundred years, including a tyrant and a legionary; the bowshot dispute was the first time anyone tried to measure it.

Ties: the Great Sanctuary; House Hagnotheidai; the archer from Delphara who measured the bowshot.

Temples · Hellenorian towns

The Temples of Carianea, Araavyna and Loutrokleion

Small towns keep small Synnaoi, or none: a rock at a harbour mouth, a shrine on top of a kiln, a colonnade of thank-offerings, and in each one a god older than the town who is still owed something.

Carianea Poseidon of the harbour mouth · Hera of the Loom · the Old Man in the cave

Salt and widowhood · divers, shipwrights, widows · drying sponge, tar, cold seawater

Carianea has no Synnaos; it has a rock. Poseidon of the harbour mouth is a rough altar on the reef at the harbour entrance, reached by boat, where the diving season opens: the first sponge of the year is laid on the altar, not sold, and the Nereids are placated with a jar of oil poured on the water by the oldest diver alive. The priest is whoever that is, at present Old Glaukos, fifty-one, deaf in both ears. On the Widows' Terraces stands the town's real temple, Hera of the Loom, a small stone house with a loom in the porch where the Matriarch's Loom of Bonds meets; every marriage in town is woven into a cloth there, and a diver's name is cut from it, thread by thread, at the Counting. The Kymothoidai, the widows' house, keep it, and their eldest, Kallirhoe Kymothois, is its priestess and the town's banker in all but name.

The forgotten and the hidden. Off the western point is a sea cave the divers pass with their eyes shut: the old shrine of Phorcys, the Titan of the sea's monsters, whom Carianea's grandmothers called the Old Man of the Deep. Nobody worships him now. The divers still leave him the second sponge of the season, wedged in a crack at the cave mouth, and say it is to stop the octopus taking their fingers. Mnasilochos the tyrant took the reef altar's offerings into his treasury his first year; the widows' council made him put them back.

Ties: Carianea; House Kymothoidai; the dying rowers Hellarchon's Shaking Rest sends home (see Hellarchon); Corinth's Aphrodite of the Rock, where Carianean wives dedicate their mirrors.

Araavyna Hephaestus of the kiln · Athena of the wheel · the Clay-Shaper

Smoky and litigious · potters, painters, kiln-masters · wood smoke, wet clay, glaze

Araavyna's Synnaos is the communal kiln. The great dome at the top of the Kiln Terraces has a shrine built against its flank with two images, Hephaestus of the kiln and Athena of the potter's wheel, and between them a hook on which every workshop hangs a sample of its best ware before the Firing. The priest is the kiln-master elected for the year, Lysippe Kerameis, who reads the omens in the colour of the smoke. At the Breaking the flawed prestige pieces are smashed before the shrine "so the god sees we keep standards", and the sherds go down the hill to Hellarchon's Clay Gate (see the Smith's House). Terra the Earthshaper has an altar at the common clay beds, kept by the Geolith Artisan Covenant's masons, and every allotment-holder pours water on it before digging.

The forgotten and the hidden. Under the oldest clay pit is a niche with a figure of a man shaping a man out of clay: Prometheus, the Titan who made the first people from earth and stole fire to warm them. The potters call him the Clay-Shaper, and the Pelopidai and the Euthymidai each claim to have found him and sue each other about it every generation. This year the communal kiln has been fired twice for an order of heavy double-walled jars, and the kiln-master has quietly stopped reading the smoke.

Ties: Araavyna; House Pelopidai and House Euthymidai; Corinth's Founders' Altar; Hellarchon's hidden Lender, whom the Voidfolk would recognise.

Loutrokleion Apollo the Healer · Asclepius · the nymphs · the Moon's dormitory

Steaming and discreet · physicians, patients, pilgrims · sulphur, incense, clean linen

Loutrokleion's gods are its springs. Apollo the Healer has the temple at the head of the valley, served by the Luminastra Alchemists, who brew the cures and the plagues' remedies under one roof; the Colonnade of the Grateful runs from the Physicians' Hall to the shrine of Asclepius, Apollo's healer son, whose Invictian disciples, the Radiant Heartwardens, send patients and pray beside the Hellenorians without discussing it. The nymphs of the springs have no temple, only niches above each pool where bathers leave a hairpin. The physicians of House Iamidai hold the priesthoods; Sostrate Iamenou, the Demarch, is Asclepius's priestess, and reads the thank-offerings aloud at the Grateful with a physician's interest in the symptoms.

The forgotten and the hidden. Above the hottest spring is a long stone hall the bath-lessees use for towels, which was once an incubation dormitory of Selene, the Titaness of the moon and of dreams, where the sick slept to be told their cure. Sostrate has quietly put beds back in it. Patients who sleep there on the full moon dream true, and three this year have dreamt of a woman walking through a mirror. Theron Oneirokrites of Hellarchon's Academy pays for reports; so does a quiet guest from Delphara's Dream Dormitory.

Ties: Loutrokleion; House Iamidai; the Dreamers' Hunt for Vesperine Ilaro; Hellarchon's Academy.

Temples · Delphara

The Temples of Delphara

A mountain where every god of the League keeps a room, one god keeps the house, and an older tenant still talks through the floor.

Pantheon building
The Dodekatheon, the Portico of the Twelve Altars, at the fourth turn of the Sacred Way
Chief priest
The Pythia Theano speaks; Hosios Chairephon Kastalides, senior of the five, runs the temple; Neokoros Theodektes Labyadas keeps the Dodekatheon
Patron gods
Apollo, the Radiant One, nine months of the year; Dionysus in the Silence; Phoebe the Visionary at the spring, unofficially
Banned here
Ares (no altar on the mountain); the Eclipsed Mirror; any sacrifice not first approved by the shiver of the goat
Trouble
The tyrant of Atticenea wants his name on his city's altar; something is drinking the sleepers' dreams

The Pantheon

The Dodekatheon is a long marble portico at the fourth turn of the Sacred Way, built after the third sacred war as the price of peace: every member city of the Amphictyony got one altar on the mountain, of equal size, in a row, so that no city could build a bigger treasury to its god and call it piety. There are twelve altars under twelve bays, each with a bronze lamp lit from the common hearth at the eastern end, where the Hearthfire Sanctum keeps the oldest fire in Hellenoria. The mountain is the thinnest place in the grey fog that walls the gods out of the world, which is why the Pythia can still speak for one, and why every city wants an altar here.

The altars run west to east in the order the cities joined. Hellarchon's Maiden, Athena, stands first, and Atticenea's Athena of the Olive stands seventh; the two flames have been forbidden to touch since a priest of one lit his taper from the other. Corinth's Poseidon of the Isthmus and Argotiko's Poseidon of the Horses quarrel each spring over whose bull dies first. Thessalonika keeps Hermes of the Gate, Thebesieas keeps Hercules with a pile of captured spearheads instead of flowers, and Delphara keeps Apollo, whose bay is a hand's breadth wider than the others, which everyone has measured. Three island cities keep Aphrodite, Dionysus and Artemis of the Islands. Two altars embarrass the priests. Helionyx keeps Helios, a Titan, and its altar was set one step lower than the rest, which the Helionyxians call the Step of Insult and polish every year. Kirimitsana's bay holds a rough stone hive to Melisseus, the bee-Titan, and nobody from the mountain has tended it in living memory. Delpharan children are paid an obol a month to keep the bees out of it, and fail.

The Neokoros sweeps, trims the lamps, and decides which delegate's priest may sacrifice on which day. It is the only priesthood on the mountain held by the House Labyadai, who are shut out of the oracle, and they treat it as a foot in the door. This year Aristeas Kotinos of Atticenea has sent a silver plaque to be fixed to his city's altar: "Rekindled by Aristeas". Theodektes has hung it, face to the wall, until the council votes on whether a tyrant's delegate is a delegate. Ephelanum has no altar and sends an observer every year to make sure the Artemis of the Islands stays smaller than its Lady.

Temples

The Temple of the Oracle Apollo, the Radiant One

The summit · Hosios Chairephon Kastalides · laurel smoke, cold water, the sweet breath of the crack

The god's house at the head of the Way, over the adyton where the Pythia sits on her tripod. The five Hosioi run it, and the senior of them, Chairephon Kastalides, 81, is the last man alive who saw the old Pythia before Theano. Every consultation begins with a goat sprinkled with cold spring water: if it does not shiver from hooves to head, the god is not at home and the day is lost. The priests' boys carry warm water for the sprinkling in winter, and are beaten for it if caught. The bay-laurel burned on the hearth is cut from one grove above the stadium, and laurel crowns for the Corinthian games' Laurel Court were once cut here too.

Ties: Apollo's guest-shrine at Helionyx; the Luminastra Alchemists' annual tithe of first remedies; House Pythokleidai; Lysandra Anthemis and the Exegetes.

The Winter House Dionysus, the God of Festivity

Below the theatre · Thyias Charikleia · wine-lees, pine torches, wet fur

When Apollo leaves for the Silence, someone has to hold the mountain, and Delphara gives it to Dionysus. His temple is small, low and plain, with a stone basin in which the god's head, a carved mask of fig-wood, sleeps in a cradle all summer. On the first night of the Silence the Thyiades, thirty Delpharan women under their leader Charikleia, wake the mask with drums and run with torches up to the snowline. Twice in living memory they have been caught in a blizzard, and the Tripod Guard has gone up to dig them out. The Winter House pours its libations from the first must of the Kastalidai presses.

Ties: House Charikleidai; House Kastalidai; the Obsidian Veins, who send "observers" to the run and are chased off.

The Shrine Before the Temple Athena Pronaia

Foot of the Way · Priestess Kydilla of Hellarchon · olive oil, fallen stone, sea-wind up the valley

The first shrine a pilgrim reaches, a round marble house to Athena "who stands before the god" at the bottom of the switchbacks. Its priestesses are sent from Hellarchon's Rock, and so is its money. That makes it the Hegemon's chapel on a neutral mountain. Kydilla, its priestess, is a sharp woman of forty who blesses pilgrims' sandals and asks them, kindly, what they intend to ask the god. Rockfalls have hit the shrine three times in a century, each time in a year when Hellarchon had pressed the Amphictyony hard; the Delpharans consider this a comment.

Ties: House Nikandridai; the Ecliptica Arcanum; the Maiden's temple in Hellarchon.

The Dream Dormitory Apollo the Healer, and the Healer's Serpents

Inside the temenos · Iphianassa Oneiropolos · cool stone, serpent musk, lamp-smoke

The long hall where the sick sleep and report their dreams at dawn. It is Apollo's, but its rites are older: a sleeper brings a honey cake for the olive-coloured Healer's Serpents, washes at the Phoibad Spring, and lies on the hide of the goat he sacrificed. Iphianassa Oneiropolos reads the dreams; a patient who dreams of a serpent, a dog or a laurel is sent to the Herbalists' Lodge with a prescription, and one who dreams of nothing is told to come back. Since Philokles vanished she has started sleeping in the hall herself, with a knife.

Ties: the Herbalists' Lodge and Kirimitsana's herb-wives; the Enchanted Muse at Persevalis; the Arcane Academy at Hellarchon.

The forgotten temple

The Serpent's Hollow lies under the Phoibad Terrace, behind a goat-pen wall. Before Phoebe held the oracle, and long before Apollo, the crack belonged to Terra, the Earthshaper, and a great serpent kept it for her. Apollo's first priests killed the serpent, built over its cave and gave its name to the Games. The hollow behind the wall is a natural chamber with a stone omphalos, rounded like an egg, and a channel in the floor where something long once lay. Goatherds stable kids there in winter because it is warm. The Geolith Artisan Covenant, Terra's masons, ask every year to restore it and are told every year that the goats need it. Old women say that if you put your ear to the omphalos you hear the mountain breathing on the other side.

Priestly houses

The Phoibadai Women of the spring · keepers of Phoebe

Crest: a crescent over running water · Motto: "She was here first" · Seat: the round shrine at the Phoibad Spring

Not a house in the Eupatrid sense, but a line of Delpharan women, mother to daughter, who have kept the Titan's round shrine since before the god came. They wash every petitioner's hair, so they see every face that goes up the Way. Every Pythia within memory has been one of them or married into them. The priests tolerate them because nobody else will wash pilgrims' hair at dawn in spring water.

  • Grandmother Ismene Phoibas, eldest, 84. Blind; recognises pilgrims by the feel of their scalp.
  • Theano, the Pythia, a Phoibad by marriage. Comes to the cell after every consultation and touches the linen strips.
  • Aglaurina Phoibas, 30, Ismene's granddaughter and Theano's likely successor. Does not want it.
  • Korinna Phoibas, 16, who washes the pilgrims' hair and has noticed Lykos counting the Dormitory's sleepers.

Ties: Lysandra Anthemis; the Grandmothers of Kirimitsana; the College of the Arc at Helionyx, whose tables set their calendar.

House Charikleidai Keepers of the Winter House · Eupatrid

Crest: a fig-wood mask in an ivy wreath · Motto: "We hold the mountain when he is away" · Seat: the house beside the Winter House

An old, small, unruly house that has led the Thyiades for nine generations. They have no share of the oracle fees and live on the winter: the Silence is when the Amphictyony audits, the delegates stay late, and somebody has to feed and entertain them. They want a seat among the Hosioi, and argue that a god who holds the mountain for three months deserves a fifth of the priesthood.

  • Charikleia, leader of the Thyiades, 52. Has run to the snowline thirty-one times and lost two toes to it.
  • Thrason Charikleides, her husband, host of the delegates' winter banquets. Knows how every delegate votes after the third cup.
  • Melitta Charikleia, their daughter, 24. No longer runs, sleeps late, and has a sweet taste in her mouth.

Ties: House Kastalidai (wine); the Dionysian altar in the Dodekatheon; the Obsidian Masquerade, which would like to recruit them.

Temples · Helionyx

The Temples of Helionyx

A white city that worships a Titan in public, keeps the god as a lodger, and schedules its prayers by the shadow of a stick.

Pantheon building
The Hall of Hours, a roofless round temple on Temple Hill whose floor is a sundial of the gods
Chief priest
Gnomonarch Asterope Kleidemou of the College of the Arc; Hierophant Lampon Kleidemos keeps the Hall of Hours
Patron gods
Helios of the Aetherian Ancients; Apollo as guest; Poseidon at the mole; Demeter at the grain quay
Banned here
Nyx and her Syndicate (night has no niche); any rite held at noon; burning anything on Temple Hill but cedar
Trouble
The storks have not come, the sun's bird is missing from the sky, and someone wants the cedar presses burned

The Pantheon

The Hall of Hours stands beside the Solar Precinct: a ring of twelve white columns with no roof, because a roof would cast the wrong shadow. Between each pair of columns is a niche for a god, and the floor is a great bronze-lined dial. Each god is honoured in the hour when the shadow of the central pillar touches its niche, so the city's piety moves round the hall with the sun. Eos, the dawn-Titan, gets the first hour, with milk and the first figs. Hermes takes the market hour, Athena the hour of the courts, Poseidon the hour the fishing boats come in. Helios is honoured at the moment the shadow is shortest, and in that moment, by law, nothing is done at all: the priests stand with their hands open and the city holds still. Apollo has the late afternoon, which his priests consider a calculated insult. Demeter has the hour of the evening bread, and Selene the dusk.

The twelfth niche, on the north side where the shadow never reaches, is walled up with plain lime. Before the Charioteer fell it held Nyx, the Mistress of the Void. After the earthquake an assembly decided that the night had been given too much honour in a city of the sun, and bricked her in. The Nightweaver Syndicate has been banned from Helionyx ever since, and people still push black olive stones into the mortar of that wall.

The Hall's keeper is Hierophant Lampon Kleidemos, 47, nephew by marriage of the Gnomonarch. He measures the shadow with a knotted cord before each hour's rite and has a bad habit of correcting other gods' priests in front of their worshippers. A small brass weight hangs by a thread beside the central pillar, and Lampon checks it every morning. He has never explained why.

Temples

The Temple of the Chariot Helios, Titan of Vitality

Temple Hill · Archiereus Polemon Phaethontides · hot gold, cedar, bird lime

The gold-domed sun-temple, its flat roof the Stork Roof. Inside, a gilded chariot with four bronze horses faces east under the lantern. Polemon Phaethontides, uncle of this year's Sun-Priest, keeps it; the Sun-Priest wears the crown only on festival days. Every fourth summer, at the Standing, four white horses in harness are driven off the outer mole into the sea "to give the god new horses", and the Argotiko breeders supply them at a ruinous price. Sun-priests may not stand in shadow on festival days, which is why they carry their own parasols and argue about whether a parasol counts.

Ties: House Phaethontidai; the sun-disc treasury and the Step of Insult at Delphara; horses from Argotiko.

The Guest-Shrine Apollo, the Radiant One

Down the side stair · Priest Lykomedes the Guest · laurel, damp, lamp-oil

Apollo lives in Helionyx as a lodger. His shrine is a vaulted room down a side stair below the sun-temple, cool, dim and full of laurel sent each spring from Delphara. Its priest is always a Delpharan, appointed by the Hosioi for ten years and called "the Guest" by everyone. The present Guest, Lykomedes, is a polite, homesick man who reports to Delphara on everything the College of the Arc publishes. The shrine holds the city's copy of every oracle Helionyx has received, including "Do not move what has fallen", and the Phaethontidai have asked three times to borrow it.

Ties: the Temple of the Oracle; the Luminastra Alchemists, who supply its healing rites; the Phaethontidai, who want the oracle reread.

The Mole Temple Poseidon, the Earth Shaker

Fallen Quarter · Priest Glaukos Aigeides · tar, salt, sun-hot bronze

A squat temple at the root of the outer mole, half built from the Charioteer's bronze plates, which the priests call the sea god's share of the earthquake he sent. Oaths for the Court of the Jettison are sworn here at dawn, hand on a ship's ram, and every shipper in a jettison case pays a drachma "to the god who took the cargo". Glaukos Aigeides, brother of the Navarch, has kept it for twenty years. The Tyrsian pilots worship here too, under another name, and leave cedar shavings on the altar.

Ties: House Aigeidai; the Two Tides priesthood of Corinth; Hellarchon's harbour Poseidon.

The Bread House Demeter, the Earth Mother

The grain quay · Priestess Hegeso Ismenis · flour dust, warm stone, sacks

Helionyx grows no grain and keeps a temple to its goddess at the quay where the Thebesian barley lands. Every cargo is blessed and then weighed in the temple porch, so that nobody cheats under the goddess's eye. The priestess, Hegeso Ismenis, is a Thebesian of the grain house who married a Halikid salt factor: the salt goes one way, the barley comes the other. This year she has begun asking for payment in advance, as the Accord now demands of cities it does not trust, and the Halikidai have taken it personally.

Ties: the Golden Scythe Accord; the Temple of the Furrow at Thebesieas; House Ismenidai; House Halikidai.

The forgotten temple

The Dawn Temple under the pans. Before Helionyx was white it was a fishing town on a lagoon, and its temple was to Eos, the dawn-Titan, on an islet facing east. When the Halikidai's ancestors flooded the lagoon for salt four centuries ago, the temple went under the brine. In a dry late summer, when the furthest pans are raked to the floor, the tops of six columns show, crusted white, and the veiled pan-workers step round them and do not rake that square. The College of the Arc keeps one sentence about it in its oldest press: "The first readings were taken from her steps." The Covenant of the Equinox, Eos's druids, have asked to visit at the autumn equinox. The Halikidai said the pans were private.

Priestly houses

House Kleidemidai Gnomonists · Eupatrid

Crest: a shadow-stick and arc, black on white · Motto: "The shadow does not flatter" · Seat: the long house behind the cedar presses

The family that has given the College of the Arc more gnomonists than any other, and four Gnomonarchs. Quiet, precise, and poorer than their influence suggests, because the College pays nothing. Asterope, born a Phaethontid, married into them at nineteen and has been a Kleidemid in everything but blood for sixty years.

  • Asterope Kleidemou, Gnomonarch, 79. Half-blind; reads the arc by touch and by her pupils' voices.
  • Lampon Kleidemos, Hierophant of the Hall of Hours. Checks the plumb weight every morning.
  • Euanthe Kleidemou, 26, his daughter, the College's best young reader. Has noticed that her readings and the published tables differ by a hair.
  • Diodotos Kleidemos, 15, a pupil. Sells tables a week early, and has been asked by a glass-grinder for the key to the presses.

Ties: the Solar Precinct; House Phaethontidai; the Phoibadai of Delphara, whose calendar the College sets.

House Aigeidai Sea-priests and navarchs · Eupatrid

Crest: a trident over a ram · Motto: "The sea takes its share" · Seat: the Ram House on the outer mole

A naval house that splits its sons between the fleet and Poseidon's altar, on the principle that one should always have a friend on the far side of a storm. They command the city's eleven warships and swear the jettison oaths. They want the Tyrsian pilots kept in the harbour, because the charts are worth more than the Kochlidai's purple, and say so in council.

  • Timokles Aigeides, Navarch. Counts the Hegemon's squadron every month and chalks the numbers on the temple wall.
  • Glaukos Aigeides, his brother, priest of the Mole Temple. Buys Tyrsian charts with temple money.
  • Nausikrate Aigeis, their late brother's widow. Keeps the house accounts, and goes out at noon.

Ties: the Mole Temple; Hellarchon's fleet; the Two Tides at Corinth.

Temples · Thebesieas

The Temples of Thebesieas

Plain stone, captured shields, and seven gods for seven gates; a city that prays the way it drills, in files, and buries what it does not understand.

Pantheon building
The Heptapylon, the seven-walled Hall of the Gates in the Temple Ward
Chief priest
Kallikles Iolaides, Priest of the Champion and keeper of the Heptapylon
Patron gods
Hercules the Champion; Demeter of the furrow; one god for each gate; Ares at the citadel gate, kept up and never thanked
Banned here
Dionysus's night rites inside the walls; the Obsidian Masquerade; the Eclipsed Mirror (except, unofficially, at the Dead Gate)
Trouble
The new channel on the Wet Plain, and the men who dug it for reasons they did not give the council

The Pantheon

The Heptapylon is a seven-sided hall at the centre of the Temple Ward, built of the same grey stone as the walls and roofed with bronze shields beaten flat. Each of its seven walls faces one of the city's gates, and against each wall stands the altar of that gate's god, kept by the gate-ward and paid for by its families. When the gate-general of a ward takes office, he sacrifices at his wall; when he lays down his command at the end of the year, he sacrifices there again, on time, because the death-law is watching.

The Grain Gate keeps Tyche, the goddess of fortune, because selling a harvest is a gamble. The Isthmus Gate keeps Hermes of the roads, and Corinthian factors leave coins on his altar that the ward priests count with distaste. The Horse Gate keeps Poseidon of the Horses, with a bronze foal given by Argotiko. The Spring Gate keeps Hercules himself. The Mothers' Gate keeps Demeter. The Hollow Gate keeps Hades, Lord of the Underworld, the only city gate in the League given to him: the ward says he is the god who keeps what is under the ground under it, and they want him paid. The Dead Gate keeps no god officially; its wall has a bare niche where widows set a three-faced wooden post of Hecate at every funeral and take it home afterwards, which the priests pretend not to see.

In the middle of the hall, on a floor of trampled earth brought in from the Muster Ground, stands the Polemarch's altar to Hercules, with the club of the founding hero in a bronze case above it. Every new Polemarch swears on the club. Melanthios Sparton swore twice and gripped it so hard the case had to be re-soldered. The hall is run by Kallikles Iolaides, who has served the Champion forty years and treats the seven ward priests as file-leaders and himself as their drill-master.

Temples

The Temple of the Champion Hercules, the Champion

Temple Ward · Priest Kallikles Iolaides · cold incense, rust, olive-wood shavings

Squat, enormous and plain, with a cult statue of the hero as a goliath that the roof was built round. Its walls are hung with captured shields, some so old their devices have rusted off. The Herakleia, every second summer, is a festival of wrestling, weight-carrying and a race in full armour; the winner carves his name on the temple's lintel, which has room for perhaps eleven more. Thebesians swear "by the Champion's club" and mean it. Pilgrims from every city come to see the hero's cradle, and the priests sell olive-wood clubs the length of a forearm.

Ties: the Thebesian treasury of captured shields and Hercules's altar in the Dodekatheon at Delphara; House Iolaidai; Epameinon Kleitarchos.

The Temple of the Furrow Demeter, the Earth Mother

Outside the Mothers' Gate · Priestess Praxithea Ismenis · barley chaff, wet earth, pig

A long barn of a temple among the first fields beyond the Mothers' Gate. At the Thesmophoria, citizen wives camp in its yard for three days, fast on the second, and on the third bring up rotted piglets from a pit to spread on the seed-corn. Men are not admitted and do not ask. The Ploughing begins here, with the Polemarch's ox blessed by Praxithea Ismenis, aunt of the Grain Gate's general, and the Circle of the Eternal Grove's elder walking beside it. The Golden Scythe Accord swears its allocations on her altar.

Ties: the Golden Scythe Accord; the Bread House at Helionyx; House Ismenidai; the olive presses of Atticenea.

The Shield-Bearer's Tomb The hero Iolaos, servant of Hercules

Outside the Spring Gate · Keeper Nikasippe Iolais · grass, bronze, old flowers

A grassy mound with a stone door, where the hero's shield-bearer is said to lie. Every pair of the Sacred Band swears here, hand over hand on a bronze shield laid on the threshold. The oath is short: "I will not run while you watch." Pairs leave a lock of each other's hair in a niche of the door, and when a man dies the keeper burns his partner's lock with him. Nikasippe Iolais, the keeper, is the only woman who attends the Naming of the Band in an official capacity, and she reads the dead pairs' oaths back to the living.

Ties: the Sacred Band and the Pairs' Ground; House Iolaidai; House Dirkaidai, keepers of the roll.

The Unthanked Altar Ares, the Warlord

The citadel gate · Keeper Phormion One-Arm · rust, blood, wind

A block of black stone at the citadel gate, older than the gate, with a bronze spear socket and no roof. Ares is not loved here; he is maintained, the way a city maintains a dangerous wall. A sacrifice of a dog is made before the Muster, by a keeper who must have lost something in war, and nobody says a prayer, only the god's name, once. The keeper is Phormion, a veteran who left his left arm on the Inland Road in the war's last decade. The Crimson Sigil of the Shattered Spear has offered three times to endow the altar with a roof. Phormion sent them away.

Ties: the Muster; the Crimson Sigil, who recruit in the Seven Gates' wine-shops; no altar to Ares exists at Delphara, and Thebesians think that wise.

The forgotten temple

The Sluice-Temple. Where the four greatest Mycairan channels meet on the Wet Plain, on a mound of brick barely above the reeds, stands a roofless shrine of cyclopean blocks with a basin in its floor fed by all four channels. The Mycairan engineers who drained the plain built it, and the carvings on its door, a woman with water running from her hands, match Tethys, the Titan of rivers. Nobody in Thebesieas worships her. The dike-wardens, who are paid by the city and feared by the landholders, leave a loaf on the basin's rim each spring because their fathers did, and they clear its inlets of reeds before they clear their own. A warden who skips the loaf is laughed at, and then quietly reassigned.

Priestly houses

House Iolaidai Priests of the Champion · Eupatrid

Crest: a shield held up by a second hand · Motto: "Behind him, always" · Seat: the Tomb House by the Spring Gate

The house claims descent from Hercules's shield-bearer, and has held the Champion's priesthood and the oath-tomb for as long as the city has records. They are respected, modestly landed and almost entirely unpolitical, which the Spartidai find useful and the Ismenidai suspicious. They want the Band kept as it is: three hundred, defensive, and sworn at their door.

  • Kallikles Iolaides, Priest of the Champion, 66. Has watched three hundred pairs swear and can tell which will hold.
  • Nikasippe Iolais, his sister, keeper of the oath-tomb. Burns the dead men's locks herself.
  • Agis Iolaides, his son, 30, of the Sacred Band. Paired with a smith's son from the Seven Gates, against his father's wishes.
  • Kleio Iolais, 12, his granddaughter, who has started sweeping the Dead Gate's niche without being asked.

Ties: the Temple of the Champion; Epameinon Kleitarchos; House Dirkaidai.

House Teiresiadai Bird-seers · Eupatrid

Crest: a staff with a bird perched on it · Motto: "The birds do not take sides" · Seat: the Seat of Augury, a stone chair on the citadel wall

The city's hereditary augurs, descended from a blind seer whose stone chair still stands on the citadel wall. They read the birds before the Muster, before the Ploughing and before any march, and the war council will not move without them. They are poor, prickly, and the only family in Thebesieas that reads Mycairan runes, a skill they have kept to themselves.

  • Manto Teiresias, head of house, 58. Saw a cloud of crows turn back over the Hollow Rock at this year's Muster and said nothing in public.
  • Erginos Teiresiades, her brother. Reads runes; has been asked by a Thessalonikan scholar, and by a dike-warden, what the tablets say.
  • Phaidra Teiresias, 19, her daughter. The best eyes in the house. Will not sit in the chair.

Ties: the Sown Hill; Dexippe of the Porticoes at Thessalonika; the Circle of the Eternal Grove.

Temples · Hellenorian towns

The Temples of Argotiko, Atticenea and Kirimitsana

Three towns with a hearth and a vote at Delphara, and each with one god it would fight for and one it would rather not discuss.

Argotiko Poseidon of the Horses · a stable that prays

Argotiko · Priest Hippokoon Xanthippides · hay, liniment, salt brought from the sea

The town's temple is the Hippeion, a stable-shaped temple to Poseidon of the Horses at the end of the Course, with a bronze stallion rearing out of a basin of seawater that is carted inland every month at the town's expense, because the god of horses is also the god of the sea and the breeders will not risk offending either half. Every foal entered in the Registry is led past the basin and sprinkled; a foal that shies is entered in red ink. The priest, Hippokoon Xanthippides, is the Demarch's brother, and the Running opens with his sacrifice of a horse that has never been ridden. Argotiko supplies the four white horses Helionyx drives into the sea, and the Horse Gate's bronze foal at Thebesieas, and keeps one of the two Poseidon altars in the Dodekatheon, where its priests race Corinth's to the first sacrifice every spring.

Forgotten and hidden. Behind the Registry Hall, in the oldest stable, a low niche in the wall holds a carved horse-headed figure and a bowl of dried dates. The grooms call it "the Foreigner" and leave dates there before a foaling. It was cut by Acheaorian grooms captured with the white mares in the Barley Truce year, and it is Kiga, the Beastmaster of the eastern pantheon. Eupraxia the Registrar has started leaving dates too.

The cult. None to speak of; the town says it has no time. The Tenebral Covenant keeps a fence among the bloodstock dealers on Buyers' Street, which is not a cult, but is close enough for the priests.

Ties: the Temple of the Chariot; Corinth's Poseidon; Kiga's temples in Persemenid.

Atticenea Athena of the Olive · and a tyrant's unfinished god

Atticenea · Guardian Charmion of the Old Tree · crushed olive, cicadas, cut marble

Atticenea's real temple is a tree. The Old Tree, on its terrace at the top of the School Steps, is held to be the first olive Athena planted, and its guardian family, the Charmionidai, have tended it for longer than the town has had walls. There is a small marble shrine beside it with a wooden image of the goddess, too old to have a face, and a lamp fed with oil from the tree's own fruit. Students swear on the tree before the Leaving. Charmion, its guardian, publicly refused the tyrant's gift of a new terrace wall.

The tyrant has answered with stone. Below the Press Quarter, Aristeas Kotinos has begun a temple to Zeus, the Storm Lord, the largest in the League by its plan, on a platform of white marble a hundred and twenty paces long. Four columns stand. The teachers he pays call it a gift to the gods; the smallholders he lends to call it the Debt. Its priest is his own appointee, a former teacher of rhetoric named Isagoras, who preaches that the storm god favours a single hand on the helm. His silver plaque hangs face-to-the-wall in the Dodekatheon at Delphara.

Forgotten. Under the School Steps is a sealed cave where the town once kept the Muses Elder, Titan of inspiration; the schools grew up over it, and the students still scratch verses on the stone door for luck.

Ties: the Maiden's Athena at Hellarchon, whose flame will not touch Atticenea's; grain from the Temple of the Furrow; Thessalonika's Porticoes.

Kirimitsana Melisseus, the Abundant Guardian · a Titan who never left

Kirimitsana · The Grandmothers of the Dozen · wax, smoke, thyme, cold stone

Kirimitsana worships a Titan in the open and has never thought to apologise. The bee-Titan Melisseus has no building. His temple is the Long Row, the line of stone hive-boles along the Beekeepers' Hall, and his altar is the hall's own hearth, where the first comb of the Smoking is laid in the fire whole. The Grandmothers are his priestesses, all twelve, and Grandmother Thymo is first among them. The rites are women's: three sisters, chosen each year, wear yellow and climb to the highest hives at dawn on the Gathering Days, and what they say on their return sets the gathering. The lowlanders call them the Bee-Women and are a little afraid of them.

The empty altar. Kirimitsana's bay in the Dodekatheon is unattended because the Grandmothers believe a Titan cannot be kept in a row with gods, and they say so to the Amphictyony's letters every year, in the same unanswerable sentence.

Hidden. Above the rhododendron line is a shrine nobody below sixty is shown: a cave of dark hives whose honey is the mad honey. The Grandmothers keep it for Melisseus's protecting face, the one that stopped a raiding column in the war. The Luminastra factor Kleitos Pharmakeus has spent nine years trying to find it.

Ties: the Phoibadai and the Herbalists' Lodge at Delphara; the Luminastra Alchemists; the Dream Dormitory's honey cakes, which are made with Kirimitsana honey and nothing else.

The Fire and the Honoured Ones: faith in Acheaoria

Ask a Magus which god the fire belongs to and he will correct the question. The fire belongs to no god. In the Magi's doctrine the sacred fire, Atar the Witness, is older than the gods: it burned before anything was sworn, and the gods themselves made their compacts in its light. That is why the codex calls every Acheaorian god a "lesser" god, and why no Acheaorian temple to any god may stand higher than the fire-temple of its city, or within sight of the flame through its screen. The gods are honoured. The fire is kept. The difference is the Magi's whole authority, and they have defended it for longer than the House of Zindar has held a throne. They may also be right in a way they do not teach: since the Veiling no god can reach the plateau except through the grey fog, and a fire kept unbroken for a century is the strongest current through it anywhere on the continent.

The gods are called the Honoured Ones (izadan). Every city keeps them together in an Izadkhaneh, a "house of the honoured ones": a pantheon hall built below and downwind of the fire-temple, with a niche or a room for each god and a lamp in every niche. Those lamps are not lit by the god's priests. Each dawn a Magus carries a taper down from the temple and lights them in turn, the Lending of the Flame. A god whose priests offend the Magi may find its lamp skipped, and a dark niche closes the god's house to custom until the debt is cleared. Nobody calls this a power. Everybody pays it.

Purity binds everyone. Fire, earth and water must not be defiled: the dead go to the towers for the vultures, never into the ground or the flame; blood, hair and nail-parings are carried out by licensed corpse-bearers; a Magus tends the fire through a veil so that his breath never touches it; and a god's priest who sheds blood in his own rites must buy a purification before his lamp is lit again (see the Magi and the Purity of Fire). The gods of the plateau long ago learned to keep their rites dry, bloodless and cold. Beast and Kiga, whose faithful kill, are honoured outside the walls.

Tolerated and suppressed gods. Acheaoria's way with a conquered people was relocation, and the relocated brought their gods. Those gods may be registered as guest-gods (mehman-izad): a niche in the guest-court of the Izadkhaneh, a yearly fee to the Scribes, a ban on public processions and, for peoples who bury their dead, a fine by the grave. Gods of the dark half of the pantheon are not tolerated at all. Lotha, the Shadow Queen, Thasmudayan, the Harbinger of the Undying, and the Faceless God have no niches anywhere; to keep their images is to keep a capital charge in the house. The Titans are not suppressed so much as forgotten on purpose: the Magi teach that they were "the first fires that went out", and leave it there.

The royal cult. The King of Kings is not a god. He carries the Farr, the royal glory, a radiance granted at his crowning by the fire and visible, to the right eyes, as a light about the head. Every Izadkhaneh keeps a Hall of the Glory with the King's image, and every satrap's oath is sworn before that image as well as before the fire. As the satraps grow bolder, the Halls of the Glory grow better kept; a satrap who lets his go dusty is announcing something.

The pilgrim circuit. The devout walk the Circuit of Five Fires: Persemenid's Temple of Breath, the undying fire of Atarabad, the Witness of Mithratal, the frontier fire of Xerastri, and back down the Royal Road and along the Garden Road to the Channel Head of Persevalis, about forty days with the post-stations. Fire may not be carried by laymen, so pilgrims carry ash: a pinch from each temple in a brass box with five sealed cells, stamped by each temple's Magi. A full box is a lifetime's honour and, since the Peace, a profitable forgery. The circuit is also the Magi's own road: the Fire Watch runs along it, and so do their letters.

Temples · Persemenid

The Temples of Persemenid

A chain of fires along the mountain, a house of all the gods beneath them, and under the house a city whose gods nobody is allowed to name.

Pantheon building
The Izadkhaneh of Persemenid, the Hall of Twenty-Three Niches, on the lower slope of the Hill of Fires
Chief priest
Keeper of the Niches Atossa Mazdani; above her, Herbad Tansar of the Hill of Fires
Patron gods
The undying fire; Hajama for the throne's valour; Zann for its rolls; Kor for its memory
Banned here
Lotha, Thasmudayan, the Faceless God; every guest-god procession within sight of the terrace
Trouble
Dark niches nobody will explain, and a hollow ring under the hill

The Pantheon

The Izadkhaneh of Persemenid stands two hundred steps below the Fire-Temple on the Hill of Fires, a long, low hall of grey stone with its back to the mountain and its doors to the garden town. Inside, a single colonnade runs the length of the building, and between the columns open twenty-three niches, one for each Honoured One the court recognises, each with a bronze lamp, an offering shelf and a small door behind it into the god's own rooms. The number is not an accident. Twenty-three peoples walk the relief on the Royal Stair, and the Sixth King built twenty-three niches so that each subject people would find its own god in the King's house. It was a generous idea, and the court has spent three centuries making it tidy: the conquered peoples' own gods were moved out to the guest-court behind the hall, and the niches were given to the gods of the plateau.

The hall is kept by the Keeper of the Niches, Atossa Mazdani, fifty-four, of the priestly house of Mazdan. She sets the rota of the niche-priests, receives the offerings, pays the Scribes their guest-god fees and answers, in all things that touch the fire, to Herbad Tansar, who sends the Magus down with the taper each dawn. Atossa is precise, devout and short of money: the court's offerings arrive late, like everything else the court pays. Her husband Mazdayasn Mazdani keeps the hall's accounts and the guest-court's register. Their son Haoma Mazdani serves as niche-priest of Zann and wants to be a Scribe instead. Their daughter Parisatis Mazdani, nineteen, carries the Hall of the Glory's censer at the Bringing, and has been noticed by Prince Tiridat.

The practical truth is in the lamps. Three niches have been dark for a year: Najm's, whose priest blessed a caravan that turned out to belong to a satrap marked "not presented"; Haku's, whose priest said something about the cloth of gold; and a third niche at the end of the colonnade, which has no god's name on it at all and which, Atossa insists, has always been dark. The court visits the Izadkhaneh twice a year. The garden town visits it every day, and has noticed that its favourite god, Jarmik of the kitchens, has the smallest niche and the busiest door.

Temples

The Lion Gate of Hajama The throne's valour

Hajama, the God of Valor · Lion-Priest Bahman Arshak · horse-sweat, bronze, cedar oil

A gatehouse temple at the Paradise's east wall, built so that the Lion's Mane Vanguard rides through it on the way to the Royal Hunt. Inside, Hajama stands as a leonin general in bronze, a campaign map cut into the floor at his feet. The Lion-Priest Bahman Arshak, a grizzled former lancer, blesses the lances before the Hunt and reads the omens from the lion's fall, which have been favourable for sixty-one years. The rite is exacting and impersonal: the god is owed the correct order of march, not love. Money comes from the satraps' squadrons, who pay for their standards to hang here, and from House Mihran, which pays more than anyone and keeps an empty saddle on a stand beside the altar. The Lion Gate's politics are simple: whoever pays for the Vanguard owns its chapel, and the satraps now pay.

Ties: the Lion Hall at Xerastri; House Mihran; the Vanguard chapel at Shir'abad D'ar (towns).

The House of the Count Zann's temple of the rolls

Zann, the Illuminator · Ledger-Mother Gulnar Zand · ink, lamp-black, dust

A plain brick temple on the terrace's lower edge where the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger swear their oath to Zann and where the Naming of the Rolls ends each year: the roll of the Ten Thousand is read before the god, every name, and the god is asked to witness that the count is full. The Ledger-Mother Gulnar Zand, an air-genasi woman whose hair moves when the room is still, keeps the temple and the master copy of the tribute ledger. Zann's priests take no side, which in Persemenid means they write down everything and are thanked for none of it. The temple's income is a tenth of a grain of silver on every tribute entry, which was a fortune once and is now a lengthening column of nothing. Gulnar has started writing "not presented" in red.

Ties: the Scribes' chapel at Mithratal; the Sandglass Circle, which hates her red ink; Mithratal's archive fees.

The Deep Lamp of Kor The Sage's Archive

Kor, the Sage of Ages · Master-Reader Vidarna Kaus · cold stone, chalk, rubbing-wax

Kor's temple is a cave. It runs back into the cliff below the royal tombs, a gallery cut by the Sage's Archive to reach the oldest inscriptions on the mountain, with a single lamp burning at its end before a deep-gnome figure of the god reading a stone. Master-Reader Vidarna Kaus is its priestess by office, since the Archive is Kor's order. The rite is to read aloud, correctly, one line no one has read that year. The Feast of the Correct Reading each autumn is attended by three scholars and a Sandglass clerk taking notes. The Deep Lamp lives on bequests and copying fees, and on parcels that go west by the Treaty Road to correspondents in Aeterna and Thessalonika, the Three Libraries.

Ties: Thessalonika; Aeterna; R'eyshar's archive (towns).

The Hall of the Glory The royal cult

The Farr of the King of Kings · Censer-Bearer Artakhshar · frankincense, gold leaf, nerves

The greatest Hall of the Glory in the empire stands on the terrace itself, the one shrine allowed above the garden town, because it holds no god. A gold image of the King of Kings sits within a ring of lamps lit from the Fire-Temple, and every satrap who climbs the stair swears before it. The Censer-Bearer Artakhshar, a eunuch of the Inner House appointed by Chief Eunuch Sparamiz, tends it and sets the order of oath-taking, which the Karin dispute. The Glory's festival is the King's crowning-day, when the image is unveiled and the court looks for the light about its head. Money: every satrapal oath carries a gift, and every absent satrap's gift is recorded as "owed". The Hall's politics are the court's politics with incense.

Ties: every Hall of the Glory, from Atarabad to Shir'abad D'ar; House Karin; the House of Zindar.

The forgotten temple

The Shrine of the Unnamed King. Below the Temple of Breath, the oldest fire on the hill, the undercroft runs down further than the Magi admit, and the draught that feeds the flame comes up through a grating set in a floor of brick stamped with a king nobody can name. The garden town calls whatever is down there the Shrine of the Unnamed King, after the well-digger's brick. Officially there is nothing. Archivist Hashmet went down there, read something, and was executed on the second day of Peaceful; the Magi have since bricked up the undercroft stair, and the dark niche at the end of the Izadkhaneh's colonnade, the one with no name, stands directly above it on the same line. Old women of the garden town leave a cup of water at that niche on the night of the Naming of the Rolls. They say it is for the guard. They do not say which guard.

Priestly houses

House Mazdan Keepers of the Niches

Crest: a lamp in an arched niche · Motto: "Each light in its place" · Seat: the Keeper's House behind the Izadkhaneh

A priestly family that has kept the Izadkhaneh since the Sixth King built it, marrying only into Magi families and other priestly houses. The Mazdani hold no land; their wealth is the right to the offerings left at the niches, which are falling, and the guest-court fees, which they collect for the Scribes and occasionally forget to forward.
