They are devout, proper and in debt to the Vaults of Equilibrium.

  • Atossa Mazdani, Keeper of the Niches — knows the name of the god of the dark niche and has sworn never to say it.
  • Mazdayasn Mazdani, her husband, register-keeper of the guest-court — keeps two registers, one for the Scribes and one true.
  • Haoma Mazdani, niche-priest of Zann — copies Gulnar Zand's red entries into his own notebook.
  • Parisatis Mazdani, censer-bearer at the Bringing — Prince Tiridat has sent her a ring, and her mother has sent it back.

Ties: Herbad Tansar's Magi; House Zarrin of Atarabad, cousins by marriage.

House Tansar Herbads of the Hill of Fires · Magi

Crest: a veiled flame over seven peaks · Motto: "Kept, not owned" · Seat: the Herbad's Lodge on the Hill of Fires

A Magi lineage that has given the Hill of Fires its herbad, the chief teaching-priest, eleven times in four centuries. The Tansar crown the King of Kings, declare the fit days for war and execution, and send the taper down to every niche in the city. They are the one check on the throne the throne has never removed, and they know exactly how far that check reaches: to the fire, and not one step past it.

  • Herbad Tansar, chief of the Magi of the Hill — crowned the present King and has never told anyone what the Farr looked like that day.
  • Magus Kirdir Tansar, his eldest son, keeper of the Fire Watch — has noticed messages in the signal chain that no Magus sent.
  • Lady Denag Tansar, his wife, keeper of the corpse-bearers' licences — knows every body that went to the towers, and the few that did not.

Ties: the Witness of Mithratal; rivals of the First Flame at Atarabad on points of doctrine; uneasy neighbours of Magus Rashnu-Vahram.

Temples · Atarabad

The Temples of Atarabad

The oldest fire in the empire on the hill, a pantheon that rents niches to foreign gods by the season below it, and a First Flame who wants the foreigners out.

Pantheon building
The House of All Roads, the Izadkhaneh of Atarabad, at the foot of the Fire Hill where the bazaar's lanes begin
Chief priest
Keeper of the Roads Farangis Zarrin; above her, Mobad Atar-Farnbag, First Flame of the Magi
Patron gods
The undying fire; Jauhar the Gilded; Bala of the scales; Najm for the deep road
Banned here
Lotha, Thasmudayan, the Faceless God; Ragarra's serpent, by a decree nobody remembers making
Trouble
Foreign gods paying rent, a First Flame who wants them evicted, and a snake no one can name

The Pantheon

The House of All Roads is the most profitable temple in Acheaoria and the least holy-looking: a great square courtyard at the foot of the Fire Hill, roofed with matting like the bazaar it opens into, with a wind-tower at each corner and a ring of god-rooms round the sides. The plateau's Honoured Ones hold the east side, nearest the fire, in rooms whose doors face the hill. The west side is the Court of Guests, twelve rooms let by the season to the gods of foreign merchants: a niche for Mercury hired by the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon, one for Hermes held by a Corinthian shipping family, one for the river-god of Khemaret that nobody has visited in two years. The rent is collected by the pantheon and a tenth goes to the Scribes as guest-god fees. The rest pays for the Lending of the Flame, the matting, the wind-towers and, it is said, most of the First Flame's own wood.

The House is kept by the Keeper of the Roads, Farangis Zarrin, sixty, of the priest-banker house of Zarrin, sister of Master of Scales Jahanbakht Zarrin at Persemenid. She is a large, cheerful, ruthless woman who has run the House for twenty-two years and quadrupled its income by treating foreign gods as foreign merchants: welcome, taxed and watched. Her husband Mehran Zarrin keeps the Court of Guests and speaks seven languages badly. Their son Rustam Zarrin is niche-priest of Jauhar and a gem-broker on the side. Their daughter Shabnam Zarrin trained as a Magus's assistant at the Fire Hill, the first Zarrin to be allowed past the screen's outer court, and carries her mother's messages up the hill and the First Flame's back down.

For Mobad Atar-Farnbag, the Court of Guests is a defilement with a ledger. He has wanted foreign shrines out of the caravanserais for a decade; now he wants them out of the House of All Roads as well, and he has the means, since every niche-lamp is lit from his fire. Since the spring the Magus with the taper has begun to skip the Court of Guests "when the wind is wrong". Farangis has answered by buying lamp-oil from the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon, lit from a Mercurial flame at Deiperduem, and the city is waiting to see whether the First Flame will call that a crime.

Temples

The Gilded House of Jauhar Merchants' temple

Jauhar, the Gilded · Gilded Priest Vologases Sekkeh · coin-dust, sandalwood, polished brass

Jauhar's temple faces the weigh-house across the bazaar's central court: a domed room hung with balances, and a hill-dwarf figure of the god counting coins into a bowl that is never full. The Gilded Vault and the Wheelwalkers are both sworn here. The Gilded Priest Vologases Sekkeh, a thin man with a jeweller's loupe on a cord, opens the Long Bargain each year by weighing a single gold coin before the crowd and announcing the god's price for it, which sets the tone of the week. Jauhar's priests take no side: they bless the buyer and the seller in the same breath. Money comes from a hundredth part of every sale sworn in the god's name, and lately from quiet fees for blessing stones that will leave the empire sewn into coats.

Ties: the Wheelwalkers' wayside shrines; the gem-trade at Deiperduem; House Suren-Pahlav, its largest donor.

The Vault-Temple of Bala The temple-bank

Bala, the Melodic · Master of Scales Pouran Dastvar · lute-strings, cold iron, ink

That a god of music and joy should keep a bank strikes foreigners as a joke; Acheaorians reply that balance is a kind of music. The Vaults of Equilibrium's Atarabad house is a temple above and a strongroom below, and its hymns are sung over the opening of the ledgers each morning. Master of Scales Pouran Dastvar is priest and banker in one; he lends to satrapies the Mithril Reserve will not touch, and has started asking for collateral that fits in a strongbox. The temple's festival is the Day of the Even Scale at the year's turn, when debts are sung aloud with a lute and one small debt, chosen by lot, is forgiven to music. Its politics: the Vaults are losing to the Reserve, and Pouran means to lose slowly.

Ties: the high temple-bank at Persemenid; the Melodic Circle at Persevalis; rival of the Reserve branch under Brokk Ironhand.

The Waystone of Najm East Gate shrine

Najm, the Explorer · Wayfinder Arzhang · dust, camel-dung smoke, rope

A rough stone pillar in the East Gate, chipped by every caravan that has touched it for luck, with a lean-to shrine beside it where a half-elf figure of Najm points down the road. Wayfinder Arzhang, half-elf himself and the son of a Wheelwalker mother, keeps it. Najm is honoured by being given room, not obeyed: the Wayfinder's whole rite is to ask each caravan master where he means to go, and to say nothing when the answer is foolish. Since two caravans were lost beyond the Zaruk'thal notches last year, the Waystone has had more custom than in a decade, and Arzhang has started cutting the names of the lost into its base. Najm's niche at Persemenid is dark; his Waystone here is not, and the court has noticed.

Ties: the pool shrine of Qa'zshahrv'in (towns); the Wheelwalkers; the East Gate.

The Kitchen of Jarmik The Benevolent Hands

Jarmik, the Benevolent · Mother Kuchak · lentils, smoke, wet bread

A temple that is a kitchen, by the Cobra Heaps, under a halfling figure of Jarmik with a ladle. Mother Kuchak, a halfling of the Benevolent Hands who came east with a relocated people forty years ago and stayed, feeds six hundred a day on the endowments of old families and the leftovers of the caravanserais. The rite is to eat, and the feast is every day. The Benevolent Hands feed the satrapies the throne has stopped feeding, carefully, and Mother Kuchak's kitchen is where the drivers of three empires' caravans eat side by side and hear the news first. The Magi tolerate her because she buys a purification every month without being asked.

Ties: Jarmik's busy niche at Persemenid; the guest-levels of Zi'rzamin Dar'a, which she supplies (towns).

The forgotten temple

The Serpent House under the Cobra Heaps. The rubble mounds outside the East Gate are not rubble. They are the fallen walls of a temple older than the fire on the hill, built to Ragarra, the Wild Fury, whom the plateau's oldest images show as a yuan-ti woman with a serpent's lower body and a storm in her hand. She is still a listed god of the pantheon, and she has no niche in the House of All Roads, no priest and no day; a decree of some forgotten King struck her from the rota and nobody has ever moved to restore her. The snake-charmers' guild that lives on the Heaps descends from her temple servants. They keep a few of her words in their charming-songs, and the snakes still answer to them. Last month the guild locked its gate.

Priestly houses

House Zarrin Priest-bankers · Keepers of the Roads

Crest: a gold scale in a wind-tower · Motto: "Weighed, then welcomed" · Seat: the Keeper's Court of the House of All Roads

An old priestly family of Bala and Jauhar, half temple and half counting-house, which has kept the House of All Roads for six generations and placed a Master of Scales in the Vaults of Equilibrium in each of them. The Zarrin are the reason the Atarabad pantheon pays its way. They are also the reason the Magi distrust it: a family that prices gods will price anything.

  • Farangis Zarrin, Keeper of the Roads — keeps a list of every foreign god's rent, arrears and worshippers, and sells copies to no one but the King's Eye.
  • Mehran Zarrin, her husband, keeper of the Court of Guests — has developed a private devotion to Mercury, which he thinks nobody knows.
  • Rustam Zarrin, niche-priest of Jauhar — blesses stones bound west and keeps a note of which family each one belonged to.
  • Shabnam Zarrin, temple assistant at the Fire Hill — has heard a dying temple servant talk about a night he swears the fire went out.

Ties: Master of Scales Jahanbakht Zarrin at Persemenid; House Mazdan by marriage; Tahmineh of the Seal, the King's Eye.

House Farnbagan Mobads of the Fire Hill · Magi

Crest: a flame behind a lattice screen · Motto: "It has not gone out" · Seat: the Mobads' Houses on the Fire Hill

The Magi lineage of the First Flame, which has given Atarabad its mobad, the senior fire-priest, for longer than the city has had walls. The Farnbagan keep the oldest flame in the empire, lit, they say, before the empire, and their whole standing in the Magi rests on that claim. They are conservative, learned and hostile to foreign practice, and they are the only family in Acheaoria that Herbad Tansar's house at Persemenid treats as an equal, which both houses resent.

  • Mobad Atar-Farnbag, First Flame of the Magi — keeps the undying fire, knows it once died, and has decided that the truth would do more harm than the lie.
  • Magus Tirdad Farnbagan, his nephew — sent to Persemenid to observe the Rite of Return, and not invited in.
  • Lady Spenta Farnbagan, the Mobad's sister, mistress of the fuel-stores — logs every load of wood and knows exactly how much the House of All Roads pays for.

Ties: House Tansar, rivals in doctrine; the Witness of Mithratal, allies against the Rite.

Temples · Mithratal

The Temples of Mithratal

In the oath-city the gods are witnesses before they are anything else: they stand round the empty court in a ring, and each one can be called to hear a promise.

Pantheon building
The Hall of Witnesses, the Izadkhaneh of Mithratal, a covered colonnade enclosing three sides of the Precinct of Oaths
Chief priest
Mistress of Witnesses Roshandokht Varzavand; above her, Magus Frawardin, the Witness of the Fire
Patron gods
The sacred fire as witness; Hakiyah the Just Scales; Vatagatal the Dutiful; Migal the Silent
Banned here
Lotha, mistress of lies, above all; the Faceless God; any oath sworn in a god's name without the fire's seal
Trouble
Witnesses for hire, a bought ordeal, and someone teaching that a man without a face cannot be bound

The Pantheon

The Precinct of Oaths is bare, and is meant to be. Its ornament is all around it: a deep colonnade on the north, west and south sides, the Hall of Witnesses, where each Honoured One has a bay with a lamp, a bench and a stone lectern facing the court. The east side is the fire. When parties swear barefoot on the stone, the fire witnesses the oath and the Magi seal it; but a covenant may also call one or more gods as secondary witnesses, and the priest of each god called comes out of his bay, stands at the lectern and says the god's name once. A covenant witnessed by the fire alone binds. One witnessed by the fire and by Hakiyah, Vatagatal and Botu'Astook binds the parties, their heirs and their horses, and costs accordingly. The price of each witness is posted on a bronze plate in each bay, and has not changed in a hundred years, which makes the Hall of Witnesses the only honest price-list in Acheaoria.

The Hall is kept by the Mistress of Witnesses, Roshandokht Varzavand, sixty-two, of the priestly house of Varzavand. She assigns the witness-priests to their bays, keeps the roll of which gods witnessed which covenant, and answers to Magus Frawardin, whose seal makes everything else matter. She is dry, exact and rather funny, a widow who has refused two Dadvar proposals on the grounds that she would end up witnessing her own marriage. Her son Arashk Varzavand is witness-priest of Hakiyah. Her daughter Vida Varzavand keeps the Roll of Witnesses, which is now the second-largest archive in the city. Her grandson Kaveh, eleven, has been taught to recite the names of all the gods without breathing, which is the house's party trick and, once, settled a lawsuit.

On the Silent Day the Hall empties: the gods' priests withdraw behind their bays and only Migal's lamp burns. During the eleven days of the Renewal every bay is manned from dawn to dusk, and the witness-fees pay the Hall's year. The Hall's quiet trouble is that a witness-priest's single spoken word can now be bought twice: once at the posted price, and once more, in a teahouse, for a slightly different pronunciation of the god's name which, under a Dadvar reading, voids the witness.

Temples

The Lantern House of Hakiyah Justice that announces itself

Hakiyah, the Just Scales · Lantern-Mother Parisa Roshanpur · lamp-oil, polished steel, saddle leather

The Lanterns of Justice keep their chapter-house at the Grove Gate, and its temple is the one building in Mithratal lit all night: a protector-aasimar figure of Hakiyah holds a lamp that is never dimmed, so that justice is visible from the walls. Lantern-Mother Parisa Roshanpur, aunt of Lantern-Captain Zarir, keeps the temple, trains the riders' souls while he trains their horses, and hears their confessions after circuit. The rite is the Lighting of the Road: a Lantern going out on circuit lights his lamp from the god's and may not let it go out until he returns. Hakiyah's priests keep strict rules; the temple takes no fees for justice, and lives on bequests from people who were judged fairly. It is poor and proud of it. Hakiyah's priests also oversee, in name, the Ordeal Grove, and Parisa has begun to distrust the man who runs it.

Ties: the Lanterns ride to Xerastri and Shir'abad D'ar; the Ordeal Grove's priest Kersasp.

The Hall of Duty Vatagatal's oath-chapter

Vatagatal, the Dutiful · Oath-Priest Garshasp Ahanin · iron filings, wool, cold hearth

A plain iron-doored hall in the Archive Ward where the Ironclad Oath renews its vow every seventh year: each sworn soldier comes to Mithratal, touches the hobgoblin figure of Vatagatal's iron hand, and repeats the promise that binds him to the throne and forbids him war on the empire's own subjects. Oath-Priest Garshasp Ahanin, once an Oath-Captain, lost an arm on the Cloudspine and found the god in the hospital. The rites are exacting and impersonal; Vatagatal is owed correct observance, not affection. The Hall's income is a soldier's day-pay at each renewal. Its politics have turned sharp: Garshasp has been asked, by three satraps in one year, whether a man sworn to the throne may defend it against a satrap who calls himself its protector. He has not answered.

Ties: the Oath chapters at Xerastri and Shir'abad D'ar (towns); Persemenid.

The Kin-House of Botu'Astook Genealogies and marriage-covenants

Botu'Astook, the Kinkeeper · Kin-Keeper Mehrnoush Tabarzad · parchment, horse, old wood

Every marriage covenant between zarates is sworn twice in Mithratal: once on the stone before the fire, and once in the Kin-House, before a centaur figure of Botu'Astook with a family tree carved up its flanks. Kin-Keeper Mehrnoush Tabarzad keeps the genealogies of four hundred noble houses and can tell a bride whom she is related to and how badly. The Kinkeeper's priests take no side, which means they record every bastard as faithfully as every heir. The festival is the Reading of the Lines in the Renewal, when the house's newest entries are read aloud. Money comes from marriage fees and from quiet fees to look up a lineage. Lately the Kin-House has had many requests from minor zarates to prove descent from the founder of the dynasty, in case the line should fail.

Ties: House Vohuman's marriage to House Tir'dad; the Sandglass Circle at Persemenid.

The Silent Lamp of Migal The god of the Silent Day

Migal, the Silent · Keeper Without Words · nothing at all; that is the point

The smallest bay in the Hall of Witnesses, and the only one with a door. Behind it a changeling figure of Migal, faceless in the true sense, stands with a finger on lips that are not quite there. Migal is the god of stealth and knowledge, and his rite is the Silent Day itself: the whole city speaks no word from sunrise to sunset, so that anything said aloud is heard and remembered. His priest is called the Keeper Without Words, takes a vow of silence for life, and writes nothing. By ancient privilege the only person who may write on the Silent Day is a royal witness, which is why Mardak the Listener, the King's Eye, is Migal's most regular worshipper and the most hated man in the city. The Silent Lamp has no fees. It has gifts, left without a word.

Ties: the shaft-rota of Zi'rzamin Dar'a, where Migal is honoured (towns); the creed of assassins, who also keep silence.

The forgotten temple

The Binding Word. The precinct was a temple before it was a court. Mithratal is named for an old covenant-spirit that the city's founders swore by long before the Magi set their fire at the precinct's eastern edge: the Covenant, or the Binding Word. It had no image. Its temple was the empty floor; its priest was whoever stood on it and told the truth. Every decade, when the masons cut the new slab at the Setting of the Stone, they find beneath the old one a thin layer of dark ash and a sequence of marks in a script nobody living reads, and every decade the Magi have them covered without comment. The oldest document in the Covenant Archives, the one read first at every Renewal, in a language no one speaks, is sworn in the Binding Word's name, and the Magus who reads it bows to the empty floor and not to the fire.

Priestly houses

House Varzavand Masters of Witnesses

Crest: an open hand raised before a flame · Motto: "Heard" · Seat: the Witness-House on the precinct's north side

A priestly family that has kept the Hall of Witnesses since it was built, and has supplied witness-priests to most of its bays. The Varzavand are poor in land and rich in standing: their roll of which god witnessed which covenant is cited in disputes across the plateau, and a Varzavand's memory is accepted as evidence. They marry Magi and Lanterns and never Dadvar.

  • Roshandokht Varzavand, Mistress of Witnesses — has noticed that three witness-priests now pronounce Hakiyah's name with an accent they did not have last year.
  • Arashk Varzavand, witness-priest of Hakiyah — honest, slow and in love with Laleh Golnar, who plays him at board games for information.
  • Vida Varzavand, keeper of the Roll of Witnesses — has found a covenant in the roll that names a god who is not in the pantheon.
  • Kaveh Varzavand, eleven — can recite every god in one breath, and is the only person who has heard the Keeper Without Words laugh.

Ties: House Golnar; Magus Frawardin; the Lantern House.

House Frawardin Witnesses of the Fire · Magi

Crest: a seal-ring in a flame · Motto: "Without the seal, a promise" · Seat: the Seal-House beside the Fire-Temple

The Magi lineage whose head holds the office of Witness of the Fire and the seal that turns a promise into a covenant. The Frawardin are the most legal of the Magi and the least mystical; they argue doctrine with the Tansar of Persemenid by letter, in numbered paragraphs. They are also the Magi most opposed to the Rite of Return, on the ground that a covenant with the dead is a covenant the dead cannot dispute.

  • Magus Frawardin, Witness of the Fire — seals every covenant, and has quietly begun refusing to seal those that call no god but the fire, which is new.
  • Magus Hutaosa Frawardin, his wife's brother, reader of the oldest covenant — the only living Magus who can pronounce it, and he has started to understand it.
  • Dinak Frawardin, his daughter, keeper of the seal-wax — has been offered a fortune for one impression of the seal.

Ties: allies of House Farnbagan against the Rite; House Tansar.

Temples · Persevalis

The Temples of Persevalis

A pantheon with no roof: each god a walled garden on the slope, each garden watered by deed, and the water lately running uphill towards something that is not a god at all.

Pantheon building
The Garden of the Honoured Ones, the Izadkhaneh of Persevalis, a ladder of walled god-gardens below the Channel Head
Chief priest
High Gardener Darya Sarvestan; above her, Herbad Shirzad of the Channel Head
Patron gods
The sacred fire; Shajar at the channel heads; Selan for the dreamers; Bala for the singers; Jisan for the deeds
Banned here
Lotha, Thasmudayan, the Faceless God; the Cult of Whispering Roots, which the city suspects is already in its orchards
Trouble
A water-god's priests and a harvest-god's priests at law over the same channel

The Pantheon

Persevalis builds gardens with buildings in them, and its pantheon is no exception. The Garden of the Honoured Ones is a long ladder of walled gardens on the slope directly beneath the Channel Head, one for each god, each fed by the channel in turn as it comes down from the fire. Water reaches the gods in the order of precedence the Magi set three centuries ago: Shajar's garden first, then Selan's, then Hakiyah's, and so on down to the guest-gods' orchard at the foot, which drinks what is left. Each garden has a pavilion with the god's lamp, a pool and a tree planted for the god and grafted from its predecessor; the oldest, Shajar's plane, is entered in the Peyvand registry as the forty-first of its line. To sit in a god's garden is an invitation, with rules, and refusing it is an insult.

The Garden is kept by the High Gardener Darya Sarvestan, forty-eight, of the priestly house of Sarvestan, gardeners to the gods for nine generations. She holds the deed to the Garden's channel, sets the rota of god-gardeners, and walks the ladder every dawn behind the Magus with the taper, checking each lamp and each sluice. She is soft-spoken, stubborn, and the best judge of a sick tree in the city. Her husband Khosrow Sarvestan keeps the guest-gods' orchard and its fees. Their son Sohrab Sarvestan is gardener of Selan's garden and an initiate of the Enchanted Muse. Their daughter Roudabeh Sarvestan, sixteen, has been apprenticed to Ustad Babak, the master channel-keeper, which no Sarvestan girl has done before.

The order of the water is the Garden's politics. The Bountiful Harvesters, Jisan's guild, hold most of the channel deeds in the city, and they have filed a claim that Jisan's garden, ninth in the ladder, has been watered short for a century and is owed the arrears, payable from Shajar's share. The River's Embrace calls this blasphemy. Herbad Shirzad, who opens the water each spring and can refuse to, has said nothing, and the Opening of the Channels is in forty days.

Temples

The Channel Shrines of Shajar The River's Embrace

Shajar, the River Guardian · Mother of Channels Taraneh Kariz · moss, cold stone, wet reed

Shajar has no single temple here; she has a shrine at every point where a channel divides, sixty-three of them, each a small arch with a triton figure and a bowl. The mother-shrine stands at the Qanat Pools beside the Water-Court, where the blind newts live, and the Mother of Channels Taraneh Kariz of the River's Embrace keeps it and walks all sixty-three in a ten-day round. The Opening of the Channels is Shajar's festival as well as the Magi's: Herbad Shirzad blesses the water, Taraneh releases it, and the city follows it down the slope in a day. Shajar's priests take no side, which in practice means they warn of floods and droughts to everyone at once and are blamed by both. Money comes from deed-holders, who pay for each shrine on their section.

Ties: the pool shrine at Qa'zshahrv'in (towns); the Water-Court at Atarabad; Persemenid's failing Paradise channel.

The Moon Pavilion of Selan The Enchanted Muse

Selan, the Enchantress · Almanac-Mistress Mahtab · night-jasmine, lamp-smoke, paper

A white pavilion in Selan's garden, open on all sides, where the Enchanted Muse keep their dream-almanac and read the moon. A high-elf figure of Selan holds a mirror turned to the sky. Almanac-Mistress Mahtab is priestess here by office. The rite is to sleep in the pavilion and bring a dream back to be written; the festival is the Night Gardens in high summer, which the Muse calls Selan's own and the Magi call a civic custom. Persevalis plans its year by the almanac. Since last summer's "spring tide of dreams", when half the city dreamed of a woman in grey walking the terraces, the pavilion has been full every night, and Mahtab has sent careful letters to Delphara and to the Arcane Academy.

Ties: the Dreamers' Hunt: Delphara, Hellarchon, Eronis; the weavers' Selan at Tabrishi'ir (towns).

The Hall of Strings Bala and the Melodic Circle

Bala, the Melodic · Keeper of the Strings Behrouz Tarzani · rosewater, wine, gut strings

A garden pavilion with a sprung wooden floor and a satyr-figure of Bala with a pipe, where the Melodic Circle rehearses, initiates and drinks. Bala's worship is warm and unruly; the rite is to play when moved and to stop when bored. Keeper of the Strings Behrouz Tarzani, an old lutenist with no front teeth, keeps the hall and its instruments. Shirin Navaz, First Voice of the Circle, sings here when she is in the city, and her songs about the satrap, and lately about the court, are first sung in this garden. By long custom what is sung is not what is said, and the Hall of Strings is the one place in Persevalis where the court's unpaid bills can be named aloud. Money comes from patrons and from the Night Gardens, when the hall plays until dawn for every gate in the city.

Ties: the Circle's hall at Mithratal; the Vault-Temple of Bala at Atarabad.

The Deed-Shrine of Jisan The Bountiful Harvesters

Jisan, the Bountiful · Deed-Priest Kambiz Kharman · grain, wax seals, rotting windfalls

Jisan's garden is the richest on the ladder and the least pleasant: a firbolg figure of the god sits among heaped windfalls left to rot, because Jisan is owed what the tree drops. The Bountiful Harvesters keep their deed-registry in the pavilion, and the Deed-Priest Kambiz Kharman is both its priest and the guild's chief registrar. Jisan's worship is quiet and self-serving: the faithful bargain for a good harvest and do not speak of what they paid. The festival is the Grafting in late winter, when new cuttings are registered by name and the Harvesters take a fee for each. Kambiz's claim against Shajar's share of the water is the city's lawsuit of the decade, and he has filed it in Mithratal, where it will be heard under a covenant nobody has read for a century.

Ties: the Harvesters at Atarabad and De'rakhtak Bon (towns); Mithratal's Hall of Witnesses.

The forgotten temple

The Old Channel. Below the Foot of the Slope, beyond the Green-Nut Orchards, there is a dry stone conduit older than any qanat, cut through the rock in a straight line and lined with tiles of a deep green glaze nobody can now make. At its head, half buried in the slope, stands a ruined arch with a woman's figure worn almost smooth, her hands full of growing things. Channel-keepers call her the Green Mother and spit for luck when they pass. The Magi say she is a nursery tale. The Peyvand registry says that the first named tree of Persevalis was grafted "from the Mother's tree at the Old Channel", and the registry does not tell nursery tales. The blue-lamped garden, where the city's oldest stories say a peri comes on the Night Gardens, sits exactly on the Old Channel's line.

Priestly houses

House Sarvestan Gardeners to the Gods

Crest: a cypress inside a lamp · Motto: "First the water, then the god" · Seat: the Gardener's House at the head of the ladder

A priestly family that has kept the Garden of the Honoured Ones for nine generations. The Sarvestan own the Garden's channel deed outright, which makes them the only priests in Acheaoria who could, in law, turn off the gods. They have never done it, and remind people of this often.

  • Darya Sarvestan, High Gardener — has found that Jisan's garden really was watered short for a century, and on whose orders.
  • Khosrow Sarvestan, her husband, keeper of the guest-gods' orchard — lets a Hellenorian merchant leave offerings to Demeter under the pomegranates and does not record it.
  • Sohrab Sarvestan, gardener of Selan's garden — dreamed of the woman in grey every night for a month and has fallen in love with a dream.
  • Roudabeh Sarvestan, apprentice channel-keeper — has walked the eastern channel further than anyone but Ustad Babak, and heard water running beneath it.

Ties: House Peyvand's registry; Herbad Shirzad; House Bagh'dar, its patrons.

House Shirzad Herbads of the Channel Head · Magi

Crest: a flame above running water · Motto: "Fire over water, never in it" · Seat: the Herbad's House beside the Fire-Temple of Persevalis

The Magi lineage of the Channel Head, which has opened the water every spring for three hundred years and claims the right to refuse. The Shirzad are gentler than the Magi of the Royal Road, garden-loving and poetic, and they are also the only Magi with an economic weapon that works: no blessing, no water, no harvest, no court supply.

  • Herbad Shirzad, keeper of the fire and the Opening — means to refuse the Opening this year unless the court pays the satrap, and has told no one but the King's Eye.
  • Magus Pashang Shirzad, his brother — keeps the fire and writes verse no one is allowed to read.
  • Golnaz Shirzad, his daughter — married into House Golab, and so sits at both ends of the court's debt.

Ties: House Golab; House Tansar, his superiors in doctrine.

Temples · Xerastri

The Temples of Xerastri

A fortress keeps its gods the way it keeps its grain: inside the inner wall, counted, rationed, and expected to hold when everything outside is lost.

Pantheon building
The Hall of Standards, the Izadkhaneh of Xerastri, a vaulted barrack-hall inside the inner citadel
Chief priest
Keeper of the Standards Gordafarid Kamandar; above her, Herbad Burzin of the frontier fire
Patron gods
The sacred fire; Vatagatal the Dutiful; Hajama for the cavalry; Kiga for the hunt; Beast, as a guest of the steppe
Banned here
Lotha, Thasmudayan, the Faceless God; the burning of the dead, which the garrison does anyway
Trouble
Soldiers who burn their comrades, engineers who make unclean fire, and a wall that hides a god

The Pantheon

The Hall of Standards stands inside the inner wall between the granaries and the Fire-Temple, a long vaulted building of the same thick brick as the citadel, with arrow-slits for windows and a door that can be barred from inside. It was built to be the citadel's last chapel and, if needed, its last barracks. Each Honoured One has a bay along the walls, and in each bay hang the standards of the regiments sworn to that god: Vatagatal's bay is crowded with the iron-grey pennons of the Ironclad Oath, Hajama's with the lion banners of the Vanguard squadrons, Kiga's with the hunting-flags of the scouts. A god with no regiment has a lamp and a bare wall. The plateau's softer gods, Bala, Selan, Jarmik, share a single bay at the end, which the garrison calls the Nursery and visits more than it admits.

The Hall is kept by the Keeper of the Standards, Gordafarid Kamandar, fifty-one, of the bowyer-priest house of Kamandar. She is a broad, grey-braided woman who served twelve years as a horse-archer before she took the lamp, and she can still put an arrow through a standard's eyelet at sixty paces, which she does at the Riding to remind everyone. She keeps the regimental rolls of oaths, sets the rota of chaplains, and answers to Herbad Burzin, who keeps the fire and the oaths of the wall-families. Her husband Giv Kamandar is master bowyer to the garrison. Their elder son Bizhan Kamandar rides with Roxana Surena at the Parthian Ravine. Their younger son Hormoz Kamandar is chaplain of Vatagatal's bay and has, the city whispers, burned a comrade on the steppe.

The Hall of Standards is the most honest pantheon in Acheaoria because it has nothing to sell: its income is a copper a month from every soldier's pay, which has been four months behind. Gordafarid has begun to pay the lamp-oil from her own purse, and Satrap Vindarna Sarvand has offered to pay it from the steppe tolls, which would make the gods his as well. She has not answered.

Temples

The Lion Hall of Hajama The cavalry's temple

Hajama, the God of Valor · Lion-Priest Bahram Shirdel · horse, leather, lamp-oil, old blood

A temple and a stable in one, at the north gate beside the March House: the Vanguard squadrons' horses are blessed in its forecourt before the Riding, and the leonin figure of Hajama inside looks down on a sand-table of the steppe frontier that the officers use as a map. Lion-Priest Bahram Shirdel, a former Vanguard officer from Persemenid sent north in disgrace, has made it his life. Hajama's rites are exacting: the god is owed the correct order of battle and gives order in return. The Lion Hall's politics are the Mihran's: House Mihran of Xerastri pays for it, and the empty saddle stands beside the altar as it does at the capital. Bahram blesses the feud every year, and has noticed that Marzban Piruz does not bow at that point in the rite.

Ties: the Lion Gate at Persemenid; the Vanguard chapel at Shir'abad D'ar (towns); the Cloudspine Feud with Duneforged.

The Oath Chapter of Vatagatal The Ironclad Oath

Vatagatal, the Dutiful · Oath-Priest Hushang Zereh · cold iron, wool, porridge

The Ironclad Oath's chapter-house in the Barracks Row holds a small iron chapel where the chapter hears its oath read each morning before drill. Oath-Priest Hushang Zereh, a dour man who has never once raised his voice, keeps it alongside Oath-Captain Arya Kardar, who commands. The rite is the morning reading; the festival is the seventh-year renewal, for which the whole chapter marches to Mithratal and back. The chapel's question this year is the old one sharpened: the Oath will fight the steppe and will not fight subjects, and the Malaunian clans who trade at the Horse Fair have begun asking to be counted as subjects so that the Oath cannot be turned on them. Hushang thinks the god would say yes. The satrap thinks the god should mind his own business.

Ties: the Hall of Duty at Mithratal; the Oath chapter at Shir'abad D'ar.

The Hunting Altar of Kiga The Predator's Guild

Kiga, the Beastmaster · Huntmistress Yasaman Yuzban · cheetah-musk, dry grass, blood on stone

Kiga's altar stands outside the walls in the Hunting Park, because the god's faithful kill and the purity laws keep blood out of the city. It is a flat stone under a tabaxi figure of the god crouched to spring, stained dark from generations of first kills. Huntmistress Yasaman Yuzban of the Predator's Guild keeps the altar and the park's cheetahs, which are trained here and sold to every satrap with a hunting park. Kiga's worship is quiet and self-serving: hunters bargain for a kill and do not speak of the price. The festival is the First Kill of the hunting season, when a young cheetah is slipped for the first time and its quarry offered on the stone. One of Yasaman's cheetahs is still loose, and three people have blamed three different men.

Ties: the Paradise at Persemenid, which buys her cheetahs; the Guild's culling rights at Persevalis.

The Steppe Shrine of Beast A guest-god at the Horse Fair

Beast, the Savage · Old Kesh the horse-shaman · horse-sweat, fermented milk, wood-smoke

Beast is a god of the Acheaorian pantheon, but at Xerastri he is honoured as the steppe honours him: a ring of horse-skulls on poles in the Horse-Fair Ground, registered with the Scribes as a guest-god's shrine and paid for by the clans. During the truce week of the Horse Fair, Old Kesh, a Malaunian horse-shaman with a shifter's yellow eyes, sleeps in the ring and settles quarrels by wrestling. The rite is to give the god room. The garrison, which rides and shoots like the Malaunians, has adopted the shrine wholesale; half the Vanguard's young officers have a horse-skull charm under their armour. Tomyra of the Lion Grass pays her respects here each year before she hears offers, and the Magi pretend not to know where the officers go after dark.

Ties: the Savage Pack beyond the qanat line; House Asbdar, which pays the clans' fee.

The forgotten temple

The Warden in the Wall. The outer wall was not the first wall here. Its Long Stretch, held by House Dezhban for nine generations, is built on a foundation of fitted grey stone far older than Xerastri, and behind the facing, at the stretch's midpoint, is a chamber the Dezhban call the Warden's Room. In it stands a figure taller than a man, of the same grey stone, with a shield and no face, facing the steppe through the wall. The Dezhban have reported their stretch sound every spring for two hundred years, and every spring before the Counting the eldest Dezhban goes into the Warden's Room alone with a lamp. The family says it is an inspection. The stone floor in front of the figure is worn in two hollows the shape of knees.

Priestly houses

House Kamandar Bowyers and Keepers of the Standards

Crest: a strung bow before a lamp · Motto: "Hold the string" · Seat: the Bowyers' Court inside the inner wall

A frontier family that has made the garrison's bows and kept the Hall of Standards for five generations, the only house in Acheaoria where the lamp passes through the women and the bow-trade through the men. The Kamandar are soldiers first and priests second, and they treat the gods the way they treat the garrison: with respect, a roll-call and no illusions.

  • Gordafarid Kamandar, Keeper of the Standards — would rather pay the gods' oil herself than let the satrap buy them.
  • Giv Kamandar, master bowyer — has been asked by the siege yards for bow-glue that does not burn, and wonders why.
  • Bizhan Kamandar, horse-archer at the Parthian Ravine — sends home letters about lights in the gorge at night.
  • Hormoz Kamandar, chaplain of Vatagatal — burned his best friend on the steppe in the war's last year and has gone down to the Howling Cellar since.

Ties: Herbad Burzin; Roxana Surena; the Ironclad Oath chapter.

House Burzin Herbads of the frontier fire · Magi

Crest: a flame inside a tower · Motto: "The last thing given up" · Seat: the Herbad's Tower beside the Fire-Temple of Xerastri

A Magi lineage that has kept the frontier fire since the citadel was built, and one of the few Magi families that has stood a siege. The Burzin hold the fire and the oaths of the wall-families; they are hard, plain men and women who have buried no one and burned no one, and who live with a garrison that does the second all the time.

  • Herbad Burzin, keeper of the fire — has begun to suspect that the yards' "unclean fire" exists, and does not know whether to tell the satrap or the Marzban.
  • Magus Mitradata Burzin, his son, keeper of the towers — the vultures have left Xerastri, and he cannot find out why.
  • Lady Arnavaz Burzin, his wife, sister of Rostam Dezhban — knows what her nephew Faramarz does at night.

Ties: House Dezhban by marriage; House Tansar.

Temples · Acheaoria · Towns

The Temples of the Acheaorian Towns

No town has a fire-temple of the first rank; most have a fire-house with a single Magus, a shrine or two, and one god the town actually lives by.

De'rakhtak Bon The Root Hall and the god of the cold levels

Jisan and Botu'Astook · Root-Reader Old Mother Sarv · damp earth, sap, cold grain

The town has a fire-house on the surface, a single Magus and a single lamp, and the town ignores it. Its real temple is the Root Hall, where the taproot is dressed and read and its readings cut into the wall for six hundred years. Officially the Hall honours Jisan, the Bountiful, and the Bountiful Harvesters pay for it, since their seed lies in the cold levels; in practice it honours Botu'Astook, the Kinkeeper, because the taproot's readings are also the town's genealogy: each family's name is cut beside the year its first child was born underground. Old Mother Sarv, the Root-Reader, is the town's priestess in all but title, and her daughter Sarvenaz and granddaughter Narges stand behind her at every Reading, learning to read sap by colour. The rite is the Reading of the Root at each season's turn; planting above follows her word, not the Frataraka's. Since the root wept red, Mother Sarv has declared no season, and the Harvesters' Deed-Priest at Persevalis has written asking, politely, whether she is aware what the delay is costing.

Ties: De'rakhtak Bon; the Harvesters of Persevalis; the cold-store trade with Zi'rzamin Dar'a.

Qa'zshahrv'in The Pool Shrine and the muqanni's god

Shajar and Najm · Pool-Priestess Golbahar Ab'kesh · wet mud, camel, hot dust

At the edge of the pool stands the marking-stone, and beside it a triton figure of Shajar under a reed awning: the Pool Shrine, kept by Pool-Priestess Golbahar Ab'kesh, sister of Arashshara Soheila, who sets the water price each morning. The sisters consult before dawn; the god's blessing and the day's price are announced together, and nobody has ever proved which one sets the other. In the caravanserai, travellers bound east touch a small stone pointing down the road, an offshoot of the Waystone of Najm at Atarabad. The town's own god is neither. The muqanni, who go down into the channel at the Clearing and come up feasted, if they come up, keep a shrine in the shaft itself, forty feet down, to a god they will not name to outsiders. Ustad Gav, their master, says it is "the one who keeps the roof up". The Magi of Atarabad send a Magus each year to purify the shaft and he has never been allowed past the first ladder.

Ties: Qa'zshahrv'in; the Channel Shrines at Persevalis; Wayfinder Arzhang at Atarabad.

R'eyshar The Servants' Shrine and the circuit of the dead streets

Haku the Liberator; the Lost One · Street-Reader Esmail Kuhan · quince blossom, broken tile, dust

The living town has a fire-house, a modest Izadkhaneh of six niches and a priest of its own: Street-Reader Esmail Kuhan, brother of the Frataraka, who lights a lamp for each vanished street as Archivist Ferdows reads its name aloud at the Naming of the Streets. Out in the Empty Quarters, among the salvagers' paths through the old servants' lanes, stands a roofless shrine the town calls the Servants' Shrine: a figure of an elf with broken shackles, worn smooth by hands. It is Haku, the Liberator, god of freedom of spirit, and his niche in Persemenid's Izadkhaneh has been dark for a year. Here his shrine has never had a lamp, and never needed one; the servants of the old town left offerings of cord. The Cult of Whispering Roots recruits here, openly enough to irritate the satrap, and tends the ruins around the shrine; the Exiled Wanderers camp by the walls at the Walking of the Circuit and leave feathers for the Lost One.

Ties: R'eyshar; the Deep Lamp of Kor at Persemenid; the Orchard Lodge of Persevalis.

Shir'abad D'ar The lion-gate chapels and a satrap's new Glory

Hajama, Vatagatal, the Farr · Lion-Priest Siyavash Tahmures · fresh plaster, horse, incense

The lesser satrapy keeps its gods in the gate. The double gate with its facing lions has a chapel in each tower: in the east, Hajama's, for the satrap's swelling Vanguard squadrons, kept by Lion-Priest Siyavash Tahmures; in the west, Vatagatal's, for the Ironclad Oath chapter, kept by the chapter's own Oath-Priest. Neither priest drinks in the other's taverns. The town's fire-house is old and small, and its Magus is owed three years' wood. What is new is the Hall of the Glory beside the Tribute Yard, rebuilt last year in marble, with an image of the King of Kings twice the size of Persemenid's, lamps on every column and a second, smaller throne to the image's right, which the Censer-Bearer describes as "for the King's protector". Satrap Vaumisa Shir'vand swears before it each month. The Scribe of the Infinite Ledger has recorded the building's cost in full and wonders what it means that the protector's throne has a cushion and the King's does not.

Ties: Shir'abad D'ar; the Lion Gate at Persemenid; the Hall of Duty and the Unwritten at Mithratal.

Tabrishi'ir The weavers' Selan and the Reading of the Books

Selan, the Enchantress · Pattern-Mother Shahla Gereh · wet wool, madder, indigo

The town's Izadkhaneh is a weaving-court: the god-niches are set into the walls of a courtyard whose centre holds a loom that is never finished. A thread is added to it each day by a different weaving house, and has been for three hundred years. The patron is Selan, the Enchantress, goddess of aesthetic inspiration, shown as a high-elf woman with a shuttle. The temple is kept by Pattern-Mother Shahla Gereh, mother of Arashshara Mehri Gereh, keeper of the strongroom keys; the house holds the temple and the strongroom together, which is why the Frataraka signs what they have already agreed. The rite of the Reading of the Books, when a girl becomes a weaver, is Selan's: the girl is shown her family's pattern-book before the goddess and swears never to copy it for another house. The Dye Days belong to Selan's garden at Persevalis in spirit; the colours are carried to the Moon Pavilion each year in a woven sampler.

Ties: Tabrishi'ir; the Moon Pavilion at Persevalis; the Kitchen of Jarmik and the bazaar of Atarabad.

Zi'rzamin Dar'a The god of the fifth door

Migal the Silent; the Lost One · Master of Air Roudabeh · cold air, goat, lamp-smoke

The town keeps no lists and no idols that could be counted. Its fire-house is a lamp on the second level, tended by whichever household holds the shaft rota that day, and the Magi have twice complained and twice failed to find it. Its two gods have shrines carved into the rock, without images. At the shaft-rota hall, a blank niche with a finger-width hole in it is Migal's: the god of silence and knowledge, honoured by a town that knows a great deal and says none of it. Below the fifth door, in the guest levels, a second blank niche is the Lost One's, god of exile and longing, where the sheltered leave a feather or a scrap of their old clothes and take nothing away. Master of Air Roudabeh, who runs the shaft rota and overrides the Frataraka in a sealing, is priestess of both by custom. The festival is the Guest Night, when the guests are fed by the town and no one asks a name.

Ties: Zi'rzamin Dar'a; the Silent Lamp of Mithratal; the Kitchen of Jarmik at Atarabad, which sends supplies.

Part VI

The Twenty Champions

Ten great spellcasters, one for each school of magic and most of the spellcasting classes, and ten great martial fighters, each of a different calling.

Asetheria keeps no census of its wonders, but the Academy's actuaries and the Magi's calendars agree on the arithmetic. One person in a hundred thousand reaches the tenth rank of any art: enough to be the best in a province, to break a siege or end a plague. The three empires and the country between them hold perhaps ninety million souls, so there are some nine hundred such people alive, most of them on somebody's payroll. Above that the table thins out like air on the Cloudspine. Seventeenth rank is one in sixty million. By rights the continent should have one or two. It has twenty, because fifteen centuries of war were a forcing-house, and because peace has not yet found anything else for them to do.

The courts list them as ten spellcasters and ten martials. None is simply a villain; several are dangerous mainly because they are right. Kallisto Pyrphoros and Aulus Custos spent thirty years trying to kill each other across siege lines and now co-sign the wards of Deiperduem. Three powers hunt Vesperine Ilaro, and one of the hunters is quietly helping her. Rashnu-Vahram and Atar-Farnbag serve the same fire and have not spoken in eleven years. Aurelie Virellarion writes to the necromancer of Persemenid by every Mithril Reserve courier, and Artabazos Mihran would like to burn her workshop. Bagoas attends every one of Shirin Navaz's performances and takes no notes.

Stat blocks are built from class levels: proficiency follows level (+6), and Challenge follows the DMG's arithmetic of damage and defence, so a soft-bodied archmage rates below a fighter of the same fame.

The Ten Spellcasters

Spellcaster · Wizard (School of Evocation) · Hellenoria

Kallisto Pyrphoros Scholarch of the Arcane Academy

She burned three fleets for Hellarchon; now she runs its Academy like a ship, keeps its cellars shut, and holds the violet sky together with her own wards.

Class
Wizard 19 (Evocation)
Race
Human
Age
64
Home
Hellarchon, the Academy Grove
Allegiance
The Arcane Academy; the Assembly, while it pays the grant
Alignment
Neutral
Patron
Athena, by Academy statute
Challenge
CR 14

Story

Born on the Road between the Long Walls to a rower and a laundress, Kallisto came to the Academy on a shipowner's scholarship meant to buy a war-mage, and he got one. She burned an Invictian transport fleet off Ephelanum and an Acheaorian squadron in the Reach, and served thirty years as fire-mage of the common fleet. Scholarch for eleven years, she runs the Academy with inventories, drills and a flat refusal to let Inquisitor Vireon of the Truth-Flame into the cellars. The Assembly has cut her grant twice since the Treaty, because the Theoric Fund cannot pay for anything useful, so the Academy now hires out ward-work and sends expeditions to Eronis under her seal.

Appearance and manner

Small, square, cropped iron-grey hair, burn-scarred forearms she never covers, reading lenses on a chain. Smells of lamp-smoke and cloves. Speaks in orders, hates waste, and is bone-dry funny when she forgets to be busy.

At the table

She treats the party as contractors: clear brief, fixed fee, paid on time. She wants Vesperine Ilaro found before Delphara or Persevalis finds her, and Vireon kept out of her cellars. She offers library access, a letter that opens doors in every League city, and spells cast at cost. In a fight she stays at the back, sculpts fire around her own people, splits enemies with wall of force, and teleports out of anything she cannot finish in three rounds.

Signature

  • The Dusk Wards — at every new moon she renews the Academy's sky-wards from the observatory roofs. The Academy says they are for weather.
  • The Kiln Ring — cast from the bronze of the Academy's first brazier; fire resistance, and it warms when someone lies to her about money.

Ties

  • Aulus Custos — enemy across thirty years of siege lines; now her co-signatory on the Treaty Wards and her weekly correspondent on notation.
  • Lysandra Anthemis — her best student, lost to Delphara; rival in the Dreamers' Hunt.
  • Vesperine Ilaro — the quarry.
  • Krates the Dog — heckled her at the Reading in Thessalonika; she set his jar alight; he lived in the ashes for a week to make the point.
  • House Erebides — Asteria Erebide is her ablest evoker; Kallisto knows what the shed with no number holds and keeps the Academy out of it.

Spellcaster · Wizard (School of Divination) · Hellenoria

Lysandra Anthemis the Exegete

She writes down what the oracle actually says, decides what it means, and has begun leaving out the parts that are true.

Class
Wizard 17 (Divination)
Race
Tiefling (Voidfolk, citizen under the Accord)
Age
38
Home
Delphara, the Temenos
Allegiance
The oracle; the Amphictyony
Alignment
Neutral good
Patron
Apollo, who has never objected to her horns
Challenge
CR 9

Story

A pitch-boiler's daughter from the Deme of the Accord, Lysandra was Kallisto's most promising diviner until she walked up the Sacred Way at twenty-six and stayed. She now heads the five Exegetes who render the Pythia's words into verse a petitioner can carry home. The Pythia, Theano, speaks over the crack on a leaf of sleep-poppy; what she says is rarely verse and sometimes not Hellenorian. Lysandra has noticed that questions from Persemenid always go first, always come out favourable, and are worded by Hosioi who have new roofs. She cannot prove it, and the Amphictyony is the one Hellenorian body that still works, so she has said nothing in public. On consultation days she casts foresight on the Pythia, not on herself.

Appearance and manner

Tall, ash-grey skin, horns swept back and capped in plain bronze, ink on every finger. Gentle voice, long pauses, laughs at her own puns. Writes everything down twice.

At the table

She wants the oracle honest and wants evidence, not rumour: ledgers, a Hosios's confession, the Vashtiri's books. She offers what a diviner can: one true answer per favour, delivered in plain prose, which in Delphara is the rarest currency there is. She will never fight if she can foresee her way out of it.

Signature

  • The Plain Copy — for every verse she issues, she keeps a prose transcript of what Theano actually said, in Infernal, in a locked chest only a tiefling can read.
  • The Reach Chart — Delphara keeps the hour-by-hour wind chart of the Aeolus Reach; she corrects it each season, with help.

Ties

  • Kallisto Pyrphoros — former teacher; rival in the Dreamers' Hunt; still sends her the Academy's lecture lists.
  • Vesperine Ilaro — Philokles of the Dream Dormitory is with her, and Lysandra reads his letters before anyone else does.
  • Ixion Keraunios — supplies the corrections to the Reach chart, for a fee and a look at the next season's page.
  • Atar-Farnbag — the Magi send Delphara one question a year; she suspects his are the only honest ones.
  • House Vashtiri — the Acheaorian treasurers of the House of the Tripod (thread 6).

Spellcaster · Sorcerer (Storm Sorcery) · Hellenoria

Ixion Keraunios Wind-Seller of the Reach

He sells the wind by the knot from a black lighthouse whose neighbours count the wrecks, and he believes every breeze he sells keeps something asleep.

Class
Sorcerer 18 (Storm Sorcery)
Race
Human
Age
52
Home
The Wreckers' Beacon, Aeolus Reach; trades at Corinth
Allegiance
Himself, his cousins, and whoever is paying this season
Alignment
Chaotic neutral
Patron
Zeus, publicly; Astraeus, Titan of the Wind, in fact
Challenge
CR 11

Story

The Keraunioi have kept the Beacon on the Reach's southern cape for nine generations, and the cove below it has been strewn with timber for all of them. Ixion was born with the weather in him: as a boy he could make the lantern flame lean against the wind. In the war he flew ahead of the common fleet calling squalls onto Acheaorian oars, and in its last year he cast the one spell no sorcerer casts twice. Since the Treaty he has sold winds: a cord with three knots, one for a fair breeze, two for a gale, three for a storm. Tyrsan pilots coming up from Mavelon's south quays buy them by the dozen, and so does every Corinthian captain who wants to make the Haulway before the toll changes.

Appearance and manner

Long, salt-white hair tied with a knotted cord, a captain's coat he never earned, bare feet. Laughs too loud, bargains in fathoms, and never sits with the wind behind him.

At the table

He is the party's fastest way across any sea and its least reliable friend. He wants Lysandra's next chart page, Nerissa's custom, and nobody asking about the cove. He offers winds, flight, and warnings of the storms that are not on any chart, which he feels coming a day early. In a fight he stays airborne, twins his lightning, and leaves when it stops being profitable.

Signature

  • Wind-Knots — the first knot is 30 drachmas and gives a steady wind of the buyer's choosing for a day; the second, 300, gives a gale for an hour (as control weather centred on the ship). The third is not for sale. Nobody who has untied one kept the ship.
  • The Moving Light — he can carry the Beacon's flame in his hand; villagers have seen it move on stormy nights.

Ties

  • Nerissa Thalassine — his best customer and occasional partner; her corsairs sail on his knots.
  • Lysandra Anthemis — sells her the Reach-chart corrections; she pays in foreknowledge.
  • Kallisto Pyrphoros — sold the Academy two storms for its weather-ward experiments and has never been paid for the second.
  • Corinth — keeps a stall by the Lechaion harbour, beside the pilots' shrine.

Spellcaster · Wizard (School of Abjuration) · Deiperduem

Aulus Severinus Custos Warden of the Treaty Wards

An Invictian-born dwarf who spent a century keeping legions alive behind his wards, and now keeps the peace from being stolen, one lock at a time.

Class
Wizard 18 (Abjuration)
Race
Mountain dwarf
Age
212
Home
Deiperduem, rooms above the archive on Treaty Square; born in the iron country near Mavelon
Allegiance
The town council of Deiperduem, paid by all three empires
Alignment
Lawful good
Patron
Janus, who keeps doors
Challenge
CR 10

Story

His family took citizenship and Invictian names in the iron country three generations before he was born, and he went into the legions as a ward-mage at nineteen. For a hundred and sixty years he warded camps, bridges and siege lines; Kallisto Pyrphoros spent thirty of them trying to burn through his work and managed it twice. When the empires needed someone all three could trust to lock the Treaty Hall, the Hellenorian delegation nominated him, on Kallisto's word. He keeps the Hall unbreakable and the Treaty unstolen, lives above the archive, and is rarely seen leaving.

Appearance and manner

Broad, bald, beard in two plaits bound with lead seals, half plate polished to a dull grey. Deadpan, patient, pedantic about notation, and quietly kind to clerks.

At the table

He wants the peace kept by the paper, not by the compounds' "household staff", whose numbers rise every quarter. He hires people to test his wards and pays well for anyone who breaks one honestly. In a fight he locks things down: forcecage, wall of force, counterspell, and his ward thrown over whoever is about to die.

Signature

  • The Treaty Wards — a guards and wards lattice over the Hall and archive, renewed daily for five years and now effectively permanent; he feels every touch on it.
  • The Geas-Lock — the lead case in the Mithril Reserve vault opens only to him and Hildra Ironhand together.

Ties

  • Kallisto Pyrphoros — co-signatory of the wards; they argue weekly by letter and would die for each other without admitting it.
  • Decimus Corvus — warded his legion for twenty years; Decimus wants him back, and lately has been asking about the vault.
  • Rashnu-Vahram — the Acheaorian compound's "household staff" include men his wards read as dead. He has reported nothing.
  • The Ironhands of Deiperduem — the Reserve branch that holds the other half of the lock (thread 9).

Spellcaster · Druid (Circle of the Shepherd) · Imperium Invicta

Sylvia Nemorina Mother of the Grove

She has led the Torchlight at Nemibano for three centuries, watched seven wardens die at the grove, and loves the eighth.

Class
Druid 17 (Circle of the Shepherd)
Race
Wood elf
Age
c. 300
Home
Nemibano, the grove below the Steps
Allegiance
Diana's grove; the Verdant Sentinel Order, when it behaves
Alignment
Neutral good
Patron
Diana, Guardian of the Grove
Challenge
CR 11

Story

The grove's priestesses have always been women and the wardens have always been men, and the two offices were designed to need each other. Sylvia has led the Torchlight round the crater lake for longer than the Imperium has kept the town's records. She tends the wood the Verdant Sentinels guard, clears the Asking from the treeline before dawn, and sits with each new warden through his first winter. The current warden, Gnaeus Ferrus, has held the grove nineteen years; she has shared his hut for twelve of them, and dreads every Challenge Day.

Appearance and manner

Brown as oak bark, hair the colour of dead bracken, a grey hind that walks at her heel and is not quite there. Warm, earthy, plain-spoken, immovable.

At the table

She heals anyone who comes to the treeline in good faith and asks for a task in return: carry a petition, cull a beast, bring back a cutting from a forest the war burned. She wants the capital to stop trying to abolish the custom and wants this year's Challenge Day to pass quietly. In a fight she summons: wolves, dryads, a bear spirit over her friends, and a storm if the grove is touched.

Signature

  • The White Hind — her totem spirit, seen by pilgrims at dusk on the far shore; Nemibano's children are told it counts the wardens.
  • The Golden Bough — only a challenger who breaks a branch from the grove's one sacred oak may fight the warden. She decides, in practice, whether the branch breaks.

Ties

  • Gnaeus Ferrus — the Rex Nemorensis; her partner.
  • Tomyra of the Lion Grass — has been seen on the rim road asking about Challenge Day; Sylvia has invited her to the Torchlight to look at her properly.
  • Decimus Corvus — led the third attempt to abolish the custom, talked with Gnaeus for an hour, and reported the arrangement "militarily sound".
  • House Ocrea and the town on the Rim.

Spellcaster · Artificer (Alchemist) · Duneforged Citadel

Countess Aurelie Virellarion Mistress of the Crucible Spire

The youngest head House Virellarion has had in two centuries, she brews elixirs for archmages, patches gladiators for free, and is trying to open a vault her ancestors sealed for good reason.

Class
Artificer 18 (Alchemist)
Race
Human (Virellarion; "subtly altered", says the gossip)
Age
33
Home
Duneforged Citadel, the Crucible Spire
Allegiance
House Virellarion; Duke Roderick Caesar
Alignment
Chaotic good
Patron
Vulcan; Anchiale, the Flame Artisan, at the bench
Challenge
CR 9

Story

Aurelie inherited the Spire at twenty-two, when her mother's last experiment took the top three floors with it. She has rebuilt them, doubled the Gilded Crucible's catalogue and made the Virellarion levitation crystals reliable enough that the Cloudspine's moving bastions have not dropped a fortress since the Treaty. She treats the bonded fighters of the Ju Colliseum for nothing, which the other houses consider vulgar. Below the Spire is the Stillflame Vault, which no Virellarion has opened in three generations; she has been picking its locks for four years.

Appearance and manner

Thin, quick, burn-freckled hands, copper hair pinned with glass rods, goggles on her forehead in court. Talks fast, forgets titles, laughs at explosions.

At the table

She is the party's best supplier of potions and its most likely employer for strange errands: an ingredient from a rift, a page of Thalor's Codex, a Nethranan glass. She offers elixirs at cost, infused gear and an honest opinion. In a fight she buffs, heals and gasses, and keeps her friends standing.

Signature

  • Memorysteel — her breastplate reforms when broken, overnight, to the shape it "remembers"; she can make one plate a year.
  • The Nocturne Draught — her ancestor Lyssira's dream-walking potion. Aurelie has the recipe and has never dared drink it.

Ties

  • Marcia Ferox — friend and patient; the only person who refuses her elixirs on principle.
  • Rashnu-Vahram — a correspondent by every Mithril Reserve courier, about souls, vessels and Jevan's Heart-Smith's Gauntlet.
  • Artabazos Mihran — her crystals hold up the bastions that broke the Mihran at the pass; he has named the Spire a target.
  • Vesperine Ilaro — Lyssira's notes describe a "glass woman" who taught her the Draught in a dream.

Spellcaster · Wizard (School of Necromancy) · Acheaoria

Magus Rashnu-Vahram Keeper of the Rite of Return

A courteous old Magus who attends every Immortal's funeral, and knows exactly why there are so few of them.

Class
Wizard 20 (Necromancy)
Race
Human
Age
88
Home
Persemenid, rooms below the Temple of Breath on the Hill of Fires
Allegiance
The throne; the Magi, in name
Alignment
Lawful neutral
Patron
Vatagatal the Dutiful, in the Rite's words; Thasmudayan, in its grammar
Challenge
CR 15

Story

Rashnu-Vahram was a junior Magus copying inscriptions under the Temple of Breath when he found the Rite of Return carved on the walls of a city older than Persemenid, sixty years ago. The war was going badly; he gave the Rite to the throne, and the Immortals have not lost a man since. He keeps the oldest rites of the Hill of Fires, stands at every Immortal funeral (rare, because an Immortal must be destroyed twice), and is unfailingly polite to everyone, including the dead.

Appearance and manner

Tall and stooped, white beard to the belt, Magus's white with ash at the hem, a cold hand. Speaks softly, listens completely, apologises to corpses before he raises them.

At the table

He wants a way to release the Immortals without the empire learning what they are, and wants the Undying Legion left alone, because they are right. He offers ancient lore, speak with dead answers obtained by ritual, and a patron at court. He fights only when cornered, with thralls in front and finger of death for whoever threatens the Rite.

Signature

  • The Rite of Return — a seven-night ritual that rebinds a fallen soldier who swore the Immortal's oath. It needs the man's name on the roll and his oath-cord; it does not need his consent, which troubles him more each year.
  • The Breath Below — the draught that feeds the Temple of Breath's flame rises from the buried city; he can hear voices in it.

Ties

  • Atar-Farnbag — the First Flame holds that the dead defile fire; they have not spoken in eleven years.
  • Bagoas — the creed keeps his secret, and would silence him with it.
  • Aurelie Virellarion — his correspondent on souls and vessels.
  • Aulus Custos — knows what stands guard in the Acheaorian compound at Deiperduem, and has kept quiet.
  • The House of Zindar — whose army he keeps alive.

Spellcaster · Cleric (Light Domain) · Acheaoria

Mobad Atar-Farnbag First Flame of the Magi

Sixty years beside a fire that has never gone out have left him half-blind, wholly stubborn, and the one man in Acheaoria the throne cannot dismiss.

Class
Cleric 20 (Light Domain)
Race
Dragonborn (gold)
Age
74
Home
Atarabad, the Fire-Temple on the Fire Hill
Allegiance
The Magi and the fire, before the throne
Alignment
Lawful good
Patron
Hakiyah, the Just Scales; the flame is truth made visible
Challenge
CR 15

Story

The Magi admitted a dragonborn novice once, on the grounds that a boy who breathed fire could hardly defile it. Sixty years later he is First Flame: keeper of Atarabad's undying fire, from which every fire-temple's flame is relit, and master of the calendar by which the empire works. He can close the bazaar for a day by declaring it impure. He wants the foreign shrines out of the caravanserais and the Invictian silver weighed honestly, and sees no contradiction between the two.

Appearance and manner

Gold scales gone the colour of old brass, eyes milky from the fire, a white mouth-veil over his breath so he will not defile what he tends. Slow, formal, kind to children, merciless to liars.

At the table

He is a conservative and an honest one. He wants the truth spoken in his temple and will heal, restore or raise anyone who tells it. He offers sanctuary, a hearing at the Hill of Fires and, once in a life, a miracle. In a fight he wards his allies, burns the unrepentant and talks throughout.

Signature

  • The Undying Fire — while he stands within sight of a fire-temple's flame, he cannot be deceived by illusion, and a creature that lies to him there feels the heat.
  • The Calendar — no coronation, war or execution is lawful on a day the Magi have not declared fit, and the days are counted from his fire.

Ties

  • Rashnu-Vahram — a fellow Magus who raises the dead under a sacred flame. Atar-Farnbag has refused him the fire for eleven years.
  • Shirin Navaz — she mocks the Magi in song; he defends her licence before the Court of Vipers.
  • Bagoas — the creed would like the Magi's records; the Magi would like the creed's.
  • The Satrap of Atarabad — whose squadrons have grown past the permitted number, on days the Magi did not declare fit.

Spellcaster · Bard (College of Glamour) · Acheaoria

Shirin Navaz First Voice of the Melodic Circle

Story

Shirin was a palace foundling who sang for the household eunuchs at six and for the King of Kings at sixteen. The Melodic Circle made her First Voice at thirty-five. Its licence is ancient and narrow: what is sung is not what is said, and a Circle poet may put a satrap's failings into verse in his own hall. This season her verses have been unusually direct. The Court of Vipers has started asking for transcripts, which, being sung, do not exist. She sang "The Debt Rides With Us" at the Mihran feast and was applauded by everyone except the Mihran.

Appearance and manner

Black hair to the knee, a setar slung across her back, laughter you can hear across a garden. Generous, reckless, impossible to embarrass.

At the table

She wants the licence kept wide and wants to know who is reading her letters. She offers introductions at every satrapal court, a song that can make a minor noble famous or ridiculous, and a garden where nobody is overheard. In a fight she charms, commands and makes her friends very hard to hit.

Signature

  • The Licence — while performing, she may say anything about any official without legal consequence; the moment the music stops, the protection ends.
  • The Night Garden Song — sung at the Night Gardens, it makes listeners forget which walls belong to whom until dawn.

Ties

  • Bagoas — they grew up in the same household; he has attended every performance for twenty years, and she suspects he is the reason she is alive.
  • Vesperine Ilaro — sheltered her one Night Gardens, with the Enchanted Muse's dream-reader three gardens away.
  • Atar-Farnbag — defends her licence before the court and is the subject of her rudest verse.
  • Roxana Surena — Shirin's song about the Ravine made her famous; Roxana has asked her, twice, to stop.
  • House Golab — her hosts and patrons in Persevalis.

Story

She remembers the Palace of Eronis with its corridors standing still, a council session, and a mirror. Then a long dream with a feathered serpent in it, and then the Mourning Cypress Walk in daylight, nine years ago, with the war still on. Since then she has slept nine nights in Delphara's Dream Dormitory under a false name and walked into a sick woman's dream to cure her; Philokles, the priest who recognised her mirror-craft, now travels with her by choice. The Arcane Academy, Delphara's Dormitory and Persevalis's Enchanted Muse all want her (thread 10). She wants to find the rest of the Council of Eronis, because she does not believe they are dead.

Appearance and manner

Pale, slight, eyes that reflect the room a moment late, a grey cloak that shows other weather. Wry, kind, lonely, and unreliable about what year it is.

At the table

She will meet the party first in a dream. She wants a guide through a world she does not know and protection from people who want her as a specimen. She offers the one thing nobody else can: memory of the Old Empires, first-hand, and a road into anyone's sleep. In a fight she vanishes, confuses and leaves.

Part VII

Systems of the Empires

Every system now exists for all three empires, each built from that empire's own model.

How the systems matrix works

Every empire on Asetheria has to feed its capital, water its cities, pay its soldiers, keep its records, punish its criminals and decide who counts as a person. Each does it differently, and the differences are where adventures start. This section lays the thirteen systems side by side: one group per system, one card per empire.

Each group opens with a comparison table. Read across a row to see how the three empires answer the same question. Name is what the system is called locally; Run by names the office or order that holds it; How it works is the official machinery; Breaking point is what five years of peace have done to it; At the table is the one-line use. The cards below the table give the full page.

Cards marked Existing polish pages already in the codex and keep all their facts. The rest are new. Every card ends with a small mechanic (prices in gp, DCs, a d6 of complications or a favour economy) and a DM note naming the real-world model.

Two rules hold everywhere. First, "now" is five years after the Treaty of Deiperduem: the Great Concord in Invicta, the Treaty of Myrianth in Hellenoria, the Peace of the Signing in Acheaoria. Court scribes who say "a decade" or "fifty years" are doing their jobs. Second, the Mithril Reserve belongs to none of the three and appears in all of them. It has its own continental card under Banking.

Political Order

Five years after the Treaty of Deiperduem, each empire still runs on machinery built for war, and each is finding out what that machinery does with no enemy to point it at.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria

The Rule of the Dominus Militum Existing · Imperium Invicta

Category: Political · Run by: General Valerius Maximus, Dominus Militum, and the Council of Legates

Overview

The Imperium Invicta was once a republic. It shed representative rule in the crucible of perpetual war and never picked it up again. The Senate still meets in the great halls of Aeterna, built for a body that decided things; today it stamps the will of the army. Above the Senate stands the Imperator's chair, empty since the war ended and kept empty "awaiting the recovery" of Iovianus Sandarion, who withdrew into seclusion in the capital. The state is run from the room next door.

How it works
  • The Dominus Militum. "Master of the Soldiers": a supreme command created as a temporary measure against an existential threat, made permanent centuries ago and never handed back. The present holder is the aging but formidable General Valerius Maximus of the gens Valeria, a veteran of the war's final decades and one of the architects of the Great Concord. His authority is absolute because the legions he led still remember being led by him.
  • The Council of Legates. The commanders of the strongest legions, each a Legatus Augusti governing a province with troops loyal to him personally. It shows the public a united front and is a viper's nest behind it. Its members include Legatus Decimus Aurelianus Corvus, the Iron Legate.
  • The demobilised legions. Millions of discharged legionaries were promised land and pensions the bankrupt state cannot pay. In remote provinces former officers have used their loyal troops to seize land and set themselves up as warlords, defying the Dominus.
  • The patrician remnant. Descendants of the senators who ruled the Republic: immense wealth, social prestige and a grievance. They fund provincial governors, sow dissent among the populace and wait for the army's grip to slip.
Now

With no external enemy, the Council's rivalry has turned inward. Each Legate is building a fief for the day Valerius dies, and none says so, because the first to say it becomes everyone else's target. The court scribes speak of ten years of peace. The veterans count five, and count what they were promised.

At the table

Authority in the Imperium is a seal, and a seal works only where its owner's soldiers stand. When the party invokes a name: the Dominus Militum's seal opens anything and is reported to Aeterna within the week; a Legate's seal gives advantage on Charisma checks with officials in his province and disadvantage in a rival's; the Senate's earns courtesy and nothing else; a patrician introduction gets money, dinner and gossip, never troops. Forging a Legate's seal is DC 15 with a forgery kit. A clerk who handles the real thing spots a fake on DC 13 Investigation.

The League of the Hellenes Existing · Hellenoria

Category: Political · Run by: the synedrion, under Emperor Thalorion IV of House Thalorid; the Hegemon of Hellarchon commands the common fleet

Overview

Hellenoria is a league of maritime city-states that survived fifteen centuries of war because nobody could take all of it at once. The independence that saved it is now its chief instability. Each city governs itself, swears loyalty to the Imperial Family and answers the Emperor's summons. Emperor Thalorion IV has not been seen in public for ten years. His proclamations still arrive, read aloud by heralds, and men who travel between cities remark that his voice sounds different in each.

How it works
  • The League. On paper, an assembly of delegates from every city-state, the synedrion, deciding matters of common interest. In practice, a forum for endless debate in which each city guards its sovereignty. The war forced cooperation; peace has let the old divisions back in.
  • The ideal and the reality. The larger cities cling to democracy. The long war empowered merchants, shipowners and commanders, who now manage the process to their own ends and leave the common citizen with a vote and a grievance. Hellarchon is ruled by "the Assembly, in theory", and by the shipowning houses in fact.
  • The tyrants. In several smaller cities charismatic men, usually former commanders, have seized power promising order. They pay lip service to the League, pursue aggressive foreign policies to prop up their legitimacy, and build navies no assembly would fund.
  • The naval hegemony. Hellarchon has the largest fleet and has always held the hegemony. Its leading strategos, the Hegemon Kleandros Nikandrides of House Nikandridai, commands the common fleet. In war this was a necessary evil. In peace it is simply evil, as far as the smaller cities are concerned.
Now

Rival alliances have formed inside the League, and Corinth funds them as a matter of routine. Two of the twelve seats of the Amphictyony of Delphara are held by tyrants' cities, and the council cannot decide whether a tyrant's delegate is a delegate. Court scribes date the Treaty of Myrianth fifty years back. It was five.

At the table

Every harbour has a different constitution, so the person to persuade changes with the port.
