Roll d6 for an unfamiliar city: 1–2 democracy managed by shipowners (pay the speaker who moves the motion, 50 gp, more next time); 3 open democracy (group Persuasion DC 14 before the assembly; on a failure the party's proposal passes in someone else's name); 4 oligarchy of the Thousand (an introduction from a eupatrid house beats any bribe); 5 a tyrant (one man, one audience, no appeal); 6 a city in faction, with two governments using the same seal.

The King of Kings and the Satraps Existing · Acheaoria

Category: Political · Run by: Shahanshah Vishtaspa III of the House of Zindar; the satraps in the provinces

Overview

An empire of immense size and fabulous wealth, defined by rigid hierarchy and the absolute power of the King of Kings, and rotting beneath the gilding from centuries of corruption, court intrigue and the resentment of its conquered peoples. The Shahanshah, Vishtaspa III ("the Magnificent" in court style) of the House of Zindar, is semi-divine, resides in the palace-city of Persemenid, and is ceremonially central and increasingly ignored.

How it works
  • The satrapies. The King's authority is absolute; his reach is not. Each province is governed by a satrap appointed by the throne, a virtual monarch whose loyalty is a matter of convenience. The office of karanos, lord over several satrapies, exists on paper. The throne has appointed none in five years, for fear of what a karanos might do with them.
  • The Court of Vipers. Noble families vie for the King's favour and plot against rivals. The eunuchs who manage the royal household wield immense influence, and the succession is often bloody. Peace has given every faction more time and money for the game.
  • The restless satrapies. Peoples conquered centuries ago never accepted the rule. The war held them down with force and the promise of protection from the other powers. With the threat gone, nationalist movements are gaining ground, and some satraps fan the flames, hoping to wake up kings.
  • The Magi. The priestly caste guards the state faith and the fire-temples. Conservative, suspicious of foreign influence, a check on the throne, and at odds with the conquered peoples' gods.
Now

At new year the satrapies' delegations climb the stair at Persemenid in the order carved on the reliefs, and every gap is seen by everyone. The court scribes speak of a decade of renaissance. It has been five years since the Peace of the Signing, and the gaps grow.

At the table

Roll d6 for a satrap's real stance: 1 loyal and frightened (obeys the letter, asks the party to carry his excuses); 2 loyal by convenience (obeys whatever costs least this month); 3 withholding tribute (generous to travellers, needs witnesses that he is poor); 4 courting a court faction (will sell the party to Persemenid for credit); 5 fanning revolt next door (wants crates moved, no questions); 6 independent in all but name (the King's seal earns a polite welcome and a guard who never leaves). Reading his household is Insight DC 15; a Scribe of the Infinite Ledger's figures tell the truth for free.

Economy

Fifteen centuries of war built three economies for one purpose; peace removed the purpose and left the machinery running.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe War Economy at PeaceThe Sea EconomyThe Tribute Economy
Run byState armouries and road contractors, patrician landowners, the Golden Harvest CovenantMerchants, shipowners and banking houses of each cityThe throne and satraps, the arashshara, the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger
How it worksLatifundia grow grain, roads move it, the state buys armsImport bread; export craft, carriage and creditGrain, spice and metal flow up as tribute and out as luxury trade
Breaking pointDemand for grain and iron collapsed with the warThe fleet was destroyed; the pirates were notSubject peoples carry the weight and know it
At the tableVeteran bandits make every road a jobEvery ship is short of crewEvery bargain is a ritual
The War Economy at Peace Existing · Imperium Invicta

Category: Economic · Run by: state armouries and forges, patrician landowners, road contractors

Overview

The Imperium is a disciplined empire modelled on its legions, with an economy built for total war. For centuries its resources went to conquest and defence. In the sudden stillness of peace the gears are grinding to a halt, showing both the strength of the machine and where it cracks.

How it works
  • Agriculture. The heartland is a patchwork of latifundia, vast estates worked by people tied to the land through serfdom and indenture. The war consolidated land into a few powerful families. The most notorious holdings are the red-earth estates inland of Ephelanum, pledged to the Imperium under the Great Concord and now worked under the Invictian Dux, who holds the harbour and garrison in condominium while the Hellenorian Archon and the priesthood hold the city. The estates grew grain for the legions. Some owners are now trying olives and vines, but the means to move and sell those goods at scale barely exist. Grain demand has collapsed, prices have crashed in surplus regions, and the countryside is restless.
  • Trade. The paved roads, once arteries of military movement, are cautiously carrying commerce. Banditry is rampant, much of it by demobilised soldiers with no trade but violence. Internal tariffs written to fund the war still strangle trade between provinces. Most ports are shadows of themselves, their fleets broken by centuries of naval war with Hellenoria. The exception is Mavelon, the caldera port whose arsenal never stopped building, where merchants from the Farshore Realms (Qart-Hadeth, Tyrsa, Khemaret, Maurash and stranger coasts) now tie up at the south harbour. Every foreign cargo and every great contract must then be registered and sealed against the master weights at Romulo, which has become the Imperium's merchant capital. A merchant class is rising, and shipbuilding pays.
  • Industry. The southern mountains give iron, lead, tin and magical ores. Mining, armouries and forges were all state-run, and the fall in military demand has thrown whole regions out of work. The Via Ferraria still carries interior iron to Mavelon's arsenal, which has turned from warships to merchant hulls faster than the mines have turned to anything.
  • Infrastructure. The road network is the Imperium's greatest asset and, after fifteen centuries of use, much of it is failing: bridges down, waystations in ruin. The state now offers repair contracts to private companies, a new and chaotic thing in a rigidly managed economy.
  • Wealth and labour. Wealth sits with the patricians and the high command. Peace has widened the gulf. Millions of veterans and war-workers have no purpose and no income.
Now

The coin is being debased to cover the gap, and the Golden Harvest Covenant has said publicly that it is being paid in bad silver.

At the table

Prices this season: wheat at a latifundium gate, 1 cp for 3 lb (half the pre-war price); in Aeterna, 1 cp a pound; a skin of Falecosa wine, 2 gp; a veteran escort, 3 sp a day and food; a bridge-repair contract, 400–1,200 gp plus whatever lives under the bridge. Road trouble, d6: 1 a veterans' toll-post flying an old unit standard, 5 sp a head; 2 bridge down, a day's detour or Athletics DC 12 to ford; 3 a provincial tariff station, 2% of cargo value, again; 4 a contractor's crew, paid, idle and touchy; 5 a legionary patrol wanting the manifest and a cut; 6 an abandoned waystation that is not abandoned.

The Sea Economy Existing · Hellenoria

Category: Economic · Run by: the merchants, shipowners and banking houses of each city-state

Overview

A confederation of fiercely independent city-states, held together by a common culture and the sea, came through the long war on naval skill and a decentralised, adaptable economy. The sea is the lifeblood. Five years of peace have been a desperate scramble to rebuild shattered fleets and take back the waves.

How it works
  • Agriculture. Rugged, mountainous land, poor for grain. The cities grow olives, grapes and citrus and import the rest. In war that dependence was the critical weakness: the Imperium's land power and Acheaoria's resources could choke the supply lines. Terracing and irrigation projects are under way, and the League still eats imported bread.
  • Trade. The soul of Hellenoria. Its merchants are famous for cunning and for going where others will not. The war wrecked the merchant fleet and the last five years have been frantic shipbuilding, old partners re-contacted and new markets probed. Finance is sophisticated: young banking houses, loans and maritime insurance. Piracy, always a menace, has been emboldened by the post-war chaos.
  • Industry. Few natural resources. Skilled craft instead: pottery from Araavyna, metalwork, and above all ships, with small hulls from Carianea and triremes from Hellarchon's yards. The secret of Hellenic fire is a closely guarded state secret and a serious deterrent.
  • Infrastructure. Maritime. The cities are built around defended harbours and the roads are sea lanes: the Long Lane, the Southern Run, the Aeolus Reach, and Corinth's Haulway across the isthmus. The war destroyed many port facilities; lighthouses are being relit and harbour defences thickened, a sign that the peace is read as a breathing space.
  • Wealth and labour. Wealth is fluid, held by merchants, shipowners and the political elite. Free citizens are many, but the metics, resident foreigners, are the backbone of the artisan and labouring classes. The war killed sailors and craftsmen; wages for both have risen, and so has reliance on foreign labour.
Now

Every yard has orders it cannot crew. The ships go down the slip faster than the men to row them can be found.

At the table

Hiring: a skilled rower, 4 sp a day (twice the pre-war rate); a helmsman, 2 gp a day. Freight on the Long Lane, 1 gp per ton per day; the Haulway at Corinth, 10 gp per hull and 1 sp per ton. A share in a voyage costs what the party likes; on the ship's return roll d6: 1 lost with all hands, share gone; 2 pirated, half recovered; 3 broke even; 4–5 +30%; 6 +80%, and someone wants to know which cargo did that.

The Tribute Economy Existing · Acheaoria

Category: Economic · Run by: the throne and the satraps, the arashshara, the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger

Overview

Acheaoria is vast and ancient, its history reaching back millennia before the long war, and it is a land of immense wealth and staggering inequality. The economy rests on central control, a sophisticated bureaucracy, and the exploitation of natural resources and conquered peoples.

How it works
  • Agriculture. Fertile river valleys along the Zheret-al-Nur produce a massive surplus of grain, fruit and spice, watered by canals, by the qanats and stored in state granaries. The King of Kings owns all land in theory; the satraps administer it. In war the surplus fed vast armies. In peace it is traded for luxuries across the continent.
  • Trade. Acheaoria holds the overland routes east. Caravans of silk, spice and precious metal draw raiders, so the empire keeps fortified caravanserais and a corps of guards on the roads. The bureaucracy taxes and tolls the trade heavily, enriching the state and breeding resentment among merchants. The southern ports are reviving, warily, as Hellenorian merchants return.
  • Industry. Gold, silver and gems, mined extensively to fund the court. Artisans excel at metalwork, carpets and fine textiles, the great exports; the carpets of Tabrishiir are the one Acheaorian thing the Imperium admits admiring. Heavy industry, iron and bronze for the armies, ran on the labour of subject peoples, and the end of the war has not ended their exploitation. The arashshara, women overseers of production and trade, run most of the workshops worth running.
  • Infrastructure. The Royal Road is an engineering marvel that moves armies, couriers and caravans across the empire. Keeping it up in the far and rebellious satrapies is a constant struggle. Yakhchals, domed ice-houses, store perishables through the summer and steady prices.
  • Wealth and labour. Grotesquely uneven. The royal family and high nobility live in unimaginable luxury; most people, including many slaves and subject peoples, live in poverty. The bureaucracy is bloated and officials at every level skim.
Now

Demobilised soldiers, many from conquered lands, have come home to hardship and discrimination. The resentment of the oppressed is a tinderbox looking for a spark.

At the table

Bargaining in Atarabad is a ritual, and treating it as a transaction marks a foreigner. Run it as a skill challenge: three successes before three failures, using Persuasion, Insight or Deception. Accepting the tea when it is offered counts as one success, once. Each success takes 10% off, to a maximum of 30%. Three failures and the price rises 10% and the merchant's Wheelwalker cousins hear about it. Prices: a Tabrishiir carpet, 40–400 gp; a pound of saffron, 15 gp; a sealed jar of yakhchal ice in high summer, 5 sp.

Grain and Provisioning

Every capital on the continent is a few weeks from hunger, and every regime knows that the first thing a hungry city does is reconsider who rules it.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe AnnonaThe Grain Law of the SitophylakesThe King's Storehouses
Run byThe Prefect of the Annona; the Golden Harvest Covenant suppliesGrain-wardens chosen by lot in each city; the Golden Scythe Accord buys abroadStorehouse-keepers of the throne; the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger audit
How it worksProvincial levy, state shipping, the horrea at Fucostia, a monthly ration by tesseraConvoy law drives grain ships home; wardens fix the price of breadTribute in kind fills the storehouses; sealed tablets draw rations for workers, soldiers and couriers
Breaking pointLegates keep the levy to feed their own troopsTyrants and the hegemon both treat the grain fleet as a weaponSatraps have stopped forwarding the grain and kept the storehouses
At the tableStopping a convoy is a political argumentA grain cargo is lawful only on its way homeA sealed tablet feeds the party across an empire, if it is real
The Annona Existing · Imperium Invicta

Category: Economic · Run by: the Prefect of the Annona, answering to the Dominus Militum; supplied by the Golden Harvest Covenant

Overview

The Annona is the Imperium's oldest promise: that no citizen of the capital will starve while the state stands. Grain is levied from the provinces, shipped under state contract, stored in the great horrea and handed out by ticket to every registered citizen of Aeterna. It began as a hedge against bread riots in the early wars and hardened into an entitlement no Dominus Militum has dared touch. Feeding the capital is not charity in the Imperium. It is the price of its quiet.

How it works
  • The levy. Each province owes a fixed measure, assessed on cultivated land rather than on the harvest, so a bad year falls on the farmer and not on the treasury. Ceres's farmers of the Golden Harvest Covenant grow most of it.
  • The river. All of it passes through Fucostia at the mouth of the Tiberius, where sea-going hulls hand over to river barges and the horrea stand wall to wall. A suspect cargo goes upriver only with an Aurum Pact certificate.
  • The ticket. Registered citizens hold a tessera, an inscribed token claimed monthly at a distribution point. Tesserae are heritable, which means a great many are held by people who have never lived in the capital.
  • The prefect. One officer holds the contracts, the granaries and the shipping. It is the least glamorous and most quietly powerful appointment in the Imperium.
Now

The war ended and the arithmetic did not improve. Levies arrive short, because the Legates have learned that grain retained is grain that feeds their own troops. The demobilised legions, promised land they have not received, drift to the capital, where a tessera is easier to obtain than a farm. A swelling population is fed from a shrinking levy by a treasury already debasing its coin, and the Covenant is paid in that coin and says so. The prefect has twice petitioned to cut the ration. Both petitions were refused, and both refusals were correct: the first thing a hungry capital does is remember that the Senate used to matter. At Fucostia the yearly Weighing has fallen three years running.

At the table

Whoever controls the Annona controls whether Aeterna is calm. A Legate who stops a grain convoy is not committing robbery; he is making an argument. The ration is five measures of wheat a month, about 70 lb: 6 sp in the market, priceless in a riot. A genuine tessera on the street costs 60 gp and comes with a dead man's name; a forged one costs 15 gp and fails at the distribution point on a clerk's Investigation DC 14. Distribution day, d6: 1 a third short, and the queue knows; 2 a Legate's agent buying tesserae for cash; 3 the Vigiles close a distribution point; 4 a barge sunk on the Tiberius bar; 5 Covenant officers refuse debased coin at the horrea door; 6 a rumour of a cut, and the Senate steps fill.

The Grain Law of the Sitophylakes New · Hellenoria

Category: Economic · Run by: the sitophylakes (grain-wardens) of each city; foreign cargoes contracted by the Golden Scythe Accord

Overview

Hellarchon grows almost nothing, and no League city grows enough. Hellenoria imports its bread and always has. The Imperium feeds its capital by levy; the League feeds its cities by law: a body of rules centuries old that bends every grain ship, every grain loan and every grain dealer toward the home harbour, and a board of grain-wardens in every city who make sure a loaf costs what the assembly says it costs.

How it works
  • The convoy law. A citizen's ship carrying grain must land at least two-thirds of it at the home harbour. No citizen or metic may lend money on a voyage that does not bring grain back. In the grain season the ships sail together under escort through the Aeolus Reach.
  • The sitophylakes. Grain-wardens chosen by lot, from five in a small city to thirty-five in Hellarchon. They register every cargo, fix the margin between grain, flour and bread, and weigh loaves in the market.
  • The dealers' cap. No dealer may buy more than fifty baskets at once. Hoarding is a capital offence, and wardens have been executed for conniving at it.
  • The Accord. Above the cities sits the Golden Scythe Accord, Demeter's farmers, which contracts the foreign cargoes and in a bad year decides which city goes short. It has no constitutional standing whatever.
Now

The hegemon's escorts now guard Hellarchon's convoys first and the League's second. Tyrants seize grain ships in their waters and call it enforcing their own convoy law. The Accord has begun demanding payment in advance from cities it does not trust. Thebesieas, the one League city that feeds itself from the Argotiko plain, has discovered it has a foreign policy. Atticenea still exports philosophers because it cannot feed them.

At the table

Grain is lawful cargo only on its way home. Running grain for a League city pays 1 gp per ton per day of voyage, plus a 10% bonus from the wardens when bread is dear. Carrying it anywhere else is smuggling: fine 1,000 gp and the ship. On the Reach, d6: 1 a tyrant's guard-ship "inspects"; 2 the escort peels off for a Hellarchene convoy; 3 pirates who know the sailing date; 4 a wind-seller offers a fair wind for a share of the cargo (Ixion Keraunios deals at Corinth); 5 the wardens find short weight (Persuasion DC 15 or a 100 gp fine); 6 a rival city's agent offers double to divert.

The King's Storehouses New · Acheaoria

Category: Economic · Run by: the storehouse-keepers of the throne; ration-tablets sealed by satrapal officials; audited by the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger

Overview

Acheaoria has no hungry capital; it has a hungry hierarchy. Grain, wine, beer and oil come in as tribute in kind and go into the royal storehouses, a chain of them along the Royal Road and around every satrapal seat. Out of them the empire pays its workmen, soldiers, couriers and court, not in coin but in rations, each issue written on a sealed clay tablet that records who, how much, by whose order and when.

How it works
  • The portion. Everyone on royal work draws a monthly portion of barley, wine and oil graded by skill: least for a labourer, more for a craftsman, most for an overseer. Women and men of equal skill draw equal portions, an arashshara draws more than most of the men she supervises, and a new mother draws a double portion for a month.
  • The tablet. No storehouse issues anything without a sealed tablet, a clay tag pressed with the seal of the official who authorised it. A traveller on royal business carries a sealed authorisation and draws his day's ration at each station on the Royal Road.
  • The audit. Every tablet is filed. The Scribes of the Infinite Ledger reconcile issues against stock, and their tally is the only figure the throne half-believes.
  • The ice. Yakhchals beside the larger storehouses keep fruit and meat through the summer, so the storehouses also set the market price of both.
Now

The storehouses belong to the throne and stand in the satrapies. Satraps who have stopped forwarding tribute have not stopped filling them; they have stopped sending the tablets. Persevalis, the satrapy that feeds the court, still sends. Shir'abad D'ar holds grain nobody will forward. The Benevolent Hands quietly feed the villages the storehouses no longer reach, and forged tablets are a growing trade.

At the table

A sealed travel authorisation draws a day's food and fodder at every Royal Road station, worth about 5 sp a head a day and far more as proof of royal business. Forging one needs a forgery kit, a seal to copy and DC 15; a keeper spots it on Investigation DC 14, or DC 18 if the party paid the seal-cutter's best price (25 gp). Storehouse, d6: 1 full and honest; 2 full, the keeper selling to the satrap's men at night; 3 empty, filed as full; 4 guarded by satrapal troops who do not recognise the King's seal this week; 5 a Benevolent Hands kitchen at the gate; 6 a Scribe of the Infinite Ledger mid-audit, glad of witnesses.

Water

Water is the one thing a city cannot import by the shipload, and each empire has built a board, an office or a hereditary trade to keep it running.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Cura AquarumThe Fountain-HousesThe Qanat Network
Run byThe curator aquarum and his water gang; the Vigiles inspect inside the wallsAn elected Overseer of Fountains in each city; the Amphictyony's oath guards the springsThe families who dug the channels; the muqanni; the Bountiful Harvesters hold the shares
How it worksThe Aqua Aeterna carries Klynin spring water sixty miles; private grants flow through stamped nozzlesSprings, tunnel-aqueducts and cisterns feed public fountains where water is freeUnderground channels from mother wells; water divided by the timed bowl at the water-court
Breaking pointUpkeep came out of the war budget, which no longer existsCisterns cracked in the war; tyrants own springsSatraps fund maintenance from tribute they no longer forward
At the tableEvery illegal pipe has a name stamped on itFouling a fountain is war on the godsA share of water is worth more than the land it waters
The Cura Aquarum New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Infrastructure · Run by: the curator aquarum, appointed by the Dominus Militum; the water gang; the Vigiles inside the walls

Overview

The Aqua Aeterna carries spring water sixty miles from the Klynin foothills to the fountains of Aeterna, most of it underground and the last four miles on a double tier of arches. Over sixty miles the channel drops a little under one part in four thousand, held across three river valleys by surveyors nobody recorded. The capital does not need it to survive (it has cisterns, wells and the river) but it needs it to be the capital: the baths, the fountains, the flushing of the drains. The board that runs it is the Cura Aquarum.

How it works
  • The tanks. The channel ends in distribution tanks that split the flow three ways: public fountains first, which may never run dry by law; then baths and public buildings; then private grants.
  • The grant. A private house gets water by personal grant, which dies with the grantee. It flows through a bronze nozzle of fixed bore stamped by the board, then into lead pipes stamped with the owner's name.
  • The water gang. Some seven hundred state slaves and freedmen: overseers, tank-keepers, inspectors, plasterers and pavers who walk the line, chip lime from the channel and patch.
  • The Vigiles. Inside the walls they inspect cisterns and outlets and can close a bath-house drawing more than its share.
Now

The maintenance office was funded from the war budget. Three spans on the upper course are shored with timber meant to last a season that has lasted four years; the Emberforge Collective has clamped them and been paid late. The water arrives brown after rain, and the capital's physicians have begun, cautiously, to write about that and about the lead. Water-thieves have multiplied: estates tapping the rural channel, householders piercing city pipes, gang-men bribed to fit a wider nozzle than the stamp admits. The gang has not been paid in full since the Treaty, which makes it cheap to bribe.

At the table

Finding an illegal tap is Investigation DC 13 in the city, DC 16 on the rural line. The name on a stolen pipe is evidence, and it is usually somebody's freedman. Fine: 100 gp per illegal outlet and the grant revoked. A bribe to widen a nozzle, 20 gp; a lawful new grant, three months and about 250 gp in fees. On the line, d6: 1 a span groaning (Athletics DC 13 to shore it before it goes); 2 estate overseers guarding a tap, with dogs; 3 an unpaid gang crew sitting down; 4 something nesting in the dark channel; 5 a Legate's surveyors measuring the line, for reasons; 6 a lime blockage, and the city's fountains dry by dusk.

The Fountain-Houses New · Hellenoria

Category: Infrastructure · Run by: the elected Overseer of Fountains in each city; the springs protected by the Amphictyony's oath

Overview

A Hellenorian city is built where there is a spring and a harbour, and the spring is the scarcer. Water reaches the city by clay pipe or by a tunnel cut through the hill and arrives at the fountain-house: a colonnaded hall in the agora where bronze lion-heads pour into basins, the water is free, and every household sends its women and slaves each morning with jars. Under every city lie the cisterns, plastered pits that catch winter rain against summer and siege.

How it works
  • The Overseer of Fountains. One of the few offices elected rather than allotted: the assembly will trust a lottery with justice but not with water. He keeps the pipes and fines anyone who washes, waters animals or draws for private use at a public spout.
  • The tunnel-aqueducts. Island cities cut water tunnels through the ridge from both ends at once, two crews steering by survey to meet in the middle. The great ones run over half a mile and are spoken of like temples; the engineers' names are carved at the meeting point.
  • The cisterns. Every house of standing has one and the city keeps great ones under the acropolis. A full city cistern is the difference between a siege of weeks and a siege of a season.
  • The oath. Every delegate to the Amphictyony of Delphara swears never to cut a member city's running water, in war or peace, and to march on any power that does. Invoked four times in fifteen centuries; each time the offender came to terms within a season.
Now

Many cisterns cracked in the war and nobody has paid to reline them, so a city that leans on its fountain-house in summer is one blocked tunnel from surrender. Two tyrants hold their cities' springs and ration the fountains as patronage. Ephelanum stands outside the Amphictyony and its oath, and knows it. At Loutrokleion the springs come up hot and are a different trade altogether.

At the table

The fountain-house is the city's morning news. An hour there with a jar gives advantage on checks to gather rumours, or Investigation DC 10 for one true rumour and DC 15 for one the Overseer wants kept quiet. Fouling a public fountain is sacrilege and an act of war under the oath: death, no jury needed. Drawing illegally costs 10 gp, a private pipe off the main 50 gp. A besieged or tyrant-held city's water, d6: 1 cisterns full and sweet; 2 half full and green; 3 cracked, a week left; 4 the tyrant's guard holds the spring and sells water; 5 the tunnel has a forgotten side-gallery wide enough for a party; 6 something has lived in the tunnel since the war.

The Qanat Network Existing · Acheaoria

Category: Infrastructure · Run by: the families who dug the channels; the hereditary muqanni; shares held by the Bountiful Harvesters

Overview

Acheaoria is mostly desert and has been prosperous for two thousand years, and the reconciliation of those two facts is the qanat. A mother well is sunk at the foot of the highlands until it strikes the water table; from it a tunnel is driven, falling more gently than the land above, until it surfaces as a stream in country where no stream should exist. A line of spoil rings marks the shafts sunk every thirty paces for air and hauling, so that from above an Acheaorian plain reads as a dotted line drawn from the mountains to a town. Where the shafts stop, so does the empire's writ: the frontier is called the Qanat Line.

How it works
  • Why it works. Water in a qanat never sees the sun, so almost none is lost to heat. It flows by gravity alone, with no lifting and no fuel. It cannot be over-drawn: the tunnel takes only what the aquifer offers at that level, so the network fails gradually and visibly rather than suddenly. Nothing built above ground in a desert survives a siege; a qanat is invisible, unburnable, and its shafts are too narrow for a man in armour.
  • Ownership. A qanat belongs to the family that dug it. Shares in its water are inherited, sold and litigated over exactly as land is.
  • The water-court. Where the channel surfaces, a cool vaulted chamber divides the flow into shares, each measured by a timed bowl and owned by deed. The Bountiful Harvesters hold most of the shares and keep the rota, which makes them a power in every city.
  • The muqanni. The diggers are a hereditary trade, well paid and short-lived. The work is done lying down in the dark, and the tunnels collapse.
  • The towns below. Many settlements are cut into the rock beside their channels rather than built over them. An Underground Town such as Zirzamin-Dara or Derakhtak-Bon is a town that followed its water down.
Now

The satrapies pay for maintenance out of tribute they are increasingly reluctant to forward to the throne, and a qanat neglected for a decade is a qanat that must be dug again. Two towns on the northern route have already been abandoned. The Magi call it a judgement. The muqanni call it a shortage of muqanni.

At the table

Water sells by the bowl. One bowl-time in a town's rota (about a third of an hour's flow every twelve days) costs 30–80 gp and waters one field; at Qa'zshahrv'in, the last certain water for four days in any direction, 200 gp. A master muqanni hires at 1 gp a day, paid in advance. In the tunnel, d6: 1 collapse (DC 13 Dex save or 2d6 bludgeoning and trapped; Athletics DC 14 to dig out); 2 bad air (DC 12 Con save each hour or one level of exhaustion); 3 a sudden surge (DC 12 Str save or swept 30 feet); 4 a side-gallery the family never mapped; 5 a satrap's men have dammed the channel upstream to put a rival's fields last; 6 someone above has pulled out the shaft's ladder-pegs.

The Public Purse

Each empire keeps one purse it cannot spend freely, and what a state cannot spend says more about it than what it can.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Aerarium MilitareThe Theoric FundThe King's Table
Run byPrefects of the military treasury; the Watchers of the Eternal Rest keep the veterans' registersEach city's theoric board; capital law guards itThe royal treasurers at Persemenid and the household of the hazarapat
How it worksInheritance and auction taxes fund land and pensions for discharged legionariesEvery surplus pays citizens to attend the festivals before anything else can claim itTribute comes in as bullion and gifts and goes out as gifts, feasts and places at the Table
Breaking pointIt owes more than it has ever held; Legates now pay their own veteransIt cannot lawfully be spent on the fleet the League needsThe court spends against tribute that no longer arrives
At the tableA veteran's diploma is a debt the party can buyA citizen paid to watch a play will not vote to sailA royal gift cannot be refused, sold or forgotten
The Aerarium Militare New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Economic · Run by: three prefects of the military treasury, appointed by the Dominus Militum; registers kept by the Watchers of the Eternal Rest

Overview

A legionary signs for twenty years and is promised, at discharge, a plot of land or a lump sum in cash. The military treasury exists to keep that promise. A Dominus Militum founded it from his own fortune centuries ago, and two taxes nobody likes have fed it since: a twentieth of every inheritance above a modest sum and a hundredth of every auction sale. While the war ran, discharges came slowly and the money kept pace. The Great Concord discharged millions at once.

How it works
  • The diploma. On discharge each man receives two hinged bronze tablets, witnessed by seven, recording his name, unit, service and entitlement. The Watchers of the Eternal Rest, Senectus's circle, hold the master registers of who was promised what.
  • The reward. Land in a veterans' colony, or cash equal to about thirteen years' pay. Land comes from state holdings or confiscations; cash from the two taxes.
  • The prefects. Three former praetors keep the treasury apart from the general one, so that its money cannot be spent on anything else. In theory.
  • The games. The aediles fund the capital's games; the Legates now outbid them. A Legate who pays for a week of games in his province's name is advertising whose purse a veteran should look to.
Now

The treasury owes more than it has ever held. Three times since the Treaty the general treasury has proposed a "reconciliation of the rolls" that would quietly cut the total; three times the Watchers refused and published the request, and the Crimson Warlords now guard their archive unasked. Meanwhile the Legates settle veterans on land seized in their own provinces and pay pensions from revenue the treasury never sees, so every settled veteran becomes a Legate's client. The Triumphant Vanguard of Glory has refused three Legates a triumph, correctly, since the Great Concord was no victory. The Legates bought games instead. The officers retire to Napplesia; the men retire to the road.

At the table

Diplomas trade. Speculators in Aeterna buy veterans' claims at a fifth of face value: a legionary's claim (face 600 gp) for 120 gp, a centurion's (face 3,000 gp) for 600 gp. Forging one needs seven witness seals (forgery kit DC 16; a Watchers' clerk spots it on DC 14). A veteran met on the road, d6: 1 paid, settled, bored and dangerous to his neighbours; 2 holding a diploma and a grudge, will sell it for 100 gp and a meal; 3 settled on a Legate's confiscated land and owes him everything; 4 riding with a warlord and calls it collecting; 5 in the capital with a tessera and nothing else; 6 a Watchers' informant, counting the others.

The Theoric Fund Existing · Hellenoria

Category: Economic · Run by: each city's elected theoric board; protected by capital law in most League cities

Overview

Every surplus in a Hellenorian city-state's treasury flows first into the Theoric Fund, which pays each citizen the price of a seat at the festivals and the day's wages lost attending them. It is the most popular institution in Hellenoria and, in the judgement of every admiral who has ever tried to raise a fleet, the most ruinous. The principle is that a citizen who cannot afford to attend the rites is a citizen only in name. The consequence is that the money is spent before anything else can claim it.

How it works
  • The payment. Two obols per festival day to every citizen on his deme's roll, counted out by the theoric board at the theatre gate as the citizens file in.
  • The law. In most League cities it is a capital offence to propose moving theoric money to military use. The prohibition was written during the war, when the assemblies feared their generals more than they feared the enemy, and it has outlived the fear that produced it.
  • The ways round. All slow. A city may vote a special levy, borrow against harbour dues, or accept a loan from the Mithril Reserve at rates that assume, correctly, that it will struggle to repay.
  • The board. Because the fund is the surplus, the theoric commissioners end up holding most of a city's purse strings. In Hellarchon they also oversee the dockyards, which they visit rarely.
Now

The naval hegemon has spent five years arguing that the fund should be opened to pay for the common fleet; the Hegemon Kleandros Nikandrides makes the speech every spring. The smaller city-states have spent five years noticing that the common fleet is berthed in the hegemon's harbour and crewed by its citizens. So the fund stays shut, the festivals are magnificent, the ships rot at their moorings, and the tyrants, who are not troubled by assemblies, build navies of their own.

At the table

The fund is why adventurers get hired: anything a city needs that is not a festival must be paid for privately, and private money hires mercenaries. A citizen who moves to open the fund is indicted for an unlawful proposal and must win Persuasion DC 18 before a jury of 501, or pay 1,000 gp and lose the right to speak in the assembly (in Hellarchon, the penalty is death). Ways round, d6: 1 a special levy (two weeks of debate, the rich furious); 2 a loan against harbour dues from Corinth's bankers; 3 a Mithril Reserve loan at 25%; 4 shame a liturgist into fitting out a ship; 5 call the voyage a sacred embassy, so the board pays for "festival transport"; 6 a tyrant offers to pay, and wants a harbour.

The King's Table New · Acheaoria

Category: Economic · Run by: the royal treasurers at Persemenid; the household of the hazarapat; audited, when permitted, by the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger

Overview

The throne does not pay; it gives. Tribute reaches Persemenid as bullion, cloth, horses and gifts, and leaves as gifts, feasts and places at the King's Table. The treasury under the platform keeps gold and silver melted into great earthenware jars; when the King needs money, a jar is broken and the ingot cut. Above it the Table feeds the court every day: thousands of mouths, a thousand animals, and a seating plan that is the empire's real constitution.

How it works
  • The Table. The King dines behind a screen, seeing and unseen. His Table feeds the household, the first regiment of the Ten Thousand and every honoured guest, and what is left goes out as pay. A dish sent from the King's own platter to a man's lodging is a public promotion.
  • The gifts. The King rewards with robes of honour, gold bracelets and torques, a horse with a golden bridle, a sword of the royal pattern. None may be sold; wearing them is the point. A royal gift is a debt paid in loyalty.
  • The Bringing. At new year every satrapy and great house carries gifts up the stair. The King gives back more than he receives, and the surplus is the measure of his majesty.
  • The treasuries abroad. The throne keeps treasuries at the great sanctuaries, richest of all the one at Delphara on the Sacred Way, where a past King of Kings dedicated a golden tripod.
Now

The court spends against expected collections rather than collections. The Vaults of Equilibrium lend against the shortfall, so the halls stay gilded and the arithmetic worsens. There are fewer jars in the cellar each year, and the King still gives back more than he receives, because giving less would be read by every satrap in the hall. A satrap who brings no gift at new year has not merely withheld money; he has refused the King's generosity, which is one step short of rebellion.

At the table

Visiting a satrap's hall without a gift imposes disadvantage on Charisma checks there; a suitable gift costs about a tenth of the favour sought. Royal gifts, d6: 1 a robe of honour (wear it at court or give offence); 2 a gold bracelet worth 150 gp (selling it is treason, though a Gilded Vault factor pays 60 gp and asks nothing); 3 a horse with an engraved golden bridle (300 gp, and recognisable anywhere); 4 a dish from the King's platter (advantage on Persuasion with court officials for a month, and three new enemies); 5 a seat at the Table on a feast day (an audience becomes possible: see the Ladder of Access); 6 a sword of the royal pattern (the bearer may be summoned to the King's service at any time, and will be).

Office and Advancement

Every empire has a ladder; the useful question is never how a man climbs it but whether the top rung still holds any weight.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Cursus HonorumThe Lot, the Liturgy and the SherdThe Ladder of Access
Run byThe Senate's registers; the real ladder runs through the legionsEach democracy's assembly, council and allotment machinesThe hazarapat, keeper of the King's door; the Court of Vipers
How it worksFixed civil offices with minimum ages and intervalsOffices filled by lot; the rich pay for ships and choruses; the over-mighty are exiled by voteRank is how close one may stand to the King, recorded on the Benefactors' roll
Breaking pointEvery rung is civil, and the state is run by soldiersThe rich rig the lot and dodge the liturgiesThe door is kept by one man, for a King who decides less each year
At the table"Praetorian" means respectable and irrelevant to violenceAny citizen may be handed an office tomorrowAn audience is a quest in itself
The Cursus Honorum Existing · Imperium Invicta

Category: Politics · Run by: the Senate's registers in Aeterna; the real ladder is the legions'

Overview

The Cursus Honorum is the fixed order in which a citizen of the Imperium holds office: a minimum age for each post, a minimum interval between posts, and no man to hold the same office twice within ten years. It was designed to stop any one family owning the state. It worked for four hundred years. It has not worked for a thousand.

How it works
  • Quaestor, 30. Audits a provincial treasury. A real job, given to nobodies.
  • Aedile, 36. Games, markets and the streets of the capital. Bought, not earned.
  • Praetor, 39. Judges. Still respected; still powerless against a Legate.
  • Consul, 42. Presides over a Senate that decides nothing. One year, then a province.
  • Why it is hollow. Every office on the ladder is civil, and the Imperium has been governed by soldiers since the Dominus Militum became permanent. A man who completes the sequence has shown that his family is wealthy and that he is patient. He has not shown that he commands anything. The Council of Legates climbed a different ladder: military tribune, prefect of a cohort, legate of a legion, then a province with the troops still loyal to him personally.
Now

Ambitious young patricians run the Cursus as fast as the law permits, paying the fines for irregularities, purely to collect the dignity before taking the military post where the real advancement lies. The aedileship has become an auction the Legates win: they fund the games their candidates give. Above the whole ladder the Imperator's chair stands empty. The one Invictian office still won outright is the oldest and least civil of all: the Rex Nemorensis at Nemibano, held by whoever kills the last one (at present Gnaeus Ferrus, nineteen years and counting).

At the table

Useful for placing an NPC precisely. A man introduced as "praetorian" is respectable, propertied and almost certainly irrelevant to anything violent about to happen, which is exactly why he may be worth talking to. Costs: an aedile's games, 3,000–8,000 gp, unless a Legate pays (and then owns the aedile); the fine for holding office early, 500 gp per year short. Roll d6 for a magistrate's real loyalty: 1–2 his family; 3 a Legate who funded his games; 4 the patrician remnant's salons; 5 the Dominus Militum's staff; 6 the law, sincerely, and he is lonely.

The Lot, the Liturgy and the Sherd New · Hellenoria

Category: Politics · Run by: each democratic city's assembly (ekklesia) and council (boule); the allotment machines in the agora

Overview

Hellenorian democrats hold that elections favour the rich and the famous, and that the only fair way to fill an office is to draw lots. In a League democracy most magistracies, every council seat and every jury are filled from citizens who put their names forward and are drawn by the allotment machine: a stone slab slotted with bronze name-tickets and a tube of black and white balls. Only offices where skill matters more than fairness are elected: generals, treasurers, the overseer of fountains.

How it works
  • The lot. A citizen over thirty puts in his ticket. If drawn he serves a year, is examined before office on his parents and his taxes, and audited after it on his accounts. No one holds the same allotted office twice.
  • The liturgy. The richest citizens pay for public goods directly: the trierarchy (fit out, crew and command a warship for a year) and the choregia (train and costume a chorus for a festival). A liturgy is an honour, a tax and a competition at once, and a good one buys votes for a decade.
  • The exchange. A man named for a liturgy who thinks a richer man has been spared may challenge him: take it on yourself, or swap your whole estate for mine.
  • The sherd. Once a year the assembly votes on whether to hold an ostracism. If it does, each citizen scratches a name on a potsherd; if six thousand are cast, the name with most goes into exile for ten years, property untouched and no crime alleged. It is not a punishment. It is a precaution.
Now

In Hellarchon the shipowning houses have learned to rig the machine: pre-sorted tickets, a bribed attendant, a tube with one ball too many. The rich dodge liturgies by turning land into "invisible" wealth (sea-loans, shares, Mithril Reserve accounts) that no assessor can see. The tyrants have abolished the lot outright. The Hegemon Kleandros Nikandrides has survived two ostracism votes; after the second, two hundred sherds pre-inscribed with his rival's name were found down a well.

At the table

A citizen PC living in a democracy rolls d20 each season; on a 1 he is allotted (d6): 1 market-warden; 2 grain-warden; 3 juror for a month; 4 a council seat; 5 envoy to a festival; 6 one of the city's magistrates. Declining costs 100 gp and standing. A choregia costs 1,000–3,000 gp, a trierarchy 4,000–6,000 gp; either gives advantage on Persuasion before that city's assembly for a year. Under the exchange, a challenger who wins Investigation DC 15 finds the hidden wealth before the swap, and the challenged must choose.

The Ladder of Access New · Acheaoria

Category: Politics · Run by: the hazarapat, chief of the court and keeper of the King's door; the Benefactors' roll kept by the Illuminated Scholars

Overview

In Persemenid, access is the whole currency: who may approach the King, how closely, and whether one may speak or must be spoken for. Acheaoria has offices by the hundred, but rank is not the office; rank is distance. A satrap who must kneel at the foot of the stair is outranked by any servant permitted to stand at the top of it.

How it works
  • The bow. Everyone who approaches the throne bows to the ground or, if of rank, bows and blows a kiss from the hand. The exact gesture a man is permitted is his rank, and everyone watches.
  • The Kinsmen. An honorific order a few hundred strong, styled the King's Kinsmen whether related or not. They greet the King with a kiss, sit nearer at the Table and may enter unsummoned on certain days. The title is for life and envied for generations.
  • The Benefactors of the King. Any man who does the throne a service may have his name and deed entered on the roll of Benefactors. A Benefactor is owed a reward, and the throne pays, sometimes to his grandson. The roll is the empire's one promise that never lapses.
  • The hazarapat. "Chief of the thousand": commander of the first regiment of the Ten Thousand and chief of the court. Every petition, visitor and letter passes him. He does not decide. He decides what reaches the man who decides.
  • The household. Cupbearer, staff-bearer, the eunuchs of the inner rooms: servants' offices that outrank satraps because they stand nearer.
Now

The King decides less each year, so the door matters more. The Benefactors' roll is in arrears: the throne owes more rewards than it can afford and pays them in titles. Two satraps have bought Kinsman rank with gifts, and the old Kinsmen call the new ones "the purchased" and will not sit beside them.

At the table

An audience is a quest. First, get on the hazarapat's list: a Kinsman's sponsorship or 200 gp to his secretary. Second, wait d4 weeks, less one week per further 100 gp. Third, learn the protocol (History or Insight DC 13; on a failure the party uses a gesture above its rank and has disadvantage on every check in the audience). Fourth, the audience: nobody speaks to the King; they speak to the official who repeats it. A deed worthy of the roll earns an entry and one major favour from the throne, collectible at the worst possible moment. At court, d6: 1 the secretary wants a favour; 2 a eunuch faction adopts the party; 3 a Kinsman takes offence over precedence; 4 a rival petitioner was moved ahead; 5 Bagoas the Nameless is in the room; 6 the King speaks directly, and the hall goes silent.

Banking and Coin

Coin is a promise about weight, and every empire is currently breaking that promise in its own way while a dwarven bank in the south keeps score.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Mint and the Money-ChangersThe Tables and the Sea-LoanThe Vaults of Equilibrium
Run byThe Imperial Mint beside the Temple of Juno; money-changers in every forum; the master weights at RomuloTable-bankers of Corinth and Hellarchon; temple treasuries such as Ephelanum'sBala's temple-bank under the Masters of Scales, house-banks, the Gilded Vault
How it worksState coin, tested at the changer's table, assayed quarterly against Juno's standardDeposits, transfers, sea-loans repayable only if the ship returnsSealed letters of credit honoured across the empire, sworn on a god
Breaking pointThe silver is being debased, and the standard itself has been swappedPiracy makes every sea-loan a gamble; the rich hide coin at the tablesIts notes are worthless outside Acheaoria; its book is full of satrapies that have stopped paying
At the tableInvictian silver loses value on the roadThe party can bankroll a voyageA sealed letter is safer than gold, until the border
The Mithril Reserve Existing · Continental

Category: Banking · Run by: House Merca of the Duneforged Citadel · Motto: "Fides in Metallo, Fiducia in Lapide" (Trust in Metal, Faith in Stone)

Overview

Not merely a place to store gold: a pillar of commerce and political power across Asetheria. Founded by the Merca family (House Merca), it runs on dwarven principles: strength, integrity and an unshakable memory for debts. Its headquarters is carved into the mountain under the Duneforged Citadel; it keeps a stone branch in every major city, the largest outside Duneforged at Deiperduem.

How it works
  • The Argentar. Licensed, public-facing bankers: advisers, agents and community figures, sworn on a shard of the original Mithril Lode.
  • The Stonework Ledger. Every transaction is chiselled into basalt ledgers in the branch vault; major accounts and transfers are duplicated by linked Runestones onto the master ledger in the mountain. Permanent and tamper-proof.
  • Fides. The business is its reputation for being unbreachable and incorruptible. Slander or successful fraud meets relentless retribution, legal and otherwise.
  • The Depositum (opening an account). Not for commoners. Prove standing by a noble's letter, a guild charter or a Founding Deposit of at least 1,000 gp. The Mark of Attunement: a drop of blood on an obsidian stone in a lead tray, tapped with a silver hammer to a Dwarvish chant; it glows only for its owner. A gnome Tabularius counts the funds, the deposit is chiselled in, and the client receives a Tessera, a heavy lead or bronze token stamped with the account number and the Reserve's seal.
  • The Receptum (withdrawal). Present the Tessera; grasp the Attunement Stone (no glow, no transaction); the new balance is carved and the old entry struck through but left legible for audit.
  • The Permutatio Aethensis (letter of credit). Fee 8–10%. A sealed Tablet of Transfer: a baked clay shell around a mithril sheet inscribed with the details and an arcane seal, closed with wax dusted with iron filings magically aligned to the origin branch. On redemption the Argentar checks the filings with a lodestone, breaks the shell, examines the plate, and for large sums casts sending to the origin branch.
  • The Mutuum (loan). Collateral (pignus) worth more than the loan: a castle deed, a magic item, a mine share, or a geas to serve the bank on default. Interest 20–25%, terms magically bound. Default means seizure, without exception or pity.
  • Security. Each branch has a Dominus Argentar (often a dwarf of Clan Ironhand), Custodes (professional soldiers in the best arms money buys) and an Arcanist-Securitas for wards and forensics. Outer vaults: adamantine doors and locks needing several officers' keys. Inner vaults: forbiddance, glyphs of warding on every surface, stone golems, sometimes a shield guardian bound to the Dominus Argentar.
Now

The Reserve is discounting debased Invictian silver against its own weight, and Lady Isolde Merca's letters go out monthly to Deiperduem and every branch master. Farshore merchants landing at Mavelon now bank here rather than trust any empire's coin. Each branch chalks its own rate by the door, and the slates disagree in instructive ways: Odvar Ironhand in Aeterna posts the gentlest discount in the Imperium, because Aeterna is where the Dominus Militum can reach him; Hulda Ironhand in Persemenid discounts Invictian silver at the door and will not lend to a satrapy at any rate.

At the table

The Reserve currently takes Invictian silver at 8 sp to the 10, Hellenorian at par, Acheaorian royal gold at par and Aksumar's foreign gold at par by weight. Spotting a forged Tablet of Transfer is DC 18 without the lodestone, automatic with it.

The Mint and the Money-Changers New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Banking · Run by: the Imperial Mint and the priests of Juno; licensed money-changers; the master weights at Romulo

Overview

The Imperial Mint is a windowless fortified workshop beside the Temple of Juno in Aeterna, the goddess of warning whose name the coin carries. Every bar is weighed twice and every worker searched twice, going in and coming out. The master weights that coin is judged against are kept at Romulo, the copy that counts, in the Hall of Weights under the Praefectus Ponderum, Lucius Vettius Libo. Between the mint and the purse stands the most Invictian figure of all: a man at a folding table in the forum, ringing coins on a stone.

How it works
  • The coin. Gold for Legates and great contracts, silver for pay and taxes, bronze for bread. Silver is the coin that matters: the army is paid in it, the Annona is bought with it, and every debt in the Imperium is written in it.
  • The changers. Licensed money-changers sit at tables in every forum, ring coins on stone, weigh them and take a cut, usually one part in twenty. Each seals the bags he has tested with his own stamp; a sealed bag passes at face without opening, so a changer's seal is worth exactly his reputation.
  • The Assay. Quarterly at the Temple of Juno, trial pieces from each new issue are weighed against the standard before witnesses. Once a formality; now the most watched morning in the city. Junia Tertulla, Keeper of the Standard, reads the figures aloud whatever they are.
  • The witnesses. A senator, a priest of Juno, a changer chosen by lot and a notary of the Oathbound Sanctum sign the Assay roll. The Sanctum keeps its copy forever.
  • The master weights. Any dispute about a weight goes to Romulo, where the master standard is unlocked only before three keyholders.
Now

The silver is being debased to pay the army and the Annona: each new issue carries a little more copper under a silvered skin. The Seekers of Eternal Truth are publishing their own assays, and the Oathbound Sanctum is in unhappy correspondence with Juno's priests. Changers in the provinces now quote two prices, one for "old silver" and one for "Concord silver", and soldiers paid in the new coin have learned the difference fast. Gold has vanished into floors and wells; Legates pay their own men in coin they strike locally, "for convenience".

At the table

Invictian silver is worth 10% less outside the Imperium and 20% less at Corinth. Spotting Concord silver by ring and weight: Investigation DC 12 with scales, DC 16 without. A changer's seal forged on a bag of light coin: forgery kit DC 15, and every changer in that forum knows his colleagues' marks (Insight DC 13 to notice the forger flinch). Hiring a changer's honest opinion of a hoard: 1 gp per 100 gp tested. Assay day, d6: 1–3 quiet; 4 a new issue lighter by a tenth; 5 riot at the changers' tables; 6 a witness refuses to sign. A changer's table, d6: 1 honest and slow; 2 buys Concord silver at par and sells it to soldiers; 3 a Seeker taking notes; 4 fronts for a Legate's mint; 5 clips every coin he touches; 6 pays in old silver, and wants to know where yours came from.

The Tables and the Sea-Loan New · Hellenoria

Category: Banking · Run by: the table-bankers (trapezitai) of Corinth and Hellarchon; temple treasuries

Overview

Hellenorian banking began with a man at a table in the agora changing foreign coin, and grew into deposits, transfers and the sea-loan. Every League city strikes its own silver, so changing is constant and the changer at his table is the first man any merchant meets. Corinth is the money market, with the Mithril Reserve and Vaults of Equilibrium on the same street watching each other; Dorgrim Ironhand keeps the Reserve's branch in Hellarchon, Hjalma Ironhand the Corinthian.

How it works
  • The table. A banker takes deposits, pays a client's debts on his word, and keeps a day-book of names and sums. His evidence is good in court, because his whole business is being believed.
  • The sea-loan. Money lent on a ship and cargo at 20–30% for the voyage, repayable only if the ship comes home. Lender carries the sea; borrower carries the market. The contract names the ports, the season and the cargo; a ship that strays off the named route forfeits the protection.
  • Temple banks. The sanctuary at Ephelanum holds deposits under the goddess's protection and lends; it is the largest single holder of coin in Hellenoria. Cities deposit their reserves there; kings and tyrants their exiles' money. Under the condominium, who audits it is a treaty question.
  • Slaves at the tables. Many tables are run by slaves and freedmen handling their masters' money. A clever one may end owning the table and his master's debts with it.
Now

Piracy has doubled sea-loan rates. The Aeolus Reach is safe only in convoy, and convoys sail when the Hegemon says so. The rich hide coin at the tables as "invisible wealth" that no liturgy assessor can see, so the bankers know which citizens are really rich better than any assembly does, and are paid well to forget. Tyrants borrow from Ephelanum against harbour dues they have not yet seized.

At the table

Lend 500 gp on a voyage at 25%; on return roll d6: 1 lost, nothing owed; 2 "lost", ship seen in another port; 3–6 repaid with interest. Raise the odds by sending a PC aboard as the lender's man (treat a 1 as a sea encounter the party can fight). Proving a "lost" ship sailed to another port: Investigation DC 14 in that harbour, and the borrower then owes double. Opening a table account: 50 gp and a citizen's introduction. Reading a banker's day-book without leave: Sleight of Hand DC 15 to borrow it overnight; it names everyone in the city hiding money. Loan trouble, d6: 1 the cargo was not what the contract said; 2 the captain is the borrower's brother-in-law; 3 a corsair offers to sell the ship back; 4 the banker has sold the loan to a tyrant; 5 the ship reaches Corinth's Haulway and is held for dues; 6 the ship comes home richer, and nobody can say how.

The Vaults of Equilibrium New · Acheaoria

Category: Banking · Run by: Bala's temple-bank; the great house-banks; the Gilded Vault for portable wealth

Overview

The Vaults are older than the Mithril Reserve and were for most of history larger. They lend on the authority of a god rather than a charter, and their notes are honoured within Acheaoria and nowhere else. For a century they have been losing ground for a reason they cannot fix: a Reserve letter is good in every major city on the continent. In Persemenid the high temple-bank is kept by the Master of Scales Jahanbakht Zarrin, who holds most of the court's debt and has begun to wonder whom he can collect it from.

How it works
  • The scale. Every Vault has a great bronze balance before Bala's altar. Deposits are weighed on it in public, so the god witnesses the sum.
  • The sealed letter. A clay envelope sealed with the issuing temple's and the depositor's seals, honoured at any Vault in the empire; covenants sworn at Mithratal back the big ones. Breaking a sworn covenant is a sin as well as a default.
  • House-banks. Family firms in Atarabad lend against harvests and collect taxes for satraps, taking their fee before the tribute moves. Master of Scales Pouran Dastvar of the Atarabad temple-bank lends to satrapies the Reserve will not touch.
  • The Gilded Vault. Gems and bullion for nobles turning estates into saddlebags; no ledger links a stone to a seller. Gem-Master Laal Firuzan keeps no records and remembers every face anyway.
Now

The Vaults lend to satrapies that have stopped forwarding tribute, and to the court against tribute that will not come. To win business from the Reserve they lend at rates it will not match, and their book is now full of provinces in quiet revolt. Pouran Dastvar has started asking for collateral that fits in a strongbox. Ziba Hormazdi, the Vaults' factor at Corinth, counts the Reserve's visitors from her window.

At the table

A sealed letter costs 3% and is good in Acheaoria; across the border a Wheelwalker discounts it 30%. A Vault loan runs at 15% against land or water shares, with a vow sworn before Bala; forging a temple seal is forgery kit DC 17, and a Master of Scales tests it on the god's balance (DC 20 to pass). Selling a stone at the Gilded Vault: three-quarters of value, no questions. A sealed letter's journey, d6: 1 honoured at once; 2 honoured, after a week, in a debased local coin; 3 the issuing temple has suspended payment; 4 the satrap's men read the seal and want a share; 5 a Wheelwalker uncle offers 70%, cash, tonight; 6 the Vault pays in gems from the Gilded Vault, and one is famous.

Information

Whoever hears first decides first, and every empire spends heavily on roads, runners and spies to make sure that is them.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Cursus LegionisRunners, Beacons and the OracleThe Eyes and Ears of the King
Run byThe state post under the Dominus Militum; the frumentariiDay-runners, beacon-keepers, Delphara's exegetes; the Ivory Chorus, unofficiallyRoyal Road couriers; the King's inspectors; the Melodic Circle, by licence
How it worksRelay stations on every road; grain-men who carry and listenFire-chains, fast feet, and petitioners who confess to the oracleA rider every day's ride; inspectors who report only to the throne
Breaking pointLegates read the post firstThe beacons now watch Hellenorian shipsSatraps feed the Eyes what they want seen
At the tableSeize a station, read a provinceAsk the oracle, pay twiceAnyone may be an Eye

The market in the middle. Deiperduem is the richest place on the continent for anyone in the business of knowing things first: three embassy compounds, the best notaries and translators, and a density of couriers and well-informed merchants that makes a Deiperdene innkeeper's silence worth more than his wine. All three systems below end there.

The Cursus Legionis New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Information · Run by: the state post under the Dominus Militum; the frumentarii

Overview

Official riders change horses at relay stations along every Invictian road, carrying orders, tax returns, dispatches and the quarterly Assay figures. The post belongs to the army, not the Senate: it was built to move legions' orders, and the roads were built to move legions. Use of it needs a warrant, a folded bronze diptych stamped with the Dominus Militum's seal and a date after which it is void. A warrant-holder may demand a fresh horse, a bed and a meal at any station, and the station-master may not ask why.

How it works
  • The stations. A posting house (mansio) every day's ride, with changing-stables (mutationes) between: forty horses, a smith, a wheelwright, a clerk with a ledger of every warrant shown. Busiest at Aepistra on the Via Septentrionalis, where the Legate's men always sit in the posting house.
  • The speeds. An ordinary dispatch goes fifty miles a day; a "feathered" letter, marked urgent with a quill tucked under the seal, rides through the night at eighty. Aeterna to Aepistra in four days; Aeterna to Mavelon on the Via Ferraria in six.
  • The frumentarii. The grain-men began as army buyers who bought grain for the legions, became couriers because they were always on the road, then spies because they were always listening. They travel as quartermasters, wear no insignia and report to the Dominus Militum's staff on the Palatine of Aeterna.
  • The cost. The provinces feed the stations: every town on a road owes horses, fodder and carts. It is the most hated levy in the Imperium after the tax-farmers.
Now

Each Legate reads his province's post before it leaves. Seals are lifted with a hot wire and replaced; the better Legates employ a forger full-time for the purpose. The Dominus answers by sending his frumentarii, which the Legates answer by bribing them, which the Dominus answers by sending frumentarii to watch the frumentarii. Meanwhile towns on the roads have stopped supplying horses they are never paid for, and a third of the northern stations are now kept by a Legate's soldiers, who decide whose warrant is honoured. Legatus Augusti Quintus Herennius Strabo's men at Aepistra have honoured every warrant shown to them since the Treaty, and copied every one.

At the table

A forged post warrant (forgery kit DC 15; DC 18 in a Legate's station) gives fresh horses and 80 miles a day. A genuine one costs 150 gp from a corrupt clerk on the Palatine and is good for a month. A frumentarius can be spotted by Insight DC 15; turning one costs 100 gp a month, and he will sell you too. Reading a sealed dispatch without leaving a trace: Sleight of Hand DC 16 with a hot wire. At a posting house, d6: 1 no horses, the town stopped sending them; 2 the station-master copies your warrant for the Legate; 3 a frumentarius shares your table and your route; 4 a feathered courier arrives and every horse is taken; 5 soldiers turn back anyone carrying letters for the capital; 6 a sealed bag of the province's post sits unguarded by the fire.

Runners, Beacons and the Oracle New · Hellenoria

Category: Information · Run by: day-runners and beacon-keepers of each city; the exegetes of Delphara; the Ivory Chorus, unofficially

Overview

Hellenoria has no state post, because the League has no state willing to pay for one. It has day-runners (hemerodromoi) who cover a hundred miles in two days, a beacon chain of hilltop fires along the coasts, harbour gossip, wedding songs and the oracle. News moves fastest by sea and slowest over the Inland Road, and the cities have always assumed that whoever pays for a messenger owns the message.

How it works
  • The runners. Each city keeps a dozen professional runners on public pay, men who run from boyhood and are fed at the town hall. A runner's message is spoken, not written; he can be stopped, but not read.
  • The beacons. A chain of fire-towers on headlands carries a handful of agreed signals (fleet sighted, city taken, come at once) from one end of the Long Lane to the other in a night. Keepers are paid by the cities whose coasts they watch.
  • The oracle. At Delphara petitioners from every city confess their plans to put a question. The exegetes, led by Lysandra Anthemis, hear everything, record more than they admit, and the oracle is the clearing-house of the League's secrets.
  • The harbour. Every captain is a newsletter. The Ivory Chorus, Aphrodite's bards, sing at the weddings where alliances are made and hear the rest before, during and after.
Now

The beacon chain that once warned of Acheaorian raiders now mostly reports Hellarchon's ships. Smaller cities have added their own signals, unknown to the hegemon: three short fires for "the Hegemon's fleet is out". The runners have found richer employers among the oligarchs, and the Ivory Chorus has noticed that its wedding-songs are being commissioned by people who have no intention of marrying.

At the table

An oracle consultation costs 10–500 gp by question; the answer is ambiguous, and the exegetes' private reading costs as much again. Harbour gossip: Investigation DC 12 for one true rumour per day in port. Hiring a city runner: 20 gp and the magistrates' consent; bribing one to carry a message twice, 50 gp. Learning the beacons' private signals: History DC 15 or a keeper's confidence. What the harbour says, d6: 1 a true report, a day late; 2 a lie planted by a Corinthian bank to move sea-loan rates; 3 a beacon lit for no reason anyone will admit; 4 an Ivory Chorus singer offers a verse that names names; 5 a runner arrives dead on his feet with a message for a man who left yesterday; 6 the oracle has already answered a question nobody admits asking.

The Eyes and Ears of the King New · Acheaoria

Category: Information · Run by: Royal Road couriers; the King's inspectors, answerable only to the throne

Overview

The Royal Road runs from Persemenid through Atarabad and Mithratal to Xerastri, with a post-station every day's ride and a fresh rider waiting. Nothing outruns it: "neither snow nor heat nor darkness" is carved over the gate of every station. Beside the road travel the Eyes and Ears, the King's inspectors, whose existence is the empire's most effective police force whether or not any of them is present.

How it works
  • The relay. A letter under the King's seal changes hands at every station, day and night; refusing a courier a horse is a capital offence. Stations keep a stable, a cistern, a scribe and a ration-store, and each issues travellers a sealed leather tag naming how much barley and wine they may draw at the next.
  • The Eyes and Ears. Inspectors who arrive unannounced in a satrapy and report only to the throne. Anyone might be one; that is the point. They carry a small gold seal shaped like an eye, shown once and never again.
  • The Melodic Circle. Bala's court musicians hold the ancient licence to put a satrap's failings into verse in his own hall. What is sung is not what is said; their songs travel the Royal Road with the caravans.
  • The hazarapat. Every report reaching Persemenid passes Hazarapat Aspachana Farnaka's secretaries first. He does not suppress; he sorts.
Now

Satraps now feed the Eyes what they want seen: prepared granaries, rehearsed petitioners, a rebel hanged in time for the visit. The Melodic Circle's licensed songs are the most honest report in the empire, and the court has started sending scribes to festivals to write them down. On the frontier, Satrap-held stations delay letters by a day when it suits them, which is long enough.

At the table

Persemenid to Xerastri in seven days by relay. A ration-tag forged well enough to eat on: forgery kit DC 14. Claiming to be an Eye is Deception DC 16 and a death sentence if caught; being mistaken for one is free and nearly as dangerous. A Circle poet will put a grievance into verse for 50 gp and a good story. On the Royal Road, d6: 1 a courier's horse dies and he demands yours, lawfully; 2 a station scribe asks too many questions, he is an Ear; 3 a satrap's officer holds the post for a day; 4 the party is mistaken for Eyes, and feasted, and followed; 5 a Melodic Circle troupe sings a verse that is clearly about the party; 6 a dead courier in a ditch, letters gone, seal intact on the bag.

Law and Justice

Each empire has a law it boasts of and a justice it actually delivers, and the distance between them is where most adventurers end up standing.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Praetor and the Bronze TabletsThe Jury Courts and the Truth-FlameThe Law That Does Not Change
Run byPraetors; patrons; the Iron Judges for soldiersJuries of hundreds; Inquisitor Vireon's Truth-FlameRoyal judges; the Lanterns of Justice; Mithratal's priests
How it worksWritten law, a praetor's edict, a patron at your sideCitizens judge citizens by lot; the censor judges ideasA sealed royal law cannot be revoked; ordeals decide the doubtful
Breaking pointNo praetor can touch a LegateJuries are bought; the Flame is fearedOld laws trap the throne itself
At the tableFind a patron before a crimeSpeak well or dieChoose the court, or the cup
The Praetor and the Bronze Tablets New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Law · Run by: praetors; patrons; the Legio Custodia Praetoriana for military law

Overview

Invictian law is written on bronze tablets set up in every forum; the originals hang at Romulo, the copy that counts. Each year's praetor issues an edict saying how he will apply them, and his successor usually copies it word for word, so the edict has become a second code. The Imperium is proud of its law and right to be: it is written, public and the same for every citizen. The trouble is getting it applied to anyone with soldiers.

How it works
  • Patronage. No one goes to law alone. A client attends his patron's morning greeting and the patron speaks for him in court. A man without a patron is a man nobody will testify for.
  • The summons. The plaintiff drags the defendant before the praetor himself; if he refuses, witnesses are called and force is lawful. The praetor decides which formula applies and names a private judge to try the facts.
  • Soldiers. The Iron Judges of the Custodia Praetoriana, the Praetorian Custodians under Legatus Varus Decianus, try soldiers; civil courts cannot. A legionary who robs a farmer is tried by his own officers, which is to say he is not.
  • The witnesses of last resort. The Oathbound Sanctum, Juno's oath-keepers, registers contracts in three cities and will produce them decades later against anyone, including the state. The Accord of Infinite Wisdom, sworn to Concordia, arbitrates for fees.
Now

Praetors are respected and powerless against a Legate, so serious disputes go to the Accord of Infinite Wisdom or to a sword. The Accord now mediates between Legates who cannot be seen to negotiate, and its fees have tripled. Demobilised veterans claim soldiers' privilege years after discharge, and the Iron Judges, who are short of work, have begun to agree. Cassia Vetra, a tribune of the Custodians seconded to the Vigiles, is the one officer in Aeterna who will hand a soldier to a civil court.

At the table

Without a patron, disadvantage on all checks in court. A patron costs a favour a month (or 25 gp a month and attendance at dawn). Contracts sworn before the Oathbound Sanctum are produced decades later against anyone; registering one costs 1% of its value. Accord arbitration: 200 gp a day, binding by custom. Arguing before a praetor: Persuasion DC 14, DC 20 against a Legate's client. Court day, d6: 1 the praetor's edict changed this morning; 2 the opposing patron outranks yours; 3 a key witness has joined a legion and is beyond summons; 4 a Sanctum brother arrives with a forty-year-old contract; 5 veterans pack the forum and shout the verdict; 6 the defendant produces a Legate's letter and the case is "deferred".

The Jury Courts and the Truth-Flame New · Hellenoria

Category: Law · Run by: the jury courts of each democracy; the Truth-Flame inquisition under Inquisitor Vireon, Third Seat

Overview

In a League democracy a case is heard by 201 to 1,501 citizens chosen by lot that morning, paid three obols, timed by a water-clock. There are no judges and no lawyers; each side speaks for itself and the jury votes at once, without discussion, by dropping a bronze ballot into one of two urns. Above the cities' courts stands an older, imperial court that judges not deeds but words: the Truth-Flame.

How it works
  • The accusers. Any citizen may prosecute; professional informers live on the rewards (a share of the fine) and on the threat of prosecution, which is cheaper.
  • The speech. A litigant may not hire an advocate, but he may hire a speechwriter and memorise the result. The best speechwriters are famous and write for both sides.
  • The penalty. Where the law fixes none, each side proposes one and the jury chooses between them. Proposing too little is fatal.
  • The Truth-Flame. An imperial inquisition that judges texts, teachings and heresies. Inquisitor Vireon, Third Seat, of Hellarchon annotates and strikes; his court has no jury, and a passage he strikes is struck in every library of the League.
Now

Oligarchs buy juries by the bench: since the rigged allotment machine was installed in Hellarchon, the right citizens are drawn on the right mornings. The Flame's list of struck passages lengthens every year, and lately includes histories of the war that disagree with the Emperor's voice. Smaller cities complain that the Flame's sittings follow Hellarchon's politics. Under the tyrants there are no juries at all, only the tyrant's hearing, which is quicker.

At the table

Defending before a jury: Persuasion or Performance DC 15, advantage with a hired speechwriter (50 gp; 300 gp for a famous one). An informer threatening suit wants 100 gp to go away. Buying a bench: 5 gp a juror, and you must know which bench. Before the Flame: the charge is the evidence; the best result is recantation (a public reading, Charisma DC 16 to sound sincere). In court, d6: 1 the water-clock has been tampered with and runs fast; 2 the jury is two hundred oarsmen who hate the rich; 3 your speechwriter also wrote your opponent's speech; 4 an informer adds a second charge mid-trial; 5 a Flame scribe takes notes in the gallery; 6 the opposition proposes death, and the jury looks interested.

The Law That Does Not Change New · Acheaoria

Category: Law · Run by: royal judges; the Lanterns of Justice, sworn to Hakiyah; the priests of Mithratal

Overview

A law sealed with the King's seal cannot be revoked, even by the King. Royal judges, appointed for life, interpret it; a judge found taking bribes is flayed and his skin stretched over the seat his successor sits on.
