The empire's law is therefore very old, very hard and full of contradictions, because the only way to fix a bad law is to seal a new one beside it and argue which governs.

How it works
  • The royal judges. A college of seven at Persemenid and one in every satrapal city, chosen from Magi-trained families and answerable only to the throne. They interpret, they never legislate.
  • The Lanterns. Roving magistrates sworn to Hakiyah who carry a lit lantern so their approach is seen, giving the guilty time to make amends. They hear the cases local courts will not touch, usually because the defendant owns the local court. Lantern-Captain Zarir Roshanpur rides from Mithratal with his lamp lit at noon.
  • The ordeal. At Mithratal the accused may drink bark-water in the Ordeal Grove, kept by the priest Kersasp; the innocent sicken and recover.
  • Covenants. Oaths sworn at Mithratal bind both parties before the god, and breaking one is tried as sacrilege, not breach.
Now

Old unalterable laws trap the throne; the court answers with new laws that contradict them, and the judges now spend more time deciding which seal is senior than deciding guilt. Satraps have begun appointing "deputy judges" with no royal warrant. The Lanterns are the only royal justice many satrapies still see, and some satraps have started meeting them at the border with an escort, to be sure the lantern is seen coming.

At the table

The ordeal: Con save DC 14 (innocent DC 10, if the dose is honest). The grove's priest sells verdicts for 300 gp. Finding a sealed law that contradicts the one charging you: History or Investigation DC 17 in a satrapal archive, then 100 gp to have a judge read it. A Lantern hears any free person's complaint for nothing. In the court, d6: 1 two sealed laws apply and both are fatal; 2 the judge's seat is visibly upholstered; 3 a Lantern is seen on the road, and the satrap releases everyone; 4 the accuser offers to settle in silver; 5 the priest at the grove asks how strong you would like the dose; 6 a Mithratal covenant you never swore is produced with your seal on it.

Armed Force

Three armies built for a war that ended in a signature, each now asking whom it serves when no enemy is coming.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe LegionsHoplites, Hulls and Hired SpearsThe Immortals and the Levy
Run byThe Dominus Militum and the Council of Legates; the fleet at MavelonEach city's generals; Hellarchon's Hegemon at seaThe throne's guards; the satraps' cavalry
How it worksProfessional legions loyal to their Legates; a navy rowed by Mavari under treatyCitizen spearmen, rich men's warships, mercenariesElite guards, a decimal levy, noble horse
Breaking pointVeterans unpaid, Legates armingThe fleet cannot be crewedThe cavalry belongs to the satraps
At the tableEvery veteran is a hirelingEvery captain is for hireEvery number is a lie
The Legions New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Military · Run by: the Dominus Militum; the Council of Legates; the fleet and arsenal at Mavelon

Overview

A legion is about 5,000 men under a Legatus Legionis; a Legatus Augusti commands several and a province. For fifteen centuries the legions were the Imperium: they built its roads, collected its tribute and chose its masters. Legions may not enter Aeterna; the Vigiles under Prefect Titus Oppius Ursus hold its walls, and the Praefectus Castrorum of the garrison, the dwarf Marcus Ulpius, counts every spear that comes through the gate. The named legions include the Red Obsidian ("the Emperor's Hammer", its Red Knights known by number, its Black Knights used as executioners), the Praetorian Custodians (the Iron Judges), the Beastlords (wolf-riders below, gryphon-riders above), the Shadow Assassins (the Cloaked Talons) and the Triform Host of soldiers, arcane archers and battle-wardens.

How it works
  • Ranks. Legatus Augusti, Legatus Legionis, Tribunus Laticlavius (a young patrician learning the trade), five Tribuni Angusticlavii, Praefectus Castrorum (the old soldier who actually runs the camp), Centurio (about 80 men), Optio, Tesserarius (keeper of the watchword), Signifer, Cornicen, Immunes (specialists excused fatigues), Legionaries; Decurio for a cavalry turma.
  • Twenty years. A legionary signs for twenty years and is promised land or cash at the end; see the Aerarium Militare. Pay comes through his Legate's paymaster, and that is the whole political problem in one sentence.
  • The fleet. Warships are built and berthed in the arsenal of Mavelon's south harbour under the Praefectus Classis, Servius Ancharius Nepos, and rowed and marined largely by Mavari islanders under treaty. Dux Publius Arruntius Celer signs for the hulls; Reiks Ansvald of the Hrodnings signs for the men.
  • The orders outside the line. The Obsidian Phalanx swears to Bellona, not to the Dominus Militum, and is quartered near the capital, never in it.
Now

Millions demobilised, unpaid. Warlords in the provinces, some of them former centurions with their centuries intact. The Council of Legates keeps its legions at full strength "against brigandage": Legatus Augusti Quintus Herennius Strabo in the north, Sextus Lollius Calvus in the south, and Decimus Aurelianus Corvus, who drills the Latium Plains garrison as if the war were next week. The Obsidian Phalanx sits at full strength outside the capital and has asked nobody's leave. Tribunus Cassia Vetra of the Custodians keeps a list of which Legates' paymasters have been buying extra grain.

At the table

Hiring a veteran: 3 sp a day; a centurion with his old century, 50 gp a week, and they choose the targets. Passing as a serving legionary needs the watchword (bribe a tesserarius 25 gp, or Deception DC 15 to bluff past a sentry). A deserter's brand is found on a strip search; harbouring one is a 500 gp fine. Raising your own troop of twenty veterans: 200 gp a month plus a Legate's blessing, or a Legate's displeasure. Legion encountered on the road, d6: 1 a vexillation building a road nobody ordered; 2 Custodians hunting deserters, and the party fits the description; 3 a Beastlord ala with a hungry dire wolf; 4 a paymaster's wagon, lightly guarded and heavily watched; 5 a century wearing a Legate's private badge over the eagle; 6 Black Knights escorting someone hooded towards the capital.

Hoplites, Hulls and Hired Spears New · Hellenoria

Category: Military · Run by: each city's elected generals; trierarchs; the Hegemon of Hellarchon for the common fleet

Overview

Every citizen who can afford a shield stands in the phalanx; the poor row the triremes. On land Hellenoria is improvised: a citizen army that trains when it remembers, fights in summer and goes home for the harvest. At sea it leads the continent. The common fleet of the League is commanded by the Hegemon of Hellarchon, Kleandros Nikandrides, berthed in Hellarchon's harbour and crewed by Hellarchon's citizens, which is why the smaller cities call it "the common fleet" in the tone other people use for "the common cold".

How it works
  • The phalanx. Eight ranks of bronze-shielded spearmen. Each man buys his own panoply (about 30 gp); the city elects ten generals a year, who command in rotation and are prosecuted when they lose.
  • The trierarchy. A rich citizen fits out and commands a warship for a year (see the liturgy). The city provides the hull; he provides everything else. The corsair-trierarch Nerissa Thalassine of Corinth is what happens when one keeps the ship.
  • Hellenic fire. A state secret siphoned from bronze tubes; burns on water and cannot be put out with it. Only Hellarchon makes it, and the siphon-crews are slaves who never leave the arsenal.
  • The rest. Thebesieas fields the only serious standing army and the Sacred Band under Epameinon Kleitarchos, three hundred sworn pairs who have never broken. Everyone else hires the Sunward Valiants, Hermes' light troops, fast and contractually impossible to pin down.
Now

Ships are built faster than crews are found. A trireme needs 170 rowers, and the free poor of the League have found that peace pays better ashore. The Theoric Fund cannot pay for war, so the fleet is paid for by liturgists who dodge, harbour dues that piracy shrinks and loans that compound. Tyrants pay better than assemblies, in cash, on time, and their navies are full of the assemblies' rowers. Thebesieas is arming with iron nobody admits buying.

At the table

A Valiant company: 1 gp a man a day; will not hold a line, will not garrison, may withdraw on a day's notice. A trireme with crew for a month: 1,500 gp, or serve as trierarch for the year (4,000–6,000 gp) and keep the glory. Rowing as a free oarsman pays 3 obols a day and gives anyone the right to speak in the assembly of the city that hired him. Stealing a fire-siphon: the city's fleet will hunt you for a year; working one without training, DC 15 Dexterity or burn yourself (4d6 fire). Contract trouble, d6: 1 the Valiants withdraw at dawn, citing clause nine; 2 half the rowers are tyrant's men; 3 the general who hired you is indicted mid-campaign; 4 the trierarch wants the prize money, all of it; 5 a Theban buyer asks about your iron; 6 Nerissa Thalassine offers a better rate.

The Immortals and the Levy New · Acheaoria

Category: Military · Run by: the throne (the Immortals, the Ten Thousand, the Ironclad Oath); the satraps (the Lion's Mane Vanguard)

Overview

The Immortals are the elite who kept defeat from becoming collapse: masked, silent, never seen eating, and never fewer than they were. The Ten Thousand guard Persemenid and are never fewer than ten thousand; when one dies, another steps into his file the same day. Their first regiment, the Golden Apples, carry spears with golden apple-weights at the butt and serve the hazarapat; a Farnaka has commanded them for forty years. Below the guard sits a levy counted in tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands, and beside it the cavalry the satraps raise and the throne merely borrows.

How it works
  • The decimal levy. Each satrapy owes men by the ten; captains of ten, hundred and thousand, each paid by the rank below's rations. The muster rolls go to the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger, who record what they are told.
  • The cavalry. The Lion's Mane Vanguard, armoured lancers on plateau-bred horse, raised and paid by satraps; Spahbed Artabazos Mihran rides with it. Horse-archers like Roxana Surena hold Xerastri and the Parthian Ravine.
  • The Ironclad Oath. Vatagatal's order, sworn to a promise rather than a satrap, and forbidden by that promise to make war on the empire's own subjects. At Xerastri, Oath-Captain Arya Kardar keeps the chapter; the throne trusts them precisely because they will not do everything it asks.
Now

Two satraps have expanded their squadrons. Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad of Atarabad filed the correct returns for every new lancer, which frightened the court more than if he had hidden them. The Ten Thousand are full of boys who have never fought; Bagabukhsha Farnaka drills the Golden Apples beautifully and has never seen a battle. The levy exists on paper, where it is enormous.

At the table

A squadron of the Vanguard costs 500 gp a month and its satrap's permission. Counting the Ten Thousand truthfully: Investigation DC 18. An Ironclad escort for a caravan: 20 gp a day for five riders, and they will refuse any order to fight Acheaorian subjects. A levy captain's muster roll can be padded or bought (200 gp per hundred "ghost" men; Scribes' audit DC 16 to catch). Muster day, d6: 1 half the hundred are the captain's cousins; 2 the horses are borrowed from the next satrapy; 3 a subject people's levy refuses to march without their own priest; 4 an Immortal stands in the file and does not breathe; 5 a Mihran recruiter asks about Duneforged; 6 an Eye of the King is counting too.

Faith and the Licensing of Magic

Every empire lets magic be done; none lets it be done without a licence, a priest or a reckoning.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Pontiffs and the Licensed CollegiaThe Academy, the Lexicon and the TribunalThe Magi and the Purity of Fire
Run byThe college of pontiffs; augurs; the magical collegiaThe Arcane Academy; the Lexicon Council; the TribunalThe Magi of the fire-temples
How it worksMagic only inside a licensed collegiumThe Academy certifies; the Council fixes words; the Tribunal fixes godsFire, earth and water must not be defiled; the dead are kept from all three
Breaking pointThe pontiffs have no headFrontier cities worship unrecognised godsThe state's Rite of Return defiles what the Magi guard
At the tableCast in public, show your licenceSpeak the wrong dialect, meet the FlameNever let a corpse touch fire
The Pontiffs and the Licensed Collegia New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Religion · Run by: the college of pontiffs; the augurs; licensed collegia such as the Artisan's Forge of Wonders and the Luminous Arcanists

Overview

Invictian religion is a contract: the state performs the rites correctly and the gods keep the state. The pontiffs keep the calendar, the state rites and the lists of lucky and unlucky days; the augurs read the birds before any public act, and an assembly can be dissolved because a crow flew left. The Vestals under Virgo Maxima Tarquitia Lucilla keep the hearth; Junia Tertulla keeps the Standard at the Temple of Juno. Arcane magic is treated the same way as a trade: lawful, useful and only inside a licensed collegium that answers for its members.

How it works
  • The licence. A collegium (the Artisan's Forge of Wonders for makers, the Luminous Arcanists for scholars, a dozen smaller) examines its members, records their spells and answers for them in court. Its seal ring is the licence. Unlicensed casting is hunted by the Speculatores Interni, the inquisitor-agents of the Praetorian Custodians.
  • The augury. No battle, assembly, founding or marriage of note without the auspices. An augur can delay anything; a general who wants to fight on a bad day needs a different augur.
  • The head. The chief pontiff was always the Imperator. The chair is empty, so the college rules itself by seniority, and the most senior pontiff is ninety-one and hard of hearing.
  • The temples. Each god keeps its own priesthood and treasury: Juno the mint and the warning, Mars the field, Bellona outside the boundary, Vulcan the arsenal fires at Mavelon.
Now

Generals buy omens from the Celestial Astromancers, Caelus's sky-watchers, and deny it; an unannounced eclipse is now a professional scandal, and a well-timed one is worth a legion. With no chief pontiff, nobody can declare a new festival, so the Legates sponsor "games of thanksgiving" instead. The collegia are swamped by veteran battle-mages of the Triform Host who learned their spells in the line and never sat an examination.

At the table

Licence: 50 gp a year and an examination (Arcana DC 14); a veteran's war-licence can be converted for 20 gp and a centurion's letter. Unlicensed casting in a city: fine 200 gp or a month in chains; casting on a state occasion without auspices, double. An augury bought from the Astromancers: 25 gp for a day, 250 gp for a campaign season, delivered sealed. Before a public act, d6: 1 the birds are favourable; 2 the augur wants a gift; 3 a rival paid for a crow; 4 the Speculatores ask for your ring; 5 the date falls on an unlucky day and the pontiffs will not shift it; 6 lightning, and every magistrate goes home.

The Academy, the Lexicon and the Tribunal New · Hellenoria

Category: Religion · Run by: the Arcane Academy of Hellarchon; the Lexicon Council; the Tribunal of the gods

Overview

Hellenoria governs magic the way it governs everything: with argument, paperwork and an inquisitor at the end. The Arcane Academy in Hellarchon, under Scholarch Kallisto Pyrphoros, certifies mages. The Lexicon Council sanctions dialects and texts, because a spell in the wrong dialect is, by Academy theory, a different spell. The Tribunal decides which gods are recognised. Behind all three stands Inquisitor Vireon of the Truth-Flame, who enforces what they decide.

How it works
  • Certification. An Academy seal opens every city's doors to a mage: lodging at a proxenos, access to temple libraries, the right to cast in an agora. Without one, a mage is a suspect.
  • The Lexicon. Approved spellbooks bear the Council's stamp. Unstamped books are not illegal; they are evidence.
  • Recognition. Worship of an unrecognised god is not banned, merely unprotected: its temples have no asylum, its priests no standing in court, its oaths no force.
  • The Voidfolk. Tiefling casters are certified under a separate register nobody outside the Academy has seen.
Now

Cities beyond the Peaks of Veilmar speak unsanctioned dialects and worship gods the Tribunal does not know. The tyrants hire uncertified mages because they are cheaper and less chatty. The Academy's examiners are hunting the last dream-walker, Vesperine Ilaro, alongside Delphara and the Enchanted Muse, and certification interviews now include questions about dreams.

At the table

An Academy seal: 100 gp and Arcana DC 15; a forged one passes casual inspection (forgery kit DC 15) but not an Academy reader (DC 20). A Lexicon stamp for a spellbook: 10 gp per spell level copied, a month's wait, and one spell may be struck. An unsanctioned book found in your pack: the Truth-Flame takes an interest. Petitioning the Tribunal to recognise a god: 2,000 gp in fees and a year. Examination day, d6: 1 passed; 2 the examiner wants a copy of your best spell; 3 your dialect is "provincial", resit next season; 4 a question about dreams, asked twice; 5 a Voidfolk candidate is refused and asks you to witness it; 6 Vireon's clerk sits at the back, taking notes.

The Magi and the Purity of Fire New · Acheaoria

Category: Religion · Run by: the Magi; the First Flame at Atarabad; the Keeper of the Rite of Return at Persemenid

Overview

The Magi tend a fire in every city that must never go out; at Atarabad Mobad Atar-Farnbag, First Flame, keeps the oldest, lit (they say) before the empire. The faith forbids defiling fire, earth or water, so the dead are exposed on towers, never burned or buried, and the vultures are sacred. The Magi are the empire's priests, judges of purity, keepers of the calendar and the only men permitted to touch the King's sacred fire.

How it works
  • Purity. Defiling a fire is a capital crime. So is blowing on one: Magi tend flames through a veil over the mouth. Corpses, blood, nail-parings and hair are impurities and must be carried by licensed corpse-bearers to the towers.
  • Arcane work. Spellcasting is lawful if it does not touch the elements impurely; a fire-mage must buy a purification each season. The Magi license casters by temple, not by school.
  • The Rite of Return. A state rite kept by Magus Rashnu-Vahram at Persemenid, publicly a rite of honour for the fallen of the Immortals, performed behind closed doors.
Now

Conquered peoples' gods clash with the Magi's purity laws: subject peoples who bury their dead are fined by the grave, and returned soldiers burn their comrades' bodies on the frontier as they did in the war. The Magi of Atarabad, through observers like Magus Tirdad, have begun asking what exactly the Rite of Return does, and Atar-Farnbag has not been invited to see it.

At the table

Carrying a corpse into a city without rites: arrest. A purification costs 25 gp and a day; a fire-mage's seasonal purification, 50 gp. Casting fire spells near a temple flame without leave: DC 15 Persuasion to talk a magus out of an accusation, or a capital charge. Hiring corpse-bearers to remove a body quietly: 10 gp, no questions. Purity trouble, d6: 1 a magus spots blood on your boots; 2 a subject village buries its dead and asks you to hide it; 3 a temple flame flickers when the party enters; 4 the vultures will not touch a body on the tower; 5 Rashnu-Vahram's servants buy a fresh corpse; 6 a magus asks you to carry a message to Atarabad, and a sealed copy to nobody.

Citizenship and Status

Who counts as a person decides everything else, and each empire draws the line somewhere different.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Orders of the ImperiumCitizen, Metic, SlaveThe Ranks of the Realm
Run byThe census; the Annona's rolls; the censors' successors in the Dominus Militum's staffEach city's deme registers; the polemarch's court for meticsThe throne, the zarates, the arashshara
How it worksPatrician, equestrian, plebeian, freedman, slave; the tessera proves the restCitizens by birth from two citizen parents; metics pay and need a sponsor; tieflings under the Voidfolk AccordAzata nobles, arashshara, free farmers with water shares, kurtash labourers, subject peoples
Breaking pointVeterans are citizens with nothingMetics do the work and vote on nothingSubject peoples outnumber everyone and came home armed
At the tableA tessera is proof of being somebodyA metic needs a sponsorRank decides the bow
The Orders of the Imperium New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Society · Run by: the census and the rolls of the Annona

Overview

Patricians hold old names, equestrians money and commands, plebeians the vote that no longer matters, freedmen their former masters' names, slaves nothing. The orders were drawn for a city-state and stretched over a continent's worth of provinces, and they still decide who may be flogged, who may appeal, who may marry whom and who eats. Nobody has held a proper census since the war began to go badly; the rolls that matter now are the Annona's.

How it works
  • The tessera. In Aeterna the grain ticket is the practical proof of citizenship: a lead token stamped with a distribution day and an arch of the Porticus. Sextus Naevius Macer, Prefect of the Annona, keeps the rolls that issue them, and his clerks are the nearest thing the capital has to a registry of persons.
  • Patricians. Descendants of the founding houses. Their privileges are ceremonial (certain priesthoods, a seat in the Senate, a red shoe) and their debts are not. The patrician remnant marries money and resents it.
  • Equestrians. Citizens assessed above a property line, once the cavalry, now the contractors, tax-farmers and junior officers. They hold the gold ring and most of the actual gold.
  • Plebeians. Everyone else with a vote. The assemblies still meet; they ratify.
  • Freedmen. Free, citizen, barred from office; their sons are not. A freedman owes his former master attendance and a share of his estate, and many of the Imperium's richest men are freedmen pretending not to mind.
  • Appeal. A citizen accused anywhere may appeal to the capital, which halts flogging and execution until the appeal is heard. A non-citizen may be flogged on a centurion's word.
Now

Veterans are citizens with land promised and none given. Twenty years of service grants citizenship to provincial auxiliaries at discharge, so the Great Concord created a million new citizens in a season, most of them hungry and many not Latin-speaking. Macer's rolls cannot hold them: a veteran without a tessera is a citizen on bronze and a beggar in the street. Forged tesserae now circulate in the Subura, and the patricians have begun quietly selling their sons' marriages to equestrian contractors and to the Legates' officers.

At the table

Citizenship by purchase: 500 gp and a patron. A forged tessera costs 25 gp (Annona clerk spots it on DC 13); a genuine one bought from a dead man's heir, 60 gp. A PC who claims citizenship under arrest must prove it: a diploma, a tessera or a witness of standing (Persuasion DC 12 with proof, DC 20 without). A status complication, d6: 1 a freedman's former master turns up to claim his share; 2 the party's patron is suddenly out of favour; 3 a provincial magistrate ignores an appeal and dares anyone to report it; 4 Macer's clerks strike a PC's name from the rolls by error; 5 a patrician offers adoption, with his debts attached; 6 a veteran mob demands the party show tesserae at a bridge.

Citizen, Metic, Slave New · Hellenoria

Category: Society · Run by: each city's deme registers; the Voidfolk Accord for tieflings

Overview

Citizenship descends from two citizen parents. Metics, resident foreigners, pay a yearly tax, need a citizen sponsor and own no land. Slaves do the harbour work. Every League city keeps its own register, so a citizen of Corinth is a metic in Hellarchon and a stranger in Thebesieas, and the League itself has no citizens at all. That is the arrangement the smaller cities insist on, because a League citizenship would be a Hellarchon citizenship by another name.

How it works
  • The deme roll. At eighteen a youth is presented to his deme, sworn on his father's word, and scrutinised; a deme that admits a false citizen can be fined, so demes guard their rolls fiercely.
  • The metic. Registers with a citizen sponsor (prostates), pays the metic tax, serves in the levy and the fleet, pays liturgies if rich, and may not own land or a house. Metics are the potters, bankers, shipwrights and physicians of every port.
  • The slave. Owned, rented out, often skilled. Many table-bankers and harbour clerks are slaves running a master's money; a slave who earns enough may buy himself free and become a metic.
  • The Voidfolk Accord. Tieflings were absorbed under a classified accord; they hold a status of their own, neither metic nor citizen. They carry an Accord token, pay no metic tax, serve where the accord says, and may not hold office. What the Accord promised them in return is not public.
Now

In Hellarchon the metics outnumber the citizens and run the yards. The war killed citizens and spared metics, who could not stand in the phalanx; the shipowning oligarchs prefer it that way, because metics cannot vote against them. Twice since the Treaty of Myrianth the Assembly has debated a mass enrolment of loyal metics; twice the Hegemon Kleandros Nikandrides has let it fail. The tyrants, who need soldiers more than pedigrees, enrol anybody, and metics are drifting to tyrannies.

At the table

Metic tax: 1 gp a year; a sponsor costs a favour (or 20 gp a year from a professional prostates in the agora). A metic without a sponsor can be sold into slavery on a citizen's suit. Grant of citizenship by Assembly decree: a great service, or 2,000 gp spent publicly on a liturgy, then Persuasion DC 17 before the Assembly. Asking about the Accord: the Truth-Flame hears. A deme complication, d6: 1 the sponsor dies and his heir wants rent; 2 an informer prosecutes a PC as a false citizen; 3 the PC is called up for the fleet; 4 a tiefling asks the party to carry a sealed petition under the Accord; 5 a slave banker offers to launder money for his freedom; 6 a tyrant's recruiter offers citizenship today.

The Ranks of the Realm New · Acheaoria

Category: Society · Run by: the throne; the azata lords of the zarates; the arashshara

Overview

Azata nobles head the zarates; arashshara, women overseers, run production and trade; free farmers hold water shares; kurtash labourers work the royal estates on rations; subject peoples carry the rest. Acheaoria does not ask whether a man is a citizen. It asks whose he is: which zarate, which satrap, which estate, which workshop. A person with no answer is a person nobody will avenge.

How it works
  • The azata. Lords of the zarates, the "free-born", who owe horse and counsel and expect the bow from all below. Houses such as Mihran and Farnaka count their rank in generations and in distance from the throne.
  • The arashshara. Overseers whose seal outranks most men's in a workshop or market. They allot rations, fix weights, hire and dismiss, and sign for the output of whole quarters. A satrap rules a city; the arashshara run it.
  • Free farmers. Holders of qanat water shares, measured in hours of flow. Lose the share and you become someone's labourer.
  • The kurtash. Bound labourers paid in portions: grain, beer and wine by the measure, recorded on clay. Men, women and children; the tablets note extra rations for new mothers.
  • Subject peoples. Conquered nations keep their own law at home and pay the King's tribute. Their nobles may rise; their peasants rarely do.
Now

Returned soldiers from subject peoples meet discrimination. The levy took them as men owed by the ten and returned them with spears, discipline and no rank. Some satraps enrol them as private horse; others turn them away, and they gather on the eastern caravan routes. The arashshara meanwhile are quietly the richest order in the empire, because peace means trade and trade passes their seals. Older azata houses call it an outrage and borrow from them.

At the table

An arashshara's pass opens any workshop; insulting one costs a merchant his licence. A pass costs a favour or 50 gp a season. Claiming a rank one lacks: Deception DC 15, then Insight DC 12 against anyone at court who watches the bow. Buying a water share: 300 gp per hour of weekly flow. Encounters by rank, d6: 1 an azata demands the party dismount and bow; 2 an arashshara commissions a delivery and pays in clay ration chits; 3 kurtash runaways beg passage; 4 a subject-people veteran captain offers his band; 5 a farmer has lost his water share to a satrap's cousin; 6 a Kinsman's servant claims the party's inn rooms by precedence.

Taxation and Tribute

Every empire taxes what it can see, and every merchant spends his life making sure it sees less.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameTribute, Tax-Farmers and TollsDues, Levies and LiturgiesTribute in Talents
Run byProvincial quaestors; the Chyrsus Syndicate; customs at Mavelon and RomuloHarbour officials; the assembly; the poletai who auction tax contractsSatraps; the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger
How it worksLand and head tribute, farmed taxes, internal tariffs, sea customsHarbour dues, war levies, rich men's liturgiesEach satrapy owes talents of silver; gifts at new year; road tolls
Breaking pointTariffs strangle trade; the farmers write the contractsThe rich hide their wealthSatraps stop forwarding
At the tableEvery seal costs a feeEvery harbour takes two per centEvery road has a toll
Tribute, Tax-Farmers and Tolls New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Economic · Run by: provincial quaestors; tax-farming companies; customs at Mavelon; registration at Romulo

Overview

Provinces pay tribute on land and heads. Difficult provinces are farmed out to the Chyrsus Syndicate, who pay up front and extract the rest. Above the tribute sit the tolls: a tariff at every provincial boundary, a duty at every port, a fee at every seal. The Imperium never designed this system. It accumulated, one emergency at a time, over fifteen centuries of war, and every layer still has an office drawing a salary from it.

How it works
  • Tribute. A tenth of the harvest on provincial land, a head tax on every adult, assessed by the provincial quaestor from a census nobody has updated. Citizens' land in the heartland pays nothing, which the provinces have noticed.
  • The farm. Where a quaestor cannot collect, the province's tribute is auctioned for five years to a company that pays the treasury a lump sum and keeps whatever it raises above it. The Chyrsus Syndicate holds most of the big farms and the Treaty Road tolls at Deiperduem.
  • Customs. Foreign cargoes land at Mavelon's south harbour and pay a quarter duty to Dux Publius Arruntius Celer's customs house; the Mavari collect their own fee at the north harbour under Reiks Ansvald's seal, and the treaty forbids either side to tax the other's quay.
  • Registration. Every foreign cargo and great contract must be weighed and sealed at Romulo against the master weights. Foreign houses such as Himilkat of the house of Magon's Qart-Hadethi office pay the seal and keep the receipts for the courts.
  • Tariffs. Internal tolls at provincial boundaries, two to five per cent, each kept by the province that charges it.
Now

The tax-farmers' contracts grow longer; the tariffs still strangle trade. Five-year farms became ten-year farms during the war and are now offered for twenty, paid in advance, because the treasury needs the lump sum more than the future revenue. Legates have begun charging their own boundary tolls and calling them "road maintenance". Farshore cargo increasingly lands at the Mavari north harbour, where the Reiks's fee is lower and the clerks less curious.

At the table

Mavelon duty 25% on Farshore luxuries, 2.5% on staples; Romulo seal 1%; boundary tariff 2–5% per province crossed. Smuggling past Mavelon: Stealth DC 15 and a Mavari pilot (30 gp). An unsealed contract cannot be enforced in an Invictian court. Bribing a customs clerk to undervalue: 5% of the duty saved, Persuasion DC 13. Tax trouble, d6: 1 a Syndicate collector claims the cargo was assessed twice and wants the difference; 2 a Legate's toll-post appears on a road that had none last month; 3 Romulo's weighers find the party's measures short; 4 north- and south-harbour clerks both claim the same cargo; 5 a farmer offers the party a share to collect from a stubborn village; 6 a quaestor wants the Syndicate's books stolen.

Dues, Levies and Liturgies New · Hellenoria

Category: Economic · Run by: harbour officials of each city; the assembly

Overview

No Hellenorian citizen pays a regular direct tax. Cities live on harbour dues, emergency levies and the rich. A direct tax on a citizen's person is the mark of a tyrant, and the democracies would sooner let a fleet rot than levy one. So every League city is funded by its harbour, its foreigners and the vanity of its wealthiest families, which makes the treasury of a maritime democracy as fickle as the weather.

How it works
  • Dues. Two per cent on everything in or out of a harbour, collected by tax-farmers who bid each year at auction. Corinth adds the Haulway, a fee per hull dragged across the isthmus, which is why the Prytanis Telestes Bacchiades can afford to be generous.
  • The metic tax. One gold a year from every resident foreigner; small, steady and resented.
  • The war levy. Voted only in emergencies, on property, assessed by the owner's own declaration. Declarations are optimistic.
  • Liturgies. The rich pay for ships and choruses, and compete to be seen paying. See the Lot, the Liturgy and the Sherd.
  • The League contribution. Each member city pays Hellarchon a share for the common fleet. Hellarchon calls it a contribution; the smaller cities call it tribute.
Now

The rich hide wealth in sea-loans and Mithril accounts, which no assessor can see. Since the Treaty of Myrianth the League contribution has been "deferred" by four cities, and the Hegemon Kleandros Nikandrides has answered by sending triremes to collect it in person, which is precisely what the cities said tribute looks like. Archias the Weigher and his fellow Corinthian factors quietly offer the deferring cities loans to pay it, at rates that put their harbours in hock.

At the table

Harbour dues: 2% of cargo value; dodging them is Deception DC 14 (a false manifest, 15 gp from a harbour scribe). Haulway fee: 30 gp per merchant hull, 60 per warship. A war levy assessment against a PC with property: Deception DC 15 to under-declare by half; an informer who proves it collects a third of the hidden sum. Harbour trouble, d6: 1 the tax-farmer is new and greedy; 2 an informer watches the party unload; 3 a Hellarchon trireme "escorts" the party's ship to collect a deferred contribution; 4 the Haulway is closed for a festival; 5 a liturgist wants the party's ship for his trierarchy; 6 a tyrant's port offers zero dues and a garrison.

Tribute in Talents New · Acheaoria

Category: Economic · Run by: the satraps; audited by the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger

Overview

Each satrapy owes a fixed tribute in talents of silver, plus gifts carried up the stair at Persemenid at new year. The figure for each province was set by the founder's scribes and revised once in a millennium. Inside his satrapy a satrap raises whatever he likes, however he likes, so long as the talents go up the Royal Road. The throne asks how much, never how.

How it works
  • The talent. Assessed by the Scribes, collected by satraps. Fixed sums: a rich river satrapy owes hundreds of talents, a desert march a few, and horses, eunuchs or incense where the land has no silver.
  • The forwarding. Silver travels in sealed convoys under satrapal guard; at Persemenid the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger weigh it, record it on clay and mark the satrapy "presented".
  • The gifts. At new year every satrapy and great house brings gifts as well as tribute; see the King's Table.
  • Tolls. Charged at every Royal Road station, on the Garden Road and at caravan gates; House Suren-Pahlav pays at more stations than anyone and complains in proportion.
  • Water. Free farmers pay a share of the harvest to whoever owns the qanat; on royal channels, the King.
Now

The Scribes' column of provinces marked "not presented" lengthens; Shir'abad D'ar collects tribute nobody forwards. Its satrap paid for a better place on the Royal Stair and has paid nothing up it since. Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad of Atarabad still forwards in full, conspicuously, and files exact returns on everything, including the squadrons he raised past the establishment. The court answers shortfalls with borrowing from the Vaults of Equilibrium, not with soldiers.

At the table

Royal Road toll: 1 sp per beast per station; a sealed royal pass waives it (forgery DC 17, death if caught). Guarding a tribute convoy pays 2 gp a day per guard and a share in the King's gratitude. Collecting arrears from a defaulting satrapy for the court earns an entry on the Benefactors' roll. Convoy trouble, d6: 1 the silver weighs short at Persemenid and the guards are blamed; 2 raiders who know the route; 3 a satrap's agent offers the party a cut to lose a chest; 4 a station-master demands the toll twice; 5 a King's Eye rides with the convoy, disguised; 6 the convoy is ordered to turn back to its own satrap.

Roads, Bridges and Upkeep

Every empire built its roads to move armies. Five years into the peace, all three are finding out what it costs to keep a road when no army needs it.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Viae and the Repair ContractsThe Lanes, the Harbours and the LampsThe Royal Road and its Stations
Run byCuratores viarum appointed by the Dominus Militum; private repair companies (redemptores)Each city's harbour-wardens; rich citizens who fund the lamps as a liturgy; the Hegemon's fleet on the Long LaneStation-masters of the throne; the rahdar (road-wardens); the Wheelwalkers and caravanserai endowments
How it worksPaved highways, milestones every thousand paces; bridges and waystations repaired by contract, paid on inspectionThe sea is the road: lanes between harbours, moles, ship-sheds and lighthouses kept by city duesOne stone road, a station every day's ride, fresh horses for the King's business and tolls for everyone else
Breaking pointContractors paid in debased coin do debased work; Legates divert crews to their own fiefsLamps go dark where no one will pay the liturgy; wreckers fill the gapSatraps keep the tolls and stop paying the station-masters
At the tableA bridge contract is a dungeon with paperworkA lit lamp is a promise, and someone pays for itA station is food, horses and a witness, if it is still manned
The Viae and the Repair Contracts New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Infrastructure · Run by: the curatores viarum, one per great road, appointed by the Dominus Militum; private repair companies bidding for contracts; the old posting-houses of the state post

Overview

The viae are the Imperium's best argument for itself. Fifteen centuries of paved road run out from Aeterna: the Via Sacra Aeterna to Romulo, the Via Septentrionalis north through Anticata to Aepistra, the Via Ferraria south through the iron country to the Duneforged Citadel, the Via Litoranea down the coast to Napplesia. Legions built them. The legions have gone home, and nobody else was taught to lay a road.

How it works
  • The curator. Each great road has a curator viarum, a senior officer who answers for its surface, bridges and milestones.
  • The contract. Since the war the state offers repairs to private companies, the redemptores. A company bids for a bridge or a ten-mile stretch, posts a bond, does the work and is paid when a curator's inspector walks it. Half the price is held back a year, in case the bridge falls.
  • The levy. Landowners along a road owe labour on it. The latifundia pay a fine instead, and the fine goes to Aeterna, not the road.
Now

Bridges are down on every road but the Sacra. Contractors paid in debased silver lay a debased road: a hand of gravel where the specification says a foot of stone. Legates commandeer crews for their own fiefs. The Chyrsus Syndicate has offered to farm the tolls of the whole Via Septentrionalis, and the curator has not said no.

At the table

A bridge contract pays 400–1,200 gp, half on inspection and half a year later, and requires a 100 gp bond. Something always lives under the bridge. An inspector passes shoddy work on a bribe of 10% of the contract, or catches it on Investigation DC 13. Each day, d6: 1 bridge down, a day's detour or Athletics DC 12 to ford; 2 veterans' toll-post, 2 sp a head; 3 a rival company's crew sabotaging a stretch it lost; 4 a Legate's soldiers impressing labourers, party included; 5 a waystation roofless, sleep in the open; 6 new paving, a contractor's name fresh-cut, and a dead surveyor in the ditch.

The Lanes, the Harbours and the Lamps New · Hellenoria

Category: Infrastructure · Run by: the harbour-wardens (limenophylakes) of each city; wealthy citizens who carry the lamp liturgy; the Hegemon's common fleet on the Long Lane and the Southern Run

Overview

Hellenoria barely bothers with roads. Its highways are water: the Long Lane from Hellarchon to Corinth and Thessalonika, the Southern Run to Helionyx and Ephelanum, the wind-strait of the Aeolus Reach. A League city builds a harbour instead: a mole, ship-sheds, a chain across the mouth and a tower with a fire on the headland. The great land works are the Sacred Way to Delphara, kept by the Amphictyony, and Corinth's Haulway.

How it works
  • The harbour-wardens. Elected each year, they collect the pentekoste, two parts in a hundred on cargo in and out, and spend it on dredging, moles and moorings. The surplus goes to the assembly, so the dredging is always late.
  • The lamp liturgy. A lighthouse is not paid from taxes. Each year a rich citizen is named to keep the light, as another is named to fit out a warship. He buys the oil and pitch and pays the keepers. A citizen who thinks a richer man was passed over may challenge him to take the duty or swap estates.
  • The lanes. The Hegemon's fleet sweeps the Long Lane and the Southern Run; everything else, whoever owns the nearest harbour.
Now

The war cost many harbours their lamps, and relighting them has become a quiet contest. Hellarchon relights the lamps on its own lanes and lets the small cities' towers stay dark, so trade routes past them. Tyrants refuse the liturgy and seize the harbour dues. On the Reach the Wreckers' Beacon keeps a light that is not always where the rocks are, and Keeper Damokles asks every sailor what the ship carries.

At the table

Harbour dues are 2% of cargo value in and again out. A night passage on a lane with no lit lamp needs a Navigation check (Wisdom, water vehicles) DC 15, DC 18 in Nereid's Veil; failure by 5 or more puts the ship on rocks for 4d10 bludgeoning to the hull. A character who carries the lamp liturgy for a year pays about 1,500 drachmas and gains advantage on Persuasion with that city's assembly for the next. Harbour, d6: 1 lamp lit, dues honest; 2 lamp dark, keeper unpaid; 3 a tyrant's men collecting double; 4 moorings silted, lighter ashore at 5 sp a load; 5 Hegemon's guard-ship checking manifests; 6 a liturgy challenge in the agora.

The Royal Road and its Stations New · Acheaoria

Category: Infrastructure · Run by: the station-masters of the throne; the rahdar (road-wardens) of each satrapy; caravanserais endowed by the arashshara; the Wheelwalkers, who use it more than anyone

Overview

Acheaoria has one road worth the name, and it is the finest on the continent. The Royal Road runs from Persemenid through Atarabad and Mithratal to Xerastri on the northern frontier, with a post-station at every day's ride. The Garden Road runs to Persevalis. The road follows the Qanat Line, because a station needs water; where the water fails, the road fails.

How it works
  • The station. A walled yard, a well or qanat outlet, stables, a storehouse and a station-master paid by the throne. Couriers with the King's seal change horses here; anyone else pays.
  • The toll. One silver piece per beast per station, collected by the station-master and owed upward to the satrap, who owes it to Persemenid.
  • The rahdar. Satrapal road-wardens patrol between stations and hang bandits at them.
  • The caravanserais. Between the stations, inns for caravans are endowed by arashshara and great houses, who name them, own them, and keep their wells.
  • The bridges. Stone where the throne built them, lashed boats where the satrap did. A boat bridge belongs to whoever holds the rope.
Now

The tolls still come in. They no longer go out. Satraps keep the money and stop paying station-masters, who then sell the fodder, the horses and finally the roof beams. North of Mithratal one station in three is unmanned. The Wheelwalkers have moved into several and run them better than the throne did, which the throne has not noticed and the satraps have.

At the table

Toll: 1 sp per beast per station; a sealed royal pass waives it. A manned station sells a fresh horse for 15 gp or swaps one for the party's own tired mount at 3 gp, and its master will witness a document or a death. Station, d6: 1 manned and honest; 2 manned, master selling the King's horses to the satrap's men; 3 empty, well fouled (Survival DC 13 to find the next water); 4 run by Wheelwalker cousins, toll halved for anyone they like; 5 rahdar hanging a man they say was a bandit; 6 a royal courier dying in the yard, sealed message in his fist.

Medicine, Plague and Quarantine

The war killed more by fever than by the sword, and every empire learned the same lesson differently: who decides a ship is clean decides who eats.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Heartwardens and the ShedsThe Physicians, the Apothecaries and the Dreaming CurePurity and the Three Medicines
Run byThe Radiant Heartwardens (healing); the Aurum Pact (quarantine), under Febris's shrinePublic physicians paid by each city; the Luminastra Alchemists; the Asklepian sanctuariesThe Magi, who decide what is pure; herb-healers and surgeons under them; the River's Embrace on water
How it worksHospitals in every major city; forty days in the isolation sheds for any suspect cargo, and an uncontested certificateFree surgeries for citizens, standardised remedies by batch, sleep in the god's dormitory for a dreamHealing by knife, by herb and by holy word, in that order of respect; impurity is the first illness
Breaking pointThe veterans' wounds outlast the hospitals; the Pact's certificate is for saleCities close their harbours by vote and starve their neighboursNeglected qanats breed fever the Magi call impurity and the satraps call someone else's problem
At the tableA certificate opens a portA batch mark is evidenceA Magus's word is a quarantine
The Heartwardens and the Sheds New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Society · Run by: the Radiant Heartwardens under Archiater Valeria Salvia; the Aurum Pact under the Master of the Sheds, Septimus Febronius Siccus; licensed physicians of the collegia

Overview

The Imperium treats the sick with one order and the dangerous with another. The Radiant Heartwardens, Asclepius's physicians, staff the military hospitals and public infirmaries of every major city, from their mother-infirmary at the Duneforged Citadel. The Aurum Pact, Febris's merchants, hold the quarantine: the isolation sheds outside every Invictian port, and the certificate that says a hold is clean. The Heartwardens decide who can be saved; the Pact decides what can move.

How it works
  • The infirmary. Heartwardens treat anyone for a fee scaled to rank, soldiers free. By oath they will not serve a siege: no poisoned wells, no advice on how disease will spread.
  • The sheds. A suspect ship unloads into the Pact's isolation sheds and waits forty days. Crew wait with it. At Mavelon the sheds stand at the end of the Farshore mole; at Fucostia they stand outside the walls, where inspector Ysolde Varn signs.
  • The certificate. The one document a harbour prefect cannot overrule; the Mithril Reserve insures against it.
Now

The military hospitals have emptied and the veterans' wounds have not healed. The Heartwardens want a public infirmary on the Campus Hastarum and cannot get the land. Men with ruined legs and no pensions go instead to the Mending Needle, which mends cheaply and collects later. Farshore trade has made the Pact rich. Patients who can travel go to the springs at Napplesia.

At the table

A Heartwarden infirmary bed costs 5 sp a day; a cure wounds 10 gp, lesser restoration 40 gp, free for a soldier with his discharge tablet. A Pact certificate costs 1 gp per ton of cargo, or 50 gp on the side for a hold nobody inspected. Forty days in the sheds: each week, every character makes a DC 11 Constitution save or catches a fever (sewer plague rules). Sheds, d6: 1 clean and dull; 2 the fever is real; 3 a merchant offering 200 gp to be let out early; 4 Febris's priest says the goddess has left, so the ship may go; 5 a rival's cargo held one day too long; 6 a sick man who is not on the manifest.

The Physicians, the Apothecaries and the Dreaming Cure New · Hellenoria

Category: Society · Run by: each city's public physician (demosios iatros), elected by the assembly; the Luminastra Alchemists under Archiatros Iasonides Phoibammon; the priests of the Asklepian sanctuaries

Overview

A League city hires its doctor the way it hires a general: by vote, for a year, with a salary from the treasury. Medicine in Hellenoria is three trades that do not much like each other. The public physicians argue from observation and charge citizens nothing. The Luminastra Alchemists, Apollo's apothecaries, sell remedies by the marked batch from their great workshop at Corinth. The Asklepian cult heals by sleep: the sick lie down in the god's dormitory and dream the cure.

How it works
  • The public physician. Elected, salaried, obliged to treat any citizen free. Hellarchon's Public Physician's Surgery stands by the customs house in the Emporion.
  • The batch. Every Luminastra preparation carries a batch mark and a record. A member who cannot produce the record of a compound he sold is expelled. Courts accept nothing else as evidence of good faith.
  • The dormitory. At an Asklepian sanctuary the patient bathes, sacrifices a cockerel, sleeps in the long hall and tells the priests the dream. The priests interpret.
  • The plague vote. No standing quarantine: in an outbreak the assembly votes to close the harbour, which takes three days, which is too long.
Now

Tyrants have abolished the public physician in two cities and kept the salary. The Luminastra guild hunts Willowheart's midwifery method; one of the two midwives Willowheart expelled now works for it at Ephelanum. Delphara's Dream Dormitory has begun asking patients about a dark-haired woman in their dreams, which is not medicine.

At the table

A citizen is treated free; anyone else pays 2 drachmas a visit. A Luminastra antitoxin costs 55 gp with batch mark, 25 gp without, and the unmarked one is genuine on a d6 roll of 4+. A night in an Asklepian dormitory costs a cockerel and a 5 gp offering: roll d20 + Wisdom modifier. On 15+ the dream names a true remedy and the next long rest ends one disease or poison; on 5 or less, the dream belongs to someone else (DM's choice of vision, or a clue in the Dreamers' Hunt).

Purity and the Three Medicines New · Acheaoria

Category: Religion · Run by: the Magi, who rule on purity; healers by knife and herb who work under their licence; the River's Embrace, who gauge the water; the Benevolent Hands, where no one else comes

Overview

In Acheaoria illness begins as impurity. The Magi teach three medicines, ranked: the knife, the herb, and the holy word, and the holy word heals best because it heals the cause. A corpse, a dead dog in a channel, blood on a threshold: these pollute, and the polluted sicken. So the Magi are the quarantine, and they enforce it with the threat that matters most: nobody may take an oath from an impure man.

How it works
  • The ruling. A Magus declares a person, house or well impure. Purification takes nine days of washing with water, sand and the cleansing rite. Until then no one eats with them.
  • The corpse-bearers. Impure by trade, paid well, married only among themselves. They carry the dead to the towers.
  • The healers. Surgeons and herb-healers are licensed by the fire-temple and pay it a tithe.
  • The water. The River's Embrace keeps the gauges and tells the Magi when a channel has gone bad. The muqanni who clean the qanats know first and are asked last.
Now

Satraps who withhold tribute also withhold the muqanni's wages. Untended qanats silt, the water stands, and the "qanat fevers" come with the summer: shaking, yellow eyes, a bad week, sometimes a grave. The Magi call it impurity and close the well. At Atarabad, under Mobad Atar-Farnbag, the most conservative Magi in the empire have closed four wells this year, and the Benevolent Hands are carrying water to the streets that drank from them.

At the table

Qanat fever: drinking from a neglected channel forces a DC 12 Constitution save; on a failure, 1 level of exhaustion and disadvantage on Constitution checks for 1d6 days; a second failure adds another level. A Magus's purification costs 5 gp and nine days; a lesser restoration from a fire-temple 30 gp, and only for the pure. Touching a corpse, or casting fire into water, earns impurity: no fire-temple or satrapal court receives the character for nine days. Well, d6: 1 sweet; 2 fouled, unmarked; 3 closed by the Magi; 4 a muqanni who will clean it for 1 gp a day; 5 a body in the shaft; 6 a Benevolent Hands water-cart.

Schools, Guilds and Apprenticeship

Every empire teaches its children to serve it, and every empire is short of teachers, because the war took the young men and the peace has not paid the old ones.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Collegia and the MasterpieceThe Gymnasion, the Academy and the PorticoesThe Tablet-House, the Workshop and the Archive
Run byLicensed collegia (the Artisan's Forge of Wonders, the Luminous Arcanists and a hundred trade guilds); schoolmasters for coinEach city's gymnasiarch; the Arcane Academy under Scholarch Kallisto Pyrphoros; free philosophers in rented colonnadesScribal masters licensed by the throne; arashshara who run the workshops; the Illuminated Scholars and the Magi's schools
How it worksA written apprenticeship, seven years, a masterpiece, a seal; the collegium answers for its members in courtCitizen boys train body and mind in the gymnasion; mages are certified by examination; philosophy is sold by the lectureClay and ink for the scribes, the loom for the workshop girls, petition and patience for the archive
Breaking pointVeterans with no trade and no apprenticeship crowd the guild doorsThe Academy keeps its monopoly; the gymnasion is a club for the richLiteracy is a state secret, and the state is breaking into pieces that each want scribes
At the tableA seal ring is a licenceAnyone may object, and the master must answerA scribe can read what the seal says; the patron cannot
The Collegia and the Masterpiece New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Society · Run by: the licensed collegia, chartered by the Senate and regulated by the praetors; the Artisan's Forge of Wonders under Magistra Opificum Tullia Sollers; the Luminous Arcanists under Lector Primus Marcus Clarius Scriptor; private schoolmasters

Overview

The Imperium does not educate its children. It licenses the people who do. A boy learns letters from a schoolmaster under a colonnade awning, for a few coppers a month and a cane, if there is a coin that month. Then he learns a trade, and the trade belongs to a collegium. A collegium is guild, burial club and court witness at once: it examines its members and answers for them before a praetor. In magic, a casting licence is a collegium's seal ring.

How it works
  • The tablet. Apprenticeship is a written contract between a father and a master: years of service (usually seven), board and clothing, and a penalty if either breaks it. It is filed with the collegium.
  • The masterpiece. At the end the apprentice presents a piece, not a speech. The Artisan's Forge of Wonders judges the object; the Luminous Arcanists make a candidate transcribe a working in notation and have a stranger cast it.
  • The grammaticus. The well-born go on to a grammar teacher and a rhetor, then the Cursus Honorum. The Lexicon at Aeterna, under Quintus Arminius, keeps the standard texts.
Now

The legions taught a million men a trade the peace does not want. Veterans crowd the collegium doors asking to be taken as apprentices at forty, and the collegia, paid in debased coin, are raising their entry fees to keep them out. Mavelon's arsenal school takes Mavari boys as apprentices, and the guild halls are filling with their marks.

At the table

Joining a collegium costs 25 gp and a sponsor; a seal ring lets a mage cast in a city without a magistrate's question. Training a tool proficiency through a collegium takes 200 days at 1 gp a day, halved for a character who already holds a related one. A veteran with the Soldier background may substitute service for half the fee. Collegium hall, d6: 1 examination day; 2 a burial collection; 3 a forged seal; 4 veterans at the door; 5 a praetor's summons for botched work; 6 a master who will take an adult apprentice, for a favour.

The Gymnasion, the Academy and the Porticoes New · Hellenoria

Category: Society · Run by: each city's gymnasiarch, a wealthy citizen who funds the oil and the teachers; the Arcane Academy of Hellarchon under Scholarch Kallisto Pyrphoros; the philosophers of the porticoes

Overview

A League citizen is made in the gymnasion. It is an exercise ground, a school and the citizens' club in one: boys wrestle and run in the morning and learn letters, music and Homeric verse in the afternoon, and at eighteen they serve two years as ephebes and swear the oath. Above that are two roads. The mages go to the Arcane Academy at Hellarchon. Everyone with a question goes to the porticoes, where philosophers rent the space between two columns and teach in public.

How it works
  • The gymnasiarch. A rich citizen names himself to the duty for a year and pays for the oil, the trainers and the teachers.
  • The Academy. A student is attached to one school and examined twice; after the second he is a certified mage. He owes the Academy one contract a season: a ward to keep, a ship to fireproof, an expedition to escort.
  • The porticoes. At Thessalonika the gymnasiarch Nikomachos Stoabiou auctions the south-facing bays by the year. A student pays by the lecture or not at all. A master who cannot answer an objection loses his students to the objector.
Now

The gymnasion was always for citizens, and now it is for rich ones: two cities have let theirs become private clubs. Atticenea still exports philosophers because it cannot feed them. The Academy wants the Invictian notation kept secret. Krates the Dog teaches in the Porticoes for nothing and sleeps in a jar.

At the table

A gymnasion membership costs 10 drachmas a year for a citizen, and is not for sale to anyone else. An Academy place costs 300 drachmas a year and an entrance trial (Intelligence (Arcana) DC 15); certification at the second examination grants an Academy seal, which lets a mage lodge with a proxenos by right. To win students in the Porticoes, make a contested Intelligence (Persuasion or Religion) check against the master in the next bay; the winner takes 1d6 drachmas a day from the loser's audience. Lose three days running and the bay goes to auction.

The Tablet-House, the Workshop and the Archive New · Acheaoria

Category: Society · Run by: scribal masters licensed by the throne; the arashshara who run the royal and house workshops; the Illuminated Scholars under Archivist-General Mehrnush Dabir; the Magi's schools for priests

Overview

In Acheaoria most nobles cannot read, and do not need to: they have scribes. Writing is a profession, not an accomplishment, and the empire runs on the men and women who can do it. A scribe learns in a tablet-house, six years of clay and ink in three scripts. A craftswoman learns in an arashshara's workshop, a priest from a herbad at the fire-temple. A noble child learns horses and the bow, and at Persemenid the Court of Pages teaches them to stand still for three hours.

How it works
  • The tablet-house. A master scribe takes boys and girls at seven. The best go to the satrap's chancery, the treasury or the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger.
  • The workshop. Arashshara run the weaving, pottery and dye workshops, and teach the workers: at Persevalis a girl becomes a weaver the day she can read the coded patterns, which record more than designs.
  • The archive. The Illuminated Scholars copy everything and lend almost nothing. Access needs a petition, a purpose and a wait. Members never own a copy. At Mithratal's Archive Ward the registrars swear the Dadvar oath not to sleep outside it.
Now

Every satrap who has stopped forwarding tribute needs scribes of his own, and is hiring them away from the throne's chanceries at double pay. The Sage's Archive has started reading old inscriptions that do not match the court's history, and its students are learning to read the ones nobody can.

At the table

A hired scribe costs 2 sp a day, 5 sp if he can read all three scripts; he can read a sealed document the party cannot, and may lie about it (Insight DC 14). A petition to the Illuminated Scholars costs 5 gp and a d6 wait: 1–2 days, 3–4 months, 5 a year, 6 refused. Learning Acheaorian script in a tablet-house takes 250 days at 1 gp a day. A character taught by an arashshara can read a workshop's woven records with an Intelligence check DC 13, and learns who owes whom.

Labour, Debt and Slavery

Every empire on Asetheria was built by people who did not choose the work. Five years of peace have flooded all three markets with hands: captives nobody ransomed, soldiers nobody paid, and debtors nobody will forgive.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Familia and the Freedman's CapHands, Metics and the Silver DemeThe Ration Tablet and the Subject Levy
Run byMasters under the praetor's edict; the latifundia owners; the census of the AnnonaEach city's slave market and deme roll; the poletai who lease the silver galleriesThe arashshara who allot rations; the azata of the zarates; the satraps' levy-clerks
How it worksChattel slaves work the estates and the houses; manumission makes a citizen with a patron for lifeSlaves are owned and rented out by the day; metics earn wages; debt-slavery of citizens is forbiddenKurtash labourers work for portions recorded on clay; subject peoples owe labour by the season
Breaking pointWar-captives are cheap and veterans are idle, so free men cannot find wagesCaptive prices have collapsed; the silver galleries kill a man a dayRations short-weighted, levies called twice, conquered peoples counting the difference
At the tableA freedman owes his patron; collect the debt or inherit the feudEvery skilled hand in a harbour may belong to someone the party has insultedA ration tablet is a passport, a pay slip and a debt ledger in one
The Familia and the Freedman's Cap New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Society · Run by: masters under the praetor's edict; the latifundia owners; Sextus Naevius Macer's Annona rolls for freedmen's citizenship

Overview

In Invictian law a household, the familia, is everyone under the master's power: wife, children, slaves and cattle, in roughly that order of legal standing. Fifteen centuries of conquest filled the familia with captives. The great estates inland of Ephelanum and on the Latium Plains, the latifundia, are worked by slave gangs who sleep in locked barracks, and the red-earth estates the Dux holds under the condominium are the worst of them. In the city, slaves are cooks, clerks, tutors and doctors, and a clever one can run his master's business better than the master.

How it works
  • The peculium. A slave may hold money "as if his own", a fund the master can take back but rarely does. Slaves save it to buy their freedom.
  • Manumission. Before a magistrate with a touch of the rod, by will at the master's death, or by entry in the census. The freedman takes his master's family name, a felt cap and citizenship, and owes his patron attendance, respect and work-days for life.
  • Debt. Citizens cannot be sold for debt, but a debtor can be seized and made to work it off on the creditor's land, which on a latifundium looks much the same.
  • Wages. A free labourer earns 1 denarius a day, in coin that buys less every quarter.
Now

The war's last captives were sold cheap, so a landowner can buy a field-hand for less than a year of a free man's wages. Millions of demobilised legionaries, promised land, find the land worked by slaves and themselves hired for harvest only. In Aeterna rich freedmen such as the Herennian clerks now outspend the patricians who freed them, and the patricians have not forgiven it.

At the table

Slave prices: field-hand 60 gp, skilled clerk or craftsman 200–500 gp, physician or tutor up to 1,500 gp. A slave buys freedom at his price plus a twentieth to the treasury. A freedman PC owes his patron three days' work a month; refusing invites a lawsuit for ingratitude (Persuasion DC 15 before a praetor, disadvantage if the patron is patrician). Inheriting a patron's freedmen gives the party their loyalty and their quarrels: roll d6 for a freedman's favour (1–3 information, 4–5 a loan of 100 gp, 6 a door into his old master's house).

Hands, Metics and the Silver Deme New · Hellenoria

Category: Society · Run by: each city's slave market and deme roll; the poletai (sellers) who lease the silver galleries; the metics' citizen sponsors

Overview

A League city calls a slave "a hand" and counts them as it counts oars. Hands row the merchant fleets, dig the clay, keep the tables of the bankers and sweep the agora. Metics, free foreigners with a citizen sponsor, do the skilled work for wages and own no land. Citizens vote, serve on juries and, in the great democracies, are proud of not working for another man. The arrangement rests on a law the cities treat as a founding myth: no citizen may be sold for debt. Long ago a lawgiver tore up the debt-stones on the fields of Hellarchon, and every citizen learns the story at the deme.

How it works
  • The silver deme. The silver galleries of Argyreia, two days from Hellarchon's harbour, are owned by the city and leased in lots to contractors by the poletai. The contractors work them with hired hands, a thousand to a lessee, in shafts a man crawls through.
  • Hiring out. A master rents a skilled hand by the day (2 obols to the master, 1 to the hand) and the hand lives where he likes. Many save and buy themselves out, becoming metics.
  • Manumission. By dedication at a temple: the god buys the slave for a price the slave has paid in, and the deed is cut on the temple wall. Some obligations remain until the old master dies.
  • Debt. Metics and foreigners can still be held for debt. Bankers in Corinth hold debtors in "the cellars" until a relative pays.
Now

Captives from the last campaigns flooded the markets, and a hand now sells for half the pre-treaty price. The galleries of Argyreia have doubled their crews and halved their care. Shipwrights in Hellarchon's yards are metics who strike when wages fall, and the shipowners answer by buying hands.

At the table

Hiring a skilled hand: 1 drachma a day. Buying one: 100–300 drachmas. A day in the Argyreia galleries: Con save DC 13 or one level of exhaustion; a week in the deep lots, DC 15. The party can buy a slave's freedom at a temple for his price plus 20 drachmas for the cutting; a freed metic ally gives advantage on Insight and Investigation in his trade's quarter.

The Ration Tablet and the Subject Levy New · Acheaoria

Category: Society · Run by: the arashshara, who allot rations and sign for output; the azata of the zarates; the satraps' levy-clerks

Overview

Acheaoria keeps fewer chattel slaves than its neighbours and says so loudly. What it keeps instead is labour owed. The kurtash work the royal estates, the palace workshops and the qanat crews on rations of barley, beer and wine, recorded on clay tablets by the arashshara. They are not sold in markets. They are assigned, moved and inherited with the estate. Above them stand free farmers who hold water shares, and around them the subject peoples, who owe the King tribute in goods and labour by the season.

How it works
  • Portions. A kurtash man draws thirty measures of barley a month, a woman twenty, a skilled craftswoman more than a man. Extra for a birth. The tablet hung at the neck is proof of who you belong to.
  • The levy. Subject peoples owe a season's work on the Royal Road, the qanats or a satrap's palace. Their own headmen pick who goes.
  • Debt. A farmer who cannot pay his water dues pledges his share, then his labour, then his children's. The Vaults of Equilibrium lend against the pledge.
  • Release. A satrap may free a household on a royal feast-day; a Magus may free one who served a fire-temple for seven years.
Now

Neglected satrapies short-weight the rations and call the levy twice in a year. At Persemenid the palace still feeds its kurtash in full, because the King's tablets are audited. Subject veterans home from the frontier have found their families pledged for water dues in their absence.

At the table

A kurtash tablet forged or bought (25 gp) lets a stranger walk any royal estate unquestioned until someone checks the register (Investigation DC 14 by an arashshara's clerk). Freeing a pledged household costs its water debt: 50–200 gp. Each season a subject village is levied twice, roll d6: 1–4 grumbling, 5 the headman asks the party for help, 6 the levy-clerk is found in a qanat shaft.

Crime and the Underworld

Peace was good for thieves. The roads opened, the soldiers came home with nothing, and every empire's watch is still organised to catch spies, not burglars.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Collegia of the NightThe Harbour BrotherhoodsThe Ceiling and the Creed
Run byThe Prismatic Shroud and the Tenebral Covenant; street collegia; the Vigiles who should stop themThe Tenebral Covenant at Corinth; informers; the Eleven and their archersThe Veilborn Syndicate in the bazaars; the Eyes and Ears; the Lanterns of Justice
How it worksCrime is organised like a trade guild with a patron and a shrineCrime is a business partner of the shipowners and a weapon in politicsCrime is tolerated under a ceiling and crushed above it
Breaking pointVeterans for hire; illusion fraud on Farshore cargoesStolen letters decide elections; informers outnumber thievesSomeone broke the ceiling at Atarabad and the satrap wants a culprit
At the tableA fence wants a patron's name before he wants the goodsProsecute a thief and his employer prosecutes youSteal small and you are a nuisance; steal big and you are a rebel
The Collegia of the Night New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Crime · Run by: the Prismatic Shroud, the Tenebral Covenant and a hundred street collegia; opposed by the Vigiles under Titus Oppius Ursus and the Speculatores Interni

Overview

Invictians organise everything into collegia, and crime is no exception. A neighbourhood collegium of "crossroads-keepers" registers a shrine, elects a magister, holds a feast for the Lares each spring and runs the protection on every shop in the block. The Senate banned such clubs three times and licensed them twice. Above the street sit two professional houses: the Prismatic Shroud, working out of the glass-sellers' arcade at Romulo with a counterfeiting room at Mavelon's north harbour, and the Tenebral Covenant, whose safe-house in Aeterna steals letters and seals rather than silver.

How it works
  • The Vigiles. Seven cohorts of freedmen fire-fighters in Aeterna, who also patrol at night and arrest petty thieves. Serious crime goes to the Prefect of the Vigiles, Titus Oppius Ursus, who has more fires than men.
  • The courts. There is no public prosecutor. A victim must bring a thief before the praetor himself, which means a victim needs a patron, and the thief usually has a better one.
  • Fences. Goods move through freedmen's shops on the Subura and through the Shroud's arcade, where a stolen object can be sold back to its owner under an illusion of being something else.
  • The Speculatores. The Praetorian Custodians' agents ignore theft entirely unless it touches a seal, a Legate or magic.
Now

Discharged legionaries hire out as muscle by the century, with their old officers as captains. The Shroud has learned to switch Farshore cargoes between the quay at Mavelon and the Hall of Weights at Romulo. A cargo sealed in Romulo and opened in Aeterna as sand is now the commonest lawsuit in the capital.

At the table

Protection costs a shop 2 sp a week; a tavern 5 sp. A fence pays a quarter of value, a third with a patron's name he recognises. To prosecute a thief: find a patron (a favour), then Persuasion DC 13 before the praetor, or DC 18 if the thief belongs to a collegium with a senator's freedman as its magister. Hiring a veteran crew: 1 gp a man a day, and they bring their own swords.

The Harbour Brotherhoods New · Hellenoria

Category: Crime · Run by: the Tenebral Covenant at Corinth; the harbour brotherhoods; informers; opposed by each city's Eleven and their public archers

Overview

A League city has no police in any sense an Invictian would recognise. A board of magistrates called the Eleven keeps the prison and executes sentences, and a few hundred public slaves armed with bows keep order in the agora and the assembly. Everything else is private. A citizen who catches a burglar at night may kill him. A citizen who wants a thief tried prosecutes him himself. Into that gap step the harbour brotherhoods: dining clubs of dockers, oarsmen and fishermen who swear an oath on a shared cup, protect their members and rent out their muscle.

How it works
  • The Covenant. At Corinth the Tenebral Covenant runs as a politics shop. It steals letters, alibis and ballots, and it stole one election outright. Its fence is on Zandar Isle.
  • The informers. Anyone may prosecute, and the prosecutor takes a share of the fine. Professional informers threaten merchants with prosecution and accept a fee not to bring it. Many are better paid than thieves.
  • Protection. Brotherhoods sell harbour safety by the cargo: a fee per hold, collected on the quay.
  • The Truth-Flame. Inquisitor Vireon has no interest in theft, only in stolen texts, which is how the Covenant's letter trade sometimes ends at his court.
Now

In Hellarchon the shipowning houses employ the brotherhoods to break metic shipwrights' strikes, and the brotherhoods expect protection in return. Tyrants' cities have no such problem: the tyrant's bodyguard is the only gang, and it collects.

At the table

Harbour protection: 1 drachma per hold per call. Hiring a brotherhood for a night: 10 drachmas a man. An informer's threat costs 20–50 drachmas to settle; refusing means a jury trial (see the jury courts). A stolen letter from the Covenant sells at 50 drachmas a page, more if it names a Treaty Guest. If the party prosecutes a brotherhood member, roll d6: 1–3 he is acquitted, 4–5 he is fined and his brothers visit the prosecutor, 6 the brotherhood counter-sues for impiety.

The Ceiling and the Creed New · Acheaoria

Category: Crime · Run by: the Veilborn Syndicate under Old Shabnam, the Ceiling-Keeper; the King's Eyes and Ears under Utana Gushdar; the Lanterns of Justice

Overview

Acheaoria handles organised crime the way it handles satraps: by agreement, until the agreement is broken. In the bazaars of Atarabad and Persemenid the Veilborn Syndicate steals under a ceiling: nothing above a certain value, nothing from a temple, nothing from the Gilded Vault. Its members who breach it are punished by the Syndicate before the satrap hears. A guild that costs a satrap less than a crackdown is never cracked down on, and the Syndicate has survived three centuries on that arithmetic.

How it works
  • The bazaar wardens. Each bazaar has wardens appointed by the arashshara, who fix weights, settle quarrels and keep the gates. They know every Veilborn by sight and take a cut called "the dust".
  • The Eyes and Ears. The King's inspectors watch officials, not thieves. A theft that embarrasses a satrap reaches them; a stolen purse never does.
  • The Lanterns. Roving magistrates sworn to Hakiyah who hear cases the local court will not touch. A Lantern who arrives with his lamp lit gives a thief a day to return the goods.
  • The creed. Above all this the assassin creed does what it is paid to do. It is not a crime syndicate in Acheaorian law. It is a hazard of court.
Now

This year's courier robberies at Atarabad broke the ceiling, and they were not the Syndicate's. The satrap wants a culprit, the Syndicate wants the real thieves found first, and both have begun hiring outsiders, which is to say the party.

At the table

The ceiling is about 50 gp: below it, a caught thief is beaten and fined double the value; above it, he loses a hand or his life. The Syndicate fences at a third of value and takes its fifth. Bribing a bazaar warden: 5 gp a week to be overlooked. If a Lantern rides into town while the party holds stolen goods, return them before nightfall or face judgment without appeal; Persuasion DC 16 to explain, with advantage if the goods are returned in front of him.

The Trade in Magic

All three empires agree that magic is too useful to forbid and too dangerous to leave unlicensed. They disagree about who should hold the licence, and the black market lives in the gap.

Imperium InvictaHellenoriaAcheaoria
NameThe Licensed Collegia and the Glass ArcadeThe Academy Seal and the Ship-WizardThe Temple Licence and the Bazaar of Lamps
Run byThe Artisan's Forge of Wonders and the Luminous Arcanists; the Speculatores InterniThe Arcane Academy under Kallisto Pyrphoros; the Lexicon Council; the Truth-FlameThe Magi, who license by temple; the arashshara, who license shops
How it worksOnly a collegium member may cast for pay or sell an item; the collegium takes a tenthAny certified mage may sell; the Lexicon stamps books; uncertified mages are tolerated by tyrantsCasters buy purification and pay the temple; items are sold by weight in licensed stalls
Breaking pointFrozen Nethranan illusions sold to patriciansMycairan bronze coming up from the silver demeSatraps buying war-magic without the Magi
At the tablePrices are fixed and receipts are evidencePrices are open and the seller may be a hereticPrices include a purification and a bribe
The Licensed Collegia and the Glass Arcade New · Imperium Invicta

Category: Magic · Run by: the Artisan's Forge of Wonders (makers) and the Luminous Arcanists (scholars); enforced by the Speculatores Interni; insured by the Mithril Reserve

Overview

In the Imperium magic is a trade, and trades have collegia.
