The conscript shafts of the first two satraps, now rubble-choked rings with a cairn of names beside each. Air comes up out of them steadily, cold, smelling of wet stone, though no water has ever been found in either. Shepherds use the second as a windbreak and claim it breathes in at night.

Ties: the muqanni guilds; the satrap's survey office.

The Snow Cistern New · summit hollow

Ice bowl below the peak · climbers, rarely · thin air, nothing

A bowl under the summit where the snowmelt pools and then goes nowhere, draining into the rock through a funnel too smooth to be natural. A haoma plant grows at its lip. The Magi say this is impossible, and one of them climbs up every few years to say it again.

Ties: the Magi; the Div.

What lives here

  • The Div of Kharveth — a hulking, horned shape deep in the mountain that does not want company.
  • Plateau rock-leopard (use panther) — the Leopard's Ledge at dusk.
  • Bone-breaker (use vulture) — circles the Ledge and drops bones from height.
  • Giant bats and bat swarms — out of the sealed shaft at sunset.
  • Earth elementals — in the Cinnabar Shafts; the collapses were not all geology.
  • Horned wild sheep (use giant goat) — the high scree.
  • Ghouls — dead convicts in the deep galleries, still mining.

What can be gathered

  • Alabaster — the Cuttings; a lamp-bowl 5 sp, a perfume jar 2 gp, a burial urn 10 gp.
  • Cinnabar — the Shafts; quicksilver and vermilion, 10 gp a pound, and a ruined body for the cutter.
  • Devil's gold — the cap-rock; worthless, sold to fools as gold.
  • Sacred haoma — the Snow Cistern lip; the Magi's sacrament, priceless and unsellable.
  • Leopard pelt — the Ledge; 50 gp, and the Predator's Guild's displeasure without a licence.

Who goes there

  • The muqanni guilds hereditary qanat-diggers — on strike rather than dig; their master, Ostad Peshang Kariz, says only "spoken for".
  • Satrap Artavasdes Nikbin new satrap of the plateau — wants wells, a legacy, and to be the one who was right.
  • Overseer Varaz the Red-Handed master of the Cinnabar Shafts — has a convict uprising coming and knows it.
  • The Magi — climb to the Snow Cistern, take a haoma cutting, and offer no doctrine.
  • Predator's Guild — licenses the leopard and protects it, against the shepherds.

Wild · Acheaoria · Frontier gorge

Parthian Ravine

Sixty miles of red rock and loud gravel on the eastern frontier: the only road an army can take, and the one place no army has ever taken.

Codex now: A dry gorge on the Acheaorian frontier, three days long and never once successfully forced — the shot that killed you comes from behind.

Claimed by
Acheaoria; held for the throne by the Warden of the Ravine at Xerastri
Terrain
Dry gorge, red cliffs, gravel floor, side-wadis
Travel
3 days to cross · Survival DC 13 (DC 17 at night)
Danger
Moderate (CR 1–5); High after dark
Trouble
Disbanded horse-archers turning toll-takers

The land

The Ravine cuts sixty miles through the Acheaorian frontier. Its walls of red rock close in places until two carts cannot pass, and its floor is gravel, which is loud. It is the only practical road east for an army, and trying it has cost the Imperium Invicta more legionaries than any battle of the long war.

The Acheaorian defence never involved holding it. Light horse met a column at the mouth, engaged, broke and fled up the gorge. The column, smelling collapse, pursued into ground where it could not form line, and the fleeing riders turned in the saddle and shot backwards without slowing. The manoeuvre is old enough that the Imperium named it after the place: Invictian officers still call any victory that turns out to be the first half of a defeat "a Parthian win". The floor is thick with arrowheads. Locals gather them by the sack, but not after dark, because the gravel is loud, and on certain nights it is loud in a rhythm nobody is making.

New lore

The treaty made the Ravine a road instead of a trap, and the throne has not adjusted. The horse-archer companies who held it for fifteen centuries were paid off in the first year of peace with land grants the satrap of Xerastri has not yet surveyed. Several companies stayed in the side-wadis anyway, and now "escort" caravans for a fee that looks a great deal like the old Imperial tolls they used to shoot at. Roxana Surena, Warden of the Parthian Ravine, rides out of Xerastri with forty riders and a writ that lets her hang anyone who charges for passage without a royal seal. She has hanged two. She has also quietly sealed eleven, because a company with a seal patrols the gorge for free.

Pilgrims have started coming the other way: Invictian veterans walking east on the Royal Road's spur to find where their friends died. The gravel-gatherers sell them arrowheads "from your cohort's day" at a silver denarius apiece. The denarius is debased, so both sides think they won.

Sites

The Kohl Workings Existing · Mine

Women's trade · shallow pits and grinding-sheds · grey dust and mutton fat

A scatter of shallow pits along the gorge where women and boys dig a soft, shining grey-black stone and carry it to the grinding-sheds at the mouth. Ground fine and worked into fat, it becomes the eye-paint worn from the palace to the caravan road. Cheap at the pit, dear at court; the difference feeds the gorge. The sheds sell to anyone with a mule and good manners, and the women who run them, under an arashshara named Parisa Kohlzan, do not haggle twice.

Ties: Persemenid court buyers; the Xerastri garrison.

The Pitch Seep Existing · Seep

State secret · garrison post · a sharp smell everyone recognises

A black pool where tar seeps from a crack and spreads over stagnant water, with a clear, sharp-smelling oil floating on top. Bones ring the edge, and gatherers do not wade in without a rope. The seep gives black pitch for hulls and roofs, and the skimmed oil is naphtha, the fluid that burns on water. A garrison post of twenty spearmen guards the pool, and keeps it a state secret from everybody who cannot smell.

Ties: the satrap of Xerastri; Hellenorian buyers curious about anything that rivals Hellenic fire.

The Vulture Crags Existing · Cliffs

Sky-burial · white-streaked rock · thermals and silence

White-streaked cliffs above the gorge, riddled with nests and ringed by wheeling birds from dawn until the thermals fail. The plateau's people lay their dead on the towers at the cliff-foot and let the Sky-Cleaners do the rest. A priest of the rite lives in a hut by the stair and answers questions about the birds, and none about the dead. Mourners use the stair; sightseers are sent to a viewing ledge half a mile off.

Ties: the Magi; the families of Xerastri.

The Narrows of the Turned Saddle New · Battlefield

The tightest point · arrowheads ankle-deep · veterans' cairns

Two days in, the walls come within thirty feet of each other for half a mile. This is where most columns broke. Invictian veterans have begun building small cairns of their dead friends' names scratched on gravel, and the horse-archer companies, to everyone's surprise, leave them alone. Gatherers do not work the Narrows at night. The rhythm on the gravel is strongest here, and it sounds like a column at the march, pace for pace.

Ties: veterans from Aeterna; the Imperial army.

What lives here

  • Warhorse Skeleton — the cavalry of dead columns, ridden on the loud nights.
  • Wight — Invictian centurions still trying to form line in the Narrows.
  • Giant Vulture — the Sky-Cleaners of the Crags, sacred and short-tempered.
  • Magmin — crawl out of the Pitch Seep when the naphtha catches.
  • Giant Lizard — sand monitors basking on the gravel bars.
  • Panther — the King's lynx and rock-leopard, hunting goats on the rim.
  • Scout — horse-archers of the old companies, now "escorts".
  • Tribal Warrior — Savage Pack hunters from beyond the qanat line.

What can be gathered

  • Kohl-Stone — the Workings; 2 cp a basket at the pit, 5 sp an ounce ground at court.
  • Black Pitch — the Seep; 1 sp a lump, sold under licence.
  • Ravine Naphtha — skimmed at the Seep; illegal to carry, 50 gp a sealed flask in the wrong hands.
  • Azurite and Realgar — side-wadis; dye-blue and poison-red, both sold at Xerastri.
  • Arrowheads — anywhere on the floor; bronze, iron and Invictian lead, sold by the sack to smiths and to grief.

Who goes there

  • Roxana Surena Warden of the Parthian Ravine — wants the gorge quiet and the companies sealed, not hanged.
  • The Lion's Mane Vanguard heavy cavalry under Hajama — rides through on parade marches; useless here and proud of it.
  • House Mihran of Xerastri cadet line of the Persemenid zarate, holders of the march — patrons of two of the old companies; they recruit in the wadis for the Cloudspine Feud.
  • Wheelwalkers road-folk under Jauhar — pay every toll, then tell the Warden who charged it.
  • The Savage Pack frontier tribe — trade leopard-skins at the eastern mouth for salt and arrowheads.

Wild · Acheaoria · Dead canal

Xeruezcho Canal

A royal sea-road cut across the desert neck, finished, glorious and dry within a generation; caravans now walk its paved bed and still pay the toll.

Codex now: A royal canal cut across the desert neck to join two seas — finished, magnificent, and abandoned within a generation.

Claimed by
Acheaoria; tolls farmed by the Chyrsus Syndicate
Terrain
Walled, paved canal bed; silted basins; dead locks; desert either side
Travel
5 days end to end in the bed · Survival DC 10 (DC 15 outside the walls)
Danger
Moderate (CR 2–7); High in the basins
Trouble
The sacred River-Dragon is dying

The land

A cut a hundred and twenty miles long and wide enough for two galleys abreast, driven across the desert neck by a King of Kings whose name has been struck from the stelae at both ends but not from the annals. It worked. For about one generation ships passed from sea to sea without unloading, the tolls were enormous, and Acheaoria ran a route no rival could reach. Stelae every ten miles announced, in four scripts, that the King of Kings had commanded the sea to join the sea, and it had obeyed.

Then it silted. The engineers had solved gradient, banks and locks; they had not solved sand, which arrives without a schedule and does not stop. Dredging cost more each year than the tolls returned. The court stopped recording the dredging figures, then stopped dredging. Long dry stretches remain, walled and paved, running arrow-straight into nothing. Caravans use them as roads: the bed is level and the walls give shade. The tolls are still collected, now for walking along the bottom of a sea-road that holds no water.

New lore

The toll is farmed. Since the treaty, the Chyrsus Syndicate has held the farm for a lump sum paid at Persemenid, and collects at each of the nine surviving lock-houses in Persemenid coin, Hellenorian drachmae or Mithril Reserve paper at a rate set the morning of payment. The Syndicate posts the rate on the old stelae, under the King of Kings' boast, in chalk. The frataraka of the canal district, Ardavan Lock-Keeper, draws a salary for maintaining a waterway and has not seen water in it.

Every few years a court engineer proposes re-cutting it; the proposal costs the treasury a feasibility study and the engineer a career. The most recent, a Magus of the Sage's Archive, argued that the canal silts faster than any canal should, and that the sand arrives at night, from the wrong direction. He was posted to a satrapy without water.

Sites

The Crocodile Pool Existing · Pool

Sacred · garlands and wine-soaked bread · white birds and river-smell

A broad pool beside the canal, lined with steps and garlanded with flowers, where a huge river-beast lies half in the water and is fed by priests of the River's Embrace with fish and wine-soaked bread. The Watching Ibis, a long-billed white bird the priests call a clerk of the god, picks food from its teeth: god and bird have a covenant. Pilgrims are admitted at dawn. Anything dropped in the pool should be left there.

Ties: the River's Embrace (Shajar); the canal-side town that lives on pilgrims.

The Nine Lock-Houses New · Tollhouses

Bureaucracy · stone gatehouses on dry locks · ink, dust and camel

Square stone gatehouses that once lifted galleys. The lock-gates are long gone for timber; the houses are toll booths, inns and Syndicate counting-rooms. Each keeps a scale, a ledger and a chalked rate. Caravans walk down a ramp into the dry chamber, pay, and walk up the far side, which takes most of a morning and is the closest anyone now gets to the original experience.

Ties: the Chyrsus Syndicate; Acheaorian tribute; Wheelwalkers.

The Dead Basins New · Silted harbours

Abandoned · ooze and drowned ships · rot and sweetness

The two turning-basins at the canal's middle were never fully drained. They hold black ooze under a crust that bears a man until it does not, and the ribs of galleys caught when the water left. Salvagers come for bronze rams and sealed jars. Few stay the night. The crust breathes, slowly, and smells sweet.

Ties: the Mother of Corruption; salvagers from R'eyshar.

What lives here

  • The River-Dragon — the sacred beast of the Crocodile Pool; vast, old, and ill.
  • Giant Crocodile — its offspring, in the wet stretches near the seaward ends.
  • Crocodile — common in the reed-choked lock chambers.
  • Young Black Dragon — lairs in a flooded lock; collects toll stelae.
  • Rot-Lords — things of the basin ooze, tended by the Mother of Corruption.
  • Gray Ooze — the lesser product of the Dead Basins.
  • Giant Scorpion — shelters under the canal walls at noon.
  • Bandit — toll-jumpers who walk the desert outside the walls.

What can be gathered

  • Pen-Reed — wet stretches; the best reed pens in the empire, 1 cp each, 1 sp at Persemenid.
  • Salt-Cedar — along the dry walls; firewood and tamarisk-manna, sold at the lock-houses.
  • Bronze rams and fittings — the Dead Basins; 20–200 gp, if you come back.
  • Sealed jars — galley cargo, still sealed: oil, wine, and once a jar of seeds from Khemaret that sprouted.
  • River-Dragon scutes — shed at the Pool; sacred, not for sale, sold anyway at 25 gp.

Who goes there

  • The Chyrsus Syndicate toll-farmers — want the rate to float and the canal to stay dry; a wet canal is a crown monopoly again.
  • Ardavan Lock-Keeper frataraka of the canal district — wants one honest report filed before he dies.
  • Priestess Shirindokht River's Embrace, keeper of the Pool — wants a cure for the River-Dragon and the town not to know it needs one.
  • Mother of Corruption continental dark cult — tends the basins as a cathedral of honest decay.
  • Wheelwalkers road-folk — the canal's most loyal customers and its loudest critics.

Wild · Acheaoria · Black ridge

Zaruk'thal Spine

Two hundred miles of black rock standing out of the sand like a fin, crossable only at eleven cut gates of a kingdom that no longer exists.

Codex now: A ridge of black stone splitting the Acheaorian desert — the old border of a kingdom that no longer exists, and still refuses passage.

Claimed by
Acheaoria; each notch taxed by the nearest satrap
Terrain
Sheer black ridge, eleven notch-gates, salt domes beneath, desert both sides
Travel
1 day through a notch; 10 days along it · Survival DC 15
Danger
High (CR 1–8)
Trouble
Two satraps disputing the Seventh Notch

The land

Two hundred miles of black rock, nowhere more than a quarter-mile wide, impassable except at eleven notches that are plainly cut rather than weathered. The cutting is older than Acheaoria and older than the treaties; the satraps' own annals give it to one of the kingdoms that came before. Each notch was a gate. Several still have the sockets, and two still have fragments of the doors, which are not stone and have not corroded.

The Spine borders nothing now. The kingdom it defended is a chapter in the chronicles and a set of ruins under the sand. But the notches remain the only crossings, so every caravan road in eastern Acheaoria still runs where a dead kingdom decided it should, and the satraps tax the crossings because the crossings are still where the crossings are. Caravan masters make a small offering at the sockets. Asked to whom, they say: to whoever is still holding the gate.

New lore

The notches are numbered from the north, and each has its own toll, its own satrap and its own grievance. The Seventh, the widest, sits exactly on a satrapy border the throne drew with a ruler on a map; for five years two satraps have each kept a toll-post at one end, so a caravan pays twice to walk a quarter of a mile. Persemenid has been asked to rule and has sent a commission, which has been in the notch for two years, taking fees.

Offerings at the sockets have grown since the peace. Caravan masters used to leave a date or a pinch of salt. Now they leave coin, and in the last two years the coin has been gone each morning. The tollmen swear they do not take it. The tollmen at the Ninth Notch have stopped leaving their post at night.

Sites

The Cold Forge Existing · Forge

Secret · a windowless smithy · iced quench-water and no sound

A black, windowless smithy beneath the ridge, so cold that the quenching trough is skinned with ice. The smiths do not speak, do not wear gloves and do not say who they work for. Their work is dark, matte and heavy: darksteel, tenebrium, infernal iron and the cold northern ironfell, all arriving by night in unmarked wagons. No visitor has found a door. Caravans passing at night say the glow from the vents is black.

Ties: buyers unknown; Ember & Anvil of Duneforged would pay to know.

The Hyena Hollows Existing · Dens

Wild · bone-white dens · bones, musk and laughter

Low hollows at the base of the ridge, strewn with bone and bleached by sun. The same families of Grave-Laughers have used them for generations, and at night their laughter carries ten miles across the plain. Giant eagle-owls nest on the ridge above; fat-tail scorpions live in the cracks below. Caravans camp elsewhere. Those with no choice sleep with a fire and a friend.

Ties: gnoll bands of the deep sand; the Savage Pack, who hunt them.

The Salt Cathedral Existing · Mine

Devout · a hall in a salt dome · lamp-oil and brine

A cavernous working hollowed from a dome of rock salt over centuries and left standing on pillars the miners chose not to cut. The hall rings when a man speaks and glitters when a lamp is lit. At one end is a miners' chapel to Vatagatal, keeper of promises; at the other, a saint's niche nobody can name. Clear and grey blocks of deep rock salt go up on ropes and sell by weight at the pit-head. The miners give a tour for a small fee and a larger tip. The chapel lamp has not gone out in living memory.

Ties: The Ironclad Oath (Vatagatal); salt buyers at Mithratal.

The Door Notch New · Gate

Eerie · the Ninth Notch · cold metal in hot sand

One of the two notches that still holds fragments of its doors: three leaves of a grey metal, each twice a man's height, hanging from sockets that should have rusted through a millennium ago. They are cool at noon. Caravans pass between them in single file and do not touch. The tollmen of the Ninth keep their post a hundred paces outside, and since last year collect only by daylight.

Ties: The Sage's Archive (which wants a scraping); the Magi (who forbid one).

What lives here

  • Giant Hyena — the Grave-Laughers of the Hollows.
  • Gnoll — bands that follow the hyenas and raid camps at the notches.
  • Behir — coils in the ridge's clefts; eats tollmen, prefers camels.
  • Earth Elemental — wakes when someone cuts a new notch. Someone keeps trying.
  • Mummy — natron-preserved dead of the old kingdom in the salt galleries.
  • Wight — gate-wardens still at their posts, mostly at night.
  • Giant Owl — the eagle-owls of the ridge-top.
  • Giant Scorpion — fat-tails in the cracks below the Hollows.

What can be gathered

  • Deep Rock Salt — the Salt Cathedral; 2 sp a clear block, more as caravans go deeper into the waste.
  • Fire-Stone — fissures on the sunward face; glows at night, 10 gp a palm-sized piece.
  • Natron — salt galleries; for embalmers and glassmakers.
  • Gate-metal scrapings — the Door Notch; forbidden, unworkable by any known forge, priceless to the Cold Forge.

Who goes there

  • Wheelwalkers road-folk under Jauhar — know which notch is cheapest this month, and charge for the knowledge.
  • The Undying Legion proscribed society under Thasmudayan — hold the dead are still enrolled; they muster at the sockets on the old kingdom's feast-days.
  • Frataraka Bahram Dozakhi toll-governor of the Seventh Notch, east end — wants the commission to rule for him, and has paid twice to make sure.
  • Frataraka Mitra Azarnush toll-governor of the Seventh Notch, west end — has paid three times.
  • The Sage's Archive inscription-readers under Kor — want the old kingdom's name, which is carved on every socket and readable on none.

Wild · Free lands · Great forest

Foloicauria Forest

The one great forest the long war never touched, because nobody who marched into it marched out as an army. It is alive, possibly awake, and divided between the mother of monsters, the Wild Elves and the gorgon's warrior-women.

Codex now: Foloicaria is a vast, ancient forest untouched by the millennium-long Continental War. Its thick canopies and dense undergrowth pulse with pure, unfiltered Nature Magic, often called "Vitalous Energy." …

Claimed by
No empire. Hellenoria's Circle of the Eternal Grove keeps the edges; Echidna and Typhon, the Heartgrove elves and Medusa's Amazons hold the interior.
Terrain
Old-growth canopy, shifting undergrowth, one fogbound peak (Mount Vaeltheruun) in the east
Travel
12 days to cross, if the paths agree · Survival DC 18
Danger
Deadly (CR 1–17)
Trouble
The forest is growing outward, and the empires have started measuring it for timber.

The land

Foloicauria is older than the empires and was untouched by fifteen centuries of their war. Its canopy is thick enough that noon looks like evening, and the undergrowth is saturated with raw nature magic, which foresters call Vitalous Energy and philosophers call a problem. The saturation mutates what lives here, not into abominations but into exaggerated versions of themselves: boars the size of carts, oaks that hold thunder in their wood, flowers that are also teeth. Most who live on its edge believe the forest is sentient. None of them believe it is friendly.

Three powers divide the interior. In the east, on fog-wrapped Mount Vaeltheruun, live Echidna and Typhon, progenitors of all monsters; from the lowlands a vast serpentine outline can sometimes be seen on the summit, and their brood roams the eastern wilds under their watch. The centre, the Heartgrove, holds the forest's single city, founded ages ago by elven clans who walked in and stayed. Over the centuries they have changed: some grow fur, some feathers, some skin like bark. They are the Wild Elves, and they keep the middle forest. In the west, Medusa rules in alliance with the Amazon tribes, warrior-women and serpent guardians who have made their territory a country of trials. The strongest warlords and archmages of all three empires steer around it. Its creatures cannot be catalogued, its paths seem to move, and something under it is asleep or pretending to be.

New lore

The peace has done what the war could not and made the forest valuable. Five years of rebuilding have stripped the hills of timber, and Foloicauria holds the last old-growth on the continent. Invictian surveyors have twice been found on the southern edge with measuring chains, and twice been found again a season later, deeper in, as trees. The Circle of the Eternal Grove insists that Hellenoria has never felled the old forest out of piety. Woodcutters on the margin say it is because the stumps grow back overnight, with the axe inside.

The edge is moving. Farmers along the border report a hedge-line that advances a few paces every spring, which matches what the Heartgrove elves told the last Hellenorian envoy: the forest is "breathing out". Nobody has yet asked what it breathed in.

Sites

The Living Stones Existing · clearing

Warm, hushed, knee-high · a forest tribe keeps it · smells of wet clay and struck flint

A round clearing where nothing grows above the knee and the rocks, veined with green, gain a few inches a year. The clay breathes; geodes open at dawn like eyes. The tribe that keeps it speaks of the place as a sleeping thing and receives visitors at the edge, politely and unmoved by coin. The clearing has begun to spread, and the tribe is quietly moving its camp.

Ties: source of Chlorophyte, Clay of Life, Gaia Geodes and the Heart Stones; watched by the Circle of the Eternal Grove.

The Mushroom Caverns Existing · caves

Damp, faintly glowing · foragers in threes · smells of earth and old bread

Linked caves under the forest floor, lit by the fungus on every wall. Three common species grow side by side and look nearly identical: one heals, one does nothing, one kills. Foragers sort them by smell, then colour, then, in the worst case, by trial. The lodge at the mouth keeps a book of the dead. It is large, and the newest pages are in a hand that grows less steady.

Ties: shriekers and violet fungus below; Luminastra Alchemists buy Embergill Bloom here.

The Woad Pits Existing · clearing

Foul, cheerful, industrious · pit-masters and dyers · smells of a mile of fermenting urine

Shallow pits where woad leaves are crushed, fermented and dried into blue cakes. The dyers are tolerated and not invited to dinner. The cakes go to the forest tribes, who paint themselves before battle, and, by a long chain of middlemen, to the Imperial dyers who colour garrison cloaks. The pit-masters trade with anyone and let no stranger sleep over. The tribes have lately ordered a new pattern, which the pit-master calls a war-sign.

Ties: Warrior's Woad; Amazon buyers from the west; Invictian dye contracts.

The Heartgrove New · Wild Elf city

Living timber, no walls · feathered and bark-skinned elves · smells of resin and rain

The forest's only city, grown rather than built: halls in the crowns of thunder-oaks, bridges of trained root, a council that meets on a fallen trunk so old it has its own soil. The Wild Elves accept guests who arrive by the right path and turn back those who arrive by the wrong one, and they will not say which is which. They trade honey, bow-staves and medicine for salt and iron needles.

Ties: uneasy truce with Medusa's west and the brood of the east; envoys to the Circle of the Eternal Grove.

Mount Vaeltheruun New · lone peak

Fog to the treeline, silence above · the brood's country · smells of musk and hot stone

A single mountain in the eastern wilds, rarely seen without its collar of fog. Shepherds on the far plains swear that on clear evenings the summit carries a coiled silhouette too large to be a ridge. Hunters who go up for chimera hide do not come down with it. The approach is marked by bones arranged with care, which suggests either worship or housekeeping.

Ties: Echidna and Typhon; chimeras, hydras and saurians.

What lives here

  • Chimera — the commonest of Echidna's brood; nests on Vaeltheruun's lower ledges.
  • Hydra — in the eastern bogs; the elves count heads to date a kill.
  • Medusa — the gorgon-queen of the west, and her lesser kin among the Amazon shrines.
  • Centaur — clans on the open glades between the three domains, paid by all of them.
  • Dryad and Satyr — in every grove that has a name.
  • Unicorn — rarely seen near the Heartgrove; the elves will not discuss them.
  • Owlbear — mutated large, even by owlbear standards.
  • Green dragon — one at least, in the tangle between the Heartgrove and the west.
  • Shrieker and Violet fungus — the Mushroom Caverns.
  • Tusker of the Thicket, Great Forest Bull — game animals the size of farm buildings.

What can be gathered

  • Chlorophyte — green ore that grows, the Living Stones; 40 gp a pound, if the tribe lets you near.
  • Clay of Life, Gaia Geode — the Living Stones; golem-makers pay anything.
  • Embergill Bloom — the beneficial cave mushroom; heals, 5 gp a cap (and its look-alike, Widow's Bell, kills).
  • Warrior's Woad — the Woad Pits; 2 sp a cake.
  • Thunder-Oak — heartwood that crackles when worked; staff-makers' timber.
  • Fly-Cap, Beautiful Lady — the red-spotted mushroom and the poison berry; both sell to physicians and to worse people.

Who goes there

  • The Circle of the Eternal Grove Hellenorian druids of Demeter — keep the edges, carry messages to the Heartgrove and veto every timber licence they hear of.
  • Silent Stalkers of the Glade Invictian woodsmen of Faunus — hired by the surveyors; the only Invictians who come back on their own feet.
  • Hippolyta Drakaina Amazon war-leader — buys woad and iron, sells safe passage through the west at the price of a trial.
  • Elder Thessa Barkhand Wild Elf speaker · bark-skinned — wants the empires to stop measuring the edge and is losing patience politely.
  • Luminastra Alchemists Hellenorian apothecaries of Apollo — send foragers to the caverns in threes, and replace them.

Wild · Free lands · Swamp

Maeotis Helos

Forty miles of reed and black water where three rivers fail to finish. It has never been conquered, pays tribute to whoever asks, and is slowly digesting a kingdom.

Codex now: The great marsh at the mouth of three rivers — impassable to armies, home to reed-cutters, and slowly digesting a fallen kingdom.

Claimed by
Everyone who sends a tax-collector; held by nobody
Terrain
Reed-sea, channels, floating islets that move with the season
Travel
4 days by punt with a guide, never on foot · Survival DC 16 (DC 22 without a guide)
Danger
High (CR 1–14)
Trouble
Three empires now want tribute at once, and the water rises when soldiers come.

The land

Where three rivers reach the sea without any of them quite arriving, the land gives up being land for about forty miles. The Helos is reed twice a man's height, black water and islands that stay islands only until the season changes. It has never been conquered, because there is nothing to hold and no way to march. Every attempt in the long war ended the same way: a column went in, the guides proved unreliable, the water rose, and a smaller column came out somewhere unintended. The reed-cutters paid tribute to whichever empire asked and went on exactly as before.

The Helos is also where a kingdom went. Pieces of worked stone come up in the nets, always the same pale stone, always carved on one face. The reed-cutters have a rule against bringing them home. The old people say the marsh took Nethrana, the Kingdom of Mirrors and Mist, because it was owed, that the debt was never fully settled, and that this is why the water rises when soldiers come.

New lore

The Treaty made the Helos a borderland on paper, which means three sets of tax-collectors where there used to be one at a time. Marshroot pays all three, in reed, and keeps the receipts. The reed-cutters greet every new official with the same courtesy and the same punt-guide, and the officials who insist on an inspection tour come back with excellent notes on the wrong part of the marsh.

The pale stones are coming up more often. Fishermen say a whole carved lintel rose to the surface at the Pelican Islands last spring, face down, and sank again when someone tried to turn it over. Collectors in Deiperduem now pay well for any piece with the carving intact, which has given the old rule against bringing them home its first real test.

Sites

The Reed-Cutters' Fen Existing · channels

Narrow, green, endless · reed-cutters and guides · smells of cut reed and lily

A web of channels just wide enough for a punt, each marked by a knot of reed on a pole, cut by generations of reed-cutters. Blue lilies open at dawn and close at noon. A guide is not optional: the channels change with the season, the knots are moved by people who want you lost, and the fen keeps what it takes. Roofing reed and the fine hollow pen-reed scribes prize both come out of here.

Ties: Marshroot Grove; the Stilted Archive buys pen-reed.

The Pelican Islands Existing · floating islets

Loud, white, drifting · fishermen and birds · smells of guano and fish oil

Reed islets in the heart of the marsh, anchored to nothing and moving a few yards a year. Pelicans, pheasants and winter cranes nest by the thousand; the black-egg sturgeon run beneath in spring. A fishermen's guild punts visitors out for a day's wage and a promise not to take eggs. One islet has started drifting against the current, and nobody punts near it now.

Ties: sturgeon roe sold upriver; the drowned lintel was seen here.

The Stilted Archive Existing · library

Damp, quiet, guarded · scribe-reedcutters · smells of mildew, ink and smoke

A library on stilts reached by a plank causeway that the keepers pull up at night. Its scribes cut their own reeds, mix their own ink and copy the texts the great libraries would rather not keep, selling sealed copies to scholars who ask no questions. A visitor must be vouched for by a scribe. A book is missing: the one the keepers forbade themselves to copy.

Ties: buyers from the Three Libraries' circle; the Whispering Eyes.

Willowheart Existing · village

One vast willow · herbalists and midwives · smells of bark tea

A village built into and around a single enormous willow standing out of the water. Its bark preparations for pain and fever are the best in the region, and its midwives are sent for from towns three days away. The bark is stripped only from allotted sections in a rite of strict supervision; taking unallotted bark is the one offence that gets a person expelled.

Ties: Willowheart Enclave; the Luminastra Alchemists buy the preparation but not the method.

The Pale Shallows New · drowned ruin

Still, clear, cold · nobody stays · smells of nothing at all

A stretch of open water in the outer marsh where the reed will not grow and the bottom, a fathom down, is paved in the pale carved stone. The carvings face upward here, and they do not show the same scene twice to the same person. The reed-cutters punt around it, never across, and say the water is "still paying".

Ties: Nethranan ruins of Eronis and Velothis; collectors in Deiperduem.

What lives here

  • Black dragon — an old one in the deep channels; the tribute the reed-cutters do not mention.
  • Lizardfolk — reed-island clans who trade with Marshroot and eat what the empires send.
  • Hydra — in the river mouths after floods.
  • Giant frog and Giant toad — everywhere, loudly.
  • Stirge — summer swarms; the reason for reed-smoke.
  • Will-o'-wisp — lights over the Pale Shallows that look like a guide's lantern.
  • Shambling mound — what a lost column becomes after a wet season.
  • Green hag — sells directions, always correct, never helpful.
  • Chuul — in the drowned channels over the pale stone.
  • Reed-Striders — long-legged marsh hunters that walk the reed-tops.

What can be gathered

  • River Reed and Pen-Reed — the Fen; thatch by the bundle, pen-reed at 1 sp a dozen.
  • Blue Water-Lotus — burned in temples; 5 sp a basket.
  • Black-Egg Sturgeon roe — spring run; worth its weight in silver upriver.
  • Healer's Leech — still pools of the Pelican Islands; physicians pay 1 sp each.
  • Willow-bark preparation — Willowheart; sold as medicine, never as a recipe.
  • Pale carved stone — forbidden by custom; 50 gp a piece in Deiperduem.

Who goes there

  • Wenna Reedmother Pile-Elder of Marshroot — pays three empires and wants a fourth receipt from nobody.
  • Tovah Brightwater Midwife-Warden of Willowheart — knows which officials' wives she has delivered, and uses it.
  • Keeper Anaxis Stilted Archive · scribe — wants the missing book found and not read.
  • Tax-collectors of three empires Praefectus, demarch and frataraka — each believes the others are the irregular ones.
  • The Enchanted Muse Acheaorian dream-readers — buy pale stones quietly; part of the hunt for Vesperine Ilaro.

Wild · Free lands · Steppe

Malaunian Steppe

Grass to every horizon and horsemen behind every column. No empire has conquered it in fifteen centuries; all three now hire it.

Codex now: Grass to the horizon in every direction — the horse country that no empire has ever conquered and every empire has hired.

Claimed by
Nobody in the sense the empires mean; the horse clans
Terrain
Treeless grassland, waterless between rivers, burial mounds
Travel
15 days to cross on horseback · Survival DC 15 (water-finding DC 18)
Danger
Moderate (CR 1–7)
Trouble
Peace has put thousands of hired riders out of work at once.

The land

A sea of grass along the continent's northern edge, past Xerastri, treeless, waterless between rivers, and owned by nobody. The Malaunian clans are mounted from the age of four. They keep no cities and sign no treaty that outlasts the man who signed it, and in fifteen centuries they have destroyed three punitive expeditions from each empire in the same way: the column advances, the steppe empties, the supply line lengthens, and the horsemen appear behind it.

All three empires solve this by hiring them. Malaunian auxiliaries ride in Invictian, Hellenorian and Acheaorian service, frequently in the same season and occasionally against each other. Nobody on the steppe calls this disloyal. A contract is with a man, not a nation. The only permanent structures are the burial mounds: enormous, thick with gold, and never robbed twice, because the first thief always manages it.

New lore

The peace was a disaster for the steppe's economy. For fifteen centuries there was always someone at war who needed horsemen; for five years there has been nobody. Riders who came home with imperial silver now find it debased, and the clans who grew used to selling sons to armies have too many sons. The result is raiding along the Royal Road's northern end, which the satraps call banditry and the clans call collecting arrears. All three empires have started hiring Malaunians again, to guard against Malaunians.

One name now crosses every clan boundary: Tomyra of the Lion Grass, a berserker hired by all and ruled by none, who has refused every contract this year. The clans read that as a sign she is waiting for a better one.

Sites

The Lion Grass Existing · grassland

Golden, shoulder-high · lions and saiga · smells of hot grass and musk

A broad stretch where the grass grows shoulder-high and the herds avoid grazing in the evening. At dawn the manes of the great cats rise above the stems like standards, and the ground is printed with a thousand hooves. The horse clans will guide a traveller across for a gift of salt. They will not guide him back. Tomyra takes her name from here, and the cats are said to give her room.

Ties: Tomyra; the Predator's Guild covets the culling rights.

The Mound Field of the Nine Khans New · burial mounds

Huge, silent, grassed over · nobody lives here · smells of turned earth

Nine kurgan-mounds in a row, each tall enough to see a day's ride from. Every one has a robbers' shaft in its side, and every robber's name is remembered, because each was the first and only one to try. The clans water their horses here and leave a cup of mare's milk on the nearest slope. Two of the shafts have been freshly reopened since the peace.

Ties: barrow-wights; gold that reaches Deiperduem's market as "old Acheaorian".

The Hiring Fair at Saltford New · seasonal market

Loud, dusty, temporary · clan riders and recruiting officers · smells of horse and roast mutton

At the one good river ford on the southern edge, the clans gather each spring to be hired. Officers from all three empires set up tents a bowshot apart and bid for squadrons. Salt, silver and iron change hands; contracts are sworn on a drawn bowstring. This year the officers outnumber the contracts, and the riders have raised their price.

Ties: Xerastri; Ironclad Legion and Sunward Valiants recruiters; the Royal Road.

What lives here

  • Mane-King of the Steppe — the great maned lions of the Lion Grass (use Lion, larger).
  • Malaunian Saiga — odd-nosed antelope herds by the ten thousand.
  • Riding horse and wild Heavenly Horses — the steppe's wealth, counted before children.
  • Plateau Wolves — winter packs (use Dire wolf).
  • Axe beak — "striders" the clans race and occasionally ride.
  • Centaur — clans who trade with the riders and despise their saddles.
  • Bulette — the land-shark; the steppe empties above one.
  • Wight — barrow-wights in the gold-filled mounds.
  • Hyena and Vulture — the steppe's undertakers.

What can be gathered

  • Banded Agate — river gravels; cut into seals and bead-strings, 10 gp a good stone.
  • Rope-Hemp — wild along the rivers; bowstrings and halters.
  • Mare's milk and kumis — everywhere; the only currency the clans trust as much as salt.
  • Saiga horn — sold to Acheaorian physicians; 5 gp a pair.
  • Mound gold — by custom untouchable; worth everything, once.

Who goes there

  • Tomyra of the Lion Grass berserker · hired by all, ruled by none — has turned down every contract this year; nobody knows what she is waiting for.
  • Khan Arpoxai Seven-Horses head of the largest clan — wants back pay from Invicta in good silver, not the new coin.
  • Roxana Surena Warden of the Parthian Ravine — recruits Malaunian horse-archers for the frontier and pays in Acheaorian gold.
  • Predator's Guild Acheaorian hunters of Kiga — want Mane-King cubs for the royal parks.
  • Caravan of the Gilded Horizon Mercury's caravaners — pay the clans for safe passage on the northern route, and double it this year.

Wild · Free lands · Valley

Shadowed Vale

A cleft so deep the sun crosses it for forty minutes a day, farmed by the most punctual people on the continent, who will not say what walks in the dark weeks.

Codex now: A valley the sun reaches for forty minutes a day — cold, fertile, and farmed by people who keep very precise clocks.

Claimed by
No empire with confidence; the Valefolk settlements govern themselves by clock and council
Terrain
Narrow deep cleft, terraced orchards, cold streams, scree walls
Travel
2 days along the floor · Survival DC 12 (DC 17 in the sunless weeks)
Danger
Low most of the year, High in the sunless weeks (CR ½–8)
Trouble
Outsiders arriving to buy the fruit and staying into winter

The land

A cleft so narrow and so deep that direct sun crosses it for about forty minutes around noon and, for eleven weeks of winter, not at all. The people are not gloomy about it. They are punctual about it, which is stranger. Every settlement keeps a sun-clock calibrated to its own patch of sky, work is scheduled to the arriving light by the quarter-hour, and a Valefolk given a time will keep it to a degree the rest of the continent finds unnerving.

The soil is superb: cold, wet and thick with washed-down mineral. The Vale exports fruit that ripens nowhere else, picked mostly in the dark by people who navigate their orchards by count of paces. When asked what is done in the sunless weeks, Valefolk say: the same things. When asked what is out during them, they change the subject, politely, every time.

New lore

The peace made the Vale's fruit fashionable. The shade-pear, white-fleshed and cold even in summer, now sells on Deiperduem's market at a silver piece apiece, and buyers from all three empires come up the valley road to bid on whole orchards. Valefolk sell gladly and insist, in every contract, that the buyer be out of the Vale by the first sunless day. Two Hellenorian factors ignored the clause last winter. Their lodgings were found swept, aired and empty, with the shutters latched from outside.

Each household keeps a lamp-ledger: who lit which lamp, when, and for how long. Lamps in the Vale are never left burning untended, and a child's first duty is to learn the count of steps from bed to door in the dark.

Sites

The Hedge of Healing Existing · physic hedge

Cold-shaded, tended · herbalists' guild, the sick · bark, crushed leaf and damp

A thick hedge along the valley's sunless side, planted generations ago by a physician and left to grow. The herbalists trim it twice a year and gather witch hazel for bruises, comfrey for bones, woundwort for cuts and the red heartberry that quiets a racing pulse. Salves are sold at a stall by the gate; the physician's lodge takes the sick for a small donation. Last autumn a third of the hedge died overnight, in a perfectly straight line.

Ties: the Radiant Heartwardens buy its salves; the Clock Hall.

The Clock Hall New · council house

Exact, ticking · the Vale council, clockwrights · brass oil and beeswax

A round stone hall at the Vale's widest point where the master sun-clock stands under an aperture in the roof. Noon is declared here and carried down the valley by runners. The council of hour-keepers meets at a time fixed eleven years in advance and has never started late. In the sunless weeks the hall keeps time by a great water-clock, and the doors are barred from the half-hour before the dark bell.

Ties: every Vale settlement; the Celestial Astromancers, who covet its tables.

The Dark Orchards New · orchards

Cold and fragrant · pickers counting paces · pear-blossom and wet stone

Terraced shade-pear and frost-plum climbing the north wall, where the forty minutes never reach. Rows are numbered by notches on the trunks. Pickers work blind and fast and sing counting songs. In the sunless weeks the notches are checked each morning, because some trees have been found with notches that were not cut by the family.

Ties: fruit buyers of Deiperduem.

What lives here

  • Shadow — common in the sunless weeks; they walk the orchard rows at exactly the pickers' pace.
  • Specter — outsiders who stayed into winter, according to the people who will not say so.
  • Bugbear — a clan in the upper scree that raids only in the dark weeks.
  • Darkmantle — in the cold caves of the walls; dropped on the unwary picking at the cliff foot.
  • Giant owl — the Valefolk's allies, fed on the clock-hall roof.
  • Swarm of bats — out at noon in winter, confused.
  • The Keeper of the Hours — the thing Valefolk will not name; see DM notes.

What can be gathered

  • Shade-pear and frost-plum — the Dark Orchards; 1 sp a pear on Deiperduem's market.
  • Witch hazel, comfrey, woundwort, heartberry — the Hedge of Healing; salves at 5 sp a pot.
  • Vale loam — washed mineral soil; gardeners of the capitals buy it by the cart.
  • Water-clock floats — the clockwrights' trade; a true Vale clock costs 50 gp and is worth it.

Who goes there

  • Hour-Keeper Odila Vane chair of the Vale council — wants the outsiders' money and the outsiders gone by the dark bell.
  • Master Physician Coren Hask keeper of the Hedge — wants to know what killed a third of his hedge in a straight line.
  • Celestial Astromancers sky-watchers — want the Clock Hall's tables for their eclipse charts.
  • Fruit factors from three empires — want a winter in the Vale to secure the next crop first.

Wild · Free lands · Mountain

Vael'Tharan Mountain

The bare, warm peak where the Titans were put down, its southern face worked into terraces and channels for hands three to five times the size of a man's.

Codex now: The peak the Titans are said to have been broken against — bare, faintly warm, and worked on one face by hands that were not human-sized.

Claimed by
No one; shrine-priests on the flank, sulphur-gatherers by custom
Terrain
Bare rock above the cedar line, warm worked terraces, sulphur vents, thin-aired summit
Travel
3 days to the Thin Places · Survival DC 15 (DC 18 above the Smoke-Steps)
Danger
High (CR 3–13)
Trouble
The warmth is rising, and scholars and cultists are racing to learn why

The land

Bare rock from the treeline up, warm to the touch on its southern face in any weather, and shaped on that face only into terraces and channels far too large to be stairs and far too regular to be nothing. Asetherian tradition puts the breaking of the Titans here. The codex records fifty-one of them, and the tradition is consistent that they did not die but were put down, which is a different thing and implies a place.

Nothing grows on the worked face. Compasses point true; water boils normally. What is wrong is scale: every feature is proportioned for something between three and five times human size, consistently enough that Hellenorian scholars have published estimates of the builders' height and been taken seriously. The warmth has never been explained. It is not volcanic. It is strongest in the channels, and strongest at night.

New lore

The sulphur-gatherers of the Smoke-Steps keep a tally-post on which each generation cuts a notch at the height the night-warmth reaches up the channels. For three hundred years the notches crept. In the five years since the treaty they have climbed a forearm's length. The gatherers now leave the mountain by noon without exception, and the Fallen-Star priests have doubled their lamps.

A popular explanation in Deiperduem's taverns: the war's magic kept the Titans drowsy, and peace is letting them wake. The Scholars dislike how well this fits their own figures.

Sites

The Smoke-Steps Existing · sulphur terraces

Yellow, breathing · sulphur-gatherers at dawn · struck flint and rotten egg

A natural stair of yellow terraces on the warm flank, cut deeper by generations of gatherers. Vents breathe a pale smoke, and at night some stones glow dull red, as if the mountain remembered the fire that broke the Titans. Brimstone is scraped off in sheets; the hottest vents leave glassy fire-stone that stays warm for days. The gatherers work in the cool of dawn and are gone by noon. A traveller who stays later has been warned.

Ties: alchemists of Duneforged and Hellarchon; the tally-post.

The Fallen-Star Shrine Existing · shrine

Windswept, swept clean · sky-priests, pilgrims on foot · lamp oil and cold iron

A small sanctuary built around a pit where a black, pitted stone lies half-buried as it fell. The priests keep a lamp beside it and sweep the ground every morning; pilgrims may not touch it. The shrine holds star metal and a few splinters of blue-white celestium that fell with it and have glowed ever since. Offerings are accepted and not discussed.

Ties: the Thin Places; the Celestial Astromancers.

The Thin Places Existing · summit terraces

Silent, too-clear light · vowed climbers · nothing; the air has no smell

Three bare terraces near the peak where the world is worn thin enough for the high powers' metals to pass through: hallowed steel, valhallium, weightless aerialite, ivorite, idyllium, prismatic ice, prismetal and patient aximium. The climb takes three days and a vow of silence. Those who come down speak of a light they cannot describe and of something below them that breathes once an hour.

Ties: the Fallen-Star priests license the climb; the Mithril Reserve buys the metal.

The Giants' Measure New · worked terrace

Huge, warm, geometric · stone giants and scholars · hot stone

The broadest worked terrace, where a channel ends in a socket the size of a house. Stone giants come here each midsummer to lay their palms in the channels and measure them with knotted ropes. Hellenorian scholars camp at a polite distance and copy the knots. Neither party has explained its figures to the other.

Ties: the Arcane Academy of Hellarchon; the Scholars.

What lives here

  • The Simurgh of Vael'Tharan — nests above the Thin Places; old enough to have seen the Titans put down, and inclined to say so in riddles.
  • Stone giant — the Measure's pilgrims, solemn and literal.
  • Cloud giant — seen around the summit at dawn, counting.
  • Salamander and magma mephit — in the Smoke-Steps vents after dark.
  • Roc — the rukhs of the warm flank, which the Simurgh tolerates.
  • Red dragon — one, sleeping in the warmest channel and growing restless with the heat.
  • Deva — the celestials of the Thin Places, who do not intervene.

What can be gathered

  • Brimstone — the Smoke-Steps; 1 sp a pound, more in Hellarchon.
  • Fire-stone — the hottest vents; warms a room for days, 10 gp a lump.
  • Star metal and celestium — the shrine; not for sale, sometimes stolen.
  • The high metals (aerialite, valhallium, aximium and the rest) — the Thin Places; fortunes, in ounces.
  • Mountain cedar and fly-cap — the lower slopes, below the worked face.

Who goes there

  • Prior Eustathe of the Star keeper of the Fallen-Star Shrine — wants the climb kept silent and the lamps fed.
  • Gatherer-Mother Zoe Kapnia head of the sulphur families — keeps the tally-post, and wants someone to tell her what the notches mean.
  • The Scholars rift classifiers — think the Thin Places are a permanent Bound Rift and want to anchor one.
  • Melted Ice continental dark cult — gathers where old things are uncovered, and has camped below the treeline.
  • Envoys of Duneforged's Countess Aurelie Virellarion, buying fire-stone by the cartload.

Wild · Free lands (Deiperduem's water) · Great lake

Varathros Lake

A war-made inland sea beside Deiperduem: safe for fifty miles from the northern shore, strange in the middle, and over its trench something chained that every empire swears it never tried to wake.

Codex now: Overview:

Claimed by
No one by treaty; the northern waters are policed by Deiperduem's Lake Board
Terrain
Deep fresh-to-brackish inland sea, reefs, islets, salt pans, a central trench
Travel
5 days to cross by sail · Survival (or Vehicles, water) DC 12 in the Crest, DC 18 in the Maw
Danger
Moderate near shore, Deadly in the Ring and Deeps (CR 2–17)
Trouble
The Broken Masts are surfacing, and so is the question of who lost

The land

Once a small, serene lake; then, during the Continental War, a sinkhole tore the land open and the hole filled over centuries with rain and cavern water. Varathros is now deep, unpredictable and dangerous, and its tides seem to remember the war that made them. The Northern Crest, fifty nautical miles out from the Deiperduem shore, is calm and settled: coastal outposts, drowned ruins, fishing fleets. Beyond, the Arcane Maw writhes without wind, magic grows stronger and stranger, and ships sometimes return decades older or before they left. Further in, the Abyssal Ring is a trench of drowned temples where prayers turn to foreign tongues; at the centre the Hadal Deeps fall away past the reach of light and, the stories say, the gods.

When the moon is high, phantom fleets replay the old battles across the northern water in silence. Everyone has seen them. Nobody agrees which side is winning.

New lore

Before the war Deiperduem was a lake-naval power governed by a Senate of Mages and Admirals. The treaty abolished the Senate with the navy; the town council and its Arbiter now rule the city, but the old Senate survives as the Lake Board, seven pilots and wizards who license every hull, collect harbour dues and issue the storm-flags. Their bureaucracy is iron-handed and their records go back further than the city's. The grey fog-dome over the harbour, "the drowned god's breath", has never lifted, and the Board charges a pilot's fee for finding the harbour mouth in it.

Each empire tells the lake its own way. Invictians say they crushed the Hellenorian fleet at the Battle of the Broken Masts and raise monuments to it; Hellenorians sing of the Stormcallers of Crythonis who broke the Imperium's line and of a Seafather-General who rode a hippocampus and never lost; Acheaorians say they never fought at all, only observed. Since the peace, the lake has started giving up wrecks from that battle along the Crest, and every one so far contradicts somebody's monument.

Sites

The Great Sanctum Library Existing · island library and lighthouse

Colonnaded, humming · librarians in pairs · vellum, lamp oil, lake wind

A rocky islet with a titanic lighthouse said to be carved from sky-glass, which hums at certain lunar alignments; some claim it was never built, only revealed. Around it stands the library that holds a copy of every written work in Asetheria, nearly. Any ship docking surrenders its books for copying; the copy is returned, the original kept. Deep copies are shelved below ground in rooms librarians enter in pairs and leave together, a rule nobody explains.

Ties: the Three Libraries circle of Aeterna, Thessalonika and Persemenid.

The Kindred Depths Existing · reef city

Lit coral, cold currents · tritons, sea elves, water genasi · brine and kelp

A reef and cave system under the Crest, home to a confederation of aquatic peoples bound by the Scaled Accord, a pact with peaceful dragons who rest coiled around ancient ruins and keep the war's secrets locked in them. The Kindred trade pearls and pilotage with Deiperduem and send an envoy to the Lake Board who attends every meeting and votes on none.

Ties: the Lake Board; the Silver Reefs.

Isle of Oracles (Mount Zharion) Existing · island sanctum

Spired, flickering · riddling apprentices · ozone and salt

A towering island in the Maw whose "lighthouse" pulses in strange colours: the Arcane Sanctum of Archmage Vaelithar, rarely seen. The apprentices speak in riddles and make offerings to the lake. Around the isle lie the Temporal Rifts, the Eddies of Memory that steal or plant recollections, and the Silver Reefs, crystal spires that warp spells and may be fossilised war titans.

Ties: the Scholars; the Arcane Academy of Hellarchon.

The Drowned Workshop Existing · ruin

Half-sunk, turning · a boat-renting fisher, divers · weed and hot metal

A stone workshop half-sunk in the shallows, its great wheel still turning slowly in the current. Divers report rooms of machinery lit by a pale light that does not come from the surface. The silt yields mechanite, meld, voidmetal, cosmilite and dripping etherplasm. This week the wheel turned faster.

Ties: Writhing Curiosity; the Mithril Reserve's buyers at Deiperduem.

The Natron Pans Existing · salt flats

White glare · rakers, moonlight hauliers · old eggs

Shallow basins on the southern shore that fill in the wet season and bake to a white crust in the dry. The crust is natron: for glass, cleaning, embalming and the washing of the dead. Rakers wear cloths over their eyes; hauliers work by moonlight. Under the crust lies a layer of something older, and a raker who broke through it has not spoken since.

Ties: glass-houses and embalmers of every coast.

The Broken Masts New · wreck field

Shallowing, spectral · salvagers, embassy agents · rotten oak

A field of masts rising out of the Crest where the lake has begun returning the battle's wrecks. One hull is plainly the Invictian flagship Domina Aeternum, split in two; another is a Hellenorian trireme with its rowers still chained; a third has a black obsidian hull nobody claims. Each embassy in Deiperduem has sent divers, quietly.

Ties: the Treaty Hall; the Abyssal Tideguard.

What lives here

  • Merfolk — the Kindred Depths, with tritons and water genasi.
  • Bronze dragon and silver dragon — guardians of the Scaled Accord.
  • Plesiosaurus and archelon — the Maw's open water.
  • Giant octopus — in the Drowned Workshop.
  • Aboleth — the Abyssal Ring; they remember the lake when it was small and trade memories for service.
  • Chuul — guards of the drowned temples.
  • Ghost — the phantom fleets, and the crews still chained at their oars.
  • Ezerantheil the Unblinking — the chained thing in the Hadal Deeps; no stat block, only consequences.

What can be gathered

  • Natron — the Pans; 2 cp a pound at the shore, three times that at a glass-house.
  • Workshop metals (mechanite, voidmetal, cosmilite, etherplasm) — the Drowned Workshop silt; the Board taxes every ounce.
  • Silver-reef crystal — the Maw; a spell focus that sometimes argues, 100 gp a shard.
  • Kindred pearls — traded, not gathered; taking one is a breach of the Accord.
  • Star-iron links — Chainfall in the Deeps; unbreakable, priceless, nearly unrecoverable.

Who goes there

  • Harbour-Master Ilsabet Corvane chair of the Lake Board — issues the storm-flags and remembers when the Board was a Senate.
  • Aulus Severinus Custos Warden of the Treaty Wards — worries the wards over Deiperduem were drawn without allowing for the lake.
  • Archmage Vaelithar master of the Isle of Oracles — unseen; the apprentices' riddles have started to rhyme with the Deeps.
  • Abyssal Tideguard Neptune's marine order — hold the Invictian embassy's salvage contract on the Broken Masts.
  • The Scholars and the Ironclad Legion on contract to the city, who escort the Board's survey boats.

Ruins of the Old Empires

Before the three empires there were two older kingdoms, and both are now ruins that the living visit for money, scholarship or bad reasons. Mycairos, the bronze-and-blood fortress kingdom, stood in the cliffs and hills of Ekran in what is now Hellenoria; it dug up "the gift beneath stone" and emptied overnight. Nethrana, the kingdom of mirrors and mist, stood on the island of Velothis with its capital at Eronis; it fell to illusion and the "Third Sun". The shared "Old Empires" chronicle copied between the three great libraries is the best source on both, and it disagrees with itself on every page.

The League of the Hellenes claims the Mycairan ruins and forbids digging without a licence from the Amphictyony; licences are sold. Nobody claims Velothis. The sea around it does that.

Ruin · Mycairos · Ekran, the Hellenorian hills

The Citadel of Mycarion

The cliff-cut heart of the bronze kingdom: halls of red stone, bronze doors that still lock, and a silence that has lasted longer than any empire now standing.

Codex now: The heart of the Mycairos empire, serving as the political and spiritual center. (New entry; drawn from the DM's Mycairos notes.)

Claimed by
The League of the Hellenes, through the Amphictyony's digging licences
Terrain
Cliff fortress, cyclopean walls, stair-shafts, rock-cut halls
Travel
2 days from the Inland Road into the hills · Survival DC 15; inside, Investigation DC 14 per level not to get lost
Danger
High (CR 3–11)
Trouble
Licensed diggers are opening sealed doors for a buyer nobody has met

The ruin

A fortress carved into the cliffs of Ekran, built to withstand siege and storm, and home in its day to warrior-kings, priests and sorcerers who held their rites in chambers no visitor was shown. The walls are of blocks so large the Hellenorians say giants laid them. The architecture favours intimidation over comfort: narrow gates, killing stairs, halls with one door. Tablets inscribed in the Mycairan runes lie in heaps in the archive rooms, most undeciphered; the phrase scholars have read most often is "the gift beneath stone".

New lore

Since the peace the Amphictyony has sold digging licences to fund the sanctuary's repairs, and three crews now camp below the citadel. They sell bronze, tablets and cursed blades to collectors at Corinth. One crew, led by a foreman with unusually good maps, has bypassed the archive and gone straight down.

Sites

The Lion Stair New · gate and approach

Steep, exposed · diggers' camps below · goat dung and dust

A switchback stair up the cliff to a gate crowned by two headless stone lions. The stair turns so that an attacker's shield arm faces the wall. The diggers have strung ropes. Every so often a rope is found cut.

Ties: diggers' camp; Corinth's antiquities dealers.

The Tablet Rooms New · archive

Dry, close · scholars, copyists · clay and old smoke

Baked clay tablets in thousands, preserved by the fire that ended the palace. Most are grain counts and bronze inventories. A few, kept apart in a sealed niche, are warnings. Copyists from the Three Libraries' circle work here under licence.

Ties: the Three Libraries; Thessalonika's Porticoes.

The Hall of Blood and Stone New · ritual hall

Red-stained, cold · nobody stays · iron and something sweet

A round chamber with a drain in the floor and channels cut in the walls, carved with creatures and symbols never seen alive. Wards of blood and stone still hold: spells cast here cost the caster 1d4 hit points per spell level.

Ties: the Vaults of Ekran below.

What lives here

  • Bronze golems (use iron golem with lightning immunity in place of fire) — door-wardens who still keep the king's hours.

The Vaults of Ekran

The tunnels the Mycairan priests found under their own citadel, older than they were, and sealed again at a price nobody survived to record.

Codex now: No entry. (New; drawn from the DM's notes on the fall of Mycairos.)

The ruin

A network of tunnels beneath the cliffs, cut by a people the Mycairans never named, filled with glyphs and artifacts. The early kings believed they had found a lost civilisation's treasury. Their priests read the glyphs and began the rites in the chambers above. The tunnels end in a ring of seal-doors of blood-red stone, each carved with a single eye, and behind them a vault nobody living has seen.

New lore

Since the war's end, shepherds in the hills report the old symptoms in the chronicles: whispers at night, strange symbols carved into stone by hands that did not remember carving them. Two goatherds have killed each other over nothing. The village priests have sent to Delphara for help and been sent a pamphlet.

Sites

The Glyph Road New · tunnel

Long, dry, humming · nothing living · chalk and blood

A straight tunnel a mile long, its walls cut floor to ceiling with glyphs that the eye slides off. Readers who stare too long carve the glyphs themselves, later, on whatever is to hand.

Ties: the Tablet Rooms above.

The Ring of Seals New · seal-doors

Warm, wet, listening · the dead of the last ritual · copper

Nine blood-red doors around a circular hall. Three are cracked. Behind each crack is darkness that breathes. The floor is scattered with the gear of the priests who performed the last binding, laid down neatly, as if their owners had simply stopped being.

Ties: the Nameless Hunger.

What lives here

  • Gibbering mouther — what the frenzy made of those who stayed.
  • Wraith and specter — the half-erased souls of the binding.
  • Black pudding — the flooded galleries.
  • Cloaker — in the high vaults of the Glyph Road.
  • Stone golem — seal-wardens, carved with the eye.

What can be gathered

  • Seal-stone chips — blood-red; an arcane focus that adds +1 to necromancy spell DCs and whispers at night.
  • Priests' regalia — gold and bronze, 200 gp a set; it remembers its owner.

The ruin

Three rings of wall on a bare hill, natural stone and brutal masonry. The outer two face outward, as fortresses should. The innermost, built last and in haste, faces inward, toward the king's hall. Survivors of the frenzy reported a pervasive sense of being watched; the inner wall was the garrison's answer. It did not help.

New lore

A shepherd-lord from the nearest deme has declared himself tyrannos of the ruin, pastures his flock in the outer ring and charges visitors a drachma to see the tholos tomb. Business has been good since the peace brought travellers. Two of his paying guests have not come out of the tomb, and he now charges two drachmas.

A beehive tomb dug into the hill, with a passage lined in dressed stone and a lintel of a single block. The king was buried here with his armour, his horses and, by the bones, his entire household. The household was buried alive.

The ruin

Velothis is ringed by turbulent waters and hidden currents, reachable only by routes the Nethranans once enchanted. Irelas was its door: magnificent docks, enchanted vessels carrying illusions, textiles and artifacts to every shore. Wrecks from Irelas still turn up across distant seas with cargo that defies understanding. The city lies ruined, its piers gone to coral that glows at night with residual magic, the coastline's strange flora shimmering under the moon and fading by dawn.

New lore

Since the war's navies went home, smugglers out of Zandar Isle have found a way through the currents and strip the moored hulls for their enchanted timbers, which sell at Corinth as charmed keels. Sailors on such keels report steering toward harbours that are not on any chart.

A military stronghold on the southern cliffs of Velothis, built to watch Mycairos across the sea. It is shrouded in fog that never lifts, and spectral lights flicker in it at night. Part IX

Calendars and Timeline

How each empire counts its days, and what happened when.

The Reckoning of the Year

Three empires share one sky and one year of twelve thirty-day months, and have spent fifteen centuries refusing to agree on what to call any of it.

One year, three names for everything

Every calendar on Asetheria counts the same year: twelve months of thirty days and five days left over, 365 in all. The skeleton is older than any of the empires. The Three Libraries' chronicle traces it to the Old Empires; the practical reason it survived is that armies, truces and grain fleets could not work without it. A herald who announced a truce "from the first of the seventh month" was understood on every side of the line, even by men who would not say the month's name aloud.

The common tongue starts the year at the spring equinox, as Invicta and Acheaoria do. The Five Days fall at the end of the year, between the last month of winter and the first of spring, and belong to no month. Hellenoria keeps the same months in the same places but begins its year three months later, at the Standing, the summer solstice that the sun-priests of Helionyx announce to the minute. Each empire has its own month-names, its own era and its own idea of which days are fit for business. Merchants on the Treaty Road write all three and trust none of them.

The arithmetic of the calendar belongs to Helionyx. Its College of the Arc has read a gnomon every clear day for six hundred years, and every serious calendar in the League is calibrated against its tables. So, quietly, is that of the Celestial Astromancers of the Imperium, and the Magi of Atarabad now come openly to compare the arc with their fire-calendar.

Why "Peaceful". Acheaorian month-names are attributes, not gods, and since the Signing the royal chancery has issued its documents in two columns, rendering each month by its meaning for foreign clerks. That is how the common tongue learned to write "the 2nd Day of Peaceful". The Magi chose the first of Rāmana for the Signing because it was the most auspicious day in the year for a covenant. The court chroniclers now say the month was named for the Peace, which reverses the order of events by about two thousand years.

Inside the month. Invictians count backwards from three fixed days: the Kalends (the 1st), the Nones (the 7th) and the Ides (the 15th); "the third day before the Ides" is a date. Hellenorians split the month into three tens: waxing, middle and waning, counting the last ten backwards. Acheaorians give each of the thirty days a name; a day whose name matches its month is a feast, and the Magi may still declare any day unfit for a coronation, a war or an execution.

Three tendays make a month, and the Five Days stand outside the week, so every year begins on a Firstday. Old Romulo still holds its market every eighth day by the ancient nundinal count, which drifts against the tenday and makes Romulan market day a small annual puzzle that Romulans enjoy explaining.

Converting dates

Let P be the year of the Peace (Year 5 now; a year before the Peace counts as minus, so 61 b.P. is P = −61). The common year, the Invictian year and the Acheaorian year all turn on the same morning.

  • Invictian: AUR = P + 1247. Romulo was founded in 1,246 b.P. (AUR 1).
  • Acheaorian, long count: Year of the Throne = P + 2012. Zindar was crowned in 2,011 b.P.
  • Acheaorian, regnal: year of Vishtaspa III = P + 19. He was crowned in 19 b.P. and presided at his first Bringing in 18 b.P. Earlier kings: look them up in the Rolls, and expect gaps (see DM notes).
  • Hellenorian: first find H, the Hellenorian year-count. From Highsun to the Five Days, H = P + 1032; from Sowing to Greening, H = P + 1031. Then the Pythiad is (H − 1) ÷ 4, rounded down, plus 1; the year within it is the remainder plus 1. Example: Lambing of Year 5 gives H = 1036, so the 4th year of the 259th Pythiad.
  • Day and month are the same in all three: the 2nd Day of Peaceful is 2 Vintage in the common tongue, the sixth day before the Nones of September (written a.d. VI Non. Sept.), and 2 waxing Pyanepsion.

Quick table for the Peace: Year 1 = AUR 1248 = Vishtaspa 20 = Pythiad 258.4 / 259.1 · Year 2 = AUR 1249 = Vishtaspa 21 = 259.1 / 259.2 · Year 3 = AUR 1250 = Vishtaspa 22 = 259.2 / 259.3 · Year 4 = AUR 1251 = Vishtaspa 23 = 259.3 / 259.4 · Year 5 = AUR 1252 = Vishtaspa 24 = 259.4 / 260.1.

Expansion

The Provinces of the Imperium

The Provinces of the Imperium

Nine provinces, nine Legates, nine armies, and one old man on a camp stool holding the map together by refusing to die.

The official map

On the chancery's wall map the Imperium is a single red field, cut into nine provinces by thin gold lines. Each province is governed by a Legatus Augusti, who commands its legions, appoints its garrison praefecti, hears its capital cases and sits on the Council of Legates, which meets on the Mons Sedis in Aeterna four times a year. The Duces of the great cities are appointed by the Dominus Militum, General Valerius Maximus, and answer to him; the Duumviri and praefecti of the towns answer to the Dux or to the office in the capital that appointed them. Taxes go up the road to the treasury. Orders come down it. That is the map.

The practical map

The gold lines are where one Legate's paymaster stops and another's begins. A Legatus Augusti pays his men, so his men are his; he houses his veterans, so his veterans are his; he lends the Dux his soldiers to collect the tax, so the Dux is, most months, his too. The wartime emergency that made provincial commands permanent has outlived the war by five years, and the Council's one unanimous wish is that nobody takes the legions away (see Political (Invicta) and Military (Invicta)). The crowd's rule of thumb: a seal works only where its owner's soldiers stand.

Four places sit outside the nine. Aeterna and its sacred line belong to no province: the Praefectus Urbi governs the city, the Praetorian Custodians under Legatus Varus Decianus hold the ground outside the line, and the Legates' retinues camp in the suburbs like guests who have stopped pretending to leave. The Duneforged Citadel is an ally, not a province; Duke Roderick Caesar was never appointed by anyone. Ephelanum is a treaty condominium whose Dux reports through Aepistra. Deiperduem is neutral by treaty, which has not stopped every Legate from asking who will hold the Ironclad Legion's six hundred there when their contract ends in spring.

Numbers, for the DM's ledger

Thirteen line legions stand in the provinces, about 65,000 men on paper and 58,000 on the pay rolls, plus auxiliary horse, marines and the Legates' private "household cohorts". The five named legions (Red Obsidian, Praetorian Custodians, Beastlords, Shadow Assassins and the Triform Host) answer to the Dominus Militum and are not counted here. The missing numbers in the line, VI, VII, XI, XIV and XVII to XIX, are legions lost in the Continental War or dissolved at the Great Concord; their veterans are the core of the problem in every province below. The Imperium's census, last taken in the war, gives some twenty-one million souls including the capital. Nobody has counted since, because the count would show how many of them are owed land.
