Latium the Plains · Provincia Latina

The province around the capital, held by the one Legate who commands his own legion in person and the only one who could be inside the line by noon.

Legatus Augusti
Decimus Aurelianus Corvus, the Iron Legate
Seat
Castra Latina, a day's march from the boundary stones
Cities and towns
Romulo, Anticata, Falecosa, Nemibano; Fucostia answers to the Annona, not the Legate
Trouble
A loyal army camped on the capital's doorstep, paid in foreign gold

The Legate and his household

Corvus is the only Council member who is a Legatus Legionis as well as a Legatus Augusti: he kept the Ninth when he was given the province, and sleeps in its camp. His household is small and military. His wife Aurelia Prima died in the last winter of the war; his only son is a hostage-guest in the Dominus Militum's household in Aeterna, which is the leash nobody mentions. His camp prefect, Fabricius Durus, recruits at the Veterans' Table in Napplesia and keeps the list of every centurion in three days' ride. His paymaster, Titus Ennius Cato, is the only man who knows where the Ninth's extra pay comes from. Corvus does not want the chair. He wants an army that is paid and ready for the war he expects within ten years, and he wants Deiperduem as the place to stand when it comes.

Legions

Legio IX Latiaris, "the Latium Legion", the Ninth: six thousand two hundred men, two hundred over establishment because Corvus takes the best of every discharged legion. Its officers carry the twelve gladii of the Ninth; Corvus wears the best of them. Tribunus Laticlavius Publius Aelius Lamia, twenty-three, a patrician boy the Senate sent to learn the trade, writes home to his mother more than Corvus would like. Ala I Latina, five hundred horse under Decurio-Praefectus Sabinus Ollo, rides the Via Septentrionalis to Anticata and watches Strabo's couriers change horses.

Towns and forts

Castra Latina is a stone camp on a low rise above the Plains, with a canabae of six thousand camp-followers who have built a theatre. Turris Bellonae, a signal tower on the Via Sacra Aeterna, can see the Mons Sedis by day and the line's lamps by night. Vicus Novus, a village of veterans Corvus settled on his own land, has a wall, which villages near the capital are not supposed to have. Up the Tiberius stands Calvus's granary villa, on an estate the southern Legate bought inside Corvus's province, which Corvus regards the way a dog regards a cat in its kennel.

Veterans

The Tent Rows at the boundary stones are full of men from the dead legions, and they call Corvus by his first name. He feeds some of them from the Ninth's stores, which is either charity or recruitment.

Warlord

Marcus "Ten-Mile" Atilius, a former primus pilus of the dissolved Legio XIV, holds a ten-mile stretch of the old forest road with his century intact and charges "road-keeping". Corvus could crush him in an afternoon and has not, which tells Atilius he is being saved for something.

Patrician estates

House Calpurnia and the gens Sulpicia hold the grain land around Romulo; the gens Varria keeps the Villa Varriana above Falecosa. All three pay the Legate's road-levy in debased coin, and he lets them.

The succession

Corvus is the hinge of the eclipse. If Strabo proclaims, Corvus crosses the line the same day "to protect the capital". He cannot move first while his son is in the Dominus's house.

Septentrionalis the North · Provincia Septentrionalis

The best-governed province in the Imperium, which is the problem: it has stopped needing the Imperium.

Legatus Augusti
Quintus Herennius Strabo, "the Squint", of the gens Herennia
Seat
The Castra Nova at Aepistra (Dux Marcus Insteius Fronto holds the city, in name)
Attached
Ephelanum: Dux Marcus Vettius Calvo reports through Aepistra
Trouble
Thirty thousand veterans housed on land granted in the Legate's name

The Legate and his household

Strabo is fifty-nine, squints from an old sling-stone, and is the most competent administrator in the Imperium. His wife Herennia Galla distributes the land grants personally, so the veterans thank her by name. Their son Quintus Herennius Bassus, nineteen, is a tribune in the Fourth and is not clever; their daughter Herennia Minor is betrothed to the Ollovici heir, a match the old families of the north call either statesmanship or a horse-trade. His nephew Gaius holds the Treaty March next door (see Limitanea). Strabo believes the Imperium breaks apart if Calvus gets the chair; he intends to prevent that by taking it.

Legions

Legio IV Victrix holds the Castra Nova under Legatus Legionis Lucius Antistius Vetus, Strabo's man to the bone. Legio XII Fulminata holds the northern road forts under Manius Acilius Glabrio, who owes the Chyrsus Syndicate more than his estates are worth. Legio XX Valeria Victrix, raised by a Valerius forty years ago, guards the Treaty Road terminus under Publius Clodius Thrasea, a Dominus's appointee whose men now wear Strabo's owl badge over the eagle. Thrasea has not decided whose legion he commands.

Towns and forts

Aepistra and its Legate's Mile; the Cursus Legionis relay station, where Strabo's strongroom holds five years of copied state post. Castellum Bubonis ("Owl Fort"), the XII's headquarters, two days north on the Via Septentrionalis. Agri Galli, the largest veterans' colony, named for Herennia Galla, four thousand families on drained marsh. Mansio Pulverea, a dusty relay stop where the Treaty Road caravans of House Suren-Pahlav water before Aepistra.

Veterans

The north has solved the veterans' problem, illegally. The land grants are real; the titles are signed by Strabo "for the Imperator". If the Dominus voids them, thirty thousand men lose their farms. If he confirms them, he confirms Strabo.

Warlord

Brannoc the Unenrolled, a cousin of the Duumvir's family who never took the Invictian name, leads three hundred native horse in the hills and burns veterans' boundary stones on old clan land. Strabo pays him not to, which costs less than a war and more than he admits.

Patrician estates

Most of the great estates are owned from Aeterna; Strabo has bought the debts of half of them. House Flavia Brannoca and the Ollovici are the province's own.

The succession

Strabo has said nothing in public about the day after the Dominus. Thirty thousand veterans with his signature on their land titles have said it for him.

Limitanea the Treaty March · Provincia Limitanea

The province between Aepistra and the neutral interior, where the Treaty Road is the economy and the nephew is the government.

Legatus Augusti
Gaius Herennius Severus, nephew of Strabo
Seat
Castellum Foederis, the last Invictian fort on the Treaty Road before Deiperduem
Borders
The free marsh of the Maeotis Helos; Briar's Valley
Trouble
Customs worth a legion's pay, collected by a legion that is never paid on time

The Legate and his household

Gaius Herennius Severus is thirty-eight, his uncle's heir in everything but name, and has spent five years being reminded of it. He is braver than Strabo and less patient. His wife Antonia Lepida comes from a Calpurnian cadet line, which gives the remnant a door into the gens Herennia and Strabo a reason to read her letters. Severus keeps a Hellenorian tutor for his sons and an Acheaorian groom for his horses, and calls this "frontier manners". He wants the customs of the Treaty Road for his own treasury and has been told by his uncle that they are promised to Arshan Suren-Pahlav if the north wins.

Legions

Legio VIII Augusta holds Castellum Foederis and the road forts under Legatus Legionis Sextus Calpetanus Festus, a slow, honest man the caravans like. Legio XVI Flavia Firma, raised from enfranchised northerners, garrisons the marsh edge under Titus Flavius Ammo, the first Legatus Legionis of native blood the Imperium has allowed in a century; his men would follow him into the Helos and some of them have.

Towns and forts

Castellum Foederis, a square fort with a customs house bigger than its barracks. Pons Salarius, a salt-market town at a bridge over the marsh outflow, two thousand people and a toll on every cart. Statio Tertia, a road post where the Chyrsus Syndicate's toll-men and the legion's customs clerks sit in the same room and collect the same coin twice. Vadum Ranarum ("Frog Ford"), a marsh-edge hamlet that pays tribute to whoever asks and keeps two sets of flags.

Veterans

Discharged men drift east along the road toward Deiperduem, where the Ironclad Legion hires. Lately the Ironclad recruiters there take only veterans of the Latium legions, and the rest come back angry.

Rebel

Mother Verrucosa, an ex-sutler with a scarred face, runs a smuggling ring of deserters through the Maeotis Helos, moving pre-debasement silver east and Acheaorian gold west. She pays the XVI's centurions better than the treasury does.

Patrician estates

Few; the land is marsh and road. House Ovinia holds the road-repair contract; the Calpurnii own salt-pans at Pons Salarius through Antonia Lepida's dowry.

The succession

Severus is Strabo's second blade: if the north proclaims, the Treaty March closes the road to Deiperduem and cuts Corvus off from his men in the neutral city.

Ulterior the Silent March · Provincia Ulterior

The northernmost province, under a Legate nobody in Aeterna has met in years, where the census lists villages that are no longer there.

Legatus Augusti
Gnaeus Domitius Laeca
Seat
Vallum Tacitum, a wall-fort on the border hills toward Hellenoria
Trouble
What the Imperium did here, and what it is still doing

The Legate and his household

Gnaeus Domitius Laeca is sixty-seven and attends the Council by proxy, sending a sealed vote and a jar of the march's honey. His household is his staff; his wife lives in Aeterna and has not seen him in nine years. He is a soldier of the old school, frugal, literal and frightening, and he believes the march must be kept "quiet". Laeca wants nothing from the succession except to be left alone, which makes him the Council's swing vote and every Legate's correspondent.

Legions

Legio XIII Gemina, "the Twins", formed long ago by merging two broken legions, holds the Wall under Legatus Legionis Lucius Tampius Flavianus. The Thirteenth recruits locally, from the sons of colonists, and serves its whole twenty years in the march. Its men speak a dialect the south finds old-fashioned.

Towns and forts

Vallum Tacitum, a turf-and-stone wall with forts every mile and a gate-town of three thousand. Argentaria, a silver-mining town worked by convict labour. Septem Casae, a colonist village built on the foundations of an older one that the maps do not name. Mutina Vetus, an abandoned town the XIII patrols but never enters.

Veterans

The XIII's veterans are settled in the march and are paid, in silver from Argentaria, which no other province can say. The cost is that they are never discharged south. A man who served on the Wall stays near it.

Rebel

The Unnamed, native hill-folk whose ancestors were "swept aside" in the founding, cut wall-patrols' throats and leave the bodies facing south. Their leader is called only the Grandmother. The chancery calls them brigands.

Patrician estates

None will hold land here. The gens Varria once did; its records of the march are the ones Inquisitor Falco wanted struck.

The succession

Laeca's vote decides whether the Council can declare the chair vacant with three Legates or needs four. Strabo writes to him monthly. Calvus sends wine. Corvus sends nothing, which Laeca respects.

Litorana the South coast · Provincia Litorana

Villas, olive terraces and grain ships along the Via Litoranea, held by the richest Legate, who has never risked a man he could pay someone else to risk.

Legatus Augusti
Sextus Lollius Calvus of the gens Lollia
Seat
The Villa Lolliana on the headland above Napplesia
Trouble
The Annona's grain passes through his ports, and some of it stays

The Legate and his household

Calvus is fifty-four, bald since thirty, and governs from a dining couch. His wife Pompilia Rufa runs the household and the villa's marriage market. His freedman secretary Lollius Chrestus knows every grain contract on the coast by the sack. His nephew Senator Publius Lollius Rufinus is his voice in the Curia, and a cousin at three removes, Praefectus Titus Lollius Varro of Anticata, is treated as his spy on the northern road whether he is one or not. Calvus wants the chair if it is cheap and the south's independence if it is not. He has put a candidate forward for sole Dux of Mavelon, and his lawyers are feeding the Skelding feud there.

Legions

Legio V Alaudae, "the Larks", from the crested helmets, holds the coast road under Legatus Legionis Marcus Stertinius Avitus, who thinks his Legate a coward and keeps it to his diary. Legio X Fretensis, the Imperium's marine legion, is split between the south harbour at Mavelon and the grain anchorages under Decimus Lollius Paetus, Calvus's cousin, who is the reason Calvus's marines can "take the south harbour" in one night. Calvus also pays two household cohorts of hired Qart-Hadethi spearmen, against the law.

Towns and forts

Napplesia, its hot springs and its Veterans' Table. Portus Lollianus, a private grain harbour Calvus built "for storm shelter", with granaries larger than Fucostia's. Salinae, salt pans and a fish-sauce works whose smell reaches the villas when the wind turns. Castra Alaudarum, the Larks' camp, a day south on the Via Litoranea. Oppidum Oleae, an olive town of eight thousand where the Legate's agent buys the whole crop at a price he sets.

Veterans

Retired officers crowd the coast. Pension arrears are worst here, because the men owed most once commanded cohorts. Stella of the Veterans' Table can name every officer within three days' ride; her own son is Calvus's man, which she knows.

Warlord

Gaius Septimius "Bucca", a discharged trierarch, holds a pirate cove at Scopuli Rubri with three captured liburnians and takes grain ships the Annona cannot afford to lose. Calvus buys the grain back from him, which is cheaper than fighting.

Patrician estates

The Lollii, of course; the gens Postumia's villas at Napplesia; and every rich family in the capital with a summer house. House Ovinia charters half the grain barges and splits the margin with Chrestus.

The succession

If the north proclaims, Calvus declares the south neutral and keeps the grain. Aeterna starves; whoever wins must buy bread from him.

Ferraria the Iron Province · Provincia Ferraria

The iron country of the Via Ferraria and the caldera port at its end, governed by an old Legate who owes his creditor more than his loyalty.

Legatus Augusti
Gnaeus Mettius Aper
Capital
Mavelon (Reiks Ansvald and Dux Publius Arruntius Celer, equal by treaty)
Trouble
A wartime treaty, a peacetime arsenal and a Legate for sale

The Legate and his household

Gnaeus Mettius Aper is seventy, gouty and cheerful, and governs from the iron-town of Ferrifodina rather than Mavelon, because the Mavelon Oath leaves no room for a third ruler and he is wise enough not to try. His second wife, Mettia Calpurnilla, is forty years younger and gambles. Their debts are held by Calvus. His son-in-law, Quintus Aemilius Regillus, is the Council's candidate for sole Dux of Mavelon; the writ waits in a strongbox. Aper wants to die in his bed with his debts forgiven, and would sign almost anything to manage it.

Legions

Legio III Ferrata, "the Ironclad Third" (no relation to the Ironclad Legion of Deiperduem, a point its men make with fists), guards the Via Ferraria and the forges under Legatus Legionis Lucius Tettius Crispus, a hard engineer who likes Dux Celer and despises Calvus. The fleet in Mavelon's south harbour belongs to the Praefectus Classis, not the Legate; the oars belong to the Thing.

Towns and forts

Mavelon, with its two harbours, two halves and one Gate. Ferrifodina, the mining town at the iron-beds, four days up the road, eleven thousand people and a permanent cough. Carbonaria, a charcoal camp that buys from Alderpool and burns faster than the forest regrows. Statio Malleorum ("Hammer Post"), a road fort where the iron convoys are counted, and miscounted, before the coast.

Veterans

Veterans of the III were promised forge-shares; the shares went to House Demetria's creditors. The Mavari crews idled by fewer launches drink with them in the north harbour, which the south side finds alarming.

Warlord

The Jackal's cousin-gang, the Tongs, rob iron convoys on the high road and sell the bars at the Broken Gate. Their chief, an ex-optio called Ferox Scaurus, was paid in pre-debasement silver by someone who wanted the convoys watched.

Patrician estates

House Sentia's yards, House Demetria's forges and the gens Arruntia's Praetorium; inland, the Ovinii own ore-carts and the roads they ruin.

The succession

Whoever holds Mavelon holds the fleet. Calvus needs the Oath broken by Mavari hands so Regillus can be installed; the Thing needs one more grievance to sail home.

Montana the Cloudspine March · Provincia Montana

The southern mountains toward the Cloudspine Ridge, where the Legate's forts guard the approaches and the real wall is an ally who was never appointed.

Legatus Augusti
Aulus Caesennius Rufinus
Seat
Porta Nubium, a gate-fort on the Via Ferraria below the Cloudspine Ridge
Neighbour
The Duneforged Citadel, ally, not province
Trouble
A march that cannot be held without Duneforged's levies, which three Legates are trying to buy

The Legate and his household

Aulus Caesennius Rufinus, fifty-one, fought beside the Caesars at the pass and is the only Legate Duke Roderick Caesar invites to dinner. His wife Caesennia Tertulla keeps the fort's school for officers' children; their eldest, Aulus the Younger, is fostered in Duneforged in Count Faris Zayida's Aegistower. Rufinus is loyal to Valerius Maximus because Valerius gave him the march; he has no plan for the day after, and is honest enough to say so.

Legions

Legio XV Martia holds the passes under Legatus Legionis Gaius Minicius Fundanus, a mountain soldier with frostbitten ears. Cohors I Montanorum, local goat-herders with slings, holds the high paths under Praefectus Ursa Varenilla, the only woman to command an auxiliary cohort, by Rufinus's signature and nobody else's.

Towns and forts

Porta Nubium, a gate-fort across the road with a town of four thousand under it. Castellum Aquilae, a signal fort that can see the Citadel's lights. Vicus Caprarius, a goat village where the March buys cheese and the Duneforged buy guides. Argentum Montis, a played-out silver camp now selling to Clan Ironhand's prospectors.

Veterans

Veterans of the pass want land on the plains, not stones in the mountains. Many have gone to Duneforged's mine camps, where the pay is in good coin and the mines hum.

Warlord

Haldric the Barren, an ex-signifer, runs a toll-gang at the old pass road and claims a war-grant from Strabo's commission "in the name of the Imperator". He is recruiting levies for the north from the same villages Gavin Caesar recruits from.

Patrician estates

Little worth owning. House Merca holds mortgages on half the march's mines; the gens Caesennia is new money from war-loot.

The succession

Strabo's courier came south to buy four hundred Duneforged levies; Rufinus let him pass, then wrote to Valerius. A Caerthain ruling on which seal to honour decides which Legate is better armed.

Klyninia the Water Mountains · Provincia Klyninia

The mountain province where the Aqua Aeterna begins, governed by the Dominus's most loyal Legate, who could turn off the capital's water with one order.

Legatus Augusti
Lucius Fabius Silo
Seat
Caput Aquae, at the aqueduct's head in the Klynin Mountain Range
Trouble
A contractor's aqueduct, a Legate's legion and a capital that drinks on trust

The Legate and his household

Lucius Fabius Silo is sixty-three and was the Dominus's chief of staff for twelve years. He is pious, thin and dutiful, keeps Valerius's letters in a cedar chest, and writes to Valeria Prisca weekly. His wife Fabia Paullina is a priestess of Juno and attends the quarterly Assay. Their son Marcus Fabius Silo is a junior tribune in the Custodians under Varus Decianus. Silo wants the succession settled lawfully and believes the Dominus will do it in time, which he will not.

Legions

Legio I Adiutrix, raised from marines in the war and given the mountains in peace, guards the aqueduct and the marble quarries under Legatus Legionis Servius Cornelius Scapula, a builder who thinks his men are wasted on sentry. The First is under strength by a thousand, because Silo will not pay in debased coin and cannot pay in good.

Towns and forts

Caput Aquae, the aqueduct's head: settling tanks, a temple of the Nymphs and a town of five thousand. Lapicidinae, the marble quarries, white dust on everything. Plumbaria, lead mines whose pipes carry the water to every fountain in Aeterna. Castellum Divisorium, the sluice-fort where the channel can be closed; its keys are kept by the Legate and the Ovinii, which is one key too many.

Veterans

Hill-farmers' sons who served and came home to no land. They work the Ovinii's repair gangs at half a legionary's pay and have begun calling the aqueduct "ours".

Warlord

Lucilia Bracata, a quarry overseer's widow, leads the quarrymen's collegium in a strike that has stopped marble for the Mons Sedis. She is not a warlord, but the chancery treats her like one.

Patrician estates

House Ovinia holds the contract to maintain the Aqua Aeterna; the gens Fabia holds summer pastures; the Varrii a ruined villa.

The succession

Whoever holds the sluice-fort holds the capital's thirst. Silo will close it for nobody. Two Legates have asked the Ovinii whether their key would be enough.

Araucaria the Forest · Provincia Araucaria

The old forest province on the forest road, where the arsenal's appetite meets the Silvanus rotation, and armies get lost on purpose.

Legatus Augusti
Marcus Plautius Silvanus
Seat
Forum Arborum, a timber town on the old forest road
Villages
Alderpool, Nemorus, Silva Caminia
Trouble
More timber ordered than the forest can give, paid in bad coin

The Legate and his household

Marcus Plautius Silvanus is fifty-eight, a forester's son who rose through the ranks and is mocked in the Curia for his accent. He sleeps in a hunting lodge, eats what he kills and enforces the rotation: which trees may be cut, and when. His wife Plautia Ursilla manages the timber contracts and has never forgiven the arsenal for paying late. Silvanus wants the forest left standing and the arsenal to pay its bills. He has no candidate for the chair and would like none of them to need his trees.

Legions

Legio XXII Primigenia, the youngest legion in the Imperium, raised in the war's last decade, holds the forest road under Legatus Legionis Quintus Tineius Rufus, ambitious and bored. Half the Twenty-Second is on road-clearing detail; the other half is on Rufus's private list of men who would march for Corvus.

Towns and forts

Forum Arborum, a timber market of six thousand with a sawmill on every stream. Castra Silvana, the XXII's camp, a stockade of whole trunks. Resinaria, a pitch-boiling hamlet that sells caulking to Mavelon's yards. Lucus Ferrarum, a ruined grove-shrine where travellers leave iron nails for the wood.

Veterans

Discharged men clear the road and are paid in timber-rights the arsenal will not honour. Many have taken the rights to Romulo to be sealed, and been told to wait.

Warlord

Calvus's lost silver: two weeks ago a private army of the southern Legate, marching north by the forest road with 2,000 gp in good coin, went off the road; the Silent Stalkers led it astray. Its commander, Tribune Vibius Marsus, now holds a ruined fort in the deep wood with three hundred men, no orders and no road home.

Patrician estates

Few; the forest is state land. House Ovinia holds the timber charter; the gens Sulpicia holds hunting rights it has not used in a generation.

The succession

The forest road is the back way from the south to the capital. Silvanus closing it, or not, decides how fast Calvus can move if he moves at all.

The Senate roster

Six hundred seats; about two hundred and forty senators attend in a normal month, and twenty matter. The factions: Remnant (the patrician remnant, led by the Calpurnii); Valerian (the Dominus's men); Herennian (Strabo's); Lollian (Calvus's); Army (ex-officers raised to the Senate, who lean toward Corvus); New Men (equestrian money); Pontiffs (members of the college that can declare the chair vacant).

Manius Curius DentatusPontiffs (swing)59His price: proof that the chair is truly empty, which he hopes nobody can give him.

The Council of Legates: seating chart

The Council meets in the Hall of the Standards on the Mons Sedis, at a horseshoe table of old campaign tables nailed together. The open end faces the Dominus Militum's camp stool. Seats were fixed by date of appointment and have been fought over ever since. Every Legate may bring two staff; they stand.

Expansion

The League of the Hellenes

The League of the Hellenes

Thirty-odd harbours, hill-towns and new colonies that swore to the Imperial Family, pay into a common fleet berthed in somebody else's harbour, and meet on Hellarchon's Rock to vote on whether they still have to.

The map as the scribes draw it

The court scribes of the Circles of Mirrors draw the League as a ring of cities around the Emperor's mirror: every member equal, every member loyal, Hellarchon first only because somebody has to keep the ships. The practical map is a hub and its spokes. Seven great cities, six towns of the old lists, a dozen lesser islands and coast-cities, and since the Treaty of Myrianth a scatter of colonies beyond the Peaks of Veilmar, the western range where the coast turns and the Lexicon Council's dialects stop.

Every member governs itself and sends delegates to the synedrion, which meets on the Akra of Hellarchon under a ceiling gilded, the allies suspect, with their own contributions. Every member pays an assessment to the League Chest, set by a Hellarchon board and kept in the back room of the Maiden's temple since the war moved it there "for safety". Every member owes the common fleet crews. The common fleet is two hundred and forty hulls on the Treaty list, berthed at Hellarchon, crewed by Hellarchon citizens and commanded by Hellarchon's first strategos as Hegemon: Kleandros Nikandrides, eleven years running.

The League's lists rank every city below the seven as a deme. Its chief magistrate may call himself archon at home; in the synedrion's minutes he is a Demarch, and he minds. The colonies rank lower still: those Hellarchon founded are governed by a harmost it sends, and the whole western frontier answers to a Strategos of the West, Demophon Akamantides, who sits at Virelyn.

Three blocs and a valve

The hegemon's bloc is Hellarchon, the cities that depend on its grain convoys, the islands it planted with its own citizens, and the colonies whose votes its harmosts cast. The Thebesian bloc is named for the army, not the money: Corinth pays, Thebesieas marches, Thessalonika supplies the precedents, and the smaller cities that resent the hegemony join whichever motion is likeliest to annoy it. Thebesieas itself has stopped attending, which costs the bloc three votes and gives it a grievance worth more. The tyrants hold four harbours and hill-towns where a strong man fed the poor and kept the club-bearers. Their delegates' votes are disputed, which makes them the hinge of every close division. The neutrals are sanctuaries, spa towns, toll-cities and colonies too new to have enemies; they sell their votes motion by motion and call it independence.

Above all of it the Imperial Family reigns. Emperor Thalorion IV of House Thalorid has not been seen in public for ten years. His letters open every session, read by his Voice, and his voice sounds different in every region it reaches.

Votes: 32 in all; a motion needs a majority of votes present. Present strength in an ordinary session, with Thebesieas absent and the four disputed seats seated: hegemon's bloc 10, Thebesian bloc 7, tyrants 4, neutrals 8 (7 when Kirimitsana does not come, which is always). Neither bloc can carry a motion without the neutrals or the tyrants, which is why both court them and neither will admit it.

Kynthos

A small, holy, treeless island where the League Chest used to sit, and where nobody has been allowed to be born or die for nine hundred years.

Ruler
Thargelia Phanodikou
Title
Archon of the Island (Demarch on the League's lists) · Amphictyony seat
Population
c. 2,500 residents; 15,000 in festival month
Patron
Leto the Graceful Mother, who gave birth here, the island says; Apollo and Artemis as her children
Harbour
The Sacred Harbour, shallow and crowded; a merchant mole on the lee side
Grudge
The Chest was "lent" to Hellarchon in the war and never came back
Hellarchon
Its creditor in theory, its client in fact

Kynthos is a dry granite hump with one hill, one sacred lake and a palm tree the island swears is the one Leto held in labour. The League was sworn here. For four centuries its contributions lay in the island's temple under a board of treasurers drawn from every member, and Kynthos lived on the fees, the festival and the dignity. In the war's last decade an Acheaorian squadron was sighted off the cape, and the Hegemon of the day moved the Chest to Hellarchon "for safety". The squadron was never sighted again. Neither was the Chest.

By old purification law nobody may be born or die on the island; the pregnant and the dying are rowed across to the islet of Rheneia, a quarter-hour away, which is consequently crowded with graves and midwives. The island has no farmland and imports everything, including its water in dry years. It still holds the League's spring festival, the Kynthia, with choruses sent by every city, and it keeps the original bronze tablets of the League's oath, which Hellarchon has twice asked to "conserve".

Houses

House Phanodikidai Temple stewards · Eupatrid

Crest: a palm between two swans · Motto: "We kept it once." · Seat: the stewards' house by the sacred lake

Keepers of the temple inventories for twenty generations. They hold the old treasurers' ledgers, which record to the drachma what was in the Chest the day it left.

  • Thargelia Phanodikou, Archon, 49 — reads the closing figure of the last ledger aloud at every Kynthia, in front of Hellarchon's envoys.
House Rhenaioi Midwives and undertakers · the islet families

Crest: a cradle and a lamp · Motto: "Across the water, both ways." · Seat: Rheneia

The families who run birth and burial on the islet. Every Kynthian is born in their hands and buried by them, and they know every family's secrets, especially the dates.

  • Myrto Rhenaia, head midwife — keeps a register of births that disagrees with the citizen roll by thirty names.

Samaris

A rich island of Hera's temple, a tunnel through a mountain and a tyrant with sixty ships, who holds the second tyrant's seat at Delphara and has never once been rude to the Hegemon.

Ruler
Lygdamis son of Aiakes
Title
Tyrannos (seized power in the war's last year) · Amphictyony seat (disputed)
Population
c. 40,000
Patron
Hera, Matron of Families, at the great Heraion on the marsh
Harbour
A double mole three hundred yards out into twenty fathoms, the deepest harbour in the League outside Hellarchon
Grudge
Hellarchon refused to send a single ship when Acheaorian raiders burned its vineyards in the war
Hellarchon
Smiling, well-armed rival; pays its assessment early, in full, and in Acheaorian darics

Samaris has three great works: the mole, the Heraion, and a tunnel a mile long driven through the mountain from both ends at once to bring water to the city. The two crews met in the middle, a cubit apart. Every Samarian child is taken to see the join.

Lygdamis was a trierarch who came home in the war's last year with three ships and a grievance, found the oligarchs negotiating with an Acheaorian satrap for protection, and took the acropolis during the Heraia while the citizens were unarmed for the procession. He has run the island since as a household: public works for the poor, a court of poets, sixty ships, a hundred archers from the Malaunian Steppe, and a policy of plundering friend and enemy alike "because a friend is more grateful when you return what you took". His navy is the largest in the League after Hellarchon's, and no assembly paid for it.

He is courteous to Hellarchon in every letter. His delegate holds Samaris's seat on the Amphictyony and votes with Atticenea's. Together they are the two tyrant seats that paralyse Delphara.

Houses

House Aiakidai The tyrant's house

Crest: a lion's scalp on a ship's prow · Motto: "Ask the sea." · Seat: the acropolis palace

Lygdamis, his two brothers and their sons. One brother was exiled for plotting; the other was found drowned. The house is now Lygdamis and nephews who smile at everything.

  • Lygdamis son of Aiakes, Tyrannos, 51 — once threw his signet ring into the sea to break his run of luck; a fisherman brought it back in a fish, and he has been nervous since.
House Geomoroi Exiled landowners · Eupatrid

Crest: an ox-yoke · Motto: "The land remembers its owners." · Seat: in exile at Corinth

The old landholding oligarchy, expelled when Lygdamis took the acropolis. They petition the synedrion at every session and borrow from Corinth's counting-houses against estates they cannot see.

  • Demoteles Geomoros, head, 70 — has drafted a motion to unseat the tyrant's delegate nineteen times and been talked out of tabling it eighteen.

Chelonia

An island within sight of Hellarchon's Rock whose old citizens were expelled in the war and whose new ones were shipped in from Hellarchon's Road, and who are finding the island has opinions of its own.

Ruler
Lysikrates Nausiou
Title
Archon (Demarch on the lists), elected by the cleruchs · Amphictyony seat
Population
c. 9,000 settlers; c. 2,000 old Chelonians, as metics on their own island
Patron

Mother, landlord and garrison; "the eyesore of the harbour" in the old Assembly's phrase

Chelonia was Hellarchon's oldest rival: a trading island of silversmiths and long-haul merchants whose tortoise coins were taken in every market when Hellarchon's owls were still a joke. In the war's darkest decade the Assembly accused the island of signalling to Acheaorian ships, expelled every citizen and divided the land into lots for four thousand of the Road's poor, who became cleruchs: citizens of Hellarchon farming another people's fields.

Two generations on, the cleruchs' grandchildren have Chelonian accents, Chelonian vines and Chelonian grudges. They pay Hellarchon's assessment and resent it. They send eight warships to the common fleet and want them berthed at home. The expelled families, who drifted back after the Treaty as metics, own the boatyards, the silver workshops and the only maps of the Secret Harbour's entrance.

Houses

House Nausiadai Cleruch farmers · first lot-holders

Crest: an owl on a vine-stake · Motto: "We were given it." · Seat: the upper lots

Descendants of the first settler to draw a lot, and so the island's oldest new family. They want Chelonia's vote cast by Chelonians.

  • Lysikrates Nausiou, Archon, 44 — has quietly stopped attending the Panegyris at Hellarchon.
House Chelonidai The expelled · silversmiths, now metics

Crest: a sea-turtle · Motto: "Slow, and home." · Seat: the boatyards below the old town

The old merchant aristocracy, back as tenants on their own island. They keep the tortoise dies hidden and strike nothing with them, yet.

  • Aiakeia Chelonis, head, 68 — was born in the expulsion boat, and holds the original deed to the Archon's house.

Thyraia

The walled pass-city under the Thunder Gate of Olympus, where the tyrant's brother collects a "votive offering" from every smuggler and every raider, and the League's common garrison is mostly priests.

Ruler
Dexippos son of Orthon
Title
Tyrannos (seized power after the second Northfolk raid)
Population
c. 7,000, and a fort of 300 hired spears
Patron
Zeus the Storm Lord of the Gate; Hermes of the road for the traders; Ares, quietly, in the tyrant's hall
Harbour
None; a river landing three days downstream, and the pass itself
Grudge
The synedrion voted a common garrison and sent a "festival of watching" instead of soldiers
Hellarchon
Far away and useless in winter; Dexippos says so in every letter

Of the three passes over Olympus, the Thunder Gate is the eastern and the weakest held, and Thyraia is the city that holds it: a grey town of stacked stone houses, goat-markets and wind, with a wall across the valley floor and the fort above it in the cloud. Its assembly argued for a season with its neighbour about who should pay for the wall, and in that season Northfolk raiders came through twice. The second time Dexippos, a captain of hired spears, held the fort with ninety men for four days while the assembly debated. He came down with the raiders' horses and was voted a guard by acclamation.

He keeps the pass. His brother Orthon commands the fort and takes a toll from every mule-train, called an offering to Zeus because a tax would need the assembly. The synedrion's common garrison arrived last year: forty spearmen, twelve priests and a choir, funded from the Theoric Fund as a festival because the Fund cannot pay for war. Dexippos feeds them, pays them better than Hellarchon does, and has begun to drill the choir.

Crest: a closed gate under a thunderbolt · Motto: "Shut it first." · Seat: the gate-tower

A family of mercenary captains who served every city in the war and were paid by most. They hold the wall, the fort and the toll.

  • Orthon son of Orthon, fort commander — keeps two ledgers of offerings, one for Zeus and one for himself, and both are accurate.

Crest: a key and a horn · Motto: "The mountain chose us." · Seat: the old warden's house, now a stable

The hereditary wardens who held the pass for six centuries and lost it in a season of argument. They want the assembly restored and themselves back on the wall.

  • Kleomenes Pylaios, head, 60 — writes to Thessalonika weekly; Thessalonika answers monthly.

Asopia

A city of three thousand on the Inland Road, within sight of Thebesieas's walls, which has been loyal to Hellarchon for four hundred years out of pure spite.

Title
Archon (Demarch on the lists), elected each spring
Population
c. 3,000; every adult citizen of Hellarchon by an old grant
Patron

None; the River Asopos ford and the Inland Road toll-stone

Hellarchon
Its only friend, which has never once sent help in time

Asopia sits on a low ridge above the river between Thebesieas and the coast, small enough to walk round before breakfast. Its fame is a battlefield: the plain below, where a League army broke an Acheaorian host eleven centuries ago, and where the Asopians still hold the Feast of the Free every fourth year, racing in armour from the altar to the trophy. Every city of the League swore to keep Asopia free and inviolate. Thebesieas has razed it twice since. Hellarchon, which granted every Asopian its citizenship in gratitude, has never arrived before the walls came down.

The Asopians are farmers, tomb-keepers and professional witnesses. They tend the war graves of half the League for a fee, swear to boundaries in other cities' lawsuits, and vote with Hellarchon in the synedrion on everything, including motions they have not read, because anything Thebesieas wants must be bad. Since the Sacred Band refilled its roll this spring, Asopia has repaired its wall with its own hands and asked Hellarchon for a garrison. The request is "under consideration".

Hereditary priests of the battlefield and its graves; the city's archons come from them more often than the lot would suggest.

Stenai

The toll-city on the Narrows at the far end of the Long Lane, where every grain ship of the Golden Scythe Accord passes under a boom chain and pays somebody, and the argument is about whom.

Ruler
Pausimachos Leonidou
Title
Archon (Demarch on the lists), chosen by the council of three hundred
Population
c. 30,000

Poseidon of the Narrows; Hecate of the crossings, whose torch-shrine lights the chain

Hellarchon
A partner it cannot afford to lose and a tenant it cannot evict

Stenai stands on a triangular headland at the Narrows, where the current runs so hard that grain ships must hug its shore to pass. The founders consulted Delphara, were told to settle "opposite the blind", and decided the people across the strait must have been blind to miss the site. The city's wealth is the current: tunny that shoal in the Horn, pilots who know the eddies, and the dues on every ship of the grain run that feeds half the League.

In the war Hellarchon put a customs house on the quay and took a tenth of every cargo "for the common defence". The war ended; the tenth did not. Stenai's council of three hundred voted to close the customs house five times in four years and has never sent the vote to the synedrion, because the grain fleet's escort comes from Hellarchon and the Narrows are full of pirates the escort keeps away. It keeps twelve warships of its own and pays its assessment on time and resentfully.

Masters of the boom for nine generations. Whoever controls the windlass controls the Horn.

Pilots of the Narrows and salters of tunny. They have no seat on the council and the best information in the city.

Virelyn

A walled harbour beyond the Peaks of Veilmar that the fleet besieged for three years and was handed at a table, whose quays are visited every autumn by a dozen ships that do not tie up.

Ruler
Nausikles Archeptolemou
Title
Harmost, appointed by Hellarchon; the Strategos of the West, Demophon Akamantides, keeps his seat here
Population
c. 11,000: settlers, garrison, and the older townsfolk who stayed

Grudge
The townsfolk remember the siege; the settlers remember being sent
Hellarchon

Virelyn is the oldest harbour on the western coast, a grey stone town at the mouth of a fjord, ten days' sail beyond the Peaks of Veilmar. Some twenty years before the Treaty it was held against the League by a foreign garrison and the hill-clans, and the common fleet besieged it for three years. The crews of twelve ships swore at the black spring under the walls, by Styx, that they would not set foot ashore until Virelyn fell to them. It never fell. The Treaty of Myrianth handed it to the League at a table in Deiperduem, and the garrison marched out under a flag of truce.

Virelyn is now a colony of Hellarchon, the seat of the western frontier and the base for every settler-ship that sails past Veilmar. The harmost governs the town; Strategos Demophon commands the station fleet and the forts along the coast. Every autumn, at the Naming of the Dead, the dozen hulls that row out of Hellarchon at each Launching and never come back anchor in Virelyn's roadstead for one night. Their boats come in for water. Their crews stay in the boats.

A second-rank Hellarchon shipowning family, given the west as a reward and a test. They hold the settler-ship contracts.

  • Nausikles Archeptolemou, Harmost, 47 — has never once gone down to the quay on the night of the dozen.

The family who keep the spring and stayed through the siege. They speak a dialect the Lexicon Council has not sanctioned.

Thalos

Thessalonika's mining and scholars' colony on Thalos Ridge, founded for copper and famous for what its first trench turned up instead.

Ruler

Title
Demarch, elected by the colonists under Thessalonika's charter
Population
c. 2,200
Patron
Hephaestus of the copper; Hermes as Thessalonika's god; Mnemosyne, kept by the scholars
Harbour
A river landing two days down the ridge; supplies come up by mule

The Truth-Flame closed its great trench, and the copper seam runs under it
Hellarchon

Thalos Ridge lies a week inland from Virelyn, beyond the Peaks of Veilmar: a long spine of red rock and pine with copper in it. Thessalonika's Porticoes and two of its mining families founded the colony in the Treaty's second year, half for ore and half because the old songs said the ridge had a story. The first trench for the copper seam opened a pit of bones. The second opened another. By the end of the first season the colonists had found eleven pits along the ridge, each holding hundreds, laid in rows with their hands bound.

The founding myth of Hellenoria says the first settlers chose peace. The Truth-Flame arrived in the colony's third year, closed the great trench "pending study", and left a censor who lives in the best house. The mine works around the closed ground at twice the cost. The colony sends copper ingots to Thessalonika, one vote to the synedrion, and, every month, a sealed report to the Porticoes that arrives opened.

Crest: a copper ingot shaped like an oxhide · Motto: "Dig straight." · Seat: the founders' house at the pithead

Thessalonikan mine-owners who put up the colony's money and want the trench reopened, bones or no bones.

  • Myronides son of Kleon, Demarch, 41 — has quietly had the seam followed under the closed ground from the side.

The scholarly families sent from the Porticoes. They have drawn every pit, counted every skull and copied every drawing three times.

  • Theanó Mnemonis, chief recorder — sends one copy to Thessalonika, one to the censor, and buries the third.

Strayhold

A colony that was not founded so much as found: settlers blown off course beyond Veilmar who landed among hill-folk speaking an old Hellenorian, beside a ring of stones with an oath cut into them.

Demarch, elected by the settlers; shares rule with the Hearth of Elders of the hill-folk

c. 1,800 settlers and perhaps 4,000 hill-folk in the valleys around

Grudge

In the Treaty's second year three settler-ships bound for Virelyn ran before a gale for six days and beached in a cove nobody had charted. The settlers called it Strayhold, the stray ships' holding, and expected to be killed. Instead the hill-folk came down with bread and spoke to them in a Hellenorian their great-great-grandparents might have used, full of words the Lexicon Council struck from the language four centuries ago. On the headland above the cove stands a ring of nine grey stones. One carries a long inscription in the same old speech. The hill-folk call it the Swearing, and say their fathers' fathers and "the mirror-lords" cut it together.

The colony is a joint settlement under a written compact of its own: the settlers' Demarch and the Hearth of Elders sit together at one fire to decide anything that touches land. It farms barley, trades wool and amber to Hespera, and has petitioned the synedrion for a seat three times. Each petition has been tabled and not voted on. A Truth-Flame clerk has visited twice and copied the stones. The second time, he was told the copy would cost him a sheep, and paid.

The family of the lead ship's captain, Road-born rowers who became landholders by accident and have no intention of giving it back.

  • Iolaos Planetides, Demarch, 39 — has learned the old speech well enough to be laughed at politely by the Elders.

Hespera

Corinth's westernmost colony, a walled market town on a far bay where the tin of the Tin Isles meets League wine, governed by six hundred merchants who agree on nothing except that Hellarchon should stay away.

Ruler

Title

Hespera was founded on a marriage. The story says a Corinthian captain landed on the day the local chief's daughter was to choose a husband by offering a cup of water, and she offered it to the stranger. Her descendants, the Gyptidai, have sat in the Six Hundred ever since; the colony is older than the war and was cut off for most of it. Since the Treaty it has boomed. Pretannic tin comes south to its quay in hide-covered boats, League wine and oil go north, and the town's warehouses hold more tin than the rest of the League combined.

The Six Hundred are merchant heads of household who sit for life; fifteen of them form the working council, and three of those the executive, and the First of the Six Hundred chairs all three. The Corinthian charter gives Corinth the casting of Hespera's foreign policy, which in practice means Hespera's delegate sits next to Corinth's in the synedrion and passes him notes. The colony keeps eighteen warships against pirates and the Virelyn station, and makes a point of never saluting the harmost's flag.

The Harbour of Night: a black-sand cove beyond Veilmar where the Voidfolk families who were not enrolled at Hellarchon were settled under the Accord, and where nothing is allowed to float that could carry a siphon.

Patron

The Voidfolk Accord enrolled the tiefling families of the war in Hellarchon's new Deme of the Accord. Not all of them fitted in the pitch-yard. Some six hundred households were offered land "on the new frontier" instead, and in the Treaty's first year they were shipped past Veilmar to a cove of black volcanic sand under a smoking hill. The Mirrored House named it Nyktos Limen. The colonists call it the Cove, and the hill the Kettle.

They are good at it. Within five years the Cove has forges, terraced vines on the warm black slopes, a fishing fleet and the best ropewalk on the western coast. It has no warships, because the Accord forbids them. It has no vote, because its citizens are enrolled in Hellarchon's Deme of the Accord, which is represented by Hellarchon's delegation. It has no leave to trade in Hellenic-fire materials, and the Kettle seeps something that smells like the shed with no number. A Truth-Flame officer comes on the monthly supply ship and stays three days.

The Synedrion

The League's council of delegates: thirty-two votes, bronze ballots, a basket for the doubtful, and an agenda written in Hellarchon the night before.

How it votes

The synedrion meets on the Akra of Hellarchon twice a year: in spring, the day after the Launching, so that every delegate climbs to the session having just watched the fleet row past; and in autumn, after the Naming of the Dead. The Emperor may summon it at any time by letter, and has done so four times in ten years, each time in a different voice.

The agenda belongs to the ten League Treasurers, Hellarchon citizens chosen by Hellarchon's Assembly, who also assess every member's contribution. A motion not on their list cannot be voted, only "heard". A member who wants something heard must find a Treasurer to table it, and every Treasurer dines at the Oarsmen's Table.

The chair is the Proedros, drawn by lot at each session from the delegates of cities other than Hellarchon: a concession won after the Chest was moved, and the only office in the League that Hellarchon cannot fill. The Proedros keeps order, recognises speakers and counts the ballots aloud. He has no casting vote. A tied motion fails.

Votes are weighted by an old schedule that nobody has revised since the war: five for Hellarchon, three each for Corinth and Thebesieas, two each for Thessalonika and Helionyx, one for every other member with a seat, none for the newest colonies until admitted. Each delegation receives one bronze disc per vote. A disc with a solid hub is yes; a hollow hub is no. The delegate closes his fingers over the hub, so the room cannot see which he holds, and drops the disc into the bronze urn. Since the tyrannies began, the discs of disputed delegates go not into the urn but into a wicker basket beside it. The Proedros announces each result twice, "with the basket" and "without", and the minutes record whichever the clerk, a Hellarchon public slave, is told to record.

Quorum is two-thirds of the members. Thebesieas's empty bench counts toward the members and not toward those present, which has twice nearly ended a session before it began.

A session: the spring sitting, this year

Dawn on the Akra, the day after the Launching. Delegates climb the marble stair past the temple, where the strongroom door is closed and a guard of Hellarchon marines stands in front of it. The council room sits in the temple's shadow: tiered stone benches, a gilded ceiling, a bronze urn, a wicker basket. Kynthos's delegate draws the Proedros's lot and is visibly delighted.

First, the libation, and the Emperor's letter. Archigrammateus Orestes Phylarchides reads it in a dry tenor with a harbour accent. It urges unity, praises the fleet and asks the cities to "remember what they swore". Thessalonika's delegate asks, as the rules allow, to see the seal. Orestes shows it at arm's length. Second, the Treasurers' report on assessments, which takes the morning; Kynthos asks for the current inventory of the Chest and is told it is "in preparation", as it has been for six sessions. Third, petitions heard and not voted: Strayhold's request for a seat, read by the clerk in eleven seconds; the Geomoroi's motion against Samaris's delegate, withdrawn at the request of a Treasurer.

In the afternoon, the motion: that command of the common fleet pass by rotation among the members with warships. Corinth moves it; Hespera seconds. Hellarchon's speaker answers for an hour on the Acheaorian squadron that was once sighted off Kynthos. The discs go in. The Proedros counts: with the basket, fourteen for and fourteen against. Without the basket, ten for and fourteen against. Either way the motion fails, and the room turns, as one, to look at Thebesieas's empty bench and its three uncast votes. Corinth's delegate walks out without waiting for the adjournment. By evening the rowers on the Road are singing a song about the basket.

The Imperial Court of House Thalorid

A household, a scriptorium and a voice in the Mirrored House on the Rock's north spur, where a dozen officials speak for an Emperor none of them will admit they have not seen.

House Thalorid reigns and does not govern. Its court is small, old and entirely made of intermediaries. The Emperor's letters arrive through a tall mirror in the Mirrored House; they are read to Hellarchon's Assembly by the Archigrammateus and carried to every other city by heralds who each receive their text separately. The Circles of Mirrors write Hellenoria's account of itself. The Lexicon Council decides what words it may use, the Tribunal what gods it may name, and the Truth-Flame what may be written about any of it. Nobody at court has authority over the fleet, the Assembly or the Chest. Everyone at court has authority over what the cities believe the Emperor wants, and in a League held together by oaths, that is enough to frighten the Hegemon.

Officials who speak for the Emperor

  • Lady Kassiane Thaloris Keeper of the Mirrored House · the Emperor's cousin — the only Thalorid seen in public; laid the robe on the goddess at the seventh-year Panegyris in his name, and has not slept well since. Suspects Orestes.
  • Archigrammateus Orestes Phylarchides First Scribe of the Circles · the Emperor's Voice at Hellarchon — the only man who claims to receive the Emperor's words directly; reads them in a dry tenor with a harbour accent. Suspects the mirror.
  • Kallirhoe Myrsinou Imperial Herald at Corinth and the isthmus — reads the same letters in a contralto with a Corinthian lilt; once received a text that contradicted Orestes's and read it anyway.
  • Ainesidemos the Herald Imperial Herald at Thessalonika — reads to the Epistates, whose letter-patent is the last still "pending instructions"; is ninety, deaf, and word-perfect.
  • Dion Akestorides Herald of the West · Virelyn and the colonies — sails the western coast with letters that arrive in an accent the colonists say is their own. The hill-folk at Strayhold call him "the mirror-lord's mouth".
  • Euphemios Parakoimomenos, keeper of the inner door — sleeps across the threshold of the Emperor's rooms, as the office requires, and says he hears the Emperor cough at night. The cough has not changed in ten years.
  • Archigenes Imperial Physician — prescribes by letter, has not examined his patient in ten years, and has never been asked to; draws a full salary and drinks.
  • Sosipatros Kyrou Logothetes of the Letter-Patents — issues and registers imperial appointments; has issued none in ten years, which makes Thessalonika's the most valuable document in the League.
  • Hagne Ladike Proto-Katoptes, head of the First Circle of Mirrors — edits the court histories; listed Selenarion of the Fourth Circle as "on leave of the mirrors", and personally dates the Treaty of Myrianth fifty years back.
  • Dorotheos Mnesiphilou Lexiarch, President of the Lexicon Council — rules which dialects are Hellenorian; has declared the old speech of the western hill-folk "a corruption", without hearing it.
  • Menekrates Oulios Hierophylax of the Tribunal — keeps the register of recognised gods; Styx and Astraeus are recognised as Titans but not "in the western manner", a phrase he has never defined.
  • Inquisitor Vireon Third Seat of the Truth-Flame · the court's censor — not of the household but in it daily; wrote "Do not acknowledge the Strayhold Accords" in a margin, and has never once asked to see the Emperor.

Expansion

The Satrapies of Acheaoria

The Satrapies of Acheaoria

On the Royal Stair at Persemenid twenty-three peoples climb in stone, each in its own dress, each carrying what it owes. The relief is the empire's official map. The working map is the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger's tribute roll, which divides the same peoples among sixteen satrapies, from the Throne Plain that pays nothing to the Zardun Highlands that pay in horses and boys. Some satrapies are one city and its fields. Some are a desert the size of a Hellenorian league. Several contain a kingdom that the Ledger records as a district and that remembers itself as a crown.

A satrap (xšaçapāvan, "protector of the realm") is a king in all but the word. He collects whatever he likes, however he likes, keeps his own court, appoints his own frataraka, and raises troops "for the roads". What he owes the throne is a fixed sum in talents of silver, set by the founder's scribes and revised once in a millennium, plus gifts at the Bringing on Sowing 1st. Against him the throne sets three checks: a King's Eye who reports past him by two routes, one to the hazarapat and one to the Chief Eunuch; a garrison commander who is supposed to answer to Persemenid for war; and the Magi, who can declare any day unfit for anything. The arashshara, who run what the province actually produces, answer to whoever pays on time.

The war held it all together. The conquered peoples were told the empire was the only thing between them and the legions, and on the frontier that was true. Five years after the Peace of the Signing the legions are busy with their own chair, the threat is gone, and the old crowns are being taken out of cellars. Some satraps fan the flames, hoping to be the king who wakes up. Most simply forward less silver every year and wait to see who notices. At the last Bringing sixteen of twenty-three peoples climbed the stair. The Scribes expect fourteen. See the King of Kings and the Satraps, Tribute in Talents and the Undying Count.

Reading the table. Tribute is the assessed figure in talents of silver a year, then what reached Persemenid at the last Bringing. A talent is about sixty pounds of silver, some 6,000 gp at the Mithril Reserve's weight; the whole roll, collected in full, would come to about four thousand four hundred talents, and last year came to about three thousand one hundred, of which the Scribes believe six hundred was borrowed from the Vaults of Equilibrium against next year.

The Throne Plain

The home satrapy, exempt from tribute since the founder, governed by the King's second son, who has filled two levels of an underground town with grain and arrow-shafts and calls it prudence.

The satrap and his zarate

The plain around Persemenid was the founder's own country, and by his grant it pays no silver. It pays in men for the Ten Thousand, in ceremony, and in the gifts of the Bringing. Its satrap is Prince Tiridat, the King's second son, of the House of Zindar: generous, loud and owed by half the garden town. The plain's dues, which by custom pay for the roads, the post-stations and the frataraka of De'rakhtak Bon, R'eyshar and, on paper, Zi'rzamin Dar'a, are collected by his household and never seen again. His household has doubled every season since the Peace. Its riders wear his colours, not the King's.

The watchers

Bagapana, the King's Eye of the Throne Plain, is a soft-spoken eunuch who reports to the hazarapat and, by a second route, to the Chief Eunuch, and has noticed that neither has asked him about the sealed doors at De'rakhtak Bon. The arashshara of the plain are the court's own: Queen Mother Irdabama holds the royal workshops and estates by right, and Arashshara Mandana Nahid'zar feeds every delegation and is owed for all of them.

The old crown

The plain has no conquered people, only the oldest one: the founding clans, whose great zarates (Mihran, Farnaka, Karin) sit on the terrace. Its "old royal line" is the one on the throne, and the question the plain asks is not whether to have a king but which. Below the terrace the answer is loudly Tiridat. On the terrace it is Crown Prince Ariaramna, quietly.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi of the Hill of Fires under Herbad Tansar crown the king and declare the days; Hajama is honoured for the throne's valour and Zann for its rolls. Water comes down the Zheret-al-Nur and through the royal qanats, which the plain's dues are supposed to maintain. Three channels north of the city have run thin for two summers; the repair money went to stables.

The garrison

The Ten Thousand and the Immortals hold the terrace and answer to the hazarapat, not the satrap. Tiridat's own force is his household cavalry, about nine hundred riders, under Captain Shapur Varaz, who guards the sealed levels at De'rakhtak Bon and lets no one past, including the frataraka.

The Satrapy of Atarabad

The richest satrapy in the empire, which pays in full, on time, with exact returns on everything, including the cavalry it is not supposed to have.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Ardavan Tir'dad of House Tir'dad governs Atarabad, the eastern caravan road and its towns, Qa'zshahrv'in and Tabrishi'ir, from a palace in the Wind-Tower Quarter. His house has held the satrapy for three generations by being useful to every King of Kings and dependent on none. He forwards seven hundred talents a year, conspicuously, files exact returns, and raises and pays Vanguard squadrons beyond the establishment, which he also files. His nephew Captain Volagash Tir'dad commands them and wants a reason. His wife, Lady Azadokht Tir'dad, keeps the satrapal granaries and knows to the sack how long the city could hold.

The watchers

Tahmineh of the Seal, the King's Eye of Atarabad, widow of a Royal Road post-master, reads every courier's bag at the Royal Caravanserai and sends her reports up the road in nine days. The satrap knows exactly what she sees and arranges for her to see it. The bazaar's senior arashshara, Shahdokht Abrisham, keeps the city weights; the caravan zarate Suren-Pahlav carries the Silk Terminus west to Deiperduem, Aepistra and Corinth.

The old crown

Atarabad was never a kingdom; it was a crossroads that every kingdom wanted. Its subject peoples are the caravan clans east of the city, who keep their own headmen and registers and are content as long as the road is open. The only nationalism here is money's: as the satrapies grow restless, portable wealth is the only kind a revolt cannot seize, and Jauhar's custom is excellent.

Fire, gods and water

The undying fire of the Fire-Temple, under Mobad Atar-Farnbag, is the most sacred flame in the empire; the Magi can close the bazaar for a day by declaring it impure. Jauhar the Gilded keeps the merchants, Najm the couriers. Water is held by the Bountiful Harvesters; Qa'zshahrv'in's pool marks fall every year, and the frataraka there, Mahrokh Qazi, has written three times about it.

The garrison

The satrap's own Vanguard squadrons, perhaps two thousand lances, plus gate-wardens he appoints. There is no royal garrison of note; the throne relies on Tir'dad's honesty, which so far has been perfect.

The Covenant Plain

The one satrapy the Scribes have never marked "not presented", governed by a man whose fortune is registering other satraps' bargains and asking no questions.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Zariadres Vohuman of House Vohuman governs Mithratal and a modest grain-plain around it. His house has held the satrapy for four generations by never once being late and never once being interesting. Its income is the archive fee, the richest tax per head in the empire, and the registry of land titles across the northern plain. Lately it has registered a great many covenants between satraps, at the standard fee. Zariadres is dry, exact and privately terrified of being the satrap under whom the record failed.

The watchers

Mardak the Listener, the King's Eye of Mithratal, attends every swearing between satraps and copies the terms to the hazarapat; he is hated because he alone may write on the Silent Day. The arashshara Simin Golnar runs the Waiting Lodges, where every party that comes to swear is fed, housed and overheard. The real sovereign is the record, kept by Azata Yazdin Dadvar, Chief Registrar, of House Dadvar.

The old crown

The plain has no lost kingdom; it has class zero, the oldest covenant in the archive, read aloud every Renewal in a language no one speaks. Every conquered people's surrender is filed somewhere below it. The restless satrapies send lawyers here before they send soldiers, because in Acheaoria a revolt that is not registered is merely a riot.

Fire, gods and water

The Witness of the Fire, Magus Frawardin, seals every covenant; without his seal an oath is a promise. Hakiyah keeps the scales and Vatagatal the duty. The Covenant Garden beneath the plane tree is watered by a single old channel, and an old tribute covenant sworn there is void "by the drying of the wells".

The garrison

Four hundred men under the satrap's brother, Arsham Vohuman, who knows every one by name. The Lanterns of Justice, under Lantern-Captain Zarir Roshanpur, answer to no satrap and carry the city's judgements across the plateau.

The Garden Satrapy of Persevalis

The only satrapy that pays the throne in something the throne cannot defer, because fruit does not wait; its satrap is growing a harvest he may no longer own.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Farrokh Bagh'dar of House Bagh'dar governs Persevalis and the plateau villages from his pavilion at the end of the Pomegranate Walk. The Bagh'dar have held the satrapy for five generations by being the most agreeable hosts in the empire and the least threatening. He forwards four hundred talents' worth in kind, in full and often early, and is owed by the court more than he is owed by anyone else. His steward, Frataraka Dariush Baghban, runs the nut orchards and reports at breakfast. His heir Kamran borrows from the Vaults in his own name.

The watchers

Parvaneh, the King's Eye of Persevalis, dines at the satrap's table so often that guests assume she is his wife. She is fond of him, loyal to the throne, and slowly realising the throne is what is robbing him. The court supply is run by Arashshara Golrokh Golab of House Golab.

The old crown

No conquered people; instead a family older than the satrapy. The Peyvand channel-keepers have walked the Persevalis qanats longer than the Bagh'dar have ruled, and write nothing down, by policy. If Persevalis has a hidden king, he carries a lamp and a measuring cord.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi of the Channel Head under Herbad Shirzad open the water each spring and can refuse to. Shajar stands where the channels divide; Selan's almanac sets the year. Four powers rule here: the satrap who hosts, the Magi who open the water, the Bountiful Harvesters who measure it and the arashshara who sell what it grows. Only the satrap is unpaid.

The garrison

Show cavalry for parades and the hunt, a few hundred riders. The satrapy cannot be defended by anything except its usefulness, and knows it.

The Northern March

A frontier satrapy split along its own walls: the satrap rules inside, the Marzban outside, and the garrison has noticed which of them pays.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Vindarna Sarvand governs Xerastri, the subsidy and the customs. The throne cut the subsidy twice since the Peace; Sarvand now pays the garrison from untaxed steppe tolls and records the tribute as "presented in kind", which the Scribes have accepted, for now. His nephew Farhad Sarvand commands a hundred new riders in stables built from stone robbed out of the Outer Wall. Sarvand is a follower, not a plotter, and he writes to Shir'abad D'ar often.

The watchers

Marzban Piruz Mihran of the Mihran of Xerastri holds the march beyond the walls and answers to the throne directly. Bagadata the Lame, the King's Eye of Xerastri, a retired engineer, limps the walls daily, counts the bricks, and has three letters to Persemenid written and unsent. Arashshara Nasrin Asbdar runs the remount trade and the Horse Fair, now a hiring fair for three empires.

The old crown

The march's subject people are its clients: Malaunian clans who take Acheaorian silver and keep their own law. They never had a kingdom to lose and want none; they want the price of a rider set by the steppe, not by Persemenid. Tomyra of the Lion Grass is uniting the clans to do exactly that, and her son has been a "guest" in Persemenid since the war.

Fire, gods and water

Herbad Burzin keeps the frontier fire and the wall-families' oaths. Vatagatal is the garrison's god and the subject of its theology: may a man sworn to the throne defend it against a satrap who calls himself its protector? Young officers wear Beast's horse-skull charms under their armour. Water is wells and the river; the qanats stop a day south of the walls, which is where the Qanat Line says the empire's writ stops too.

The garrison

Thousand-Commander Datis Kamboj, Commander of the Walls, reports to the satrap for pay and to the Marzban for war, and has found only one of them pays. Roxana Surena, Warden of the Parthian Ravine, keeps sealed companies the satrap thinks are his. An Ironclad Oath chapter holds to the throne.

The Satrapy of Shir'abad D'ar

A lesser satrapy behind a lion-carved gate that collects the full tribute of a wide district, forwards none of it, and has had its lions re-cut early.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Vaumisa Shir'vand of House Shir'vand rules Shir'abad D'ar and a frontier district of dry pasture and wells three days wide. His house has held this lesser satrapy for three generations and has begun to think of it as a greater one. He paid House Karin for a better place on the Royal Stair and has paid nothing up it since: two hundred and forty talents a year, withheld, while collection has not slackened. The difference buys a covered riding school, stables for six hundred horses in a town that needs two hundred, and an over-strength Vanguard under his brother-in-law, Spahbed Arshak Karin. His wife, Lady Apama Shir'vand, born Karin, reads the court letters first.

The watchers

The King's Eye was recalled last year and has not been replaced; the satrap sent the hazarapat a gift the same month. Scribe Farnaz Daftari of the Infinite Ledger records every refusal and has begun to fear for her life; her brother Kurosh makes a second copy of every page and hides it. The district's arashshara, the wool-mistresses of the Tribute Yard, count the goods laid out; different people count the goods that leave.

The old crown

Shir'vand is not a conquered prince. His subject people are the Tamarkhi, horse-clans of the steppe edge whose khans were broken by the Sixth King and who still bury their chiefs with a gilded bridle "for the ride home". Their old line, the Khans of the Nine Felts, survives in a herder called Ulduz Tamarkh, who has been offered a gilded bridle by Shir'vand and the price of a free steppe by Tomyra. The Tamarkhi have no love for Persemenid and less for the man who taxes them in its name.

Fire, gods and water

A small fire-temple under Herbad Mehrdad keeps the oaths, and the satrap's Hall of the Glory has been allowed to gather dust, which in Acheaoria is a public statement. Hajama is the riders' god; the Tamarkhi keep Beast at a horse-skull cairn outside the walls. Water is wells, and the satrap's new stables drink more of it than the Lion Gate Quarter.

The garrison

Six hundred Vanguard horse, raised and paid locally, against Oath-Captain Zhubin Arzan's two hundred of the Ironclad Oath, sworn to a throne that has not written in a year. The two forces share one street and no taverns.

The Satrapy of the Ruhaniin Vale

A desert of oases ruled from a city stacked up a sinkhole spring, where caste is the cistern you were born above and the satrap is a cadet of the shahs he replaced.

The satrap and his zarate

Spirits' Rest, the civilised core of the Dasht-a Khaliq, is governed from Kharnesh on the Eye of Havar. Satrap Mardonak Havari styles himself "shah" of Kharnesh, which the court allows as a courtesy. It is not a courtesy. The Havari were the old shahs of the Vale; the throne broke the senior line four centuries ago and raised a cadet branch as satraps to keep the water-castes quiet. Mardonak's tribute caravans have arrived a third short four years running: three hundred and twenty talents of four hundred and eighty, with letters about sandstorms.

The watchers

The King's Eye is Esmat the Cistern-Counter, a former water-clerk who measures the sluices at night and the satrap's sincerity by day. The arashshara of the water-guild hold the sluice keys, which matter more than the satrap's seal; their head, Arashshara Tahmineh of the Sluice, decides whose side the keys are on.

The old crown

The Vale's people are the Kharneshi, ranked by tier: the highest houses draw first, the lowest drink what falls. The upper-tier families are the old nobility, the Lords of the First Draw, and they remember a shah who ruled from the top terrace with no satrap above him. The senior Havari line survives on the lowest tier, in a potter named Kayan Havari, whom the lower castes call the Shah-in-the-Well. The Sahari, who decide who arrives in the Vale, take no side and charge for it.

Fire, gods and water

A fire-temple on the top terrace keeps the Magi's calendar; Shajar's shrines stand at every division of water. The Spring itself is registered as a guest-cult, the Mother of the Eye, and its offerings are dropped into the sinkhole. The Vault of Silt, where six qanats meet under a ward the muqanni call "the lid", keeps half the city's water; if it fails, Kharnesh is dry inside a week.

The garrison

Twelve hundred spearmen of the satrap's, mostly from the upper tiers, and a royal marzban's fort at Ostakhan on the edge of Zahr al-Mawt that went silent in the second year of peace. The satrapal ledger still draws its pay. Someone collects it at Kharnesh, in person.

The Satrapy of Khamsin's Reach

Rock desert, petrified pine and singing obelisks, and a satrap paying his tribute in full with money borrowed against sand that has not yet buried him.

The satrap and his zarate

The south-east of the Dasht is governed from the Rose-Cliff City of the South, a rock-cut city of carved façades around a spring that drops a finger's depth each year. Satrap Hormozd Sangtarash, of a minor zarate of stone-cutters raised to the satrapy after the war, forwards his hundred and twenty talents on time. The desert advances; at dawn it sometimes swallows ten miles of somebody's land, and the satrapy's tax base shrinks every season while its assessment does not.

The watchers

Dilnaz of the Stair, the King's Eye of the Reach, is young, posted here as a punishment, and has noticed the silver arrives from the Vaults of Equilibrium's Atarabad house rather than from the satrapy. The Rose-Cliff's frataraka, Kerdir Rigi, has begun selling the wells by the hour; the arashshara of the incense and carnelian trade, led by Arashshara Banu Sorkh, buy the hours.

The old crown

The Rasafi cut the Rose-Cliff before Acheaoria existed and were ruled by queens whose tombs are the grandest façades. The Rasafi nobility, the Houses of the Façade, still sit in the tomb-fronts on feast-days, and the last queen's line is kept by the eldest daughter of the House of Raqim, Saluma Raqim, who keeps the tomb keys and has never been asked to swear to anyone. Rasafi nationalism is not angry. It is patient, and it assumes the empire will dry up first.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi keep a small temple below the spring and do not like the obelisks. The Rasafi honour Astraeus, Titan of the Wind, as a registered guest-god, and the Stormcallers' Choir tends the singing stones; farmers in the wadis keep Drummern and Pag. There are no qanats worth the name. There is the spring, and the hours sold from it.

The garrison

Five hundred desert spearmen and a camel troop. Blue dragons tax the caravans by lightning, and the garrison has learned to schedule around them.

The Kharveth Plateau

A dry plateau around one snowcapped mountain nobody will dig under, governed by a new satrap who means to be the man who did.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Artavasdes Nikbin, new, governs the plateau from Sangbast, an alabaster-cutters' town at the foot of the Mountain of Kharveth. His house is small and court-made; he bought the appointment with a reform plan, and the plan is wells. He forwards two hundred talents, much of it in porphyry from the royal quarry, and he is a reformer and a fool in about equal measure.

The watchers

The King's Eye, Old Varahran, has watched four satraps and outlived three, and spends his reports on the muqanni rather than the satrap. The arashshara of the alabaster yards, Arashshara Roshanak Sangi (no relation to the princess, as she says twice a day), sells to every satrap's residence on the plain.

The old crown

The plateau's old people are the Kuhani quarrymen, whose petty kings once cut their names into the mountain's lower face and whose surrender is a covenant of class three at Mithratal. The real lords here are not kings but diggers: the muqanni guilds, hereditary and unreplaceable, whose master, Ostad Peshang Kariz, has called a strike rather than sink a shaft within a day's ride of Kharveth. The guild's power is the satrapy's oldest nationalism: no one else knows where the water is.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi have no doctrine on Kharveth, which for the Magi is itself a position. Migal is the diggers' god and Jisan the deed-holders'. Every qanat on the plateau runs clean of div, which the muqanni say is the point of not digging at the mountain.

The garrison

Three hundred guards for the royal quarry and a prison mine on the lower flank, under Hazarbed Gushnasp, who is short of convicts and has been sent conscripts instead.

The North Shore of the Kaspiran

A salt-sea coast of fishing towns full of discharged spearmen, a falling shoreline, and a satrap claiming every yard of mud the sea gives up.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Arzhang Kaviani governs the north shore of the Kaspiran Seas from Bandar Siyah, the Black Harbour, whose quays now stand two hundred yards from the water. His house, a fishing zarate turned salt-farmer, has held the shore for two generations. He forwards a hundred and eighty of two hundred and sixty talents and blames the sea, which is at least falling. His real business is the lawsuit: the treaty-maps were drawn to the old waterline, and he claims all the new land on his side.

The watchers
