The King's Eye, Nushafarin the Salt-Wife, buys sturgeon-egg at the quay and knows every night-digger by lamp. The arashshara of the salt-pans, Arashshara Farangis Namaki, sends the black egg up the Royal Road in ice and keeps the profit off the satrap's books.

The old crown

The shore people are the Namaki, salt-folk who claim descent from the drowned city the Magi say does not exist. Their headmen, the Lords of the Low Water, keep a list of the drowned city's kings back to a name no one can read. Every column that comes up out of the mud makes the list longer and the Namaki prouder. Since the Peace their discharged spearmen have come home to villages that cannot feed them, and night-digging is an industry and a politics.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi forbid excavation and condemn the finds; the fire-temple at Bandar Siyah is the only building on the shore with a guard. The Namaki keep Saeronis, the River of Secrets, as a registered guest-god: every river runs into the Kaspiran and nothing runs out, so every secret ends here. Fresh water is the shore's real poverty; the qanats from the uplands are old and two are failing.

The garrison

Four hundred marines without ships, under Captain Ardeshir Mahi, who spends his nights arresting diggers and his days buying from them.

The South Shore of the Kaspiran

The rival shore: sturgeon money, re-cut waterline marks, and a satrap paying in full because he expects the throne to rule in his favour.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Kamdin Shurabi governs the south shore from Namakdan, a salt town built on the old flats. His predecessor re-cut the war-era waterline marks and sold "reclaimed" shore that was still underwater; Kamdin hanged the surveyor and kept the money. He forwards two hundred and twenty talents in full, on time, with a petition about the new land attached to every convoy. He is the most loyal man on the Kaspiran, and his loyalty is a lawsuit.

The watchers

The King's Eye, Sepideh Waterline, measures the marks herself every season, and her figures and the satrap's disagree by a hand. The sturgeon trade belongs to the arashshara of the ice-houses, chief among them Arashshara Homa Shurabi, the satrap's aunt, who sells to House Nahid'zar at Persemenid and lends to the satrap at interest.

The old crown

The south shore's Namaki are the same people as the north's, cut in half by a line drawn on a map, and their Lords of the Low Water marry across the sea in defiance of both satraps. The oldest of them, Grandmother Gelareh of the south, keeps the half of the king-list the north does not have. Both satraps would like the list. Neither would like the Namaki to read it together.

Fire, gods and water

The fire-temple at Namakdan is newer and richer than Bandar Siyah's, paid for with sturgeon. Saeronis is kept here too, in the same guest-court niche, and the Magi skip her lamp whenever a column surfaces. Fresh water comes from three upland qanats in good repair; Kamdin spends on them, which is why he can afford to pay.

The garrison

Three hundred spearmen and twelve fast boats, under Captain Babak Navi, who chases north-shore diggers across the lagoons and sometimes catches south-shore ones.

The Satrapy of Ushtan

A river kingdom turned canal satrapy turned dry road, where caravans pay a toll to walk the bed of a dead sea-road and the river's sacred dragon is dying.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Farnadat Kanarang governs Ushtan from Kemrud, a walled river city at the western end of the Xeruezcho Canal. His house is a plateau zarate posted here by the King's grandfather to hold a people who never asked for it. The canal's tolls, still collected for walking along a dry bed, are farmed by the Chyrsus Syndicate, which pays him a fixed sum and keeps the rest. He forwards ninety of three hundred talents and says the Syndicate owes the balance; the Syndicate says the same of him.

The watchers

Ziba the Toll-Reader, the King's Eye of Ushtan, reads the Syndicate's ledgers, which are better kept than the satrap's and less honest. The river trade belongs to the arashshara of the reed-boats and the date-groves, led by Arashshara Nikta Ushtani, who is Ushtani herself and sits on both sides of every question.

The old crown

The Ushtani were the Kingdom of the Two Banks before the canal, ruled by the Lords of the Flood, who rode the river at its rising on the back of a sacred dragon. Their nobility, the Bank-Houses, still hold the date-groves and the ferry rights. The old royal line lives in Princess Shaduyeh Nahrani, who keeps the Flood-Crown in a cellar under her grove and took it out at the last rising, briefly, in front of three thousand people. The movement calls itself the Dredgers: they want the river back where the canal stole it, and the empire out of the way while they move it.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi's temple at Kemrud stands higher than any Ushtani shrine, by law. Shajar is honoured as the river's guardian; the Ushtani say Shajar is a plateau name for their dragon. The River-Dragon is registered as a guest-cult, and it is old, sick and shrinking with its river. The canal's silted basins steal the river's spring flood; the qanats of the east bank were never dug, because the Ushtani never needed them.

The garrison

Eight hundred plateau spearmen in the river citadel under Hazarbed Mazdak Kanarang, the satrap's son, and Syndicate toll-guards who are better paid and better armed.

The Satrapy of the Spine

A satrapy that is mostly a wall of black rock and eleven gates cut by a kingdom nobody can name, still held by the descendants of its wardens.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Ashkan Darband governs the west face of the Zaruk'thal Spine and the toll-roads through its notches from Darvazeh, a gate-town in the Fifth Notch. His house, a zarate of road-wardens, has held the satrapy for six generations. He forwards a hundred and eighty talents in full; the notches make it easy. His grievance is the Seventh Notch, the widest, which sits exactly on a border drawn with a ruler: for five years he and the satrap of the Vale have each kept a toll-post at one end, and a caravan pays twice to walk a quarter of a mile.

The watchers

The King's Eye, Kuchak the Tollman, is a former notch-clerk who knows the toll by heart and the satrap's cut by arithmetic. The salt and natron trade belongs to the arashshara of the galleries, led by Arashshara Shirin Namakdar. The commission Persemenid sent to settle the Seventh Notch has been there two years, taking fees; Frataraka Mitra Azarnush of the west end has paid it three times.

The old crown

The Notch-clans are the descendants of the gate-wardens of the kingdom that cut the Spine. They have no king and no kingdom, only the oath their ancestors swore at the door-sockets, and they still keep it: caravan masters leave offerings at the sockets "to whoever is still holding the gate". The clans' elders, the Socket-Keepers, are the satrapy's real nobility, and the satrap's house married into them three times to be allowed to collect.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi keep a fire in the Fifth Notch and Vatagatal's shrine beside it; the clans keep the Gate-Oath, which is unregistered because no Scribe can say to whom it was sworn. Water comes from salt-dome springs under the ridge, sweet where they rise and brine a mile away.

The garrison

Notch-wardens, about six hundred, hired from the clans, under Warden-Captain Hirbod Socketborn. On the old kingdom's feast-days other wardens stand at the sockets, mostly at night, and the living ones stand back.

The Satrapy of Halvan

The rain-fed wheat belt on the empire's western edge, whose old rain-kings are remembered at every autumn storm and courted, lately, from the Treaty Road.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Hutana Vaspar governs Halvan from Halvanshahr, a granary city a few days east of the Treaty Road. His house is a plateau zarate of the old war-party, posted west to feed the armies; with the armies gone, grain prices have crashed and the dry-farmers cannot pay. He forwards two hundred of four hundred and fifty talents and says the rest is in the granaries, which it is, rotting. He is honest, overworked and pessimistic, and the only satrap who has asked the throne to lower an assessment.

The watchers

The King's Eye, Afsoon of the Granaries, counts sacks and rumours with equal care and has reported Invictian and Hellenorian visitors in the satrapy six times this year. The grain trade is run by the arashshara of the threshing floors, led by Arashshara Taraneh Gandomi, who sells west along the Treaty Road at Deiperduem prices and pays the satrap in Invictian silver that weighs less every quarter.

The old crown

The Halvani were a kingdom of rain-kings, whose king walked out into the first autumn storm each year and was struck or spared by it. Their nobility, the Houses of the Threshing Floor, still hold the dry-farm villages. The royal line survives in Arvand Halvanid, the Rain-Prince, who teaches fencing at Deiperduem and dines in two foreign compounds a month. The movement, the Autumn Drum, beats the old storm-call at every harvest, and the satrap has stopped arresting the drummers because there are too many.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi keep the granary fire at Halvanshahr. Drummern and Pag rule the dry-farming belt, where wheat lives or dies by the autumn storms; Jisan is the deed-holders' god. Halvan has few qanats and needs few; rain is its water, which is why its people never needed the empire's engineers and never learned to fear their withdrawal.

The garrison

A thousand men under Hazarbed Siavash Vaspar, half of them demobilised veterans re-enlisted for bread, and a road-garrison on the Treaty Road that watches the west more than the province.

The Zardun Highlands

A mountain kingdom of serpent-queens that has paid its tribute in horses and boys for six centuries, and stopped three years ago.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Aspandas Kuhyar governs the Zardun Highlands from Dezh-e Zard, the Yellow Fort, in the lowland valley at their foot, which is as far up as his writ reliably runs. His house has held the satrapy for two generations and the valley for all of them. The Zardun tribute is a hundred and sixty talents assessed in horses and eunuchs, an old punishment, and none of it has come down from the hills in three years. The satrap reports "late snows".

The watchers

The last King's Eye of Zardun was found at the bottom of a well. The new one, Payam the Quiet, does not drink water he has not drawn himself. The arashshara of the lowland markets, led by Arashshara Mahin Kuhyar, the satrap's sister, trade salt and iron up the passes for wool and honey, and are the only Acheaorians the hill villages let in.

The old crown

The Zarduni are ruled, among themselves, by the Mothers of the Mountain, a matrilineal nobility of clan-queens. Their royal line, the Serpent Queens, was supposed to end with the conquest; it went into the caves instead. The present claimant, Queen Mahsati of the Coils, was crowned in a cavern three summers ago, the same summer the tribute stopped. The Zarduni do not have a nationalist movement. They have a kingdom, and it has stopped pretending otherwise.

Fire, gods and water

The Magi's fire burns at Dezh-e Zard and nowhere above it. The Zarduni keep Ragarra, whose words survive in their snake-songs, and the Lost One, god of the relocated, for the families carried off to the plateau. Water is snowmelt and springs; there are no qanats because the highlands never needed them, and the lowland ones run on Zarduni snow.

The garrison

Fifteen hundred men in the Yellow Fort and four pass-forts under Hazarbed Tahmasp Kuhyar. Two of the pass-forts have not been relieved since autumn.

The Inland Shore

Acheaoria's coast on the sea the three empires share, where the satrap rules the harbour, the League rules the sea lanes, and the islands rule themselves.

The satrap and his zarate

Satrap Shahvar Daryabeg governs the Inland Shore from Marvaridan, a pearl harbour and the empire's only real port on the inland sea. His house is a shipping zarate that owns half the merchant hulls Acheaoria still floats. He forwards a hundred and fifty of two hundred and ten talents; the rest, he says, is owed by the islands, which he claims and which do not agree. Azadeh Atoll has never paid tribute to anyone and celebrates the fact annually; Bahrami Rock takes pay for its light from both the League and Acheaorian shipping; Parvaz Cay nets birds and ignores everyone.

The watchers

The King's Eye, Mehrnoush of the Quays, watches Hellenorian hulls more than the satrap, and reports both. The pearl trade belongs to the arashshara of the drying-yards, led by Arashshara Yasaman Davani, who sells pearls to Corinth through Zandar Isle and declares a tenth of them.

The old crown

The Davani islanders were a thalassocracy of pearl-kings before the empire came down to the coast. Their nobility, the Captains of the Banks, still own the pearl-beds by inheritance and dive them by right. The old royal line lives on Azadeh Atoll in Old Davan the Ninth, who calls himself King of the Banks and fishes his own lagoon. The movement is a joke on the mainland and a creed on the islands: the sea was never conquered, only the harbour.

Fire, gods and water

The fire-temple at Marvaridan is the westernmost on the circuit. Kar'r'rga is the islands' god, honoured by pearl-divers and crews, and the Magi count him a guest-god in all but name. Fresh water is the islands' weakness: cisterns and rain, and in a dry year they buy it from Marvaridan, which is the satrap's only real lever.

The garrison

Six war-galleys, three seaworthy, and eight hundred marines under Navarch Kourosh Daryabeg, the satrap's brother. The League's patrols outnumber them.

The Royal Court: who stands nearer than a satrap

A satrap rules a province; a cupbearer pours the King's wine. In Persemenid the cupbearer outranks the satrap, because he stands nearer.

The satrapies are governed from the provinces and judged from the terrace. A satrap's fortune rises or falls on what fifteen people say to the King of Kings, or keep from him. The factions below are the court's own: the Gate (House Farnaka and the hazarapat, backing Crown Prince Ariaramna), the Inner House (the eunuchs under the Chief Eunuch), the Below (Prince Tiridat's party in the garden town), the Stair (the old precedence houses), the Fire (the Magi), and the creed, which belongs to no one. The Shadow Court belongs to all of them and is not on the list.

  • Hazarapat Aspachana Farnaka chief of the court · the Gate — keeper of the King's door and commander of the first thousand of the Ten Thousand; patient, sleepless, sure the empire can be saved by protocol. Every King's Eye reports to him.
  • Chief Eunuch Sparamiz Master of the Inner House · the Inner House — runs the household, the harem and the King's calendar; plump, pleasant and indispensable; receives every King's Eye's second report, and trusts it more than the first.
  • Queen Mother Irdabama arashshara of the royal estates · her own — eighty, never once audited; holds the one income of the House of Zindar that is not falling, and a secret about Prince Tiridat.
  • Bagapana King's Eye of the Throne Plain · the Inner House — a soft-spoken eunuch who reports on the King's own son, by two routes, and has started a third.
  • Utana Gushdar Master of the Eyes and Ears · the Gate, officially — keeper of the roll of King's Eyes, who appoints them, pays them and buries them; suspects the hazarapat reads every report before it reaches him, and has started sending the interesting ones by the Chief Eunuch's route instead.
  • Cupbearer Hushang Meydar Royal Cupbearer · the Below — tastes the King's wine, pours it, and has borrowed against Tiridat's accession; his cellar-keeper is Bagoas the Nameless, whom he considers a dull, reliable man.
  • Censer-Bearer Artakhshar eunuch of the Inner House · the Inner House — appointed by Sparamiz; tends the incense before the throne and sets the order of oath-taking, which the Karin dispute.
  • Chamberlain Mitradata Khvaraz Chamberlain of the Bedchamber, a eunuch · the Inner House, wavering — the last man to see the King each night; Zarduni-born, sent down as tribute at nine, and lately reading letters from the mountains.
  • Lady Rodaba Farnaka the hazarapat's wife · the Gate — keeps the list of who has been refused audience and when, which is the more dangerous list; most of the restless satraps are on it.
  • Azata Sukhra Karin Master of the Stair · the Stair — keeps the order of approach at the Bringing and walks the gaps because the book says so; his cousin sold Shir'abad D'ar its better place.
  • Mazdayar Spandiyad acting Treasurer of the Hours · the Stair, frightened — twenty-six, holding keys he was never trained for; asks everyone for advice, which is how the court learned the treasury is short.
  • Herbad Tansar Herbad of the Hill of Fires · the Fire — keeps the calendar, crowns the king, declares the days; no coronation, war or execution is lawful on a day he has not called fit, and every faction is courting his calendar for next winter.
  • Magus Rashnu-Vahram Keeper of the Rite of Return · the Fire, and himself — stands at every Immortal funeral; wants the Immortals released without the empire learning what they are.
  • Bagabukhsha Farnaka captain of the Golden Apples · the Gate — drills the first thousand twice a day to hide that he has never seen a battle; would be the first sword drawn in a palace coup, on whichever side his uncle chose.
  • Arashshara Mandana Nahid'zar provisioner of the Bringing · creditor of the throne — feeds every delegation and knows to the cup what the court owes her; the first person at court to know when a satrapy's delegation will not come, because it cancels the lamb.

Expansion

Daily Life

Daily Life in the Imperium

A marble city on the outside and a brick one within: the Invictian day runs on the dole queue, the patron's door and the baths, and everyone counts the hours from dawn because the sundials are the only clocks most people trust.

A day, hour by hour

Invictians count twelve hours of daylight from dawn and twelve of night from dusk, so an hour is longer in summer than in winter and every appointment is approximate. The Vigiles' horn marks sunrise and sunset inside the sacred line; the rest is guesswork and bells.

The poor: a veteran's family on the sixth floor. Marcus Tullius Naevus, discharged three years, his wife Aelia, her mother and two children rent one room and a cupboard at the top of a block in the Insulae, where the rent is lowest because the stairs are longest and the fire comes up them first.

  • Before dawn. Aelia carries the night-jar down six flights to the fuller's vat on the corner (he pays nothing for it and charges for the laundry). Marcus joins the tessera queue at the dole portico on the Mons Cerealis, which forms in the dark.
  • First to third hour. Bread and a twist of salt fish from a counter in the street, eaten standing. Marcus takes the grain to the miller-baker who grinds it for a cut. The children go to the schoolmaster's awning in a colonnade if there is a coin for him this month; otherwise they carry water.
  • Third to sixth hour. Day work, if any: the saccarii at the river wharves hire at dawn and the late are not hired. Aelia spins, mends, and sells the spun wool to a weaver on the ground floor. Her mother holds the room, because an empty room in the Insulae is a room someone else is living in by evening.
  • Sixth to eighth hour. The heat stops everything. A cup of posca, a nap on the floor, a dice game in the stairwell.
  • Eighth to ninth hour. The baths. The family goes to the cheapest house within four streets, a quadrans each, children free. This is where Marcus hears of work, where Aelia hears of rooms, and where both hear which Legate is paying veterans this month.
  • Dusk. Supper from the thermopolium counter: lentils, a sausage if it was a good day. No cooking at home; the room has no hearth, only a charcoal brazier the landlord forbids and everybody uses.
  • Night. Carts are allowed into the city only after dark, so the streets are loudest when the poor are trying to sleep. Marcus checks the bucket of sand by the door. Everyone in the Insulae knows where the nearest Vigiles station is.

The rich: a patrician house in the Horti. Gaius Calpurnius, a cousin of House Calpurnia, keeps a ground-floor domus with a garden behind it in the Horti.

  • Before dawn. The door-slave opens the vestibule to the clients already waiting on the bench. Gaius receives them in the atrium in order of rank: a freedman with a lease, two veterans with diplomas, a baker who wants a word with the Prefect of the Annona. Each gets a coin or a promise, and the coin is called the little basket.
  • First to sixth hour. To the Forum with his clients walking behind him, because a man is measured by the length of his tail. A lawsuit in the basilica, a sacrifice, a meeting of the Senate that decides nothing and is attended anyway.
  • Sixth hour. A light meal standing: bread, olives, cold meat.
  • Eighth hour. The great baths, never the private bath at home when there is business to be done. Exercise in the palaestra, an hour in the hot room, a massage, letters dictated to a secretary on the bench.
  • Ninth hour to late. The cena: three couches, nine guests, seven courses on a good night, a reader or a dancer between them. Guests bring their own napkins and take leftovers home in them. Political careers are made and broken at this table more often than in the Curia.

Homes

The insula is a block of brick-faced concrete six or seven storeys high round a light-well, shops at street level, the shopkeeper sleeping on a mezzanine above his counter. The first floor is the good floor: several rooms, glass in some windows, a lease. Above it the rooms shrink and the rent falls until, at the top, a family lives in one room under the tiles. There is no water above the ground floor and no latrine above it either. Most blocks belong to House Ovinia through middlemen, and the middlemen sublet. The domus turns its back to the street: a blank wall, a narrow door, the atrium with its rain-pool open to the sky, the shrine of the household gods by the hearth, the wax masks of the ancestors in cupboards, and a garden behind. Outside the capital, the rich live in villas and the poor in whatever the villa needs them to live in.

Food and drink

The poor eat puls (spelt or barley porridge), bread from the dole grain, moretum (crushed cheese, garlic, herbs and oil, spread on bread), chickpeas, lentils and cabbage. Garum, fermented fish sauce, goes on everything; the cheap grade is called allec and is the sludge at the bottom of the vat. Street counters sell lucanica sausage, fried fish and hot chickpeas in a paper of fig leaf. The drink is posca, sour wine cut with water, which the legions issue and the veterans still prefer. The rich eat patina (an egg-set dish of anything), sea bream, oysters, roast kid, dormice in honey and poppy seed, and finish with mulsum, honeyed wine, and fruit from the provinces. Libum, a cheese-cake, is baked for the household gods and eaten by the children afterwards. A cheap meal in the capital costs a sestertius; a loaf, an as.

Clothing and what it signals

Everyone wears the tunic. Only a citizen may wear the toga, which is heavy, white, hot and impossible to work in, so in practice it comes out for court, the patron's door, funerals and the census. A senator's tunic carries the broad purple stripe; an equestrian's the narrow stripe and a gold ring. A married woman wears the stola over her tunic and covers her hair outdoors. Freeborn children wear the bulla, a locket-amulet, until they come of age. In Aeterna every registered citizen over ten wears a bronze tessera on a cord, and it is the first thing a stranger looks at (see Status). Veterans keep the studded military belt, and wearing one when you have not served is a quick way to be beaten in a wine-shop. Dark cloth is mourning; chalk-whitened togas mean a man is standing for office.

Marriage, birth and coming of age

Birth. The father lifts the newborn from the floor to acknowledge it. A girl is named on the eighth day and a boy on the ninth, and given the bulla. Coming of age. At fifteen or sixteen a boy dedicates his bulla to the household gods and puts on the plain white toga of manhood, and his father walks him to the Forum to be enrolled; a girl comes of age by marrying, usually at fourteen to eighteen. In Aeterna the tessera cord at ten is the real threshold, and the dole office's register is a better record of births than the census. Marriage. Betrothal with an iron ring on the fourth finger of the left hand; a dowry, returnable on divorce; the bride in a flame-coloured veil, her hair parted with the point of a spear, carried over the threshold so she does not stumble on it. Divorce is easy and common among the rich. Among veterans, marriages contracted on the frontier are being registered for the first time in the capital, with the Aerarium arguing about whose pension the widow gets.

Funerals and the dead

No one is buried inside the sacred line, so the roads out of every city are lined with tombs, and the dead are read on the way in and out. The poor are buried by subscription to the Cycle of the Eternal Bloom, a few asses a month for a niche in a columbarium, an urn, a name and a funeral meal; for most citizens it is the most important contract they will ever sign. Patricians walk their ancestors in procession: actors wear the wax masks of the family's consuls behind the bier, and a son gives the eulogy in the Forum. A coin goes in the mouth for the passage. The dead become the Manes and are fed at the tomb on feast days; the restless dead, the Lemures, are driven out of the house each year at midnight by the head of the household, barefoot, spitting black beans over his shoulder without looking back.

Schooling and literacy

A schoolmaster teaches letters and sums under an awning in a colonnade from dawn to midday for a few asses a month a child, with a cane. The sons of the comfortable go on to a grammaticus for literature and then a rhetor for speaking, which is the only education the Imperium considers complete. Girls of good family learn at home. Perhaps one city-dweller in four can read a shop sign, an election notice painted on a wall or a dole list; fewer can write a letter. Veterans read army forms, which is why they read diplomas so carefully. Wax tablets for everyday, papyrus for anything that matters, bronze for the law.

Medicine and who heals

The Radiant Heartwardens staff the hospitals, originally built for the legions, and by oath will not serve a siege; a veteran with his diploma is treated free in principle and after a long wait in practice. A trained physician, often Hellenorian or Hellenorian-taught, charges a denarius a visit and more to set a bone. The poor go to the temple first, sleep in the porch and hope for a dream, then to the wise-woman on the stair with her herbs and her curses, then to the barber, who pulls teeth. Votive clay legs, eyes and wombs hang by the hundred in every healing shrine. Fever in the Gullet in late summer is expected and counted.

Crime and punishment

Inside Aeterna the only lawfully armed men are the Vigiles, freedmen with axes and buckets who fight fires first and thieves second; they arrest at night and the Praefectus Urbi tries their prisoners at dawn. Nobody goes to law alone (see Law): a patron speaks for a client, and a man without one loses. A citizen can be fined, exiled or, for the worst crimes, executed cleanly, and may appeal; a non-citizen can be flogged on the spot; a slave or a convicted bandit is crucified on the road outside the gate where the traffic can see. Bath thieves are the commonest criminals in the city, and the commonest revenge is a lead curse tablet dropped in the bath's drain naming the stolen tunic. Veteran gangs collect "protection" from blocks whose landlords will not pay the Vigiles enough to call.

Entertainment and gambling

The Circus Aeternus holds three hundred thousand for the chariots; the four racing colours have their own taverns, songs and street fights, and a man's colour is as fixed as his gods. The arena gives beast-hunts in the morning, executions at noon and gladiators after. The theatre has given up tragedy for mime, which is cheaper and lewder. In the street: tali (knucklebones) and dice, the board game of twelve lines, and the soldier's game of robbers on a scratched grid. Gambling for money is lawful only during the midwinter festival, when slaves dine with their masters, and is practised all year, everywhere, in the back of every wine-shop. Legates now pay for games in their own names, and the crowd has noticed whose name is on the awning.

Work and wages

  • Day labourer at the wharves: 1 sestertius (2 sp 5 cp) a day and a loaf, when hired.
  • Skilled craftsman (mason, smith, fuller): 1 denarius a day at face; the denarius is worth 8 or 9 sp in fact and falling at every Assay.
  • Schoolmaster: 2 asses a month per pupil; a good grammaticus, 10 denarii a month per pupil.
  • Legionary: about 46 denarii a year after stoppages; a centurion, ten times that.
  • A top-floor room in the Insulae: 2 denarii a month, paid weekly; a first-floor flat, 30 denarii a year; a domus in the Horti, 500 a year and more.
  • A tessera bought on the Mons Cerealis: about 60 denarii, triple its price before the Great Concord.
  • Burial subscription to the Cycle: 2 asses a month, or a lump sum of 3 denarii.

Taboos and manners

Step over a threshold right foot first. Never name the dead after dark. Do not carry a drawn blade inside the sacred line. A citizen in a toga does not carry his own parcels. Spilling salt or oil at a meal is a bad omen, and a sneeze is answered with "salve". At dinner, guests recline on their left elbows and eat with their right hands; sitting up is for children and slaves. At the baths the order is warm, hot, cold, and talking business in the cold pool is the height of manners. Speaking ill of the empty Imperator's chair is not yet a crime; it is merely noted.

Three things outsiders always get wrong

  • The poor live at the top. Height is poverty in Aeterna: the cheapest rooms are the highest, because the stairs are longest and the top floors burn first.
  • The dole is not charity. The tessera is a citizen's proof of being somebody, and suggesting that the Annona is alms for the poor is an insult to the family that has drawn on it for nine generations (see Grain).
  • The toga is not everyday dress. Visitors arrive expecting a city in white wool and find a city in brown tunics. A foreigner who wears a toga is either a fool or claiming citizenship, and both are punished.

Daily Life in Hellenoria

Everyone is outdoors, everyone is arguing, and everyone is paid by the public purse to do something: sit on a jury, row a ship, watch a play. The house is for women, slaves and sleep; the city is the street, the harbour and the hill where the Assembly meets.

A day, hour by hour

Hellenorians reckon by the sun and the market: "when the agora fills" is mid-morning, "when the agora empties" is noon. The courts run on water-clocks, and a speaker's time is literally poured out.

The poor: a rower's household on the Road. Nikias son of Lykos rows in the third bank of a trireme, when there is a voyage, and lives with his wife Phila, their three children and his widowed sister in two rooms of a four-storey tenement leaning on the inner face of the Long Walls.

  • Before dawn. Phila or the sister fetches water from the fountain-house at the end of the lane; the women's queue there is the Road's real assembly. Barley cakes from yesterday, dipped in watered wine.
  • Dawn. Nikias walks down to the Shipsheds to learn whether his ship sails. It mostly does not. If not, he goes early to the Agora to be drawn for a jury: the allotment stones decide, and three obols is a day's bread for five.
  • Mid-morning. Phila sells figs and baskets from a mat at the edge of the market; citizen women of the poor work in public because they must, and the rich pretend not to see them. The children run errands for the rope-walk at the foot of the wall.
  • Noon. Bread, olives, a bowl of lentil soup. Sleep in the shade.
  • Afternoon. If he sat on a jury, Nikias is home with his pay and an opinion about the defendant. If not, he caulks for a Voidfolk pitch-boiler at day rate, mends nets, or sits in the barber's shop, which is where the Road decides how it will vote.
  • Evening. Supper is the main meal: barley, a fish or a piece of octopus, greens, cheese. On festival days the family eats meat, because the sacrifice is shared out, and each citizen draws two obols from the theoric board at the theatre gate.
  • Night. Lamp oil is dear, and the Road goes to bed with the sun, except on Assembly eves, when the wine-shops stay open and the oligarchs' men buy rounds.

The rich: a shipowner's house at the top of the Road. Demophon Euxenides, a cousin of the head of the house, owns eleven merchant hulls and funds one warship a year as a public duty, as men of his house have done for generations.

  • Dawn. A libation at the courtyard altar and a word with the steward. His wife Kleito, who will not leave the house today, holds the storeroom keys and the account of every jar behind them.
  • Morning. To the Agora with two slaves behind him, then to the Emporion to see his factors and the metic bankers at their tables. Money is borrowed against cargoes not yet landed, at what the law calls sea-interest and everyone else calls robbery.
  • Noon. A light meal at a friend's. The barber's, for the news, because the rich go to the barber too.
  • Afternoon. The gymnasion: wrestling, oil, the strigil, and conversation that is the real business of the class. His sons train here; the Arcane Academy's students argue in the colonnade.
  • Evening. The symposion: couches in the men's room, a mixing-bowl of wine and water at the ratio the symposiarch sets, songs, riddles, a flute-girl, and the game of flicking wine-lees at a target. Kleito does not attend. She knows what was said by morning.

Homes

A Hellenorian house shows the street a blank whitewashed wall and a door, and turns inward to a courtyard with an altar and a well or cistern. The men's dining room opens near the door; the women's rooms are upstairs or at the back, where visitors do not go. The poor live in mud-brick on stone footings, two or three rooms round a shared yard, or in tenements like the Road's, four storeys of rooms let by the month. Burglars in Hellenorian slang are "wall-diggers", because it is easier to dig through mud-brick than to pick a lock. Furniture is sparse: couches, stools, chests, a loom. A wealthy house shows its wealth in painted pottery and bronze, not in rooms.

Food and drink

The meal is sitos, the staple, and opson, whatever goes with it. Sitos is maza, kneaded barley cake, for the poor and wheat bread for the comfortable. Opson is cheese, olives, onions, garlic, figs and above all fish: sprats and anchovies for the poor, tuna and eel for the rich, and a man who eats too much opson for his bread is mocked as a fish-glutton. Phake, lentil soup, is the poor man's dinner and the philosopher's boast. Kykeon, barley gruel with pennyroyal and grated cheese, is drunk by labourers and by initiates of the Mysteries. Wine is always mixed with water, two or three parts water to one; drinking it neat is what Malaunian horsemen do. Honey cakes for the gods, sesame sweets for children, octopus grilled on the quay for anyone with an obol. Meat is a festival food, because it comes from sacrifice. The grain-wardens fix the price of bread (see Grain), and a riot starts the day they fail to.

Clothing and what it signals

The chiton, a tunic pinned at the shoulders, and over it the himation, a large wrapped cloak, for anyone with leisure. Workers wear the exomis, a short tunic fastened on one shoulder to leave the arm free. Young men and riders wear the short chlamys. Long hair on a man means horses and old money; a shaved head means mourning or slavery; a beard means an adult citizen; a long beard and a ragged cloak mean a philosopher, or someone who wants to be taken for one. A purple border costs twelve thousand Helionyx shells and announces it. Citizen women of good family go veiled in the street; poor women and metic women often do not. The Voidfolk of the Deme of the Accord cap their horn-tips in silver or bronze on civic occasions, as another citizen would wear a wreath. There is no dress that marks a metic or a slave, which visitors find maddening and Hellenorian conservatives complain about in every generation.

Marriage, birth and coming of age

Birth. A wreath of olive on the door for a boy, a tuft of wool for a girl. On the fifth day the father carries the child at a run round the hearth, which makes it part of the house; on the tenth it is named, usually for a grandfather. Coming of age. At eighteen a citizen's son is presented to his deme, examined for age and free birth, and enrolled as an ephebe for two years of service; with the fleet half laid up, ephebes now spend those years guarding the Long Walls and repainting shipshed numbers. A girl dedicates her toys and a lock of hair to Artemis before her wedding. Marriage. A pledge between the bride's father and the groom, a dowry that goes back with her if the marriage ends, a ritual bath in water carried from a sacred spring, and a torchlit procession by cart to the groom's house, where she eats a quince and is showered with nuts and dried figs at the hearth. Brides are fourteen to eighteen, grooms nearer thirty. The Ivory Chorus sings at every marriage that matters, which means every alliance, and repeats nothing.

Funerals and the dead

The women of the family wash the body, dress and crown it, and lay it out for a day with its feet to the door; they lament and tear their cheeks, and hired mourners sing where the family cannot. Before dawn on the third day the procession carries the dead out of the city, because no one is buried inside the walls: in Hellarchon through the Clay Gate, where grave monuments line the road for half a mile. An obol goes in the mouth for the ferryman. Burial or burning, then a meal at the family's house, offerings at the grave on the third, ninth and thirtieth days, and once a year after. The dead go down to the house of Hades as shades, thin and thirsty, and libations are poured to them through a pipe into the grave. Initiates of the Eleusinian Mysteries expect a better place and do not say what it is. Sumptuary laws cap what a family may spend, and every great family breaks them. The war dead are buried publicly, one stone per ship, with an empty bier carried for the missing; at Delphara most new questions to the oracle are about them.

Schooling and literacy

At seven a citizen boy goes to three masters: the grammatistes for letters and sums, the kitharistes for the lyre and the poets, the paidotribes for wrestling. A slave, the paidagogos, walks him there and back and canes him on the way. Literacy among citizen men is high, because the Sherd requires every voter to scratch a name on a potsherd and the Assembly posts its decrees on whitened boards. Women of good family learn at home, if their fathers allow it; metic children learn their parents' trade and letters at the counter. Older youths pay a sophist, and a speech-writer can be hired by the hour (two drachmas buys a man to argue anything). The Arcane Academy, the Porticoes of Thessalonika and the gymnasia are where the rich finish, and the Truth-Flame watches all three.

Medicine and who heals

Physicians are craftsmen who travel, set up a surgery in a rented shop and advertise by curing someone visible. Some cities pay a public physician to treat citizens free; Hellarchon pays two. The sick who can travel go to the healing sanctuaries of Asklepios to sleep in the dormitory and dream the cure, or to the hot springs at Loutrokleion, where diet is prescribed by the cupful. Midwives deliver children and know more medicine than most physicians. Country people trust the herb-cutters, and the druids of the Tranquil Hand Enclave treat anyone, citizen or not, in exchange for an argument about the land. A physician's visit costs a drachma; a night in a healing dormitory, an obol and a cake for the sacred snakes.

Crime and punishment

There are no police. A citizen who catches a thief drags him before the magistrates himself; public slaves with rods keep order in the Assembly and nowhere else. Any citizen may prosecute, so professional informers live on the rewards and on the threat (see Law). Juries of hundreds, paid three obols, decide by majority before supper. Punishments are fines, loss of citizen rights, exile by the Sherd, confiscation, and for the gravest crimes death: hemlock for a citizen, the plank for a slave or a pirate. A slave's testimony is admissible only under torture, which is why rich men send their slaves abroad before a trial. Hubris, the deliberate humiliation of a free person, is a crime in itself. The Truth-Flame tries ideas rather than acts, and its court has no jury.

Entertainment and gambling

The theatre above all: three tragedies and a satyr play in a day at the Dionysia, comedies that name living politicians, and every citizen paid two obols by the Theoric Fund to watch. The gymnasion and its races; the great games at Delphara and the Isthmian Games at Corinth, on which the whole League bets. In the street: knucklebones, dice, a board game of five lines, cockfights and quail-tapping (a quail is set in a ring and flicked on the head; if it backs out, its owner loses). At symposia, the wine-lees game and drinking songs passed round with a myrtle branch. Gambling houses are frowned on, and every harbour has three.

Work and wages

  • Rower in peacetime: 3 obols a day while afloat. In the war it was a drachma, and the cities still argue about who promised it.
  • Juror: 3 obols a day. Assembly attendance in Hellarchon: a drachma a meeting, if you arrive ahead of the red rope.
  • Skilled worker (mason, carpenter, caulker) on public works: a drachma a day, citizen, metic or slave alike; an architect, two.
  • Theoric pay: 2 obols a festival day per citizen on the roll, about sixty festival days a year in Hellarchon.
  • Metic tax: a drachma a year for a man, half for a woman, plus a citizen sponsor who expects favours.
  • Rent: two rooms on the Road, 3 drachmas a month; the lease of a courtyard house below the Rock, 300 drachmas to buy.
  • A day's barley for one man, about an obol at the fixed price; a jug of ordinary wine, an obol; a fish worth eating, three.

Taboos and manners

Do not drink unmixed wine, eat from the common dish with the left hand, or forget the libation before the first cup. Never refuse a suppliant who holds the altar; never strike a herald. Ask a citizen woman's name in public and you have insulted her family: outside the house she is "the wife of" or "the mother of". Spit into the fold of your cloak to turn bad luck, and do not discuss the terms of the Voidfolk Accord where a stranger can hear, because the Truth-Flame hears. A guest is sacred for three days and a nuisance after. Above all, do not boast: the gods punish it, and so does the Sherd.

Three things outsiders always get wrong

  • You cannot tell a citizen by looking. Metics, slaves and citizens dress alike; asking a man his status in the street insults the citizen and threatens the slave.
  • The Theoric Fund is not a bribe. To a Hellenorian, being paid to attend the rites is what makes a poor man a citizen at all; calling it a bribe is calling the city a brothel (see the Public Purse).
  • The Voidfolk are citizens. The tieflings of the Deme of the Accord vote like any other deme, and a visitor who treats them as metics or slaves will find that the Road takes their side.

Daily Life in Acheaoria

A life measured in water-hours, bows and gifts: the Acheaorian day is arranged around the qanat's rota, the fire that must never be insulted, and the certainty that every encounter between two people has a correct order of precedence.

A day, hour by hour

The Magi mark the day in five watches of prayer, beginning at sunrise, and the fire-temples sound them with a bronze bell. In the country the real clock is the water: a family's share of the qanat comes round on a fixed rota, by day or by night, and when it comes everyone works.

The poor: a share-holding farmer on the Garden Road. Bagdat of the third shaft, his wife Arta, their four children and his brother's widow farm eight jarib of wheat, melons and pomegranates in a qanat village a day below Persevalis. They own one bowl-time in the village's twelve-day rota, about a third of an hour's flow, and it is the most valuable thing they will ever possess.

  • Before dawn. This week the share falls in the second hour after midnight. Bagdat and his eldest son stand at the sluice with a lantern while the kadkhuda's man sinks the timing bowl in its basin; when it fills and drowns, the water goes to the next man. Arguments about whose bowl was dropped late are the village's chief entertainment.
  • Sunrise. The first prayer, facing the sun, with the hearth-fire fed a stick of clean wood. Bread baked yesterday on hot pebbles, yoghurt, a handful of dates, sweet tea if there is sugar.
  • Morning. Field work while it is cool. Arta and her sister-in-law spin and dye at the courtyard pool; the wool goes to the arashshara of the district workshop, who weighs it, writes it on a tablet and pays in barley or in pashiz. The younger children scare birds off the melons.
  • Noon to mid-afternoon. Nobody works in the heat. The family eats in the cool room under the wind-catcher, then sleeps.
  • Afternoon. Bagdat takes a turn on the village's corvée: three days a month clearing silt from the qanat's shafts with the muqanni, who are paid and he is not.
  • Sunset. Prayer, then the main meal: a pot of lentil and noodle pottage, bread, onions, cheese, and on good days a little mutton. The men sit at the teahouse by the village pool and hear what the Royal Road courier said at noon.
  • Night. The hearth is banked, never put out. The door is barred against wolves and tax-gatherers, in that order.

The rich: an azata household in Persemenid. The lord of a lesser zarate keeps a courtyard house in the Garden Town below the platform; his wife, Lady Parysatis, is arashshara of three weaving workshops and a vineyard, and signs with her own seal.

  • Sunrise. Prayer before the household fire with a magus in attendance. A bath in the house's own tank, fed by its own share of the Water-Court.
  • Morning. The lord rides up the stair to the Terrace of Columns to wait. Waiting is most of court life: in the right antechamber, at the right distance, for a summons that may come in a month. Parysatis receives her overseers in the women's court, checks the tablets, and settles a dispute between two dyers with a sentence nobody appeals.
  • Noon. A meal of many small dishes laid on a cloth: rice with saffron and barberries, stewed fowl with walnuts and pomegranate, flatbread, herbs, sherbet cooled with ice from the house's own yakhchal.
  • Afternoon. Sleep through the heat in the summer room below ground, where the wind-tower pulls air over a pool.
  • Late afternoon. Polo on the Square below the bazaar, or a ride into the hunting park if he holds the right; for Parysatis, visits, which are negotiations conducted over fruit.
  • Evening. A long dinner in the garden pavilion, a singer of the Melodic Circle if the house can afford one, wine (the Magi drink it, so may anyone), and a game of nard. Decisions taken drunk are reviewed sober the next morning, and decisions taken sober are reviewed drunk; it is an old custom and the court still keeps it.

Homes

The Acheaorian house turns inward and downward. Thick mud-brick walls, a single door from the lane, a courtyard with a pool and a fruit tree, rooms round it, and below ground a summer room where the heat cannot reach. A house of any standing has a wind-tower pulling cool air down over water; in Atarabad's Wind-Tower Quarter they stand on every roof of consequence and are counted like servants. The great houses keep a domed yakhchal beside them, filled with winter ice from shaded pools and opened in summer for sherbet. The poor live in one or two rooms of the same plan, share a courtyard and a hearth, and roof their lanes with matting. In the desert villages the houses are domed so the roof needs no timber, and a family's status is how near its door stands to the point where the qanat surfaces.

Food and drink

Bread first: sangak, baked on a bed of hot pebbles, and thin flatbread slapped on the wall of the clay oven. The poor eat ash, a thick pottage of lentils, chickpeas, noodles and herbs topped with dried whey; abgusht, mutton and chickpeas stewed in a clay pot, the broth eaten with bread first and the meat mashed after; yoghurt, cheese, onions, dates and melons. The rich eat rice: chelow steamed so the bottom forms a golden crust that guests compete for, rice with saffron and barberries, lamb kebab, fowl in walnut and pomegranate stew, quince, pistachio and rosewater sweets. In summer a jar of yakhchal ice turns syrup into sherbet and rice-starch noodles into paludeh, eaten with rosewater and lime. Tea, sweet and strong, is drunk all day and offered to every visitor; refusing it is possible and remembered. Dugh, salted yoghurt with mint, is the labourer's drink. Wine is lawful and the court's; the Magi drink it at rites. A bowl of teahouse stew costs a few pashiz; a jar of ice in high summer, 5 sp.

Clothing and what it signals

Everyone wears trousers, men and women, rich and poor, which Invictians and Hellenorians find hilarious until they ride for a week. Over them goes a long-sleeved tunic and, for anyone of standing, the kandys, a coat worn over the shoulders with the sleeves empty. Commoners wear undyed or madder-red wool and a cloth wound against the dust; azata nobles wear dyed silk, a felt cap with flaps, and gold. The gold matters: bracelets, torques and robes given by the King are royal gifts that may be worn and never sold, and a courtier is read by what he has been given. The Magi wear white, with a cloth over the mouth before the fire so that breath does not touch it. An arashshara wears her seal on a cord at the wrist and turns it outward when she enters a workshop. Kurtash labourers on the royal estates wear what the estate issues, and the ration tablet hung round the neck.

Marriage, birth and coming of age

Birth. A fire is lit beside mother and child and kept burning for forty days to keep the dark away. On the sixth night the family names the child, and a scribe writes the name under the father's. A kurtash mother draws an extra ration for the birth, more for a son, and the tablets show it. Coming of age. At fifteen a magus ties the sacred cord round the young person's waist three times over a white undershirt, and from that day they pray as adults and can be punished as adults. A noble boy is taught three things from five to twenty: to ride, to draw the bow and to speak the truth. Court boys are raised as pages at the King's gate, which is where they learn whom to bow to. Marriage. A contract sealed before a magus and witnesses, with fire present: a bride-gift from the groom's family, a dowry from hers, and her house name kept for life. Zarate marriages are treaties and are negotiated by the women. A village wedding lasts three days, a noble one seven, and the bride sits before a mirror and two lamps while the contract is read, and answers only on the third asking.

Funerals and the dead

A corpse is the most polluting thing in the world, so it may not touch earth, water or fire. Within the day a dog is brought to look at the body, to drive off the corruption, and the corpse-bearers, a hereditary guild who live apart and are paid well for it, carry it on an iron bier to the Silent Towers, where the dead are laid out on the stone for the vultures; at Persemenid they stand on the north spur of the Hill of Fires. When the sun and birds have finished, the bones go into an ossuary in the tower's well. The family stays indoors three days, cooks no meat, and keeps a lamp lit where the body lay. On the dawn of the fourth day the soul crosses the Bridge of the Account: for the truthful it is broad as a road and a fair girl waits at the far end; for the follower of the Lie it narrows to a blade. Kings lie in tombs cut high in the cliff, so that they touch neither earth nor water. Conquered peoples who bury their dead do so outside the Qanat Line or pay a fee not to be seen doing it.

Schooling and literacy

Most Acheaorians cannot read and do not need to. Those who can are scribes, Magi, merchants and arashshara, and the arashshara are the largest literate group in the empire after the scribes, because a workshop cannot be run without tablets. Scribes train for years under the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger in three scripts and two languages. The Magi teach temple boys the hymns by heart, because the holy word is spoken, not written. Everyone else learns by memory: poems, genealogies, water-rotas and the order of precedence, all recited, and an illiterate kadkhuda can recite his village's every share and its history for three generations.

Medicine and who heals

There are three kinds of healer: the healer by the knife, the healer by herbs and the healer by the holy word, and the last is held best, because he cures without cutting. The Magi heal by word and by the purification of nine nights for anyone who has touched the dead. Herbalists sell in their own lane of every bazaar. A surgeon must cure three foreigners before he may cut a believer, and if he kills three he is barred for life; the foreigners are rarely told. Eye disease from dust and glare is the commonest ailment, and kohl from the Parthian Ravine is worn by men and women as much against the sun as for beauty. Where satraps have stopped feeding their people, the Benevolent Hands run kitchens and wells that also serve as clinics, carefully and without saying so.

Crime and punishment

Each bazaar lane has a warden and each district a frataraka with armed men, and the satrap's court sits above them. The Lanterns of Justice ride with a lamp lit at noon, so the guilty have an hour's warning to make amends, which a surprising number do. A sealed law cannot be changed (see Law); a doubtful case can be sent to the ordeal at Mithratal's grove. Punishments are public and physical: the bastinado, branding, the loss of an ear or the nose for a repeat thief, death for treason and for the third conviction of lying under oath. The worst sentence short of death is the loss of a water share, which ends a family. Theft in the bazaar is organised: the Veilborn Syndicate works under a ceiling it never breaks, and a merchant robbed above that ceiling knows it was not the Syndicate. The King's Eyes and Ears report on officials, not on thieves.

Entertainment and gambling

Polo on the great squares, played by nobles and watched by everyone. The Royal Hunt and its lesser imitations in every satrap's park. Wrestling in the houses of strength, domed gymnasia where men swing wooden clubs to a drum and chanted verse. Storytellers in the teahouses recite the deeds of kings in instalments, and stop at the cliff-edge of a story to collect coins. Music from the Melodic Circle at Persevalis, and from every village fiddler who claims to have studied there. The board game is nard, played with dice, and the dice are where the gambling happens; the Magi disapprove, and play at home. Betting on polo and on horse-races runs through the bazaar's tea-sellers. The Bringing at the new year is the great show of the empire, and the absences from it are discussed for months.

Work and wages

  • Kurtash labourer on a royal estate: a monthly ration of thirty measures of barley for a man, twenty for a woman, wine or beer on feast days, and no coin at all.
  • Free labourer in a city: about 5 sigloi a month, paid weekly in pashiz by the bazaar gang-masters.
  • Master muqanni: 1 siglos a day, paid in advance, because nobody argues with the man who knows where the water is.
  • Weaver in an arashshara's workshop: 3 to 8 sigloi a month by skill, plus barley; a master carpet-knotter, more than a junior scribe.
  • A bowl-time in a village rota: 30 to 80 gp to buy, 200 at Qa'zshahrv'in (see Water).
  • A bed in a caravanserai's far court, 5 sp a night; a teahouse meal, a few pashiz; a pound of saffron, 15 gp; a carpet from Tabrishiir, 40 to 400 gp.

Taboos and manners

Never pollute the elements: do not blow on a fire with your breath, throw rubbish into it, spit or urinate in running water, or bury anything dead in the earth. Never lie, and never call a man a liar unless you mean to fight him; the word is far stronger than in any other tongue. Do not name the King. Greet an equal with a kiss on the lips, a near-equal on the cheek, and a superior by bowing and kissing your own fingers towards him; getting this wrong in public is a social catastrophe. Offer three times and refuse twice: a host offers, a guest declines, the host insists, and only the third offer may be accepted. Take shoes off on carpets. Eat with the right hand. A posted price is an insult: bargaining is a courtesy, and a stranger is expected to fail at it.

Three things outsiders always get wrong

  • The women run the workshops. An arashshara's seal outranks most men's in any market or workshop; asking whose daughter she is, or looking past her for the man in charge, costs a merchant his licence (see Status).
  • The Silent Towers are piety, not desecration. Westerners call exposure barbaric; Acheaorians think burying a corpse in the earth is a deliberate poisoning of the world, and say so.
  • The first "no" is not an answer. Refusal, praise and gifts are all a ritual of three; the visitor who takes the first refusal at face value has gone home without the contract, and the visitor who accepts the first offer has been rude.

Daily Life among the Mavari of Mavelon

Free spear-bearers in cave-houses above their own harbour, rowing the Imperium's ships for wages and never for orders: the north side of Mavelon lives by fish, ship-shares and the keel-silver, and settles its quarrels by law, by man-price, or at the Gate on festival nights.

A day, hour by hour

The Mavari day runs on the tide, which comes through the Race twice a day and decides when the fish market opens, when boats can leave and when the tide-mills on the south shore turn. Nobody on the north side owns a sundial; the Lawspeaker's bell at the Thingstead marks noon, and the Gate opens at sunrise when two keys turn.

The poor: a fishing family in the Hollows. Wido Keelbreaker, a Hrodning oarsman laid off when his quinquereme was laid up, his wife Thorgund, their three children and his mother live in a two-room cave-house cut into the pumice of the Hollows, with a whitewashed front, a peat fire and a sheep in the back room in winter.

  • Before dawn. Thorgund blows the peat back to life and sets barley porridge on. Wido and his eldest go down the switchback stair to the North Harbour to take the family's share-boat out on the ebb through the Race.
  • Sunrise. Across the caldera, at the Gate, the Reiks's key-bearer and the Dux's turn their keys. Mavari who work on the south side, forge hands, caulkers, Wido's sister who sells herring at the south fish-stalls, file through and are counted.
  • Morning. Thorgund spins and keeps the house; the grandmother mends nets on the step and runs the children. The eldest girl carries peat and water. The younger children are on the slips, where they learn Invictian from the shipwrights and teach the south-side boys Mavari curses.
  • Turn of the tide. The boat comes in; the fish market opens at the turn, without a customs post, because the fish are untaxed by the Oath. What is not sold is gutted and hung to dry on the racks above the shingle.
  • Afternoon. Wido sits on an upturned boat with the other idle oarsmen and watches the south harbour's empty slips. If the arsenal is hiring caulkers at day rate, he crosses the Gate; if the Skeldings are in the alehouse, he goes home a different way.
  • Evening. Fish stew, flatbread, curds, ale. In the long evenings the clans visit each other's cave-rows, and someone always recites.
  • Night. The Gate shuts at sunset. A Mavari caught on the south side after dark needs a reason, and "I was drinking with a trierarch" is accepted surprisingly often.

The rich: a ship-share household at the Thingstead. Mavari wealth is not land; it is shares in ships, the right to a cut of every voyage and every catch. The Reiks's own wife, Fridugund, holds the Hrodnings' shares and the keel-silver accounts, and her day is the model every ship-share wife follows.

  • Sunrise. The Reiks walks down to the Gate and turns his key himself, as Ansvald has done every morning of his reign. Fridugund takes the keys of the hall's storerooms and the silver chest from her belt and checks what is owed.
  • Morning. Shipmasters come up to the hall to settle shares from last week's voyages; she reckons in her head and has a scribe tally on a stick. The Reiks hears petitions on the bench outside, standing, and anyone with a spear-ring may speak to him without leave.
  • Noon. The Lawspeaker's bell; bread, mutton, ale at the long hearth. Guests from the south side are fed first, by custom.
  • Afternoon. The Reiks crosses to the Gate Court if a case needs both rulers, or to the yards; Fridugund visits the clan elders' wives, which is where the Thing's votes are actually counted.
  • Evening. The hall's long table: forty people, mead, a skald, and on the nights the Dux's son and Hildegund visit, the boy who is Aulus at one grandfather's table and Audwin at this one.

Homes

The north side lives in cave-houses cut back into the soft pale pumice: a whitewashed front wall with a door and one window, a front room with the hearth, a back room cut deeper where it is cool in summer and warm in winter, and storage niches carved into the walls. A family that prospers cuts another room. Rows of them climb the cliff in terraces linked by stairs worn into troughs, and a clan's cave-rows are its fortress, its address and its vote. The greatest clans build timber halls on the rim, roofed with ship-timber turned keel-up. Down at the harbour the boat-sheds are timber, and the young unmarried men sleep in them in summer.

Food and drink

Herring above all, fresh, salted, smoked or soured in barrels; cod split and dried on the racks; mussels from the caldera walls, which the south side will not eat because of the arsenal's outfall and the north side eats because it collects them upstream. Barley porridge with butter for breakfast, keel-bread (a hard rye flatbread baked for voyages that keeps for a month) for the boats, curds and whey-cheese, mutton from the sheep grazed on the outer flank, and blood-sausage at slaughter time in autumn. Sea-stew is whatever the boat brought, boiled with onions and barley. The drinks are ale, sour whey cut with water for work, and mead for feasts. The ram sacrificed at the Midsummer Thing is eaten by the whole assembly, and a man who refuses his share has refused the law. South-side wine has crossed the Gate with the Gate Marriage and is now drunk at weddings, to the annoyance of the old.

Clothing and what it signals

Men wear wool trousers bound at the calf, a long tunic and a cloak pinned at the right shoulder, so the sword arm is free; a free man's cloak-pin is bronze or silver and inherited. Women wear a long dress under an apron-dress held by two brooches, and from the brooches hang the household keys, scissors and a knife; a woman who wears the keys runs the house, and in the clans that means the ship-shares too. The spear-ring, an arm-ring of twisted silver, marks a free spear-bearer of the Thing, and taking it off in public is how a man renounces his clan. Long hair is free; cropped hair marks a man outlawed or in mourning. Young Mavari who cut their hair short and wear the Invictian tunic are called key-turners on the north side and natives on the south, and know it.

Marriage, birth and coming of age

Birth. The father takes the newborn on his knee and sprinkles it with water, which makes it his; on the ninth night it is named, never for a living relative, because a name has room for only one. A child whose father is drowned takes its mother's name and nobody remarks on it. Coming of age. At fifteen, at the Midsummer Thing, a boy or a girl of a free family takes the spear-ring before the Lawspeaker and may then speak at the Thing, fight at the Gate and be held to the law. The children of the Gate Marriage will choose at their spear-taking which name to answer to, and both halves are waiting. Marriage. The groom's family pays a bride-price, the bride brings a dowry of household goods and a ship-share if she has one, and on the morning after the wedding the husband gives her a morning-gift that is hers alone. The vows are sworn at the Hof on a ring from the ring-board. A marriage across the Gate is held twice, once at the Hof and once in the south, and registered at the Gate Court, which keeps both names.

Funerals and the dead

The drowned have no bodies and need none: at the Night of the Oars each autumn the hof-wife reads the names of everyone the sea took that year, and each family carries the dead man's oar down to the Keelhall to stand with the oars of his fathers. A third of the fathers on the north side are remembered by an oar. Those who die ashore are washed, dressed in their best, given a coin and a knife, and laid in the deep cave-tombs at the back of their clan's rows, the entrance sealed with a stone carved with a ship. The dead sail to the hall of Saiwar, the sea-father, and those who died well row in his ship; the ship-mother Kiliga keeps the living afloat. The funeral feast lasts as long as the ale, and the heir does not take his place on the dead man's bench until he has drunk the inheritance-cup and sworn a deed. A death caused by another is owed a man-price, paid to the kin, and the Skelding feud is about the Imperium paying a fine to its own treasury instead.

Schooling and literacy

Mavari children are taught on the slips and in the boats: knots, tides, stars, the Oath at the Gate by heart, and enough Invictian to be cheated in it less. Their own letters are runes, cut on sticks for tallies, ship-shares and memorials, and most adults can read a rune-stick and few can read a page. The Lawspeaker carries the law in memory and recites a third of it at every Thing, so that it is all heard every three years. The arsenal school on the south side takes promising Mavari boys as apprentices, and the guild halls' four centuries of apprentices' pieces include, now, a good many with Mavari marks.

Medicine and who heals

The hof-wife and the wise-women of each clan set bones, sew wounds and give herbs; bone-setting on the slips is a skill passed down in families, and a good one is paid in fish for life. The Baths of Mavelon on the High Crescent, fed by the volcano's hot springs, open before dawn for the forge shifts and take Mavari forge hands, which makes them the one place both halves sit naked together, and the source of half the city's gossip. The arsenal's hospital, staffed by the Radiant Heartwardens, treats Mavari crewmen on fleet business free, under the Oath, and everyone else for a denarius.

Crime and punishment

Within the north side, the Thing's law: injuries are priced by a tariff the Lawspeaker recites, from a lost finger to a life, and paid to the injured or their kin. The Thing's spear-wardens enforce it; a man who will not pay or will not come is declared nithing at the Thing, outlawed, and may be killed by anyone without man-price. Cases between the halves go to the Gate Court, an Imperial iudex and a Mavari doomsman side by side, and if they cannot agree the rulers have nine days. The Gate Fights on festival nights are lawful brawls on the neck, broken up by the south's Vigiles and the Thing's spear-wardens together at the third hour; a man who draws iron at one is outlawed by both sides at once. Theft from a boat is the north side's worst ordinary crime and is punished by the loss of the thief's share in his own.

Entertainment and gambling

Rowing races across the caldera between clans, and once a year between a Mavari crew and a south-side crew, which is the year's biggest bet. Flyting, a duel of insults in verse in the Reiks's hall, judged by the room; a good flyter is admired more than a good fighter and gets a byname for life. Wrestling on the shingle. Skalds reciting the Burning of the Slips. The board game is the Reiks's table, a king and his guard against attackers on a grid, played on every upturned boat. Dice and knucklebones in the alehouses. The Bridge Walk, the Midsummer Thing, the Keel-Silver and the Night of the Oars are the four days the whole north side keeps.

Work and wages

  • Mavari freeman oarsman in the fleet: 120 denarii a year by the Oath, paid whether the ship sails or not, while he is on the roll; the fleet that carried ten thousand Mavari oarsmen now carries four thousand.
  • Steersman: double an oarsman's pay, and a Mavari steersman sails with every Invictian master.
  • Caulker or forge hand on the south side: 1 denarius a day at face, paid in the debased coin the Mavari now weigh.
  • Keel-silver: a tithe on every hull launched, about 200 denarii for a trireme and 400 for a quinquereme, shared among the clans at the Hof; launches have fallen from nearly thirty a year in the war to six.
  • A basket of herring at the north fish market: 2 asses, untaxed; at the south stalls, 3 asses and a market fee.
  • A free spear-bearer's man-price by the Lawspeaker's tariff: 200 denarii in silver, or its value in ship-shares.

Taboos and manners

Never name a child for a living relative: it is a public wish for his death, and the Skeldings did exactly that this spring. Never call a Mavari "oar-slave". Never whistle in a boat, turn a boat against the sun, or say the word "drown" aboard. Stand when you speak to the Reiks and look him in the eye; kneeling to him is an insult to him and to you. Guests are fed first and asked their business after. A woman's keys are not touched by anyone else, and a man who takes a ship-share wife's keys has stolen the household. Do not pass the Gate with a drawn blade or an unpaid debt.

Three things outsiders always get wrong

  • The Reiks is not a client chieftain. He is the Dux's equal by sworn treaty, holds a key to the Gate, and is called "Reiks", never "chief"; the Mavari know exactly what "chieftain" means in Invictian mouths.
  • The Gate Fights are not riots. They are a calendar custom with an agreed end, and an outsider who calls the Vigiles to a Gate Fight, or joins one with a weapon, has broken a peace both halves were keeping.
  • A fine is not a man-price. Paying the state for a death is, to a Mavari, paying the wrong people and calling the matter closed; it is how the Skelding feud started and how most Mavari feuds start.

Daily Life in the Duneforged Citadel

A city of shifts, tiers and dust: the Duneforged day is told by a bronze giant on the wall and the bells of the blast-houses, and every family knows to the step how far it lives from the mountain's top and the mountain's bottom.

A day, hour by hour

The citadel tells time by Talos. Three times between dawn and dusk the bronze guardian walks the outer wall on a circuit it has never varied, and the city's day is divided into the first, second and third walks. The furnaces work round the clock in three shifts, and the shift bells of the Furnace Ring are the night's clock.

The poor: a quarrying family on the cut face. Merrin of the Fourth Shaft cuts stone in a family gang; his wife Ysolde keeps a terrace plot and works a half-shift sorting ore; her father, forty years a miner, coughs in the back room; their two sons are fourteen and eleven. They live in three rooms of terraced housing in the Quarrymen District, with a hoist rope running past the door.

  • Before dawn. The night shift comes up and the day shift goes down; Merrin and his elder son meet the gang at the sledway. Breakfast is a heel of furnace bread and a cup of thin beer.
  • First walk. Ysolde carries the family's water ration up from the Rockpools in two jars; the keepers mark her token. She works the terrace plot until the sun clears the ridge.
  • Morning. Her half-shift at the sorting floor below the Dune Mines' adits, where women and boys pick ore from spoil by hand. The younger boy is at the guild school until noon, because Ysolde has decided he will be a smith and not a miner.
  • Second walk. The gang eats underground: a miner's pasty, onion and goat in a crust thick enough to hold with filthy hands, the crust thrown to the shaft for luck.
  • Afternoon. The old man sits on the step and tells the neighbours which galleries hummed in his day. None did.
  • Third walk and dusk. The gang comes up grey from head to foot. The men go to the bath-houses at the Rockpools, which are cheap and hot, then to the Parched Ox to read the slate for work and grievances. Supper: chickpea and goat stew, terrace greens, the bread.
  • Night. Bed early. The furnace bells ring the shift change at midnight, and nobody in the Lower City hears them any more.

The rich: a Count's household on the Helm. Lady Benedetta Zayida, a cousin of the Count, keeps a household of thirty in a mansion cut into the topmost plateau of the Helm, under the Aegistower.

  • Dawn. A servant brings warm water piped from the Geomantic Forge's vents; the household prays at the shrine of Juno. Her steward reads her the Rockpools' levels and the ore assays, which in this house are read like the weather.
  • First walk. The Citadel Cathedral for an oath-swearing at the Temple of Juno: a cousin's marriage contract, witnessed and sealed, with a Mithril Reserve clerk present because the dowry is in ore-shares.
  • Second walk. A long meal with guests: Serathal trout, roast ibex from the crags, terrace fruit, wine brought up by caravan from the Imperium at four times its price.
  • Afternoon. The Ju Colliseum's House Ring, where nobles bet land and marriage pacts and the Zayida, as the house that hears fighters' petitions, are watched as closely as the fighters.
  • Evening. Dinner, then the Gilded Imperator Casino, where the Helm drops to the Middle City and dice have replaced the battle-roar. The talk this year is of the Great Martial Festival, the Mihran name on the register, and which families have quietly bought land in the Imperium.

Homes

Where you live is what you are, and it is measured vertically. The Lower City is terraced housing cut into the rock face, three or four rooms with stone shelves for furniture and a door onto a hoist path, cool in summer and dusty always. The Middle City is shopkeepers, smiths and stallholders living above their work in houses built against the wall-stone, with a shared roof-terrace for drying and gossip. The Upper City is mansions carved into the plateaus, with piped water, glazed windows of Mavelon glass and heat drawn from the geothermal vents. Dwarves of Clan Ironhand live where they please and prefer to live deep. Every house in the citadel has a cistern jar, a lamp-niche by the door and a water token on a nail.

Food and drink

The citadel cannot feed itself, and every meal admits it. Grain comes up by caravan; the terraces grow vegetables, fruit and fodder. The poor eat furnace bread, millet and barley loaves baked against the outer walls of the blast-houses on the furnaces' waste heat; miner's pasty; chickpea and goat stew; lentils, onions, terrace greens; and gallery mushrooms grown in worked-out shafts. The cheese is hard goat cheese from the Cloudspine pastures. Beer is brewed thin for work and thick for the Parched Ox, where the house beer is spiced with ridge thyme; Clan Ironhand brews a black stout it sells by the cask and will not explain. The rich eat trout from Lake Serathal, ibex, cedar-smoked mutton and imported wine, and display imported wheat bread at table because everyone knows what it cost to bring it up the mountain. Water is never wasted: a full cup left on a table is a rudeness.

Clothing and what it signals

Lower City people wear leather aprons, dust-cloths and heavy boots, and the dust gets into the creases of the skin and does not come out; "clean hands" is what the Lower City calls anyone above it, and it is not a compliment. Smiths wear their guild's mark burned into the apron and, on feast days, their best work. The Middle City dresses in Invictian style with a mountain cloak over it. The noble houses wear their colours and their metal: Caerthain the Duke's storm-grey, Vulkrim the smith's iron, Merca silver, Virellarion alchemical stains worn as proudly as embroidery. Bonded fighters of the Ju Colliseum carry the obsidian chain-mark on the wrist; a fighter who has won his five and been freed keeps the mark and adds a gold ring through it. Miners wear their shaft-name on a tin tag at the throat, so that the body can be named if it comes up.

Marriage, birth and coming of age

Birth. The child is registered at the Citadel Archives by name, house or shaft, and tier; a miner's child is given a lamp, unlit, which hangs by the door until the child goes down. Coming of age. In mining families it is the first descent, at fourteen, when the boy or girl goes down with the family gang and lights the lamp below; in smithing families it is the apprentice's first piece, judged by the guild; in the noble houses, presentation before the five altars of the cathedral at sixteen. Marriage. Sworn at the Temple of Juno, where oaths bind. Among the poor it is a gang matter: a marriage joins two gangs' claims, and gang-masters negotiate it. Among the nobles it is a banking matter, with dowries in ore-shares, forge rights or Reserve accounts, and a Mithril Reserve clerk at the altar. The Allotment of terrace plots every seventh year redistributes by household, and a rush of weddings before it is expected.

Funerals and the dead

The mountain keeps its own. Miners killed below are left where they fell if the gallery cannot be cleared; the gallery is sealed, the names cut on the seal, and their lamps are put out at the Parched Ox in front of the whole room. Those whose parties never signed back in at Drakkur's Expeditionary are read aloud each year at the Reading of the Open Lines, and the shop does no trade that day. The Lower City buries its dead in niches cut in the old quarry faces. The Furnace Ring families burn theirs in a blast-house at shift change, and a pinch of the ash goes into the next pour, so that the dead are in the iron. The nobles lie in the crypt of the Citadel Cathedral. The dead are believed to go into the mountain, to Vulcan's forge or to the Titans under it, and the hum in the lower shafts has made the Lower City think about that more than it would like.

Schooling and literacy

The guilds run schools for their apprentices from ten to fourteen, because a smith must read an order and an assay, and literacy among Duneforged artisans is higher than anywhere in the Imperium. Miners' children learn from the gangs, and many miners read shaft-marks and tally-sticks and nothing else.
