The noble houses hire tutors from Aeterna and the Arcane Academy, and the Virellarion train their own in the Crucible Spire. The Citadel Archives keep every registration, assay and contract since the Caerthain took the mountain, and the chancery Latinises every name it writes, which citizens resent when they see it.

Medicine and who heals

The commonest killer is the miners' cough, from dust, and the commonest treatment is to stop mining, which nobody can afford. The Lower City goes to bone-setters and wise-women and to the bath-house keepers, who know more about burns than most physicians. The Middle City buys from alchemists: the Virellarion's Molten Crucible sells potions to the Upper City and its apprentices sell cheaper ones, of variable honesty, to everyone else. A physician trained in the Imperium charges a denarius a visit. Willowheart bark comes up by caravan for fevers and is the most trusted medicine in the citadel. A healing potion costs fifty gold pieces, more than a miner earns in a season.

Crime and punishment

The Duke's officers keep the peace in the Middle and Upper City and the Adamantine Line under Commander Daud guards the walls, the Helm and the Duke. In the Lower City the real court is the back table at the Parched Ox, whose rulings have no force and are obeyed, because a man who ignores one does not get hired. Formal sentences are fines, bond-debt, the deep galleries, and for the worst crimes the death matches of the Ju Colliseum, where criminals and bond-debtors fight; five sanctioned wins earn a petition to House Zayida for pardon. Using the surname "Caesar" without the right is an offence. Since the hum began, the deep galleries have stopped being a sentence anyone can enforce, and the Lower City has noticed that the Duke has not found a replacement.

Entertainment and gambling

The Ju Colliseum above all: yield duels, chain fights, mass pits, and every five years the Great Martial Festival, which is this year. Commoners bet coin in the Circle of Bone, nobles bet land and marriages in the House Ring, and the Gilded Imperator Casino takes everyone's money between bouts. Below that: dice and knucklebones at the Parched Ox, arm-wrestling for drinks, betting on how many circuits Talos will walk before something interrupts him (it has never happened, and the odds are long), watching the Serathian Fleet's airships come in to their moorings, and the annual reading of the Rockpools' levels, which is attended like a play.

Work and wages

  • Deep-gallery miner: 2 denarii a day, the best wage in the citadel for the shortest life; quarryman, 1 denarius.
  • Ore-sorter (women and boys): 1 sestertius a half-shift.
  • Journeyman smith: 1 to 2 denarii a day; a master armourer of the Furnace Ring, 5 and up, and a commission price on every blade.
  • Rockpools keeper: 1 denarius a day and the most important lower-city friendship anyone can have.
  • Rent: three rooms on the cut face, 3 denarii a month; a Middle City house over a shop, 150 a year; a Marketplace stall, heritable, changes hands for 2,000 denarii and up.
  • A water token for a household's daily ration is issued free; extra water, bought from a keeper, costs an as a jar and more in a dry year.
  • All wages are reckoned in denarii, which the Mithril Reserve's counter in the Marketplace discounts like everyone else's.

Taboos and manners

Never whistle underground, and never put out another person's lamp, even by accident. Do not step into Talos's path on the wall, and do not touch him. Do not admire a blade in the Furnace Ring unless you mean to buy it, because admiring it is asking the price. Never waste water. Never claim a shaft-name you have not worked. At the Parched Ox, sit where the room puts you. A noble greets a smith with his title and a smith greets a noble with his trade, and nobody on the mountain bows lower than the waist.

Three things outsiders always get wrong

  • Duneforged is not an Invictian province. It is allied to the Imperium, not appointed by it; its lords are Duke, Marquis and Count in the common tongue, and calling the Duke "the Dux of Duneforged" to his face is a provincial insult.
  • The Lower City is not powerless. The Rockpools keepers hold the water for every tier, the Quarrymen supply every gang, and the Parched Ox decides who is hired; the Upper City knows it and the visitor does not.
  • The Ju Colliseum is a court as well as a show. Judgment champions settle lawsuits, bond-debtors fight their way free, and a fighter's fifth win is a legal petition; treating it as mere bloodsport insults the Sanctum of Hoplodamus and half the families in the stands.

Daily Life among the Road Peoples

Three peoples who belong to no empire and are needed by all of them: the Wheelwalkers who carry the goods, the Malaunian riders who are hired to guard them and to take them, and the marsh-folk of the Maeotis Helos who pay tribute to everyone and are ruled by no one. They share one conviction, that a roof is the beginning of being owned.

A day, hour by hour

The poor: a reed-cutter's family at Marshroot. Hild Wennasdaughter, her husband Corran, their two children and his father live on one platform of Marshroot Grove, a room of reed walls on piles above black water.

  • Before dawn. Corran checks the eel-traps from the platform edge while the mist is still down. Hild blows up the fire in its clay tray, never on the boards. Breakfast is reed-root cake and smoked eel.
  • Morning. The adults punt out to the cutting beds in the Reed-Cutters' Fen; reed is cut waist-deep with a hooked blade and bundled in fathoms. The grandfather and the children mend nets and watch for strangers, and a stranger in a boat is reported to the Pile-Elder before he has tied up.
  • Noon. Fish and bread eaten in the punt.
  • Afternoon. Bundles stacked on the drying platforms; a buyer's barge from the dry land takes them for roofing and matting. If a tax-collector came today, he is paid in reed, promptly, and the village makes sure he leaves before dark.
  • Evening. Pike or waterfowl stewed with marsh greens; the walkways fill with neighbours; songs about the channels and where they used to run.
  • Night. No lights burn late, because fire is the only thing a reed village fears more than soldiers.

The rich: a Wheelwalker convoy-master's family on the Treaty Road. Mehrnaz of the Wheels, a niece of Javid, the senior uncle of the Wheelwalkers, runs a convoy of nine painted wagons between Atarabad and Deiperduem with her husband, her brothers, their wives and children, and four road cousins.

  • Before dawn. The wagons are yoked by lantern; the youngest children sleep on through it on the bales. Mehrnaz reads the day's tolls aloud from memory: who charges what, where, and which of them is a cousin.
  • Morning. On the road. The convoy pays every toll without argument, including the Chyrsus Syndicate's, then tells the next Warden who charged it.
  • Noon. A halt at a post-station or a well; tea, flatbread and dried fruit; the children are taught sums on the toll-receipts.
  • Afternoon. The day's second stage. Her husband rides ahead to the evening's caravanserai to bargain for the yard.
  • Evening. The wagons are drawn into a ring in the caravanserai yard or on the Caravan Fields; the family eats together round one pot, the cousins from the other wagons come to trade news, and Mehrnaz writes nothing down. The convoy's books are in her head, which is why the Wheelwalkers are never robbed of their accounts.

On the steppe there is no rich and poor in the empires' sense, only more horses and fewer. A Malaunian band's day begins at first light with the herds driven to water, mare's milk drawn and set to ferment in a hide bag hung by the tent door, and the men and women of fighting age riding out to hunt, to scout or to visit the next band's tents. The heat of the day is spent in the shade of the felt; the evening is the meal, the stories and the arguments about which contract to take now that nobody is at war.

Homes

Wheelwalkers own no fixed property by custom: the painted wagon is the house, and a permanent house is the beginning of decline. Their headquarters in Atarabad is a courtyard full of carts, because it may not have a roof. Malaunians live in round felt tents on a lattice frame, packed onto two horses in an hour; the hearth is in the centre, the place of honour faces the door, and men sit on one side and women on the other. The marsh-folk live on reed-roofed platforms on piles; at Marshroot the whole village moves its walkways when the channels move, leaving the old piles standing, and at Willowheart the houses are built into and around one enormous willow, so that the tree is wall and shelter at once.

Food and drink

Wheelwalkers eat Acheaorian road food from one pot: cumin stew of mutton and chickpeas, flatbread baked on an iron sheet over the fire, dried apricots and mulberries, pistachios, and sweet tea all day. Malaunians live on milk and meat: kumis, fermented mare's milk, mildly drunk-making and drunk by everyone; qurut, balls of dried curd that keep for a year in a saddlebag; mutton boiled in its own broth; and on long rides, blood drawn from a horse's neck vein and drunk warm, which the riders do not discuss with outsiders. Bread is a luxury bought at the hiring fairs. The marsh-folk eat eels, pike, carp, ducks and duck eggs, reed-root cake made from flour pounded out of the rhizomes, smoked fish, marsh greens and wild rice, and brew a thin sour beer from the grain they take in trade for reed.

Clothing and what it signals

Wheelwalkers dress as well-off Acheaorians do, in trousers and a long coat, but in the colours of their convoy families, and every Wheelwalker wears a small bronze wheel on a cord; a road cousin's wheel is iron until his third journey. Malaunians, men and women, wear trousers, soft boots, a belted coat and a felt cap with long flaps; a rider's wealth is in gold plaques sewn on the coat and the horse's harness, and a great warrior is tattooed on the arms and shoulders with running beasts. Marsh-folk wear oiled leather and reed capes in the wet season and go barefoot on the walkways; a Willowheart midwife wears a willow-bark band on the wrist, and is sent for, and let through, by people who would stop anyone else.

Marriage, birth and coming of age

Wheelwalkers marry within allied families, and every marriage is a business merger negotiated by the aunts; an outsider joins only by marrying in or by being adopted as a road cousin after three journeys. A child is born in the wagon and given a wheel at its naming; at fourteen it drives its first stage alone. Malaunians put children on horseback at four. Coming of age is the first hunt, and for a fighter the first contract. At a wedding the bride races the groom on horseback and is expected to win; a groom who lets her win too obviously is mocked for a year. A bride-price is paid in horses. Marsh-folk marry within the marsh, after a summer of courting by punt; the couple build their own platform, and the village helps sink the piles in a day. Willowheart's Midwife-Warden keeps a register of every child the enclave has delivered across three empires, and some noble houses would pay a great deal to see it.

Funerals and the dead

Wheelwalkers take their dead to the nearest Silent Tower on the Qanat Line, as other Acheaorians do; beyond it, they lay the body on a high place, unburied. The dead person's wagon-wheel is taken off, and in the courtyard of carts at Atarabad the walls are hung with wheels, one for every Wheelwalker who died on the road. Malaunians raise mounds: a common rider under a low barrow with his bridle and bow, a great one under a kurgan with horses, servants' grave-goods and gold. A cup of mare's milk is left on the nearest slope by anyone who waters horses there. The dead ride on with their horses, and the grass over a mother's grave becomes the rider's grass-name. Marsh-folk lay their dead in a reed boat, weighted, and push it out into the Pale Shallows, where it sinks without a mark. The old people say the marsh is owed a debt, and that the dead pay some of it.

Schooling and literacy

Wheelwalker children learn sums, tolls, four languages and the family's routes before they learn letters, and most learn letters too, in three scripts, because a forged receipt is the commonest attack on a convoy. Malaunians do not write and regard a signature as a promise that outlives the man, which is exactly what they will not give: a contract is with a man, sworn on a grass-name, and the steppe keeps it in memory. Marsh-folk mostly cannot read; the tribute receipts nailed to Marshroot's meeting-house wall, from all three empires and two that no longer exist, are read by the Pile-Elder and by nobody else.

Medicine and who heals

The road peoples' medicine is Willowheart: its bark preparations for pain and fever are the best in the region, sold across three empires, and its recipe is sold to nobody. Its midwives are sent for from towns three days away. Wheelwalkers carry Willowheart bark, kohl, and a cousin who can set a bone; they buy the rest in the next bazaar. Malaunians treat wounds with hot iron and felt, sweat out fevers in a closed tent over hot stones and burning hemp, and trust their own horse-doctors over any physician; a rider who cannot ride is cared for by his band until he can, or until he chooses not to be.

Crime and punishment

Wheelwalkers have no crime against each other that cannot be settled by money and the aunts, because cheating a partner means cheating a relative; the one unforgivable act is to cheat a cousin's customer, and the punishment is that no cousin in any city will carry for you again. Malaunians settle killings in horses, and refuse to pay at the cost of a feud; the worst sentence is to be put out of the tents, which on the steppe is death delayed. Marsh-folk expel: taking unallotted bark at Willowheart is the one offence that gets a person sent away, and at Marshroot a thief loses his place on the platform. No empire's law reaches far into the Helos, because no column that enters it comes out where it meant to.

Entertainment and gambling

Malaunians race horses, shoot from the saddle at a gallop, wrestle, and play goat-grabbing, two teams on horseback fighting over a headless carcass across a mile of grass; they gamble on all of it with knucklebones, horses and next year's contracts. Wheelwalkers bet on everything that moves on the road, play nard in every caravanserai, and tell stories that are, on inspection, intelligence reports. Marsh-folk race punts, hold eel-catching contests and sing long songs about channels that have moved; at the Moving, when the village shifts a walkway in a day, everyone works and everyone drinks.

Work and wages

  • Wheelwalker carriage: about 1 gp per hundredweight per ten days on the Treaty Road; from Qa'zshahrv'in eastward, the far-cousin premium doubles it.
  • A road cousin on his first journey: keep, a share of a share, and an iron wheel; after three journeys, a full share.
  • Malaunian rider hired with his own three horses: 1 gp a day in the war, paid in silver; at the Hiring Fair at Saltford now, half that, and the silver is debased.
  • A guide across the Lion Grass: a gift of salt. Back again: no price will do.
  • A fathom-bundle of Marshroot reed at the buyer's barge: 2 cp; a roof's worth, 3 gp.
  • A Willowheart bark preparation: 5 sp a dose at the enclave, three times that in Ephelanum; a Willowheart midwife for a noble birth, 10 gp and her keep.

Taboos and manners

Wheelwalkers: never build a roof for a Wheelwalker or offer one a house; it is a curse. Never haggle with a cousin's cousin about a toll they have already paid. Malaunians: never step on the threshold of a tent, never pass between a rider and his horse, never refuse kumis, and never name a band in a treaty as if it were a family. Marsh-folk: never light a fire on bare boards, never bring a pale carved stone home from the nets, and never let a tax-collector stay the night.

Three things outsiders always get wrong

  • The Wheelwalkers are not vagrants. They are among the richest families on the Treaty Road and the best-informed; mistaking a convoy for tinkers costs a merchant his contacts in every city at once.
  • A Malaunian who rides against you is not a traitor. A contract is with a man, not a nation, and the rider who guarded your caravan last season and raids it this one has broken no promise he made (see Tomyra of the Lion Grass).
  • The marsh is not empty and not conquered. The Helos pays tribute to everyone and obeys no one; tribute is a courtesy the marsh extends, and armies that mistook it for submission are part of the reason the marsh owes nobody anything.

Expansion

The Gods of Asetheria

Many names, fewer gods

Titans first. Before the empires had gods, the world had the Aetherian Ancient Titans. They were put down rather than killed. Their temples still stand, in the Citadel Cathedral at Duneforged among other places, and under the Forum at Aeterna, where the Titan of Time's columns are mistaken for part of a basilica. Every imperial priesthood teaches that its gods won that war. None of them agrees on which gods did it.

Three empires, one sky. The Invictian, Hellenorian and Acheaorian pantheons are often the same powers under different names, and the priests know it. The codex already admits several pairs. The Forgeflame Artisans are Hellenorian smiths "working under Vulcan's Invictian name", and the Emberforge Collective is the mirror image, Invictian citizens sworn to Hephaestus. At Ephelanum the Treaty names one goddess twice, Artemis in the Hellenorian text and Diana in the Invictian, and gives her two birthdays. Invictians swear to Nike's Order of Morning's Rise and Asclepius's Radiant Heartwardens under their Hellenorian names. The thieves of Nyx and the druids of Terra keep chapters in both empires. Acheaoria's gods match less neatly. Its Magi say the western gods are its own gods, badly translated.

The Ascended came to the continent from beyond and took root among its peoples. Their temples cross every border, and no imperial college fully licenses them. Invicta lodges them outside the sacred line. Hellenoria's Tribunal neither recognises them nor bans them. The Magi call them guests who stayed too long.

The Dreaming Gods (Horthonel, Kaelrath, Saeronis, Tzarash, Urakh-Rynis, Vaedoris, Velkora) sleep at the edges of the world and reach it through dreams. They have few temples. Their faithful find them, which is why the Dreamers' Hunt for Vesperine Ilaro worries all three priesthoods. The Outer Gods come from beyond the world, and their attention is a catastrophe. They are not worshipped so much as served.

What a cleric receives. A state priest is a magistrate with an altar, and most priests cast nothing. Spells are the god's side of a private bargain. They go to whom the god chooses, not to whom the college ordains. Every college registers its clerics, because a man who can call fire without a licence is a political problem. A cleric of one god can usually serve that god's other names without losing a spell, though not without losing friends. No god has walked the waking world since the Greying six centuries ago: the grey fog walls every pantheon, Titan and Outer power out of the mortal plane, and what reaches a cleric is grace filtered through it, strongest at the altar, where the grey is thinnest.

The Invictian Pantheon

Thirty-eight gods kept by contract: the right rite on the right day, paid for by the state, whether or not anybody believes.

Invictian religion is a civic contract. The gods are honoured so that the state prospers. Rites are performed correctly whether or not anyone believes in them, and a god's temple is as much a public institution as a holy place: it owns land, takes deposits and sues. The College of Pontiffs keeps the register of licensed gods and the calendar of their days. The Rex Sacrorum at Romulo keeps the correct version of every rite and the first image of every god. The Imperator was always Pontifex Maximus, and the chair is empty. Since the Great Concord the old gods have been losing customers to veterans' cults, foreign guests and the Ascended. The priests blame the debased coin, and are not entirely wrong.

Jupiter the Stormlord, Optimus

Thunder, Authority · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: eagle over a thunderbolt · Holy day: the Ides of every month; the Feast of the Thunder in Iunius

King of the gods, lord of the sky and guarantor of every oath of command. Asetherian iconography shows him as a seated goliath with the thunderbolt across his knees. Jupiter does not love the Imperium; he keeps it, as a magistrate keeps a ledger. His rites are exacting and impersonal. Correct observance buys order, and nothing else is on offer.

Worship today. A Legate swears his command to Jupiter and leaves his first spoils with him, so the cult has had little income since the Concord and much attention. The gilded roof on the Arx has gone green because it is regilded only after a victory.

Temples. Jupiter Optimus on the Arx of Aeterna, the apse of the Pantheum (temples); Jupiter Lapis, a flint in the Atrium of the First Gods at Romulo (temples); the Capitolium and the Shrine of the Standards at Aepistra (temples).

Orders. The Stormlord Vanguard, his oath-keepers under arms, who swore to the Treaty on his steps and distrust what they swore.

Of a cleric or paladin. Never break a sworn word, and never let another's go unpunished. Serve the office, not the man in it. The Flamen Dialis may touch no iron and take no oath; his clerics carry both.

Hook. Lightning strikes the Arx on a clear day and splits the oath-stone. The Vanguard want it read as an omen against the Treaty, and they want a cleric to say so.

Juno the Protector of Bonds

Protection, Oaths · Lawful Good · Symbol: the scales of the Standard; a goose · Holy day: the Kalends of every month; the Matronalia on the Kalends of Martius

Queen of the gods and keeper of the sworn bond, in marriage, in contracts and in coin. Her iconography is a changeling, a face that alters with the oath sworn before it, which her priestesses read as a warning about how many faces a promise has. Her priests keep strict rules in the belief that right order is itself a kindness.

Worship today. Juno is the goddess of money now, because the Mint and the Standard sit inside her precincts. The quarterly Assay is held on her steps. When the figures are read, everyone in Aeterna learns how far the silver has fallen. Her cult is the most trusted in the Imperium and the most frightened.

Temples. Juno of the Warning on the Arx at Aeterna (temples); Juno of the Weights, mother of all her temples, over the master standards at Romulo (temples); a cella of the Capitolium at Aepistra (temples); the Temple of Juno in the Citadel Cathedral at Duneforged, where oaths are sworn at her font and the citadel's coin is assayed (temples); her seal on the Oath-Stone of the Keelhall at Mavelon (temples).

Orders. The Oathbound Sanctum, who witness and hold the continent's contracts and do not forget.

Of a cleric or paladin. Keep every oath and witness others' truthfully. Protect the bound party: the wife, the debtor, the hostage. Never weigh false.

Hook. A hairline crack has opened across Juno's seal on the Keelhall's Oath-Stone at Mavelon. The nine Mavari spear-ring marks on the other face are untouched. Both halves of the city want a priestess to say what that means before the Gate Fights do.

Minerva the Sage of Wisdom

Creative Arts and Crafts · Chaotic Evil · Symbol: an owl; a stylus · Holy day: the Quinquatria, five days from the 19th of Martius

Goddess of craft, skill and the made thing, third of the Capitoline triad, painted on every guild hall with her stylus. Her iconography is a kenku, the bird that can copy any voice but has none of its own. The state Minerva is respectable. The goddess is not. She is jealous of mastery, gives it at a price, and ruins rivals who are better than her chosen.

Worship today. Two cults share her name. The public one inspects apprentices, blesses tools at the Quinquatria and licenses enchanters. The hidden one is a scatter of artisans who have sold something for skill: their sight in one eye, their children's talent, a rival's hands. Its shrines are hunted, and the college says it does not exist.

Temples. A cella in every Capitolium, at Aepistra (temples) among them; the left hand of Jupiter in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples); the owl in the Atrium at Romulo (temples).

Orders. The Artisan's Forge of Wonders, which treats enchantment as a craft with a guild examination.

Of a cleric or paladin. Make something better than anyone has made it, and let no one take the credit. Never teach freely.

Hook. A Mavelon shipwright's apprentice has carved a figurehead that weeps. His master wants it burned. The Artisan's Forge wants to buy it. The boy wants to know what he promised in his sleep.

Vesta the Guardian of the Sacred Fire

Home, Warmth · Lawful Good · Symbol: a lamp; she has no image · Holy day: the Vestalia in early Iunius; the Vigiles' Night on the Kalends of December

Goddess of the hearth, public and private. The codex's iconography gives her a halfling's shape, but her temple has no statue, only a fire. She is the most conservative of the gods and the kindest. Her priests keep strict rules because a hearth that is neglected for one night goes out.

Worship today. Every Invictian house keeps her at its fire, and every city keeps a civic hearth lit from Romulo's. The six Vestals hold the wills of the rich, which makes the temple a bank and its virgins the most discreet notaries in the empire. On the Vigiles' Night every fire in Aeterna is put out and relit from Vesta's flame, carried by runners down the Via Sacra Aeterna.

Temples. The round Temple of Vesta on the Hearth at Romulo, under the Virgo Maxima Tarquitia Lucilla (temples); the lamp in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples); a civic hearth in every licensed city.

Orders. None under arms. The Vestals answer to the Rex Sacrorum and to nobody else.

Of a cleric or paladin. Keep the fire. Feed the guest at your hearth, whoever he is. Never strike fire with iron.

Hook. A dead senator's will deposited with the Vestals names a son nobody knew of. The Vestals must deliver it. The family would prefer they did not.

Janus the Gatekeeper

Transitions, Passages · True Neutral · Symbol: a two-faced head; a key and a staff · Holy day: the Agonium on the 9th of Ianuarius; the first words of every rite

God of doors, beginnings and the line between one state and the next. His iconography is a tiefling, two-horned and two-faced, looking out and in. Janus takes no side, holding that a door is neither friend nor enemy to those who pass. Every rite in the Imperium begins with his name.

Worship today. Every temple pays his priest a copper for the first sacrifice. His doors at Romulo stand open in war and are shut in peace. Whether they have been shut since the Concord depends on whom you ask. The Senate's calendar says yes, every Concordialia, "for the first time in twelve centuries". The Ianitor says nobody has dared. Travellers touch his milestone shrines; householders salt their thresholds at the turn of the year.

Temples. The Gate of Janus at Romulo, under the Ianitor Aulus Sempronius Atratinus (temples); a niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples); the Shrine of the Milestones at Anticata, where he faces the capital and the road at once (temples); the threshold shrine at the Gate of Mavelon.

Orders. The Gatekeepers of the Eternal Threshold, a secret society guarding arcane boundaries, who visit his priests unannounced.

Of a cleric or paladin. Begin nothing without asking whether it should be begun. Guard the threshold you are given. Never stand in a doorway to argue.

Hook. At Mavelon's Gate the threshold shrine's two faces have both turned south overnight. The Mavari say Janus has chosen a side.

Mars the Champion of Valor

Warfare, Glory · Lawful Evil · Symbol: a spear and the twelve shields · Holy day: the Kalends of Martius; the dances of the Salii in Martius and October

God of war and father of the Invictian people, second only to Jupiter. His iconography is a half-drow in the legion's crest. Mars is not cruel for its own sake; he is owed, and he collects. His worship is a hierarchy of obligation. He rewards those who serve his ends without question, and his priests are effective, feared and well organised.

Worship today. Mars is a god with nothing to do. His month opens the year and once opened the campaigning season. The Salii still dance his shields home every autumn and argue each spring over whether to dance them out. Discharged legionaries keep his altars in every Tent Row and pray for back pay in a war god's name.

Temples. The twelve shields in the Atrium of the First Gods at Romulo (temples); the outer half of the Pantheum at Aeterna, outside the sacred line (temples); an altar in every legionary fortress.

Orders. The Crimson Warlords, the Imperium's most decorated order, now a fraternity of unemployed veterans with excellent contacts.

Of a cleric or paladin. Win, and be seen to win. Pay your men before yourself. Leave no oath to Mars unpaid in blood, yours or another's.

Hook. A Crimson Warlord offers the party a commission: find a war. Any war, anywhere, that the Treaty does not cover.

Bellona the Warbringer

Warfare, Shadow Tactics · Lawful Evil · Symbol: a spear over a broken cup; a torch · Holy day: the Day of Blood, the 24th of Martius

Goddess of war as it is declared and waged: the ambush, the night march, the spear thrown into enemy ground. Her iconography is a hobgoblin in a black helm, and her priests are proud of it. Where Mars is glory, Bellona is method. She rewards obedience and punishes hesitation.

Worship today. Her temple stands outside the sacred line, where armed men may gather. Before it is the war column, over which the fetial throws a spear to declare war. No spear has been thrown in five years, and everyone in Aeterna knows exactly where the spear is kept. Her armed priests, the Bellonarii, cut their arms on the Day of Blood and offer what runs.

Temples. The Temple of Bellona and the War Column on the Campus Hastarum at Aeterna, under the Bellonarius Lucius Atilius Serranus (temples).

Orders. The Obsidian Phalanx, heavy infantry sworn to the war rather than the state, quartered beside her temple.

Of a cleric or paladin. Strike first and from the dark. Obey the chain of command above you, and own the one below. Never surrender a standard.

Hook. A Bellonarius dies in a tavern brawl with a fresh cut on his arm, though the Day of Blood is months away. Someone is making offerings out of season.

Neptune the Sovereign of the Deep

Oceans, Sovereignty · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a trident · Holy day: the Neptunalia, the 23rd of Quintilis (Iovianius)

God of the sea, of fresh water and of the ground beneath both. His iconography is a triton with a crown of barnacles. Neptune is not a kind god. He is owed correct observance, and his rites are propitiatory rather than grateful: a ship is blessed so that the god will leave it alone.

Worship today. No Invictian captain sails an unblessed keel, so Neptune's cult is rich wherever ships are built. Since the Peace the navy builds fewer warships and the merchants more, and the priests have quietly raised the blessing fee. At the Neptunalia sailors build shelters of branches on the shore and sleep out of reach of the tide.

Temples. The blue Temple of Neptune on the High Crescent forum at Mavelon, kept by the priest Aulus Vibius Nauta and guarded by Lucius Pontius Ancora, Master of the Tideguard, facing Vulcan's across the paving, and the first place in the south aisle of the Keelhall (temples); a niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples); the trident in the Atrium at Romulo, in the cupboard that was Hope's (temples); Neptune of the Fords at Aepistra (temples).

Orders. The Abyssal Tideguard, marines and salvors who hold the sole right to consecrate a hull.

Of a cleric or paladin. Give the sea its due before you take from it. Rule what is yours, and do not reach past the tide line for more. Bury no one at sea without rites.

Hook. A Qart-Hadeth trader at Mavelon refuses the Tideguard's blessing and sails anyway. Three days out the sea is glass, and nothing on board will move.

Vulcan the Artisan of Creation

Craftsmanship · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: hammer and tongs over an anvil · Holy day: the Volcanalia, the 23rd of Sextilis; the Quenching at Mavelon on the Kalends of December

God of fire and the forge, worshipped of old outside the walls for fear of his flame. His iconography is a warforged, a made thing that makes. His rites are exacting and impersonal. The god is owed correct observance, not affection, and he repays it with work that holds.

Worship today. Vulcan is the god of the iron economy. Mavelon's arsenal, Duneforged's forges and every smithy on the Via Ferraria keep his altar, and his priests stamp the proof marks on blades. At the Volcanalia small fish are thrown into the forge-fire in place of lives. Across the border, Hellenorian smiths pray to him under his Invictian name and dislike being asked why.

Temples. The Forge of Vulcan in the Citadel Cathedral at Duneforged, a working forge for an altar under High Smith-Priest Hadrian Voss, on which the Duke spends lavishly (temples); the Temple of Vulcan of the Arsenal at Mavelon, facing Neptune's, whose priests have not crossed the forum in a generation (temples); a niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples); the anvil in the Atrium at Romulo (temples).

Orders. The Forgeflame Artisans, Hellenorian smiths working under his Invictian name. Their mirror image is the Emberforge Collective, Invictian smiths sworn to Hephaestus.

Of a cleric or paladin. Make it sound. Never put your mark on poor work. Keep the fire outside the walls when you can, and away from the grain when you cannot.

Hook. Blades proof-marked at Mavelon are turning up in the hands of Thebesieas's hoplites. The priest who stamped them wants to confess, but only to someone who can protect him from the arsenal.

Mercury the Trickster of Trade

Commerce, Cunning · Lawful Good · Symbol: a winged staff and a purse · Holy day: the Mercuralia, the Ides of Maius

God of commerce, roads, messages and the clever word. The codex calls him a trickster and makes him Lawful Good, and both are true: Mercury loves a sharp bargain, kept to the letter. His iconography is a tabaxi, quick-footed and curious. His priests keep strict rules on weights and seals, because trade is a trust and a trick at once.

Worship today. Mercury is the god of the Peace. The Treaty Road, the Farshore cargoes at Romulo and the caravans at Aepistra have made his priests the richest in the Imperium after Juno's. At the Mercuralia merchants sprinkle their goods with water from his well to wash away the year's lies. Couriers touch his foot before they ride.

Temples. Mercury of the Square at Romulo, which lodges licensed Farshore gods as guests (temples); Mercury of the Terminus and the Guest-Fire at Aepistra (temples); the Vault of Mercury in the Citadel Cathedral at Duneforged, where every Dominus Argentar swears his oath (temples); the south aisle of the Keelhall at Mavelon (temples); the Shrine of the Milestones at Anticata (temples); a niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples); Mercury of the Fields among the toll-booths at Deiperduem (temples); a rented niche in the Court of Guests at Atarabad (temples).

Orders. The Caravan of the Gilded Horizon, his own long-haul company on the Treaty Road.

Of a cleric or paladin. Keep the letter of every bargain and use every advantage it allows. Carry the message, whatever it says. Never cheat a guest.

Hook. A Gilded Horizon wagon reaches Deiperduem with its seals intact and its cargo turned to river stones. The factor swears by Mercury that no one opened it.

Ceres the Harvest Mother

Agriculture, Prosperity · Neutral Good · Symbol: a wheat-ear and a torch · Holy day: the Cerealia, the 12th to 19th of Aprilis

Goddess of grain, fertile land and the commons. Her iconography is simply a human woman with flour on her hands, and the plebs like that. Her faithful are expected to help where they can and are given wide latitude in how.

Worship today. Ceres is the goddess of the Annona, and the Annona is failing. Every citizen's dole token is checked in her portico, so her temple is where the queue forms and where riots start. Grain now buys more than silver, and the tithe her temple takes in kind has made it rich while the hill goes hungry. At the Cerealia foxes run through the Circus with torches tied to their tails.

Temples. The Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Mons Cerealis at Aeterna, under Plautia Rufina (temples); Ceres of the Estates outside the south gate of Aepistra (temples); Ceres of the Annona in the Temple of Portunus at Fucostia, who receives the First Hull's first sack (temples); Diana and Ceres of the Camp outside the garrison at Ephelanum (temples); the red-bound sheaf in the Atrium at Romulo (temples).

Orders. The Golden Harvest Covenant, the farmers' guild that supplies the dole and can therefore starve the capital.

Of a cleric or paladin. Feed the hungry before the rich. Count the grain honestly. Leave the gleanings in the field.

Hook. A Covenant granary at Fucostia is full by the ledger and empty by the lamp. The priestess who reported it has been transferred to a hill shrine with no road.

Diana the Guardian of the Grove

Hunting, Adventure · Chaotic Good · Symbol: a crescent and a bow · Holy day: the Ides of Sextilis, the Torchlight

Goddess of the hunt, the woodland, the boundary and the moon, worshipped in groves rather than buildings. Her iconography is a firbolg, huge and gentle until it is not. Her worship is warm and unruly: the faithful honour her by acting on generous impulse rather than by keeping a rite.

Worship today. Diana is the goddess of the frontier and of women. At the Torchlight the crater lake of Nemibano is ringed with torches and walked by women; the warden of the grove does not attend. She is also a treaty question. At Ephelanum the Invictian text names the city's goddess Diana and the Hellenorian text names her Artemis, and each side's procession is a claim.

Temples. The roofless Grove of Diana at Nemibano, held by the Rex Nemorensis Gnaeus Ferrus, its rites led by Sylvia Nemorina (temples); Diana and Ceres of the Camp, the garrison's temple at Ephelanum (temples); Diana Equestris, the White Mare, at Aepistra (temples); a niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples).

Orders. The Verdant Sentinel Order, wardens of the sacred groves and boundaries, who walk Romulo's sacred line each Februarius.

Of a cleric or paladin. Protect the grove, the boundary and the woman in childbed. Hunt cleanly and only what you need. Go where the map stops.

Hook. The Invictian Dux of Ephelanum means to carry Diana's image through the sanctuary on the Ides, past the Hellenorian guards. He wants a cleric of Diana walking in front.

Venus the Goddess of Beauty

Beauty, Light of Love · Chaotic Good · Symbol: a dove on a myrtle branch · Holy day: the Veneralia, the Kalends of Aprilis

Goddess of love, beauty and the luck that comes with them, and by old legend mother of the Invictian people. Her iconography is a tiefling with a gilded tail, which Hellenorians find funny and Invictians do not. Her worship is warm and unruly. The faithful honour her by acting on generous impulse.

Worship today. At the Veneralia women of every rank bathe her images and then bathe together in the men's baths, by ancient right, with myrtle in their hair. Patrician families claim descent from her son and spend the day proving it. Since the Lechaion Marriage, Aeterna's matrons have taken to visiting Corinth's goddess of love under her other name.

Temples. A niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna, between Janus and the empty niche (temples); Venus of the Harbour in the Keelhall at Mavelon, whom sailors' wives pray to (temples); the white Temple of Venus of the Bay at Napplesia, where retired officers' widows remarry (temples); honoured beside Aphrodite of the Rock at Corinth (temples).

Orders. None of her own in the codex. The Hellenorian Ivory Chorus sings for her under Aphrodite's name.

Of a cleric or paladin. Make beauty where there is none and protect it where there is. Never force love. Never mock an honest lover.

Hook. Calpurnia Secunda writes to her mother from Corinth asking for a statuette of Venus from the Pantheum's own workshop. The letter is in cipher, and the cipher is not House Calpurnia's.

Concordia the Unifier

Unity, Peacekeeping · Lawful Good · Symbol: two clasped right hands · Holy day: the Concordialia, the Kalends of September

Goddess not of peace but of agreement, which the Imperium learned to tell apart in its own civil wars. Her temple was raised to mark a reconciliation, not a victory. Her iconography is a half-elf, a figure of two peoples. Her priests keep strict rules in the belief that right order is itself a kindness.

Worship today. The Dominus Militum decreed the Concordialia in Year 1, and Concordia has never been so fashionable or so hollow. On the Kalends of September every city sacrifices to her for the Great Concord. In the same week the Legates who praised her hire mediators to divide provinces they cannot be seen to discuss.

Temples. No great temple of her own is entered in the register this century, and her altar is raised in every forum at the Concordialia. At Deiperduem, where the Treaty forbids temples, she has a room in the House of Three Doors and a waist-high altar against the Treaty Hall, licensed as "a fixture", on which the three envoys lay olive each year (temples).

Orders. The Accord of Infinite Wisdom, arbitrators who record and never enforce; the Order of the Silver Flame, knights who intervene between factions and are resented by all of them.

Of a cleric or paladin. Stand between, not beside. Seek the agreement both sides can keep, not the one that is right. Never draw first in a parley.

Hook. Two Legates ask the Accord to witness a private boundary between their provinces. The line runs through a village whose people were not invited.

Victoria the Goddess of Triumph

Victory, Honour · Chaotic Good · Symbol: wings, a palm branch and a laurel wreath · Holy day: the Kalends of Sextilis; the day of any Triumph

Goddess of victory, whose altar once stood in the Senate house. Her iconography is a leonin with spread wings. She is the generous half of war: honour to the winner, mercy to the beaten, and the wreath for whoever earned it. Her worship is warm and unruly.

Worship today. A goddess of triumph in an empire forbidden to win anything. The Treaty makes a Triumph impossible, and none has been awarded in five years; three Legates have been refused. Her priests curate the old trophies, polish the chariots and wait. The Ludi Aeterna are held in her name, and the crowd is understood to be voting.

Temples. No temple of hers is entered in the codex. Her winged statue stands over the Senate's altar at Aeterna, and her trophies are kept for the next Triumph.

Orders. The Triumphant Vanguard of Glory, keepers of the Triumph, now curating parades for a war that ended in a treaty.

Of a cleric or paladin. Win honestly or not at all. Spare the beaten who yield. Give the wreath to the soldier who earned it, not the general who paid for it.

Hook. The Vanguard has found a loophole: a Triumph may be awarded for a victory over a non-signatory. A Legate is shopping for a non-signatory to defeat.

Phoebus the Illuminator

Light, Heavenly Knowledge · Neutral Evil · Symbol: a bronze mirror catching the sun · Holy day: the Ludi Phoebei, the 6th to 13th of Quintilis (Iovianius)

"The bright one": the sun as the eye that sees everything and tells whoever pays. Hellenorians know him as Apollo's radiant face; Invicta kept the light and dropped the healing. His iconography is a sun elf, beautiful and faintly bored. His worship is quiet and self-serving. The faithful bargain for advantage and rarely say what they paid.

Worship today. Phoebus is the scholars' god and the spies'. Mages who want their work legible pray to him; so do men who want a rival's secrets brought into the light. His games in high summer are the most expensive in the calendar after the Ludi Aeterna, and the cheapest to attend.

Temples. None of his own is entered in the register; he is honoured at the Ludi and in the collegia's chapels. The sun-priests of Helionyx say the Invictians pray to half a god.

Orders. The Luminous Arcanists, who make magic legible; the Sable Codes Circle, who make forbidden magic legible to themselves.

Of a cleric or paladin. Bring hidden things into the light, and choose who sees them. Never leave a debt of knowledge unpaid. Never look away.

Hook. A Luminous Arcanist offers the party a lens that shows any written lie glowing red. She wants it tested on the Assay ledgers first.

Pluto the Lord of the Hidden, "the Host"

Underworld, Forbidden Knowledge · Lawful Evil · Symbol: a key; a cake of spelt and salt · Holy day: the three nights the Mundus opens, 24 Sextilis, 5 October and 8 November

Lord of the underworld and of the riches buried in the earth: silver, the dead and the things the dead knew. His iconography is a tiefling in a dark crown. His worship is a hierarchy of obligation; he rewards those who serve his ends without question, and his priests are feared and well organised.

Worship today. Pluto's name is not on the college's register, and his worship inside a sacred line is unlicensed. Miners on the Via Ferraria pray to him anyway before they go down. In Aeterna his devotees call him only "the Host" and leave a cake of salt and spelt on a capped shaft on the three nights the dead were once allowed up.

Temples. The Mundus in the Horti at Aeterna, a hidden shrine over the paupers' pits (temples); miners' altars in the mountain workings of Duneforged.

Orders. The Shadowhand Collective, infiltrators who trade in secrets more than gold.

Of a cleric or paladin. Keep what is buried buried until it is owed. Collect every debt. Speak to the dead with respect; they keep accounts.

Hook. A silver vein at Duneforged opens into a chamber of old coins stamped with no empire's head. The miners will not touch them until a priest of the Host says whose they are.

Fortuna the Wheel of Fate

Luck, Fortune's Change · Neutral Good · Symbol: a wheel and a horn of plenty · Holy day: Fors Fortuna, the 24th of Iunius

Goddess of luck, turning her wheel and pouring from her horn. Her iconography is a wood elf with a blindfold pushed up on her brow, as if she had just taken a look. She is kinder than her reputation. Her faithful are expected to help where they can, because the wheel turns and everyone is on it.

Worship today. Every soldier, gambler and grain-factor in the Imperium carries her token. At Fors Fortuna the poor row down the Tiberius to her old riverside shrines and come back drunk, garlanded and broke. Since the coin began to fall, the city has preferred to pray to luck than to Juno.

Temples. No temple of hers is in the codex. Her riverside shrines below Aeterna on the road to Fucostia are unregistered and very busy.

Orders. None of her own. Every dice-house claims her.

Of a cleric or paladin. Share good luck; it is on loan. Help the man the wheel has crushed. Never curse a bad throw out loud.

Hook. At the Gilded Imperator Casino in Duneforged a dealer has won forty times in a row. He says Fortuna is paying a debt. The house wants to know whose.

Faunus the Keeper of the Plains

Wildlife, Serenity · True Neutral · Symbol: a horned mask · Holy day: the Lupercalia, the 15th of Februarius

The horned god of the countryside, the flocks and the open plain. His iconography is a tabaxi resting in long grass. Faunus is serene, not gentle; his priests take no side, holding that the plain must stay in balance whoever profits. He speaks in the wind through grass, and shepherds still sleep on fleeces to hear him.

Worship today. Faunus belongs to the Latium Plains and the herdsmen, and the plains are being parcelled out to veterans who were promised land. At the Lupercalia young men run the old wall of Romulo in goatskins, striking women with thongs for fertility, while the college tries to look elsewhere.

Temples. The horned mask in the Atrium of the First Gods at Romulo (temples); field shrines across the plains, a stone and a pair of horns.

Orders. The Silent Stalkers of the Glade, Invictian woodsmen who take game, guide armies and read a forest better than any map office.

Of a cleric or paladin. Keep the herd whole and the plain open. Take no more than the land will give back. Listen before you speak.

Hook. Surveyors marking veterans' allotments on the Latium Plains keep finding their stakes pulled and laid in a circle around a single horned stone.

Pomona the Guardian of the Orchard

Fruits, Harvest · Neutral Good · Symbol: a basket and a pruning knife · Holy day: the Picking, the first day of the apple harvest in September

Goddess of fruit trees, gardens and the patient work of grafting. Her iconography is a halfling with a pruning knife. She is a homely goddess and a stubborn one: she wants the work done properly and the trees outlasting the gardener. Her faithful are expected to help where they can.

Worship today. Pomona is honoured in every walled garden and every orchard on the hills around Aeterna. Her cult has a flamen of its own, the least important flamen in the college and the only one who brings fruit to its meetings. Orchardists hang their first apple on her branch at the Picking and sell the rest at prices the grain guilds envy.

Temples. The basket in the Atrium of the First Gods at Romulo (temples); the orchard-altars of Falecosa and Nemibano.

Orders. The Harvestwrights' Guild, smaller, richer and more particular than the grain guilds; the College of the Starlit Lute, bards who keep the Imperium's memory of its countryside.

Of a cleric or paladin. Plant what you will not live to eat. Graft, mend and prune; never fell a fruiting tree. Share the windfall.

Hook. A Harvestwright orchard near Falecosa bears silver-skinned fruit overnight. The Starlit Lute has a song about that, and it does not end well for the owner.

Flora the Blooming Spirit

Flowers, Renewal · Neutral Good · Symbol: a wreath of spring flowers · Holy day: the Floralia, the 28th of Aprilis to the 3rd of Maius

Goddess of flowers and the spring, of everything that blooms before it bears. Her iconography is a dhampir crowned with roses, life and pallor together, which her priests explain as the bloom that lasts a week. Her faithful are expected to help where they can.

Worship today. The Floralia is the most riotous festival in the Imperium. There are games, actresses, hares and goats loosed in the Circus, beans thrown to the crowd, and coloured clothes instead of white. The college disapproves of it every year in writing. The Legates fund it every year in coin, because the plebs remember who paid for the flowers.

Temples. No temple of hers is entered in the codex. She is honoured at the Floralia games in Aeterna and in the rose-gardens of the Horti.

Orders. The Everbloom Circle, a magical society of growth and grafting whose work takes a decade to show.

Of a cleric or paladin. Make the world bloom, briefly and often. Celebrate what will not last. Never cut flowers for a funeral you caused.

Hook. The roses of the Horti bloomed in midwinter over the Mundus. The Everbloom Circle wants samples, and the gardeners want no one digging.

Proserpina the Goddess of Fertility

Fertility, Rebirth · Neutral Good · Symbol: a pomegranate split open · Holy day: the Return at the spring equinox; the Descent at the autumn equinox

Daughter of Ceres, carried down to the underworld, whose return each spring brings rebirth. Her iconography is a wood elf with dark earth on her feet. She is the goddess of the seed in the ground, which is to say of hope and burial at once. Her faithful are expected to help where they can.

Worship today. Proserpina's cult does the Imperium's funerals for the poor and its seasonal mysteries for everyone. Her order holds the burial contracts of half the plebs, paid a copper a month for life. Since the debasement those coppers buy less burial every year, and the order has not said what happens when the contract runs short.

Temples. She shares her mother's temple on the Mons Cerealis at Aeterna as Libera (temples), and keeps chapels in the cemeteries along every Invictian road. At Deiperduem she is the other unnamed god of the Three Stones on the Quiet Ground, where her Cycle and Senectus's Watchers keep the war dead of three empires (temples).

Orders. The Cycle of the Eternal Bloom, funerary rites, seasonal mysteries and the burial contracts of the poor.

Of a cleric or paladin. Bury the dead properly, whoever they were. Plant after every burial. Return what was taken, in its season.

Hook. A Cycle undertaker asks the party to recover a contract-holder's body from a Legate's private cemetery, where it was buried without rites to hide how he died.

Cybele the Earthen Mother

Flora, Wilderness · True Neutral · Symbol: a mural crown and two lions · Holy day: the Megalesia, the 4th to 10th of Aprilis

The Great Mother of the mountains and wild places, brought into the Imperium in a desperate war to save it. Her iconography is a half-eladrin, an elf of the turning seasons. Her priests take no side, holding that the wild must stay in balance whoever profits.

Worship today. Cybele is a foreign goddess who was naturalised and never quite trusted. Her eunuch priests dance with cymbals in the streets at the Megalesia and are forbidden to be citizens. Her image is a black stone carried in procession. Mountain folk of the Klynin range pray to her where they will not pray to Jupiter.

Temples. No licensed temple. Her black stone is kept at Aeterna, and her hill shrines line the Aqua Aeterna up into the Klynin Mountain Range. Above the lake at Nemibano an ivy-choked cave holds her older shrine, from before Diana came; Sylvia Nemorina keeps it clear (temples).

Orders. None in the codex sworn to her alone. Druids of the Tranquil Hand Enclave honour her beside Terra.

Of a cleric or paladin. Defend the mountain and the forest against the plough and the axe. Protect the city that keeps your shrine. Leave the wild a share of everything.

Hook. The aqueduct engineers want to cut a new channel through one of Cybele's hill shrines. Her galli have chained themselves to the stones.

Bacchus the Bountiful Spirit

Revelry · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a thyrsus and a two-handled cup · Holy day: the Liberalia, the 17th of Martius; the Treading at Falecosa

God of wine, freedom and revelry, the Invictian face of Dionysus. His iconography is a satyr with a wine-skin. He is unpredictable, and so are his faithful; he is honoured by being given room rather than by being obeyed.

Worship today. The Senate banned his night rites centuries ago and has been banning them since. The public cult is a vintner's god of pressing-floors and good years, honoured at Falecosa's Treading and every harvest supper. The private cult meets masked, after dark, and the Speculatores keep a file on it that grows every year of the Peace.

Temples. The Temple of Liber Pater by the consecrated presses of Falecosa, a station on the pilgrims' Iter Sacrum (temples); Liber in the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera at Aeterna (temples).

Orders. The Masque of Eternal Revelry, a secret society of ecstatic rites and elaborate masks.

Of a cleric or paladin. Free what is bound, including yourself. Share the cup. Never refuse a guest at a feast or a stranger in a mask.

Hook. A Masque invitation arrives for one of the party, sealed with a vine leaf and addressed to a name they have never told anyone.

Cupid the Heart's Arrow

Love, Emotional Healing · Chaotic Good · Symbol: an arrow with a heart-shaped head · Holy day: the eve of the Veneralia, the last day of Martius

Son of Venus, god of desire, whose arrows wound gods and mortals alike. His iconography is a half wood elf with a quiver. The codex gives him two faces: love that strikes, and the healing of a broken heart. His worship is warm and unruly.

Worship today. Cupid is a household god of lovers and widows. Girls leave arrows at his shrines before they marry, and the bereaved break one afterwards. Veterans' wives who waited fifteen years for husbands who came home strangers have made him popular again in the Tent Rows.

Temples. No temple of his is in the codex. He is honoured beside his mother in her niche in the Pantheum at Aeterna (temples) and at every wedding.

Orders. The Thorned Eye Cabal, assassins who strike with deadly beauty, whose victims rarely understand why the blade was drawn.

Of a cleric or paladin. Heal the heart that can be healed. End the love that poisons. Never strike from jealousy.

Hook. A widow hires the party to find who sent her a Thorned Eye arrow, a silver one, which by the cabal's custom means a killing has been bought out of love.

Caelus the Celestial Scholar

Astronomy, Celestial Knowledge · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a wheel of seven stars · Holy day: the solstices, and the Reading of the Arc on the Kalends of December

The sky itself, the oldest father, older than the gods who live beneath it. His iconography is an air genasi, a figure of wind and star. His rites are exacting and impersonal; he is owed correct observance and gives order in return, the order of the seasons and the stars.

Worship today. Caelus has no festival crowds. He has calendars, eclipse tables and the omens the Imperium's generals refuse to admit they buy. His astromancers now attend the Reading of the Arc at Helionyx openly, the first Invictian priests to sit in a Hellenorian temple by invitation since the war.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. His observatories sit on the roofs of the collegia at Aeterna, and his priests travel to Helionyx each winter.

Orders. The Celestial Astromancers, sky-watchers who sell calendars, eclipse warnings and omens.

Of a cleric or paladin. Observe, record and predict. Never alter a table to please a patron. Keep the calendar true.

Hook. The Astromancers have predicted an eclipse on the next Dies Sandarionis. They have been offered a great deal to predict it on a different day.

Aurora the First Light

Dawn, New Beginnings · Neutral Good · Symbol: a rose-coloured torch · Holy day: every dawn; the Matralia on the 11th of Iunius

Goddess of the dawn, who renews herself every morning. Her iconography is an aasimar with a torch. She is the patron of second chances, new ventures and the shift that starts before sunrise. Her faithful are expected to help where they can.

Worship today. Bakers, watchmen and apothecaries keep her small altars and greet her at first light. Since the Concord, discharged legionaries starting again on unpaid land have adopted her, and "Aurora's coin", a copper left at a crossroads at dawn, has become their prayer for a fresh start.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. She is honoured at dawn altars on the eastern gates of every Invictian city and in the dispensaries of her apothecaries.

Orders. The Dawnfire Alchemists, apothecaries of dawn-gathered preparations and the Imperium's best burn treatments.

Of a cleric or paladin. Give everyone a second chance and some a third. Begin each day's work before the sun. Never despair at night.

Hook. The Dawnfire Alchemists need dew gathered from the war column at Aeterna at first light on the Day of Blood. The Bellonarii do not let anyone near it.

Veritas the Keeper of Truth

Truth, Illumination · Lawful Good · Symbol: a well with a mirror at the bottom · Holy day: the four Assay days, the Kalends of Martius, Iunius, September and December

Truth personified, said to hide at the bottom of a sacred well. Her iconography is a plain human woman holding a mirror. Her priests keep strict rules and expect the faithful to keep them too, in the belief that an accurate account is itself a kindness.

Worship today. Veritas was a philosophers' goddess, invoked in lecture halls and law courts and otherwise ignored. Then her circle began investigating the coinage. Now her followers stand outside Juno's temple at every Assay with wax tablets, recording the figures and the faces of the men who read them. It has made her popular with the plebs and dangerous to know.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. Her well-shrine stands in the law courts of Aeterna, and her circle meets in a borrowed portico.

Orders. The Seekers of Eternal Truth, philosophers who investigate claims and publish their findings, and have petitioned to watch the Assay from inside the strongroom.

Of a cleric or paladin. Tell the truth, all of it, to whoever asks in good faith. Publish what you find. Never lie, not even to an enemy; say nothing instead.

Hook. A Seeker hands the party a wax tablet as she is arrested. It holds four columns of figures and a single word: "Mavelon".

Nemesis the Goddess of Retribution

Vengeance, Balance · True Neutral · Symbol: a measuring rod and a bridle · Holy day: none fixed; the day after any Triumph

Goddess of retribution, who brings down those who rise beyond their due. Hellenorians honour her under the same name. Her iconography is a tiefling with a measuring rod. She takes no side; her priests hold that the scales must balance whoever profits, and that excess is a crime whether or not it breaks a law.

Worship today. Gladiators pray to her before they fight, and her shrine stands at the gate of every arena. In a Triumph, a slave once rode behind the general whispering her warning. With no Triumphs, her priests have turned to the Legates who behave as if they had won one, and they are keeping lists.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. Her shrines stand at the arena gates, the Ju Colliseum at Duneforged among them, where Marcia Ferox touches the rod before every bout.

Orders. The Scales of Eternal Justice, who pursue not crime but excess, usually against people who have broken no law at all.

Of a cleric or paladin. Bring down the proud and the swollen. Measure before you strike. Never take more vengeance than was owed, or you become the next target.

Hook. The Scales have named their next target: a beloved patron of the party, guilty of nothing but too much good fortune.

Trivia the Keeper of Secrets

Sorcery, Forbidden Knowledge · Chaotic Evil · Symbol: a three-faced torch at a crossroads · Holy day: the last night of each month, at the dark of the moon

"Of the three ways": goddess of crossroads, sorcery and the night, the Invictian name for what Hellenorians call Hecate. Her iconography is a yuan-ti, a serpent with a woman's face. Her worship is dangerous to the faithful and everyone near them. Most of her shrines are hidden and her cults are hunted.

Worship today. Unlicensed casting is a crime in the Imperium, so Trivia is the patron of every hedge-witch, sorcerer and wise woman the collegia will not admit. Suppers are left at crossroads on the dark of the moon, and the poor eat them before dawn, which the goddess is said not to mind.

Temples. None licensed. A hidden crossroads shrine lies under the Vault Streets of Romulo, where three archive tunnels meet (temples).

Orders. The Arcane Veil of Mysteries, a cloaked society of spellcasters who speak in riddles and act through proxies.

Of a cleric or paladin. Learn what is forbidden. Keep three secrets for every one you tell. Never refuse a traveller at a crossroads.

Hook. A Speculator offers the party their own licences, free, in exchange for the location of a crossroads shrine. He already knows one of them has prayed there.

Spes the Embodiment of Aspiration

Hope, Inspiration · Neutral Good · Symbol: a flower held up in the right hand · Holy day: the Kalends of Sextilis

Goddess of hope, honoured in times of crisis, shown holding a flower before her. Her iconography is a human girl lifting her skirt to step forward. Her faithful are expected to help where they can and are given wide latitude in how.

Worship today. Romulo keeps the copy that counts of everything except Hope. Her temple burned in a siege three centuries ago and was never rebuilt, and her cupboard in the Atrium was given to Neptune. Her cult survives in the Tent Rows and the dole queues, where people pin paper flowers to their tunics at the Kalends of Sextilis. Nobody organises it. Every year there are more flowers.

Temples. The forgotten temple of Spes under the caravan yard at Romulo (temples); no licensed temple anywhere.

Orders. None in the codex.

Of a cleric or paladin. Give hope where there is none, and make it honest. Begin the work even if you will not finish it. Never sell a false hope.

Hook. A petition to rebuild the temple of Spes is circulating in the Tent Rows. It has forty thousand marks on it. Somebody important wants to know who started it.

Senectus the Patron of Rest

Rest, Peaceful Death · True Neutral · Symbol: a staff and a lamp burnt low · Holy day: Dies Parentales in Februarius; the Discharge at Napplesia in October

Old age personified, the gentle end of a long life. His iconography is an old human with a staff. He takes no side, holding that every life deserves its end and that the end should be paid for. He is the god of the pension as much as of the deathbed.

Worship today. Senectus was a minor god until the legions came home. Millions of veterans were promised pensions the state cannot pay, and his circle administers them. At the Discharge each autumn the year's retired officers are welcomed at Napplesia by those already settled, and the crowd grows larger every year of the Peace.

Temples. No temple of his own. His altar stands in the pension offices and at the Discharge at Napplesia, and he is one of the two unnamed gods of the Three Stones on the Quiet Ground at Deiperduem, kept by his Watchers with the Cycle (temples).

Orders. The Watchers of the Eternal Rest, who administer the pensions and are the reason the veteran arrears are documented.

Of a cleric or paladin. Honour the old. See that what was promised is paid. Sit with the dying; never hurry them.

Hook. A Watcher clerk has found that ten thousand pensions are being paid to dead men. The money is still being collected. He wants witnesses before he takes the ledger to the Senate.

Somnus the Patron of Reflection

Sleep, Dreams · True Neutral · Symbol: a poppy and a horn of sleep · Holy day: the longest night, at the winter solstice

God of sleep, who lives in a cave where no light comes and the river of forgetting flows. His iconography is a high elf with closed eyes. He takes no side. His priests hold that sleep must come to everyone, guilty and innocent, and that dreams are reflection, not prophecy.

Worship today. Physicians, insomniacs and the grieving pray to him. Poppy-sellers keep his image. Since the Dreamers' Hunt began, his small cult has been watched closely by the Speculatores, who cannot tell a priest of sleep from a dream-walker and are not inclined to learn.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. His sleeping-houses, where the sick sleep beside his image, stand by the baths of Napplesia.

Orders. None in the codex.

Of a cleric or paladin. Bring rest to the restless. Guard the sleeper. Never enter another's dream uninvited.

Hook. Patients in a Napplesia sleeping-house all dream the same island, and wake with salt on their lips.

Juventus the Spirit of Vitality

Youth, Endurance · Chaotic Good · Symbol: the boy's amulet laid aside · Holy day: the Day of the Toga at the Liberalia, the 17th of Martius (shared uneasily with Bacchus)

Goddess of youth, especially of young men coming of age to bear arms. The codex writes her name Juventus; older inscriptions say Juventas. Her iconography is an aasimar runner. Her worship is warm and unruly.

Worship today. Every Invictian boy puts on the man's toga before her and drops a coin in her chest, which once paid for his first kit. There are no recruits now. Juventus is becoming the goddess of a generation with nothing to do, and the young men who pray to her pray for something to happen.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. Her shrine has a chapel on the Arx at Aeterna, inside the Temple of Jupiter, by an old ruling that youth must not leave the city's god (temples).

Orders. None in the codex.

Of a cleric or paladin. Run, climb, try. Protect the young from the old men's wars and the old men's peace. Never grow tired of starting.

Hook. Young men in Aeterna's Insulae have formed running clubs under Juventus's name. They train at night with wooden swords, and someone is paying for the swords.

Vis the Goddess of Strength

Strength, Resilience · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a clenched fist lifting a stone · Holy day: the Lifting, at the Great Martial Festival every fifth year

Force and strength personified, the power behind every deed. Her iconography is a dragonborn bearing a boulder. Her rites are exacting and impersonal; she is owed correct observance and gives order in return, the order of the stronger.

Worship today. Vis is a soldier's goddess without a state's. Labourers, porters, wrestlers and mercenaries keep her stone. At the Great Martial Festival at Duneforged, this fifth year of the Peace, the Lifting opens the games: a stone of her weight raised by any who can.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. Her stone stands at the Ju Colliseum at Duneforged and in the Ironclad Legion's barracks at Deiperduem.

Orders. The Ironclad Legion, sworn to raw force as a principle, hired by all three empires and trusted by none.

Of a cleric or paladin. Be strong, and endure. Keep the contract your strength was hired for. Never use your strength for someone who has not paid for it, or against someone who has.

Hook. The Ironclad Legion's contract at Deiperduem comes up for renewal. Each empire has quietly offered more than the city.

Mutunus the God of Union

Physical Union, Sensuality · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a knotted girdle · Holy day: none fixed; every wedding night

God of marital union and fertility, invoked at weddings. His iconography is a half-orc, broad and frank. He is unpredictable, and so are his faithful; he is honoured by being given room rather than by being obeyed.

Worship today. Mutunus is an embarrassment to the college and indispensable to everyone else. Brides make a quiet offering at his little shrines before the wedding, and the knot in the bride's girdle is tied in his name. Patrician families who want heirs pay his priests well and say so to nobody.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. His old shrine once stood below the Mons Cerealis at Aeterna before a patrician bought the ground; his altars are household ones.

Orders. None in the codex.

Of a cleric or paladin. Bless honest unions. Untie no knot you did not tie. Never shame a body for what it wants.

Hook. House Calpurnia needs proof that the Lechaion Marriage was consummated by Invictian rite. The only witness is a priest of Mutunus who has since gone missing in Corinth.

Febris the Harbinger of Ailments

Plagues, Mischief · Chaotic Evil · Symbol: a cup of cold water · Holy day: none; she is propitiated when fever comes

Goddess of fever, propitiated at three temples so that she would spare the city. Her iconography is a centaur, which the physicians say is because fever gallops. Her worship is dangerous to the faithful and everyone near them, and most of her shrines are hidden.

Worship today. Febris is prayed to, not loved. Mothers hang amulets on sick children's beds in her name, begging her to move on. Her one licensed cult is a merchant compact that holds the quarantine, which is the most profitable form of worship in the Imperium.

Temples. No licensed temple. Her old fever-shrines stand in the marsh quarters below Aeterna; the Aurum Pact keeps her shrine in its isolation sheds outside Fucostia (temples) and beside the House of Guest Gods at Mavelon (temples).

Orders. The Aurum Pact, a merchant compact sworn to her: they hold the quarantine, and the quarantine is why they are rich.

Of a cleric or paladin. Fear her, feed her and keep her at the gate. Close the harbour when she comes. Never bring her into a house that has not paid.

Hook. The Aurum Pact has quarantined a Farshore ship at Mavelon for a fever nobody aboard has. Its cargo is pepper, and the price at Romulo has doubled.

Arcus the Spectrum

Prismatic Nature, Trickery · Chaotic Good · Symbol: a bow of seven colours · Holy day: the first rainbow after the spring rains

The rainbow, the bow in the sky that Hellenorians call Iris, messenger between heaven and earth. His iconography is an aarakocra in plumage of every colour. Arcus is a trickster and a merry one: light bent, a thing seen from one side and not the other. His worship is warm and unruly.

Worship today. Arcus is a children's god, a dyers' god and a thieves' god. Dyers at Mavelon's Dyers' Fields pray to him for true colour. Illusionists keep his prism. Thieves pray to him for misdirection, and say a prayer of thanks when a rainbow lets them slip away in the rain.

Temples. No temple is entered in the codex. He has a dyers' altar in the Dyers' Fields at Mavelon.

Orders. The Prismatic Shroud, a crime syndicate of illusion and misdirection whose operations are known and whose members are not.

Of a cleric or paladin. Show people another side of things. Trick the proud, never the poor. Carry messages between those who cannot speak to each other.

Hook. A Prismatic Shroud job has gone wrong: an illusion meant to last an hour has lasted a month, and a whole street in Romulo now looks like the Hellenorian quarter of Deiperduem.

The Ascended

Thirty-seven gods who came from beyond, took root among the peoples, and are claimed by no empire's college.

The Asetherian Ascended came to the continent from beyond and took root among its peoples. Their worship crosses the borders of all three empires, and none of the imperial priesthoods fully claims them. Ascended feasts are dated by the common tongue's months, because no empire's calendar will carry them. In the Imperium they are unlicensed: they may be worshipped, but not inside a sacred line. So their altars stand where the foreign altars always stand, on the far bank at Aeterna, in the Canabae at Aepistra, on Mavelon's native north side and on the quays. A licensed god's priests may own land and sue; an Ascended priest may do neither, and so their temples are held in a layman's name, usually a merchant's. They are thick at Deiperduem, where the Treaty forbids temples and the gods lodge as guests in the House of Three Doors (temples), and among the veterans, who met them on campaign and found them more interested in individuals than the state gods ever were.

Tyr God of Justice

War · Lawful Good · Symbol: balanced scales on a warhammer · Holy day: the Day of the Even Hand, 15 Vintage

The maimed god of justice, who gave his hand to bind a wolf and judges with the hand that is left. Asetherian iconography shows him as an aasimar with one hand. His priests keep strict rules in the belief that right order is a kindness.

In the Imperium today. Veterans who saw Legates hang the wrong men brought Tyr home. His priests sit as unofficial judges in the Tent Rows and the canabae, where the praetor's court costs more than the dispute. The magistrates call it usurpation. The plebs call it the only court that is free.

Temples. His one-handed altar stands on the far bank at Aeterna and in the arbitration courts of Deiperduem. No order in the codex is sworn to him; the Lanterns of Justice of Acheaoria honour him beside Hakiyah.

Of a cleric or paladin. Judge without fear or favour. Pay the price of justice yourself. Never punish without a hearing.

Hook. A Tent Row court of Tyr has sentenced a Legate's tribune in his absence. The tribune is coming to collect the judge.

Torm God of Courage and Self-Sacrifice

War · Lawful Good · Symbol: a right gauntlet held upright · Holy day: the Day of the Gauntlet, 1 Highsun

The loyal fury, god of duty, courage and the guard who does not leave his post. His iconography is an aasimar in plain mail. His priests keep strict rules, and his paladins keep stricter ones.

In the Imperium today. Torm is the Ascended the legions trust. Centurions who held a line until relieved, and the men who were relieved, keep his gauntlet in their kit. His worship is unlicensed, so his shrines stand in the canabae outside every fortress, and the officers pretend not to visit.

Temples. His shrine in the Canabae at Aepistra; a chapel of the Adamantine Line's veterans at Duneforged. No order in the codex is sworn to him.

Of a cleric or paladin. Stand your post. Protect those who cannot protect themselves. Accept the cost of your duty; never pass it to another.

Hook. A sentry of Torm has stood at an abandoned frontier post since the Concord, because no one came to relieve him. His legion was disbanded four years ago.

Tempus God of War

War · True Neutral · Symbol: a flaming sword upright · Holy day: the eve of any battle; the Feast of Swords, 1 Sowing

The Foehammer, god of war as weather: it comes, it favours no side, and it honours whoever fights well. His iconography is a goliath in battered armour. His priests take no side, holding that war must be fought fairly whoever profits.

In the Imperium today. Tempus is the god of the mercenary and the career soldier, and the Concord has given him many new worshippers who have nothing to fight. His priests bless both sides in a duel and keep the rules of the Gate Fights at Mavelon, which both the Mavari and the Imperials accept.

Temples. His sword-altar on Mavelon's north side at Mavelon; mercenary chapels at Deiperduem. No order in the codex is sworn to him, though half the Ironclad Legion prays to him beside Vis.

Of a cleric or paladin. Fight honourably and well. Never kill a herald or a beaten foe who yields. Honour a brave enemy.

Hook. A priest of Tempus is asked to judge a duel between a Mavari spear-bearer and an Imperial tribune at the Gate. Both sides expect him to cheat for them.

Bane God of Tyranny

War · Lawful Evil · Symbol: a black hand, fingers together · Holy day: the Day of the Black Hand, 1 Frostmonth

The Black Lord, god of tyranny, fear and the rule of the strong over the weak. His iconography is a hobgoblin warlord. His worship is a hierarchy of obligation; he rewards those who serve without question, and his priests are effective, feared and well organised.

In the Imperium today. Bane's worship is forbidden in all three empires and quietly practised in all three courts. In the Imperium he appeals to the Legates' officers, who admire order and have stopped believing it will come from Aeterna. His priests offer a simple creed: the chair is empty, and someone will sit in it.

Temples. None openly. A black-hand mark has been found scratched in the Castra Nova at Aepistra and in barracks at Aeterna. No order in the codex is sworn to him.

Of a cleric or paladin. Rule or be ruled. Strike fear before you need to strike. Never forgive defiance.

Hook. A centurion confesses to the party that his whole cohort has sworn to the Black Hand, and he cannot remember taking the oath.

Helm God of Protection

Life, Light · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a staring eye on an upright gauntlet · Holy day: the Long Watch, the longest night of Frostmonth
