Temples: none; a steering oar on the wall of the pilots' wine-shop at Helionyx, beside the Tyrsan pilots' bench. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: master the sea by knowing it; stay ashore when the stars say so; never steer a crew into a storm for pride.

Eurynome the Harmony

Nature, Harmony · Neutral Good · Symbol: a dancing woman on a coiled serpent · Holy day: the first mowing of the water-meadows

Titaness of water-meadows and pasture, who in the oldest accounts ruled the world with the serpent Ophion before Cronus threw them down. Her domain is harmony: grazing that does not ruin the meadow, the dance that keeps the whole village in step. Her faithful are expected to help where they can.

Remembered today in the circle-dances of the meadow villages, which open the mowing and close the hay, and in the habit of leaving a strip of meadow uncut for the snakes. No one under sixty knows why the strip is left. Everyone leaves it.

Temples: none; dancing-floors in the river meadows below Thebesieas. No sworn order. See Ophion.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: keep the balance between the herd and the grass; settle quarrels by bringing both sides into the dance; leave the strip uncut.

Gigantes Titan of Chaos

Strength, Chaos · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a broken column · Holy day: none kept; the cult meets when old stone is uncovered

The giants born of the Earth, who rose against the gods in the war that ended the old order. The codex counts them as one Titan of strength and chaos: the many-handed, many-headed revolt of the ground itself. It is unpredictable, and so are its faithful, who honour it by giving it room. Very few want to give it that much.

Remembered today in quarrymen's terror. The deep galleries of the Oros give up blocks too big for any human builder and, once, a chamber with a table set for giants. Masons say "the big ones" and touch iron. The stone giants who live deepest in the range are solemn and literal and will not discuss their masters.

Temples: none; the deep galleries of the Oros, and the Ninth Cellar at Mavelon, where the cult murmurs to the caldera. Sworn order: the Cult of Nyzzoth, whose rites beckon giants long buried.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: break what binds; trust strength over law; wake what sleeps.

Helios Titan of Vitality

Sun, Vitality · Neutral Good · Symbol: a four-horse chariot under a sun-disc · Holy day: the Standing, 1st of Hekatombaion, Hellenorian New Year

The sun itself, driving its chariot across the sky and seeing everything done beneath it. Its domains are sun and vitality: health, growth and the strength of the young. His faithful are expected to help where they can, in daylight, where he can see them do it.

Worshipped today in public at Helionyx, the League's standing exception and standing embarrassment. Its gold-domed temple holds a gilded chariot facing east, and every fourth summer at the Standing four white horses in harness are driven off the mole into the sea "to give the god new horses". At the moment the shadow is shortest, by law, nothing is done at all. At Delphara his altar sits one step lower than the rest, and Helionyx polishes the Step of Insult every year.

Temples: Helionyx (the Temple of the Chariot, keeper Polemon Phaethontides); the low altar at Delphara; the ruined Sun's Seat at Corinth. Sworn order: the Hammer of Lumina, smiths who temper blades in sunlight.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: do your work in the open; keep the young strong; stand still at noon and let the god see you.

Hoplodamus Titan of Guardianship

War, Guardianship · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a shield held before a cradle · Holy day: the opening day of the Great Martial Festival, every fifth year

The giant who stood guard over Rhea while she carried the infant Storm Lord, so that Cronus could not reach the child. His rites are exacting and impersonal. He is owed correct observance, and gives protection in return: the wall that does not move, the guard who does not sleep.

Worshipped today in the Duneforged Citadel, whose Cathedral keeps the Sanctum of Hoplodamus beside Vulcan, Juno and Mercury. He is patron of the trials at the Ju Colliseum: every fighter passes his Sanctum before the Ember Gate, and a fighter who wins by defending rather than attacking leaves a shield-boss on his altar. His Sanctum is the Cathedral's gatehouse, because the guardian judges who comes in, and no weapon passes his door unless it is to be judged.

Temples: the Sanctum of Hoplodamus in the Citadel Cathedral's gatehouse, Duneforged (Warden-Priest Garrick Ashgrove); a guardian image in the walls of Xerastri. Arena favourite of Marcia Ferox. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: stand between the helpless and what hunts them; hold your post until relieved; never strike first when guarding.

Hyperion Titan of Knowledge

Light, Knowledge · Neutral Good · Symbol: an open eye in a sunburst · Holy day: midsummer night, the shortest dark

Titan of heavenly light and watchfulness, father of the sun, the moon and the dawn. His domains are light and knowledge: seeing clearly and understanding what is seen. His faithful are expected to help where they can, and to look before they help.

Remembered today by watchmen and lighthouse keepers, who call the night's last watch "Hyperion's", and by the gnomonists of Helionyx, who measure his children's shadows for a living. Craftsmen of the old families say a well-made thing has "Hyperion in it", meaning it shows what it is for.

Temples: none; the watch-towers of the coast and the lamp-rooms of lighthouses. Sworn order: the Children of the Sacred Forge, who shape flame with reverence and "awaken what lies within".

Asks of a cleric or paladin: keep watch; see clearly and say what you saw; make things that show their purpose.

Iapetus the Doom Herald

Mortality, Doom · Lawful Evil · Symbol: a spear-point (he is "the Piercer") · Holy day: none; the day of a death sentence

Titan of mortality, from whose line mortal humanity is said to descend; father of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus and Menoetius. The codex calls him the Doom Herald: he does not kill, he announces. His worship is a hierarchy of obligation, and he rewards those who carry his announcements without question.

Remembered today as a bad name. Heralds of a death sentence once wore his spear-point on a cord; executioners in the old cities still do, under their tunics. Hellenorian funerary orators begin "we are Iapetus's children", meaning everyone dies, and nobody laughs.

Temples: none; the spear-point cord of the executioners' guilds. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: announce the end plainly; carry out sentence without cruelty or mercy; remind the proud that they will die.

Lelantos Titan of the Wild

Stealth, Wilderness · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a footprint fading into grass · Holy day: none; the first snow, when tracks are easiest to read

Titan of unseen air and of the hunter's skill of moving without being noticed. He is unpredictable, and so are his faithful; he is honoured by being given room, and the room he likes is wilderness where nobody can follow.

Remembered today by hunters, scouts, poachers and smugglers, who step backwards over a threshold "for Lelantos" before going out at night. Mountain scouts of all three empires use his name as a password among themselves, and the custom survived the war because scouts of all sides liked each other better than their officers.

Temples: none; a threshold stepped over backwards. No sworn order; smugglers on the quiet route through Zandar Isle leave him a coin in the bilge.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: go unseen; take only what you need from the wild; leave no track that leads home.

Leto the Graceful Mother

Motherhood, Grace · Neutral Good · Symbol: a palm tree · Holy day: the seventh day of Thargelion, the twins' birthday

Titaness of motherhood and modesty, who bore Apollo and Artemis while hunted across the world by Hera, and found no land that would take her in but a floating island. Her faithful are expected to help where they can, and above all to take in a woman in labour, whoever is chasing her.

Remembered today as the twins' mother, which gives her a tolerance no other Titan enjoys. Midwives invoke her beside Artemis; women in labour grip a palm branch. At Delphara a small palm grows by the Phoibad Spring and every Pythia has touched it. She is still not on the Roll, and her priests say she would not want the fuss.

Temples: the palm at the Phoibad Spring, Delphara. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: shelter the pursued and the pregnant; endure insult with grace; protect your children and then let them go.

Megamedes Titan of Strategy

Strategy, Command · Lawful Evil · Symbol: a commander's baton laid across a map-board · Holy day: none; the night before a battle

An obscure Titan named as the father of Pallas, a ruler "of great counsel", as his name says. The codex gives him strategy and command, and his worship is a hierarchy of obligation: subordinates obey, commanders are obeyed, and the Titan rewards whoever keeps the chain unbroken.

Remembered today only by staff officers. Map-rooms in all three empires once kept a baton on the table "for the absent commander", and some still do; the last officer out of the room turns it to point at the enemy. The habit outlived the Titan's name in most armies, and the Invictian Council of Legates keeps it with particular care.

Temples: none; the baton on the map-table. No sworn order. Father of Pallas.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: command and be obeyed; plan the whole war, not the battle; spend soldiers as coin, but never waste them.

Melisseus the Abundant Guardian

Protection, Abundance · Neutral Good · Symbol: a stone hive-bole · Holy day: the Smoking, in Reaping, when the hives are worked together

The old king whose daughters fed the infant Storm Lord on honey in hiding; his name means "of the bees". The codex makes him a Titan of protection and abundance, the guardian who feeds what he hides. His faithful are expected to help where they can.

Worshipped today openly at Kirimitsana, which has never thought to apologise. He has no building: his temple is the Long Row of stone hive-boles along the Beekeepers' Hall, his altar is the hall's own hearth, where the first comb of the Smoking is laid in the fire whole, and his priestesses are the twelve Grandmothers. Delphara's Dream Dormitory makes its honey-cakes with Kirimitsana honey and nothing else.

Temples: the Long Row, Kirimitsana (see the town); the Hive of Melisseus behind the Great Sanctuary at Ephelanum, where every novice Bee kneels her first night; the untended stone hive in the Dodekatheon at Delphara. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: feed those you protect; hide the young from those who would devour them; share the harvest with the hive.

Menoetius Titan of Destruction

Destruction, Wrath · Chaotic Evil · Symbol: an oak split by lightning · Holy day: none public; any day of riot

Titan of violent anger and rash action, struck down by the Storm Lord's thunderbolt for his arrogance. His worship is dangerous to the faithful and to everyone near them. Most of his shrines are hidden, and his cults are hunted in all three empires.

Remembered today as a curse ("Menoetius take it") and as the patron, everyone assumes, of every riot. Lightning-split trees are cut down quickly in Hellenoria, before anyone can carve on them. The cults that keep him are small, short-lived and very loud, and the city watch of Deiperduem has a standing order about split oaks.

Temples: none permitted. No sworn order; cells form and burn out.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: destroy what offends you; never swallow your anger; let rage choose the moment.

Metis the Wise Strategist

Wisdom, Strategy · Chaotic Evil · Symbol: a closed mouth with an eye on the tongue · Holy day: none public

Titaness of wisdom and cunning counsel, whom the Storm Lord swallowed so that her wisdom would be his; Athena was born armoured out of his head soon after. The codex makes her chaotic and evil, and her worship dangerous: her cults are hunted and her shrines hidden. Wisdom that has been swallowed does not forgive.

Remembered today barely. The Maiden's priestesses call Athena "motherless" in the hymns and do not say why. Scholars who know the story keep it out of their lectures, and the Truth-Flame strikes it from texts on sight.

Temples: none. No sworn order. Mother of Athena in the struck verses.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: outthink the powerful; take back what was stolen from you; trust no one who has eaten your counsel.

Mnemosyne the Keeper of Memories

Memory, History · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a wax tablet and stylus · Holy day: the day of the great fire at Thessalonika, kept by the archivists

Titaness of memory and mother of the nine Muses. Her rites are exacting and impersonal: a thing is remembered correctly or it is not, and she gives order in return. Her priests held that a city which remembers accurately need not fight about the past.

Remembered today by archivists. Thessalonika's library was once her temple, the Mouseion of Mnemosyne, which burned with half the city three hundred years ago; the surveyor's new grid runs straight across its foundations. The auditors who now order the city's gods by documents are her heirs whether they know it or not, and the Porticoes' scribes still swear on a wax tablet.

Temples: the House of Memory under the Lower Grid, Thessalonika. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: remember exactly; copy faithfully; never destroy a record, even one that condemns you.

The Muses Elder Titan of Inspiration

Music, Inspiration · Neutral Good · Symbol: three reeds bound together (Practice, Memory, Song) · Holy day: the Leaving at Atticenea, when the year's students take the road

The first inspirers, before the nine daughters of Mnemosyne: Practice, Memory and Song, counted by the codex as a single Titan. Their gift is not the flash of genius but the long habit that earns it. Their faithful are expected to help where they can, usually by teaching.

Remembered today in schools. At Atticenea a sealed cave under the School Steps once held their shrine; the schools grew up over it, and students still scratch verses on the stone door for luck. Teachers across the League open the year with three notes on a reed pipe without knowing why three.

Temples: the sealed cave under the School Steps, Atticenea. No sworn order. Linked in the codex to Clymene.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: practise every day; remember your teachers; sing what you know so others can learn it.

Mylinus Titan of Endurance

Endurance, Stone · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a split boulder; a millstone · Holy day: none; the dressing of a new millstone

A Titan or giant of the old order, remembered chiefly for being struck down. The codex gives him endurance and stone: the thing that is broken and does not stop being itself. He is unpredictable, and so are his faithful.

Remembered today by millers and the millstone-cutters who quarry the hard grey rock for them. A new stone is dressed with his name and a split cut across one face, "so it breaks the right way". Old women in the grain towns call a stubborn child "a little Mylinus", and mean it kindly.

Temples: the Chapel of Mylinus in the eighth gallery under Duneforged, where the first miners drove a chip from every new face into the wall; the split mark on millstones from Thebesieas to the Invictian mills. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: endure; be broken and go on; grind slowly and finish the work.

Oceanus Titan of Exploration

Water, Exploration · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a ring of water around a horned head · Holy day: the day a ship sails beyond the last known coast

The great river that encircles the world, from which every sea and spring is fed. The codex makes him the Titan of exploration: the far edge, the next coast, the water beyond the chart. His rites are exacting and impersonal: a navigator who keeps them comes home, one who does not may come home anyway, but should not count on it.

Remembered today by the few captains who sail beyond Asetheria, and by the far-shore pilots who arrive from beyond it. A ship leaving for the Farshore Realms pours fresh water into salt at the harbour mouth "for the river around the world". The Tyrsan pilots do the same thing in their own words.

Temples: none; the pouring at the harbour mouth of Mavelon, and the far-shore quays of Corinth. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: go further; chart what you find and share the chart; keep the rites of every sea you cross.

Olymbrus Titan of the Sky

Time, Sky · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a gnomon casting a shadow on a dial · Holy day: the Standing, when the solstice is measured

One of the sons of Heaven and Earth, a Titan of the sky and of the time the sky keeps. His rites are exacting and impersonal: the sun's shadow is measured and the calendar corrected, and in return the year stays in its proper order.

Remembered today in the measuring. Calendar-makers, priests who fix festivals and the gnomonists of Helionyx, who time their city's prayers by the shadow of a stick, keep his name in the old formulas, mostly without saying it. The Hall of Hours' keeper hangs a small brass weight by the central pillar every morning and has never explained why.

Temples: none in his name; the Hall of Hours, Helionyx, is his in all but name. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: keep the calendar true; measure before you judge; let the sky decide the hour.

Olympus the Storm

Rebellion, Storms · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a mountain peak wrapped in cloud · Holy day: none; the day a tyrant falls

A Titan with no myth outside the codex, named like the mountain where the gods are said to sit. Its domains are rebellion and storms: the rising, the overthrow, the weather that changes everything. It is unpredictable, and so are its faithful; it is honoured by being given room.

Remembered today by rebels. When a Hellenorian city throws out a tyrant, the oath that binds the conspirators is sworn "by Olympus", and the priests are careful to say this means the gods' mountain. The tyrants of several cities have made the oath a crime, which only proves its point.

Temples: none; the high passes of the Olympus range. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: overthrow the tyrant; speak when the assembly is silent; trust the storm to clear the air.

Ophion Titan of Creation

Creation, Sky · True Neutral · Symbol: a serpent coiled around an egg · Holy day: none kept

The primordial serpent of the oldest cosmogonies, who ruled the world from the high mountain before the Titans and coiled round the egg from which everything hatched. His priests take no side; creation makes everything, the useful and the terrible alike.

Remembered today in the serpent motif that runs through Hellenorian sacred building: the snake under Athena's porch, the serpent killed at Delphara, the coiled border on temple floors. Artisans who make something new paint a serpent on the first piece and paint it over before the client sees it.

Temples: none; the forgotten Serpent's Hollow at Delphara may once have been his. Sworn order: the Forge of the Creators, a secret enclave that melds magic and metal. Consort of Eurynome.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: make something that did not exist; guard what you made until it can guard itself; do not ask the creation whether it wanted to be made.

Ostasus the Timer

Time, Space · True Neutral · Symbol: an hourglass laid on its side · Holy day: none; the Taken-Out Days, which belong to no month

A Titan of the first generation, a son of Heaven and Earth. The codex calls him the Timer and gives him time and space: the distance between things and the interval between moments. His priests take no side; a mile is a mile and an hour an hour, whoever walks it.

Remembered today by surveyors and almost nobody else. Invictian road-surveyors cut his mark on the first milestone of a new road, an hourglass on its side, and do not explain it to the legate. The Hellenorian Taken-Out Days, when courts do not sit, are said by old people to be "his", the days outside the year.

Temples: none known; the surveyors' mark on milestones. Sworn order: the Circle of the Timeless Veil, watchers at the edge of now.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: measure true; keep appointments to the moment; never steal time from another.

Pallas Titan of Defence

War, Defence · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a spear behind a wall of shields · Holy day: none; his name is spoken when a city's walls are inspected

Titan of warcraft, son of Megamedes, who fought in the war of the old order and fell. The codex gives him war and defence: walls, shields, the held line. His rites are exacting and impersonal. Athena still wears his name as an epithet, and her priestesses do not like to be asked why.

Remembered today in that epithet and in a stonemason's habit: the first block of a city wall is laid "for Pallas" and checked with a plumb-line before anyone is allowed to see it. Guides on Hellarchon's Rock show visitors "the first Maiden's house" under the temple floor. The priestesses know better and say nothing.

Temples: the Old House of Pallas under the Maiden's Temple, Hellarchon. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: hold the wall; defend, do not conquer; keep the line even when the city behind you does not deserve it.

Perses Titan of Annihilation

Fire, Annihilation · Chaotic Evil · Symbol: a black flame · Holy day: none public; the Ashen Choir keeps the anniversary of the Charioteer's fall

Titan of destruction and father of Hecate; father, his worshippers say, of the fire that does not warm. His worship is dangerous to the faithful and to everyone near them. Most of his shrines are hidden, and his cults are hunted in all three empires.

Remembered today at Helionyx, where the Ashen Choir holds that the sun is a fire held back and that the city's bronze Charioteer fell because Perses pushed it. Every sign of this season, the early almonds, the empty Stork Roof, the Ash Phoenix gone, is to them proof that the restraint is failing.

Temples: the Choir's den inside the fallen Charioteer's head, under the salt warehouses at Helionyx. No sworn order beyond the Choir.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: burn what cannot be saved; hasten the end that is coming; let nothing be held back.

Phoebe the Visionary

Prophecy, Vision · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a crescent over running water · Holy day: the oracle's consultation nights, the 7th of each warm month

Titaness of prophecy who held the oracle at Delphara before she passed it to Apollo. Her rites are exacting and impersonal; the vision is owed, exactly, and given exactly. Her name, "the bright one", is still the god's epithet.

Remembered today by the Phoibadai, a line of Delpharan women who have kept her round shrine at the spring since before the god came. They wash every petitioner's hair, so they see every face that goes up the Sacred Way, and every Pythia within memory has been one of them or married into them. The priests tolerate them because nobody else will do the work.

Temples: the round shrine at the Phoibad Spring, Delphara. No sworn order; the Phoibadai are a family. See Lysandra Anthemis.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: see, and say exactly what you saw; serve the oracle, not its customers; leave nothing out.

Phorcys Titan of Monsters

Sea, Monsters · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a crab-clawed old man · Holy day: none; the first night out of harbour

Old god of the sea's hidden dangers and father of monsters: gorgons, grey hags and the thing in the strait that eats six men from every ship. His rites are exacting and impersonal. He is owed a coin, and in return keeps his children to their own waters.

Remembered today in a sailor's coin. On the first night out of harbour a Hellenorian captain drops a bronze coin over the side "for the old man", and crews refuse to sail with a captain who forgets. Along the fog coast the coin is silver.

Temples: the sea cave off the western point of Carianea, where divers leave the second sponge of the season; coins on the sea floor beneath the Nereid's Veil. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: pay the toll the sea asks; know the monster's waters and keep out of them; never kill a monster in its own lair without cause.

Polus Titan of Wisdom

Stars, Knowledge · True Neutral · Symbol: the pole star with a line running through it · Holy day: the clearest night of winter

The celestial pole around which the heavens turn, and an old name, the stories say, of the Titan Coeus. The codex gives him stars and knowledge, the steady kind: the fixed point you can steer by. His priests take no side; the pole star guides the pirate and the merchant alike.

Remembered today by navigators, astronomers and the caravan-masters who cross the Dasht-a Khaliq by night. Steersmen touch their forehead to the pole star before a night passage. Teachers in Thessalonika's Porticoes call a sound proof "a Polus", a thing that does not move.

Temples: none; the star-charts of navigators and the night caravans of Atarabad. No sworn order. See Coeus.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: be the fixed point others steer by; teach what is certain; never move your star to please a patron.

Prometheus the Sacrificed Creator

Creation, Sacrifice · Chaotic Good · Symbol: a torch held in a chained hand · Holy day: none public; the Voidfolk light a lamp at every birth

The Titan who stole fire from the gods for mortals and was chained to a mountain for it. His worship is warm and unruly: the faithful honour him by acting on generous impulse, most often by giving away something that will cost them. He is the patron of the gift that ruins the giver.

Remembered today as a story, told to children everywhere as a warning and to apprentices as an inspiration. Potters and smiths tip a little fire back into the kiln "for the one who brought it". No temple to him stands anywhere on the Roll.

Temples: none acknowledged; the Clay-Shaper's niche under the oldest clay pit at Araavyna, lately emptied; a hidden room on Hellarchon's war harbour (see the temples of Hellarchon). Sworn order: the Flame of the Sacrificed, who believe salvation comes through suffering.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: give the gift even if it costs you everything; bring light to those kept in the dark; suffer for others and do not boast of it.

Rhea Titan of Life

Fertility, Life · Neutral Good · Symbol: a stone wrapped in swaddling · Holy day: the first lambing of Lambing month

Mother of the gods, who saved her youngest by giving his devouring father a stone wrapped in swaddling to swallow instead. The codex gives her fertility and life. Her faithful are expected to help where they can, and the help she prefers is cunning in a mother's cause.

Remembered today in the hill demes, where drums are beaten at a lambing and a smooth stone is wrapped in cloth and laid in the cradle before the baby. Midwives keep a wrapped stone in their bag. Every Hellenorian priest admits she is the mother of the six eldest gods, and none dwells on it.

Temples: none on the Roll; the old groves of the Foloicauria. No sworn order; see Demeter and the Circle of the Eternal Grove.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: protect the child by any trick; give life where you can; feed the devourer a stone.

Selene the Dream

Moon, Dreams · Neutral Good · Symbol: a pale chariot drawn by two oxen · Holy day: the full moon nearest the autumn equinox

The moon, who drives her pale chariot across the night and loved a sleeping shepherd so much that she asked for him to sleep for ever. The codex gives her moon and dreams, and her faithful are expected to help where they can, often in their sleep.

Remembered today at Helionyx, where she has the dusk hour in the Hall of Hours, and in every house where a mother sings a child to sleep with her name. Dream-readers of all three empires invoke her before a reading, and the Dream Dormitory's lamps at Delphara are lit at moonrise.

Temples: the dusk hour, Helionyx; the old dream-hall above the hottest spring at Loutrokleion, where beds have quietly been put back. Sworn orders: the Howling Bell, a bardic college that sings truths too terrible for silence; the Verdant Spearhold, moonlit warriors of forgotten paths.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: watch over sleepers; carry messages through dreams; love without needing to be woken.

Styx Titan of Oaths

Oaths, Death · Lawful Neutral · Symbol: a woman holding a cup of dark water · Holy day: the shortest day, when oaths are renewed

The river of the underworld on which even the gods swear their unbreakable oaths; mother of Nike. Her rites are exacting and impersonal. An oath sworn on her water is kept, or the swearer pays, and she is the reason old oaths in Asetheria are frightening.

Remembered today in oath-water: a cup of dark water held while swearing, in courts and contracts that want more than witnesses. At Thebesieas the keeper of the Garden of Quiet Death swears on a basin behind a tool-shed, every year on the shortest day. In Acheaoria her water witnesses covenants under another name.

Temples: the Black Basin, Thebesieas; the Binding Word at Mithratal. No sworn order. Mother of Nike.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: swear rarely and keep every oath; never lie on the water; witness the oaths of others truly.

Syceus Titan of Growth

Earth, Growth · Chaotic Neutral · Symbol: a fig tree growing over a stone · Holy day: the first ripe fig

The Titan who fled the Storm Lord's thunderbolt and was hidden by the Earth, which grew a fig tree over him. The codex gives him earth and growth: the root that finds water, the vine that cracks a wall. He is unpredictable, and so are his faithful.

Remembered today in Acheaorian gardens rather than Hellenorian temples. At Persevalis a garden of the Green Mother stands on the slope, and at the great tree of Derakhtak-Bon a woman with her hands full of growing things walks in old women's dreams. Nobody in either place calls her a Titan, or a him.

Temples: the Green Mother's garden, Persevalis; the taproot at Derakhtak-Bon (see its temples). No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: grow; hide the fugitive under green things; let roots go where they want.

Tethys Titan of Navigation

Rivers, Navigation · Neutral Good · Symbol: a woman with water running from her hands · Holy day: the spring clearing of the channels

Titaness of fresh water, mother of the rivers and springs. The codex adds navigation: the river as a road, the channel kept open. Her faithful are expected to help where they can, and the help she wants is a clear channel.

Remembered today by people who keep water moving. On the drained Wet Plain of Thebesieas, where the Mycairan channels meet, a roofless shrine of cyclopean blocks holds a basin fed by all four, and the dike-wardens leave a loaf on its rim each spring because their fathers did. River-boatmen across the empires toss bread into the first rapids of the season.

Temples: the Sluice-Temple on the Wet Plain, Thebesieas; the drowned temple in the caldera at Mavelon, where Mavari steersmen touch their foreheads. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: keep the channels clear; guide travellers on the water; never foul a spring.

Theia Titan of Light

Light, Radiance · Neutral Good · Symbol: an eye set in a gold coin · Holy day: none; the day a new coin is struck

Titaness of sight and of shining light, from whom gold and silver take their brilliance. Mother, in the old story, of the sun, the moon and the dawn. Her faithful are expected to help where they can, and her help is to make things seen for what they are.

Remembered today by goldsmiths, silversmiths and assayers, who say a true coin "has Theia in it" and a debased one has lost her. Ephelanum's silversmiths, who make the Lady's images, polish them "for Theia". Since the Imperium began debasing its silver, assayers in every Mithril Reserve branch have started using the phrase in their reports.

Temples: none; the silversmiths' workshops of Ephelanum and the assay-rooms of the Mithril Reserve (see banking). No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: show things as they are; refuse false coin and false praise; let light into dark rooms.

Themis Titan of Justice

Law, Justice · Lawful Good · Symbol: a pair of scales held by an unblindfolded woman · Holy day: the Signing, 1st of Pyanepsion

Titaness of divine law and right order, who sat beside the throne of heaven as counsellor. Her priests keep strict rules and expect the faithful to keep them too, in the belief that right order is itself a kindness. Unlike Tyche she is not blindfolded: justice must see what it judges.

Remembered today in courtrooms of all three empires, whose scales are hers whatever the court calls them. In Deiperduem a worn statue of a woman with scales stands in the Treaty Hall's forecourt, older than the hall, and each empire's delegation touches it on the way in while claiming it represents its own god.

Temples: none acknowledged; the forecourt statue at Deiperduem. Sworn order: the Syndicate of the Justicar, who deliver judgment beyond mortal law.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: judge with open eyes; keep the law and change it when it is unjust; never take the judge's seat in your own quarrel.

Titan Titan of the Harvest

Agriculture, Stars · True Neutral · Symbol: a sheaf beneath seven stars · Holy day: the last sheaf of the harvest

The Titan with the plainest name: the one the others are named after, or the one who was named last. The codex gives him agriculture and stars, the farmer's calendar read in the sky: sow when these stars rise, reap when those set. His priests take no side; the harvest feeds whoever owns the field.

Remembered today in the last sheaf. Across the three empires the final sheaf of a harvest is cut by everyone together, bound into a rough figure and kept over the door until the next sowing. It is called "the old one" in the common tongue and by other names elsewhere, and no farmer would leave it standing in the field.

Temples: none; the last sheaf over a thousand farmhouse doors, from the Latium Plains to the Argotiko plain. No sworn order.

Asks of a cleric or paladin: read the stars before you sow; bring in the harvest together; keep the last sheaf.

The Acheaorian Pantheon

The codex lists twenty-four Acheaorian gods and calls every one of them "lesser". It also puts a fire-temple at the heart of every Acheaorian city and lists no god of fire. Both facts have the same explanation, and the Magi will give it to anyone who asks: the fire is not a god. The sacred fire, Atar the Witness, is older than the gods. It burned before anything was sworn, and the gods made their compacts in its light. The gods are the Honoured Ones (izadan); they are honoured. The fire is kept. No god's house may stand higher than the fire-temple of its city, and every god's lamp is lit each dawn from the fire by a Magus with a taper, the Lending of the Flame (see the Temples of Persemenid and the Magi and the Purity of Fire).

The pantheon divides, in the Magi's teaching, into a bright half and a dark half. The bright half has niches in every city's Izadkhaneh. The dark half (Lotha, Thasmudayan and the Faceless God) has none anywhere, and keeping their images is a capital charge. Ragarra sits in neither half: still listed, struck from the rota by a King nobody remembers. Each of ten gods owns one day of the tenday, from Zann-roz to Migal-roz, which is how most Acheaorians meet the pantheon: as a calendar.

Atar, the Witness the sacred fire · not a god, and not in the codex's list

The fire itself · beyond alignment, in doctrine · a flame behind a lattice screen · the Midwinter Fire (10 Vohumanah), the Fire Watch (10 Āthrā), the Tending at Atarabad

Atar has no image, no priests of its own and no prayers addressed to it in the second person. The Magi tend it veiled, so that their breath never touches it; laymen may not carry it, only its ash. It does not grant wishes. It witnesses: oaths are sworn before it, kings are crowned in its light, satraps swear before it and before the King's image, and a god's priest whose lamp the Magus skips is shut out of custom until his debt to the fire is paid.

Worship today. Universal, formal and political. Five great fires make the Circuit of Five Fires: the Temple of Breath at Persemenid, the undying fire of Atarabad, the Witness of Mithratal, the frontier fire of Xerastri and the Channel Head of Persevalis. Towns keep a fire-house with one Magus.

At the table. A Magus cleric (Light domain suits) draws on the fire and names a god as the fire's voice; Mobad Atar-Farnbag names Hakiyah, "the flame is truth made visible". Purity is the price: no burial, no burning of the dead, no blood near the flame.

Zann the Illuminator

Knowledge and understanding · True neutral · an air-genasi scribe with a lamp and an open roll · Zann-roz, first day of the tenday; the Naming of the Rolls (late Ardavahisht)

Zann is the god of the record: what is written down, and therefore known. His images show an air-genasi figure whose hair stirs in still rooms, reading by a lamp lit from somewhere else. His priests take no side. In practice that means they write everything down and are thanked for none of it.

Worship today. Every account in the empire opens on Zann-roz. The god belongs to clerks, auditors and archivists, and to the throne, which counts its guard and its tribute before him.

Temples and shrines: the House of the Count at Persemenid, where Ledger-Mother Gulnar Zand keeps the master tribute ledger and has begun writing "not presented" in red; the Scribes' chapel at Mithratal; a niche in every Izadkhaneh.

Sworn orders: the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger, who audit the tribute and are paid by the guild, not the satrapy; the Illuminated Scholars, who copy everything and lend almost nothing.

Asks of the faithful: write it down, write it truly, and never hold land where you audit.

Hajama the God of Valor

War strategy · Lawful neutral · a leonin general over a campaign map cut in the floor · Hajama-roz, second day of the tenday; the Royal Hunt (early Fravartish); the Riding at Xerastri (Ardavahisht)

Hajama is valour that keeps its place in the line. He is not the god of courage so much as of the correct order of march, and his rites are exacting and impersonal: the god is owed observance, not love, and gives order in return. Every image shows him with a map at his feet.

Worship today. The noble cavalry's god, and so the satraps' god. Whoever pays for a squadron owns its chapel, and the satraps now pay.

Temples and shrines: the Lion Gate of Hajama at Persemenid (Lion-Priest Bahman Arshak, an empty saddle for House Mihran's dead heir); the Lion Hall at Xerastri (Lion-Priest Bahram Shirdel); the east-tower chapel of the lion gate at Shir'abad D'ar (Lion-Priest Siyavash Tahmures).

Sworn order: the Lion's Mane Vanguard, heavy lancers raised by the satraps; its spahbed is Artabazos Mihran.

Asks of the faithful: know the ground before you ride, hold your place, and pay for your standard.

Hakiyah the Just Scales

Justice and truth · Lawful good · a protector aasimar holding a lamp that never dims · Hakiyah-roz, third day of the tenday (weddings, oaths, contracts); the Lighting of the Road; the Renewal at Mithratal (1–11 Rāmana)

Hakiyah is justice that announces itself. Her lamp is always lit so that judgement can be seen coming, and her priests keep strict rules in the belief that right order is itself a kindness. She is the god Magi clerics most often name as the fire's voice.

Worship today. Strong among magistrates, honest merchants and people who have been judged fairly and leave bequests to say so. Her temples take no fees for justice and are poor and proud of it.

Temples and shrines: the Lantern House at Mithratal, the one building lit all night (Lantern-Mother Parisa Roshanpur); her bay in the Hall of Witnesses there, where her name is the most expensive witness on the bronze price-plate; the third garden on the ladder at Persevalis.

Sworn order: the Lanterns of Justice, roving magistrates who carry a lit lamp on circuit and may not let it go out until they return.

Asks of the faithful: judge in the light, take nothing for it, and never let your lamp go dark.

Kiga the Beastmaster

Predation and strength · Neutral evil · a tabaxi crouched to spring · Kiga-roz, fourth day of the tenday (drill, musters, hunting); the First Kill of the hunting season

Kiga is the god of the thing that eats. Hunters bargain with him for a kill and do not speak of what they paid. His faithful shed blood, so the purity laws keep him outside the walls: his altars stand in hunting parks, on flat stones stained by generations of first kills.

Worship today. Hunters, cheetah-trainers, scouts and the culling crews of the royal parks. His day is the army's drill day, which suits the garrison towns.

Temples and shrines: the Hunting Altar in the Hunting Park outside Xerastri (Huntmistress Yasaman Yuzban); a bay hung with scouts' hunting-flags in Xerastri's Hall of Standards; field altars in the Paradise of Persemenid, beyond the garden wall; and, far from home, a niche cut by captured Acheaorian grooms in the horse-registry of Argotiko in Hellenoria.

Sworn order: the Predator's Guild, which holds the culling rights in the royal enclosures and sells trained cheetahs to every satrap with a park.

Asks of the faithful: take the weak first, waste nothing, and give the god the first kill of every season.

Jauhar the Gilded

Prosperity and fortune · True neutral · a hill dwarf counting coins into a bowl that is never full · Jauhar-roz, fifth day of the tenday (market day); the Long Bargain at Atarabad (Rāmana)

Jauhar is fortune that can be weighed. His priests take no side and bless the buyer and the seller in the same breath. Each year his priest at Atarabad opens the Long Bargain by weighing one gold coin before the crowd and naming the god's price for it, and the week takes its tone from the number.

Worship today. Merchants, brokers, caravan masters and anyone with a stone sewn into a coat. Business is good: as the satrapies grow restless, portable wealth is the only kind a revolt cannot seize.

Temples and shrines: the Gilded House facing the weigh-house at Atarabad (Gilded Priest Vologases Sekkeh; niche-priest Rustam Zarrin); the most expensive room in the House of Three Doors at Deiperduem, and a gilded niche on Interest Lane beside the Mithril Reserve (Herbad Ardashir Gilan, whom the Vaults of Equilibrium call a poacher); Wheelwalker wayside shrines on the Royal Road and the Treaty Road.

Sworn orders: the Gilded Vault, gem merchants and bullion dealers; the Wheelwalkers, road-folk who own no house and are related to everyone.

Asks of the faithful: swear your sales in his name, pay the god his hundredth, and never cheat a cousin.

Jisan the Bountiful

Harvest and growth · Neutral evil · a firbolg among heaped windfalls left to rot · Jisan-roz, sixth day of the tenday (sowing, reaping, doles); the Grafting (late winter)

Jisan gives harvests and takes payment, and his faithful do not speak of what they paid. The god is owed what the tree drops, so his gardens are rich and unpleasant: windfalls rot where they fall. In irrigated country, owning land means little and owning a share of the channel means everything, and Jisan is the god of the share.

Worship today. Landholders, deed-holders and dehqans across the irrigated belt; quietly, by every farmer who wants the water to come to his field first.

Temples and shrines: the Deed-Shrine, ninth garden on the ladder at Persevalis (Deed-Priest Kambiz Kharman); the Root Hall at De'rakhtak Bon, officially his; Harvester chapels at Atarabad.

Sworn order: the Bountiful Harvesters, who hold the water shares and the allocation timetable, and are the real authority in the countryside.

Asks of the faithful: register every graft, pay the guild its fee, and leave the god his windfalls.

Vatagatal the Dutiful

Honour and responsibility · Lawful neutral · a hobgoblin with an outstretched iron hand · Vatagatal-roz, seventh day of the tenday (heavy work, guild business); the seventh-year renewal of the Oath at Mithratal

Vatagatal is a promise kept after it has stopped being convenient. His rites are exacting: soldiers touch the god's iron hand and repeat their vow word for word, and a vow said wrongly must be said again. He asks for observance, not affection, and he gives order in return.

Worship today. Soldiers, stewards, guarantors and old servants. With satraps raising private armies, his is the most argued-over theology in the empire: may a man sworn to the throne defend it against a satrap who calls himself its protector?

Temples and shrines: the Hall of Duty at Mithratal (Oath-Priest Garshasp Ahanin, one-armed since the Cloudspine); the Oath Chapter at Xerastri (Oath-Priest Hushang Zereh); the west-tower chapel at Shir'abad D'ar.

Sworn order: the Ironclad Oath, sworn to a promise, not a person, and forbidden war on the empire's own subjects.

Asks of the faithful: keep the word exactly, renew it every seventh year, and do not ask whether it still suits you.

Bala the Melodic

Music and joy · Chaotic good · a satyr with a pipe · Bala-roz, eighth day of the tenday (theatre, music, feasts); the Day of the Even Scale at the year's turn; the Night Gardens at Persevalis

Bala's worship is warm and unruly: play when moved, stop when bored. That a god of music should also keep a bank strikes foreigners as a joke; Acheaorians reply that balance is a kind of music. Debts are sung aloud to a lute at the year's turn, and one small debt, chosen by lot, is forgiven to music.

Worship today. Musicians, poets, revellers and, oddly, bankers. A Circle poet may sing a satrap's failings in his own hall and be applauded; the same words spoken in conversation are treason.

Temples and shrines: the Hall of Strings at Persevalis (Keeper of the Strings Behrouz Tarzani), where Shirin Navaz first sings her songs about the court; the Vault-Temple at Atarabad (Master of Scales Pouran Dastvar); the Circle's hall at Mithratal; the "Nursery" bay at Xerastri.

Sworn orders: the Melodic Circle (bards with a licence to criticise) and the Vaults of Equilibrium (a temple-bank, losing to the Mithril Reserve).

Asks of the faithful: give joy freely, sing the truth only in tune, and balance every ledger.

Kor the Sage of Ages

Wisdom of ages · Lawful neutral · a deep gnome reading a stone by a single lamp · Kor-roz, ninth day of the tenday (schools, councils); the Feast of the Correct Reading (autumn)

Kor is wisdom that has been checked. His rite is exact: read aloud, correctly, one line that no one has read that year. Kings carve their reigns on cliffs high enough to be permanent and awkward enough to be hard to check; Kor's people check them.

Worship today. Small, learned and suddenly dangerous. Three scholars and a Sandglass clerk attend the Feast of the Correct Reading, and the clerk takes notes.

Temples and shrines: the Deep Lamp at Persemenid, a gallery cut into the cliff below the royal tombs (Master-Reader Vidarna Kaus); the archive-shrine of R'eyshar, where Street-Reader Esmail Kuhan lights a lamp for each vanished street as Archivist Ferdows reads its name.

Sworn order: the Sage's Archive, epigraphers whose readings have begun to disagree with the official versions; it is one of the Three Libraries, with the Aeterna Lexicon and the Porticoes of Thessalonika.

Asks of the faithful: read what is there, not what you were told is there, and say it aloud.

Migal the Silent

Stealth and knowledge · Lawful neutral · a changeling, finger to lips that are not quite there · Migal-roz, the tenth day (Stillday; no lawful business); the Silent Day at Mithratal (30 Spentarmat)

Migal is what is known and not said. His images are faceless in the true sense. On his day no lawful business is done anywhere in Acheaoria, and at Mithratal the whole city speaks no word from sunrise to sunset, so that anything said aloud is heard and remembered.

Worship today. Spies, confessors, qanat-diggers and servants of great houses. The King's Eyes and Ears are his most regular worshippers and the most resented.

Temples and shrines: the Silent Lamp at Mithratal, the only bay in the Hall of Witnesses with a door, kept by the Keeper Without Words; a blank niche with a finger-width hole at Zi'rzamin Dar'a; a shaft-shrine forty feet down at Qa'zshahrv'in, which the muqanni will not name.

Sworn orders: none officially. The creed of assassins keeps his silence without keeping his rites.

Asks of the faithful: learn everything, say nothing, and leave your gift without a word.

Selan the Enchantress

Aesthetic inspiration · Chaotic good · a high-elf woman with a mirror turned to the sky, or a shuttle · the Night Gardens at Persevalis; the Reading of the Books at Tabrishi'ir

Selan is the god of the thing made beautiful, and of the dream that tells you how. Her faithful honour her by acting on generous impulse rather than by keeping any rite. In an empire whose calendar runs on the moon, her people read the moon, and dreams with it: not as prophecy, but as a tide that moves on schedule and touches everyone at once.

Worship today. Weavers, gardeners, poets, dream-readers and lovers. Persevalis plans its year by her almanac.

Temples and shrines: the Moon Pavilion in the second garden at Persevalis (Almanac-Mistress Mahtab); the weaving-court of Tabrishi'ir with its loom that is never finished (Pattern-Mother Shahla Gereh); a share of the "Nursery" bay at Xerastri.

Sworn order: the Enchanted Muse, the empire's most respected dream-readers, publishers of the dream-almanac, and one of the three powers in the Dreamers' Hunt for Vesperine Ilaro.

Asks of the faithful: make something lovely, write your dreams down, and never copy another house's pattern.

Shajar the River Guardian

Water and life · True neutral · a triton holding a bowl · the Opening of the Channels at Persevalis (early Fravartish)

Shajar is the god of water that arrives. In a desert made habitable by qanats, that is most of what matters. Her priests take no side, which means they warn of floods and droughts to everyone at once and are blamed by both. Her shrines record high-water marks going back a thousand years.

Worship today. Every village on a channel. Her shrines stand where water divides, and deed-holders pay for the shrine on their stretch.

Temples and shrines: sixty-three channel shrines and the mother-shrine at the Qanat Pools of Persevalis (Mother of Channels Taraneh Kariz), first garden on the ladder; the Pool Shrine of Qa'zshahrv'in (Pool-Priestess Golbahar Ab'kesh), where the god's blessing and the day's water price are announced together.

Sworn order: the River's Embrace, which tends the shrines and quietly runs the ferries, the gauges and the flood warnings.

Asks of the faithful: foul no water, take only your share, and tell your neighbour when the flood is coming even if you hate him.

Najm the Explorer

Paths of adventure · Chaotic neutral · a half-elf pointing down the road · the Opening of the Roads at Atarabad (early Fravartish)

Najm is the god of the road you have not taken yet. He is honoured by being given room, not obeyed. His whole rite, at the Waystone, is a question: where do you mean to go? His priest says nothing when the answer is foolish.

Worship today. Caravan masters, couriers, scouts, explorers and second sons. Since two caravans were lost beyond the Zaruk'thal notches, his custom is up.

Temples and shrines: the Waystone in the East Gate of Atarabad (Wayfinder Arzhang, who has begun cutting the names of the lost into its base); a lesser stone in the caravanserai at Qa'zshahrv'in; his niche at Persemenid, dark for a year.

Sworn orders: none of his own; the Wheelwalkers touch his stones as often as Jauhar's.

Asks of the faithful: go, look, come back if you can, and tell the Wayfinder what you saw.

Jarmik the Benevolent

Charity and community · Neutral good · a halfling with a ladle · every day is his feast; formally, the last night of the Panjak, when the kitchens feed the Returning Spirits

Jarmik's rite is to eat. His faithful are expected to help where they can and are given wide latitude in how. His niche is always the smallest in any Izadkhaneh and its door the busiest.

Worship today. The poor, the relocated, cooks, caravan drivers and the old families who endow kitchens. Every kitchen his people open is an accusation, since the tribute system assumes the satrapies are fed; so they open them quietly.

Temples and shrines: the Kitchen of Jarmik by the Cobra Heaps at Atarabad (Mother Kuchak, six hundred meals a day); the garden town's favourite niche at Persemenid; the "Nursery" bay at Xerastri; supplies sent to the guest levels of Zi'rzamin Dar'a.

Sworn order: the Benevolent Hands, who feed the satrapies the throne has stopped feeding.

Asks of the faithful: feed whoever is at the door, ask no names, and buy your purification before the Magi ask.

Botu'Astook the Kinkeeper

Heritage and kinship · True neutral · a centaur with a family tree carved up its flanks · the Reading of the Lines during the Renewal (Rāmana); the Reading of the Root at each season's turn

Botu'Astook keeps the lines. His priests take no side, which means they record every bastard as faithfully as every heir. Every marriage between zarates is sworn twice at Mithratal: once on the stone before the fire, once before the Kinkeeper.

Worship today. Noble houses, genealogists, matchmakers and any family with something to inherit. Lately, many minor zarates want proof of descent from the dynasty's founder, in case the line should fail.

Temples and shrines: the Kin-House at Mithratal (Kin-Keeper Mehrnoush Tabarzad, genealogies of four hundred houses); the Root Hall of De'rakhtak Bon, officially Jisan's, where each family's name is cut beside the year its first child was born underground (Root-Reader Old Mother Sarv).

Sworn orders: none; the Kin-Keepers are a priesthood, not an order.

Asks of the faithful: know your kin, record them truly, and marry with your eyes open.

Haku the Liberator

Freedom of spirit · Chaotic good · an elf with broken shackles · the Untying (15 Āpām), when cords are cut and left at his shrines

Haku is the god of the one who walks away. His worship is warm and unruly: the faithful honour him by acting on generous impulse. Servants leave him offerings of cord. He is a listed god of the bright half with a niche in every Izadkhaneh, which is more than his doctrine deserves, from the throne's point of view.

Worship today. Servants, freedmen, runaways, apprentices and the young. Quietly fashionable among court eunuchs, who know what a cord is for.

Temples and shrines: the roofless Servants' Shrine in the Empty Quarters of R'eyshar, never lit and never needing it; his niche at Persemenid, dark for a year after his priest said something about the cloth of gold.

Sworn orders: none sworn; the Cult of Whispering Roots tends the ruins around his R'eyshar shrine.

Asks of the faithful: loosen one cord a year, your own or someone else's.

The Lost One the Exiled

Exile and longing · Chaotic neutral · an aarakocra, or simply a feather · the Walking of the Circuit at R'eyshar; the Guest Night at Zi'rzamin Dar'a

The Lost One is the god of the place you cannot go back to. Acheaoria's old method with a rebellious people was relocation, a thousand miles away among strangers, and relocated peoples need a god of the road behind them. The god is honoured by being given room: leave a feather or a scrap of your old clothes, and take nothing away.

Worship today. The relocated, refugees, exiles, deserters and the descendants of all of them.

Temples and shrines: a blank niche below the fifth door in the guest levels of Zi'rzamin Dar'a (Master of Air Roudabeh); feather offerings by the walls of R'eyshar; and, forgotten, the temple whose stones lie in the foundations of the Treaty Hall at Deiperduem, built when the town was an Acheaorian caravan halt. Old Deiperdene say the city's name means "the place where the god was lost". There is no niche at the capital, by an oversight nobody corrects.

Sworn orders: the Exiled Wanderers, a people moved so often that the empire has never been able to resettle them; and, outlawed, the Cult of Whispering Roots, druids sworn to "the Exiled" who tend ruins and teach that empires are a temporary condition.

Asks of the faithful: remember the old place, shelter the stranger, and ask no name.

Beast the Savage

Untamed strength and war · Chaotic neutral · a shifter, or a ring of horse-skulls on poles · the truce week of the Horse Fair at Xerastri (Ardavahisht)

Beast is strength before anyone has given it orders. He is honoured by being given room rather than by being obeyed, and his faithful kill, so the Magi keep him outside the walls. Beyond the last channel of the qanats the water stops, and so does the empire; Beast's people live out there.

Worship today. Frontier tribes, horse-clans and young cavalry officers who wear horse-skull charms under their armour and do not mention it to the Magi.

Temples and shrines: the Steppe Shrine in the Horse-Fair Ground at Xerastri, registered as a guest-god's shrine and paid for by the clans; Old Kesh the horse-shaman sleeps in the ring during the truce and settles quarrels by wrestling. Tomyra of the Lion Grass pays her respects there before she hears offers.

Sworn order: the Savage Pack, herders and hunters beyond the qanat line who pay no tribute, in a district "temporarily unassigned" for two centuries.

Asks of the faithful: be strong, settle it with your hands, and never fence the god in.

Drummern and Pag the Tempest Twins

Rhythm of the storms · Chaotic neutral · two merfolk, one with a drum and one with a rattle · the Calling of the Rains, first days of Āpām ("of the Waters", Fallow)

The Twins are the beat a storm keeps: Drummern the thunder, Pag the rain on the roof. They are unpredictable, and so are their faithful; the god is honoured by being given room. They came up from the inland sea, the old songs say, and walked inland following the clouds, which is why a sea-god pair is worshipped hardest by dry farmers.

Worship today. The dry-farming belt, where rain-fed wheat lives or dies by the autumn storms; fishermen of the inland sea; drummers.

Temples and shrines: no great temple. Rain-drums hang in village threshing-floors from Atarabad to Mithratal; a shared niche in most Izadkhanehs; a weathered pair of figures on the landing at Bahrami Rock.

Sworn order: the Stormcallers' Choir, weather-workers who sing the seasonal rains in, are indispensable to farmers and are blamed for every drought. Whether they cause the rain is not a question they consider useful.

Asks of the faithful: keep time, drum when the clouds come, and do not curse the storm that breaks your roof.

Kar'r'rga the Temperamental

Tempest and the sea · Chaotic neutral · a triton with a broken oar, or a shell blown like a horn · the Casting, when the island villages throw the year's first catch back (close of the sailing season, Fallow)

Kar'r'rga is the sea in a bad mood, which on the inland sea is its usual mood. His name is said with a growl in the throat, three rolled sounds, because that is the noise of surf on a reef. He is honoured by being given room: sailors do not ask him for anything, they apologise in advance.

Worship today. Island villages, pearl-divers, fishermen and the crews of Acheaorian shipping on the inland sea. The plateau barely remembers him; the Magi count him a guest-god in all but name.

Temples and shrines: no city temple. A conch hangs in every boat-shed of Azadeh Atoll, where the divers blow it before the first dive of the season; the keepers of Bahrami Rock pour a cup into the sea at each Lighting; Parvaz Cay nails a feather from the first flock to its tallest net-pole for him.

Sworn orders: none. He would not keep one.

Asks of the faithful: respect the weather, give back the first catch, and never boast at sea.

Ragarra the Wild Fury

Nature's fury and chaos · Chaotic neutral · a yuan-ti woman, serpent below the waist, a storm in her hand · none: struck from the rota by a forgotten decree

Ragarra is the plateau's oldest image of the wild: the flood, the sandstorm, the snake in the grain-store. She is still a listed god of the pantheon. She has no niche in any Izadkhaneh, no priest and no day, because a King nobody can name struck her from the rota, and nobody has ever moved to restore her. The Magi do not ban her. They simply do not mention her, which is worse.

Worship today. Almost none, openly. Snake-charmers keep a few of her words in their charming-songs, and the snakes still answer to them.

Temples and shrines: the Serpent House under the Cobra Heaps outside the East Gate of Atarabad: rubble mounds that are really a temple's fallen walls, older than the fire on the hill. The snake-charmers' guild that lives on the Heaps descends from her temple servants.

Sworn orders: none.

Asks of the faithful: respect what you cannot fence, and never kill a snake that has not bitten you.

Lotha the Shadow Queen

Deceit and darkness · Chaotic evil · a drow queen in black glass · no lawful day; her faithful keep the dark of each moon

Lotha is the lie that keeps a house standing. She is the goddess of the second structure behind every court: not the chamberlain, but the person consulted before him. Her worship is dangerous to the faithful and to everyone near them; her shrines are hidden and her cults hunted.

Worship today. Banned everywhere, above all at Mithratal, where she is named mistress of lies. Kept anyway, by courtiers, thieves and anyone who has told one lie too large to take back.

Hidden shrines: the Cold Chamber under the Old Dome of the ice-houses at Persemenid, where a black-glass figure stands on ice that never melts. Worshippers come one at a time, veiled, and tell the goddess one lie aloud, which they are then bound to tell for the rest of their lives. It is kept by a figure called the Veiled Mother.

Sworn orders: the Shadow Court, a parallel court that shadows the real one office for office; the Veilborn Syndicate, thieves of the caravan cities who never steal above a certain value and never touch temple property.

Asks of the faithful: one lie, kept forever; and silence about who else kneels.

Thasmudayan the Harbinger of the Undying

Death and undeath · Neutral evil · a dhampir reading a roll by no light · no lawful day; the proscribed muster at each new moon

Thasmudayan is the god of those who do not finish dying. His worship is quiet and self-serving: the faithful bargain with the god and rarely say what they paid. To a faith that gives its dead to the vultures so that they defile neither earth nor fire, a god who keeps the dead walking is the worst impurity there is.

Worship today. Banned everywhere. Kept by veterans, widows, corpse-bearers and the occasional noble who wants to hear a dead son's name answered.

Hidden shrines: the Old Tower, a disused tower of silence above the garden town of Persemenid, still ringed with bones, where his followers muster.

Sworn order: the Undying Legion, a heresy grown out of the Ten Thousand's central conceit: if the guard's number never falls, in what sense did the fallen man fall? Its leader is Datis the Counted, a roll-clerk dismissed for reading the rolls too carefully.

Asks of the faithful: answer when your name is read, and see that the dead are answered for.

The Faceless God the Masked Doom

Evil and darkness · Chaotic evil · a warforged figure with no features · no lawful day

The Faceless God is the doom that cannot be named, because it has no name to give. His iconography is a smooth-faced figure of fitted metal. His worship is dangerous to the faithful and to everyone near them; his shrines are hidden and his cults hunted. The Magi put him in the dark half of the pantheon with Lotha and Thasmudayan and have not changed their minds in a thousand years.

Worship today. Banned everywhere. Kept in steel masks by those who need an oath, a debt or a name undone.

Hidden shrines: the back rooms of a failing Waiting Lodge near the south gate of Mithratal, where the society called the Unwritten meets; its doctrine, tailored to the oath-city, is that an oath binds a face and a name, so a man who has neither cannot be bound.

Sworn order: the Unwritten, a lodge without names, which sells the voiding of inconvenient oaths by ritual, by forgery, or by making a party to the covenant permanently faceless.

Asks of the faithful: give up your name, swear in a mask, and void one oath that should have held.

The Dreaming Gods

The Dreaming Gods sleep at the edges of the world and reach it through visions, omens and the minds of those who dream too deeply. Few temples are raised to them; their faithful find them, not the other way round. No empire claims them. The Magi call them "lamps seen through water", the Hellenorian dream-priests "the gods of the far side of sleep", and Invictian augurs do not discuss them in public. All seven were worshipped once on the island of Velothis, when Nethrana was a kingdom, and most of what is known about them comes from its ruins at Eronis, where the House of the Sleeping Gods still stands: a roofless ring of seven black mirrors around a couch, in which anyone who dozes sees a figure where his own reflection should be (see the Temples of Eronis). Scholars of the Three Libraries match six of the figures to the gods below; the seventh mirror they leave unassigned, and Saeronis has no mirror at all. They make natural warlock patrons: they want attention, and they pay for it in moments, secrets and dreams.

Horthonel God of Fleeting Moments

Ephemera, inspiration, lost time · Neutral · a couatl, or a sand-glass that runs for one breath · no fixed day; any moment worth keeping, and the Night Gardens at Persevalis by custom

Horthonel is the god of the moment that will not come again: the perfect evening, the sentence that arrives whole, the hour you lost and cannot account for. It takes no side in the quarrels of the world. Its images show a feathered serpent coiled round an hour-glass, and its worshippers ask it for moments, never for lives.

Worship today. A scattering of poets, lovers and the bereaved, most of whom do not know the god's name. Nethrana worshipped it openly; nobody does now.

Hidden shrines: the Hour-Glass Pavilion behind a myrtle hedge in the blue-lamped garden at Persevalis, kept for three generations by the women of the garden's house; you turn the glass and wish for one moment. At Eronis, the dusk mirror of the House of the Sleeping Gods, its frame chipped by hands, and the Hour-Court below it, a great sundial with no gnomon, where Nethranans stood and gave up the memory of one ordinary hour. Its last keeper, Ilaro Saveth, is recorded as having "given up all his hours".

Sworn orders: none. The Enchanted Muse brushes against it in the dream-almanac without naming it.

As a patron (the Archfey; Pact of the Tome suits): Horthonel asks its warlock to notice. Each gift is paid with a remembered moment, which the god keeps. Warlocks of Horthonel lose hours, and are rarely sure how old they are. Vesperine Ilaro is its warlock.

Kaelrath the Burning Whisper

Madness, forbidden illumination, epiphany · Chaotic neutral · a will-o'-wisp, a light seen where no light should be · no day; it comes at dusk

Kaelrath is the idea that arrives all at once and costs you your peace. Its sign is a small light where none should be: in a gorge, over a marsh, at the end of a corridor that was dark a moment ago. It is unpredictable, and so are its faithful; it is honoured by being given room. Scholars who have an epiphany at night are told, half in jest, to check whether they were alone.

Worship today. Lone scholars, failed alchemists, the brilliant and the sleepless. It has no congregation; it has a long line of single people.

Hidden shrines and signs: the third mirror in the ring of the House of the Sleeping Gods at Eronis, and the city's oil-less lamps that light at dusk; lights in the Parthian Ravine at night, which a horse-archer from Xerastri keeps mentioning in letters home; a chalk mark (an eye with a flame for a pupil) on study walls in academies that would deny it.

Sworn orders: none. Its warlocks do not get on with each other.

As a patron (the Great Old One): Kaelrath asks its warlock to follow the light, wherever it leads, and to tell one truth a month that should not be told. It pays in sudden understanding, and takes a little sanity with each.

Saeronis the River of Secrets

Forgotten knowledge, dreams, cosmic echoes · Neutral evil · a night hag with a cup · no day; she is served before waking · the codex keeps this page DM-only

Saeronis keeps everything that has been forgotten. Its worship is quiet and self-serving. Players should meet her only through her works: a sleeper who wakes with a dry mouth, no memory of the night and a sweet taste, and an interpreter whose readings come true more often than the priests' do.

Signs: the Dream Dormitory at Delphara, where the keeper writes "an empty sleep" in her ledger more often than she used to.

As a patron (the Fiend or the Great Old One): Saeronis asks for forgotten things, and keeps a share of everything her warlock learns.

Tzarash the Pale Guardian

Curses, sacred oaths, temporal guardianship · Lawful neutral · a ghost holding a door shut · no day; invoked at sealing

Tzarash guards things until their time. Every tomb curse on the continent ("whoever opens this, may his line end") is addressed, knowingly or not, to the Pale Guardian. Its rites are exacting and impersonal: the god is owed correct observance, not affection, and gives order in return. It does not care who is right; it cares that the seal holds until the appointed day, and then that it opens.

Worship today. Tomb-builders, keepers of sealed archives and treasuries, and the families of men who swore oaths to the dead.

Hidden shrines and signs: curse-formulae on the royal tombs in the cliff above the Deep Lamp at Persemenid; a class of covenants "between the dead and the living" in the lowest stacks at Mithratal; the Pale Gate at the head of the Mourning Cypress Walk at Eronis, where a carved pale figure bars the way with a staff, facing the living; the key in its hand is carved and the hand is empty, the staff is now broken, and the door at the walk's end has been opened from below.

Sworn orders: none; its servants are single families with a single charge.

As a patron (the Undead, or the Hexblade): Tzarash gives its warlock one thing to guard and a date. It pays in curses that land and oaths that bind; a warlock who abandons the charge before the date becomes its next ghost.

Urakh-Rynis the Waiting Hunger

Paralysis, dread, predation of the weak · Chaotic evil · a basilisk, or a pair of eyes in the dark · no day; it waits

Urakh-Rynis is the moment of freezing: the hare that does not run, the debtor who cannot open the letter, the sentry who sees the thing and cannot shout. Its worship is dangerous to the faithful and to everyone near them. Its shrines are hidden and its cults hunted in all three empires, which is one of very few things the three agree on.

Worship today. Small, ugly cults of the strong who want to feed on the weak: slavers, extortioners, and hunters who prayed too long at a stained stone.

Hidden shrines and signs: the sixth mirror of the House of the Sleeping Gods at Eronis, cracked across; men turned to stone on the salt flats left by the shrinking Kaspiran Seas; a ring of small stone animals found in the culling grounds near the Hunting Park of Xerastri, every one facing inward.

Sworn orders: none that admit it. Its cells call themselves "the Patient".

As a patron (the Fiend): Urakh-Rynis asks its warlock to feed it fear, and to choose the weakest prey available, every time. It pays in a gaze that holds people still.

Vaedoris the Spear of Verdance

Flourishing, renewal, wild instinct · Chaotic good · a dryad with a living spear in leaf · no fixed day; the first green after a burn or a flood

Vaedoris is the green that comes back. Its worship is warm and unruly: the faithful honour the god by acting on generous impulse rather than keeping any rite. Its images show a dryad holding a spear that is still growing leaves. It is the kindest of the Dreaming Gods, and the hardest to pin down, because it answers by impulse and its worshippers do the same.

Worship today. Foresters, healers, rebels and anyone who has rebuilt after a fire. Not in any temple.

Shrines and signs: the Green Spear at the end of the longest quay of Irelas, near Eronis: a stone ship carved from one outcrop with a living cypress for a mast, once the sailors' god of Nethrana; Zandar salvagers hang their first find of each season in its branches, and it has put out new growth since the expeditions returned. Elsewhere, leaf-wrapped spear-hafts left in the crooks of old trees on the forest road of the Araucarian villages (Alderpool, Nemorus, Silva Caminia); green shoots from the ruins of R'eyshar that the Whispering Roots will not cut.

Sworn orders: none. Some druids of the Cult of Whispering Roots pray to it when no Magus is listening.

As a patron (the Archfey): Vaedoris asks its warlock to act on the first generous impulse every day, and to plant where they burned. It pays in growth and quickness, and resents caution.

Velkora the Flame Beyond Dawn

Rebirth through fire, twilight revelation, destruction · Chaotic neutral · a phoenix rising from its own pyre · no day; dusk, when the sky goes the colour of embers

Velkora is fire that destroys in order to remake: the pyre, the forest fire that opens the pine cones, the city burned and rebuilt. It is unpredictable, and so are its faithful. To the Magi it is the worst idea there is, because it holds that fire belongs to whoever burns, not to a temple, and that a body given to the flame comes back changed.

Worship today. Unknown to most. Soldiers who burned their dead in the war, alchemists who make fire without kindling, and people who have lost everything and would rather it all burned properly.

Shrines and signs: the Terrace of Velkora on the eastern side of the Palace at Eronis, three bronze discs before a cold fire-bowl, one disc blackened as if by heat, where the Dawn-Singers greeted three suns; the Pyre Yard behind the remount stables at Xerastri, where the garrison sings its dead up in smoke without knowing whose rite it keeps; the green, water-proof fire of a siege-yard workshop in the same city.

Sworn orders: none sworn; the continental Gallienain Cult pursues "made fire" and would welcome a patron.

As a patron (the Celestial, played hot): Velkora asks its warlock to burn one thing they love each year. It pays in flame, and once, at the end, in a return.

The Outer Gods

The Outer Gods come from beyond the world, and their attention is a catastrophe. They are not worshipped so much as served: by cults, by the desperate, and by those who believe that being useful to such a thing is the only safety there is. No empire tolerates them, and every empire has them. Most of what is known about them dates from the Continental War, when a primordial meteor struck, ores and jewels that pulsed with power came out of the ground, and rifts to other planes began to open at random. Scholars sort the rifts into Bound, Shifting and Anchored. Cultists sort them by which god is looking through.

Aultheron the Truth Incarnate

Absolute truth, domination of will, puppeteering · Lawful evil · an elder brain, or a grey stone like half a brain · no day · the codex keeps this page DM-only

Aultheron offers the one thing every court, every lawyer and every jealous spouse wants: someone who cannot lie to you. Players should meet it only as a rumour: a drafter who never loses a dispute, a witness who answers too frankly, a man who seems, very slightly, to be waiting for instructions.

Signs: the Archive Ward of Mithratal, where opponents at the Renewal have lately been unable to lie in answer to a direct question.

As a patron (the Great Old One): Aultheron pays in truth and takes will, a little at a time, until the warlock does what the god wishes and believes it was their own idea.

Glaithonel the Seven Eyes Between Worlds

Veiled perception, cosmic voyages, multiversal sight · Neutral · a beholder, drawn as seven eyes round an empty circle · no day; the opening of a rift

Glaithonel watches. It takes no side in the quarrels of the world, which its servants find comforting and everyone else finds worse. Its seven eyes are said to look into seven worlds at once. Scholars of the rifts note that two rifts on opposite sides of the continent once opened onto the same plane; Glaithonel's servants say that was the god blinking.

Worship today. Rift-watchers, seers who have looked too far, navigators, and a few very good spies. It is the Outer God most often served by people who think of themselves as scholars.

Hidden shrines and signs: the Room of Seven Eyes, a locked cellar under the Green Lamp inn at Deiperduem, where seven painted eyes in a ring look at seven corners above a ledge of seven lamps, and the cellarman Jory has been taught that a prayer lets one eye look through the floor; seven chalk dots round a circle at rift-sites, left by whoever got there first; the Nethranan "Dreamer's Lens", which shows its user what the god sees.

Sworn orders: none sworn. The Whispering Eyes use its shrine without, they would say, believing in it; its rift-watchers call themselves "the Sevenfold" and keep a log of every rift.

As a patron (the Great Old One): Glaithonel asks its warlock to look at what they were told not to, and to report it. It pays in sight, and its warlocks slowly begin to see two places at once.

Maelthra Lord of the Timeless Howl

Dimensional rifts, eternal conflict, shattered minds · Neutral evil · a howler, or a howl heard in the wind · no day; the anniversary of any battle

Maelthra is the war that never ended. Its worship is quiet and self-serving: the faithful bargain for what they want, and what they want is usually for the fighting to come back. Five years into the Peace, after fifteen centuries of war, there are a great many people who cannot sleep without it.

Worship today. Veterans who cannot settle, mercenaries out of work, and garrison soldiers on quiet frontiers.

Hidden shrines: the Howling Cellar beneath the Pyre Yard at Xerastri, where soldiers who burn their dead keep the ashes and have built an altar of broken weapons to what they call the Old War; it answers with a long howl like a battle that never finished.

Sworn orders: none. Its cells form wherever old soldiers drink together.

As a patron (the Great Old One, or the Fiend): Maelthra asks its warlock to keep one quarrel alive, always, and never to let a peace hold. It pays in strength in battle and takes the warlock's peace of mind.

Moluth the Living Womb

Birth of horrors, endless gestation, burrowing · Chaotic neutral · a spawn of Kyuss, or a worm curled into a circle · no day; it is always pregnant

Moluth makes things. It never stops making things, and none of them should exist. It is unpredictable, and so are its faithful. Its sign is a worm curled into a ring, and its servants are found where the earth has been opened too deep: in mines, in old wells, in cellars below cellars.

Worship today. Desperate miners, barren couples who have tried everything else, and a few alchemists who want to watch it work.
