Hidden shrines and signs: worm-rings scratched into abandoned galleries of the deep mines near Duneforged, which the miners close with salt and stone; pale, blind animals that should not breed coming up through the old qanat breaches near De'rakhtak Bon.

Sworn orders: none. Its cults are families, and they grow.

As a patron (the Great Old One, or the Undead): Moluth asks its warlock to carry something, plant it somewhere deep, and come back to see what was born. It pays in vitality, and the warlock's body slowly learns to heal in shapes it was not born with.

M'roth and Theal-Koroth the Twins

Cosmic collapse, eternal cycle, unbound potential · Chaotic neutral · two elemental myrmidons, one crumbling and one forming · no day; their servants mark the turn of every cycle

The Twins are the Outer Gods' most philosophical pair: M'roth pulls everything down, Theal-Koroth fills the space with what might be. Their servants teach that nothing is lost, only returned to potential, which sounds hopeful until you notice that they mean cities. They are unpredictable, and so are their faithful.

Worship today. Alchemists of the Gallienain stripe, people who believe the Peace is only a pause, and elementalists who have looked into a rift and liked what they saw.

Hidden shrines and signs: paired cairns at rift-sites, one built and one pulled down by each visitor; a dead caravanserai on the eastern caravan routes beyond Atarabad, where every wall has been taken down and rebuilt a little to the left.

Sworn orders: none. Its circles meet in pairs and never count beyond two.

As a patron (the Genie, played as an elemental power, or the Great Old One): the Twins ask their warlock to unmake one thing and make one thing every season, in equal measure. They pay in elemental power, and dislike anything that stays the same.

Thaun-Mirrath the False Saviour

False hope, shapeshifting, imprisoned power · Chaotic evil · an aboleth, or three pale warm stones in salt water · no day; it calls in sleep

Thaun-Mirrath promises to free you from whatever binds you: debt, a satrap, a marriage, the law. It shows itself, in dreams and in the light of Shifting Rifts, in whatever shape you most hope for. Its worship is dangerous to the faithful and to everyone near them, its shrines are hidden and its cults hunted, and it is the only god on this page that is, in a literal sense, in prison.

Worship today. The desperate and the bound: debtors, conquered peoples, unhappy wives, slaves. It finds them in dreams.

Hidden shrines: the Drowned Room beneath the snake-charmers' compound at Atarabad, reached by a well dry for eighty years, where a basin of Kaspiran salt water holds three pale stones warm to the touch; those who sleep beside it dream of a vast patient thing under the falling sea. Its keeper is Margir Shahrokh, master of the charmers.

Sworn orders: none yet.

As a patron (the Great Old One): Thaun-Mirrath asks its warlock to free others, then to bring them to the water. It pays in shapeshifting and in hope, and every gift loosens its prison a little.

The Black Veil Shroud of Cosmic Night

Oblivion, annihilation, void consumption · Neutral evil · a shadow demon, or a strip of black cloth over a name · no day; the night without stars

The Black Veil is the end of being remembered. Its worship is quiet and self-serving: the faithful bargain to have something erased (a crime, a debt, a rival, a past) and rarely speak of what they paid. Its sign is a strip of black cloth laid over a written name.

Worship today. Criminals, the shamed, the hunted, and people who would like a record to stop existing. Its cells often pose as devotees of the night-goddesses of other pantheons, which those pantheons resent.

Hidden shrines and signs: blank entries in archives that were full last year: the tribute rolls in the House of the Count at Persemenid have three; a black cloth nailed over a family name on a tomb, with the name beneath gone from the stone.

Sworn orders: none that leave a record.

As a patron (the Fiend, or the Undead): the Black Veil asks its warlock to erase one name a year from every place it is written, including memory. It pays in shadow and in being overlooked; its warlocks are hard to remember, even by their friends.

Zarakhal the Slumbering Core

Primordial chaos, stellar dreams, reality shifting · Chaotic neutral · a star spawn, or a black star with a burning heart · no day; nights of falling stars

Zarakhal sleeps, and the world it dreams of is not quite this one. It is unpredictable, and so are its faithful; they honour it by giving it room. Its servants say that when it stirs, the world shifts slightly to match its dream, and that the shifts are getting larger.

Worship today. Star-gazers, rift-miners who handle the war's strange ores, madmen, and a surprising number of jewellers. Every empire has outlawed it; none can say exactly what the law forbids.

Hidden shrines and signs: chips of black star-iron set into rings and worn by people who dream of stars; nights when the stars over the continent are briefly in the wrong places, noted in the Magi's fire-calendar and nobody else's.

Sworn orders: none. Its dreamers recognise each other by the dream.

As a patron (the Great Old One): Zarakhal asks its warlock to sleep where it tells them and to remember what they dream. It pays in power over chance and space, and the warlock's surroundings grow a little less stable.

Expansion

Orders, Guilds and Faiths

Orders, Guilds and Faiths

Asetheria has three empires, one treaty and more than a hundred sworn bodies that outlived the war which made most of them necessary. Every one is tied to a god, and most to an empire. Each also belongs to one of the three loose alignments the codex calls factions: the Impartial, who serve whoever pays and whoever asks (banks, mercenaries, couriers, tax-farmers); the Virtuous, the guilds, healers and knights who think the peace is worth keeping and mostly agree on how, which is their weakness; and the Occult, the cults and outlawed societies that survive by staying in pieces.

The war gave these bodies a job. The peace has taken it away, and five years in each of them is finding out what it is now for. The Imperium's military orders have no enemy and full rolls. Hellenoria's guilds keep a League alive that its own cities are tearing at. In Acheaoria the orders sworn to the throne are watching the satraps stop paying it. Meanwhile the continental bodies, the bank, the toll-farmers and the cults, are doing better than at any time in fifteen centuries.

The cards below give each order's patron, faction, seat and current head, where its houses stand in the cities, what it wants this year, what it asks of members, a hook, and a DM secret. Leaders and chapter-houses already named in the city sections are reused here; follow the links. The summary table lists them all at a glance.

Invictian orders

Abyssal Tideguard Military order · marines and salvage

Neptune's marines: they hold the harbours, own the wrecks, and alone may bless a keel, which is the part that pays.

Neptune · The Impartial · Mavelon, south harbour · Archinauta Lucius Pontius Ancora

Harbour defence, wreck clearance and salvage rights in every Invictian port, and the monopoly on consecrating a new hull. No Invictian captain sails an unblessed keel and the order sets the fee. Its rites buy Neptune off rather than thank him, and its officers are fatalists to a man.

Chapter-houses: the mother-house on the arsenal side of Mavelon's south harbour, next to the warship slips; a salvage station on the lower Tiberius at Fucostia that blesses the barges; the Invictian embassy's salvage contract on the Broken Masts of Varathros Lake; escort crews for grain hulls in the Aeolus Reach.

Now: the war footing is gone and the monopoly is not. The Senate argues about that. The order wants a pilot school opened to Invictians under the treaty, so it can stop paying Hellenorian pilots to take it through Nereid's Veil.

Joining: two years at the oar or the diving-bell and an oath taken waist-deep at night. Members get a share of salvage. They must also attend every launching, however small.

Accord of Infinite Wisdom Philosophical circle · arbitrators

Concordia's mediators. They write the agreements nobody else can get signed, and never lift a finger to enforce one.

Concordia · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Temple of Concord · Concordant Aemilia Pacata

Arbitrators for hire: commercial disputes, inheritance, boundaries and, more and more, the business between Legates who cannot be seen to negotiate. They draft, witness and keep copies. They do not take sides, even when one side is plainly right, and they never enforce. That is why all three empires still use them.

Chapter-houses: the Temple of Concord at Aeterna, below the Arx; a hearing room in the Treaty Hall quarter of Deiperduem; a correspondent at Mithratal, where covenants are sworn.

Now: the Praetors are respected and powerless against a Legate, so serious disputes come here or go to the sword. Fees have tripled. The Accord wants a standing seat as mediator to the Council of Legates, and it is afraid of getting one.

Joining: a written examination and three years as a copyist. Members swear never to hold office or own land in a district where they have arbitrated.

Artisan's Forge of Wonders Magical society · licensed collegium

Minerva's makers: enchantment as a trade, with an apprenticeship, an examination and a guild mark.

Minerva · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Aventine workshops · Magistra Opificum Tullia Sollers

A candidate presents a piece, not a spell, and is judged on the object. The society holds that a wonder that cannot be repeated is an accident, which annoys every other magical order on the continent. Its work is unfashionable, expensive and extremely reliable. As a licensed collegium it examines its members, records their workings and answers for them in court; its seal ring is a casting licence.

Chapter-houses: the guild hall and proving-shop at Aeterna; a fitting-shop beside the arsenal at Mavelon; a buyer's office in the market of the Duneforged Citadel, where it trades blows and patents with House Virellarion.

Now: officers still buy here. So, discreetly, do Hellenorian ones, and the Forge wants that trade made legal under the treaty before somebody prosecutes it.

Joining: seven years' apprenticeship, then a masterpiece. Dues are a tenth of sales. A member who sells an unmarked piece loses the ring.

Aurum Pact Merchant compact · quarantine

The fever-goddess's merchants: they hold the quarantine, and the quarantine is why they are rich.

Febris · The Impartial · Mavelon, the isolation sheds · Master of the Sheds Septimus Febronius Siccus

The Pact handles cargo nobody else will touch, keeps the isolation warehouses outside every major Invictian port, and certifies a hold as clean. Harbour masters accept the certificate and the Mithril Reserve insures against it. Quarantine works by refusing to move goods, which ruins people, and the Pact's rates in an outbreak are remembered for a generation.

Chapter-houses: the isolation sheds at the end of the Farshore mole in Mavelon's south harbour, where every foreign cargo waits before it goes to Romulo's Hall of Weights; the warehouses outside the walls at Fucostia, where inspector Ysolde Varn signs the certificates; a quieter anchorage at Zandar Isle.

Now: Farshore trade has made them rich. Their certificate is the one check the harbour prefects cannot overrule, and the Pact wants it kept that way.

Joining: survive a season in the sheds. Members take a share of fees and an oath never to certify by eye.

Celestial Astromancers Magical society · sky-watchers

They sell the calendar openly and the omens privately, and the Imperium's generals deny buying either.

Caelus · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Tower of the Sky · Augur Servius Caelianus Vigil

The public trade is the calendar: planting dates, sailing seasons, festivals and eclipses, predicted well enough that an unannounced eclipse counts as a professional scandal. The private trade is augury, and that is where the money is. Appointments are kept in a cipher, and the order has survived four purges by proving that it burned the book.

Chapter-houses: the Tower of the Sky in Aeterna; a factor at Helionyx, Quintia Caelestina, who pays the gnomonists' pupils for the solar tables a week before the Reading; watchers on the Latium Plains and at the Fallen Star Shrine on Vael'Tharan Mountain.

Now: with no chief pontiff, nobody can declare an omen void, and a well-timed eclipse is worth a legion. The order wants the Shadowed Vale's Clock Hall tables, and it wants Helionyx never to learn that the Imperium's calendar is calibrated against its arc.

Joining: mathematics, a sworn silence, and ten years of night duty. Members are paid by the reading.

College of the Starlit Lute Bardic college · rural memory

Pomona's singers keep the Imperium's countryside in song, and the war has handed them a great deal to remember.

Pomona · The Virtuous · Romulo · Precentrix Gaia Pomonia Rustica

Planting songs, grafting songs, and harvest cycles that run for hours and change from one district to the next. Held in performance rather than in writing, it is the most complete record of rural Invictian life anywhere. When a village is destroyed, the College sends someone to learn its variants before the survivors scatter.

Chapter-houses: the song-house at Romulo, which sends members every year to record the district's farm songs, the oldest attested; collectors at Falecosa, where Ione of the Lute is taking down the terrace songs; circuits through the Araucarian forest villages.

Now: Ione reports that the newest verses at Falecosa are about burning. The College wants the capital's buyers kept off the terraces long enough to finish the record.

Joining: learn one full harvest cycle by ear. The College feeds and boots its members. They must sing anywhere they are asked, once.

Crimson Warlords Military order · veterans' fraternity

Mars's own order: the most decorated soldiers on the continent, now unemployed, unpaid and very well connected.

Mars · The Impartial · Aeterna, the Campus Hastarum hall · Primus Pilus Gnaeus Marcius Rutilus

The honours are real and so is the battle record. Peace left the order with several thousand men who trust each other and have nothing to do. It keeps its halls, rites and rolls, and the halls have become the place a Legate goes for men who will not ask what the work is. Nobody proposes dissolving Mars's order and survives the proposal.

Chapter-houses: the great hall on the Campus Hastarum, outside the sacred line, which feeds two thousand men a day; an uninvited guard on the veterans' rolls in Romulo's Vault Streets; quiet recruiters at Mavelon; friends at the Veterans' Meadow in the Klynin range.

Now: to be needed again. The hall has not yet asked anything of the men it feeds, and everyone is waiting to see what it will ask.

Joining: a decoration for valour, two sponsors, and a night vigil before Mars Ultor. Members must answer a muster call within three days.

Cycle of the Eternal Bloom Religious order · burial society

Proserpina's order buries half the Imperium's poor by subscription, and keeps a better census than the treasury.

Proserpina · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Horti columbarium · Mater Florens Aelia Verna

Its funerals are performed as the first half of something rather than an ending. In practice it is a burial club: a small monthly due buys a proper rite, a plot and a recorded name, the difference between being buried and being disposed of. Its registers are the best population records in the Imperium. The treasury has twice asked for them, and twice been refused.

Chapter-houses: collectors on every stair of the Insulae; the columbarium at the end of the ridge in the Horti, whose roses grow over dead the order still counts as members; the Quiet Ground at Deiperduem, kept jointly with the Watchers of the Eternal Rest; rim chapels in the Briars Valley.

Now: veterans in the top floors of the Insulae are subscribing in thousands, and the dues are paid in debased coin. The order wants the Mint to honour old prices for burial. It also finds Shaking Rest's marks at about one funeral in forty.

Joining: anyone may subscribe; the clergy serve a year among the dead first.

Emberforge Collective Guild of smiths · structural iron

Hephaestus's smiths: Hellenorian technique, Invictian citizenship, and a long memory for being condescended to.

Hephaestus · The Virtuous · Mavelon, the Mill Banks · House Demetria, masters of the Collective

Bridge fittings, siege frames, aqueduct clamps: the unglamorous iron that holds the Imperium together. They are not armourers and dislike being taken for them. Working to Hephaestus rather than Vulcan is, in the Imperium, a statement.

Chapter-houses: the forge-terraces of the Mill Banks, run by House Demetria; the families' halls in Aeterna's Far Bank; bell-founders who cast the pilot bells of Nereid's Veil; buyers at the calamine diggings of the Klynin range.

Now: since the Treaty they repair instead of build, including three spans of the Aqua Aeterna, and are paid late for all of it. They want payment in Mithril Reserve paper, not the new silver.

Joining: born to a guild family or adopted by one. Members must answer any call to the aqueduct.

Everbloom Circle Magical society · slow botany

Flora's mages graft and wait, and publish a decade later. Their spells feed provinces.

Flora · The Virtuous · Nemibano hill farms · Hortulana Prima Calpurnia Viridis

Horticultural magic so slow most societies deny it is magic. The Circle produced grain that ripens three weeks early on the Latium Plains, a vine that survives Acheaorian frost, and a blight cure that took thirty-one years. Their answer to the scoffers is that those people will be hungry later.

Chapter-houses: test terraces in the hills near Nemibano; trial plots on the Latium Plains; a seed-room at Aeterna; an exchange with the Harvestwrights at Falecosa.

Now: the Annona is failing and the Circle's early grain is suddenly political. The Golden Harvest Covenant wants the seed licensed through it; the Legates want it for their own estates.

Joining: bring a cross you have kept alive for five years. Members swear never to sell a living line outside the Circle.

Golden Harvest Covenant Guild of farmers · the Annona

Ceres's grain guild supplies the dole, which means it can starve the capital.

Ceres · The Virtuous · Aeterna, Mons Cerealis · Magister Frumenti Publius Cerealis Varro

The principal supplier of the Annona. Ceres was always the plebeians' goddess, and the Covenant speaks of the dole as the state's obligation to the people and of itself as the instrument of that obligation, which is a larger claim. It has been paid in debased coin and has said so in public. It does not have to finish the threat.

Chapter-houses: the hall beside Ceres' temple on Mons Cerealis, with the dole office in the portico; a strong chapter at Aepistra; buyers across the Latium Plains, who take the clean rye and leave the black.

Now: a tariff on Khemareti grain, which arrives at half the Annona's price, and payment in old coin. The Legates are holding provincial grain back for their troops.

Joining: own or work grain land. Dues are paid in kind.

Harvestwrights' Guild Guild of orchardists

Pomona's fruit-growers are smaller, richer and fussier than the grain guilds, and they write nothing down.

Pomona · The Virtuous · Falecosa terraces · Insitor Maximus Decimus Helvius Surculus

Grafting is the whole art. Invictian orchards run cultivars kept going by cutting for four hundred years, each with a name, a registry entry and a known parent tree. Membership requires a graft that has survived three winters. The guild is politically invisible and quietly wealthy, and means to stay both.

Chapter-houses: the registry and mother-trees on the Falecosa terraces; orchards around Romulo; a stall of named fruit in Aeterna's markets.

Now: standing advice to members is to sell to whoever holds the road this month. They want the capital houses buying Falecosa's terraces to keep the old trees.

Joining: present the graft. Dues are paid in scions.

Luminous Arcanists Magical society · notation

Phoebus's mages make magic legible, and every other society calls it vandalism.

Phoebus · The Virtuous · Aeterna, beside the Lexicon · Lector Primus Marcus Clarius Scriptor

Two centuries building a written notation in which a working can be recorded, checked and taught: hand a colleague a page and get the same result. The Arcanists think magic is obscure because its practitioners profit from obscurity. They are a licensed collegium, examining scholars and answering for them in court.

Chapter-houses: a reading room beside the Aeterna Lexicon at Aeterna; a copying-room at Romulo; a correspondence with the Porticoes of Thessalonika.

Now: to publish the notation openly under the treaty. The Arcane Academy of Hellarchon would rather it stayed a monopoly; so would the Sable Codes Circle, for darker reasons.

Joining: transcribe a working in notation and have a stranger cast it. Members pay a tenth and teach a term each year.

Oathbound Sanctum Religious order · oath-keepers

Juno's order witnesses the continent's promises and can produce them against anyone, decades later.

Juno · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Arx · Pronuba Maxima Livia Fida

A contract sworn before the Sanctum goes into a register copied, sealed and stored in three cities. The order will produce it against anyone, the state included. It keeps a formal relationship with the Temple of Juno, which keeps the coin standard for the same goddess by the same logic: a coin is a promise about weight.

Chapter-houses: the first register on the Arx; the second at Romulo; the third at Deiperduem. Brother Septimus Auctor is notary in residence at Mithratal's Archive Ward, where the two registries check each other's documents: the only Invictian–Acheaorian legal link the war never cut.

Now: the debasement is a broken promise in the goddess's own name. The correspondence with Juno's priests is unhappy and growing.

Joining: a vow of record, never to destroy a written word. Notaries are paid per seal.

Order of the Silver Flame Fighting order · interveners

Concordia's knights stand between the factions instead of fighting for one, and both sides resent them for it.

Concordia · The Virtuous · Romulo, the chapter house · Grand Warden Aulus Concordius Stator

Where the Accord of Infinite Wisdom mediates, the Silver Flame intervenes: the Order puts itself physically between parties in conflict and refuses to move. It takes no side and so is attacked by both. Its casualties in the long war were appalling for an order that never once mounted an offensive. The two Concordian orders are on strained terms.

Chapter-houses: the chapter house in Romulo's Caravan Suburb, whose knights also guard the city vaults; a growing presence at Aepistra, which locals read as a sign of what is expected; a picket house at the edge of the Campus Hastarum.

Now: all its work is inside the Imperium, between Legates' retinues, between veterans and the Vigiles, between grain convoys and the people who want them. It needs recruits it cannot pay.

Joining: stand one night in the Tent Rows unarmed and come back. Knights own nothing; the Order feeds them.

Radiant Heartwardens Religious order · healers

Asclepius's physicians staff the Imperium's hospitals, and by oath they will not serve a siege.

Asclepius · The Virtuous · Duneforged Citadel, the Infirmary · Archiater Valeria Salvia

The great healing order of the Imperium: military hospitals and public infirmaries in every major city. A Heartwarden may treat soldiers but may not help reduce a city. No poisoned wells, no advice on how disease will spread. Three times in the long war the order withdrew from a campaign, and three times the campaign went worse for it.

Chapter-houses: the mother-infirmary at the Duneforged Citadel; the physicians who go in and out of the sealed wing at Aeterna where Iovianus "recovers", and say nothing, which is their oath; patients sent to the springs at Napplesia and to the Colonnade at Loutrokleion; buyers for the salves of the Shadowed Vale's Hedge of Healing.

Now: the military hospitals have emptied and the veterans' wounds have not healed. The order wants a public infirmary on the Campus Hastarum and cannot get the land.

Joining: five years' training and the oath. Physicians take no fee from the poor and double from Legates.

Scales of Eternal Justice Philosophical circle · auditors

Nemesis's circle pursues excess, not crime, and its targets have usually broken no law at all.

Nemesis · The Impartial · Aeterna, the Rhamnusian Stoa · Censor Hostilia Rigida

A philosophical circle in name and an audit in practice. Members compile holdings, honours and fortunes, and the rate at which they accumulate. When a case is ripe, the Scales publish. They do not prosecute or threaten; they put the arithmetic of someone's rise in front of people who had not added it up. It works appallingly well.

Chapter-houses: a reading-hall in Aeterna; correspondents at Delphara, where they audit the sanctuary uninvited and have pointed out, in writing, that it produces nothing and is extremely rich; a clerk at Deiperduem's Counting Ward.

Now: the circle is compiling on the Council of Legates, and everyone concerned knows it. Its next publication is expected before winter.

Joining: a sample audit of a stranger's fortune, accurate to a tenth. Members give up their own property to the circle on entry.

Seekers of Eternal Truth Philosophical circle · investigators

Veritas's philosophers investigate claims and publish the findings, and this year the claim is the coinage.

Veritas · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Well-House below the Arx · Quaesitor Gaius Puteus Verax

Any claim will do: a miracle, a boundary, a genealogy, a battle report. The method is documentary and slow, and the findings are published whether or not anyone wanted the question asked. Truth hides at the bottom of a well, the old line says, and the Seekers take that as a practical warning.

Chapter-houses: the Well-House by the Arx, a stair's descent from the Assay at the Temple of Juno; correspondents at the Porticoes of Thessalonika; a copyist at Romulo, checking the master weights.

Now: they are publishing their own assays of Invictian silver against the Temple of Juno's records. The treasury offered them a subsidy. They published the offer.

Joining: disprove something you believed. Members swear to publish anything they find, including about the circle.

Silent Stalkers of the Glade Guild of hunters · guides

Faunus's woodsmen take game, guide armies and read a forest better than any map office.

Faunus · The Impartial · Silva Caminia · Old Faunia Semita, Mistress of the Path

Hunters first and guides more profitably. Invictian columns in wooded country hire them, and a guided column against an unguided one has decided at least two campaigns. They are paid well and treated badly, and know both. They will not hunt where the god has been heard, which the legions call superstition until the wood turns out to be held.

Chapter-houses: the lodge at Silva Caminia, where they recruit the best Semitae guides and take them away; stations along the Araucarian forest road at Nemorus and Alderpool; contract guides on the Foloicauria's edge, hired by surveyors, who are the only Invictians that come back on their own feet.

Now: no armies to guide. Surveyors and timber-buyers pay instead, and the Stalkers dislike where they are being asked to lead them.

Joining: walk a stretch of the forest road blind and name every knot in the cord. Pay is by the day.

Stormlord Vanguard Military order · oath-keepers under arms

Jupiter's order swore to the Treaty itself, and now guards a peace it does not trust.

Jupiter · The Impartial · Aeterna, the Capitoline barracks · Legatus Fulminis Titus Statilius Tonans

The Imperium's treaties are sworn in Jupiter's name, and the Vanguard swore this one: its officers stood witness at Deiperduem. Their oath binds them to the peace, not to the state that made it, so the Vanguard is the one Invictian body formally obliged to oppose an Invictian war of aggression.

Chapter-houses: the barracks below Jupiter's temple at Aeterna; an honour-guard of twelve at the Treaty Hall of Deiperduem, the only Invictian soldiers the city admits; a post on the Aepistra road.

Now: the Council of Legates is testing the edges: provincial actions, punitive expeditions, matters framed as policing. The Vanguard has accepted every framing so far. Inside its halls the argument is bitter.

Joining: legion service and an oath at the Capitol. Members forfeit any land grant from a Legate.

The Obsidian Phalanx Military order · heavy infantry

Bellona's heavy infantry serve the war, not the state. Their loyalty is a live question, and they are at full strength.

Bellona · The Impartial · Campus Hastarum, the ancient quarters · Legatus Bellonae Servius Atrox

Bellona's temple stood outside the sacred line, because war is conducted beyond the walls. The Phalanx has been quartered accordingly for eight hundred years, near Aeterna and never in it. It is the heaviest infantry the Imperium fields, and its oath is to Bellona, not the Dominus Militum. Nobody cared about the difference until now.

Chapter-houses: the ancient quarters beside the Aeterna Garrison on the Campus Hastarum; a depot at Mavelon for the arsenal's shields; recruiters at Anticata's veterans' field.

Now: the Council asks whether an order sworn to war owes anything to a peace. The officers decline to answer, which is an answer. It has asked nobody's leave to stay at full strength.

Joining: legion veterans only, sworn at Bellona's column by casting a spear. Paid from the order's own temple estates.

The Dawnfire Alchemists Guild of apothecaries · burns

Aurora's apothecaries gather before sunrise, keep perfect records, and make the best burn salve in three empires.

Aurora · The Virtuous · Ephelanum, the Invictian quarter · Mater Matuta Lucilla Rorata

Every preparation is made from material cut in a fixed window before dawn, so members keep hours nobody would choose and can prove exactly when a batch was made. Their speciality is burns: salves, dressings and staged treatment, developed for Vulcan's smiths and refined in the war. Every field surgeon in three empires buys it from the same supplier.

Chapter-houses: the dawn-gardens on the red-earth estates outside Ephelanum, on the Invictian side of the Condominium; a dispensary at the arsenal of Mavelon; a stall supplying the forges of the Duneforged Citadel.

Now: Ephelanum's Archon wants the dawn-gardens taxed as sanctuary land, and the Dux wants them exempt as Imperial estate. The guild wants the dispute settled before it has to choose a side.

Joining: a year of dawns without missing one. Members share profits by batch.

The Order of Morning's Rise Mercenary company · contracts it can win

Nike's mercenaries take only wars they expect to win, so their refusal is a political event.

Nike · The Virtuous · Aeterna, the Hall of Wings; field seat at Corinth · Captain-General Lucius Albinus Ortus

Before signing, the Order assesses the campaign and declines anything it judges unwinnable, publicly and with reasons. That makes their acceptance an endorsement and their refusal a scandal. Their record is superb and slightly fraudulent, which they cheerfully admit.

Chapter-houses: the Hall of Wings at Aeterna, its paperwork seat; the standing garrison of the gates of Corinth's Upper Fortress under the Polemarch of the Rock, the nearest thing to an endorsement a company can earn; escorts on the Inland Road out of Larnakidai warehouses.

Now: since the Treaty it has refused every offer put to it, and every offer has come from an Invictian Legate. Corinth, meanwhile, pays on time, and the Order is loyal to whoever does.

Joining: veterans with a winning record and a reference from an enemy. Shares are paid only on victory.

The Vigiles Night watch and fire brigade

Seven cohorts of freedmen with axes and buckets, and the only lawfully armed men inside Aeterna's sacred line.

The city's fire (no patron order) · The Impartial · Aeterna, seven cohort stations · Prefect of the Vigiles Titus Oppius Ursus

No legion may stand inside the line, and the Vigiles are the compromise that made the law survivable. They patrol by night, fight fires with siphons and vinegar blankets, and may break down a door or pull down a neighbour's house to starve a blaze. They are not soldiers and say so. They are also the only armed body a Legate cannot lawfully command.

Chapter-houses: a station every four streets in the Insulae; pairs patrolling the Far Bank; the cohort prisons, whose prisoners the Praefectus Urbi tries at dawn.

Now: veterans have beaten the Vigiles twice this year and the Council of Legates declined both times to intervene. Prefect Ursus has begun quietly enrolling veterans of his own.

Joining: freedmen of six years' residence. Six years' service brings full citizenship, which is the real pay.

Triumphant Vanguard of Glory Military order · keepers of the triumph

Victoria's order guards the triumph's conditions, in a peace that ended without a victory.

Victoria · The Virtuous · Romulo, the Caravan Suburb hall · Master Spurius Nonius Probus

A triumph was never a parade. It is a legal award with conditions: a threshold of enemy dead, a war concluded, a general holding the right command. The Vanguard polices them. The Treaty of Deiperduem ended the fighting without a victory, and by the Vanguard's rules no triumph is owed to anyone for it.

Chapter-houses: the hall in Romulo's Caravan Suburb, which holds the triumphal regalia; the Triumph's route in Aeterna, by custom its own ground on the day.

Now: three Legates have applied; three have been refused, correctly. Spurius Nonius Probus now travels with six guards. The order wants a ruling from somebody with the authority to give one. Nobody has it.

Joining: a decoration won in a war the Imperium won. Membership is closed in practice; the youngest member is fifty-one.

Verdant Sentinel Order Military order · knights of the grove

Diana's knights keep the groves and the edges of the Imperium, and the frontier obeys them before the capital.

Diana · The Virtuous · Ephelanum forest commandery; the Grove at Nemibano · Commander Octavia Venatrix

The Sentinels are the only Invictian authority most frontier villages ever see, so they have picked up duties no charter gives them: settling disputes, licensing hunts, escorting tax collectors who would otherwise not come back. Their oldest custom survives at one grove, where the warden holds his post until another takes it from him in single combat.

Chapter-houses: the commandery in the forest behind Ephelanum; the grove at Nemibano, where Gnaeus Ferrus, Rex Nemorensis, has held the post for nineteen years and the order enforces the farmland rules (no iron plough within sight of the lake, no fire on the slope, no deer hunted); wardens at the Steps; the Boundary Walk at Romulo, where knights re-mark the sacred line.

Now: the capital wants the grove custom abolished, and Sylvia Nemorina wants the order kept honest. Knights in the Klynin range are siding quietly with veterans who squat the sacred springs.

Joining: a year's vigil in the woods; knights forswear hunting for sport.

Watchers of the Eternal Rest Philosophical circle · pensions

Senectus's circle keeps the record of every veteran's unpaid pension, and will not amend it.

Senectus · The Impartial · Romulo, the Vault Streets · Senex Primus Appius Canus

Pensions, annuities, the disposal of estates and, above all, veterans' entitlements. The Watchers hold the registers of who was promised what on discharge, the most inflammatory documents in the Imperium. Three times since the Treaty the treasury has proposed a reconciliation that would quietly reduce the total owed. Three times the Watchers declined and published the request.

Chapter-houses: the veterans' rolls in Romulo's Vault Streets, kept there instead of in Aeterna and now under a Crimson Warlords guard nobody asked for; a pension office at Anticata's Veterans' Field; the Quiet Ground at Deiperduem, shared with the Cycle; arrears postings at Napplesia, which answers loudest.

Now: to publish the full arrears figure. They know what it will do.

Joining: clerks over forty only, by long custom. The circle pays little and pensions its own members generously.

The Five Legions Military · the Imperium's named legions

The Imperium's five legions with names, each built for one job and each now owned in practice by somebody.

Mars and Bellona · The Impartial · Aeterna, the Campus Hastarum · Dominus Militum General Valerius Maximus

The codex's military roll names five special legions apart from the line: Legio Rubrum Obsidianum, "the Emperor's Hammer", numbered Red Knights and Black Knights in overgeared shock formation; Legio Custodia Praetoriana, the Praetorian Custodians; Legio Bestiarum Dominus, the Beastlords; Legio Umbrae Sicarii, the Shadow Assassins; and Legio Arcanum Bellatorum, the war-mages. In law all five answer to the Imperator. In practice they answer to the Dominus Militum, and each has a Legate on the Council who would like it to answer to him.

Stations: the Custodians at Aeterna, outside the line, under Tribunus Cassia Vetra, who keeps a list of which Legates' paymasters have been buying; the Red Knights on the Latium Plains near Decimus Aurelianus Corvus's garrison; the Beastlords in the iron country inland of Mavelon; the war-mages split between Aeterna and Aepistra.

Now: the five are the only formations still paid on time. Every Legate is courting their officers.

Joining: by selection from the line, never by application. The Shadow Assassins select without asking.

The Adamantine Line Military order · the Citadel's legion

The Duneforged Citadel's own legion is older than the primordial brood, which means it survived whatever the brood was.

House Caerthain's oath (no patron order) · The Impartial · Duneforged, the Iron Parade Grounds · Commander Daud, the Royal Protector

The legion of the Duneforged Citadel, raised before the primordial brood and tempered by decades of war since. It held the Cloudspine Ridge against a coalition and broke the Acheaorian advance at the pass. Commander Daud keeps the Duke's person, hence the nickname; Vice-Commander Meagan Foster keeps the legion running; Gavin Caesar commands the standing garrison.

Stations: the Iron Parade Grounds beside the Furnace Ring; the Skyward Bastions on the Cloudspine, repositioned by levitation crystal; the caravan escort rota over the pass, half honour guard, half watch.

Now: to hold the ridge without a war, against House Mihran, which wants one. Daud signs the cedar-cutting licences himself, because the Serathian Fleet's hulls are cut on the Cedar Stair.

Joining: citizens of the Citadel, sworn before House Caerthain. Pay is in Mithril Reserve scrip, which is worth something.

The Serathian Fleet Military order · airships

Caerthain airships that drop into battle like hawks, and the reason a mountain house commands the sky.

House Caerthain · The Impartial · Duneforged, the high moorings · Wing-Commander Elspeth Harrow

Sleek, magically lifted airships founded, by the house's own account, by Empress-Lady Vaelis Caerthain. The Fleet turned a house that held mountains into one that held the air above them. Its hulls are cut from Cloudspine cedar and lifted by the Virellarion crystals, which have not dropped a fortress since the Treaty.

Stations: the moorings above the Citadel; patrols over the Skyward Bastions and Lake Serathal; a shipwrights' exchange with Mavelon, which knows hulls but not lift.

Now: the Fleet wants the prototype, the Sovereign Star, finished. Countess Aurelie Virellarion says the crystals for it need a material House Virellarion refuses to name.

Joining: Citadel-born, light, and unafraid of heights. Airmen are paid double the Line's rate and die at three times it.

Ember & Anvil Shop · House Vulkrim's foundry

"Steel forged in dragonfire, enchanted by the stars": the Vulkrim foundry that arms the Citadel's guard and anyone who can pay.

Vulcan · The Impartial · Duneforged, the Middle District · Master-Smith of House Vulkrim

The Vulkrim family's showroom foundry, supplier to royalty, war colleges and monster-slayers. The catalogue runs from a runed longsword (300 gp) and a mithral-lined shield to matched ceremonial sets. Prices move with the market: a quarter off in a glut, a quarter on when stock is rare. The heavy work is done in the Geomantic Foundries in the ridge below; the forge in town is for show and fitting.

Where: the Middle District by the Marketplace, near the Gilded Crucible and Clan Ironhand's counters.

Now: peace has cut the army orders, so the shop courts adventurers and foreign officers. It would pay well to learn who runs the Cold Forge in the Zaruk'thal Spine, whose vents glow black.

Dealing: customers, not members. Commissions need a deposit of half and a Citadel guarantor.

The Gilded Crucible Shop · House Virellarion's atelier

"Where essence meets excellence": elixirs for archmages, nobles and divine emissaries, sold by the Virellarion family.

Minerva · The Impartial · Duneforged, the Middle District · Lord Ambrose Virellarion

The alchemist's atelier of House Virellarion. Healing potions at 50 gp, an elixir of clarity at 300, heroism at 750, alchemist's fire, frost capsules; prices swing a quarter either way with demand. Countess Aurelie doubled the catalogue after rebuilding the Crucible Spire; her brother Ambrose keeps the shop.

Where: the Middle District, near the Marketplace and Ember & Anvil.

Now: it wants a licence to sell in Aeterna, where the Artisan's Forge of Wonders has blocked it for a decade.

Dealing: customers only. Rare preparations need a sample of the buyer's blood "for calibration", which most customers do not question.

Hellenorian orders

The Amphictyony of Delphara Religious league · the sanctuary council

Twelve cities, twenty-four delegates and one power: the right to close the oracle. It is the last Hellenorian body still obeyed without argument.

Apollo of Delphara · The Impartial · Delphara, the council house on the Sacred Plain · Hieromnemon Eudoros Pythokles

The Amphictyony owns nothing and governs nothing beyond the sanctuary. It sets the festival calendar, audits the treasuries, fixes the bounds of the sacred land and decides who may consult. Delegates swear never to raze an Amphictyonic city or cut its water, and to march against any power that does. Three times it has enforced the rule that the olives of the sacred plain may not be farmed for profit, by sacred war.

Houses: the council on Delphara's Sacred Plain, which audits the Hieromnemon every winter in the Silence; licensing agents at the ruins of Mycarion; none at Ephelanum, which insists loudly that the Amphictyony has no jurisdiction there.

Now: to keep the Golden Tripod's money quiet, keep the tyrants' names off the altars, and keep the oracle the one thing no city can afford to lose.

Joining: a city joins, not a person. Delegates are chosen by their cities and paid by the sanctuary.

Circle of the Eternal Grove Druidic circle · keepers of the Foloicauria

Demeter's druids keep the last old-growth forest in Hellenoria, and remind the League that agreements have terms.

Demeter · The Impartial · the Foloicauria edge · Archdruid Melanthe of the Edge

Keepers of the Foloicauria and of an argument Hellenoria has lost three times. Demeter's displeasure is a famine, not a thunderbolt, and that is the Circle's whole leverage: it does not threaten, it observes that the grove is party to an agreement. Initiates are taken young and taught by degrees, and nothing at the centre of the teaching has leaked in eight centuries.

Houses: the edge-groves of the Foloicauria, which it keeps while older things hold the interior; field-corner groves on the Wet Plain of Thebesieas, where elder Kallirhoe Thesmia speaks at the Ploughing and the city defers to the Circle on land; the cutting rotation agreed generations ago with Alderpool across the border; letters to the druids of Pretanna.

Now: Kallirhoe has warned the Thebesian council about "the channels" three times this year. The Circle wants the Mycairan dikes left alone and every timber licence vetoed.

Joining: taken as a child or not at all. The Circle feeds its own and asks one secret kept forever.

Fate's Spindle Circle Philosophical circle · chance and destiny

Tyche's philosophers study luck as a science, and lend money on it.

Tyche · The Impartial · Corinth, the Stoa of Fortune · Moirarch Klotho Euboulides

A philosophical society that ponders destiny, chance and the threads that bind lives, and treats them as a woven pattern that is always shifting. In Corinth that is not idle. The Circle tabulates luck: wrecks, harvests, dice, the rise and fall of houses. It sells its tables to underwriters, and is the only philosophical school with a bad-debt ledger.

Houses: the Stoa of Fortune on Corinth's Street of Counting Houses; a dicing-hall in the Isthmian Quarter; correspondents among the shipowners of Hellarchon.

Now: to price the peace. The Circle's tables put the odds of a League war within five years at one in three, and it would like someone to pay it to be wrong.

Joining: throw a hundred casts of the knucklebones and record them; the Circle judges the record, not the luck. Members tithe their winnings.

Forgeflame Artisans Guild of smiths · fire-watch

Hellenorian smiths sworn to Vulcan's Invictian name, an old compromise nobody involved enjoys discussing.

Vulcan · The Virtuous · Hellarchon, the Kerameikos forges · Protomastor Hephaistodoros Kaminos

The long war produced this sort of arrangement and nobody has managed to undo it. Vulcan is fire in both aspects, forge and conflagration, so the Artisans keep the fire-watch rites as seriously as the smithing. Their halls are the fire stations of three League cities, and members turn out for any blaze, guild property or not.

Houses: the forges and fire-hall of Hellarchon, whose finished bronze goes out through the harbour; fire-halls at Corinth and Thessalonika; a standing trade with the Emberforge Collective at Mavelon.

Now: the younger members want to revert to Hephaestus. The elders point out that the Emberforge Collective already has that name, that the two guilds trade constantly, and that the argument has never survived an actual order book.

Joining: seven years at the forge and a night on the fire-watch roster. Fire duty is unpaid and compulsory.

Geolith Artisan Covenant Guild of masons

Terra's masons quarry the Oros and build every temple in the League, slowly, and ask the mountain's leave first.

Terra · The Virtuous · the Oros quarries; hall on Hellarchon's Akra · Master Mason Aristeides Lithourgos

Permission is asked before a face is opened, and part of every quarry's output is left uncut. The crews will not work a face opened without the rite, and no amount of League money has ever changed that. A Covenant temple is expected to outlast the city around it, and the ruins tend to bear this out.

Houses: the galleries and Pentelic Terraces of the Oros range, where Aristeides opened the new galleries and insists stone is stone; the hall beside the Akra; silent cutters at the Lamplit Quarries of Nereid's Veil; masons who crossed to Mithratal under safe-conduct to cut the last Setting of the Stone.

Now: to restore the old serpent-channel by the Dream Dormitory at Delphara, refused every year because the goats need it, and to keep the Mithratal contract that proves stone crosses borders.

Joining: carry stone for a year without cutting it. Masons are paid by the finished course.

Ivory Chorus Bardic college · wedding-singers

Aphrodite's singers attend every marriage that matters, which means every alliance, and they repeat nothing.

Aphrodite · The Virtuous · Hellarchon, the Chorus House by the Agora · Archikoryphaia Melitta Charitonis

In a city-state a marriage is an alliance, and the Chorus is present at the negotiation of nearly every important one: composing the songs, witnessing the contracts, hearing everything said before, during and after. They do not sell what they hear. A Chorus singer is safe to talk in front of, and that is why they are always invited.

Houses: the Chorus House near Hellarchon's Agora, whose senior singer dines monthly with the Hegemon's wife; a house at Ephelanum; singers at every symposium on the Long Lane. Unofficially, the League's best information service.

Now: wedding-songs are being commissioned by people with no intention of marrying. The Chorus wants to know who is buying its ears.

Joining: a voice, a memory, and a vow of silence sworn at Aphrodite's altar. Singers are paid by the wedding and fed by the house.

Luminastra Alchemists Guild of apothecaries

Apollo heals and Apollo infects, and these apothecaries train on poisons first.

Apollo · The Virtuous · Corinth, the great workshop · Archiatros Iasonides Phoibammon

The guild supplies most of the League's apothecaries. Preparations are standardised and batches marked, and a member who cannot produce the record of a compound he sold is expelled. That is liability, not ethics, and it makes Luminastra product the only medicine Hellenorian courts accept as evidence of good faith. The guild also holds the continent's most complete poison catalogue and will not sell from it.

Houses: the largest workshop at the end of Corinth's Street of Counting Houses, where every ingredient on the continent passes; the temple dispensary at Ephelanum; an annual tithe of first remedies to Apollo at Delphara; buyers on the thyme slopes of Kirimitsana and at Willowheart.

Now: Willowheart's method, not just its medicine. The enclave will not sell it, and one of the two midwives Willowheart expelled last year now works for the guild at Ephelanum.

Joining: survive the poison course. Members buy their own batch-seal and pay a fiftieth of sales.

Obsidian Veins Magical society · ecstatic practice

Dionysus's mages keep no records, repeat nothing, and get results nobody can explain.

Dionysus · The Occult · Hellarchon, the theatre's undercroft · Thiasarch Bromia, called the Unwritten

The opposite of the Luminous Arcanists, and pleased about it. The Veins work in altered states (wine, exhaustion, rhythm and worse) on the principle that the self is the obstacle. Results are real, sometimes spectacular and almost never repeatable, which the society calls a category error, not a failure. No records, since a record implies someone else could do it again.

Houses: the undercroft of the theatre at Hellarchon, busiest at the Dionysia; "observers" sent to the vintners' run at Delphara's Winter House, who are chased off every year; a thiasos in the vineyards of Araavyna.

Now: the League tolerates them and keeps them away from anything structural. They want a working in the Academy's violet dusk, which they think is the largest unfinished ecstasy in the world.

Joining: three nights in the hills, and come back changed. There are no dues, which is why nobody can find the treasury.

Primalhorn Kin Family and tribe · hill herders

Pan's people of the high pastures wear the horn with pride and answer to no city.

Pan · The Impartial · the Oros and Olympus uplands · Old Aigipan, the Horn-Father

A tribal family bound by ancestral rites and a deep tie to the wild, marked by the horns its men and women wear. Some are satyr-blooded, some not, and the Kin do not ask. They herd goats on the high pastures the cities do not want, guide anyone who pays, and frighten anyone who does not. Their panic, they say, is a gift from the god.

Houses: summer folds on the Olympus range, where they sell cheese to the pass-forts and their silence to the raiders; winter grazing in the Oros, alongside the quarries; a horn-market at Argotiko where they trade with the horse-breeders.

Now: the League has started granting their pastures to veterans and tyrants' friends. The Kin want their grazing written down for the first time, and distrust the idea.

Joining: by blood, or by surviving a winter in the folds. The Kin share all herds.

Sunward Valiants Mercenary company · skirmishers

Hermes's mercenaries march faster than anyone expects, never hold a line, and never break a parley flag.

Hermes · The Virtuous · Hellarchon, the muster-yard on the Long Walls · Hegetor Phaidros Ptenos

Light infantry and skirmishers who are gone before the reply arrives. A Valiant company will not hold a line or garrison, and reserves the right to withdraw on notice. That sounds worthless until someone needs a pass seized before dawn or a supply train cut three valleys away. They carry heralds' privileges, and in a century no Valiant has broken a parley flag. That clause is not negotiable.

Houses: the muster-yard by the halfway tower of the Long Walls, which they will not garrison; the hiring-house under the fallen torso in Helionyx's Fallen Quarter; dispatch boats ordered and prepaid at the Carianea sheds; recruiters at the Malaunian hiring fair.

Now: Hellarchon hires them for speed, Helionyx for salt-road defence, and the tyrants for everything. The Hegetor wants contracts only with the League, and cannot afford it.

Joining: outrun a Valiant over a stade in armour. Pay is high and by the day.

The Crimson Sigil of the Shattered Spear Military order · Ares's broken spears

Ares's order fights under a broken spear and turns every defeat into the next war.

Ares · The Impartial · Thebesieas, the Hollow Rock · Polemarch-of-the-Sigil Lykourgos Rhexenor

Ares has no altar on Delphara's mountain, and his order has no friends in the Amphictyony. The Sigil takes the broken spear as its sign: a shattered weapon still cuts, and loss is fuel. It is controlled destruction for hire, siege-breakers and wall-takers who believe battle cleanses. The cities hire them for sieges and then pay them to leave.

Houses: a chapter in the Hollow Rock on the plain of Thebesieas, the one city that likes them; a mess at the Olympus pass-forts; a broken-spear shrine at Atticenea, where the tyrant pays them retainer.

Now: Thebesieas is arming with Mavelon iron, and the Sigil means to be its edge. It wants a war, and has read the Fate's Spindle odds.

Joining: each recruit breaks their own first spear before the altar. They are paid in plunder.

The Ecliptica Arcanum Magical society · planned magic

Athena's mages plan a working three weeks before they cast it, and so rarely need anything impressive.

Athena · The Virtuous · Hellarchon, the Academy Grove · Archon of the Arcanum Theano Metidis

Contingencies drawn, sequences rehearsed, failure modes assigned. An Ecliptica mage on a battlefield is usually doing something dull, decided weeks earlier, that removes the need for anything impressive. They regard the Obsidian Veins with complete incomprehension: Dionysian practice makes marvellous stories, the Ecliptica say, and they are in the business of outcomes.

Houses: a hall in the Academy Grove, beside the Arcane Academy and loyal to Kallisto Pyrphoros; the house on Helionyx's Evening Terraces, where housemistress Hipponoe wants the cedar presses copied before "somebody careless" burns them; a shrine-office at Athena Pronaia, Delphara.

Now: the Helionyx solar records, before the Celestial Astromancers get them; and a share in the Dreamers' Hunt, planned properly.

Joining: pass the Academy's examinations and draft a campaign plan that survives a hostile reading. Members serve the League fleet in war.

The Golden Scythe Accord Guild of farmers · the grain allocation

Demeter's grain accord decides which Hellenorian city eats in a bad year, with no constitutional standing at all.

Demeter · The Virtuous · Hellarchon, the Emporion · Sitophylax Demaratos Ismenides

Hellenoria imports its bread and always has. The Accord manages the shortfall: contracting cargoes, allocating them and, in a bad year, deciding which city goes short. Its power rests on one fact, that every city needs the next allocation more than it needs to punish the last.

Houses: the contract-hall in Hellarchon's Emporion, which holds the Long Lane grain contract with House Nikandridai; the First Frost blessing at Thessalonika's Sea Wall; the Thebesian seat held by House Ismenidai, who sell the only real surplus in the League; factors at Corinth and Helionyx, which pays for its bread in salt.

Now: the tyrants are testing it, and the Accord has begun demanding payment in advance from cities it does not trust. Khemareti grain could break it.

Joining: cities and grain-houses hold seats; clerks are hired. Seats are inherited and sold.

The Hearthfire Sanctum Religious order · keepers of the civic hearth

Hestia's order keeps the fire every colony is founded with, and it has never let it go out.

Hestia · The Virtuous · Delphara, the common hearth · Hestiarch Aglaonike of the Prytaneion

A colony is founded by carrying fire from the mother city's hearth, and that act, not a charter, makes it a daughter instead of a rival. The Sanctum controls the fire, so it holds an unspoken veto over Hellenorian expansion. It has used it twice, both times against tyrants proposing colonies that were obviously garrisons. Neither refusal was explained, and neither colony was founded.

Houses: the oldest fire in Hellenoria at the eastern end of the common hearth at Delphara; the civic fire in the Prytaneion of Hellarchon's Agora; a house at Ephelanum; a flame in each pass-fort on the Olympus range.

Now: a tyrant has asked for fire for a "colony" on the Malaunian side of the mountains. The Sanctum wants to refuse without starting a war.

Joining: girls and widows, sworn for thirty years. The Sanctum is endowed and pays nothing.

The Matriarch's Loom of Bonds Family society · the widows

Hera's society of matriarchs weaves a thread for every family and cuts one for every death, and it runs Carianea.

Hera · The Impartial · Carianea, the Widows' Terraces · Kallirhoe Kymothois, eldest of the Widows' Council

A family society kept up by generations of matriarchs, who treat kinship and duty as threads in a sacred loom. At Carianea, where diving kills men young, widows hold more property than anywhere in the League, and the Widows' Council meets under the Loom's protection. Marriages are arranged at the Loom, debts are settled there, and its ruling on whether a boy may dive is final.

Houses: the long white house on the Widows' Terraces, with a thread on the loom for every diving family; sister looms in Hellenorian ports that lose men to the sea; a bond-register shared with the Ivory Chorus.

Now: Hellarchon wants Carianea's sons for the fleet. Kallirhoe tolerates the tyrant exactly as long as no son of hers is levied.

Joining: a widow, a mother of divers, or a woman adopted by one. Members pledge a thread and a share of the house.

The Tempest Wrath Conclave Military order · storm-war

Zeus's war-order believes battle cleanses, and its marines come in on the storm.

Zeus · The Impartial · the Aeolus Reach, the Wreckers' Beacon · Keraunarch Brontes Aigaios

A military order of storm-marines and thunder-callers who board in bad weather on purpose. They believe chaos is power and that a battle fought in a storm is judged by Zeus himself. The League fleet used them as the edge of every winter action in the war. In peace they are hard to employ and harder to dismiss.

Houses: the old fort by the Wreckers' Beacon on the Aeolus Reach, where Ixion Keraunios sells winds and they buy; a hall near the Long Walls; a shrine of the thunderbolt at the Olympus pass-forts.

Now: a war, or at least a storm-season contract. Corinth pays them to escort the Haulway's winter traffic; Hellarchon pays them not to escort it.

Joining: swim a winter strait in a storm. Pay is high, irregular and often in wreck-salvage.

Tranquil Hand Enclave Druidic circle · healing and mediation

Druids of two empires, sworn to Terra, heal the land and argue its case with the cities.

Terra · The Impartial · Loutrokleion, the hot springs · Speaker Ianthe Hydrias

A union of druids from several traditions, Hellenorian and Invictian, who heal and restore: spoiled wells, burnt hills, poisoned fields from fifteen centuries of war. They mediate between nature and civilisation, often between a village and its own forest, and take no side but the ground's.

Houses: a retreat above the springs at Loutrokleion, under its old convention of neutrality; a cell in the hill farms of Nemibano, on good terms with Sylvia Nemorina; walking healers on the border marches where the battles were fought.

Now: to clean the battlefields before they are farmed. The Legates want the land cleared quickly for veterans' grants; the Enclave wants it cleared properly.

Joining: heal something that cannot thank you. Members own nothing and travel.

Acheaorian orders

Benevolent Hands Charity guild · kitchens and wells

Jarmik's charity feeds the satrapies the throne has stopped feeding, carefully, and never says so.

Jarmik · The Virtuous · Atarabad, the Kitchen of Jarmik · Mother Kuchak, the First Ladle

Kitchens, wells and almshouses endowed by old families. Every kitchen they open is an accusation, so they open them quietly, name them after donors, and thank the local satrap for a permission he never granted. The endowments are tied in perpetuity, and seizing them would frighten every noble house in the empire. Two satraps have tried, and both were persuaded they had misread the paperwork.

Houses: the Kitchen of Jarmik by the Cobra Heaps at Atarabad, where Mother Kuchak, a halfling who came east with a relocated people forty years ago, feeds six hundred a day and three empires' caravan drivers eat side by side; almshouses along the Royal Road; wells in the neglected northern satrapies.

Now: the charmers' guild at Atarabad has not opened its gate in a month, and its children have stopped coming to supper. Mother Kuchak wants someone to go in. The Hands also want the endowment deeds re-registered at Mithratal before a third satrap tries.

Joining: cook, carry, or give. Donors' names go over the door; workers' names go nowhere.

Bountiful Harvesters Guild of farmers · water shares

They own the qanat shares, which makes them the real power in the Acheaorian countryside.

Jisan · The Virtuous · Atarabad, the Water-Court on Fire Hill · Mirab-Master Kourosh Abyar

Owning land means little where the qanats water it; owning a share of the channel means everything. The Harvesters' real business is the rota: which field takes water, for how long, in what order. Their ledgers are older than the dynasty and count as evidence in satraps' courts. A satrap who quarrels with them finds his estates watered last, strictly by the rota.

Houses: the Water-Court at the foot of Fire Hill, where clerks divide the flow by timed bowls; most shares and all the bowls at Persevalis's Channel Head; the rota at Mithratal's Garden Ward; the water shares of Persemenid's lower city; the guild's grain reserve in the deep cellars of Derakhtak-Bon.

Now: the Predator's Guild has been buying shares, and the eastern channels at Persevalis run faster than the slope allows. The Harvesters want both explained.

Joining: hold a share. Clerks serve twenty years before they may hold one.

Gilded Vault Guild of merchants · gems and bullion

Jauhar's gem-dealers sell the only fortune a satrapy in revolt cannot seize: a stone sewn into a coat.

Jauhar · The Impartial · Atarabad, the Wind-Tower Quarter · Gem-Master Laal Firuzan

Land can be confiscated and debts repudiated, but a stone travels. As the satrapies grow restless the Vault's business has swollen, and changed: fewer jewellers, more nobles turning estates into something that fits in a saddlebag. The Vault keeps no ledger linking a stone to a seller. The satraps know exactly what that means.

Houses: the headquarters behind a door with no sign in Atarabad's Wind-Tower Quarter; oaths sworn at the Gilded House before the Gilded Priest Vologases Sekkeh; a counter at the end of Duneforged's Marketplace; back rooms at Persemenid.

Now: to stay out of politics while carrying half of them. The Veilborn Syndicate never touches the Vault, which is why this year's courier robberies were not the Syndicate's.

Joining: name a stone by touch in the dark. Members pledge a stone of their own as surety.

Lanterns of Justice Roving magistrates

Hakiyah's judges ride with a lamp lit at noon, so their approach is visible for an hour.

Hakiyah · The Virtuous · Mithratal, the Lantern House · Lantern-Captain Zarir Roshanpur

The Lanterns ride circuit through the satrapies hearing cases the local courts will not touch, usually because the defendant owns the court. The lit lantern means a corrupt official has an hour to release the prisoner, restore the property, or run. The order thinks that is the better outcome: its purpose is remedy, not punishment. A murdered Lantern is a lit lamp left in the road, and the empire has learned what that does to a province.

Houses: the Lantern House by the gate of Mithratal's Ordeal Grove; the circuit through Shir'abad D'ar twice a year; a privilege, older than anyone can document, forbidding them to ride within sight of the terrace at Persemenid.

Now: the satraps have stopped running when they see the lamp. Zarir Roshanpur has never yet had to use his sword on a man who saw him coming, and expects to soon.

Joining: a judge's training and a vow to carry the lamp unhooded. Lanterns own a horse and a lamp.

Melodic Circle Guild of bards · the licensed critics

Bala's court musicians are the only people permitted to call a satrap a fool, provided they sing it.

Bala · The Virtuous · Persevalis · Shirin Navaz, First Voice

What is sung is not what is said. A Circle poet may put a satrap's failings into verse in his own hall and be applauded; repeat it in conversation and it is sedition. The Circle guards the licence ferociously, expels members who abuse it, and is in practice Acheaoria's press.

Houses: the First Voice, Shirin Navaz, at Persevalis, singing the satrap's failings in his own hall; the local hall at Mithratal, singing nightly in the Waiting Lodges, where Ruzbeh the Unhurried writes a couplet for every day a party waits; licensed couriers on the Royal Road.

Now: this season's songs are about the court itself. The Court of Vipers has asked for transcripts, which, being sung, do not exist.

Joining: perform before the Circle's elders and survive their criticism. Members are paid by patrons and protected by the licence.

Predator's Guild Guild of hunters · culling rights

Kiga's hunters do the killing the royal hunt was never meant to do, and are paid in meat and water.

Kiga · The Impartial · Persemenid, the Paradise lodge · Master of the Cull Babak Shirgir

The hunting parks are stocked far beyond what the land supports, and without culling the herds sicken and the farms around them fail. The Guild holds licensed culling rights across the plateau, including inside royal enclosures. Paid in meat and hides, it has escaped the currency troubles and is comfortable.

Houses: the lodge in the Paradise of Persemenid; culling rights in the parks of Persevalis; a hide-market in Xerastri's bazaar, shared with the Savage Pack; leopard licences on the Mountain of Kharveth; reed-tiger rights on the Kaspiran shore; rot-lion bounties in the Dasht-a Khaliq.

Now: the masters are buying water shares from the Bountiful Harvesters, the kind of quiet accumulation that ends up mattering. They also covet Tomyra's lion grass on the steppe.

Joining: bring a licensed kill with the hide intact. Members take a share of meat by rank.

Scribes of the Infinite Ledger Merchant-scribes · tribute auditors

Zann's accountants audit the tribute, and their column of refusals is the truest map of the empire.

Zann · The Impartial · Persemenid, the House of the Count · Ledger-Mother Gulnar Zand

Paid by the guild, not the satrapy; rotated before attachments form; forbidden to hold land where they have worked. It is the best-designed institution in Acheaoria and it is failing anyway, because a satrap who will not open his books cannot be compelled. So the Scribes record the refusals. The column marked "not presented" is the most accurate measure of how much of the empire still works.

Houses: the plain brick temple on the lower edge of the terrace at Persemenid, where Gulnar Zand, an air-genasi, keeps the master tribute ledger and the roll of the Ten Thousand is read each year; Scribe Farnaz Daftari at Shir'abad D'ar, recording every refusal; the Clerks' Marks on the Kaspiran shore.

Now: three covenants registered at Mithratal describe what each party will do "should the roads to the west be closed". The Scribes want someone at court to read their report.

Joining: an examination in three scripts and a vow of no property. Scribes are paid in coin from the guild's own temple.

The Enchanted Muse Magical society · dream-readers

Selan's moon-readers chart dreams like tides, and half the empire plans by their almanac.

Selan · The Virtuous · Persevalis · Almanac-Mistress Mahtab

The Healer's Sanctuary treats dreams as diagnosis; the Muse treats them as a tide that moves on schedule, touches everyone at once and can be predicted. It publishes an almanac, and so many officials plan by it that its predictions have begun to fulfil themselves. The Magi have never condemned the Muse, and the Muse takes care not to find out why. The calendar is the Magi's.

Houses: the chapter at Persevalis, which plans its betrothals, sowings and lawsuits by the almanac; dream-readers on expedition at Eronis; a reader posted three gardens from Shirin Navaz during the Night Gardens.

Now: the almanac marked last summer's Night Gardens as a "spring tide of dreams", and half the city dreamed of the same woman in grey. The Muse is hunting her: Vesperine Ilaro, the last Nethranan dream-walker (the Dreamers' Hunt), against Delphara's Dormitory and the Arcane Academy.

Joining: keep a dream-journal for a lunar year that the readers can check against the almanac. Members serve by night.

The Exiled Wanderers Family and tribe · the relocated

The empire moved them so often that they no longer have a home province to be sent back to.

The Lost One · The Impartial · no seat; the drove-roads · Grandmother Gol-Bano, by consent

Acheaoria's old answer to a rebellious people was relocation, a thousand miles away among strangers. The Wanderers descend from groups moved so often that the point was lost. They work as drovers, harvesters and messengers, and settled Acheaorians regard them with contempt and unease. The unease is older: everyone on the plateau knows that a family's place is an administrative decision, and decisions are revisited.

Houses: camps outside the caravanserais of Atarabad and on the Caravan Fields of Deiperduem; harvest-gangs at Persevalis; drovers on the Royal Road. Mother Kuchak of the Benevolent Hands came east with one of their trains forty years ago.

Now: a treaty clause lets displaced persons claim land "where their families were settled before the war". The Wanderers have far too many claims and no single one.

Joining: be taken in on the road. They share everything except their stories, which never agree.

The Illuminated Scholars Magical society · archive-keepers

Zann's archivists copy everything and lend almost nothing, because an archive that lends is being edited by its borrowers.

Zann · The Virtuous · Persemenid, the Royal Archive · Archivist-General Mehrnush Dabir

Tribute rolls, land grants, genealogies and two thousand years of administrative letters. Access requires a petition, a purpose and usually a wait, and the Scholars are not embarrassed about it. They work closely with the Scribes of the Infinite Ledger; the joke goes that the Scribes find out what is true while the Scholars find out what was previously claimed.

Houses: the Royal Archive on the terrace at Persemenid; the registry at Mithratal's Archive Ward; correspondents at Thessalonika.

Now: the Whispering Eyes are selling material that can only have come from the Scholars' deep shelves. The Archivist-General wants the leak found without admitting there is one.

Joining: a scribal training and a petition to the god. Members never own a copy of anything.

The Immortals Military order · the elite unit

For every Immortal who fell, two were said to rise, and the empire would like that to stay a figure of speech.

Hajama, officially · The Impartial · Persemenid, beneath the drill-ground · Spahbed Vindafarna the Unchanged

The elite of the Acheaorian army, and the reason the empire's losses in the war never became a collapse. Acheaoria lost vast ground and paid heavily in people. The Immortals are what it did not lose. They have not lost a man in sixty years, and an Immortal funeral is rare, because an Immortal must be destroyed twice.

Houses: barracks under Persemenid's drill-ground, where rumour says the ground rings hollow; the Hill of Fires, where Magus Rashnu-Vahram keeps the oldest rites and stands at every Immortal funeral; detachments on the frontier at Xerastri.

Now: nothing to fight, so they parade. Khemareti priest-embalmers have asked twice to witness the Rite of Return, and the court has twice said there is nothing to see.

Joining: chosen from the line after death, though the army says "after distinction". Pay goes to the family, forever.

The Ironclad Oath Military order · sworn to the throne

Vatagatal's soldiers swear to a promise instead of a satrap, which makes them the throne's best tool and its most awkward.

Vatagatal · The Impartial · Persemenid, the Oath-Hall · Oath-Marshal Daryush Peymanzad

A satrap cannot suborn them, because he did not raise them. Nobody can order them to break the oath, and the oath forbids war on the empire's own subjects. The Court of Vipers has spent five years discovering how much of the current unrest that clause covers. So far: most of it.

Houses: the Oath-Hall at Persemenid; the chapter house in Xerastri's Inner Citadel under Oath-Captain Arya Kardar, who will fight the steppe but not subjects and is not sure which the clans are this year; the chapter at Shir'abad D'ar under Oath-Captain Zhubin Arzan, on correct and cold terms with the satrap; the chapel at the Salt Cathedral in the Zaruk'thal Spine.

Now: the court wants a ruling that rebels are not "subjects". The Oath wants its terms left alone.

Joining: swear the Oath before Vatagatal's iron and wear the iron collar. Paid from the royal treasury, when it pays.

The Lion's Mane Vanguard Military order · noble heavy cavalry

Hajama's armoured lancers are the satraps' pride, and are paid by the satraps.

Hajama · The Impartial · Persemenid, the Lion Gate · Spahbed Artabazos Mihran, first lance

Armoured lancers from the noble houses of the satrapies on heavy plateau horses, the most impressive force on the continent. The flaw is old: the squadrons are raised and paid by the satraps, not the throne. For fifteen centuries an outside enemy kept the question theoretical. There is no longer an outside enemy.

Houses: the gatehouse temple at the east wall of the Paradise, where Lion-Priest Bahman Arshak blesses the lances before the Royal Hunt; House Mihran, its largest private contributor, whose stables stand beside the eastern wall; the satrap's oversized squadrons at Atarabad and Shir'abad D'ar.

Now: two satraps have grown their squadrons past the permitted size and filed the correct paperwork. The Scribes forwarded it and nobody acted. Artabazos Mihran wants a war with Duneforged before the King dies.

Joining: a noble's son with a horse, a coat of scale and his satrap's nomination.

The River's Embrace Religious order · river shrines

Shajar's priests keep the river gauges and run the ferries, and know when the water is safe because they measure it.

Shajar · The Virtuous · Persevalis, the Channel Head shrines · High Gauge-Keeper Anahid Rudsar

The shrines have recorded high-water marks for over a thousand years. A priest can tell a village what the river did in a comparable year and what it will probably do this one, and that accuracy is the whole of the order's standing. It also runs most of the ferries, which is less holy and more lucrative.

Houses: shrines at the channel heads of Persevalis; the river-mouth shrines and ferries on the Kaspiran shore, whose priests know which boats go out at night; the Crocodile Pool on the old Xeruezcho Canal, where Priestess Shirindokht feeds the River-Dragon and wants a cure for it before the town learns it needs one.

Now: the eastern channels at Persevalis run faster than the slope allows, and the gauges say the Kaspiran is falling faster than any record. The order wants the Magi to listen.

Joining: a year of reading the gauge at dawn and dusk. Ferry fares feed the order.

The Sage's Archive Magical society · epigraphers

Kor's readers check the kings' cliff inscriptions, and have begun to disagree with the official history.

Kor · The Virtuous · Persemenid · Master-Reader Vidarna Kaus

Acheaoria's kings record their reigns on cliff faces, in several languages, high and hard to check. The Archive checks them. About a decade ago it began publishing readings of the older inscriptions that do not match the court's history: a usurpation called a succession, a defeat called a punitive expedition, a satrapy that appears and then does not. The Archive says it is only philology.

Houses: the reading-house at Persemenid, which Crown Prince Ariaramna reads in private and agrees with too often; copies exchanged with the Aeterna Lexicon and the Porticoes of Thessalonika (the Three Libraries), copied in secret on the top floor of the House of the Seven Quills at Deiperduem; Haftvad on expedition at Eronis's Bronze Camp, copying the three-suns mural.

Now: to keep reading. The Court of Vipers has not decided whether to agree that it is only philology, and the senior members are making copies.

Joining: read an inscription in three scripts. Members swear to copy before they argue.

The Savage Pack Frontier tribe · beyond the qanat line

Where the last channel ends, the empire ends. The Pack lives out there and pays no tribute.

the Beast · The Impartial · beyond the Qanat Line · the Old She-Wolf, Gurgana

Herders and hunters organised by kin, not satrapy. Officially they are Acheaorian subjects in a district whose administration is "temporarily unassigned", and have been for four hundred years. They trade hides and knowledge of the deep country and raid in bad years. The satraps send punitive expeditions in a good decade and subsidies in a bad one, and the Pack can tell which decade it is faster than the satraps can.

Houses: trading days in Xerastri's bazaar, beside the Predator's Guild; leopard-skin trade at the eastern mouth of the Parthian Ravine; gnoll-hunts in the Hyena Hollows of the Zaruk'thal Spine.

Now: the garrison at Xerastri taxes the steppe trade it is meant to suppress, and the subsidies have stopped. This is a bad decade, and the Pack knows it.

Joining: by blood or by hunting with them through a winter.

The Stormcallers' Choir Magical society · rain-singers

They sing the seasonal rains in, are thanked for good years, and are driven out in droughts.

Drummern and Pag · The Impartial · the Dasht-a Khaliq, the Stone Choir · Choir-Mother Baran Avazeh
