Found here: pine-nuts (2 sp a pound, roasted 1 cp a cone); myrtle sprigs for weddings; a bed at the inn (4 sp); and a free place to sleep under the trees.

Hook: a courier's body was found under the third pine, his satchel empty, a myrtle sprig in his hand.

River Tiberius

Sites along the River Tiberius, the founding river that runs from the hills through Aeterna to its port at Fucostia.

The Jet Strand River shore

Codex now: A black cliff-foot on the Tiberius where polished jet and honey-coloured amber wash up after the spring floods.

A stretch of black clay cliff on the Tiberius' upper reaches, where the spring floods cut the bank and leave the shore strewn with dark, light stones. The cliff gives jet, black and warm in the hand, and the flood-wrack sometimes carries a lump of northern amber that has travelled down the river from somewhere far upstream. In the first week after a flood the strand is crowded; after that, the dealers have bought it all.

Now: the beachcombers are mostly bargemen's widows, who hold the strand by a custom older than the river curators and see off newcomers with sticks. Their spokeswoman is Widow Tullia Nigra, who has worn the same jet necklace for thirty years and can tell strand-jet from cheap imported coal at a glance. Dealers come up from the capital with bags and short tempers.

Found here: raw jet (1 sp a lump at the strand), mourning-rings of it carved by the widows (2 gp; ten times that in the capital), and in a good week a flood-borne piece of amber (5 gp up). The Cycle of the Eternal Bloom buys jet for its funeral regalia.

Hook: a piece of amber with something trapped inside, a seal ring, has been found twice. Someone is dropping them upstream, and the second ring bore a Legate's crest.

The Kingfisher Reach River reach

Codex now: A calm green stretch of the founding river where blue birds dive and the winter is gentle for a week each year.

A quiet reach between two bridges, its soft banks pitted with burrows. The water is green and slow, the willows trail in it, mint grows along the edge, and a bird of impossible blue flashes along it at dawn. In midwinter there is a week of dead calm that the villagers call by the bird's name. Bargemen call it the halcyon week and refuse to fight, sue or collect debts during it, and several contracts in the capital fall due on the first day after.

Now: a fisherman's family, the Alcedinii, have lived on the bank for ten generations and will tell any visitor which burrows are occupied. Their head, Old Marcus Alcedinius, keeps the river shrine at the upper bridge. Fishing rights belong to the river curators, whose bailiffs patrol on market days and are bribed with eels.

Found here: a free walk; eels and river fish from the family (2 cp); a halcyon feather charm, sold only during the calm week, said to keep a marriage peaceful (5 sp).

Hook: the calm has not come this winter. The fishermen say the birds have left, and nobody has seen where. Every contract due after the halcyon week is now in dispute.

The Travertine Cuts Quarry

Codex now: Warm white terraces beside the river where hot springs lay down stone as fast as the quarrymen cut it.

A line of pale terraces beside the Tiberius where hot springs run over the rock and lay down a creamy stone as fast as the quarrymen cut it. The cuts look like frozen waterfalls, and the pools between them are warm enough for bathing in winter. Every great building in the capital wears this travertine; the older heaps of volcanic tufa are kept for backing walls.

Now: the quarry pays its dues to the river priests as well as the state, a habit nobody has been brave enough to stop. Its master is Gaius Tiburtius Calx, whose family has cut here for six generations; his books show orders down by half since the war ended and the Dominus Militum's great buildings stopped. A bathhouse by the springs charges for the pools, and passing painters pay the quarrymen in drawings.

Found here: travertine by the block (15 gp a cartload delivered to Aeterna); bathing in the warm pools (2 cp); and sketches of quarrymen by famous hands, pinned up in the bathhouse.

Hook: the springs' flow has changed twice this year. A hydrologist from the capital believes someone is diverting it, and the quarry's stone is growing more slowly.

Klynin Mountain Range

Sites of the Klynin Mountain Range, the spring-bearing hills that feed the Aqua Aeterna.

The Calamine Diggings Mine

Codex now: Pale pits in the Klynin hills where brass-makers buy the stone that turns copper to gold, and a bitter salt crusts the walls.

Pale, crumbling pits in the lower hills where the ore the brass-makers call the gold-maker is dug, and the workings are crusted with a bitter white salt. The calamine turns smelted copper to brass; the crust is scraped for alum, which dyers use to fix colour. The diggers wear scarves and complain of a taste in the mouth that never leaves. Their water-office licence forbids washing ore within a mile of a spring, so the ore goes downhill dry, on mules, at twice the cost.

Now: brass-founders from Mavelon keep a standing contract and send a wagon each week; the capital's foundries buy the rest. The diggings' foreman is Vibia Calaminaria, a widow who took over her husband's gang and runs it better. Smugglers wash ore in the springs anyway and sell it cheaper in Aeterna, and the water-office walkers fine the honest diggers to make up their quota.

Found here: calamine (5 sp a sack), alum (1 gp a pound), and brass blanks from a small illicit smelter in the next valley, which the coin Assay would very much like to find.

Hook: the diggers have begun finding old tools in the lowest cut, made of a metal no one has seen, and are quietly selling them in the capital.

The Green Gallery Copper mine

Codex now: A copper working in the Klynin foothills whose walls weep green, where miners cut malachite for paint and bead.

A long adit driven into the foothills along a copper vein, named for its walls: the rock is stained green to the roof, and in wet weather the water that runs down it is green too. The miners come for copper, but the money is the banded malachite that lines the gallery, cut into beads and ground into paint, and the verdigris scraped from old timbers. Every tool is wrapped in green dust by the end of a shift. The best seams run toward the hollow, and the miners stop where the rock begins to sound like a drum.

Now: the Imperial surveyors keep a post at the mouth, because the spring-bearing range is jealously watched; a buyer with a stamp from Aeterna may enter, anyone else buys at the gate. The foreman, Septimus Viridius, keeps a list of men who did not stop at the drum-rock. It is short and he is proud of that.

Found here: malachite beads (1 sp a string), ground green pigment (5 sp a pot, prized by the capital's painters' guilds), verdigris, and copper ingots by contract.

Hook: a miner offers to sell what he knows about the gallery's drainage. The surveyors at the mouth say he is a liar and would like to talk to anyone he talks to.

Cloudspine Ridge

Sites of the Cloudspine Ridge, held by House Caerthain of the Duneforged Citadel.

The Cedar Stair Mountain forest

Codex now: A stepped slope of black-green cedar on the high ridges, where carpenters from three empires come for timber that outlasts them.

A series of narrow shelves on the ridge, each crowded with dark, slow-growing cedars whose timber does not rot and does not warp. Loggers work the stair by rope and winch, and a felled trunk is lowered down the cliff on a cradle of green poles that is itself half a day's work. Pale-flowered mountain spikenard grows in the crevices above, and perfumers pay to have it gathered.

Now: the Duke licenses each tree. The Serathian Fleet's airship hulls are cut here, which is why the licences are signed by Commander Daud and not by the forester. The forester, Wendel Ashby, is a lean old Duneforged man who knows every tree on the stair by its scars and resents the Commander's signature on every one. The ridge forts will give a traveller a bed.

Found here: mountain cedar by licence only (a mast-grade trunk 50 gp, standing; more delivered); spikenard (5 gp an ounce); and offcuts sold by the loggers, enough for a chest or a bow-stave, for a few silver.

Hook: a cedar felled last spring had a sword-blade grown into its heart, of an old Caerthain pattern.

The Ibex Crags Cliffs

Codex now: Sheer grey cliffs where wild goats stand on ledges no hunter can reach and a great eagle rides the wind above them.

Sheer grey limestone towers, ledged and fissured in a way only a goat could love. Cliff-goats stand motionless on the edges, horned wild sheep graze the lower terraces, and the King's Eagles ride the updrafts above, taking kids from the ledges. The largest eyrie sits on a pinnacle the soldiers have named after a general, and the general has never been told.

Now: eagle-catchers lower themselves on ropes to rob the eyries; a trained eagle sells at Duneforged for the price of a house, and the Ju Colliseum's beast-pens take the untrainable ones. The catchers' headman is Corra Hawkmoth, missing two fingers and an ear, who leads the rope-teams herself. The ridge forts let a hunter pass for a share of the meat. The eagle, they say, takes a share of the hunter.

Found here: eagle chicks (500 gp, unhatched eggs 200 gp, if the catchers will sell to you); goat and sheep hides; ibex horn for bows; and rope-guides for the brave (5 gp a day).

Hook: the great eyrie holds something that glitters. The soldiers of the nearest fort have been arguing for a month over who gets to look.

Briar's Valley

The one site of Briar's Valley, the thorn-walled valley where a militia died forty years ago.

The Thorn-Rows Thicket

Codex now: A tangle of choking vines and spiked hedges at the valley's heart, where the thorn grew inward and the plants have learned to hunt.

The oldest part of the thorn-brake, where forty years of unpruned growth have knit into a living wall. The vines move in still air. The rows have the shape of a field that was planted and forgotten, and they run in straight lines like ranks, the gaps between them exactly a shield's width. Rusted spearheads hang in the canes at head height. Assassin vines tighten on anything warm, creeping kudzu swallows the old walls, and moorroot grows along the damp northern edge. Nothing that enters is easy to find again.

Now: nobody rules the valley. The rim villages keep the road to the edge and no further, and charge a fee for a guide. The guides are a quiet, scarred lot; the eldest, Brannagh of the Rim, lost her father in the massacre and has walked further into the rows than any living person. A land-hungry Legate wants the pasture opened and has sent surveyors, twice.

Found here: a guide to the edge (5 sp); moorroot (a bog-herb for fevers, 1 sp a bundle); assassin-vine cuttings, which an alchemist will buy and a sane man will not carry.

Hook: the Legate's second surveying party went in a month ago. Their chains came out, laid in a straight line along a gap between the rows. They did not.

Shadowed Vale

The one site of the Shadowed Vale, the cleft where the sun crosses for forty minutes a day.

The Hedge of Healing Physic hedge

Codex now: A cold-shaded hedge in the valley where the sun lingers forty minutes and the herbalists gather their salves.

A thick hedge along the Vale's sunless side, planted generations ago by a physician and left to grow. The herbalists' guild trims it twice a year, on dates fixed decades ahead, and gathers what it gives: witch hazel for bruises, comfrey for bones, woundwort for cuts and the red heartberry that physicians use to quiet a racing pulse. Everything it gives is useful to the wounded, and everything comes slowly.

Now: the hedge's keeper is Master Physician Coren Hask, who keeps the trimming schedule and the physician's lodge, and will not start a cut one minute early. The lodge takes the sick for a small donation; the Radiant Heartwardens buy its salves by the cask. Outsiders now come to buy and stay into winter, which the Valefolk dislike.

Found here: salves from a stall by the gate (bruise salve 2 sp, bone-knit poultice 5 sp, heartberry draught 1 gp); a bed at the lodge for the sick; and a healer's kit made up to order (5 gp).

Hook: last autumn a third of the hedge died overnight, in a perfectly straight line. The guild blames a rival; the roots are rotting from below.

Oros Mountain Range

Sites of the Oros Mountain Range, the hill demes and marble quarries above the Hellenorian coast, whose stone faces temples as far away as Aeterna.

Bloodstone Scree Scree slope

Codex now: A long slope of dark green stone flecked with red, where, they say, the blood of a hero turned the rock.

A long slope of loose dark-green stone flecked with red as if splashed. The shepherds say a hero was wounded here and his blood turned the rock; the stone-pickers do not believe it and come anyway. The slope is steep and loose, and a climber who disturbs it brings down a slide that rattles like a bag of coins. Bloodstone is carried by soldiers as a charm against wounds, and pebbles of banded seal jasper are bought by engravers by the sack.

Now: the pickers are hill-deme families under the komarch of the nearest village, Komarch Pheidon Lithaios, who takes a tenth of every sack and sells the reddest stones to the Luminastra Alchemists. Since the peace, demand from soldiers has collapsed and demand from alchemists has tripled, which the pickers find puzzling and profitable.

Found here: bloodstone (a tumbled charm 5 sp, a good red-flecked piece 10 gp), seal jasper for engraving (1 sp a pebble), and a picker to guide you onto the slope (2 sp, and walk where she walks).

Hook: one stone near the top is flecked with fresh red. It stays wet when the weather is dry, and the alchemists have offered a hundred gold pieces for it.

The Beekeepers' Hall Guildhall

Codex now: A low stone lodge on the Oros slope where the hill villages weigh, grade and seal their honey, and the thyme smell reaches the road.

A low stone lodge on the slope where the beekeepers of the hill villages bring their combs once a year for weighing, grading and sealing under the hall's stamp, a bee inside a ring of thyme. The cellar holds the villages' reserve, and a jar sealed here carries a name that sells in Hellarchon at three times the price of unsealed honey. The honey is dark, flavoured with mountain thyme, and the wax goes to the candle-makers of three cities.

Now: the hall is run by the beekeepers' guild under the Golden Scythe Accord, and its grader this year is Melitta Thymaris, a stern woman whose family have graded for six generations. The annual grading draws buyers from three cities. A beekeeper who cheats is expelled, and his bees are said to leave with him.

Found here: sealed thyme honey (5 sp a jar; the best grade 2 gp), beeswax (1 sp a pound), mead from the hall's own press, and propolis salve for wounds.

Hook: a village's honey has been graded higher than its quality. The grader before Melitta has a new house and a debt that vanished, and he is her uncle.

The Boar Thicket Scrub

Codex now: A dense hillside scrub where a tusked beast the size of a pony is hunted by heroes, and tortoises carry the old lyres' shells.

A dense, thorny scrub on the foothills, impassable except by the tracks the boars cut and the tunnels the partridges use. Hunters go in with spears and dogs and come out with stories, a few of which are true. Slow hill tortoises graze its edges, and the lyre-makers buy their cast shells; rock-partridges burst out of the brush when the dogs come near.

Now: the village at the thicket's edge hosts a hunt each autumn and feeds the hunters, living and dead. Its komarch, Komarch Agrios Kapros, keeps the hunt-register and buries the losers. The great tusker has killed four would-be heroes since the treaty, most of them young eupatrids seeking a name in a peace that gives them none. Their families blame the beast; the village blames the heroes.

Found here: a place on the autumn hunt (10 gp entry, which pays for the feast and the funerals); boar-tusk charms; tortoise shells for lyres (1 gp); and partridge with wild thyme at the village tavern.

Hook: the old boar of the stories has been seen again. A hunter who shot at it found his arrow gone and his hand marked with a crescent.

The Hellebore Cliffs Sea cliff

Codex now: A sea-wind-blown cliff of pale rock where physicians climb for the dark-rooted cure of madness and the mandrake that shrieks, they say, when pulled.

A pale limestone cliff above the sea, scoured by wind, where dark-rooted hellebore grows in the cracks and the League's physicians send a man with a rope each spring. The plant cures the mad and kills the sane, they say, and the dose is whatever the physician is brave enough to give. A sheltered cleft at the foot holds mandrake and adder's-tongue, which the gatherers pull by tying a dog to the root.

Now: the gatherers' guild admits climbers by examination, and a guide is mandatory. Its master is Kleobis the Rope, sixty, who has climbed the cliff every spring for forty years and buys his dogs from the village below. Physicians of Delphara buy most of the harvest for the oracle's own physicians.

Found here: black hellebore root (5 gp, dried; a poison if you are not careful), mandrake (25 gp, pulled the proper way), and a guided climb (5 gp, after the examination).

Hook: a climber has been found at the cliff's foot every spring for three years. Each held a hellebore root and was smiling.

The Lodestone Shelf Ore ledge

Codex now: A bare ledge on the Oros range where iron ore pulls a compass needle off true and shepherds will not sleep.

A broad grey ledge high on the range, bare of grass, where the iron ore is so strong that a needle swings off north and a loose nail creeps across a table. The shepherds will not pasture here, because the sheep will not settle, and they tell of a man who tied his boots with iron and could not leave. It is the best source of lodestone on the coast. A good piece lifts a handful of nails and fetches a month's wages in any port with a chart-maker.

Now: nobody owns the shelf and nobody wants to. Stone-hunters go in pairs and leave their metal behind, and sell to the chart-makers of Corinth and Hellarchon. The most respected of them is Amyntor the Barefoot, who walks up without nails in his boots and comes down with a sack of stones.

Found here: lodestone (a small piece 5 gp, a strong one 50 gp); compass needles magnetised on the spot by the hunters for a silver piece.

Hook: a party that loses its way on the shelf finds its compass useless, and then its steel tools pulling toward a single point in the rock.

The Olive Terraces of Oros Olive groves

Codex now: Stone-walled terraces climbing the Oros slopes, planted with olives older than the League and tended by families who inherit the trees by name.

Terrace upon terrace of dry-stone walls climbing the slopes, each planted with olive trees that have names, owners and a place in a will. The oldest are hollow shells that still bear fruit. Wild juniper lines the wall-tops, and the shepherds burn it for its smoke. The autumn harvest is a village event with songs, ladders and a feast at the press. These are the people who actually live on the Mountain, and they dislike the quarries' dust on their leaves.

Now: the terraces are held under the Golden Scythe Accord by forty families. The oil is pressed at the deme press, kept by Demarch Elaia Gerontis, who also keeps the register of trees: four thousand names. A visitor at harvest is given a bowl of new oil with bread.

Found here: new oil (5 sp a jar), cured olives, juniper smoke for curing meat, and an olive-wood bowl from a tree that died in the war (2 gp). The families will not sell a tree, but they will sell what it makes.

Hook: one ancient tree is said to be older than the Titans' fall, and two families are suing over who owns it. The case has reached the League's court and both sides need witnesses.

The Pentelic Terraces Marble quarry

Codex now: White-and-gold quarry steps on the Oros range, the source of the marble that every Hellenorian temple wants and few can afford.

A flight of enormous quarry terraces cut into the range, each step a clean wall of fine white stone with a faint golden cast where the iron weathers out. The cut blocks are lowered on timber ramps and ox-sledges down a paved slide to the sea, and the road is worn into a trench by eight centuries of carts. A block from the upper steps has been quoted at the price of a ship.

Now: the quarries are leased by the Geolith Artisan Covenant, which cuts on its own schedule; the joke in the League is that a temple is finished when the Covenant is, not when the city is. The quarry-master is Master Lysippos Leukolithos, who has not taken a rival's order out of turn in thirty years. The quarry-masters admit visitors on feast days to walk the lower steps; the upper ones are for the cutters and the stone-priests.

Found here: marble by the block (a plain building block 50 gp at the slide; upper-step stone by negotiation); offcuts and chips for mosaic; and stone-carvers who will cut a grave stele (from 20 gp).

Hook: the upper terraces have been closed for a year, officially for safety. A cutter says they cut into a hollow and found a carved floor.

Elysian Plains

Sites of the Elysian Plains, the bowl of grass honoured by every Hellenorian city and claimed by none, under the Amphictyony of Delphara.

Silphium Hollow Guarded hollow

Codex now: A sheltered fold in the plain where the last wild stand of a famous, nearly vanished herb is guarded by a family with a long memory.

A sheltered fold in the plain, fenced and watched, where one family guards the last wild stand of a herb that once paid for cities. It is tall, coarse and ordinary-looking, and every attempt to cultivate it elsewhere has failed. Around it the family grow bitterwort and golden calendula, which look enough like it at a distance to decoy thieves.

Now: the family are the Silphidai, headed by Old Battos Silphides, eighty-one, who has never left the hollow for more than a night. They sell a single stalk each year to the highest bidder in a sealed auction at the gate; the winner is blindfolded on the way out. No stranger is let in. Last year's stalk went to an Acheaorian buyer for the price of a small estate.

Found here: the annual stalk, at auction (last year, 4,000 gp); calendula and bitterwort from the decoy beds (1 sp a bundle), which some buyers purchase anyway in hope.

Hook: a rival house hires the party to get inside the fence and take one cutting, just one.

The Dreamfields Poppy and crocus fields

Codex now: Red-and-pink fields of poppy and autumn crocus on the plain, where the harvesters work in silence and are kept awake by shifts.

A stretch of the plain's edge turned over to poppies and autumn crocuses, scarlet in spring and mauve in autumn. The harvesters work in silence, one watching while two cut, because the fumes from the cut heads send a worker to sleep on his feet. The watcher shakes anyone who sits down. A harvester who sleeps in the field is left one night, by custom, before anyone goes to fetch him.

Now: the fields are worked by three villages under a single komarch, Komarch Hypnia Morphis, who sells the poppy to physicians across the League and to the Luminastra Alchemists, and the crocus to physicians who prescribe it in tiny doses for aching joints and larger ones for the unwanted. The Dream Dormitory of Delphara takes a tithe of the poppy-milk for its sleepers.

Found here: poppy-milk (5 gp a vial; a sleep draught), crocus corms (the physicians' gout cure, deadly in excess), and dried poppy heads. A stranger is not welcome in the fields at harvest; the villagers are polite about it.

Hook: the gangs are paid in poppy-milk. A man who tried to leave found he could not, and his brother wants him back.

The Horse Meadows Pasture

Codex now: A rolling green plain where the sweating, golden horses of the king are bred and the wolves keep the herds honest.

A rolling green plain where the horse-breeders run their herds, and where the grass is said to grow in the shape of the wind that blew a week ago. The horses are slim, long-legged and golden-coated, and they sweat as if they bled; a foal sells for a village. Wolves come down from the hills each winter and the herders keep their fires burning. Fallow deer winter in the far meadows.

Now: the herds are the Imperial stud of House Thalorid in name, though no Imperial officer has inspected them in ten years. The breeders' master, Hipparchos Chrysippos, sells to all three empires and says the foals are sired by something in the deep plain. Acheaorian buyers pay in gold and ask no questions; Invictian buyers ask and pay less.

Found here: a golden horse (a yearling 2,000 gp, a trained warhorse more; buyers welcome in spring), ordinary riding horses from the lesser herds (100 gp), and wolf pelts from the winter culls.

Hook: a mare has foaled something with a scar like a brand. The breeders have not told anyone, and a buyer from Xerastri wants to see the foal.

Maeotis Helos

Sites of the Maeotis Helos, the reed-sea that pays tribute to whoever asks; see also Marshroot Grove and Willowheart.

The Pelican Islands Floating islets

Codex now: Reed islets in the great marsh where pelicans, pheasants and cranes nest and the sturgeon run beneath them.

A cluster of floating reed islets in the heart of the marsh, anchored to nothing and moving a few yards each year. Bill-bag pelicans and pheasants nest by the thousand and grey cranes winter here; in the deep channels beneath, the black-egg sturgeon run in spring, and in the still pools the healer's leech waits for a bare leg. The islets are loud, white with guano, and smell of fish oil.

Now: a fishermen's guild runs punts to the islets. Its master, Old Skarphe the Poler, has punted the channels for fifty years and refuses to say which empire he pays tribute to this year, on the grounds that it changes. The guild sells sturgeon roe upriver, and three tax-collectors now ask for a share of it.

Found here: a day's trip (a day's wage and a promise not to take eggs); sturgeon roe (5 gp a crock, salted); smoked fish; healer's leeches for physicians (1 sp each, live in a jar).

Hook: one islet has started drifting against the current, and has anchored itself to something. The fishermen say it is a hand. Nobody punts near it now.

The Reed-Cutters' Fen Channel maze

Codex now: A maze of channels in the great marsh where punts glide through walls of reed and the water-lilies open each morning like blue lamps.

A web of narrow channels cut by generations of reed-cutters, each just wide enough for a punt and marked by a knot of reed on a pole. The reeds rise twice a man's height. The water is thick with blue lotus that opens at dawn and closes at noon, gathered for temples that burn its petals. Roofing reed comes from here, and the fine hollow pen-reed that scribes pay extra for.

Now: the cutters are free families who pay tribute to whoever sends a collector and work exactly as before. A guide is not optional: the channels change with the season, the knots are moved by people who want you lost, and the fen keeps what it takes. The guides' headwoman is Myrrhe Knotwife, who ties every knot on the main channels herself and can read a stranger's knot like a signature.

Found here: roofing reed (1 cp a bundle), pen-reed (1 sp a dozen, the Stilted Archive's preferred supplier), dried blue lotus (5 sp an ounce; temple incense and a mild dream-draught), and a guide (2 sp a day; do not go without).

Hook: a channel cut last year leads somewhere that is not on the cutters' map, and the cutter who cut it does not remember doing so.

The Stilted Archive Library on stilts

Codex now: A library on wooden stilts in the middle of the marsh, where the scribes who cut the reeds also copy the books that need to be forgotten.

A library on wooden stilts in the middle of the marsh, reached by a plank causeway the keepers pull up at night. The scribes cut their own reeds, mix their own ink and copy the texts the great libraries would rather not keep, selling sealed copies to scholars who ask no questions. Dampness is the archive's enemy and the smell, mildew, ink and smoke, its signature. The books are kept in cedar boxes hung from the rafters, above the water's reach.

Now: the archive's head keeper is Keeper Anaxis, a former scholar of the Porticoes of Thessalonika who left under a cloud and will not say which. A visitor must be vouched for by a scribe. Buyers come from the Three Libraries' circle; the Whispering Eyes buy too, through intermediaries.

Found here: sealed copies of rare and forbidden texts (from 50 gp, by the page-count and the danger); copying to order (a month, and a promise); pen-reed, ink and good advice on keeping a book dry.

Hook: a book is missing: the one the keepers forbade themselves to copy. Its absence has attracted three separate buyers, each sure the others stole it.

Malaunian Steppe

The one site of the Malaunian Steppe, the sea of grass beyond Xerastri.

The Lion Grass Grassland

Codex now: A golden stretch of steppe where the manes of the great cats and the antlers of the strange antelope show above the grass at dawn.

A broad golden stretch where the grass grows shoulder-high and the horse-clans avoid grazing their herds in the evening. At dawn the manes of the great cats rise above the stems like standards, and the ground is printed with a thousand hooves: the odd-nosed saiga in their herds, and in winter the shaggy two-hump camels. The steppe-lions, the Mane-Kings, hunt in prides of twenty.

Now: no clan owns the Lion Grass. The clans will guide a traveller across for a gift of salt; they will not guide him back. Tomyra of the Lion Grass takes her name from here, and the cats are said to give her room. The Predator's Guild covets the culling rights and has sent agents to buy them from clan chiefs who do not believe anyone can own them.

Found here: a guide across (a pound of salt); lion pelts from clan hunters (100 gp, worth three times that at Persemenid); saiga horn, prized by physicians; and camel-hair felt.

Hook: a herd of saiga has moved west as if fleeing something. The horse-clans have not said what, and they have begun to move their own herds after them.

Varathros Lake

Sites of Varathros Lake, whose northern waters are policed by Deiperduem's Lake Board. The great Sanctum library on its islet is listed under unplaced sites below.

The Drowned Workshop Ruin

Codex now: A ruined stone workshop half-sunk in the lake, still turning slowly, where the lost craft of an older people lies in the silt.

A ruined workshop half-sunk in the shallows, its stone walls green with weed and its great wheel still turning slowly in the current. The lake-fishers avoid it. The few divers who have gone in report rooms of machinery lit by a pale light that does not come from the surface. The silt around it yields clicking mechanite, amorphous meld, lightless voidmetal, pale cosmilite and dripping, weightless etherplasm.

Now: a fisher's hut on the nearest shore rents boats and tells stories. The fisher, Nikasia the Ferrywoman, has rented boats to divers from every embassy in Deiperduem and from the Writhing Curiosity, and buys back what they bring up to sell to the Mithril Reserve's buyers. The stories agree on the wheel and disagree on everything else.

Found here: a boat (5 sp a day), a diving weight and rope; silt-dredged materials sold by Nikasia (mechanite 25 gp a lump; etherplasm 100 gp a vial, kept stoppered); and her stories, free with a boat.

Hook: the wheel turned faster this week. Something in the workshop has been wound.

The Natron Pans Salt flats

Codex now: White crusted flats on the shore of Varathros Lake where the lake gives up its salt, soda and a smell like old eggs.

A series of shallow basins on the lake's southern shore that fill in the wet season and bake to a white crust in the dry. The crust is natron: a soda-salt used for glass, for cleaning, for embalming and for the washing of the dead. The rakers heap it with wooden rakes and wear cloths over their eyes against the glare. A cart-road runs to the lake's southern port, and the hauliers are a hard, silent breed who work by moonlight to avoid the heat.

Now: the pans are the main source of natron for every glass-house on the coast and every embalmer in the south. The rakers' boss is Gorgo Halmyra, a broad, sun-blackened woman who sells to all comers and pays the Lake Board's levy without complaint, because the Board's boats keep the pirates off the cart-road.

Found here: natron by the sack (2 sp, more at the coast); soap and washing-soda; and embalmers' grade natron, sifted, for those preparing the dead (1 gp a jar).

Hook: the crust has a layer of something older beneath it. A raker who raked too deep hauled up a bronze mask and stopped talking.

Vael'Tharan Mountain

Sites of Vael'Tharan Mountain, the warm peak where the fire broke the Titans, claimed by no one.

Smoke-Steps Sulphur terraces

Codex now: A stair of yellow terraces climbing the warm flank of Vael'Tharan, where the mountain breathes sulphur and the fire-stone glows at night.

A natural stair of yellow terraces on the warm flank, cut deeper by generations of sulphur-gatherers. Vents along the steps breathe a pale smoke that smells of struck flint and old eggs, and at night some stones glow a dull red, as if the mountain remembered the fire that broke the Titans. Brimstone is scraped off in sheets; the hottest vents leave glassy lumps of fire-stone that stay warm for days after they are cut.

Now: the gatherers work the steps by custom, not licence, and record their takings on a tally-post at the foot. Their head is Gatherer-Mother Zoe Kapnia, a lean old woman with yellow fingernails who decides each morning which steps may be worked. The gatherers work in the cool of dawn and are off the mountain by noon. A traveller who stays later has been warned.

Found here: brimstone (1 sp a pound; alchemists of Duneforged and Hellarchon buy by the cartload), fire-stone (10 gp a lump, warm for days; a fine hand-warmer and an alchemist's reagent), and sulphur matches.

Hook: the glowing stones are brighter each year, and Gatherer-Mother Zoe has begun leaving offerings on the top step. She will not say to whom.

The Fallen-Star Shrine Shrine

Codex now: A small, windswept sanctuary on the mountain's warm flank where a black stone fell from the sky and the priests have kept it ever since.

A small sanctuary on the warm flank built around a pit in which a black, pitted stone lies half-buried where it fell. The priests keep a lamp burning beside it and sweep the ground every morning. Pilgrims come on foot and are not allowed to touch it. The shrine holds star metal, the iron that falls from the sky, and a few splinters of blue-white celestium that fell with it and have glowed ever since.

Now: the sky-priests are a handful of men and women from all three empires who have renounced their old gods for the stone. Their elder is Prior Eustathe of the Star, who licenses climbers to the Thin Places above and is courted by the Celestial Astromancers, who want the shrine's records. The shrine is open to pilgrims at dawn. Offerings are accepted and not discussed.

Found here: a pilgrim's blessing (an offering of your choosing); a licence to climb to the Thin Places (a vow of silence and a donation); and, very rarely, a filing of star metal for a smith (500 gp, if the priests agree).

Hook: the stone is warmer each year. A priest has begun recording the temperature and has told no one the figures.

The Thin Places Summit terraces

Codex now: Three bare terraces high on the mountain where the world is worn so thin that the high powers' metals can be gathered by a patient climber.

Three bare terraces near the peak, so high that the air is thin and so quiet a climber hears his own blood. The light is wrong: too clear, too sharp, as if a veil had been lifted. The sky-priests say this is where the world is worn thin enough for gifts to pass through. The terraces give hallowed steel, shining valhallium, weightless aerialite, white ivorite, harmonic idyllium, cold prismatic ice, shifting prismetal and heavy, patient aximium. The climb takes three days and a vow of silence.

Now: the Fallen-Star priests license the climb; the Mithril Reserve buys most of what comes down, through an agent at the mountain's foot, Factor Brennus Ironhand, a young dwarf of the clan who has never been allowed to climb himself. Those who come down speak of a light they cannot describe and of something below them that breathes once an hour.

Found here: nothing for sale on the terraces themselves. At the foot, the Reserve's factor pays for celestial metals by weight (aerialite 500 gp an ounce, and up) and sells climbing gear.

Hook: someone has been climbing the terraces to take, not to gather. The metals are less bright each month, and something is aware.

Sites Without a Region

Four sites the codex lists under no region. They are placed here as other pages place them: the great Sanctum library on its islet in Varathros Lake; the rose-cliff city on the edge of the Dasht-a Khaliq; and the Iron Parade Grounds and the Shattered Pass at the Duneforged Citadel and beyond the Cloudspine Ridge.

The Great Sanctum Library Library and lighthouse

Codex now: The continent's great library — every text copied twice, one copy never lent, and a catalogue nobody has seen the end of.

A colonnaded precinct on a rocky islet in Varathros Lake, under a titanic lighthouse said to be carved from sky-glass, which hums at certain alignments of the moon. The precinct claims to hold a copy of every written work in Asetheria. The claim is not quite true, and is closer to true than any rival would like. It acquires by an old and legally awkward custom: any vessel docking at its harbour surrenders every book aboard for copying. The copy is returned. The original is kept. Complaints are heard sympathetically and have never once resulted in a return.

Now: everything is held twice: a reading copy that circulates and a deep copy shelved below ground, in rooms librarians enter in pairs and leave together, a rule with no stated reason that has never been relaxed. The catalogue, some hundreds of volumes, is the real treasure, since a book that cannot be found is not there. The current Catalogue-Keeper, Hypatios Grammeus, is elderly, and has begun quietly training two successors instead of one: Doris and Kallias, who are not told about each other.

Found here: a reader's ticket (1 gp a month, references required); copying to order (from 1 sp a page, a season's wait); and the harbour office where your own books are taken.

Hook: a party's ship docks and its spellbook is taken for copying. The copy they get back has one spell more than the original.

The Rose-Cliff City Abandoned rock-cut city and temple

Codex now: A city carved down into the rock of a desert gorge, rich beyond reason on water it hid, and empty since the routes moved.

Approached through a gorge two carts wide and half a mile long, which opens without warning onto rose-red facades cut forty feet into the living cliff. Nothing here was built. It was removed. The city grew rich by controlling a caravan road and stayed rich by a trick its neighbours never solved: the country around has no visible water, but the city had cisterns, channels and settling tanks cut inside the rock, fed by flash floods that elsewhere simply killed people. A besieger camped on dry ground while the city drank. The routes moved, and rock-cut cities cannot follow.

Now: the most complete abandoned city on the continent, facades and channels intact, cisterns filling every wet season for nobody. No satrap claims it; it is not the inhabited rock-town further south whose frataraka sells wells by the hour. Caravans shelter here and rarely stay two nights. The only resident is a hermit-guide, Old Nabih, who lives in a tomb by the gorge mouth and charges a copper to show the way to the great temple-facade.

Found here: clean water, free, for the drawing; shelter; carved stone fragments that collectors in Deiperduem pay for, though Nabih asks that you take nothing.

Hook: the complaint is always the same and always slightly embarrassed: the city is too well kept. Sand does not drift as far in as it should, and the channels are never blocked. Someone, or something, is maintaining the drainage of a city empty for four hundred years.

The Iron Parade Grounds Legion barracks and drill field

Codex now: This Grounds houses the legion of DuneForged Citadel called The Adamantine Line

A great flat field cut out of the mountain's shoulder below the Helm, paved in iron-grey stone and ringed by barracks dug into the rock, where the Adamantine Line drills, lives and keeps its standards. The Line is older than the citadel's present walls and older than some cities of the Imperium: a legion said to have been raised before the primordial brood, its reputation tempered through generations of war. Its men wear black-iron scale, march in a silence broken only by drums, and parade before the Duke on the anniversary of Kaelen's stand.

Now: Commander Daud, "the Royal Protector", commands the Line and keeps the Duke's person, whence the nickname the court gave him; he also signs the Cedar Stair's timber licences. Vice-Commander Meagan Foster actually runs the legion: drill, pay, discipline and the roster. The Line garrisons the Skyward Bastions in rotation; Gavin Caesar's standing garrison drills on the same field and is not part of it, a distinction the Line insists on.

Found here: the parade, open to the public on feast days; recruiting, by examination only (the Line takes one applicant in twenty); a sutler's yard selling Line-issue boots and cloaks to veterans who are entitled to them, and to others who are not.

Hook: Vice-Commander Foster is short of men for the Festival watch and hires outsiders as auxiliaries, which the Line has not done in a century.

The Shattered Pass Forbidden zone

Codex now: Northeast ridge of the Duneforeged Citadel, beyond the [insert mountain name.]

A forbidden zone on the citadel's northeast ridge, beyond the Cloudspine, among jagged peaks and shadowed cliffs. Ancient rockfalls, crumbling bridges and sudden snowstorms make it nearly impassable even for seasoned climbers, and the citadel's ruling council has closed it by decree. It is bounded on the north by the Edge of Echoes, a sheer cliff that falls into endless mist; on the east by the Maw of Thorns, a gorge of razor-sharp natural rock spires; on the south by Sentinel's Watch, a collapsed outpost marked with broken banners and warning sigils; and on the west by the Sealed Gate, a reinforced stone barrier whose runes glow faintly when approached.

Now: the Sealed Gate is watched from Sentinel's Watch by a picket of the Adamantine Line under Centurion Ivo Marrick, who reports every glow of the runes to Vice-Commander Foster. The guards call the air elemental that haunts the approaches "the Wind That Votes". Rumour says the pass is cursed, haunted by the spirits of outcast warriors and guarded by sentient winds that whisper secrets and threats at night.

Found here: nothing lawful. Entry without the Duke's seal is a capital offence. Drakkur's Expeditionary will not outfit a party for it, and says so loudly enough that people ask why.

Hook: since the hum began in the Dune Mines, the Sealed Gate's runes have glowed every night, and Centurion Marrick wants someone expendable to find out which side of the Gate the glow is coming from.

Hellarchon

Arcane Academy Academy

Codex now: Hellarchon's renowned school of magic, which draws ambitious magi from across the planes.

A walled olive grove inside the city wall, which was moved out two hundred yards in the war to take the grove in. The court scribe Selenarion called it the place "where reality is reshaped by will alone". That is true by about the same margin. Lecture halls, warded vaults and three slim observatories that appear, from the harbour at dusk, to float. The violet sky over the city at that hour is popularly blamed on ancient magic, and the official histories footnote the claim to a vault record nobody may read.

Now: Scholarch Kallisto Pyrphoros runs it like a ship and refuses the Truth-Flame the cellars. Theron Oneirokrites, Reader of Dreams, runs the Academy's share of the Dreamers' Hunt. The Voidfolk evoker Asteria Erebide is its brightest pupil.

Found here: scroll-copying at 50 gp a spell level, item identification for a fee and a signature, tutors by the hour. The Academy buys orpiment, realgar, mountain crystal and reports of strange sleepers, paying up to four thousand drachmas for a sleeper who wakes speaking a language nobody taught her.

Hook: Inquisitor Vireon offers the party a writ to inspect "the second level of the cellars, which does not exist", and Kallisto offers twice as much to lose it.

The Agora of Hellarchon Agora

Codex now: Hellarchon's agora: market, assembly ground and the place anyone may speak.

An open square framed by stoas beneath the Rock, loud from dawn: fish and figs in the morning, courts in the colonnades, and the League's rule that anyone may speak and everyone will answer. The Courts of the Lot pick juries with slotted allotment stones, five hundred and one jurors to a case at three obols a day. The round Tholos houses the councillors on duty, the Prytaneion keeps the civic fire, and the Mint strikes the owls within earshot of the fishwives. Allied envoys wait here to be heard by the Assembly that commands the League's fleet.

Now: the Agoranomos Pheidippos Lakratou checks weights and the bread price, and fines with relish. On Assembly mornings public slaves sweep the square with a rope dipped in red ochre; a citizen with red on his cloak loses his attendance pay.

Found here: fresh owl coinage at the Mint's window, juror tickets, a philosopher for an afternoon (two drachmas, or a meal), and every rumour the Council will table tomorrow.

Hook: before the next great vote, the ochre rope keeps finding the same two hundred cloaks, all from the Road.

The Gymnasion of Hellarchon Gymnasion

Codex now: Hellarchon's gymnasion: exercise ground, school and the citizens' club.

Running track, wrestling floor and colonnaded rooms where teachers lecture and old men talk politics, all inside the Academy Grove. Hellarchon's young magi train their bodies and their arguments in the same colonnades, so the wrestling floor smells of olive oil and, now and then, ozone. A bout ends the moment anyone casts; the rule is cut into the starting sill, because it needed to be.

Now: the gymnasiarch, Lysimachos Chabriou, is a retired pankratiast with a ruined ear, paid by the city and sponsored by House Nikandridai. He keeps a list of students who flinch at fire. Asteria Erebide is not on it.

Found here: trainers for hire, wrestling lessons at three drachmas, cheap Academy tutors who will teach a cantrip for a meal, and the best gossip about who is failing which examination.

Hook: a wrestler collapsed mid-bout with frost on his lips. Nobody cast anything, the referee swears, and the referee is an Academy lecturer.

The Long Walls of Hellarchon Fortification

Codex now: The walls that join Hellarchon's hill city to its harbour two miles below, making one fortress with a port inside it.

Hellarchon was built twice, the old town on its rock and the harbour two miles below. Two walls run the whole way between them, a long bowshot apart, so the city cannot be starved while the fleet holds the sea. In the war the countryside came inside and never left. The road between the walls became a town: tenements four storeys high lean on the wall faces, rope-walks run along their feet, and every courtyard is a workshop. Hellarchon's wealth is on the hill. Its population is on the road.

Now: the elected wall-commissioner, Nausikles Andronou, holds the repair budget and the keys to the nine towers. The fleet's rowers live here and vote as one; the Sunward Valiants keep a muster-yard by the halfway tower and refuse to garrison it.

Found here: a bed for two obols, rope, sailcloth, oars, rowers for hire by the season, and sleep-readers paid by the Academy to listen for strange dreamers.

Hook: a stretch of wall near the halfway tower rings hollow when a cart goes by, and Nausikles has fined three people for saying so.

The Silver Drifts Mine

Codex now: Mine tunnels and washing-floors in the hills behind the naval city, where slaves and free miners dig lead and silver for the fleet.

A day's walk into the hills: tunnels, spoil-heaps and washing-floors that run white with crushed stone. The ore is lead with a thin vein of silver, dug by slave gangs under free overseers. The state owns the hills and leases the galleries for a fee and a share. The fleet is paid for by the silver, and the miners are paid in less.

Now: House Euxenidai holds the richest leases, and its lease-overseer, Mnesarchos Kallion, runs them with a tally-stick and a whip. Nobody is allowed to count the miners; the overseers say the number changes too fast to be useful.

Found here: lead pigs by the talent, sling-bullets by the basket, and silver that leaves only as ingots under guard for the Mint's owls. The washing-floors are open to visitors in the dry season. The tunnels are not.

Hook: a free-born foreman offers the party a share if they will hold the washing-floor gate for one night. He says the miners are rising. He does not say who is paying him.

The Spice Wharf Market

Codex now: A fragrant quay where ships from the farthest east unload cassia, pepper and ginger, and the whole harbour smells like a feast.

A long stone quay in the Emporion, east of the war basins, lined with warehouses sealed at night with three locks. Monsoon captains from Maurash and Sabaian traders in sewn-plank hulls unload sacks that smell of cinnamon and fire. Every pinch is weighed in front of the buyer and in front of the tax-clerk. A pickpockets' guild works the crowd with tidy discipline and, it is said, pays dues.

Now: the harbour-master, Glaukos Timonos, collects the dues. Bagadata Daryavand of the metic banking house weighs the pepper for the tax-clerk and notices more than he is paid to.

Found here: trade cassia, black pepper and root of warmth, priced by the pinch (pepper at a drachma an ounce on the quay, five by the time it reaches a village); Sabaian incense; sample bags at the Long Stoa; and a windowless Mithril Reserve branch at its end.

Hook: a ship has docked carrying no spice. Glaukos logged it as pepper, and one crate has already gone ashore.

The Temple Precinct of Hellarchon Sanctuary

Codex now: The walled sacred ground of Hellarchon, home of its patron's temple and its dedications.

The Rock's walled temenos: one gate, a marble stair, and on the summit the Maiden's temple, white stone visible a day out at sea. Altar outside, cult image within, and every open space crowded with dedications from citizens who want Athena and their neighbours to know what they gave. The Greater Panegyris ends here each year, after its procession up from the harbour behind a new robe for the goddess. Behind the cult room is a strongroom that holds the League Chest.

Now: the priestess of the Maiden, Hagne Eteoboutadou, keeps the rites and the inventory of dedications. Lady Kassiane Thaloris, the only Thalorid ever seen in public, lays the robe on the image in the Emperor's name.

Found here: votive owls and lamps, a guide for an obol (who will point out the windowless Mirrored House on the north spur), and the allies' delegates, who meet under a gilded ceiling they suspect they paid for.

Hook: Corinth's delegate asks the party to count the League Chest. Hagne will allow it on the one day a year the strongroom is aired.

The Theatre of Hellarchon Theatre

Codex now: Hellarchon's open-air theatre, cut into the hillside for festival drama and the assembly.

A curve of stone seats cut into the Rock's south slope above a round dancing floor. Plays are staged only at festivals, in competition, before the whole citizen body. This is the theatre of the Dionysia: for four days a year the comedies mock the powerful under a licence that does not extend to the rest of the calendar. When weather drives the Assembly off its hill, it meets here instead, which is why so many plays are about politics.

Now: the theatre-warden, Philon Kerameos, assigns seats by tribe and keeps the mask store. Kleito Euxenide funds choruses whose comedies mock her own father, and they sell out. The Obsidian Masquerade sits masked in the upper rows and is not asked to leave.

Found here: seat tokens at two obols, paid back to citizens by the Theoric Fund; masks and costumes for hire; and the year's scripts, copied and sold the morning after.

Hook: this year's prize comedy has a joke about "shed one hundred and twelve and a half". The Truth-Flame wants the author. So does the Hegemon.

Corinth

The Agora of Corinth Agora

Codex now: Corinth's agora: market, assembly ground and the place anyone may speak.

Every Hellenorian city has its agora, and Corinth's is the busiest and least decorous in the League: an open square of stoas off the Street of Counting-Houses, crowded with shippers, toll-farmers and every people on the continent. Anyone may speak and everyone will answer, usually in four languages at once. Corinthian tolerance is a business decision, and the square is where the business is done.

Now: the Agoranomos, Hermon Tlesimachou, a citizen outside the clan, holds the market weights and turns a blind eye for a fee he publishes. The Bacchiad Council sits in the Prytaneion on the north side, and the Order of Morning's Rise posts a pair of guards at each corner.

Found here: Atarabad silk from the Suren-Pahlav factor, Qart-Hadeth tin, Corinthian bronze, Araavyna jars, sea-loans on any captain, and "Delpharan copies" of the Aeolus wind-chart at five drachmas, which is a tenth of the real price and a fair guide to their value.

Hook: a grain captain whose sister ship went down on an off-chart day wants the man who sold him his chart, and the stall is empty this morning.

The Copper Smelts Foundry

Codex now: A smoky quarter by the two harbours where ore from the islands is turned into the metals that arm and ornament the League.

A grimy quarter beside Lechaion, the western harbour: furnaces, casting-pits and the sheds of founders who have worked the same alloys for six generations. Ore comes in from the islands and tin from Qart-Hadeth; bronze and brass go out the same way. The air tastes of metal and the harbour water has a green sheen.

Now: House Glaukotidai runs the founders' hall. Old Damophilos died last month, and his widow Kyra Glaukotis keeps the hall, the hostel for buyers and her silence. Strangers are not let near the furnaces, and the apprentices wear scars that explain why.

Found here: copper and tin ingots, bronze, the yellow brass of temple doors and trumpets, and, for buyers the guild trusts, the gold-tinged alloy the League simply calls Corinthian (a bowl costs what a farm does).

Hook: the Corinthian alloy recipe is missing from the guild strongbox, and Damophilos's two sons are blaming each other. Kyra hires the party and asks them not to tell either son who hired them.

The Gymnasion of Corinth Gymnasion

Codex now: Corinth's gymnasion: exercise ground, school and the citizens' club.

Track, wrestling floor and lecture rooms in the Isthmian Quarter, beside the stadium. It trains the athletes of the Isthmian Games, the League's second-greatest, held every two years under a truce even tyrants keep. Corinth's version of the citizens' club admits anyone who can pay, which other cities think vulgar and Corinth thinks is the point.

Now: the gymnasiarch, Timanthes Korinnou, a former Isthmian runner, manages sponsorships the way the Street manages loans. Every rich house sponsors an athlete; the haulers sponsor one too, by subscription, and cheer him louder than the rest.

Found here: trainers and masseurs, wrestling bouts with side bets, athletes for hire as bodyguards between Games, and oil at three times the agora price.

Hook: the haulers' runner has been offered a fortune to lose. He asks the party to find out who is paying, because the purse came wrapped in a Bacchiad cloth.

The Haulway of Corinth Ship Haulway

Codex now: A paved track across the isthmus on which whole ships are dragged overland between Corinth's two seas.

Between Corinth's two harbours runs a paved track with grooves cut for wheeled cradles, on which whole ships are dragged from one sea to the other. A cargo that crosses saves several days and a dangerous cape, and Corinth charges accordingly. It never stops: ox teams, capstans, and the shriek of a hull winched across stone. The season's first ship is crewed across by the city's magistrates, who are notoriously bad at it, and the haulers bet on how many fall off.

Now: House Larnakidai holds this year's toll-farm and pays its haulers on time. The Haulmaster, Archelaos Bacchiades, oversees the toll-houses, and Nerissa Thalassine escorts convoys to both mouths.

Found here: passage by keel-length, measured against a bronze rod at each toll-house (a light galley crosses in half a day for about forty drachmas); mules for silk bales; haulers by the day.

Hook: a Hellarchon captain swears the eastern rod is shorter than the western one, and wants witnesses for a measuring.

The Laurel Court Garden

Codex now: A cloistered garden beside the games stadium where victors are crowned and the acanthus grows in carved profusion.

A cloistered garden beside the isthmus stadium where Games victors are crowned with laurel cut that morning by the priest. The columns are capped with carved leaves, and living acanthus has been allowed to grow between them until stone and plant are hard to tell apart. The masons come here to copy it for their capitals.

Now: Euagoras, priest of the Court, cuts the victors' laurel with a bronze sickle and is afraid of something. During the Games only victors, judges and the very rich get in; afterwards the crowd is let in to touch the trees.

Found here: the Victor's Laurel (not for sale, in theory), bear's-breeches cuttings for gardeners, and masons' sketches of the capitals at a drachma a sheet.

Hook: someone is cutting the laurel at night and selling wreaths to men who did not win. One of them has just been crowned at Delphara with a Corinthian wreath.

The Lyre-Makers' Row Street

Codex now: A street of luthiers by the stadium where tortoise shells become the sounding-boards of every music-school's instruments.

A street of luthiers near the stadium, every window full of lyres in every state of completion. The best are made on shells the maker chose himself and cured for a year before stringing; a passing musician can tell a row-made lyre by the first note. The shells come from hill villages, on the understanding that the animals go back to the wild after a season.

Now: the master of the row, Terpsikles Ainetou, judges every shell and sits on the panel for the Isthmian music contests. A player may try any instrument; a serious buyer is offered a seat, a cup and a long lecture.

Found here: student lyres at 5 gp, row-made concert lyres from 30 gp, strings of gut and of twisted silk, and repairs done while you wait and listen.

Hook: the tortoise supply is failing, the luthiers have begun buying from poachers, and a shell has turned up carrying a hill village's mark. The luthiers swear they returned those tortoises.

The Temple Precinct of Corinth Sanctuary

Codex now: The walled sacred ground of Corinth, home of its patron's temple and its dedications.

The temenos crowds the slope above the Lebes, the eastern harbour, round as a cauldron. Poseidon of the Isthmus holds the chief temple, and every open space is crowded with dedications. The port's temples are unusually well endowed and unusually busy. They cater to sailors, which is to say they run on the money of men who may not come back.

Now: the precinct's vow-keeper, Nausiphanes Lebetos, serves the Eastern Tide under the Archiereia Pherenike Isthmiadou in the Two Tides rite, performed at both harbours at once and ended by a race back to the centre. He writes sailors' vows on bronze tags and files them by ship.

Found here: votive anchors, safe-voyage vows at a drachma, a deposit chest where a sailor can leave his pay before he sails, and blessings in any language he can afford.

Hook: a sailor back after three years finds his deposit gone. The priests say it passed to the god when his ship was posted lost.

The Theatre of Corinth Theatre

Codex now: Corinth's open-air theatre, cut into the hillside for festival drama and the assembly.

A curve of seats above a round dancing floor in the Isthmian Quarter, newer and gaudier than any other in the League. It is new money's favourite gift to the city. Corinth's rich sponsor its festivals lavishly and are looked down on by older cities for it. Twice a year the citizens outside the clan meet here to acclaim what the Bacchiad Council has already decided.

Now: the theatre-warden, Glykera Damophantou, sells the sponsorships and keeps the seating list. Each sponsor's name is cut into the seat-backs he paid for, and re-cut when someone pays more.

Found here: seats from an obol to a gilded front-row chair at 10 gp, painted scenery, hired choruses, and an audience that heckles in six languages.

Hook: at the last acclamation the dockers sat in a block and stayed silent. The Prytanis wants to know who told them to.

The Upper Fortress of Corinth Citadel

Codex now: The fortified rock above Corinth, the strongest position in Hellenoria, never taken by assault.

A fortified rock rises above the isthmus and commands both harbours. It is the strongest position in Hellenoria, has never been taken by assault, and has a spring inside its walls that has never run dry, which is why nobody has seriously tried. Aphrodite's temple stands on the summit, rich in sailors' offerings. Below it, in vaults cut into the rock, lies the Bacchiad treasury. Corinth has never needed much of an army: it has the rock, a modest fleet, and the money to hire other people.

Now: the Polemarch of the Rock, Deinias Bacchiades, holds the keys. He voted against the Lechaion Marriage and has not dined with his cousin Lykon since. The Order of Morning's Rise garrisons the gates under contract.

Found here: a view of two seas, myrtle wreaths and sailors' votives at Aphrodite's temple, and nothing else for sale.

Hook: Deinias asks the party to test the gates "as raiders would", at night, and to report to him alone.

The Wise Owl Inn Inn

Codex now: A rambling inn beside the old city wall where a little yellow-eyed owl presides over the common room and the landlord's secrets.

A rambling three-storey inn built against the old city wall above the Lebes, its common room dark with generations of smoke. A little owl lives in the rafters, fed by the landlord and treated by the regulars as the house's conscience. Business here is done in whispers, and the owl is thought to listen. The sign shows the owl of the wise goddess.

Now: the landlord, Tolmides, keeps twelve beds and three rules, recites them on arrival, and credits the owl with knowing things he should not. Ixion Keraunios drinks here between sales of wind on the quay.

Found here: a bed at four obols, a cellar of excellent local red, a quiet corner for a contract, and introductions to pilots, sponsors and men who fix games.

Hook: the party's private conversation of last night is repeated to them, word for word, by a stranger on the quay.

Delphara

The Agora of Delphara Agora

Codex now: Delphara's agora: market, assembly ground and the place anyone may speak.

Delphara's agora is small and exists to serve pilgrims. It sits in the Lower Town at the foot of the Sacred Way: lodging brokers, sellers of goats and cockerels, money-changers, and guides who explain the treasuries for a fee. The League's rule holds here too, that anyone may speak and everyone will answer, but the town's own rule comes first: what is asked at the temple is not repeated in the town.

Now: House Labyadai licenses every guide and holds a third of the beds. Euthymos Labyadas runs the lodging brokers from a bench under the east stoa and owes money in Corinth. The town's small assembly argues about drains and the price of goats here, and is not allowed to argue about anything else.

Found here: a goat certified fit for sacrifice (2 gp in spring, 6 gp in a Games year), a bed from a drachma to a fortune, a licensed guide at three obols a turn of the Way, and pilgrims' letters of credit at the Mithril Reserve vault under the north stoa.

Hook: a question asked under the guides' seal has been repeated word for word in a Hellarchon wine-shop. Aristomache Labyadis wants the leak found quietly.

The Dream Dormitory Temple

Codex now: A long, cool hall in the oracle's precinct where the sick sleep among harmless snakes and wake with a cure or a riddle.

A long, cool hall in the temenos, lined with cots and patrolled by slow, olive-coloured snakes nobody has ever seen bite. The sick are admitted after a ritual bath and a night of fasting, and lie down to sleep. In the morning they tell their dreams to a priest, who reads them as a prescription. The Healer's Serpents have been bred in the temple for six hundred years and the priests know each by name.

Now: Iphianassa Oneiropolos keeps the hall and is frightened for the first time in her life. Her junior priest Philokles vanished after reading one pilgrim's dream.

Found here: a night's incubation for a donation (custom says a drachma; the rich give more), dream-readings, shed serpent skins sold as charms, and no guarantees.

Hook: a pilgrim from Atticenea was cured by a dream that was "not a standard dream". Iphianassa, an Acheaorian "almanac clerk" and an Academy "student of winds" each hire the party separately to find Philokles first.

The Gymnasion of Delphara Gymnasion

Codex now: Delphara's gymnasion: exercise ground, school and the citizens' club.

Track, wrestling floor and colonnades on the Phoibad Terrace, below the spring where every petitioner washes before going up. It trains for the Pythian Games, where the musical contests come before the athletics, the opposite of every other games in Hellenoria. So the music-schools outnumber the wrestling-masters, and the runners practise to pipes.

Now: the gymnasiarch, Aristonoe Phoibados, is a retired kithara champion who runs the music-schools and tolerates the athletes. Runners from Thebesieas and riders from Argotiko dominate the Games, and train here for a month before each.

Found here: lessons on the kithara and the pipes, a bath in water the priests call pure, cold plunges at dawn, and judges' gossip about who will win.

Hook: a Thebesian runner is accused of washing at the Phoibad Spring without paying the purification fee, which disqualifies him. He says he was told he could.

The Herbalists' Lodge Guildhall

Codex now: A quiet courtyard behind the oracle's temple where physicians and herb-wives trade cures, warnings and the day's gossip.

A quiet courtyard behind the oracle's temple, planted with pots and hung with drying bunches, where the city's physicians and the village herb-wives meet to trade. It is the only place in Delphara where the two talk as equals, and the lodge-keeper makes sure they do.

Now: Myrrhine of Kirimitsana keeps the lodge, listens well and prescribes better. The herb-wives come down from Kirimitsana and the hill villages twice a month; the physicians come when they are stuck.

Found here: temple hyssop, garlic and spiral-flowered birthwort for the midwives, madness-cure hellebore under lock and key (sold only with a physician's mark), and free advice to anyone with a complaint.

Hook: a new physician, Zopyros, is selling cures that work too well. The lodge suspects he is poisoning villagers to create the need.

The Oracle of Delphara Oracle Temple

Codex now: The temple at the summit where petitioners pay to put their question to the god.

At the top of the Sacred Way stands the temple of the oracle. The god answers on the seventh day of each of the nine warm months. The Pythia, a Delpharan woman over fifty in a girl's white dress, washes at the spring, goes down beneath the floor and sits on a bronze tripod over a crack that breathes a faint, sweetish air. Consultation is not free: the petitioner pays for the sacrifice, the attendance and the interpretation, and the fee scales with who is asking. In winter the god is absent, the temple shuts for the Silence, and the town empties.

Now: Theano the Pythia, a vintner's widow of fifty-eight, speaks. The five Hosioi decide which questions reach her and in what order. The Exegetes under Lysandra Anthemis turn her words into verse a petitioner can carry home.

Found here: a consultation (a man pays about 10 gp, a city a talent), the bean-lot in the porch on other days for an obol, and the right to ask first, which belongs in perpetuity to the Acheaorian throne.

Hook: Theano cannot read, but she remembers every word she has spoken, and she has noticed that the verses sent home do not always match.

The Oracle's Vineyards Vineyard

Codex now: Terraced vines on the sanctuary's lower slopes, tended by temple slaves and harvested to a calendar the oracle sets.

Terraced vineyards on the lower slopes of the Sacred Plain, owned by the temple and worked by its dependants. The harvest begins on the day the oracle names, and a vintner who picks a day early or late loses the year's wine to the god. A stand of Thunder-Oak on the upper edge is held sacred, and its acorns go to the priests' swine.

Now: Moschion, priest of the vines, names the harvest day "as the god directs". House Kastalidai keeps the boundary stones and owns the best private vines just outside the plain; their wine reaches pilgrims a fortnight before the temple's, labelled "from the oracle's slopes", which is strictly true.

Found here: temple wine at the gate, blessing included in the price (a jar at 3 gp); Kastalid wine in the Lower Town at half that; acorn-fed pork in season.

Hook: a boundary stone has moved forty paces, turning a strip of new vines into sacrilege. Reporting it could start a sacred war. Ignoring it is perjury.

The Temple Precinct of Delphara Sanctuary

Codex now: The walled sacred ground of Delphara, home of its patron's temple and its dedications.

In Delphara the temple precinct is the whole city's reason for being. The Sacred Way climbs past twenty-three treasuries to the walled temenos of Apollo, the Radiant One: oracle temple, great altar and a forest of dedications within two hundred paces. Eleven treasuries are kept up by the cities that built them; the rest belong to cities that no longer exist. The Acheaorian Treasury, the House of the Tripod, stands at the sixth turn and is the richest building on the mountain.

Now: Kleobule Pythokleia, Epimelete of the Treasuries, keeps the inventories. Captain Hagnon's Tripod Guard, a hundred and twenty men with bronze-shod staves, keeps order on the Way. Mehrdad Vashtir, treasurer of the House of the Tripod, is generous to every priest's widow on the mountain.

Found here: votive tripods and laurel, a guided climb (three obols a turn), and the view from each treasury's porch, which its city's keepers will describe at length.

Hook: Kleobule has found a chest in the House of the Tripod that is on no list, and asks the party to witness its opening before her uncle hears of it.

The Theatre of Delphara Theatre

Codex now: Delphara's open-air theatre, cut into the hillside for festival drama and the assembly.

Cut into the mountain above the temple, on the High Seats, with a view down the valley of olives that is considered part of the performance. It holds the Pythian musical contests and, each spring and autumn, the Amphictyony's sessions: twenty-four delegates in the front row, the town watching from above. The stadium is higher still, with nothing above it but Thunder-Oak.

Now: Hieromnemon Eudoros Pythokles presides at the sessions and has put off, for three sessions running, the vote on whether a tyrant's delegate counts as a delegate. The theatre-keeper, Glaukippos Hymnou, tunes the echo stones and seats the delegates.

Found here: free seats at sessions (standing room only in a Games year), pipers and singers for hire between contests, and the best place on the mountain to watch who talks to whom.

Hook: the Atticenean tyrant's delegate must reach the autumn session alive, in time for the vote on whether he is a delegate at all.

Ephelanum

The Basilica of Ephelanum Law Courts

Codex now: Ephelanum's hall of law: courts, contracts and the property registers under one roof.

A long roofed hall on the Forum Line with an apse at the far end where the magistrate sits. Cases are heard, contracts witnessed and property registered under one roof and in public. Ephelanum's basilica hears the sanctuary's lending cases, for the temple here is also a bank, and the boundary suits of the Red Plain. Both governments dispute whose law applies, so a case may be heard twice, once in each language, with two verdicts.

Now: two benches share the apse on alternate days. The Procurator of the Estates, Sextus Afranius Bassus, sits for the Dux; a Hellenorian court of jurors drawn by lot sits for the Archon. The registers are kept by a clerk who belongs to neither side, Philemon Diglossos, and is paid by both.

Found here: harvest-loan contracts, land deeds in two languages, notaries at a drachma a seal, and, at the Fair, futures on next year's barley.

Hook: a farmer won his boundary suit in the Hellenorian court and lost it in the Invictian one on the same day. Both verdicts order his neighbour's wall pulled down, on opposite sides.

The Baths of Ephelanum Public Baths

Codex now: Ephelanum's public baths, where the city does its bathing, its gossip and most of its business.

Invictian baths are civic, cheap and nearly universal: cold, warm and hot rooms over a furnace-heated floor, an exercise yard, and benches enough for a city's business. These stand at the harbour end of the marble street and serve pilgrims as much as citizens: the first stop for anyone landing by sea, before they climb to the goddess. In festival season they run from dawn to midnight and still queue.

Now: the baths are the one building the treaty assigns to both governments. The Archon, the Hierarchis and the Dux meet monthly in the warm room as the joint board, arriving at the same moment through three different doors. The bath-master, Gnaeus Sulpicius Lavator, stokes the furnaces and keeps the minutes in two languages.

Found here: a bath for a copper, a massage for two, festival ribbons sold from a stall in the yard (real ones, mostly), and every rumour that matters by noon.

Hook: Vettia Prisca, the Dux's wife, bathes daily and asks the party, in good Hellenorian, to find out who left a note in her towel.

The Ephelanum Garrison Legionary Camp

Codex now: The legion's camp at Ephelanum, kept outside the sacred line as Invictian law requires.

Invictian law keeps soldiers outside a city's sacred boundary, so the garrison stands beyond the walls on the Garrison Road: a rectangular camp on the standard plan, a gate on each side, the headquarters at the crossing of the two main streets. Beside it stand the military granaries where the plain's grain tithe for the southern garrisons is stored. Ephelanum's real protection has always been its sanctuary status; the camp is small and largely ceremonial.

Now: Tribune Gnaea Laelia Rufa commands one under-strength cohort, paid late and in debased coin. Dux Marcus Vettius Calvo keeps the praetorium. His son Lucius, a tribune, is in love with a novice of the Bees.

Found here: surplus legionary kit sold out the back gate, Diana's crescent amulets from the silversmiths' second moulds, and legionaries who will work a harvest day for wages.

Hook: the camp's paychest arrived from Aepistra a quarter short, and the cohort has heard.

The Forum of Ephelanum Forum

Codex now: Ephelanum's civic square, where law, market and religion share one pavement.

The paved, colonnaded square at the commercial end of the marble street that runs from harbour to sanctuary. Proclamations are read here, the price of bread is argued in public, and the silversmiths sell votive temples, silver sheaves and little silver oxen for the First Furrow. A bronze strip two fingers wide crosses the paving: the treaty line. A stall that straddles it pays two taxes.

Now: the Agoranomos Lysikles Thrasonos runs the market on the Hellenorian side; the Praefectus Portus's men tax the other. At dawn in harvest season day-labourers stand on the Hellenorian side of the strip to be hired for Invictian estates.

Found here: votive models in two moulds (the Lady with her stag, Diana with her hounds, same price), festival ribbons, harvest labour by the day, and grain-brokers who will quote next year's price.

Hook: a silversmith has set his stall exactly on the strip and refuses to pay either tax, citing the goddess. Both governments want him moved, and neither will be first.

The Great Sanctuary of Ephelanum Temple

Codex now: The vast temple at the end of Ephelanum's marble street, visible far out to sea, and the city's reason to exist.

At the end of the marble street stands a temple large enough to be seen well out at sea, its colonnade alone a century's work. It is also a bank: it holds deposits under sanctuary protection, lends against next year's harvest, and is by some measures the largest single holder of coin in Hellenoria. Around it lies the goddess's ring of sacred field, vineyard, olives and white cattle. Each spring the Image is carried down the marble street to the harbour and back in the Procession of the Image, and since the treaty it loops through the barley so the Lady can see the crop.

Now: Hierarchis Melissa Aristarchis holds the sanctuary, its bank and its land. The priestesses, called the Bees, keep its hives and its ledgers. The Neokoros Megabyxos keeps the temple guard, the asylum (a bowshot from the altar) and the boundary-cord.

Found here: harvest loans at one in ten for citizens and one in eight for everyone else, deposits that no army has dared touch, festival ribbons, and asylum.

Hook: a boundary-stone between the goddess's ring and the Rubrian latifundia has moved forty paces in a night, and under its old place lies a carved stone older than the temple.

The Red-Earth Sheds Workshop

Codex now: Long sheds behind the sanctuary where red clay is washed, dried and sealed in jars for painters and the pious.

A row of long sheds behind the sanctuary where red earth dug from a hill across the bay is washed in troughs, dried in trays and sealed in small jars with the sanctuary's stamp. The workers have red hands and red hair, and so do their children. The sheds are open to pilgrims after the morning rite; the priests encourage questions and the shopkeeper encourages purchases.

Now: the shed-master, Phoibe Miltoureia, a lay sister of the Bees, runs the washing and the stamp. The hill the earth comes from belongs to the Rubrii, and Gaius Rubrius Fenestella has sued the sanctuary for clay-rent in both courts and won in one.

Found here: Sinopic red, a painter's best vermilion earth, at 2 gp a jar; a smaller pilgrim's jar for the forehead at a drachma; and painters' pigment by the sack for workshops with a letter.
