Hook: the sanctuary's stamp is being forged in the port's lower market. The sanctuary has not noticed, or has decided not to.

The Tyrian Vats Dye-works

Codex now: A reeking dye-works on the temple-port's far shore where snails and insects are crushed into the colours of kings.

A long row of vats on the far shore, downwind and downstream of everything, where the stench is the first thing a visitor notices and the last thing a resident does. Shell-heaps taller than the sheds stand on the beach, and the workers are stained from the wrist down. Tyrsan dyers from the Farshore Realms taught the vats their purple, which is why the works are named for a rival.

Now: the dye-master, Kanake Porphyreia, runs the vats and sells to whoever comes by boat. The legionaries of the Garrison Road march past holding their noses.

Found here: the true purple reserved by law for rulers (a border's worth costs a farmer's year), scarlet-grain red that rivals it, and the two together, which make a robe a village could not afford.

Hook: a vat of true purple has been stolen. The thief will be found by the colour of his hands.

Helionyx

The Agora of Helionyx Agora

Codex now: Helionyx's agora: market, assembly ground and the place anyone may speak.

Awnings strung between the white walls shade the square. In this city people gather in the shade, not the sun, and business stops dead at noon. The Court of the Jettison sits here at dawn and is cited by every maritime court in the League. By mid-morning the sea-loan brokers have written the day's bottomry, loans on ships repaid only if the ship comes home. The Mithril Reserve branch is the only building on the square that is not white. It is grey basalt, and nobody has dared to report it.

Now: House Halikidai, the salt house, dominates the brokers' benches. Theron Halikos, the Prytanis's son, sits as a jurist of the Jettison court, ambitious and bored. Hrefna Ironhand, Dominus Argentar, buys next season's purple on forward contracts from her grey door.

Found here: salt by the cart, bottomry at a quarter to a third for the season, Jettison judges for hire as arbitrators, smoked glass for visitors at a drachma, and nothing at all between noon and mid-afternoon.

Hook: a ship jettisoned a sealed cargo off the Salt Flats. Under the Law of the Jettison every shipper aboard must now pay a share of something nobody will name.

The Almond Slope Orchard

Codex now: A southern hillside that flowers white in midwinter, a month before anything else, and gives the sun-city its sign of spring.

A hillside above the Evening Terraces planted with almond trees that flower in the depth of winter, a pale haze against the brown hill. On the first day of blossom the sun-priests walk up and proclaim the end of the cold, whatever the weather, and the city holds a feast. The herb-gatherers' paths along the upper edge are lined with silver-leaved Saviour's Sage.

Now: the slope is temple land, kept by an orchard-warden of the College of the Arc, Bion Amygdalou, who records the first blossom beside the College's shadow-readings. Hegesias Phaethontides, Sun-Priest of the year, wants this winter's early blossom certified as an omen before the council votes on raising the fallen Charioteer.

Found here: Early Almonds (a drachma a measure, five in the week of blossom), Saviour's Sage for fever tea, almond-blossom honey, and a crowd.

Hook: the almonds blossomed three weeks early this year. The sun-priests say it is an omen, and nobody agrees which. Hegesias wants a certificate; the Halikidai want it lost.

The Gymnasion of Helionyx Gymnasion

Codex now: Helionyx's gymnasion: exercise ground, school and the citizens' club.

On the Evening Terraces, the gymnasion keeps the hours of the sun: exercise at dawn, lectures in the shade at noon, and the astronomers' pupils at the arc by evening. Its colonnades have deep roofs and its track runs east to west so nobody runs into the glare. The College of the Arc takes its novices from the pupils who can sit still longest.

Now: the gymnasiarch, Kleitos Heliodorou, is a former navarch's oarsman who teaches geometry with a rope and a stick. The Ecliptica Arcanum's housemistress Hipponoe lectures here at noon and recruits.

Found here: lessons in astronomy, navigation and geometry at two drachmas, copies of last year's solar tables, and pupils who will sell next year's a week before the Reading.

Hook: the Invictian factor Quintia Caelestina is paying pupils for the tables early. One pupil has sold her a copy with figures that differ from the published ones by a day.

The Solar Precinct of Helionyx Observatory

Codex now: An open court with a gnomon and a graduated arc, read every clear day for six hundred years.

At Helionyx's highest point is the solar precinct: an open court with a gnomon at its centre and a graduated arc cut into the pavement, read and recorded every clear day for six hundred years. Six centuries of tables are kept in cedar presses along the north wall. At the summer solstice, the Standing, the exact moment is announced and the whole city falls silent. The year's tables are published at the Reading of the Arc before scholars from three empires.

Now: the College of the Arc, thirty life-sworn gnomonists under Gnomonarch Asterope Kleidemou, half-blind from sixty years of reading shadows, holds it. No court day or assembly may sit on a day the College has not reckoned. Magus Tirdad of Atarabad's Fire-Temple observes, and is too polite to mention what he has found.

Found here: the published tables (a copy at 5 gp), calendar reckonings for contracts, and a place in the crowd at the Standing.

Hook: Hipponoe of the Ecliptica Arcanum wants the cedar presses copied before "somebody careless" burns them, and asks the party to get her in at night.

The Stork Roof Temple roof

Codex now: The great flat roof of the sun-temple, where a dozen storks nest in the shadow of the gold dome and are forbidden to be harmed.

The wide flat roof of the sun-temple on Temple Hill, reached by a spiral stair and crowned with a gold dome that blinds ships at sea. A dozen stork nests sit among the chimneys, each a mass of sticks the size of a cartwheel. The priests treat the birds as lodgers whose rent is luck, and the city's children watch them with spy-glasses from the neighbouring towers.

Now: Pelagon, keeper of the Stork Roof, records the date of the first arrival each year, and the farmers consult the record before they sow. The roof is open to anyone who climbs the stair. The storks are not impressed by anyone.

Found here: a view over the white city, shed feathers sold as luck-charms by the temple boys, and Pelagon's record, which goes back two hundred years.

Hook: no stork has returned this spring. Pelagon has told nobody, is leaving offerings, and begs the party to climb the roof at night and find out why the birds will not land. The gold dome is warm to the touch after dark.

The Temple Precinct of Helionyx Sanctuary

Codex now: The walled sacred ground of Helionyx, home of its patron's temple and its dedications.

The city's sacred ground crowns Temple Hill beside the solar precinct, where the gnomon's shadow has been read every clear day for six hundred years. The walled temenos holds the sun-temple of Helios, the Titan who is the sun, with its gold dome and the Stork Roof above; Apollo is kept as a guest in a lower shrine down a side stair. Dedications are gilded, and at noon the precinct is too bright to look at.

Now: the Sun-Priest of the year, Hegesias Phaethontides, wears the gold crown, pays for the Standing and has his name cut into every contract. He has hired a Corinthian engineer to plan the raising of the fallen Charioteer. The real priesthood, the College of the Arc, lets him.

Found here: gilded sun-discs, votive chariots, a blessing for a voyage south, and the year's name for your contracts.

Hook: the Corinthian engineer has been found measuring the temple's foundations at night, and the College wants him gone before he finishes.

The Theatre of Helionyx Theatre

Codex now: Helionyx's open-air theatre, cut into the hillside for festival drama and the assembly.

Cut into the Evening Terraces, it faces away from the afternoon sun by design, and performances begin at dusk. The assembly meets here after dark too, by lamplight, and the city considers it the only civilised hour for either. Night is social in Helionyx, and the terraces below the theatre are the liveliest streets in the League once the sun is down.

Now: the theatre-keeper, Eudora Lychnou, controls the lamps, which in this city means she controls when the assembly can start. Prytanis Philinna Halikis presides from the front row.

Found here: seats at an obol, grilled octopus and almond cakes on the steps, lamp oil by the jar, and the night's political rumours.

Hook: on the night of the vote on raising the Charioteer, the lamps fail.

Thebesieas

The Agora of Thebesieas Agora

Codex now: Thebesieas's agora: market, assembly ground and the place anyone may speak.

The Muster Ground: an agora that doubles as a parade ground, its earth trampled hard by farmers' carts and hoplites' feet. At the Muster every citizen of military age presents himself and his equipment here for inspection, and inspectors from other wards check his greaves. On other days it is a market for barley, horses and harness. The magistrates' court stands on the east side, with the walled Garden of Quiet Death behind it.

Now: the Mithril Reserve branch and the Corinthian factors' counting-rooms face the court across the square. Archias the Weigher, a Corinthian factor, weighs grain for a living and other things for a better one. Lykophron Ktesiou, Hellarchon's proxenos, counts spearheads at the Muster for the Hegemon's office.

Found here: barley and wheat by the cartload, Argotiko horses, armourers who fit a breastplate in a day, and the cheapest bread in the League.

Hook: a spearhead turns up at the Muster with a badly filed arsenal mark. Lykophron offers the party a fortune for it; Epameinon Kleitarchos asks them to bring it to him.

The Citadel of Thebesieas Citadel

Codex now: The inland city's fortress, with its own water: built by a city that expects to be attacked by land.

Thebesieas expects to be attacked by land, and the Sown Hill says so: heavy walls of its own, gates that are real gates, granaries for a year and a spring that has never failed, so that it can hold out after the lower city falls. The citadel keeps the roll of the Sacred Band, a bronze tablet re-cut at every Naming, when the living answer for the dead.

Now: Agathon Dirkaios of House Dirkaidai keeps the spring and the roll, and reads the names at the Naming without notes. Polemarch Melanthios Sparton sits with the Seven gate-generals in the council hall. The new arsenal behind it is closed to visitors, and its storemen are forbidden to discuss what is in it.

Found here: nothing for sale, though the spring water is given free to anyone who asks, by an old law, and the walls can be walked with a gate-general's leave.

Hook: the rubbings of the Mycairan tablets are missing from the citadel archive, and Dexippe, the Thessalonikan scholar who had been trying to buy them for two years, has suddenly stopped asking.

The Garden of Quiet Death Garden

Codex now: A walled physic garden in the inland city where the state grows the plants it uses on its condemned, with a keeper who tends them gently.

A walled garden behind the magistrates' court, planted with the poison-plants the state uses for execution and the herbalists use for medicine. The beds are labelled in tidy script: this one kills slowly, this one kills quickly, this one is a cure in a very small dose. The key to the gate is held by the chief magistrate, who in Thebesieas is the Polemarch.

Now: Sosipatros, a gentle old man with gloved hands, tends it alone. He answers any question, offers nothing, and has never lied.

Found here: Judge's Hemlock, Stinking Nightshade, Nightsbane and the pretty, deadly Beautiful Lady. A physician may visit with a magistrate's note and take a measured dose; nobody else takes anything.

Hook: a bed of hemlock has been disturbed. Sosipatros says he did not do it, and he has never lied before. The Polemarch wants it settled before the Naming of the Band.

The Gymnasion of Thebesieas Gymnasion

Codex now: Thebesieas's gymnasion: exercise ground, school and the citizens' club.

The Pairs' Ground, where the city's citizen phalanx is made. Boys become hoplites here, drilled in eight-deep files until they can wheel without looking, to a standard the maritime cities cannot match. The Sacred Band lives here in the long barracks called the Pairs' Hall, two cots to a bay, fed at public cost. Old men watch from the colonnade and argue about the oblique advance as other cities' old men argue about philosophy.

Now: Epameinon Kleitarchos, Lochagos of the Sacred Band, drills the Band at dawn; the drill-master of the ephebes, Pagondas Ismenou, drills everyone else and shouts louder. This spring's Naming read three hundred living names for the first time since the Treaty.

Found here: drill instruction for foreigners (rarely granted, 5 gp a month), shield-straps and spear-shafts from the gymnasion's own workshop, and sparring partners who do not hold back.

Hook: a new recruit to the Band has no pair, and the Band has never sworn a man alone. He asks one of the party to swear with him at the shield-bearer's tomb.

The Temple Precinct of Thebesieas Sanctuary

Codex now: The walled sacred ground of Thebesieas, home of its patron's temple and its dedications.

The sanctuary of Thebesieas is plain by League standards, and the other cities never let it forget. Its dedications are captured arms, some so old nobody remembers whose they were. Hercules's temple, the city's patron who was born here, the city says, is squat and enormous. Demeter of the furrow keeps a side altar, and an altar of Ares stands at the citadel gate, kept up and never thanked.

Now: the priest of Hercules, Kallikles Iolaides, keeps the captured arms oiled and the votive clubs counted. Widows of the war tend the Demeter altar and outnumber the priests.

Found here: votive clubs and little bronze lion-skins, a blessing on new armour (a drachma), and a guide to the captured shields who will tell you which city lost each one, loudly, if a Hellarchene is listening.

Hook: a shield in the dedications bears the device of a Hellarchon trireme that was officially lost at sea with all hands, and its trierarch's family wants it back.

The Theatre of Thebesieas Theatre

Codex now: Thebesieas's open-air theatre, cut into the hillside for festival drama and the assembly.

Thebesieas built its theatre late and reluctantly, in the Temple Ward. It is used more for the reading of the Sacred Band's roll than for plays. A visiting Thessalonikan company once performed a comedy here, and the audience was polite. The Shield Assembly, in which only men who can afford a full panoply vote, meets here to elect the Polemarch.

Now: the theatre-warden, Kadmilos Thersandrou, is a veteran with one arm who keeps the seat-stones swept and the roll's stand polished. At the Naming of the Band the living stand in the orchestra and answer for the dead, name by name.

Found here: free seats, honey cakes at the Naming, and a Thessalonikan troupe once a year, which comes for the fee and leaves early.

Hook: at this year's Naming a name was answered that is not on the roll, by a voice from the empty top row.

Thessalonika

The Agora of Thessalonika Agora

Codex now: Thessalonika's agora: market, assembly ground and the place anyone may speak.

The tidiest agora in the League: a planned square on the city grid, its stoas glazed against the northern cold and warmed by braziers from the First Frost to spring. It is the busiest market north of the Long Lane, where a horse, a slave, a cask of pickled tunny and a copy of any book on the continent can be bought before noon. Anyone may speak and everyone will answer, though here the answer usually comes with a reference.

Now: every quarter the Epistates, Eudoros Anaxilaou, hangs the city's full audit on whitened boards by the speakers' step, so nobody can call him illegitimate. The chief auditor, Sosipatra Lysimachou, has refused his signature twice and kept her post both times. Debts are recorded here and called on the day.

Found here: steppe horses and felts, amber (one with a wasp inside sells to Persemenid for its weight in gold), salt fish, glazed-cloth winter cloaks, and copies of the audit at an obol.

Hook: one line in this quarter's audit, the "steppe retainer", has risen by a third in five years. Sosipatra has asked in writing what the city buys with it, and wants a witness when she asks aloud.

The Gymnasion of Thessalonika Gymnasion

Codex now: Thessalonika's gymnasion: exercise ground, school and the citizens' club.

Thessalonika's gymnasia, behind the Porticoes of the upper town, are as much academies as exercise grounds: the old men who wrestle at dawn lecture at noon. Courtyards are enclosed and windows glazed, for this is the coldest city in Hellenoria. Their porticoes host the Disputation, five days in which scholars argue positions assigned by lot, enormously popular and heavily bet on. A scholar may have to defend the opposite of everything he has written.

Now: the gymnasiarch, Nikomachos Stoabiou, auctions the south-facing teaching bays each year. Krates the Dog sleeps in a storage jar at the east end and heckles everyone. The gymnasia take fee-paying students from all three empires, and a few steppe children enrolled as the sons and daughters of horse-dealers.

Found here: lectures at an obol, private tutors in any subject, a bet on the Disputation, and the scholars' post, whose sealed letters travel uninspected.

Hook: the party is drawn by lot into the Disputation and must argue that the Emperor is present.

The Sea Wall of Thessalonika Fortification

Codex now: The long wall along Thessalonika's bay, guarding a waterfront of warehouses.

Thessalonika lies on a curved bay behind a long sea wall, with numbered warehouses along the waterfront and a citadel on the slope above. It is the tidiest large city on the continent, built to a plan it still follows. Ships tie up in the order they were sighted, and the clerks will tell you so before you ask. The statutory grain reserve sits in the granaries behind the harbour gate, each jar sealed by the auditors with a lead tag on a cord; breaking a tag is a capital charge.

Now: the harbour-master, Nikanor Chrysou, is elected by the shippers and answers to the auditors. House Boreadai ships the grain south to Hellarchon and Corinth. The harbour is blessed on the day ice first appears in the upper town's fountains; a late frost is an omen.

Found here: grain by the shipload, rope from the four-hundred-pace ropewalk, pickled tunny, passage south on the Long Lane, and a berth fee published to the obol.

Hook: a granary seal has been broken, and the jar inside held no grain. Sosipatra wants the culprit; Phila Anaxilaou, who clerks for the auditors, wants the party to find him first.

The Temple Precinct of Thessalonika Sanctuary

Codex now: The walled sacred ground of Thessalonika, home of its patron's temple and its dedications.

The sanctuary stands in the upper town among the academies, above the Grid Agora. Its chief temple is Hermes of the Gate, god of eloquence and of thresholds, with Athena kept in the academies. Its priests bless the harbour on the day the first ice appears in the fountains, and the date is entered in a series four hundred years long. The dedications are tidy, catalogued and mostly books.

Now: the priest of Hermes of the Gate, Aristokles Kerykides, keeps the frost register and the sacred threshold-stone, which every steppe envoy must step over with his right foot first. At the midsummer Horse Fair the priests carry the god's staff to the Horse Gate for the Exchange of Cups.

Found here: votive herms, travellers' blessings, a reading of the frost register for omens (a drachma), and hospitality-tokens for foreigners with business in the city.

Hook: a frost that never comes has happened twice in four hundred years. This year the fountains are still unfrozen at midwinter, and the harbour cannot be blessed.

The Theatre of Thessalonika Theatre

Codex now: Thessalonika's open-air theatre, cut into the hillside for festival drama and the assembly.

Cut into the slope above the Grid Agora, it holds the Reading, where new works are read aloud and heckled before publication; several careers have ended on its stage. The Assembly meets here monthly. It can refuse a levy, and does about once a year to prove it still can, but it passes the steppe retainer every spring without debate.

Now: the theatre-warden, Aristokleia Anagnostou, schedules the Reading and seats the heckling scholars by school, so the fights are contained. Zenon Pinakides, a careless copyist, boasts here of "certain correspondents abroad".

Found here: seats at an obol, new books read aloud before anyone can buy them, and copyists from Ink Row who will sell the text by evening.

Hook: a copyist dies at his desk with a page of the Old Empires chronicle that matches none of the three sources, and it was due to be read at the next Reading.

Aeolus Reach

Emery Shore Beach

Codex now: A black, glinting beach where the sea grinds a hard grey stone to powder that polishers pay well for.

A short black beach on the Aeolus strait, beyond the Torpedo Shallows, where a hard grey rock breaks from the headland and is ground to grit by the surf. The beach glints in the sun. The grit is gathered by hand into sacks and carried up a goat-path to the polishers' sheds. The wind here is the strait's own, and it carries a sting.

Now: six families of gatherers live in huts above the beach under an old woman called Melaina Smyridou, who weighs every sack and sells to the sea-captains who call. Corinth's gem-cutters and the Luminastra Alchemists buy most of the fine powder.

Found here: Island Emery, the abrasive that cuts gems, marble and, with patience, steel (5 sp a pound for fine powder), black flint, and goat cheese.

Hook: a gatherer's child has found a signet ring in the grit with the mark of a shipwrecked house. The family wants it sold quietly.

The Fig Orchards Orchard

Codex now: Sun-baked orchards above the strait where fig-growers hang wild branches in the trees to bring the wasps that ripen the crop.

Dry orchards on the sheltered slope above the strait, where the growers hang branches of wild fig in the cultivated trees each summer so that tiny wasps carry pollen between them. The practice looks like superstition and works like a machine. Along the cliff edge, women in white head-cloths gather the gum of the Weeping Mastic trees.

Now: three families share the slope, and their eldest, Theokritos Sykeas, decides the day the wild branches go up. The mastic-gatherers sell to the Knot Shrine on the northern head, which burns it.

Found here: Wasp-Figs fresh in season and dried by the string (a copper a string), mastic by the pinch for chewing, incense and medicine, and a taste before buying, which is expected.

Hook: the wild-fig branches have been going missing. Someone is trying to ruin one family's harvest.

The Petrel Stacks Sea stacks

Codex now: Rock pillars in the strait where storm-birds nest and the water below is thick with ink-fish, snail and eel.

Tall rock pillars rising from the strait, white with guano and shrieking with birds. The wind is made here, the sailors say, and the petrels that nest on the stacks are the first to flee when a storm is coming. The water at their feet is rich with ink-fish, purple-snail and moray. Egg-climbers work the lower ledges in spring.

Now: the pilots' guild of the Reach watches the stacks from the headland and posts the petrels' movements on a board at each harbour. The upper ledges belong to harpies, who sing the climbers up and do not always let them down.

Found here: petrel eggs in spring, purple-snail for the coast towns' dye-works, ink-fish for scribes, and a free storm warning for anyone who watches the birds.

Hook: the petrels left a week early. The harbour-master says there is no storm. The sailors disagree.

The Pumice Flats Shore

Codex now: A grey shore where the sea throws up floating stone, and every boy on the strait knows how to sell it.

A wide grey shore on the strait where, after a storm, the sea leaves a drift of floating rock, light as bread and rough as a cat's tongue. Boys comb the tideline at dawn with baskets, and the drift is sold by the sack to scribes, bathers, hull-scrubbers and anyone with a callus. After an off-chart storm the flats are buried knee-deep, and nobody asks where so much stone came from.

Now: a market at the north end opens after every storm, run by Kerkyon the Sack-Man, who buys from the boys and sells to the Hellarchon scriptoria. He also hires the boys out by the day.

Found here: pumice at a copper a stone or a drachma a sack, black flint from the dunes, and boys who know every rock on the strait.

Hook: after the last great storm the drift included a floating island of pumice with a door in it.

The Torpedo Shallows Bay

Codex now: A sandy bay where the fishermen step carefully, because the flat grey fish in the sand deliver a blow like a hammer.

A broad sandy bay on the strait, its bottom so flat and pale that a swimmer can see the shadows of fish. The fishermen shuffle their feet as they wade, because the sand hides a flat, grey, round fish that delivers a numbing shock when trodden on. Some men take it as a cure for headaches and some as a warning.

Now: the fishermen's headman, Narkissos Thalamou, sells live Numbfish to the coast's physicians and keeps a tally of who has been struck. A visitor who wades barefoot is warned once.

Found here: live Numbfish in water-jars (2 sp each; physicians hold them to a patient's brow for headache and gout), salt fish, and a boat across to Emery Shore.

Hook: a fisherman's body was found in the shallows, unmarked and smiling. The coroner says it was the fish; the coroner is being paid.

The Wreckers' Beacon Lighthouse

Codex now: A lighthouse of black stone on the strait's southern cape whose keepers say they save ships, and whose neighbours say they sink them.

A tall black lighthouse on the strait's southern cape, with a fire-basket that burns pitch and a keeper's house that has seen more weather than visitors. The keepers claim to guide ships through the rocks; the villagers have seen the light move on stormy nights, and the cove below is strewn with timbers. Never-Landing Swifts wheel round the lantern at dusk, and the keepers tally them as a weather-sign.

Now: Keeper Damokles has held the job ten years and built three new houses in the valley. Ixion Keraunios, the Wind-Seller of the Reach, lives in the tower's upper room and sells his winds in Corinth.

Found here: a bed in the keeper's house (the keeper asks what the ship carries, which is a reasonable question for a lighthouse), knotted wind-cords that really work at 10 gp a knot, and salvage in the next valley's markets.

Hook: a grain captain hires the party to find who forged his wind-chart; the trail leads to the Beacon's own keepers.

Nereid's Veil

The Lamplit Quarries Quarry

Codex now: Marble quarries cut underground by lamplight on an island in the sea-fog, where the stone glows faintly when it is cut.

Galleries mined from beneath, by lamplight, into the marble heart of an island inside the sea-fog. The stone is translucent enough that a lamp behind a thin slab shows through, and the cutters work by lamp because the galleries are too deep and the fog too thick for daylight. The quarrymen work in silence by rule, so that nobody answers a voice by accident. A cutter's wage is good, and his lungs are not.

Now: the quarry-master, Lampros Lychnites, will let a sculptor in and nobody else. The Geolith Artisan Covenant buys most of the marble and sends its own silent masons to cut it. Boats come in on the tide, guided by a bell.

Found here: Lamp-Quarried Marble, prized for statues because it takes light into the flesh (40 gp a block before shipping, shipped only with a pilot paid in advance), fire-stone veins for lantern-makers, and island emery from the spoil.

Hook: the fog around the island has a voice, and the night shift reports that it knows their names.

The Sponge Banks Reef

Codex now: Clear, rocky shallows off the foggy coast where free-divers cut sponge and coral and net the red fish that die in colours.

A broad shelf of clear rocky water just inside the sea-fog, where the free-divers of the coast work from open boats. A diver goes down on a stone with a knife and a net, cuts what he can in one breath, and is hauled up with his lungs on fire. Divers wear wax in their ears, which they consider the most important tool of the three. Their widows keep the nearest tavern.

Now: the divers' guild sells a day on a boat and is run by Kymo Spongeia, a diver's widow who keeps the tavern, the guild's purse and the list of the drowned. Merfolk trade with the divers at the outer edge and will not enter the deep fog either.

Found here: Diver's Sponge for baths and physicians, Blood-Coral from the sea-caves at 10 gp an ounce, and the Dying Mullet, served live at oligarchs' tables for the show of colours as it dies.

Hook: a diver came up with a coral branch that was not red but black, and cannot say what he saw below.

Olympus Mountain Range

The Gods' Table Grotto Cave

Codex now: A shining cave high on Olympus whose walls are lined with clear crystal, and where, shepherds say, the gods once dined.

A cave high on the Olympus range, its walls lined with clear six-sided crystal that throws a morning sunbeam into a hundred points. A long flat slab at its centre, set with twelve hollows, has been called the gods' table since before the first shepherd. Pilgrims leave honey cakes, oil and wine in the hollows. In the morning the offerings are gone and the hollows are clean.

Now: a priest of the mountain, old Orestheus Kryonos, keeps the way and charges for the climb. He says the gods dislike company, and the offering plate says otherwise. Crystal-cutters work the outskirts under licence; the table's own walls are not cut.

Found here: Mountain Crystal, clear as ice and cold in the hand, cut for lenses, cups, scrying spheres and the eyes of statues (25 gp a clear fist); mountain honey; and a guided climb at 2 gp.

Hook: last night the honey cakes were not taken. The shepherds are terrified, and Orestheus has gone up alone to find out why.

The Yellow Cleft Mine

Codex now: A sulphur-stained crack in the high rock where gold-yellow and blood-red poison-stones are mined by men who do not expect to be old.

A narrow crack in the Olympus rock, yellow at the lip and red at the bottom, where the mineral that painters call gold and poisoners call something else is dug out by hand. The smell is garlic and struck matches. The men who work here cover their faces with wet cloth and are paid twice the going rate. It is a day's climb above the last shepherd's hut.

Now: the cleft-boss, Stygnos Arsenikou, runs a crew of the condemned and the desperate on contract to the Arcane Academy, which buys more than painting requires and does not explain why. A guide is a good idea and a mask is a better one.

Found here: Orpiment from the upper wall and Realgar from the deeper cuts (2 gp an ounce, deadly to process), brimstone from the walls, and wolf's-bane on the scree below.

Hook: a rival buyer has been paying the miners to mark the rock with a cross when a seam is rich, and a rich seam has been collapsing within a week.

Foloicauria Forest

The Aurochs Glades Glade

Codex now: A chain of green clearings deep in the old forest where huge wild cattle graze under the eye of bears and the old hunters' ghosts.

A chain of green clearings deep in the forest, each a mile across, joined by trails that the great beasts have worn into the ground. The glades have no villages, no roads and no signs, and the hunters who know them keep their knowledge to themselves. The Great Forest Bull and the shaggy Hill Bison graze in the open; the dark edges are the den-country of the Mountain Brown Bear.

Now: centaur clans graze the open glades between the forest's three domains and are paid by all of them. A hunter needs a licence from the forest-wardens of the Circle of the Eternal Grove and a guide from the tribe; a second-hand tale of a glade is not a licence. The Circle's warden for the glades is Agrotera Boukolis, who issues four licences a year.

Found here: aurochs horn and hide (a pair of horns sells for 50 gp in Hellarchon as drinking-horns), bear pelts, and a centaur guide for a price in salt.

Hook: someone has been killing the bulls and taking only the horns. The wardens suspect a buyer in the capital.

The Living Stones Clearing

Codex now: A deep forest clearing where green-veined rocks grow like fungus, clay breathes and geodes open at dawn like eyes.

A circular clearing deep in the forest where the stones are warm, the soil is soft and nothing grows taller than a man's knee. The rocks are veined with green and gain a few inches each year. The clay breathes, and geodes open at dawn like eyes. A forest tribe keeps the clearing and speaks of it as a sleeping thing.

Now: the tribe's elder, Rhizome-Mother Daphnaia, receives visitors at the edge, politely, patiently, and unmoved by money. The Circle of the Eternal Grove watches the clearing and sends word to the Heartgrove.

Found here: Chlorophyte, the green ore that grows (40 gp a pound, if the tribe lets you near), the soft Clay of Life and opening Gaia Geodes that golem-makers pay anything for, and the beating red Heart Stones, which the tribe will not sell at any price.

Hook: the clearing has begun to spread, and the tribe is moving its camp. They have asked an outsider to find out why before it reaches their winter ground.

The Mushroom Caverns Cave

Codex now: Damp, glowing caves under the forest floor where three kinds of fungus grow side by side: one that heals, one that does nothing, and one that kills.

Connected caves beneath the forest, damp and faintly lit by the fungi on every wall. The three commonest species look nearly identical: one heals, one does nothing, one kills. Foragers come in threes and sort them by smell, then colour, then, in the worst case, by trial. Shriekers and violet fungus guard the lower galleries.

Now: the foragers' lodge at the cave mouth is kept by Mykes the Counter, who keeps a book of the dead. It is large, and the newest pages are in a hand that grows less steady. The Luminastra Alchemists send foragers here in threes, and replace them.

Found here: Embergill Bloom, the beneficial mushroom (heals; 5 gp a cap), Nullcap, which does nothing and is sold as Embergill by cheats, Widow's Bell, which kills, and the red-spotted Fly-Cap on the entrance ledge.

Hook: a forager returned with a basket of Widow's Bell labelled as Embergill Bloom. The lodge wants to know who relabelled it.

The Woad Pits Clearing

Codex now: Foul-smelling pits in a forest clearing where leaves are fermented into blue, and the warriors who use it paint themselves for war.

A clearing dotted with shallow pits where woad leaves are crushed, fermented in urine and dried into blue cakes. The smell carries a mile. The dyers are cheerful, tolerated, and not invited to dinner. The cakes go to the forest tribes, who paint themselves before battle, and, by a long chain of middlemen, to the Imperial dyers who now colour garrison cloaks.

Now: the pit-master, Glaukon Isatides, trades with whoever has coin and lets no stranger stay overnight. Amazon buyers from Medusa's west come for the cakes, and Hippolyta Drakaina's people pay in iron.

Found here: Warrior's Woad at 2 sp a cake, blue dye by the jar for cloth, and an unforgettable smell, free.

Hook: the tribes have begun painting a new pattern, and so have the Amazons. Glaukon says it is a war-sign, and someone wants to know whom they mean to fight.

Persemenid City

The throne-city's named sites: the terrace where the empire is staged, and the working rooms underneath that keep the staging fed, watered and lit.

The Audience Hall of Persemenid Throne hall

Codex now: The columned hall on the platform: the largest roofed space on the continent, where the King of Kings receives.

The Hall of Audience stands on its own raised floor at the heart of the Terrace of Columns: the largest roofed space on the continent, its cedar roof carried on seventy-two columns crowned with paired bull-heads. Here the King of Kings receives the satrapies, and here nothing is accidental, from the height of each step to the hour the light falls on the throne. Petitioners are told the room was built to make a man feel small. It works on satraps too.

The first regiment of the Ten Thousand holds the platform and quarters along its north edge. It is drawn from the old nobility, which makes it a guard and a hostage-house at once. The hall's daily order belongs to the hazarapat, Aspachana Farnaka (House Farnaka); its keeper of floors and hangings is the eunuch Usiris the Measurer, who replaces the carpets by the inch so that no visitor ever sees a worn one.

To be had: nothing for sale. A seat in the gallery on a reception day costs a bribe of about 10 gp to the right usher, and a place nearer the throne costs a favour.

Hook: a satrap's envoy asks the party to learn, before tomorrow, which column he will be seated by. Last year's envoy was seated behind one.

The Caravanserai of Persemenid Caravanserai

Codex now: The great walled inn at Persemenid where caravans stable, sleep and trade.

A caravanserai is a walled courtyard inn built for caravans: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Persemenid's is the Royal Caravanserai, where the Royal Road enters the town, and it is the heart of the Quarter of Tongues. Before the Bringing it receives every satrapy's delegation, lodges them in the order the tribute relief shows, and sends them up the stair the same way.

The rest of the year it is a foreign quarter in one building: Invictian factors on the west gallery, Hellenorians on the south, steppe horse-dealers in the yard. The keeper is Hamid Kaarvan, a heavy, patient man who has run it for twenty-two years under contract to House Nahid'zar, which feeds and beds every delegation and is owed for most of them.

To be had: a bed for 5 sp, a stall for 2 sp, an interpreter in any of nine tongues for a silver a morning, and the best gossip in the city for free if you sit in the yard long enough.

Hook: Hamid has rooms reserved for a delegation that has not come for three years. Someone keeps paying for them.

The Fire-Temple of Persemenid Fire-temple

Codex now: The house of Persemenid's sacred flame, kept by the Magi and never allowed to die.

Every Acheaorian city of any size keeps a fire-temple: a heavy, plain building around an inner chamber where the Magi tend a flame that must never go out. The public may look at it through a screen and may not approach. Persemenid's chief temple stands on the Hill of Fires, first of the chain of fire-houses along the mountain's spine from which the Magi mark the Fire Watch, signalling from temple to temple across the plateau to Atarabad. The oldest of the chain, the Temple of Breath, burns on a draught rising out of the rock itself.

The temple is kept by Herbad Tansar, who crowns the king and sets the calendar; no coronation, war or execution is lawful on a day he has not declared fit. His fuel-master, Magus Dadbeh, weighs and logs every load of juniper.

To be had: blessing of a journey (1 sp), a lamp lit from the sacred flame for a new hearth (1 gp), and a fit day for a wedding, which has a waiting list.

Hook: the signal fire from Atarabad came a night late. The Magi say weather. The courier says otherwise.

The Royal Stair of Persemenid Ceremonial stair

Codex now: The great stair up to Persemenid's platform, wide enough for ten horsemen abreast and lined with the tribute relief.

The platform stands forty feet above the plain, reached by a double stair of shallow steps wide enough for ten horsemen abreast. It is meant to be climbed slowly. Along it runs the tribute relief: every subject people in its own dress, carrying what it owes, so a visitor climbs beside the whole empire bringing gifts. At the top is the Gate of All Peoples and its winged bull-guardians (the Royal Stair).

At the Bringing, every satrapy that still acknowledges the throne climbs in the order the relief shows. Which ones do not come is the year's real news. The order belongs to House Karin, Masters of the Stair, under Azata Sukhra Karin, who walks through the gaps where absent delegations should be because the book says so.

To be had: guides at the foot, mostly children, a copper to name the carved people beside you and a silver to say whether they came this year.

Hook: Varaz Karin is selling better places in the procession. A delegation that bought one wants the party to make sure nobody notices.

The Treasury of Hours Vault

Codex now: A columned vault beneath the royal palace where the King of Kings keeps the metals he will not spend and the strange ones nobody can name.

A vast vault beneath the Inner House, its pillars carved with the hours of the day and its doors opened only at the hour the king chooses. It holds the empire's tribute in bullion, ingots of orichalcum, white platinum that no smith in the empire can melt, a single plate of adamantium the court believes older than the dynasty, and a room the keepers do not enter after dark.

The keys belong by appointment to House Spandiyad. Last spring the treasurer, Bagapata Spandiyad, resigned and will not say why. His nephew Mazdayar, twenty-six and untrained, now holds the keys and asks too many people for advice. The house clerk, Ispitamu, is the only person alive who knows the full inventory, including what is missing.

To be had: nothing. A visitor to the palace sees the great door and nothing else. A Spandiyad will sometimes pay well for discreet help, as long as it comes from outside the court.

Hook: Mazdayar asks the party to count something in the vault that his clerk refuses to count.

The Water-Court of Persemenid Qanat head

Codex now: Where The Qanat Network surfaces at Persemenid and the city's water shares are measured out.

Acheaorian cities live on water brought underground from distant hills by the qanats. Where the channel surfaces there is a water-court: a cool vaulted chamber where the flow is divided into shares, each measured by a timed bowl and owned by deed. Persemenid's lies in the Garden Town below the platform, beside the ice-houses and the siege cisterns, and it feeds both the town and the three channels of the Paradise.

The Bountiful Harvesters hold most of the shares and all of the bowls. Their clerk of the court is Ab-Shenas Raham, a quiet woman who can hear a cracked bowl from across the chamber and keeps the rota in a ledger chained to the wall. Water law is hers before it is the satrap's.

To be had: a water share, if one ever comes up, for the price of a good house; a bowl's worth of flow for a season for about 30 gp; and cold water by the cup at the court door for a copper.

Hook: the westernmost Paradise channel measures short again. Raham wants someone to walk the tunnel and find where the water goes.

Acheaoria: the Throne Plain

Sites the codex files under the empire itself rather than a city: the royal demesne outside Persemenid's walls.

The Paradise of Persemenid Royal garden

Codex now: The King of Kings' walled hunting garden — an artificial wilderness watered by qanat, where the empire's fitness to rule is demonstrated annually.

A wall of fired brick eleven miles around, enclosing watered woodland in a country that has none: cedar, plane and fruit trees in ranks, streams led from three qanat channels, and deer, boar, onager and lion kept at numbers the land could never support. The word means simply "walled around". Every satrap keeps a lesser one, and the size of a man's garden is understood to be the size of his claim (the Paradise).

Once a year the King of Kings hunts here before the court. The beasts are driven, the ground is chosen, and a man of the Ten Thousand stands within a spear's throw. What is demonstrated is not the king's courage but the empire's ability to stage the world as it wishes. The Warden of the Paradise is Azata Mehrdad Shikarbān, old and courteous; the Predator's Guild culls the surplus, and House Mihran keeps its horses beside the eastern wall.

To be had: venison and lion-skins from the cull, through the warden's steward; a day's ride inside by royal pass only.

Hook: the western channel has failed for two years, and the dying trees on that side are being cut at night by order of the court. A woodcutter has found something in the stumps.

Atarabad City

The caravan city's sites: a ring of inns, a hill of fire and water, and the fields and sheds that make its silk and saffron worth stealing.

The Caravanserai of Atarabad Caravanserai

Codex now: The great walled inn at Atarabad where caravans stable, sleep and trade.

A caravanserai is a walled courtyard inn built for caravans: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Atarabad's is not one building but a ring of them, one at each road (the Caravanserai Ring), and each is a small foreign quarter of whoever travels that road. The Western Caravanserai on the Treaty Road houses Invictian and Hellenorian factors, with the Mithril Reserve's stone branch beside it; the Royal Caravanserai serves the road to Persemenid; the eastern yards speak tongues the city scribes cannot write. On the Opening of the Roads they all send their first convoy out on the same morning.

The ring's keepers answer to the Satrap's Warden of Gates, Kaveh Darvazeh, but the Western house is leased to House Suren-Pahlav, whose steward Mihrdad Sarband decides who gets a gallery and who sleeps by the camels.

To be had: beds from 3 sp, a place in a westbound convoy (about 2 gp a day's stage), Invictian coin weighed rather than counted, and an introduction to Dominus Argentar Brokk Ironhand.

Hook: a westbound convoy needs guards who will not ask what is in the twelfth wagon.

The Cobra Heaps Rubble

Codex now: Rubble mounds outside the caravan city where the snakes sun themselves, the mongooses patrol and the charmers ply their trade.

Old rubble mounds outside the East Gate, left by the demolition of a dozen forgotten buildings, whose cracks and hollows the snakes were glad to move into. The den belongs to the Hood-Asp. A guild of charmers holds rights to the ground and keeps the mongoose called the Snake-Warden as a working partner. Locals give the heaps a wide berth, and drovers bound east fill their waterskins inside the gate rather than walk past.

The guild master is Margir Shahrokh, lean, scarred on both wrists, who has handled asps since he could walk and locked the guild's gate last month without telling the satrap why.

To be had: a demonstration for a few coins; asp venom by the vial (about 25 gp, under the counter); antivenom paste the guild swears by (5 gp); a trained mongoose, if a charmer likes you. The guild does not let strangers handle the snakes.

Hook: a snake of a colour no charmer recognises has been seen on the heaps. Margir wants it caught alive and quietly.

The Fire-Temple of Atarabad Fire-temple

Codex now: The house of Atarabad's sacred flame, kept by the Magi and never allowed to die.

Every Acheaorian city keeps a fire-temple: a heavy, plain building around an inner chamber where the Magi tend a flame that must never go out. Atarabad is oriented on its own, a squat building on the highest ground of the Fire Hill, where the Magi hold that the flame has never once been extinguished. The Magi's houses, schools and wood-stores climb the slope around it, and every load of fuel is weighed, blessed and logged.

The temple is the seat of Mobad Atar-Farnbag, First Flame of the Magi, who keeps the calendar, the guild oaths and the power to close the bazaar for a day by declaring it impure. His deputies are the hereditary Mobads of the Farnbagan line. He wants foreign shrines out of the caravanserais.

To be had: oath-witnessing for guild contracts (2 sp), blessed ash for a caravan's first wagon (1 sp), a fit day for departure, and an ember in a sealed brass pot to found a new hearth-shrine (25 gp and a Magus's approval).

Hook: a dying temple servant asks for the party by name and wants to confess to someone who is not a Magus.

The Mulberry Sheds Workshop

Codex now: Rows of warm, whispering sheds where silkmoths eat mulberry leaves all day and the whole building sounds like rain.

Long wooden sheds behind the dye-yards of the Silk Quarter, warm and humid and loud with ten thousand mouths chewing leaves. The worms are fed four times a day by women who sleep in the sheds in season, and the cocoons are stifled in steam before the moths can break out. The sheds house the Tabrishi'ir silkmoth, bred for a pale, strong thread that may not leave the city in raw form.

The sheds belong to House Abrisham, whose head, Arashshara Shahdokht Abrisham, also keeps the city weights. The breeding floors are run by Nushin Abrisham, the best breeder in the house.

To be had: reeled thread by the skein (about 3 gp), finished silk through the bazaar, and tea in the front room, which is as far as any buyer is admitted. Eggs are never sold.

Hook: someone is selling the house's eggs to a competitor. By old custom the penalty is the loss of both hands, and Shahdokht would rather the culprit vanished than be found.

The Saffron Terraces Fields

Codex now: Lilac-carpeted terraces above the caravan city that flower for ten days a year and are picked by hand before the sun is up.

Terraced fields above the caravan city, bare for fifty weeks and lilac for ten days, when the crocuses open together and must be picked before the sun wilts them. Every household in the district goes out at dawn, and the red threads are plucked at the kitchen table that night. A cheaper crocus, poor man's saffron, grows in a lower field and is sold, occasionally, as the real thing.

The terraces are held in strips by some three hundred families. The harvest-warden is Arashshara Farideh Zafarani, who sets the picking days with the Magi and seals the season's weight. Her cousin Kamran Zafarani, of the bazaar's third lane, sells the best saffron in the city and some of the worst, at the same price.

To be had: saffron at roughly 15 gp an ounce in season, double out of it, when the shops are empty. The ten days are a festival, with music on the terraces and free bread at dawn.

Hook: a rival merchant has proof that Kamran adulterates his saffron and wants someone to carry it to the keeper of the weights without being knifed on the way.

The Water-Court of Atarabad Qanat head

Codex now: Where The Qanat Network surfaces at Atarabad and the city's water shares are measured out.

At the foot of the Fire Hill the qanat surfaces into a cool vaulted chamber where the flow is divided into shares, each measured by a timed bowl and owned by deed. Fire above, water below: the city's two oldest authorities share a hill and not much else. The Bountiful Harvesters hold Atarabad's shares, which makes the guild one of the city's powers despite having no seat on anything.

The court's master is Ustad Jamshid Abkhan, a broad, cheerful Harvester who keeps the rota and the bowls and settles more disputes between merchant houses than the satrap does, because a house that loses its water loses its garden, its staff and its standing within a month (water).

To be had: a season's bowl of flow for a caravan yard (about 40 gp), a sworn copy of a share-deed (5 sp), and the coldest water on the road east.

Hook: two great houses of the Wind-Tower Quarter both hold deeds to the same bowl. Both deeds are genuine.

Mithratal City

The oath-city's sites: every one of them exists to make a promise stick, or to decide what happens when one does not.

The Caravanserai of Mithratal Caravanserai

Codex now: The great walled inn at Mithratal where caravans stable, sleep and trade.

A caravanserai is a walled courtyard inn built for caravans: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Mithratal's began as one and multiplied into the Waiting Lodges, a ward of walled houses, each with one gate, where parties to a covenant wait out the intervals the law requires between drafting and swearing. Rival parties are lodged at opposite ends by custom and meet only in the teahouses, where the boards are always out and the poets always in.

The lodges are run by House Golnar under Arashshara Simin Golnar, who seats rivals at opposite ends of every room and has prevented more feuds than the Lanterns. The Great Lodge's day-keeper is her steward Behruz Panahi, who keeps the arrival book and never lets two hostile parties sleep under one gallery.

To be had: lodging by the interval (a season's room about 12 gp), a board and partner for nard or chess, a poet to make couplets of your waiting (Ruzbeh the Unhurried charges by the day), and a drafter's introduction.

Hook: a party has lost a fortune at the dice-board during its interval and wants the covenant renegotiated before the other side learns why.

The Covenant Archives of Mithratal Archive

Codex now: Where every covenant sworn in Mithratal is drafted, registered and read out at the annual Renewal.

Mithratal's wealth went into the buildings around the precinct, and the richest of them is this one (the Archive Ward). Three walls, each higher than the last; a moat of raked sand that shows every footprint; doors that open only to two keys held by different families. Inside, every covenant sworn in the city is drafted, registered and kept. At the Renewal every standing covenant is read out by class, from dawn to dusk in shifts, and any party wishing to dispute one must do so then or hold its peace another year.

The Archives answer to the Chief Registrar, Azata Yazdin Dadvar of House Dadvar, whose family has drafted the empire's bargains for three hundred years. Registrars swear never to sleep outside the ward more than one night in seven.

To be had: registration of a covenant (fees by stake; the richest tax per head in the empire), a sealed certified copy (2 gp), a Dadvar drafter (from 50 gp, more if the other side has one).

Hook: a proxy of House Mihran has filed notice against a clause of the Peace of the Signing. If nobody answers in the precinct on the eleventh day, the clause lapses.

The Covenant Garden Garden

Codex now: A shaded court in the oath-city where contracts are sworn under the oldest plane tree and the water-channels never run dry.

A square court in the Garden Ward, shaded by one enormous plane tree, the Plane of the Wells, whose roots have drunk a channel of clean water for six hundred years. Contracts of consequence are sworn under its branches with the parties' hands in the channel, and a bargain broken after such an oath is said to dry the offender's wells. The beds around it hold temple hyssop, cut by the oath-priests to purify the parties before they swear.

The garden is kept by the oath-priest Mobad Nikrooz, a stooped, exact man who trims the hyssop with silver shears and charges for swearing by the hour and by the stake. He answers to the Witness of the Fire, Magus Frawardin, whose seal makes the oath binding.

To be had: an oath under the plane (from 5 gp an hour, plus a share of the stake), bundles of temple hyssop (1 sp), and the court is open to anyone with lawful business.

Hook: the channel tastes wrong. Nikrooz has not noticed; a water-carrier has, and is frightened to say so.

The Fire-Temple of Mithratal Fire-temple

Codex now: The house of Mithratal's sacred flame, kept by the Magi and never allowed to die.

Every Acheaorian city keeps a fire-temple: a heavy, plain building around an inner chamber where the Magi tend a flame that must never go out. Mithratal's burns at the eastern edge of the Precinct of Oaths, behind its screen, and the Magi witness every covenant sworn in the city. Parties face the flame barefoot on the stone. A covenant sworn with one's back to it is held to be no covenant at all, which has decided at least one famous dispute.

The Magi of the precinct are led by the Witness of the Fire, Magus Frawardin, tall, silver-bearded and slow to speak. Without his seal an oath is merely a promise. His sealing clerk, the young Magus Arash Mehrdel, keeps the impressions of every seal set beside the parties'.

To be had: the Witness's seal on a registered covenant (fee by class), purification before swearing (1 sp), and a chip of an old floor-slab blessed at the fire (prized in Persemenid; about 10 gp).

Hook: a party swears a covenant, and that night Arash finds the seal impression in his register does not match the seal on the copy.

The Ordeal Grove Grove

Codex now: A circle of grey trees beside the oath-city where the accused drink bark-water and the gods are asked to judge.

Beyond the south gate (the Grove Gate), inside a low wall, stands a circle of grey, gnarled ordeal trees ringed by tall king's candle stalks marking the consecrated ground. Those accused of lying under covenant may choose the ordeal: a cup of water in which the bark has soaked. The innocent are sick and recover; the guilty die. The priests hold that the gods decide. The survivors hold that the dose does.

The grove is closed except on ordeal days, when the crowd is large and quiet. Its priest is Kersasp, whose verdicts are famously consistent and whose house is famously new. The Lantern House stands by the gate, and the Lanterns of Justice under Lantern-Captain Zarir Roshanpur ride from it (law).

To be had: nothing lawful. Bark is not sold. Ordeal-day crowds support a market of amulets, prayers and remedies said to settle the stomach, all useless.

Hook: a man accused under covenant asks the party to find out, before his ordeal day, what Kersasp has been paid and by whom.

The Precinct of Oaths Covenant court

Codex now: The open stone court at Mithratal's centre, where oaths are sworn and every road ends.

Mithratal is laid out so that every road runs to the place where oaths are sworn: an open court, roofless, floored in one expanse of dressed stone and empty of decoration. It is named for the Binding Word, the old covenant-spirit for whom the city is named. A new slab is laid in the floor each decade, cut by the Geolith Artisan Covenant, and the chips of the old one are prized across the plateau.

Once a year, on the Silent Day, nothing said in the city is binding, and the precinct fills with people who come simply to say aloud what they think where it does not count. The court is policed by the archive guard and kept by the Precinct Warden, Azata Mehran Sangdel, whose single duty for nineteen years has been to see that nothing is ever added to the court but stone.

To be had: nothing. Selling in the precinct voids any oath sworn that day. Witnesses for hire wait at its edge (1 sp a swearing).

Hook: someone has carved a mark into the newest slab overnight. Sangdel wants the carver found before the Renewal, when the mark might be read as a party's sign.

The Water-Court of Mithratal Qanat head

Codex now: Where The Qanat Network surfaces at Mithratal and the city's water shares are measured out.

Where the qanat surfaces in the Garden Ward there is a cool vaulted chamber where the flow is divided into shares, each measured by a timed bowl and owned by deed. In Mithratal the shares are themselves covenants, registered at the Archives and read out with the rest at the annual Renewal. A water share here can be disputed only once a year, which makes it the safest property on the plateau.

The Bountiful Harvesters keep the bowls and the rota under Ustad Parvin Ab-Dast, an elderly Harvester who reads each share's covenant aloud before she opens its sluice, every morning, because the covenant says so. Her apprentices have learned the whole rota by heart from hearing it.

To be had: a registered share, very rarely, at a price several times Atarabad's; a sworn reading of a share-covenant (5 sp); and a lawyer's education by sitting in the chamber for a season.

Hook: a share registered seven generations ago has no living holder. At the Renewal, whoever disputes it first may claim it, and three parties are racing to be first.

Persevalis City

The garden city's sites follow the water down the hill: fire and pools at the top, the satrap's avenue in the middle, dust and orchards at the foot.

The Caravanserai of Persevalis Caravanserai

Codex now: The great walled inn at Persevalis where caravans stable, sleep and trade.

A caravanserai is a walled courtyard inn built for caravans: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Persevalis's sits at the Foot of the Slope, exactly where the green ends and the plateau's ordinary dust begins, and it smells of both. The Garden Road convoys load here for Persemenid: fruit packed in snow-straw, sealed baskets of cuttings, cases of rosewater, and the court's sherbet ice coming back the other way.

The keeper is Arashshara Nargess Bastani, a widow who runs the yard like a ship and sells space by the cubit. She works on contract to House Golab, which ships most of the court supply through her gate.

To be had: a bed for 3 sp, packing straw and baskets, a place in a Garden Road convoy (fruit convoys move fast and do not wait for stragglers), and sealed cuttings with pedigrees from the bazaar's agents.

Hook: a fruit convoy left last summer with an extra passenger in grey whom nobody booked. Nargess remembers her, and three different foreigners have now asked.

The Fire-Temple of Persevalis Fire-temple

Codex now: The house of Persevalis's sacred flame, kept by the Magi and never allowed to die.

Every Acheaorian city keeps a fire-temple: a heavy, plain building around an inner chamber where the Magi tend a flame that must never go out. Persevalis's stands at the top of the terraces, at the Channel Head, where the water enters the city, and its motto is "fire over water, never in it". Each spring the Magi bless the Opening of the Channels, and until they do, no sluice in the city may be raised.

The temple is kept by Herbad Shirzad, a sharp, dry man of a Magi house that has held this fire for generations. He has let it be known he will not open the east channels this year until someone explains where the water goes. This makes him, for the season, the most powerful man in the satrapy.

To be had: blessing of a new garden's first channel (2 gp), a fit day for grafting, and a place at the Opening of the Channels, the city's great spring festival, if you are a deed-holder or know one.

Hook: the satrap asks the party, privately, to give the Herbad an explanation before the Opening, whether or not it is true.

The Green-Nut Orchards Orchard

Codex now: Dusty orchards on the plateau's edge where the pistachio crop is the satrapy's quiet fortune and the harvest is picked before dawn.

Long rows of low, grey-leaved trees on the plateau's edge, planted in dry ground and watered by qanat. The nuts split with a sound like a snapped twig, and the harvest is picked before dawn, when the shells are cool and the air is still. The fallow strips between the rows are sown with old emmer, the old wheat the orchard families will not give up. A good year buys the satrapy a new bridge.

The orchards and the plateau villages are run by the Frataraka Dariush Baghban, the satrap's steward, who reports at breakfast. The pickers live in mud-brick rows below the first terrace and walk up into the gardens only to work.

To be had: green nuts at harvest, sold in the orchard by the families, who haggle in earnest (about 2 sp a pound, five times that in Persemenid); emmer flour; and seasonal work for anyone willing to rise at three.

Hook: the qanat that waters the east orchards has been blocked, and a dead man was found in the shaft. The families want him identified; Dariush wants him forgotten.

The Pomegranate Walk Garden

Codex now: A long garden avenue of fruit trees and rose hedges, where the satrap's guests are served wine and bound by the seeds they eat.

A long avenue lined with pomegranate trees on one side and hundred-petal roses on the other, ending in the pavilion where Satrap Farrokh Bagh'dar entertains (the Pomegranate Walk). The fruit is cut at table, and guests are told that every seed eaten is a promise, and that the promise is remembered. The roses go to the copper stills of the city, and their water to the court.

The walk is public in the mornings, when petitioners wait under the trees. The pavilion is by invitation only, and invitations are written on rose petals pressed into paper, which fade in a week. The steward of the pavilion is Bijan Gol-Afshan, who counts the seeds left on each guest's plate and reports to House Bagh'dar.

To be had: a morning walk (free), rosewater by the flask from the stills (5 sp), and, with an invitation, dinner, wine and the satrap's ear for one course.

Hook: a guest was found dead at the pavilion with his mouth full of seeds. The satrap says he choked. His family does not.

The Qanat Pools Reservoir

Codex now: Cool, dark reservoirs at the mouths of the underground channels, where blind newts swim and nightingales sing in the garden above.

Stone-lined pools at the tunnel mouths beside the Water-Court, where the qanats bring the garden city its water. The water is cold and clear, the walls are green with moss, and the air smells of wet stone. Pale blind newts swim in the first pool, and at dusk the night-singers in the garden above make the place famous with lovers and poets.

The pools belong to the channel-keepers of House Kariz, a hereditary guild with its own saints and its own jokes, under Ustad Babak Kariz. A keeper will lead a visitor down to the first pool. Beyond it, the way is not for the casual.

To be had: a guided descent to the first pool (5 sp), a blessing-dip for a new bride (1 gp, by custom), and, for those who can fight and keep quiet, paid work further down.

Hook: the channels flow in a direction they did not last year. Babak wants hired hands to go further down the east qanat than anyone has gone.

The Water-Court of Persevalis Qanat head

Codex now: Where The Qanat Network surfaces at Persevalis and the city's water shares are measured out.

Persevalis is the water-court made into a city. Water runs along every terrace, and the right to each channel is written into the deed of the house it passes. At the Channel Head the flow is divided by deed, each share measured by a timed bowl of perforated copper. The higher the garden, the older the deed and the earlier the water; the lowest terraces drink what the upper ones have washed their feet in, and say so at every lawsuit.

The Bountiful Harvesters hold most of the shares and all of the bowls. Their master here is Ustad Kourosh Pahnab, a dignified Harvester in a green coat who rules on terrace disputes from a stone bench in the chamber and is said never to have drunk wine, on principle.

To be had: a channel deed with a house (prices begin where most adventurers' fortunes end), a ruling on a terrace dispute (fee 1 gp, appeal to the satrap free and useless), and sworn copies of deeds (5 sp).

Hook: a low-terrace family has proof that an upper garden takes an extra bowl at night, and asks the party to sit up and watch.

Xerastri City

The frontier fortress's sites: two walls, the things kept behind the inner one, and the places where the steppe is let in on purpose.

The Caravanserai of Xerastri Caravanserai

Codex now: The great walled inn at Xerastri where caravans stable, sleep and trade.

A caravanserai is a walled courtyard inn built for caravans: stabling and storerooms below, lodging above, one fortified gate shut at night. Xerastri's stands inside the outer gate on the Horse-Fair Ground, with great yards around it. During the Horse Fair the steppe clans are let into the outer city to trade there under truce. It is heavily policed and very profitable. The truce-stone by the gate bears the clan-marks of every chief who has sworn the Fair peace.

The rest of the year the yards hold remounts and recruiters, and since the Peace a corner has been chalked off as "the Hiring Ground", where foreign agents bid openly for Malaunian archers. The caravanserai is run for House Asbdar by its yard-master, Sohrab Asbdar, Arashshara Nasrin's son, who can price a horse by its walk.

To be had: remounts (a steppe horse about 60 gp at the Fair), felt, mare's-milk spirit, a bed for 2 sp, and a contract for Malaunian archers, if you can outbid three empires.

Hook: Tomyra has cut the newest and deepest mark on the truce-stone, and her rider is asking every foreigner in the yard who speaks for Xerastri.

The Fire-Temple of Xerastri Fire-temple

Codex now: The house of Xerastri's sacred flame, kept by the Magi and never allowed to die.

Every Acheaorian city keeps a fire-temple: a heavy, plain building around an inner chamber where the Magi tend a flame that must never go out. Xerastri's stands inside the inner wall with the granaries and the wells. The fire is one of the things Xerastri will not give up, and the Magi keep a coal of it in a sealed brass pot, ready to be carried out if the citadel falls. The Herbad's Tower beside it carries the motto "The last thing given up".

The fire is kept by Herbad Burzin, who also holds the oaths of the wall-families: every family that owns a stretch of the outer wall renews its oath at the flame each spring before the Counting.

To be had: oath-witnessing (1 sp), a soldier's blessing before a posting (free, by old custom, to anyone in the garrison), and an ember for a new barracks hearth.

Hook: one of Tomyra's riders has asked the Herbad whether a Malaunian may swear on the fire. Burzin has not answered and wants advice from someone who is neither Magus nor soldier.

The Hunting Park Reserve

Codex now: A walled royal game reserve outside the frontier fortress, where trained cheetahs, falcons and lynxes are flown at hares for the garrison's sport.

A walled reserve of scrub and meadow outside the walls (the Hunting Park), kept by the garrison for its officers' sport. Huntsmen train cheetahs to run at hares from horseback and falcons to take birds from the sky, and the tufted king's lynxes are kept in cages for display. The huntsmen are half Malaunian, and the park is the one place where garrison officers and steppe men sit together without a truce.

The cheetahs are run by Qutlugh the Hooded, a Malaunian huntsman in the satrap's pay; the mews by the falconer Ashkan Baz-Dar. Officers' guests are welcome. A commoner who wants to see a cheetah run must befriend a huntsman.

To be had: a day's hunting as an officer's guest; hides and carcasses from the cull; a trained falcon (about 100 gp, and a year's waiting list); a cheetah, never.

Hook: a cheetah has been freed from its cage and not recovered. Three people blame three different men, and one of the three is an officer.

The Inner Citadel of Xerastri Citadel

Codex now: The older inner wall enclosing Xerastri's citadel, granaries and wells: what the city keeps if it loses everything else.

The older inner wall encloses the citadel, the granaries, the wells and the fire (the Inner Citadel). The space between the walls is where most people live, and everyone understands that in a serious assault that space is expendable. The empire's best siege engineers are stationed here with nothing to besiege, and keep the engines in order anyway, testing them on the first of each month by throwing stones at a hill that has never done anything to anyone.

Satrap Vindarna Sarvand (House Sarvand) keeps his residence here. The engineers answer to Chief Engineer Ustad Mehran Zarrinkamar; the granaries to the Keeper of Stores, Azata Golshan Anbari, who can say to the day how long the citadel could hold, and has been asked to stop saying it in public.

To be had: little for outsiders. Engineers will sell old engine parts and siege-craft lessons for a price; the Ironclad Oath's chapter house recruits here.

Hook: Mehran Zarrinkamar's chest is missing from his quarters. He says it held only drawings.

The Outer Wall of Xerastri Fortification

Codex now: The taller of Xerastri's two walls, facing the Malaunian Steppe.

Xerastri is two walls and a ditch with the city between them. The outer wall faces the Malaunian Steppe and is the taller (the Outer Wall). Every stretch belongs to a family responsible for its upkeep, and at the Counting of the Wall each spring the families formally report on their sections. A failed stretch shames a family for a generation; a sound one for nine generations makes a family close to noble. Once a year the garrison rides out in full muster in view of the steppe, and everyone on both sides understands the message.

House Dezhban holds the longest section; its head, Azata Rostam Dezhban, reads the Counting aloud. The gate-towers carry the horn-signals: one blast, riders seen; two, riders coming; three, nobody laughs.

To be had: a walk on the wall with a family's leave, which is how most visitors see the steppe; mortar-work for hire every spring; and arrows by the sheaf at the wall-stores.

Hook: a stretch rang hollow at the Counting. The family swears it was sound last year.

The Water-Court of Xerastri Qanat head

Codex now: Where The Qanat Network surfaces at Xerastri and the city's water shares are measured out.

Xerastri's wells are inside the inner wall, and its water-court is kept there too, a vaulted chamber where the qanat surfaces and the flow is divided by timed bowls into deeded shares. In a siege, water is the citadel's argument. In peacetime it is the satrap's: the garrison's share is set by the satrapal ledger, and when the subsidy is late, the Married Lines' bowl runs short first.

The Bountiful Harvesters keep the bowls under Ustad Mahvash Chah-Kan, a former garrison widow who took the guild's oath after her husband fell on the steppe and is the only Harvester in the empire who carries a sword in the chamber.

To be had: drinking water at the citadel gate (free to the garrison, a copper to others), a share-deed if a wall-family dies out, and in a siege, nothing at any price.

Hook: the women of the Married Lines say their bowl has been cut by a third. Mahvash says the order came from the satrap's office, in writing, and she wants the writing checked.

Dasht-a Khaliq

The Divine Wastes' named sites: the royal diggings in the red hills, the rest-houses that keep the crossing alive, and the black glass where nobody sensible goes.

Blue-Vein Pit Mine

Codex now: An open pit in the desert where blue copper ore and sky-blue stone are dug out of red rock by the thousand baskets.

An open pit sunk into the red rock of the great desert, where a vein of blue copper ore runs close to the surface. The work is done by gangs with baskets and ropes, a thousand baskets a day in the cool months, and the dust of the pit is the same blue as the stone, so a gang climbing out at dusk looks like a procession of ghosts. It is one of the Royal Diggings and pays its tithe to the satrap of the Vale.

The weigh-house is run by the satrap's counter, Clerk Hormoz Sangtarash; the pit itself by three foremen who hire and fire the gangs. The deeper cuts give small pockets of lapis, which the foremen pocket before the weigh-house sees them.

To be had: ground azurite pigment by the pound at the cistern (about 1 gp at the pit, rising with every day's distance), water for a caravan at the pit's cistern, and lapis, quietly, from a foreman's sleeve.

Hook: the lapis skimming is an open secret. Hormoz offers the party a reward to prove it, and the foremen offer a knife to anyone who tries.

The Caravan Stone Inn

Codex now: A walled rest-house at a desert crossroads where every caravan master has carved a name, and the cook's cumin is famous on three continents.

A walled rest-house at a desert crossroads east of Atarabad, named for the single huge stone in its courtyard on which every caravan master has carved a name for a thousand years. The cook's stew of caravan cumin, red-hand leaf and a scatter of sweet-root is the only reason many travellers choose this route. The stone is the only reason the cook has not been poached: her family's name is at the bottom of it, older than any other.

The cook and keeper is Mother Golpari, small, loud and eighty, who has fed the Wheelwalkers and the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon for sixty years. Her grandsons hold the gate.

To be had: a bed (4 sp), a bowl of the stew (5 cp, worth a silver), cumin by the pouch, water for the camels, and a place on the stone, for which a carver is expected to buy the common room a round.

Hook: one name on the stone has been scratched out. Golpari swears she did not do it. The name was a satrap's.

The Carnelian Washings Riverbed

Codex now: Dry riverbeds in the desert where red and green stones are sifted from gravel by lines of washers in the cold of dawn.

Dry riverbeds on the desert's northern fringe where, in the season of flash floods, red and green pebbles wash down from the hills and settle in the gravel. The washers work in lines in the cold of dawn, sifting with wicker trays and calling out each good stone like a bid. Most of it is carnelian, warm as a sunset. Now and again a fleck of green desert emerald sets the whole line cheering.

The washers' licences are issued by the satrap's counter, but the dealers' tents at the end of the line decide the price. Their senior is Dealer Arsalan Kahrobaie, a soft-handed man who buys for the seal-cutters of Mithratal and never raises his voice.

To be had: a washer's licence (2 sp a season), carnelian at the tents (5 gp a good stone, three times that cut in Mithratal), and the occasional emerald, at whatever the dealers say.

Hook: a washer who sold outside the ring was found dead in the dry bed at dawn. His widow has his last stone and wants it sold where the ring cannot reach.

The Honey-Palm Oasis Oasis

Codex now: A green pool in the desert ringed with tall date palms, a cotton field and a market for everyone who survived the crossing.

A deep spring in the red desert ringed with tall palms whose fruit is the sweetest on the plateau. The oasis is a village, a market and a rest-house in one, with a field of white tree-wool and, in the palms' shade, a patch of sweet-root the children dig for. Every caravan that crosses the waste stops here three days to sleep, trade and bury whoever did not make it. Water is sold by the skin at a price posted on a board, and the board is repainted every week.

The headman is Kadkhuda Yazdan Nakhli, genial and watchful. A back room behind the rest-house buys what the scavengers bring out of the Scar Fields.

To be had: dates, cotton, sweet-root, a bed (3 sp a night, 1 sp per camel), water by the skin (price on the board), and directions to the next well, for a price.

Hook: the spring has dropped a hand's breadth since the last caravan. Yazdan is hiding it from the market.

The Myrrh Wadi Grove

Codex now: A dry, thorny watercourse in the desert where the resin trees are cut by night and the gum is sold by weight against gold.

A dry watercourse winding through the desert, lined with low, thorny, grey-barked trees that weep tears of resin when cut.
