The collectors work at night to avoid the heat, nick the bark by lamplight and return at dawn for the hardened tears. The trees are the bitter myrrh of the caravan trade; a larger, scented cousin, the caravan resin tree, grows on the upper bend.

The wadi is held by the resin-wardens, a desert clan under Warden Hamdan Sabri, who collect a toll from every caravan master and give a clay seal in return. A trader without a seal is a smuggler by definition.

To be had: bitter myrrh at about 4 gp a pound with the seal (for temples and embalmers), resin incense, and the seal itself (toll by camel-load), which is good at every market as far as Persemenid.

Hook: a rival tribe offers the party good silver to find out how the wardens' trees stay so green in a drought year.

The Onager Plain Plain

Codex now: A flat red plain where wild asses run faster than horses, and the lizards and jackals wait for what the sun leaves.

A wide, flat, stony plain where the only shade is a rock and the only water is a well that moves. The wild asses of the waste graze at dawn and dusk and run at the sight of a rider, faster than any horse and with a stamina that makes the royal hunters swear. Gold-coat jackals follow the herds; sand monitors and buried horned vipers live in the cracks.

There is no keeper but the well-finder, Old Rashid Chahju, a nomad who walks the plain each month and marks the well's new place with a cairn. Caravans pay him in tea and flour. The royal hunt crosses the plain once a year, and a traveller who meets it is invited to join, and does not refuse.

To be had: onager hides and meat, if you can catch one; the well's location (a sack of flour to Rashid); and a royal hunt's favour, if you ride well in front of the right noble.

Hook: the well has moved half a mile in one month, further than ever before. Rashid wants company when he goes to find it.

The Purple Quarry Quarry

Codex now: A royal quarry in the desert hills, closed to all but the emperor's cutters, where the stone of kings is dug out of the red hills.

A guarded quarry in the red hills of the desert, worked by convicts and royal cutters and closed to everyone else by a wall and a garrison. The stone is purple-red speckled with white, imperial porphyry, reserved for the throne; a column of it is a boast of the highest order. The lower faces give a grey-pink granite, red syenite, which any builder may buy. The road out is paved for the stone alone, and its carts bear the royal seal.

The quarry is commanded by Quarry-Master Bardiya Sangbor, an old royal cutter who answers to the Treasury, not the satrap. A visitor needs the satrap's seal to pass the gate. Without one, the garrison does not ask questions.

To be had: red syenite at the lower yard (by the cartload), porphyry offcuts, which are illegal to own outside the court and sold anyway in Atarabad, and work for stonecutters who can keep quiet.

Hook: the convicts have been carving something on the hidden walls of the pit. A guard who looked has asked for a transfer.

The Scar Fields Wasteland

Codex now: A stretch of black, glassy desert where the divine war left its mark, and strange stones that burn, scream or sink are picked up by the desperate.

A broad stretch of fused black ground on the margin of Zahr al-Mawt, ridged and glassy and warm even at midnight, where the divine war melted the desert. Scavengers go in masked and in pairs and come out with black obsidian, ember-hot hellstone, dull daemon iron, burning inferno crystal, cold dripping styxium, pitted carceri-metal and the shrill shrieking steel that sings when struck. Hell hounds hunt the ridges.

The oasis rest-house keeps a ledger of those who went in, kept by Scribe Nasrin Daftarkhan, who also notes who came out. The finds are sold in the back room at the Honey-Palm Oasis, where prices depend on the buyer's nerves.

To be had: a guide (10 gp a day, essential), a priest (advised), and the metals, illegal to sell in three empires, which keeps the price up: a palm of hellstone fetches about 50 gp.

Hook: the fields have grown a mile in a year. A scavenger says the ground is breathing out, and Nasrin's ledger shows more going in than coming out.

The Truffle Flats Flats

Codex now: Pale, flat desert ground after a thunderstorm, where the nomad women dig for the desert's secret delicacy by smell.

A stretch of pale, flat ground that is dead nine months a year and lively for three, when the winter thunderstorms bring the sand-truffles up beneath the crust. The nomad women go out at dawn after a storm, read the cracks, and kneel to dig with short knives. The truffles are eaten raw with salt or roasted in embers. The Stormcallers' Choir is said to sing the rains onto the flats and is blamed for every khamsin.

The diggers' senior is Bibi Shahrbanu, whose knife-handle is worn to the shape of her hand. The women do not share the places they know, not even with each other.

To be had: sand-truffles at the oasis markets (about 2 gp each at Persevalis), a morning's digging with the women for a fee and a tip, and Shahrbanu's opinion of the weather, which is better than the Choir's.

Hook: a buyer from the capital has been bidding up the price, and one woman has been followed home.

The Turquoise Diggings Mine

Codex now: A sky-coloured scar on a dry hill where the satrap's miners follow robin's-egg veins, and every stone is counted.

A scar of blue-green rock on a dry hill, worked in a honeycomb of galleries too low to stand in. The miners are paid by the stone and searched at the gate, and the satrap's clerks count every piece by colour before a sack is sealed. A hard stone of the royal blue is worth more than a ruby here, and a soft one is worth a flogging if it goes missing. The best stones go to the King of Kings' own jewellers.

The diggings are run by the satrap's Overseer, Azata Firuz Shahbazi, a meticulous man who counts in his sleep, with a weigh-house open to licensed dealers on market days.

To be had: turquoise at the weigh-house for licensed dealers (5 to 50 gp a stone); everyone else sees the hill from the road. A dealer's licence costs a bribe and a sponsor.

Hook: a missing stone the size of a pigeon's egg is the reason for the new searches. The miners know where it is.

Kaspiran Seas

The shrinking salt sea's shore sites: pink water, grey trees, and a sea that gives up a little more every decade.

The Flamingo Lagoons Lagoon

Codex now: Salt-pink shallows on the inland sea where a million pale birds stand in the water and the sunset makes the whole lagoon blush.

A string of shallow, salt-pink lagoons on the shore of the inland sea, shimmering with algae and brine shrimp, where the flame-waders feed in their thousands. At dusk the whole surface turns the colour of embers, and on windless evenings sailors have steered for it, taking it for a burning harbour. Wading in is forbidden, and the herders enforce it with sticks.

A herder's hut at the southern end serves tea and tells tourists nothing they do not already know. It belongs to Gholam the Pink-Footed, a weathered old herder whose family has kept the lagoon custom for as long as the birds have come, and who collects the moulted plumes for the milliners of Persevalis.

To be had: tea and flatbread at the hut (2 cp), flame-wader plumes (about 5 sp each), natron from the flats, and a view, which is free.

Hook: the lagoons have begun to turn grey. The herders blame a spring that has changed; the plume-hunters blame the herders.

The Salt-Cedar Shore Shore

Codex now: A feathery grey-green fringe along the inland sea, where the trees weep salt and the wrack smells of wormwood.

A broad belt of feathery, grey-green salt-cedar along the inland sea, its leaves crusted with salt drawn up from the soil and shed in a white drift. Silvery sea-wormwood grows in the sandy hollows behind, bitter and good against worms and bad liquor. The wind smells of wormwood and old brine. Reed-tigers den in the thickest stands, and the herders know which stands.

There are no villages, only herders who winter here and drink from salt-lined wells. Their winter headman is Kadkhuda Ilkhan Shurab, who welcomes travellers to his felt tent and serves salty tea; the sandbreaker crews of the Dasht buy cuttings from him by the cartload.

To be had: salt-cedar cuttings and dye-galls, sea-wormwood by the bundle, shelter and salty tea, and a herder's guidance past the tiger stands.

Hook: the sea has fallen another hand's breadth, and the trees now mark an old shoreline. Something is showing beneath the new sand.

Mountain of Kharveth

The lone peak's working flank: the soft white stone, the poisonous red one, and the ledge where the shepherds pay their toll.

The Alabaster Cuttings Quarry

Codex now: Honey-white cuttings on the flank of Kharveth, where soft stone is carved into lamps and perfume jars and the wind carries white dust.

Pale cuttings low on the mountain, where the stone is so soft a mason can carve it with a knife. It is white with a warm honey cast, and a lamp set inside a jar of it glows like a coal. The workshop village at the foot turns out perfume jars, lamp-bowls and burial urns by the thousand, and everything in it, people included, wears a skin of white dust.

The cuttings are worked under licence from the new satrap, Artavasdes Nikbin; the village is run by its carvers' headman, Ustad Kamal Marmarchi, whose family carves the lamps for the tombs of Persemenid. The stone is easy to carve and slow to forgive a careless blow, and a finished jar is worth ten times the block.

To be had: a lamp-bowl (5 sp), a perfume jar (2 gp), a burial urn (10 gp), and commissions by the carvers' doors; the market at the cuttings' foot is the place to buy a gift of the stone.

Hook: the carvers have never cut the lowest face, and cannot say why. The satrap has ordered it opened.

The Cinnabar Shafts Mine

Codex now: Deep, hot shafts in the mountain's side where red ore is cut by condemned men, and the air is poison to anyone who stays.

Narrow shafts sunk into the mountain's red side, worked by prisoners under guard because no free man will take the job. The ore is bright red, the air thick and sweet-tasting, and a man who works the face for a year loses his teeth, then the steadiness of his hands, then his mind. The cap-rock above holds flecks of brassy devil's gold that fools take home. The deepest shaft was sealed after the second collapse; the convicts say it was sealed from both sides.

The shafts are fenced and the road watched. The master is Overseer Varaz the Red-Handed, who deals with buyers at the lower gate and never lets them go up. Peace has emptied the war prisons into his shafts, and the new convicts are soldiers who know how to organise.

To be had: cinnabar for quicksilver and vermilion (about 10 gp a pound, at the lower gate only) and devil's gold, which is worthless.

Hook: a prisoner has smuggled out a plate of silver-white metal that flows like water and will not be held. He will trade it for his life.

The Leopard's Ledge Crag

Codex now: A cold rock shelf on Kharveth where a pale cat hunts goats at dusk and a bone-eating vulture drops its meals on the stones.

A broad, cold shelf of broken rock high on Kharveth, above the line where shepherds take their flocks. Goat tracks cross it every morning, and the bones at the cliff-foot say what happens to the goats by night. A plateau rock-leopard hunts here, and the bone-breaker circles above, dropping what the cat leaves onto the rocks to crack the marrow.

The shepherds of the village below leave a goat on the ledge each year as a toll; the custom is kept by their headman, Dehqan Bahador Kuhzad. The Predator's Guild licenses the leopard and protects it, against the shepherds. A hunter who wants the pelt is told that the leopard has never been seen by a man who came looking.

To be had: nothing for sale on the ledge. A licensed pelt is worth about 50 gp, an unlicensed one the Guild's displeasure.

Hook: the toll goat was taken early this year, and a child went missing the same night. The village suspects the cat; the tracks say otherwise.

Parthian Ravine

The frontier gorge's sites: women's pits, a state secret everyone can smell, and the cliffs where the dead are given to the birds.

The Kohl Workings Mine

Codex now: Grey-black pits in the dry gorge where a soft, shining stone is dug for eye-paint and for the women who sell it.

A scatter of shallow pits along the gorge, where women and boys dig a soft, shining grey-black stone and carry it to the grinding-sheds at the ravine's mouth. Ground fine and worked into fat, it becomes the dark eye-paint worn from the palace to the caravan road. It is cheap at the pit and dear at court, and the difference is what feeds the gorge.

The sheds are run by Arashshara Parisa Kohlzan, who sells to any trader who arrives with a mule and good manners and does not haggle twice. Her buyers include the court at Persemenid and the officers of the Xerastri garrison.

To be had: kohl-stone at the pit (2 cp a basket), ground kohl at the sheds (about 1 sp an ounce here, 5 sp at court), and fat-and-kohl paint in small horn boxes, which also keeps the glare off a rider's eyes.

Hook: one grinder is mixing a pinch of something else into the paint she sells to the garrison officers. The effect is slow, and someone wants the Xerastri command blind on a set date.

The Pitch Seep Seep

Codex now: A black pool in the dry gorge where tar rises through the rock and a thin, burning oil floats on the water.

A broad pool where black tar seeps from a crack in the rock and spreads across stagnant water, with a clear, sharp-smelling oil floating on top. Bones ring the edge, and gatherers do not wade in without a rope. The seep gives black pitch, dug in lumps to seal hulls and roofs, and the skimmed oil is ravine naphtha, the fluid that burns on water, which armies pay a king's ransom to hold.

A garrison post of twenty spearmen guards the pool for the satrap of Xerastri, under Pasban Khosrow Naftgir, and keeps it a state secret from anyone who cannot smell.

To be had: black pitch under licence (1 sp a lump); naphtha, illegal to carry, about 50 gp a sealed flask in the wrong hands. Magmin crawl out when the oil catches.

Hook: the oil has begun to burn by itself in the heat of the day, and the post has not sent its monthly report. The smell of burning has arrived instead.

The Vulture Crags Cliffs

Codex now: White-streaked cliffs above the gorge where the great scavengers wheel and the sky-burial towers wait for their dead.

White-streaked cliffs above the gorge, riddled with nests and ringed by wheeling birds from dawn until the thermals fail. The people of the plateau lay their dead on the stone towers at the cliff's foot so that they do not defile earth or fire, and let the Sky-Cleaners do the rest. The families of Xerastri bring their dead here, three days' ride, rather than use a nearer tower.

A priest of the rite, Dastur Mehrnush, lives in a hut by the stair. She answers questions about the birds, and none about the dead. The stair is open to mourners; sightseers are sent to a viewing ledge half a mile off.

To be had: nothing for sale. The priest accepts offerings of meat for the birds and lamp-oil for her hut, and will bless a mourner's journey home.

Hook: a body was taken from a tower, and not by the birds. Mehrnush has not reported it.

Xeruezcho Canal

The dead sea-road's one living holy place.

The Crocodile Pool Pool

Codex now: A garlanded pool beside the royal canal where a sacred river-beast is fed by priests and watched by the white birds.

A broad pool beside the old royal canal, lined with steps and garlanded with flowers, where a huge river-beast, the River-Dragon, lies half in the water and is fed by priests with fish and wine-soaked bread. The Watching Ibis, a long-billed white bird the priests call a clerk of the god, picks food from its teeth, and the priests say god and bird have made a covenant. The canal-side town lives on the pilgrims.

The pool is kept by the priests of the River's Embrace under Priestess Shirindokht, a calm, tired woman who has fed the beast for thirty years. Pilgrims are admitted at dawn. A visitor who drops anything in the pool is advised to leave it.

To be had: a dawn blessing (1 sp), garlands, and shed River-Dragon scutes, which are sacred and not for sale, and are sold anyway at about 25 gp.

Hook: the beast is ill, and the priests have not told the town. Shirindokht wants a healer who can keep a secret. If it dies, a younger, wilder one will come.

Zaruk'thal Spine

Sites under the black ridge of the dead kingdom: a smithy no one can enter, dens no one wants to, and a hall of salt the miners have made holy.

The Cold Forge Forge

Codex now: A black, windowless smithy beneath the black ridge where the metals that drink light are worked by smiths who do not speak.

A windowless smithy beneath the black ridge, so cold that the water in the quenching trough is skinned with ice. The smiths do not speak, do not wear gloves and do not say who they work for. Their work is dark, matte and heavy: light-drinking darksteel, shadow-ore tenebrium, ember-veined infernal iron and the cold northern ironfell, all of it arriving by night in wagons without markings. An armourer who has seen one of their pieces will not describe it.

No visitor has found a door. The caravans that pass at night say the glow from the vents is black. The only named figure is the wagon-master the tollmen call Grey Tahm, who pays the Seventh Notch in old coin and never in daylight.

To be had: nothing openly. Gate-metal scrapings from the Door Notch would be priceless here, if anyone dared sell them. Ember and Anvil of Duneforged would pay to know who the buyer is.

Hook: the smiths are making a single item, and have been for sixty years. They are nearly done.

The Hyena Hollows Den

Codex now: A set of low, bone-white dens in the black stone where the laughter at night is the only sound for ten miles.

Low hollows at the base of the black ridge, strewn with bone and bleached by sun. The same families of Grave-Laughers have used the dens for generations, and at night their laughter carries ten miles across the plain, to the discomfort of every caravan camped within earshot. Giant eagle-owls nest on the ridge above; fat-tail scorpions live in the cracks below. Gnoll bands follow the hyenas and raid camps at the notches.

No one keeps the hollows, but the Savage Pack hunts them, and its tracker Garsha Two-Knives sells guidance to caravans that must camp nearby. Caravans camp elsewhere. A traveller who has no choice is advised to sleep with a fire and a friend.

To be had: hyena hides, owl feathers, scorpion venom from Garsha (about 15 gp a vial), and a safe camping place, for a price.

Hook: the hyenas dig at one spot every night. The caravaners say a body is buried there that wants out.

The Salt Cathedral Mine

Codex now: A vast hall carved by miners out of a salt dome beneath the black ridge, with pillars of crystal and a chapel the miners keep.

A cavernous working beneath the Spine, hollowed out of a dome of rock salt by centuries of miners and left standing on pillars of salt they chose not to cut. The hall rings when a man speaks and glitters when a lamp is lit. At one end the miners have carved a chapel to Vatagatal, keeper of promises; at the other, a saint's niche nobody can name. The chapel lamp has not gone out in living memory.

The miners' guild is led by Ustad Ramin Namakzad, whose crew hauls clear and grey blocks up on ropes and sells them by weight at the pit-head. The chapel is tended by his sister Shahnaz, who trims the lamp at every shift change.

To be had: deep rock salt (about 2 sp a clear block, more as caravans go deeper into the waste), natron from the side galleries, and a tour for a small fee and a larger tip.

Hook: the miners say a second hall lies beneath this one, and that the lamp in the chapel is there to keep something from walking up.

Expansion

Myths and Legends of Asetheria

Myths and Legends of Asetheria

What people say happened, told the way they tell it: by a fire, at a wake, over the third cup, to a child who will not sleep. Every story here is wrong somewhere. That is what makes it useful.

Historians on this continent have the calendar's timeline, the Three Libraries' chronicle and the dated accounts of the war. Everybody else has stories. A legionary's widow in the Latium Plains, a Mavari net-mender, a Magus's pupil and a Malaunian horse-girl will each tell you how the world began, why the gods stopped answering and who will come back to save it, and none of them will agree. They are telling the truth as it reached them, through grandmothers, temple-schools and propaganda.

Each myth below is given in a storyteller's voice, with a note on who tells it and where. Under each is a What is true note for the DM. Players can hear any of these in a tavern. The notes are for you alone.

How the World Was Made

Five peoples, five beginnings. They agree that there were Titans first and gods after, and on nothing else.

The Furrow of Janus Invictian

Told by an old evocatus, a recalled veteran, to recruits around a brazier at the Aeterna Garrison on the eve of the Kalends of Martius. Every legion has its version; this is the one the Ninth tells.

"Sit down. No, on the ground. Your grandfathers sat on the ground for this.

"Before anything there was the Gap, and the Gap had two sides, and Janus stood in the middle of it facing both ways. That is why he has two faces. He was the first one standing anywhere, so he was the first one with a job. On one side of him was everything that would be. On the other was everything that was. And the two sides wanted to fall into each other and be nothing again.

"So the Titans came up out of the falling. Big lads. Fifty and one of them, the Pontiffs say, and the Pontiffs count everything. The Titans were the weight of the world: one held the hours, one held the deep water, one held the hills up, one kept the stars from wandering. Good workers. Terrible masters. When they wanted a valley, they leaned on a mountain. When they wanted rain, they wrung out the sea. Men lived under them the way you live under a centurion who drinks.

"Then Jupiter. Jupiter was the son of the Titan of Time, the one whose columns are still under the Forum, where the money-changers lean on them. He looked at his father eating every hour as soon as it was born and he said: enough. He did not do it alone. That is the point of this story, so listen. He took his brothers and sisters and he made them a contubernium: eight to a tent, everyone carries something. Juno carried the oath. Mars carried the spear. Vulcan carried the fire. Ceres carried the bread, which nobody remembers and which is why they won.

"They did not kill the Titans. You do not kill the ground you are standing on. They put them down: they made them lie still and they put a line round them, the way the Founders ploughed the line round Romulo. Then Janus shut the door on them and kept the key, and the gods walked out into the world, measured it in paces, and handed it to the people who would keep it in order. That is us. The world was a camp before it was a city, and a city before it was an empire. If you forget which, you lose all three.

"Now. Why are the gods quiet these days? Because the camp is built, and a good general does not stand over the men who dig. Go to bed."

The Quarrel of the Loom Hellenorian

Sung in the theatre at Thessalonika as the prologue to the Dionysia, in the version the Porticoes approve. The comic chorus sings the second half differently every year.

In the beginning was Chaos, which is not disorder but an open mouth: the yawn before speech. Out of the yawn came Night, and out of Night came the Egg, and out of the Egg came Desire, which is why the world is restless and always will be. Desire made Earth want Sky, and their children were the Titans, too many and too large, crowded under their father's weight until their mother handed the youngest a sickle.

So the Titans ruled, and the age was golden, the old poets say, because nobody had to work and nobody was allowed to think. The Titans wove the world on a great loom: one held the warp of hours, one the weft of the sea, and men were the knots, tied in and forgotten.

Then Athena came out of her father's head fully armed, which is to say that thinking came into the world already prepared to defend itself. She asked the question the Titans had never been asked: why is it woven like this? The Titans had no answer, because they had never needed one. That was the end of them. The war that followed was ten years long, and the gods won it because they argued with each other the whole time and the Titans never learned to argue at all.

When it was done, the gods cut the loom down and gave the threads to the cities, one each. That is why every city of the League has its own patron and its own law, and why the League is a quarrel that never ends. A people that agreed with itself would be woven again.

The comic chorus's version, last year: "And the gods cut the loom down, and gave the threads to the shipowners of Hellarchon, who sold them back to the cities at interest."

The First Fire and the Two Spirits Acheaorian

Recited by a herbad, a teaching priest, to boys and girls at the fire-school of the Fire-Temple of Persemenid, each line repeated back. The Magi teach that this is not a story, and that the class will be examined on it.

Before the first day, there was the Light that thinks and the Dark that hungers, and between them nothing at all. Repeat.

The Light that thinks made the world in seven works: first the sky of stone, then the water, then the earth, then the plant, then the bull, then the man, and last the fire, which runs through all the others as blood runs through the body. Repeat.

The Dark that hungers came up through the seven works and spoiled them. It put salt in the water, so that the seas shrink. It put stones in the earth, so that the plough breaks. It made the Titans out of the spoiled earth, great idols of weight and appetite, and the Titans lay across the world like a fever lies across a man. Repeat.

Then Hajama, who is Valor, and Kor, who is the Sage of Ages, and Zann, who is the Illuminator, took the fire out of the seven works and lit it in one place, on the mountain at the middle of the world, and the Titans who were made of spoiled earth were melted where they lay. That fire was the first fire. Every fire in every temple is lit from it, from coal to coal, without one gap in all the ages. Repeat.

The western gods were there. They held the Titans' arms. The Magi do not deny it. Repeat.

A man's whole life is a fire kept in a temple: he must feed it with good thoughts, good words and good deeds, and never let the Dark that hungers put it out. When the King of Kings sits upon the throne, the fire is kept for everyone. That is why there is a throne. Repeat, and then go and fetch the wood.

The Old Man's Loft Mavari

Told by a grandmother in the Hollows on the north side of Mavelon, mending nets on the step of a cave-house, to whoever sits still. She is paid in fish and gossip.

"In the beginning there was the sea, and the sea was cold, and in the sea there was a cow made of salt. Yes, a cow. Who else would lick the world into shape? She licked the ice for three days and out came a man's hair, a man's head and then a whole man, very surprised, and he was the Grandfather.

"The Grandfather looked around and he saw the Giants. Big, stupid, made of rime and rock. The Giants were the weather and they were the hills, and they were very, very bored. A bored giant eats ships. So the Grandfather got his sons together and they made a plan, which was the first plan, and the plan was this: get the biggest giant drunk.

"They brewed for a year. They brewed in a cauldron the size of the caldera, and that is why the caldera is round. The giant drank it all and lay down on the mountain to sleep it off, and while he slept the sons cut him up. His blood is the sea. His bones are the cliffs. His teeth are the rocks in the Race that you are not to sail through at ebb. His skull they put up over everything for a roof, and that is the sky, and it leaks.

"The other giants they did not kill, because a man does not waste good enemies. They tied them down under the mountains and set the sons to watch them. The sons are the gods of the Invictians and the Hellenes and the eastern folk. They wear foreign names now. They did well for themselves.

"And the Grandfather? He went up into the loft over the sky with a jug, because the work was done, and he has been up there ever since. The Skyhall, we call it. He laughs. He drinks. Sometimes he leans over and throws a stone down for luck, and sometimes the stone hits somebody, and that is luck too. That is why we leave a cup out on the roof at the Thing. A man who has done his work should not drink alone."

The Mare Who Ran Out of the Dark Malaunian Steppe

Sung by a horse-girl of the lion-grass clans at a mare's-milk feast beyond Xerastri; collected by a Wheelwalker who traded salt for the song and swore the clan would not mind. It is short. Steppe songs are short because the singer has to ride in the morning.

There was the Dark, and there was the Grass, and the Grass did not know it was grass because nothing had run across it.

Out of the Dark ran the Mare. She was white. Where her hooves struck, the ground knew it was ground. Where her breath went, the wind knew it was wind. She ran and ran and the world followed her to see where she was going.

Behind her came the Stone Riders, who were the Titans. They were too heavy to ride her. They wanted to hold her still so they could own the grass. They built walls across the steppe to trap her, and the walls are the mountains.

She ran between the walls and she foaled as she ran, and her foals were the gods. Some foals went west and grew fat in stone houses. Some went north and learned to swim. Some went east and sat on cushions and grew beards. One foal stayed on the grass. That one is ours. We do not tell anyone its name, because the others would come and try to stable it.

The Stone Riders chased her to the warm mountain in the south, and there the foals turned on them, and the Riders fell off the world. The Mare kept running. She is still running. That is why the grass moves when there is no wind.

Do not build walls. Walls are how the Stone Riders came. The cities of the King and the Legates and the ship-men are all walls. When the walls fall, the Mare will come back across the grass, and everyone will know where they stand.

The Breaking of the Titans

Every child knows that the Titans were broken against Vael'Tharan. Every adult knows that "broken" is not the same as "dead", and lowers their voice.

Told by Brother Oruntas, a lamp-keeper of the Fallen-Star Shrine on the mountain's warm flank, to pilgrims sitting on the cold north steps (the only steps where pilgrims are allowed to sit after dark). He tells it every night. He has told it, he says, eleven thousand times.

"Put your hand on the stone. Warm, yes? It is always warm. You are touching the oldest grudge in the world.

"There were fifty-one of them. The Titans. The priests of every empire give them different names and every name is true, because a Titan was not a person with a name; it was a thing the world does, given a body. One was Time. One was the Deep. One was Weight, one was Hunger, one was Height, one was the Long Sleep. When they walked, the world happened in their footprints.

"The gods were small then. Smaller than you think. They had been born of the Titans, or had come up beside them, or had come from elsewhere — it depends which priest is talking — and they had one thing the Titans did not: they could change their minds. The Titans could not. A mountain cannot decide to be a valley.

"So the gods fought them with the one weapon a Titan could not answer: surprise. They drew the Titans one by one to this mountain. How? Some say with a feast, some say with a challenge, some say each Titan was told that the others were plotting against it and came to see. That one I believe. And when all fifty-one were here, on these terraces — look at the size of them; those are not stairs, those are seats — the gods lit the fire under the mountain.

"Not ordinary fire. The first fire, the Magi say. The fire that is inside everything, called out of everything at once. The mountain melted and the Titans melted with it. They did not die. They could not die; they were what the world does. But they were broken: pressed down into the mountain, and under the mountain, and under the world, into the Sleep. And the gods stood on the cooling rock and divided the world between them, and that took longer than the war.

"Now. You have heard that the Titans dream. That the mountain is getting warmer. That the gatherers have moved their marks. All true. And you will hear in Deiperduem that the Titans are waking because the war is over. That is tavern talk. The truth is plainer: something that was holding them down has started to let go. Go to sleep. If you dream of a very large hand, do not shake it."

Why the Gods Went Silent

Six centuries ago the gods stopped walking the world and started speaking only through the altar. Everybody has an explanation. Three are popular. None is right.

The common tongue calls it the Greying. Invictians call it the Closing of the Bright Court, Acheaorians the Veiling. Before it, gods walked on battlefields; after it, they answered prayers, healed through their clerics and sent dreams to the oracle, but never came. The grey fog that every sailor has seen at the edge of a rift, and every dying soldier claims to have seen at the end of a road, is the visible part of it. The stories below are the three most told. You will hear them in that order of volume.

I. The Gods Turned Their Backs the Punishment

Preached by a barefoot street-prophet on the steps of the Temple of Juno on Assay days, when the crowd is already angry about the coin. Versions are preached in every empire.

"You want to know why the gods are silent? Look at your hands. There is star-ore on them. Your grandfathers' grandfathers picked it up off the battlefield and made swords of it, and with those swords they tore holes in the sky, and through those holes they called down the gods to fight their wars for them. Mars against Ares! Hajama against Mars! Brother gods made to kill each other's priests for the sake of a border!

"And the gods said: enough. They drew the grey over their faces as a mourner draws his cloak. They went home and shut the door. They still hear you. They still feed the clerics, because they are merciful. But they will not come down again until we are worthy of it, and we are not worthy, are we? Five years of peace, and the Legates are still building their private armies. The fog will lift when we deserve it. Pray. Fast. Stop debasing the coin."

II. The Sky Was Wounded the Wound

The scholars' story, as told by a junior Arcanist of the Arcane Academy to paying students in a wine-shop below the Academy, at the violet dusk. The Scholars at Deiperduem tell a drier version.

"Forget the priests. The gods did not choose anything. Consider the facts. The great star fell in 873. Within twelve years the Three Circles tore the first great rift. Within a few decades the rifts were everywhere, and wherever a rift opened you could see the grey at its edge. The fog did not come from the gods. It came from the holes.

"Think of the world as a skin. Every rift is a wound in it. A wound scabs. The grey is the scab: the world's own defence, closing over the damage. It does not care what it keeps out. It keeps out the things beyond the rifts, which is good, and it keeps out the gods, which is unfortunate, and it will keep them out until the skin has healed. Which it will not, because we keep cutting. Every battle-magus who called down a storm on the Narrows made it thicker.

"So: no gods, because of us. But not punishment. Medicine. And medicine can be studied. That is why the Academy exists. One day, someone will learn to lance it."

III. The Gods Lost a War the War Above

Whispered by Dreaming-God cultists, by Ascended heretics, and by a great many soldiers of all three empires who survived the Starfall's battlefields. The fullest form is told by a one-eyed half-orc rower in the bilge of a Hellenorian grain ship.

"The gods didn't go quiet. The gods went to war, and they lost.

"My grandfather's grandfather was at Three Circles. He saw something come through the middle ring that wasn't a god and wasn't a devil. It had no face. It looked at Mars, and Mars stepped back. You never heard about that, did you? No. Because the priests would rather you thought the gods chose to leave.

"Something from Outside came through the holes. The Outer ones. The gods fought it in the sky, up where we can't see, and the grey is the smoke of that battle. Some say the gods are still fighting, and that's why they can only spare a trickle of grace for us. Some say they lost and they're prisoners, and the priests are praying to an empty jail. And some say the thing that won is up there now, sitting where the gods used to sit, and the clerics' spells come from it, and it's letting us think nothing has changed.

"Why do you think there's always a chair empty somewhere in the stories? Pass the water."

The Night of Five Stars, as the Peoples Remember It

Late in Fallow, 873 b.P., five lights fell. The chronicles argue about whose land they hit. Ordinary people remember something else: what their grandparents were doing that night.

The official accounts are in the Night of Five Stars. These are the folk versions, which are older, stranger and more often right about small things.

The Night the Lake Was Born Invictian, Nemibano

Told by the torch-bearing girls of Nemibano to visitors on the Ides of Sextilis, during Diana's Torchlight, while walking the shore of the crater lake.

"There was no lake here. There was a valley with a farm in it and a shepherd called Turnus who would not pay his tithe to the grove. On the Night of the Stars the green-blue star came over the hills sideways, the way a stone skips, and the sky went the colour of a drowned man. It struck Turnus's valley. In the morning the valley was full of water to the brim, and no river runs in and no river runs out, and it has never dropped one finger since. Turnus's farm is at the bottom. On still nights you can hear his dog. Diana took the star for herself and keeps it in the deepest water. That is why the lake is cold in Dustmonth. Do not swim past the third torch."

The Fourth Arrow Hellenorian, the Sacred Way

Told by mule-drivers on the Sacred Way to pilgrims who complain about the climb.

"Apollo loosed five arrows that night, friend, and he loosed them because he was angry at all three empires at once, which shows good sense. Four arrows had jewels for heads. The fourth went into the mountain of the giants in the south, and the mountain whistled for a year: the wind came out of the hole the arrow made and sang one note. Shepherds went mad from it. Then a king came and took the arrowhead and the whistling stopped, and the king put the jewel in his crown and sailed away to the edge of the world, and the wind followed him. That's why the Aeolus Reach blows the way it does. All the wind in the world is going after its jewel."

The Stone at the King's Door Acheaorian, Persemenid

Told by the water-sellers of the Throne Plain, who claim descent from the family that found the stone, to anyone who buys a cup.

"My grandmother's grandmother's grandmother was drawing water at the qanat mouth when the brown star came down. It did not burn. It did not shine. It came down like a sack of grain dropped off a roof, and it made a hole the size of a donkey, and in the bottom of the hole was a stone no bigger than my fist that four oxen could not lift. The King's men came and tried. Ten men, then forty. The Magi came and prayed over it. Then the King came himself, the Shahanshah of that day, and he did not try to lift it. He sat down beside it. He said: if it will not come to the palace, the palace will come to it. And they built the palace over the stone, and since then the earth under Persemenid has not shaken once. That is why we say: a patient king is a king whose house stands."

The Night the Sea Went Out Mavari

Told in the north-harbour drinking-halls of Mavelon when the talk turns to tides.

"The night the stars fell, the sea went out of the caldera. All of it, all at once, the way it goes before the great wave. Old Hroth's boat was sitting on the bottom on its keel in the moonlight, and he climbed out and walked about on the floor of the bay picking up fish. Then the sea came back. He was not there to tell us what he found on the floor, because the sea took him. But his son said his father had shouted something, just before. He shouted: 'There's a door down here!'"

The Night the Mare Stumbled Malaunian

Told by the lion-grass clans; the steppe saw the great light pass overhead going east.

"The Mare stumbled. Everyone heard it. The big star was her hoof striking a stone. Four sparks flew from the stone and the cities fought over the sparks, and the big stone they could not pick up, so they fought over the hole. The Mare got up and kept running. The cities are still fighting over the hole."

Hero Legends

Seven heroes the continent still argues about at weddings. Two may still be alive. One may never have existed.

Iovianus and the Gladius of the Furrow Imperium Invicta

Told by a professional reciter in the Forum of Aeterna, who performs the Deeds of Iovianus in nine cantos for a copper per canto. Most listeners pay for canto IX and leave.

"Hear of Iovianus Sandarion, son of a ditch-digger, son of a ditch-digger, who was born with a callus on his right hand.

"In the sixty-fifth year before the Peace the Imperium was not one thing but seven: the Legates had divided the provinces like a cloak at a dice-game, and every Legate called himself the saviour of the Republic. Young Iovianus served in all their armies by turns and was flogged in most of them. At twenty he found, in the Founders' Hut at Romulo, in the earth floor where no one had dug for twelve hundred years, a short sword with a bronze blade that had been used to cut the first furrow. The Pontiffs say the blade was not there the day before.

"He carried it to the camp of every Legate in turn and laid it on their table. He said: 'This is the line. Are you inside it, or outside it?' Four knelt. Two fought him and lost. One poisoned himself before the sword arrived, which saved everyone time. And so the Imperium was unified, and the Senate gave him the chair, and he refused the crown three times, the way a good Invictian should.

"Thirty-five years he held the line against the Hellenes and the King. Then came the Destructive Star. For a day and a night they fought above the field, and at dawn Iovianus struck the sorcerer down with the gladius of the Furrow, and the Star fell and was not found. Then the Imperator came home, made the peace with his own hand, and went into his house in Aeterna to rest. He is resting still. His chair is kept warm. When the line is threatened, he will come out. Another copper for the epilogue."

Astraphael, Who Went Out by the Violet Door Hellenoria

Told by an old trierarch's widow on the quay at Hellarchon as the violet dusk comes down, to children who ask why the sky goes that colour.

"Astraphael was a boy from nowhere. From a burned town on the eastern shore, so small that nobody remembers its name, which is why he said he came from every town. When the cities fled to the capital after the King's thirty campaigns, he was rowing in the bilge of a shipowner's galley because his family could not pay the passage. One night the galley was caught by the King's ships off the Reach. The boy came up out of the bilge and looked at the sky, and the stars came down into his hands. Every King's ship burned. That is why he was called the Destructive Star.

"He made the League. Not the shipowners, whatever they tell you. He went from city to city and said: we can be burned one at a time or stand together, and the cities believed him because he could set the sea on fire. For fifty years he held the north against the West and the East together.

"Then he met the western tyrant in the air above the battlefield, and they fought a day and a night, and neither could beat the other. And Astraphael saw that the war would never end by fighting. So he opened a door in the sky with his own hands and stepped through it, so that the West would have nothing left to fight. That door is the violet you see. He left it open. He'll come back through it when the League has need of him.

"No, I don't know why it's always at dusk. Ask the Academy. They know more about that door than they say."

Zindar the Road-Builder Acheaoria

Recited at the court of Persemenid by the royal reciters on the anniversary of the throne, and told quite differently by caravan drivers at the caravanserai.

The court's version. "Zindar Rashan al-Khavari was born of the line of the first fire, and the Light that thinks set its seal upon his brow. The tribes of the desert warred upon each other for water. Zindar did not war. He built. He laid a road from well to well, and set a station at each day's end, and whoever walked the road drank at his stations. In seven years every tribe walked his road. In the eighth they crowned him on the plain where the palace stands. He is the first of the Kings of Kings, and his house shall rule while the road is kept."

The drivers' version. "Zindar was a water-carrier. A boy who carried skins for a lord of R'eyshar, and the lord beat him. So one night he ran with the skins. He knew where every well was, because he'd carried water to every one of them. He sold water to the tribes for a promise, and the promise was: when I need you, ride. When he had enough promises, he called them in. The lord of R'eyshar woke up surrounded. That's how a road is built: one promise at every well. And that's why a King of Kings is only a King of Kings while he keeps the stations stocked. Ask the satraps."

Kaelen the Stormwall Duneforged

Sung by the miners of the Duneforged Citadel at the change of shift, and told to every child of House Caerthain on the night before their first armour.

"Five hundred in the pass. Fifty thousand coming up. Three days.

"On the first day Kaelen held the narrows with the shields, and the East broke on the shields like water on a wall. On the second day the shields were spent, and he held the narrows with spears. On the third day the spears were spent, and he held it with the dead, stacking them across the road. On the fourth morning the East came up again, led by a young lord on a white horse with a lance taller than a tree.

"And Kaelen went to the cliff and put his hand on the mountain. He said: 'I have nothing left to give you but this.' And the mountain answered him. It came down. All of it, the whole south face, on the East, on the young lord, and on Kaelen. Nobody found him after. Nobody found the lord.

"But listen. When the miners dig deep into the old pass, they hear knocking. Three knocks, then a pause, then three. That is the signal the five hundred used to say: still here. So we knock back."

Vaelis Caerthain, Who Walked on Air Duneforged

A nursery tale of the Citadel, told by nurses to the Caerthain children; also sung by the airship crews of the Vaelis, the flagship named for her, in a coarser version.

"Once there was a lady of the Caesars who was not allowed to fight, because she was a lady and because her brothers were very bad at sharing. So she climbed. Every morning she climbed higher up the Ridge than anyone had, and she watched the hawks, and she asked them how they did it.

"The hawks said: we do not fly, little lady. We stand on the wind. The wind is a floor, if you know where to put your feet.

"So she learned where to put her feet. And one day, when the East came over the Ridge in the snow and the passes were all closed and her brothers were trapped on the far side, she stepped off the top of the Ridge and walked across the sky to them, with a lantern, and showed them the way home over the clouds. The East looked up and saw a woman walking on the air with a light in her hand, and they turned round and went home.

"Then she taught the smiths. She told them where the wind's floor was, and the smiths made ships that could stand on it. That is the fleet. That is why every airship carries a lantern at the bow, even in daylight."

The crew's version ends: "and that is why every airship captain is a woman who climbed out of a window to get away from her brothers."

Hrodmar Under the Water Mavari

Told at the Thing on the north side of Mavelon by the Lawspeaker, once a year, on the night the Mavari remember the Taking. Nobody else may tell it that night.

"When the Invictians came into the caldera with their ships, our king was Hrodmar, and Hrodmar was in his hall. They came to the hall with swords and said: give us the island. Hrodmar said: the island is not mine to give. It belongs to the Thing. They killed him in his hall for that answer. That is what their books say, and their books are right about the killing.

"But their books do not say what we did with him. We took Hrodmar down to the water at night, with his sword on his chest and his crown under his hands, and we put him in a boat with no oars, and we pushed the boat out into the middle of the caldera. It did not drift. It went down, straight down, with the king sitting up in it.

"He is down there still, on the floor of the bay. He is waiting for the Thing to ask him back. When a Mavari drowns honestly, at sea, at work, he goes down to Hrodmar's hall and takes a bench. The hall is getting full. One day there will be enough of us down there, and Hrodmar will stand up, and the sea will go out of the caldera again the way it did on the Night of the Stars, and he will walk up out of it with all of them behind him.

"Not tonight. Pour the cup."

The Castaway of the Spice Wharf Farshore

Told by Tyrsan pilots in the foreign quays of Mavelon and in the guild square at Romulo, in a mixture of four languages; the version below was taken down by a Romulan registrar who had to seal a contract for one of the pilots and was kept waiting.

"Hanno-of-the-Long-Swim was a Qart-Hadeth man. His ship broke up in a fog two days off this coast, a grey fog that came up out of a calm sea with no wind, and every man on her drowned but him. He swam. He swam for three days, and on the third night the fog thinned and he saw a stair. A white stair, coming down out of the grey into the sea, and he climbed out of the water onto it because what else would you do?

"He climbed until his legs would not climb. At the top there was a gate, and a man in a grey robe with no face opened it for him, and pulled out a chair. Hanno sat at a long table. A voice at the end of the table asked him where he had come from and where he was going. He told it about Qart-Hadeth and Tyrsa and the tin roads to the Isles, and the voice listened to all of it and laughed in the right places. Then the voice said: 'Go and tell them, then.' And he woke up on the beach below the Mavelon cliffs, dry, with a copper coin in his hand that nobody has ever matched to any mint.

"He spent the rest of his life sailing between the Farshore and Asetheria telling everyone everything. That's why there's trade. He's the father of all of us who bring news. Pilots touch that coin for luck: it's in the Tyrsan pilots' shrine on the Spice Wharf. They charge you to touch it."

Monster Legends

The continent's unique creatures, as their neighbours describe them. Stat blocks live in the bestiary. These are the stories that get people killed.

The Bronze Man Who Counts the Walls Talos of Duneforged

Told by Duneforged mothers to children who climb the outer wall.

"Talos walks the wall three times a day because Vulcan told him to count it, and he has never finished counting. Every time he gets to the end he thinks he missed a stone, so he starts again. If he finds a child on the wall, he counts the child. And then he has to start again, and he is very cross about it. Get down. And never, ever touch his ankle. There's a nail in it, and the nail is holding the god's fire in, and if it comes out the fire comes out with it, all at once, over the whole Citadel."

The Mouth That Drinks Three Times Charybdis of the Reach

Told by pilots at the Wreckers' Beacon to new oarsmen, while they are still sober enough to remember it.

"She was a Titan's daughter who drank too much at her father's wedding. When the gods put the Titans down, she was too drunk to run, so they chained her to the floor of the Reach and left her thirsty. Three times a day she remembers she's thirsty and drinks the strait. The wind-chart and the drinking-chart are the same chart because the wind is her breathing in. Pay the wind-seller and listen to the pilot. If you hear the water go quiet, row the other way. If you see bare rock, it's too late; pray."

The Bird That Dies for News The Ash Phoenix

Told by the solar priests of Helionyx, who keep the register of its deaths.

"The phoenix dies so that the sun need not. When something terrible is about to happen in the world, the god sends the bird to burn instead, and the bird's death pays for a little of the disaster. We record every death. Look at the register: the phoenix burned on the Night of Five Stars. It burned the day the Three Circles opened. It burned the night the Destructive Star went out. It burned at dawn on the day of the Signing, and the peace held. It has not burned since. Some of us think it is waiting. Some of us think it is saving itself for something large."

The Hind Who Looks Back The Cerynitian Hind

Told by wardens of the Verdant Sentinel Order in the Araucarian villages, usually to a hunter who has just asked where to find her.

"Diana made her the night after the gods divided the world, to show the other gods that some things are not for taking. She runs because running is her proof. Every hunter who sees her thinks she's looking back at him to see whether he'll chase. She isn't. She's looking back to see whether he's worth leading somewhere. Three men in two hundred years have followed her without trying to shoot her. All three came back with something: a spring nobody had mapped, a lost child, a deserter's grave. The ones who shot at her came back with nothing, and could not track a cow for a year."

The Thing That Hates Water The Div of Kharveth

Told by the muqanni, the qanat-diggers, around the shaft-heads below the Mountain of Kharveth.

"Before the first qanat, the div owned all the water under the mountain. He kept it underground, in the dark, so that nothing could grow and the people had to come to him on their knees. The first muqanni dug a tunnel to the water and led it out into the light, and the div has been angry ever since. He can hear you dig. He can hear you breathe in a tunnel. He won't step into running water, so we keep the channel flowing whatever it costs. If a qanat goes dry, the div comes down it. That's why the satrap who stops paying the diggers is not just a thief. He is opening a door."

The Bird That Answers Once The Simurgh of Vael'Tharan

Told by the Magi to pupils who ask how the throne knows the future, and by Hellenorian scholars who failed to get an audience.

"The Simurgh has seen the world end three times. She was old when the Titans were young. She saw them broken, she saw the first fire lit, she raised the first phoenix from an egg she found in the ash. She will answer one question, once, for anyone who waits long enough on the mountain. Zindar climbed to ask her how to unite the tribes, and she said: carry water. Every King of Kings since has sent one petitioner in his reign. Every answer is written in the Sealed Book at the Sage's Archive. Nobody reads the Sealed Book but the King, and the King reads it alone."

The Bull-Serpent in the Deep Water The Ophiotaurus

Told by Titan-cultists in whispers and by the Academy's first-year students as a dare; the version below is from a fisherman of the Maeotis Helos, who swears he has seen it.

"Whoever burns the guts of the black bull-snake can undo what was done to the Titans. That's what the old men say, and that's why the gods hid it. It swims under the marsh, in the black water where the reeds go down forever. I saw it once. Black head like a bull, and behind it a coil as long as a street, going down. It looked at me. It didn't look like a monster. It looked like it was guarding something. My cousin went out with a harpoon the next spring. We found the boat."

The Owl at the Shutter The Strix

Told by grandmothers of the Latium Plains while nailing iron over a new baby's door.

"A strix was a woman once. She did something, or something was done to her, and nobody set it right, so she set it right herself, and it ate her. Now she listens at shutters for a sleeping house where somebody has done what was done to her. Iron over the door, because iron is a promise kept; she cannot cross a promise. And if you hear a big owl on the roof, think hard about whether anyone in the house owes anyone something. Then pay it before morning."

Other creatures have stories too short to need a section: the Peri of Persevalis, who must be left one gate unlatched on the night of the Night Gardens; the Eclipsed Empousa, about whom every traveller is told "look at her feet"; the Lemures, driven out with black beans nine times over; and the Sanctum Sphinx, which appears in the lost places below.

Lost Places: Cities, Treasures and Roads

Six legends everybody knows and nobody has finished. Each has a real trail. The party can follow it.

The Sun-Fortress of Lytheris

The legend, as told by Hellenorian sponge-divers: "On the south cliff of the mist island there's a fortress where the Old Ones lit a third sun. It's still lit. Down inside the rock. If you anchor under the cliff on a still night, the water glows."

The trail. The ruin is Lytheris on Velothis, reached through the port ruin of Irelas. Divers from Azadeh Atoll know the anchorage. The glow is real. The Nethranan mural at Eronis shows three suns, and the sponge-divers' "still lit" is the Third Sun's echo.

The Deep Stacks of the Sanctum

The legend, as told by copyists of the Three Libraries: "Under the Sanctum there is a library with every book ever burned. The sphinx guards it. Answer her question and you can read anything. Answer wrong and you can never read again."

The trail. The Alexandria Sanctum exists, the Sphinx sits at the stair to the deep shelves, and her rule is exact: a wrong answer closes the stacks to you forever. The Three Libraries' copying circle wants someone to get in for them.

The Gold Barge of the Xeruezcho

The legend, as told by Wheelwalkers at the caravanserais: "When the canal was abandoned, the last tribute barge of the old satrap was halfway along it. A whole year's gold. The water went down and the barge sat in the mud, and the sand came and covered it. It's still there, under a dune that moves."

The trail. Follow the dry bed of the Xeruezcho Canal. The moving dune is real, and so are the barge's mooring-rings in the canal wall. A Mithril Reserve map at Deiperduem marks "item: barge" with a date.

The City Under the Throne

The legend, as told in the bazaars of Persemenid when the ground hums: "The palace has a cellar, and the cellar has a cellar, and under that there's a street. A whole city, with lamps still burning. Zindar found it. That's why he built here."

The trail. Start at the Royal Stair and the Water Court, where an old qanat runs lower than any qanat should. The Naming of the Streets lists eleven lanes nobody can find above ground.

The Singing Seam

The legend, as told by airship crews in the Citadel's taverns: "Vaelis found the floating stone by following a song. Up the Ridge, past where the eagles nest. Find the song and you'll never need to recrystal a hull again."

The trail. Vaelis's journals at the Crucible Spire; the high Cloudspine Ridge above the Furnace Stair; a still day, and an ear for one high note. The grounded hulls Cedar Stair and Kestrel give House Caerthain a reason to pay.

The Eagle of the Lost Legion

The legend, as told in every legion camp: "The legion that marched into the grey and never came out. They had the eagle with them. Find the eagle and you can call them back, all six thousand, and they'll follow whoever holds it."

The trail. The lost eagle is listed in the Imperium's own registers. The legion's last camp is said to be in the Shadowed Vale, where the fog lies thickest on the ground in winter. Veterans of the Discharge tell of hearing a trumpet sounding the old marching call on foggy nights.

Prophecies in Circulation

Eight prophecies people repeat, sell and act on. Each has a source, a reading and a counter-reading.

The Third Sun

"Beware the Third Sun, for what is seen shall not be saved." The last line of Nethrana.

The popular reading: the first sun is the ordinary one, the second is the violet scar over Hellarchon, and the third will end the world. The Academy's reading: a power source, still to be found. The Magi's reading: the Starfall's great meteor was the first; two more stars will fall.

The Return of Iovianus

"When the line is crossed, the Imperator will come out of his house." Chalked on walls in Aeterna since the Discharge.

Veterans' reading: when the state fails to pay the pensions, Iovianus will come out and pay them. The Council of Legates' reading: "the line" is the treaty; a war would bring him back, which is an argument for war. Valerius Maximus's reading: it is sedition.

The Star Through the Violet Door

"He will return when the League has need of him." The Selenarion's approved edition.

The cities' reading: Astraphael will return to break the shipowners' hold on the League. The shipowners' reading: the League's need is defined by the Assembly, which they own. The Truth-Flame's reading: unlicensed.

When the Patient Stone Moves

"When the stone at the King's door is moved, the house of Zindar falls." Persemenid proverb.

The court's reading: it cannot be moved, so the house is eternal. The satraps' reading: the stone is a metaphor for tribute. The engineers' reading: it has moved; a finger's breadth in five years.

The Five Made One

"Five fell; one will rise; whoever holds the five holds the sky." Star-ore traders' saying, since the Starfall.

Treasure-hunters' reading: collect the gems, rule the world. Academy reading: the gems together can lance the fog. Magi reading: blasphemy.

The Last Dreamer Wakes the Sleepers

"The last who walks in dreams will open the eyes of those who sleep." Delphara's Dream Dormitory, a reading of 4 b.P.

The Academy's reading: Vesperine Ilaro will wake the Dreaming Gods; she must be caught. The Enchanted Muse's reading: she will wake the sleeping Nethranan knowledge. Vesperine's reading: she has not said.

When the Walls Fall, the Mare Returns

A steppe song, sung on the Malaunian Steppe and lately heard in Xerastri's markets.

The steppe's reading: the cities will fall, and the clans will ride into a free world. Xerastri's reading: a raid is coming. The Scholars' reading: the "walls" are the fog.

Expansion

Artefacts and Arms

How to use the armoury

The Continental War ran for fifteen centuries, and a war that long leaves a great deal of hardware lying about. Some of it is ordinary: a pawned legion breastplate, a fire-pot nobody admits to selling. Some of it is old enough that the empires which made it are now ruins with tourists. A little of it is the reason the war went the way it did, and the people who own those pieces would like nobody to write them down. This part writes them down.

Seven groups follow. The Relics of the Old Empires are Nethranan glass and Mycairan bronze, dug out of Velothis and the Ekran hills and sold at Corinth with or without their curses. The Arms of the Imperium, Hellenoria and Acheaoria are each empire's signature pieces, from legion standards to Hellenic fire. The House treasures of Duneforged are the codex's own artefacts: the Vulkrim forge-relics, the Merca banking magic, the Virellarion alchemy, the Zayida's instruments of rule, and an airship nobody discusses. Materials gives crafting rules for every ore the codex lists as an Ore. Common magic is what a fourth-level party can actually buy.

Every card gives rarity, type, attunement and a value in gp. Values are what a willing seller asks in a city with a Mithril Reserve branch; double them in a town, halve them when the seller is in a hurry. Rules follow the DMG: a +1 item adds to attack and damage rolls (or AC), saving throw DCs are fixed unless stated, and "regains charges at dawn" means dawn. Prices in drachmas, denarii or darics are local asking prices; the Reserve changes them at its posted rate and takes a tenth.

Three rules hold everywhere. First, the Treaty of Deiperduem lists "arms of the war" in a schedule nobody has finished reading, so carrying a famous weapon across a border is a diplomatic question, not a customs one. Second, the Mithril Reserve's Arcanist-Securitas will identify any item for 100 gp and keep a note of who brought it in. Third, the big pieces have owners, and owners have memories.

Relics of the Old Empires

Nethrana made things out of glass, mist and other people's attention; Mycairos made things out of bronze and blood. Both are gone, and both left stock. Since the peace the Amphictyony has sold digging licences at the Citadel of Mycarion, Zandar Isle smugglers have found the current-road to Irelas, and every dealer in Corinth has a back room. Rule of thumb: Nethranan pieces lie to the mind; Mycairan pieces remember their owners.

Dreamer's Lens Nethranan glass

Rare · wondrous item · requires attunement · 2,500 gp (the Academy pays 4,000)

A palm-sized disc of grey glass, slightly warm, ground so thin it flexes. As an action you can look through it to cast augury without components; the lens shows the answer as a glimpse of the two futures. Once per dawn, when you or a creature you can see within 30 feet makes an attack roll, ability check or saving throw, you can use your reaction to look through the lens and roll a d20; the creature uses your roll instead of its own.

Each use after the first in a day forces a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw. On a failure you take 2d6 psychic damage and cannot tell dream from waking until you finish a long rest: you have disadvantage on Wisdom (Insight) and Intelligence (Investigation) checks, and the DM may describe one thing each hour that is not there.

Lore. Fragments turn up in the fog of Lytheris, where the Council of Eronis kept the lenses that watched Mycairos across the sea. Whole lenses are rare; the Prismatic Shroud buys chips by the ounce.

Hook. A lens bought in Corinth keeps showing the same future: the party standing in an empty hall of mirrors at Eronis, next to a woman in grey.

Customs Mirror Shard Nethranan glass

Uncommon · wondrous item · no attunement · 400 gp

A hand-sized triangle of silvered glass from the walls of the Mirror Customs House. The shard has 3 charges and regains 1d3 at dawn. As an action you can expend 1 charge and hold it towards a creature within 15 feet. The creature makes a DC 13 Charisma saving throw. On a failure you see it "as it would be taxed": you learn every object it is concealing on its person, whether it is disguised or under an illusion, and the rough value of its purse. The creature knows it has been inspected.

If the last charge is expended, roll a d20. On a 1 the shard inspects you instead and shows your secrets to everyone looking at it.

Lore. The customs house at Irelas checked every cargo for illusion. Its mirrors still work, and smugglers out of Zandar Isle chip them off by the sack.

Hook. A Romulo customs registrar has started using a shard on Farshore factors. Three of them have since left the city at night, and one left a dead man behind.

Charmed Keel Irelas hull-timber

Uncommon · wondrous item (ship fitting) · no attunement · 500 gp

A length of black, salt-proof timber stripped from a moored Nethranan hull. Scarfed into the keel of a vessel of up to 100 feet, it increases the ship's speed by 1 mile per hour, and the ship's navigator has advantage on checks to avoid becoming lost at sea or in fog. Fitting it takes a shipwright three days.

Each night the ship spends at sea, roll a d20. On a 1, at some point before dawn the helmsman steers towards a harbour that is on no chart. The crew notice only if the officer of the watch succeeds on a DC 15 Wisdom (Perception) check. What waits there is the DM's: usually a Bound Rift, and usually Irelas as it was.

Lore. Sold at the Lechaion as "charmed keels" since the war's navies went home. The pilots' shrine there will no longer bless a ship that has one.

Hook. A merchant hires the party to find her husband's ship, which made harbour last month at a port with a lighthouse that has not stood for nine hundred years.

Glass Mask of the Council Nethranan glass

Very rare · wondrous item · requires attunement · 18,000 gp

A face-mask of clear glass, featureless except for a faint frost where the mouth would be. While wearing it you have resistance to psychic damage and advantage on saving throws against illusions, and you can cast dream (save DC 17) once per dawn. While you are asleep wearing the mask, you can see and hear the dreams of any sleeping creature within 60 feet.

Curse. Each time you cast dream with the mask, make a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw. On a failure your reflection lags a heartbeat behind you. After three failures your reflection shows another face, you cannot remove the mask, and on nights of your choosing (the DM's) something else dreams through you.

Lore. The Council of Eronis sat masked so that no member could read another's face. Seven masks are recorded. One is in the Arcane Academy's cellar at Hellarchon, one was on the face of a corpse in the Palace of Eronis two years ago and is not there now.

Hook. The Enchanted Muse offers the party a fortune to carry a mask to Persevalis without looking into it.

The Book of Lost Hours Nethranan glass and vellum

Artefact · wondrous item (pact tome) · requires attunement by a warlock or wizard · not for sale

A thin book with glass covers, written in Nethranan glyphs that shift with the light. Each page holds an hour that someone has forgotten. While attuned, you can use it as a spellcasting focus and gain these properties. Minor: you know the cantrips minor illusion and message, and you can read any page as an action to relive its hour as a vivid dream (learning what happened in it). Major: you can cast modify memory (save DC 18) three times per dawn; a memory you remove is written onto a new page. Mirror-craft: once per dawn you can cast dimension door, entering one mirror large enough to hold you and leaving by any other mirror you have seen.

Destroying it. Every page must be read back to the person who lost its hour.

Lore. The pact tome of Vesperine Ilaro, the last dream-walker, who carries it everywhere. Three powers hunt her, and at least one of them wants the book more than the woman.

Hook. A page has been torn out and sold. The buyer in Delphara has been dreaming an hour from the Council's last session and has stopped eating.

The Third Sun Nethranan weapon

Artefact · wondrous item (lens-lantern) · requires attunement · priceless

A lens of white glass the size of a cartwheel, made to sit in the bronze socket over the Gate of the Third Sun at Lytheris. The lens is missing. The socket is still warm.

Lit, the Third Sun sheds a pale light to a radius of 1 mile. A creature in the light must succeed on a DC 22 Wisdom saving throw at each dawn or become unable to tell dream from waking: it is charmed by the attuned bearer, treats illusions as real (no check to disbelieve), and acts out its dreams while awake. A creature that fails three saves in a row is unmade, as if it had never existed; only a wish brings it back, and only its family remember it.

The DM should treat this as a campaign endpoint, not a weapon for the party. The Third Sun has no minor properties.

Hook. Three empires' agents are racing to Lytheris. The party is the fourth, and the only one that wants the socket broken.

Mycairan Bloodblade Mycairan bronze

Rare · weapon (shortsword or scimitar) · requires attunement · 2,000 gp to a Corinth dealer, 50 gp to an honest one

A leaf-shaped bronze blade with a groove down its length that is always faintly red. You gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this weapon. When you reduce a creature to 0 hit points with it, the blade gains 1 charge (maximum 3). When you hit with it, you can expend 1 charge to deal an extra 2d6 necrotic damage.

Curse. Once attuned, you cannot part with the blade willingly. At each dusk you must wet the groove with blood; your own will do (1d4 piercing damage). If you do not, or if you speak ill of the old kings in the blade's hearing, make a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw. On a failure, the next time you roll initiative the blade makes your first attack against the nearest creature, friend or not.

Lore. The Mycarion diggers sell them by the dozen. Every one was used in the frenzy that emptied the bronze kingdom, and they know it.

Hook. A Corinth collector has bought forty bloodblades in two years and paid extra for the bloodiest. He keeps them in a room with no windows, and lately he has been feeding them.

Mycairan Priest's Regalia Mycairan gold and bronze

Uncommon · wondrous item (pectoral, armlets and diadem) · requires attunement · 200 gp a set

A bronze pectoral, two armlets and a gold diadem, stamped with the knotted glyph of the Ekran priesthood. While you wear the full set, Mycairan constructs (the bronze golems of Mycarion, the door-wardens, the bronze bulls) treat you as a priest of the old kings: they do not attack you unless you attack them, and they open doors for you. You have advantage on Intelligence checks about Mycairos.

It remembers its owner. When you first attune to it, make a DC 12 Wisdom saving throw at the end of your next long rest. On a failure you dream the priest's last ritual and gain no benefit from that rest. In the Vaults of Ekran you have disadvantage on saving throws against the effects of the thing behind the seals; the regalia was made to bring it food.

Hook. The Gallienain Cult is buying sets at three times the price. They need a priest's regalia for every door they mean to open.

Death-Mask of Korythos Mycairan gold

Rare · wondrous item · requires attunement · 6,000 gp to collectors; "priceless" to the family

A hammered gold mask of a bearded king with his eyes closed. While wearing it you have darkvision to 60 feet, you are immune to the frightened condition, and once per dawn you can cast speak with dead; the corpse answers in the old tongue of Mycairos, which you understand while you wear the mask. Undead of Mycairan origin within 60 feet know exactly where you are.

Lore. The mask lay on the walled-in king of Korythos of the Bronze Wall, whose garrison shot at his hall for days. The local tyrant sells tickets to the tomb. The king's wight wants the mask back, and attacks anyone carrying Mycairan bronze.

Hook. A noblewoman of Thebesieas wants the mask for her family shrine and swears her house descends from the king. She is right, and the mark in her blood will wake when the mask touches her face.

Arms of the Imperium

The Imperium armed millions of men to the same pattern and then sent most of them home with a promise. Its magic is the magic of standards, offices and kit: things that make a soldier one of a line, and a magistrate harder to argue with. Since the Great Concord, legion gear has been turning up in pawnshops from Anticata to Napplesia, and the Council of Legates has started asking which of it was ever returned.

Gladius of the Ninth Legion sword

Rare · weapon (longsword; a long-pattern gladius) · requires attunement · 4,000 gp

A plain cavalry-length gladius with a bone grip and the numeral IX punched into the tang. You gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon. Once per dawn, as a bonus action, you can give the Legion's Word: up to six allies within 60 feet who can hear you can each use their reaction to move up to half their speed without provoking opportunity attacks. Allies who end that movement adjacent to another ally gain a +1 bonus to AC until the start of your next turn.

Lore. The Ninth Legion carried a dozen of these as officers' swords; the best of them hangs at the belt of Legatus Decimus Aurelianus Corvus, who fights behind a shield wall of his own veterans and makes them hit harder before he hits at all. The other eleven were issued, recorded and never handed in.

Hook. Corvus will pay 500 gp and a favour on the Council of Legates for each missing gladius returned, no questions asked. Two of the men holding them are now Duumviri of their towns.

The Eagle of the Thirteenth Legion standard

Very rare · wondrous item (aquila standard) · requires attunement by a creature proficient with martial weapons · not for sale (theft of an eagle is treason)

A gilded bronze eagle, wings raised, on a pole shod with iron. While you hold it, allies within 60 feet who can see it have advantage on saving throws against being frightened. Once per dawn, as an action, you can raise it: up to ten allies who can see it gain 10 temporary hit points and can immediately end one effect on themselves that is causing them to be charmed or frightened.

While an enemy of the Imperium holds the eagle, every soldier who served in its legion has disadvantage on Charisma checks made to command or persuade other Invictians, until it is recovered.

Lore. The Thirteenth lost its eagle at Praetor's Fall in the last decade of the war, and its survivors were folded into other legions in disgrace. Every legion says its eagle is a god; the Thirteenth's men have spent twenty years proving it.

Hook. The eagle has turned up in a Qart-Hadeth factor's crate in the guild square at Romulo, registered as "bronze bird, decorative, one". The factor wants it sealed by the master weights and shipped. Four thousand veterans want it back.

Lorica of the Evocatus Veteran's armour

Rare · armour (breastplate; segmented plate) · no attunement · 1,500 gp (pawned for 200)

Banded steel plates on leather straps, polished by thirty years of somebody's sweat. You have a +1 bonus to AC while wearing this armour. You can don or doff it in half the usual time, and you cannot be surprised while you are awake and on watch.

Lore. Issued to the evocati, veterans recalled for a further term, and supposed to go back to the armoury when they left. Millions of men were promised land and pensions the state cannot pay; the armour is what many of them got instead. The pawnshops of the Insulae and the Veterans' Field are full of it.

Hook. The Aerarium Militare has ordered the armour recalled. The veterans have refused, a Vigiles cohort has been told to enforce the order, and half the Vigiles are veterans.

Assay Scales of Juno Temple instrument

Uncommon · wondrous item · no attunement · 300 gp (a temple set: 1,200)

A bronze balance in a walnut case with a set of stamped weights.
