Reading the gaps. Nothing reaches Deiperduem by water; Varathros Lake is its own sea and connects to nothing. The five Acheaorian cities have no sea lane among them: the empire's harbours are small southern ports and islet stations like Bahrami Rock, and what moves by sea from them moves through Zandar Isle. A cargo from Hellarchon to Persemenid goes by ship to Corinth and then a month by road, or it goes to Zandar Isle and nobody writes it down.

Short legs to the towns. Anticata, a day's march north of Aeterna. Falecosa and Nemibano, a day or two into the hills. Fucostia, a day down the Tiberius by barge and two back, or two by the river road. Napplesia, three days down the Via Litoranea from Fucostia or a day by sea, and two more by sea to Mavelon. Argotiko, a day's ride beyond Thebesieas. Qa'zshahrv'in, four days east of Atarabad on the caravan road, the last certain water. Zandar Isle, two days' sail from Mavelon or Corinth, three from Hellarchon or Fucostia; Irelas on Velothis lies three days beyond it through currents only Zandar boats will name.

The routes, stage by stage

One card for each road and lane in the routes table. Prices are in gold, silver and copper for the DM's ledger; travellers pay in local coin. Invictian denarii are discounted by a quarter to a third at any counter that can read an assay, and at most that cannot. Roll the named encounter table once a day on roads (twice on the Treaty Road), once a day at sea, and once a night in the wilds.

Via Sacra Aeterna Aeterna – Romulo · half a day

Roll: Invictian roads, or Romulo streets at the far gate · Papers: none for citizens; foreigners show a travel warrant at the Romulo gate

Stages. Out of Aeterna by the Porta Sacra; the Tomb Mile, where the patrician dead line both verges and the remnant's freedmen sell flowers at their masters' tombs; the Janus shrine at the sixth milestone, where travellers turn a bronze head to face the way they are going; the Hall of Weights at Romulo, where every Farshore cargo and every great contract must be sealed. A walker leaves after breakfast and is in Romulo for a late lunch. There is one inn on the whole road, the Two Faces at the shrine, and it survives on people waiting for processions to pass.

Costs. Two toll-posts, each bought by the season by a different syndicate: 1 cp a walker, 2 sp a cart, 5 sp a litter, processions free. A hired litter with eight bearers, 5 sp. A guide who will get a cart registered at the Hall of Weights before the noon bell, 1 gp; the sealing itself costs one part in a hundred of the declared value, and declaring less is the commonest crime in Romulo.

Hazards. Too short to rob and too rich not to. Pickpockets work the processions; the toll-farmers work everyone else. A cart whose seals do not match its manifest is held at the Romulo gate until a Hall clerk walks out to it, which can be a day.

Seasons. On festival days the road is closed to wheels from dawn to dusk, and on the Vigiles' Night the flame is carried from Romulo to Aeterna on foot and everyone else waits. In late summer the dust is so bad that patricians travel at night by torchlight and the toll-posts charge double for the lamps.

Set piece: the right of way. A Qart-Hadethi tin convoy racing to reach the Hall of Weights before the price-board changes meets a patrician funeral coming the other way at the Janus shrine. The road is one cart wide between the tombs. The factor offers the party 20 gp to get his wagons past; the dead man's son offers nothing and remembers faces. The shrine-keeper, asked, says the god faces both ways and is no help at all.

Via Septentrionalis Aeterna – Anticata – Aepistra · six days on foot, four mounted

Roll: Invictian roads; by night near the old lines, battlefield · Papers: travel warrant, stamped at each Legate's checkpoint

Stages. Day 1: Anticata, which exists because a day's march out of Aeterna ends there; sleep at the Milestone inn and buy the news by the cup. Day 2: the mansio at Ad Pontem, where the bridge has been down for four years awaiting a private contract and a ferryman has grown rich. Day 3: Castellum Rubrum, a posting-house now kept by a Legate's soldiers, who decide whose warrant is honoured. Day 4: the vineyard stage at Tres Tabernae, three inns that have hated each other for a century and all water the wine. Day 5: Statio Ianuaria, the provincial boundary, where the portorium is taken. Day 6: past the Castra Nova, two miles out, into Aepistra. From Aepistra the Treaty Road spur runs east to Deiperduem (see the Treaty Road), and a branch road runs five days north-east to Ephelanum, carrying the Dux's orders and the condominium's grain tithe.

Costs. A posting-house bed 4 sp, 6 sp with stabling; a meal 1 sp; fodder 5 cp a beast. The Ad Pontem ferry, 1 sp a head and 5 sp a cart, and the ferryman's cousin sells the planks that would mend the bridge. Portorium at the boundary: one part in forty of goods in transit, assessed by a publicanus who values debased denarii at three-quarters face. A Legate's checkpoint stamp, free by law and 2 sp in fact.

Hazards. Demobilised legionaries collecting "the pension" at ruined milestones, with receipts. Posting-houses with no horses, because the towns that owe them stopped sending animals they are never paid for. Frumentarii sharing tables. Every warrant shown north of Statio Ianuaria is copied for Legatus Augusti Quintus Herennius Strabo.

Seasons. Spring floods take the Ad Pontem ferry out for a week at a time; the ferryman charges for waiting. Autumn is the veterans' season: harvest work ends and the roads fill with men who were promised land. Winter is dry, cold and the fastest time to travel.

Set piece: the receipt. Twelve veterans under a former optio stop the party at the ninth milestone past Anticata, take "the pension" (2 sp a head, politely) and hand over a wax receipt stamped with an old legion's eagle. Two stages on, a second band demands the pension again, sees the receipt and waves them through. A frumentarius at Castellum Rubrum wants that receipt very badly: the eagle belongs to a legion the Council of Legates officially disbanded, and somebody is still keeping its books.

Via Ferraria Aeterna – iron country – Mavelon; south to the Duneforged Citadel · six days to Mavelon, three weeks to the Citadel

Roll: Invictian roads; south of the forks, forest; on the ridge, mountains and the Cloudspine Ridge · Papers: travel warrant; a Thing permit to carry iron north through the Gate of Mavelon

Stages. Four days south-west from Aeterna through the iron country, sleeping at forge-towns where everything tastes of charcoal, to the Ferraria fork. West two days to the Iron Landing on the mainland shore, where the old forest road brings Alderpool's charcoal down, and across the strait by barge to Mavelon's inner caldera and the arsenal terraces. South from the fork, seventeen days of ore road: convict stages where the yards' labour sleeps in pens, three Legates' checkpoints a few days apart, the long climb, and finally the Duneforged Citadel under the Cloudspine. Beyond the Citadel the ridge road runs four days to Kaelen's Pass and down into Acheaoria, open to trade by treaty, escorted every yard by the Adamantine Line.

Costs. Forge-town beds 3 sp and soot included. The strait barge, 2 sp a head, 1 gp a cart, and the Landing's tally-man counts the iron in every load for both the Dux and the Reiks. On the ore road each Legate's checkpoint takes its own toll, 5 sp a wagon, so a convoy pays three times for one road and the Gilded Horizon passes the cost to the Citadel. Adamantine Line escort over Kaelen's Pass: free, compulsory and watching.

Hazards. Ore convoys are slow and worth stopping. Escaped convicts in the forest stages. Checkpoint soldiers who "find" an irregularity in the second Legate's stamp. On the ridge, Mihran blood-hunters who ride up with the Acheaorian caravans and ask, courteously, whether anyone in the party is related to House Caerthain.

Seasons. Kaelen's Pass is shut by snow for about ten weeks in deep winter; caravans caught above the Skyward Bastions shelter in them, and the Bastions do not always stay where the caravans left them. The iron country's spring mud adds two days to the Citadel journey. In high summer the arsenal works through the night and the Iron Landing barges run until the haze is too thick to see the far shore.

Set piece: the third checkpoint. At the last Legate's post before the climb, the optio in charge has not been paid in four months and has closed the road "for inspection" until someone pays him. A Duneforged ore convoy of forty wagons, a Gilded Horizon coach and an Acheaorian caravan coming down from the pass are all stacked up outside his gate, and the caravan has a Mihran outrider. The optio will take 50 gp to open. The Citadel's convoy master will not pay a bribe on principle. The Mihran will, if he can choose who goes through first.

River Tiberius Aeterna – Fucostia · a day down by barge, two back; two days by the river road

Roll: Invictian roads on the towpath; in flood, the River Tiberius entry · Papers: none; grain barges carry an Annona tally

Stages. Down from Aeterna's river wharves past the bridges and the dozen ferrymen, through the water-meadows to the towpath village of Vicus Salinarum (salt-pans, eels, an inn on stilts), and out to Fucostia at the mouth by dusk. Coming back, the barges are hauled upstream by oxen on the towpath, and the night is spent at Vicus Salinarum whether you like eels or not.

Costs. Passage on a grain barge 3 sp down, 5 sp up (you will be asked to help with the ropes at the bends). A private boat with two oarsmen 2 gp a day. Wharf dues at either end, 1 sp a passenger, 1 gp a ton of cargo, waived for the Annona.

Hazards. The Annona convoy is short and a Legate who stops one is "making an argument": a stopped convoy means guards nervous enough to fire on any boat that comes alongside. Drowned dead in weighted sacks, on the nights the river remembers them.

Seasons. Spring flood makes the downstream run half a day and the upstream haul impossible for a week; the river road floods at the meadows and adds a day. In late summer the low river grounds the deepest barges at the Salinarum bend, and the Annona's grain sits on mud while the capital counts its days.

Set piece: the empty barges. The party's barge is the last in a convoy of twelve. Halfway down, at the bend, the bargemaster asks them to stand on the cargo hatches when the Annona inspector's skiff passes, because the hatches are the only full ones. Behind the inspector's skiff comes a Legate's galley, and the Legate wants to see inside every hatch.

Via Litoranea and the Imperial sea lanes Fucostia – Napplesia – Mavelon; Mavelon – Corinth · seven days by the coast road, three by sea

Roll: coast by road; sea and complications at sea afloat; the Gate of Mavelon on arrival · Papers: travel warrant; at Mavelon, the Aurum Pact's landing certificate for any Farshore cargo

Stages. By road: Fucostia to Napplesia in three days by fishing towns and retired admirals' villas, then four days along the cliffs to the Iron Landing and the barge across to Mavelon. By sea: Fucostia to Napplesia a day, Napplesia to Mavelon two, coasting and putting in at night. From Mavelon the open lane runs three days to Corinth's Lechaion quay, or two to Zandar Isle and two more on to Corinth if the captain prefers not to be counted.

Costs. Coast-road inns 5 sp, and Napplesia's 2 gp, because the villas set the price of everything. Deck passage on a coaster 5 sp a day; a berth 2 gp a day. Mavelon's harbour dues depend on the harbour: the north harbour takes silver by weight for the Reiks, the south harbour takes denarii for the Dux, and the Farshore Quays add the customs-house toll, one part in eight, on everything foreign.

Hazards. Pirates emboldened by the peace, who strike between Napplesia and Mavelon where the cliffs give no anchorage. Mavari and Imperial crews feuding in port; a ship that docks on the wrong side has picked a side. Customs galleys of the Abyssal Tideguard who want to see the iron manifest of anything Corinth-bound.

Seasons. The Imperial sailing season runs from the spring rites to the autumn storms; in winter the sea is "closed" by custom and the navy's insurance, and only grain hulls and fools sail. The Mavari sail all year from the north harbour and say the closed sea is an Invictian superstition.

Set piece: the scrap cargo. A Corinth-bound merchantman offers the party cheap passage because it needs extra hands. The hold is full of "scrap iron for Lechaion" that is plainly new spear-blanks. A Tideguard galley closes on the second morning out, and the captain asks the party which of them is a good liar. Thebesieas has paid for this iron; the Dux of Mavelon has been told about it; the Reiks's harbour-master loaded it.

The Long Lane Hellarchon – Corinth – Thessalonika · two days to Corinth, three more to Thessalonika

Roll: sea, complications at sea; through the strait, the Aeolus Reach · Papers: a proxeny letter for each city you land at; the harbour Fiftieth at each

Stages. Out of Hellarchon's war harbour, two miles below the rock, coasting west past Carianea and the little crew-ports that resent where the ships are berthed, to Corinth's Lechaion quay on the second evening. North from Corinth through the Aeolus Reach, one day under sail if the chart is honest, with the Knot Shrine on the northern head and the Wreckers' Beacon on the southern cape, then two more days up the grain coast to Thessalonika. Hellarchon's own ships run Hellarchon to Thessalonika direct in four days and do not call at Corinth on principle.

Costs. Deck passage 4 sp a day (2 drachmas and some obols), a berth 1 gp 5 sp. The harbour Fiftieth, one part in fifty on cargo, at every League port, and a landing fee of an obol a head. A Delpharan wind-chart, genuine, with the Amphictyony's tripod stamp, 50 gp; a forged one, 5 gp and possibly your life. Ixion Keraunios's knots, sold at Corinth, 25 gp a knot.

Hazards. The Hegemon's warships "escorting" other cities' grain convoys, which means inspecting them, which means fees. Charybdis three times a day in the Reach. Corsairs who are also Corinth's navy when it suits Corinth.

Seasons. The sailing season is long but the Reach's two off-chart days a season are not on any calendar. The grain run from Thessalonika comes south in late summer, and for a month the Lane is a column of hulls nose to tail under Hellarchon's triremes. In winter the Lane closes north of Corinth and the coast road (eight days, five mounted) takes the post.

Set piece: the escort. A Thessalonikan grain convoy of thirty hulls is met at the mouth of the Reach by four Hellarchene triremes offering escort "under the League's protection", at a drachma a ton. The convoy's commander refuses. The triremes fall in behind anyway. Halfway through the Reach the wind does something the chart says it will not, and only one side has a copy of the second chart.

The Southern Run Hellarchon – Helionyx – Ephelanum · two days to each

Roll: coast and sea; at Ephelanum, the condominium's two customs posts · Papers: proxeny letter for Helionyx; at Ephelanum both a proxeny letter for the sanctuary and a travel warrant for the harbour

Stages. South from Hellarchon, two days to Helionyx and its salt-pans and fallen colossus, then two more to Ephelanum, where the harbour is silting and the pilot charges more each year to find the channel. By land the same journey is nine days: the coast road to Helionyx in five, then four through the salt country, sleeping at pilgrim hostels that face the sea so the guests can see the goddess's ships come in.

Costs. Passage as on the Long Lane. At Ephelanum, two sets of dues: the Invictian Dux's harbour toll (one part in forty, in denarii, at a rate that favours denarii) on the quay, and the Archon's sanctuary tax (an obol a head, two at festival time) at the inner gate. The silting-channel pilot, 1 gp a ship and rising. A pilgrim's bed in the sanctuary hostels, 3 sp with a votive lamp included.

Hazards. Invictian customs at the condominium inspecting Hellenorian ships and Hellenorian priests inspecting Invictian pilgrims. Sandbars that move every winter. Farshore spice ships that do not know the channel and pay anyone who claims to.

Seasons. At festival time the Run is a single procession of pilgrim ships and the price of a berth triples. The two treaty texts set the goddess's festival on different days, so there are two festival seasons, and each side regards the other's as a provocation. Winter gales close the Run for a month; the land road stays open and smells of salt.

Set piece: whose goddess. On the Invictian festival day the party's ship is boarded at the harbour mouth by the Dux's customs officers, who want to know why a silver statue of the goddess is aboard. Ten minutes later a temple launch arrives with the Archon's priests, who want to know why Invictians are touching it. The statue is the party's employer's votive offering. Each side wants it registered with them, which settles which side's goddess it is.

The Aeolus Reach The wind-strait on the Long Lane · one day to pass under sail

Roll: sea (high on off-chart days, sea) and complications at sea; see sea travel for Charybdis · Papers: none; the pilots' guild asks to see the chart

Stages. Twenty miles between two headlands. Ships wait off the southern approach for the chart's hour, tie a knotted cord at the Knot Shrine if they have a boat to send, and run the strait in one tide of daylight. Nobody anchors inside. On the southern cape the Wreckers' Beacon offers a bed to any sailor who asks, and Keeper Damokles asks what the ship carries. On the northern head there is a shrine, a lodestone quarry and a bronze dragon's cave nobody goes into.

Costs. A pilot of the Reach families, 10 gp for the passage; with the second chart, which marks Charybdis's surges, 30 gp, paid in advance. A genuine Delpharan wind-chart, 50 gp. Ixion Keraunios's knots, 25 gp each, one knot a day of fair wind; rope sold as his on the Pumice Flats, 2 sp.

Hazards. Charybdis, three surges a day on no schedule anyone sells cheaply. Forged charts with the off-chart days moved by a week. Harpies on the upper Petrel Stacks. On off-chart days, the Keraunic Hydra and loose air elementals, and the Beacon lights no fire.

Seasons. Peace has tripled the traffic, and the queue at the southern approach can be two days in the grain month. Twice a season, unannounced, the Reach delivers something not on the chart; old pilots read the order in which the Knot Shrine's cords come undone and claim a day's warning.

Set piece: the double-sold wind. The party's captain has bought three of Ixion's knots. So has the captain of a Corinthian trireme entering the north mouth at the same hour. When both untie their first knot, two fair winds meet in the middle of the strait, the sea stands up between them, and Charybdis surges early. Ixion, asked afterwards, says the knots were sold honestly and the contract said nothing about exclusivity.

The Sacred Way Corinth – Delphara · three days on foot, two mounted; or a day's sail to Delphara's harbour

Roll: Hellenorian roads; above the treasuries, mountains · Papers: a proxeny letter from your own city or a pilgrim's token from the Amphictyony

Stages. Out of Corinth by the Isthmian gate; first night at the Spring of the Theoroi, a walled hostel where sacred envoys of rival cities sleep in separate wings; second night at the foot of the switchbacks, among the goat-sellers and the votive-makers; third day up the switchbacks past the treasuries of the cities, each a small marble house of loot, to Delphara. By sea it is a day from Corinth to the western harbour and the pilgrim landing, and an easy half-day up; this is how most pilgrims and most of the wine come.

Costs. Hostel beds 2 sp; a pilgrim's goat for the fee, 5 sp at Corinth, 2 gp at the foot of the switchbacks, 5 gp at the top. Each city whose stretch of road the Way crosses takes its own toll, 3 obols a head at a tyrant's post, with a public word of thanks to the tyrant. The consultation itself is priced by the Amphictyony, and the Acheaorian treasury's stipend means the King of Kings asks first.

Hazards. Treasury guards of rival cities brawling on the switchbacks over precedence. Pilgrims who want protection and pay in olives. Hellarchon's agents delaying the theoros of a small city until he misses his consultation day.

Seasons. Consultation days are reckoned from Helionyx's solar tables, so the road is empty for weeks and then impassable for three days. In winter the oracle is silent and the upper switchbacks ice over; the hostels close and the goat-sellers go home.

Set piece: precedence. On the narrowest switchback the treasury escort of Thebesieas, carrying captured shields to their council's treasury, meets the escort of a Hellarchon theoros coming down. Neither will step to the cliff side. Behind the party come three hundred pilgrims and a goat that has eaten a votive. The priestess of the treasuries arrives, appoints the party arbiters by sacred custom, and leaves.

The Inland Road Corinth – Thebesieas – Argotiko – Deiperduem · ten and a half days on foot, seven and a half mounted

Roll: Hellenorian roads; past Argotiko, plateau; near Deiperduem, the Treaty Road · Papers: a proxeny letter, or a Haulway permit for goods; Thebesieas asks for neither and inspects anyway

Stages. From Corinth's isthmus up through olive country two days to Thebesieas, where the Sacred Band drills on the plain below the walls. A day's ride, a day and a half on foot, to Argotiko on the horse plain, all corrals and horse-copers. Then seven days east across the uplands, with stopping places that were war camps and are now inns kept by men who served in them: the Tripod Wells, the Shield Ford, Hippias's Barn (a stable that sells beds), and Last Hellas, a hamlet whose name every Deiperduem clerk has asked it to change. The road ends at the toll-booths of the Caravan Fields outside Deiperduem's east gate.

Costs. Inns 4 sp, Argotiko's 6 sp with a horse-dealer at breakfast. Remounts at Argotiko, a sound horse 60 gp, a war-trained mount 300 gp, below the Hellarchon price. Thebesieas has no right to inspect carts and inspects them, 1 drachma a cart and a look under the tarpaulin. Chyrsus Syndicate toll at the Deiperduem end: written, fair, and not negotiable.

Hazards. Thebesieas inspecting carts for the wrong reasons, and Argotiko's riders inspecting Thebesieas's inspectors. Smuggled Invictian iron on its way up from Corinth (the Mavelon Contract). Mycairan ruins two days off the road into the hills at Ekran, and the people who come out of them.

Seasons. Remount season in spring fills the road with horse-herds for a fortnight and the inns with horse-copers for longer. The olive harvest empties it of hoplites, who go home whatever they were doing. Upland snows can close the Shield Ford stage for a few days in midwinter.

Set piece: the inspection. A file of Thebesian hoplites stops the party's caravan outside Thebesieas and finds, under the party's employer's olive jars, a hundred spearheads stamped with a Mavelon arsenal mark. The lochagos is delighted; these are his. He offers to pay the carriage. Then he notices the party, who were not told what they were carrying, and two Argotiko riders on the ridge who have seen everything.

The Royal Road Persemenid – Atarabad – Mithratal – Xerastri · sixteen stages; seven days by relay

Roll: the Royal Road; beyond Mithratal, steppe; at the frontier, the Parthian Ravine · Papers: a royal road pass, shown and recorded at every station

Stages. A post-station every day's ride, each a walled yard with a well, a fire-altar, stalls for forty horses and a station-master with a ledger. Four stages from Persemenid across the throne plain to Atarabad and its Royal Caravanserai, where the King's Eye, Tahmineh of the Seal, reads every courier's bag. Three stages north to Mithratal, where caravan contracts and court marriages are sworn. Nine stages north again, the stations further apart and more often held by a satrap's men than the King's, to Xerastri on the frontier, with the Parthian Ravine and the Malaunian Steppe beyond. On foot the whole road is about twenty days; mounted, sixteen; by relay, seven.

Costs. With a royal road pass, a day's food and fodder at every station, worth about 5 sp a head a day, free. Without one, the station-master sells the same for 1 gp and a bed in the courtyard for 5 sp, if he likes you. The road-tax at each satrapy boundary, one part in twenty on goods; a "gift" to a satrap-held station to stop it delaying a letter by a day, 5 gp. Caravanserai lodging at Atarabad, 5 sp a night with the gate shut at dark.

Hazards. Post-stations unpaid in the restless satrapies, whose masters hold royal riders for bribes. Tribute "lost" between stations. The King's Eyes and Ears, who are everywhere and dress as nobody. Beyond Mithratal, steppe raiders, though the clans that stopped raiding now camp at Xerastri's Horse Gate and sell horses instead.

Seasons. The Opening of the Roads in spring sends every caravanserai's first convoy out on the same morning. The khamsin, the hot wind off the Dasht-a Khaliq, closes the southern stages for days in early summer; riders wait it out inside the station walls with cloths over their faces. North of Mithratal winter is steppe winter, and the stations keep a sledge.

Set piece: the held rider. At a station two stages short of Mithratal, the party finds a royal post-rider who has been held three days by the station-master, who wants a bribe the rider cannot pay. The rider's bag carries a sealed order for the Satrap of Xerastri. The station-master is a satrap's man, the satrap does not want the order to arrive, and the rider will be dead of a fever by the fourth day, which the station-master has already written in his ledger.

The Garden Road Persemenid – Persevalis · two days for a laden convoy, one mounted

Roll: the Royal Road (the Garden Road uses the same table) · Papers: a royal road pass, or a Persevalis provisioner's seal for the court's convoys

Stages. The shortest important road in Acheaoria. From Persemenid past De'rakhtak Bon, the throne plain's cold stores where Persevalis fruit waits for the court; one night at the Pomegranate Station, a post-station with a walled orchard and a water channel through the courtyard; and on to Persevalis and the Channel Head the next afternoon. Riders do it in a day and arrive smelling of roses.

Costs. The Pomegranate Station's bed is 8 sp because it is beautiful. The court's convoys go free; everyone else pays the satrap's garden-toll, 1 sp a head and 1 gp a cart, collected at a gate in a hedge. Water for animals is charged by the trough on this road, the only one where it is, because every drop is somebody's channel.

Hazards. Not bandits, who know better, but leverage: the satrap of Persevalis knows the court cannot eat without him, and his road-wardens stop a convoy whenever a payment is late. Muqanni disputes over channels that cross the road. Dream-readers of the Enchanted Muse watching the inns for a particular sleeper.

Seasons. Fruit season fills the road with convoys moving at night under wet cloth to keep the fruit cool. Blossom season fills it with courtiers. In the hot months the cold-store ice-wagons from De'rakhtak Bon run before dawn and anyone in their way is fined.

Set piece: the late payment. The court's quarterly payment to Persevalis is a week late. At dawn the satrap's road-wardens close the hedge-gate on the court's own fruit convoy, with the party travelling alongside, and announce an inspection for blight that will take exactly as long as the payment does. The convoy's eunuch-steward has a feast in two days for the King of Kings and forty wagons of peaches going soft.

The Qanat Line Wherever the dotted line of shafts runs · the edge of the empire's writ

Roll: desert (mid or high in the Dasht-a Khaliq); in towns, the Royal Road · Papers: a royal road pass is honoured where the water flows and laughed at where it does not

Stages. Not a road but a line you follow: the mounds of the qanat shafts, a spoil-heap every hundred paces, marching across the dry country toward a town. Following the shafts means water every day; leaving them means carrying it. Travellers stop at the mother-wells, at the shaft-heads where the muqanni camp, and at the towns the channels feed. Where the shafts stop, the empire stops. Two northern towns have been abandoned in five years because their channels failed and no muqanni came to clear them.

Costs. Water is sold at the shaft-heads, 1 cp a skin for people and 1 sp a trough for camels, more where the channel is low. A muqanni guide who knows which channels are live, 5 sp a day. Crossing the Dasht-a Khaliq away from the Line takes eighteen to twenty-four days by caravan and a Survival check most days.

Hazards. Dry shafts that look like live ones. A fall down a shaft (DC 13 Dexterity save at night or in a sandstorm, 3d6 falling damage and a climb in the dark). Local headmen who sell water from a royal channel as their own. Beyond the Line, the khamsin and things that hunt by thirst.

Seasons. The channels run fullest in late spring, from the mountain melt. In high summer the shaft-heads ration and the queues at the wells become politics. In autumn the muqanni go down to clear the year's collapses, and a channel being cleared gives no water for a week.

Set piece: the last shaft. Following the Line north toward a frontier town, the party finds the shafts dry for a day's march and a crew of muqanni sitting at the head of a collapsed tunnel, refusing to go down: the last man who did came up describing a room under the channel that was there before the qanat. The town at the end of the line has four days of water in its cisterns. The muqanni will go down if someone goes first.

The Treaty Road Aepistra, Corinth and Atarabad – Deiperduem · nine to twelve days from each end

Roll: the Treaty Road, twice a day, one roll always a merchant; in the city, Deiperduem streets · Papers: each empire's own on its stretch, or a letter of neutral passage from Treaty Hall

Stages. Three roads ending at one row of toll-booths in the Caravan Fields. From the west, the Via Septentrionalis spur runs east from Aepistra, nine or ten days on foot or with a wagon train, seven mounted, by posting-houses that become roadhouses run by Wheelwalker cousins as the Imperium's writ thins. From Hellenoria, the Inland Road past Argotiko. From the east, the Acheaorian caravan track from Atarabad's Western Caravanserai, twelve days by camel train and eight mounted, caravanserai to caravanserai. The last day of each road crosses the neutral ground, where by treaty no soldier may march and the Ironclad Legion patrols on contract.

Costs. A seat in a Gilded Horizon coach, 2 gp a day, three services a week, the guard captain knows every toll. Chyrsus Syndicate tolls, written and fair: 2 sp a head, 1 gp a cart, 5 sp a camel, collected at the booths and receipted. Caravanserai lodging 5 sp. Ironclad Legion "fees" for a patrol that happens to escort you, 1 gp a day. Wheelwalker letter-carriage to Persemenid, a silver.

Hazards. Every courier is someone's spy and every spy is someone's courier. Toll-gates on bridges claimed by three parties at once. Zandar Isle smugglers with olive jars that slosh wrongly. On the eastern track, the gap between the last Acheaorian station and the first Deiperduem milestone, where nobody's law runs and Suren-Pahlav's factor pays a daric a day for guards who can read three scripts.

Seasons. The anniversary of the Signing fills the road with delegations a week before and empties it the day itself. The Opening of the Roads in spring sends Atarabad's convoys west on the same morning. Winter rains turn the western spur's unmended stretches to mud and add two days.

Set piece: three armies at one fire. A night at a roadhouse on the neutral ground. Veterans of all three empires share the hearth and the same battle story, and it goes well until someone names the general. At the same table, a Treaty Hall notary of the Brass Scales carries the only certified copy of a land clause three parties want changed by one line, and one of the veterans is not a veteran. The Ironclad patrol outside cannot intervene without a fee, and the fee has already been paid by someone.

The Farshore lanes Over the outer sea to Mavelon, Corinth and Hellarchon; overland and on the monsoon to Atarabad

Roll: sea, complications at sea; overland, the Royal Road and desert · Papers: the Aurum Pact's landing certificate at Mavelon; the harbour Fiftieth at Corinth and the Spice Wharf; a royal caravan seal at Atarabad

Stages. Weeks, not days. From Qart-Hadeth across the southern sea, ten to fourteen days to Mavelon's Farshore Quays in a fair season. From Tyrsa and Khemaret, three weeks, coasting where coasts exist. From Maurash, on the monsoon to Acheaoria's southern harbours in about forty days and by caravan to Atarabad in twenty more, or the whole way to Mavelon by sea in three months if the captain is brave. From the Seric Throne, the caravan roads east of Atarabad take most of a year; last year, for the first time, a ship did it by sea. Pretannic tin-ships come down from the misty north in five or six weeks and land at Mavelon's north harbour, out of the Dux's sight.

Costs. Passage on a Farshore merchantman is not sold by the day but by the voyage: 50 gp Qart-Hadeth to Mavelon, 150 gp Maurash to the southern harbours, a fortune and a recommendation to sail on a Seric ship. Mavelon's customs-house takes one part in eight on Farshore goods; every cargo must then be sealed at Romulo before it is sold inland. Corinth and Hellarchon take the Fiftieth and ask fewer questions. Atarabad takes a tenth and asks a great many.

Hazards. Every empire wants to be the only door, and each would rather a cargo sank than landed at a rival's. Plague ships, which is why the Aurum Pact's isolation sheds stand at Mavelon's mole. Storms that have no name in any Asetherian language.

Seasons. The monsoon decides the east: it blows toward Acheaoria for half the year and away for the other half, and a Maurashi captain who misses the turn waits six months in port. The western ocean is crossed only in high summer, and only twice in living memory has anyone from Ixtal done it.

Set piece: the isolation shed. A Sabaian incense ship arrives at Mavelon with the festival a week away and its master dead of a fever. The Aurum Pact puts the ship in the isolation sheds for forty days. Every temple in the Imperium needs that incense. Someone offers the party 500 gp to get the cargo off the mole by night, and the ship's surviving mate swears the master died of poison, not fever.

Sea travel

Two empires are sea powers and one is not. The Imperium builds warships at Mavelon and grain hulls everywhere, and has never been at ease on water it cannot see across. Hellenoria is a league of harbours whose hegemon is whoever has the most triremes. Acheaoria sails the shrinking Kaspiran Seas, owns a scatter of southern harbours and islet stations, and has hired other people's ships for every war it fought at sea. Speeds below are for a day's run in fair weather; crews are full complements; passage prices are what a captain asks a stranger.

The Aeolus Reach and Charybdis

The chart. A ship passing the Reach with a genuine Delpharan wind-chart passes in a day on a DC 12 Wisdom (Survival) or water vehicles check by the helmsman; without a chart, DC 20, and a failure costs a day standing off and a roll on the sea table. Spotting a forged chart takes a DC 15 Intelligence (Investigation) check, DC 18 for the ones with the copied tripod stamp; a pilot of the Reach families spots one on sight and charges for saying so.

Off-chart days. Twice a season. When a ship enters the Reach, roll a d20; on a 1 it is an off-chart day (a captain who has had the Knot Shrine's cords read by an old pilot, 5 gp, knows the night before on a 1–2 on a d6 that it is coming). On an off-chart day the passage check is DC 20 even with a chart, encounters use the high sea table, and a failed check by 5 or more drives the ship onto the Petrel Stacks or the Wreckers' Beacon's cove: 4d10 bludgeoning damage to the hull and the keepers come down with lanterns.

Charybdis. Three surges a day at hours only the pilots' second chart predicts. A ship carrying a pilot with the second chart avoids them. Otherwise roll a d6 when the ship is mid-strait: on a 1 the whirlpool surges within a mile. Run it as a short skill challenge: the helmsman makes water vehicles or Wisdom (Survival) checks and the crew make a group Strength (Athletics) check at the oars or sheets, DC 15 each, three rounds. Two or more successes in the three rounds pulls clear. One success: the ship is spun, takes 3d10 bludgeoning damage, loses a day and anything not lashed down, and each creature on deck makes a DC 13 Strength saving throw or goes overboard. No successes: the ship is pulled under unless the party can stop it (a control water spell, a knot of Ixion's untied at the right moment, the bronze dragon of the northern head deciding it feels like it). Charybdis' Tears, salt-glass beads prized by water-mages, are found on the bare rock after a surge by anyone brave enough to land.

Wind for sale. One of Ixion Keraunios's knots, untied, gives one day of fair wind: the ship's day's run increases by half, and the passage check through the Reach is made with advantage. He does not guarantee exclusivity. The rope knots sold on the Pumice Flats are rope.

Nereid's Veil: navigation by ear

Inside the Veil sight is worth nothing. Pilots steer by the surf on known rocks, by the forty bronze bells of the Bell Line, and by counting strokes. A crossing takes two days with a pilot, in four legs of half a day each.

Each leg, the helmsman makes a Wisdom (Perception) check relying on hearing alone. DC 12 for a licensed pilot of the coast families (who has proficiency and has spent a decade learning the bells), DC 15 for an apprentice or a sailor who has crossed with a pilot at least three times, DC 18 for anyone else. A deafened helmsman fails automatically. A helmsman with wax in his ears is immune to the voices but makes the check with disadvantage, which is why pilots never use wax and divers always do. A bell spell, a trained hound or a familiar with keen hearing grants advantage; light and darkvision do nothing.

On a failure, the leg is lost (add half a day) and roll a d6: 1–2, the hull scrapes a reef, 2d10 bludgeoning damage; 3–4, the ship drifts toward the sound of the Sponge Banks and the merfolk come to look; 5–6, nothing but fog. Two failures in a row and the helmsman hears a forty-first bell, in tune, that nobody laid. Following it is a choice.

The voices. Once per leg, every creature aboard that can hear makes a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw as the fog calls them by name. On a failure the creature answers, or walks to the rail and must be stopped. A helmsman who answers is relieved by League standing order and never takes the helm in the Veil again. A creature that answers three times over the course of its life has made a promise it cannot remember.

Pilots. About sixty licensed pilots on the whole coast. A licensed pilot costs 50 gp a crossing, paid in advance, since the families doubled their fees; House Pelagonides charges more and is worth it. An apprentice costs 25 gp and may already be answering in his sleep.

Borders and papers

The Treaty opened the roads and every chancery immediately invented a document to close them again. Papers are checked at city gates, provincial boundaries, harbours, post-stations and wherever a soldier is bored. A party with the right papers pays the official toll. A party without them pays more, waits longer, or goes round.

The Invictian travel warrant tessera viatoria · Imperium Invicta

Issued by: a Dux's or Legate's chancery, or the Prefect of the City at Aeterna · Cost: 5 gp, plus a clerk's "speed" of 1 gp · Valid: one province, one year

A folded wooden tablet, wax inside, the bearer's name, origin, height, scars and errand on the left leaf and the issuing seal on the right, with a space for stamps. Citizens carry it on the viae; foreigners must, and are asked for it at every city gate, every Legate's checkpoint and the provincial boundary at Statio Ianuaria. Each checkpoint stamps it, and each stamp is copied into a ledger that goes to that Legate, not to Aeterna. A warrant issued by one Legate is honoured in another Legate's province "at the discretion of the post", which means a stamp fee of 2 sp. It does not grant post horses; that needs the post warrant, a bronze diptych with the Dominus Militum's seal and an expiry date, issued to officials and almost never sold (black-market price 200 gp and a long fall if caught).

Forgery. Forgery kit, DC 15 for a travel warrant (the wax is easy, the seal is not), DC 18 to pass a Legate's station whose clerk keeps the seal-book. A gate guard checks with passive Investigation 10; a Legate's clerk, 14; a frumentarius, 16 and a conversation. A forged post warrant is DC 15 to make and DC 18 at a Legate's station, and gives fresh horses and 80 miles a day until somebody compares ledgers.

Caught. Forged papers are a capital matter in theory and a 50 gp fine in practice, unless the Legate whose seal was copied wants an example.

The Hellenorian proxeny letter proxenia · the League of the Hellenes

Issued by: a city's proxenos, the citizen who represents a foreign people's interests · Cost: 2 gp and a gift (wine, a dinner, a favour) · Valid: until the proxenos dies or falls from favour

There is no League passport. Each city decides who may land, buy and sue there, and a foreigner's standing depends on having a proxenos: a citizen of that city who has taken your people as his guests. His letter, on papyrus with his ring-seal, says who you are and that he answers for you. With it you may lodge, trade, enter the agora and appear in court; without it you are a stranger, may be refused at the harbour, and pay the metic's tax of a drachma a month if you stay. Hellarchon issues a "common letter" under the Council's seal, 10 gp, that it claims every League city must honour; most smaller cities honour it slowly and resentfully, and cities held by a tyrannos want their own letter from the tyrant's household (5 gp and public thanks). Mages carrying an Arcane Academy seal lodge with a proxenos by right.

Forgery. Calligrapher's supplies or a forgery kit, DC 13; a proxeny letter is just a letter. The danger is the check: a suspicious magistrate sends a boy to the proxenos's house, and within the hour the proxenos either recognises his own hand or does not. A DC 14 Charisma (Persuasion or Deception) check, or a gift of 5 gp, persuades the magistrate not to bother. Hellenorians forgive forgery more readily than ingratitude: a forged letter is a fine; a real one abused is a feud with the proxenos's whole family.

Other papers. Corinth's Haulway permit for goods across the isthmus; a pilgrim's token from the Amphictyony for the Sacred Way (free, and every hostel honours it); a Reach pilot's receipt; and, at Ephelanum, both a proxeny letter for the sanctuary and an Invictian warrant for the harbour.

The Acheaorian royal road pass halmi, the sealed authorisation · Acheaoria

Issued by: the King's chancery at Persemenid, or a satrap's · Cost: free on royal business; to private travellers 10 gp, plus rations "at cost" · Valid: one journey, the route written on it

A sealed document of leather or clay listing the bearer, his companions and animals, the route station by station, and the day's ration of flour, wine, oil and fodder each station must issue. Every station-master records it and issues the ration, about 5 sp a head a day. A royal pass carries the King of Kings' seal and is honoured, in law, everywhere; a satrap's pass carries the satrap's seal and is honoured in his own satrapy and, increasingly, nowhere else. On the frontier, satrap-held stations honour the satrap's seal over the King's and delay royal passes by a day when it suits them. A cheaper "road pass" without rations, 2 gp from any frataraka, lets a traveller use the road and buy at the stations.

Forgery. Seal impressions are hard: forgery kit DC 17 for a satrap's seal, DC 20 for the King's, and the King's Eyes and Ears keep registers of every seal in use. A station-master checks with passive Investigation 12 and a ledger; a King's Eye, 17. Bribing a station-master to accept a doubtful pass costs about a day's rations for the whole party, and he writes the bribe in the ledger as "spoilage".

Caught. Forging the royal seal is an offence against the King's majesty. The forger is handed to the Court of Vipers, and not usually seen again.

Neutral and odd papers Deiperduem, Duneforged, Mavelon, the Farshore quays

Where the three systems meet, and where they do not reach

  • Letter of neutral passage, Treaty Hall, Deiperduem: drawn by a notary of the Brass Scales and sealed by the Arbiter's clerk, 25 gp and a week. By treaty all three empires must honour it on the Treaty Road and in their embassy compounds; in practice it is honoured on the Treaty Road and examined everywhere else.
  • Chyrsus toll receipt: not a passport, but on the Treaty Road a traveller without a receipt from the last booth is assumed to have dodged one, and pays again.
  • Adamantine Line token, Kaelen's Pass: a brass disc issued to each traveller in an escorted caravan; travellers on the ridge without one are assumed to be Mihran, smugglers or both.
  • Thing permit, the Gate of Mavelon: the Mavari assembly's leave to carry iron north through the gate. Without it the Reiks's guards confiscate the iron or demand a man-price.
  • Aurum Pact certificate: nothing from a Farshore ship lands on Mavelon's south mole without one; 2 gp a passenger, 1 gp a bale, and up to forty days in the isolation sheds if the inspector does not like your cough.
  • Mithril Reserve letter of credit: not a travel paper, but honoured at every branch in every city, and the closest thing to a passport the continent has. Gate guards who would stop a stranger let a Reserve client through.

Travel complications

Roll once on a long journey, or whenever the road has been too quiet. For sea voyages use complications at sea; at Mavelon, the Gate.

d20 travel complications
d20ComplicationWhat it costs or opens
1The bridge is out, and a private contractor is "assessing" it.A day's detour, or a ferry at five times the usual price. The contractor works for a Legate.
2A lame horse, or a camel that sits down and will not get up.Half a day, or 60 gp for a new animal at the next station. The station-master's cousin sells horses.
3The posting-house has no horses: the town stopped sending them.The party walks the next stage, or bribes a courier (5 gp) for his spare.
4A party member's papers name the wrong province, satrapy or proxenos.A day at the gate while a clerk writes to someone. 5 gp shortens it.
5The coin is refused: Invictian silver at a third off, or not at all.Every price on this leg is a quarter higher unless the party has darics, drachmas or Reserve paper.
6A flood, a khamsin, a fog or an early snow closes the way.1d4 days' delay. Everyone else is waiting too, at the same inn, with the same rumours.
7A sick companion: road fever, bad water or a well that tasted of copper.One character has the poisoned condition for 1d3 days unless a DC 13 Wisdom (Medicine) check finds the cause.
8The inn is full of a delegation travelling to Deiperduem.Sleep in the stable, or be invited to dinner by a diplomat who wants a favour carried.
9A toll the party has never heard of, collected by men with a document.2d6 gp, or a fight with men who may be legal. Roll a d6: on a 1–3 they are.
10A fellow traveller attaches himself: a pedlar, a pilgrim, a runaway.He is useful for three days and then someone comes looking for him.
11A festival in the next town: no rooms, no business, the road blocked by a procession.A day's delay, and a chance to be blessed, cursed or recruited.
12A guide's "short cut".Roll on the local wilds table for the night; the short cut takes as long as the road.
13A Wheelwalker convoy claims a party member as a long-lost cousin.Free food and news for a week; the cousin's debts as well.
14A courier dies at the party's camp, his bag sealed.Deliver it, open it or burn it. Each choice is somebody's crime.
15A party member is mistaken for someone with a bounty on him.A watch patrol, a bounty hunter, or a grateful stranger who thinks he owes a debt.
16The caravan master announces a new fee halfway, where turning back costs more.5 gp a head, or leave the caravan and cross the next stage alone.
17Demobilised soldiers on the road, hungry, armed and owed money by someone.Bread buys an escort; an insult buys a fight; a promise buys trouble later.
18Something valuable is lost or stolen in the night.A pack, a letter, the papers. It turns up for sale at the next market.
19An omen: an eagle, a dead snake, a fire that will not light, a child's prophecy.Hirelings and drovers refuse to go on for a day unless a priest is found or paid (1 gp).
20A good turn: a fair wind, an empty inn, a caravan heading the same way at the same price.The leg takes a day less. Something will be asked in return, later and politely.

Expansion

Names and Tongues

Names and Tongues

Everyone on Asetheria is named twice: once by their mother and once by whoever wrote them down. This part gives the DM both, for every people the party is likely to meet, and the words to use when meeting them.

How to use this part

Each people below has a short account of how its names work, how to address its great officials, and what to call someone when the party wants a fight. Then come three d20 tables: given names, family or house names, and nicknames or epithets. Roll one column or pick across a row. A name from the first table plus one from the second is a citizen; add the third and you have someone the neighbours talk about.

Names carry politics. An Invictian with a Legate's family name was probably enfranchised in that Legate's army and still owes him a vote. A Hellenorian who gives his deme instead of his father is from Hellarchon and wants you to know it. An Acheaorian whose house name has an apostrophe in it is either from an old zarate or is very anxious you should think so. A Deiperdene councillor has no surname at all, by law. The tables are built so these signals come out by themselves.

The languages follow the names, then the manners. A party that bows correctly before the Satrap of Persevalis and salutes correctly before the Dux of Mavelon will be remembered; a party that gets either the wrong way round will be remembered longer.

Invictian Names

Three names for a citizen, one for a slave, and a heated legal argument about whether a woman has any.

How names work

The three names. A male citizen carries the tria nomina: a praenomen (personal name), a nomen (the gens, always ending in -ius) and a cognomen (a nickname that hardened into the name of a family branch). Publius Arruntius Celer is Publius, of the gens Arruntia, of the "Quick" Arruntii. Only about eighteen praenomina are in use and every one has a standard abbreviation, so documents read "P. Arruntius Celer" and a family that names five sons in a row Gaius tells them apart by cognomen, rank or bruise.

Women. A daughter takes the feminine of her father's nomen and nothing else: every daughter of Marcus Calpurnius is Calpurnia. Sisters are told apart by order (Maior, Minor, Secunda, Tertia) or by a pet name used at home and never in a contract. Calpurnia Secunda, whose marriage to Lykon Bacchiades is the talk of Corinth, has a first name only her nurse remembers. Since the war, widows who run estates have started adding their late husband's cognomen, and the patrician remnant considers this the end of civilisation.

Freedmen and new citizens. A freed slave takes his former master's praenomen and nomen and keeps his slave name as a cognomen: the slave Felix becomes Marcus Calpurnius Felix, and everyone who hears it knows exactly where he came from. A provincial enfranchised for service takes the nomen of the commander who enrolled him. In fifteen centuries of war that meant millions, and it means the Council of Legates today has whole provinces named after it. A man called Lollius in the hill country is very likely a client of Legate Sextus Lollius Calvus, and when the Legate needs votes, cohorts or a crowd, the name is the invoice.

Agnomen. A great victory adds a fourth name from the beaten enemy or the field. They were common in the war and are now handed out by the Senate for very little. The Senate voted one to a Legate last year for "pacifying" a district that had not been at war.

Children of the camp. Soldiers could not legally marry while serving, so a generation of legion children carries the mother's name, or the legion's: "Castrensis" (of the camp) is a cognomen in every frontier town, and the demobilised veterans now waiting for land they were promised give their sons names like Fidus and Patiens without irony.

Address and rank

Invictians address officials by office in speech and by rank-epithet in writing. A Dux is vir illustris on paper and "Domine" (lord) or "Dux" to his face; a senator is vir clarissimus, a great equestrian official vir perfectissimus, a lesser one vir egregius. A Legatus Augusti is "Legate" and expects nothing more, which is how you know he is dangerous. The Dominus Militum, General Valerius Maximus, is "Dominus" in speech and Dominus Militum on paper. Nobody living may be hailed Imperator. Soldiers used to give it to generals after a victory; since the chair was left empty "awaiting Iovianus", the shout is treason by edict, and two Legates have quietly let their men use it anyway.

Between equals, Invictians use the praenomen with friends, the cognomen in company and the nomen in court. Use a man's praenomen uninvited and you have claimed to be his family or his master.

Insults

"Furcifer" (gallows-bird, a slave fit for the fork) and "verbero" (whipping-boy) are the classics. "Homo novus", a new man, is said with a smile by patricians and is the worst thing in the language to a rich equestrian. "Lixa" (camp-follower) is for anyone who profited from the war without fighting it. Since the Assay began, "Juno's coin" means someone who looks like silver and is not. To a veteran, "ration-eater" (one who lives on the failing Annona) starts fights in every tavern from Aeterna to Fucostia. And "wait for Iovianus" means "never": it is said of debts, promotions and land grants, and Vigiles have been known to arrest people for saying it in public.

Hellenorian Names

One name, a father, a city, and if you are rich enough a house whose name is plural because it means all of you at once.

How names work

One name and a father. A Hellenorian has one personal name, usually a compound that means something: Kleandros "glory of men", Nikandros "victory of men", Lysandra "freer of men". Formally he adds his father in the genitive: Damon Lysiou, Damon son of Lysias. First sons are named for their paternal grandfather, so names alternate down a family like a ladder, and anyone who knows the custom can guess a man's son's name before he has one.

Deme and city. In Hellarchon a citizen gives his deme instead of, or after, his father: "Damon son of Lysias, of Aktaia". Since the reforms that made demes the voting units, giving your deme is a political act, and new-made citizens give it loudest. Abroad, every Hellenorian becomes his city: Philon the Corinthian, Ismene the Theban. Calling a Corinthian "the Hellarchonian" is a mistake you make once.

Houses in -idai. The great families, the shipowners and the old landed eupatrids, are known by a clan name in the plural: the Nikandridai, the Bacchiadai, the Erebides. A man of the house carries the singular masculine (Kleandros Nikandrides, Telestes Bacchiades), a woman the feminine (Melantho Erebide). Only members by blood or formal adoption may use it. A clan name advertises a common ancestor, real or bought, and three of Hellarchon's shipowning houses invented theirs within living memory.

Women's names in public. The old custom, still kept in Thebesieas and among Corinth's oldest families, is that a respectable woman is not named in public while she lives: she is "the wife of Telestes" or "the daughter of Lykon". In Hellarchon, where women sit on the Council by lot and teach at the Academy, the custom is dead and laughed at. In a Theban law-court, naming a citizen's wife aloud is an insult the court will note.

Short forms. Every name has a pet form ending in -on, -o or -is (Nikon for Nikandros, Kleo for Kleoboule or Kleandros, Lysis for anything with Lys- in it). Short forms serve either sex and are what slaves are called, which is why calling a grown man of good family by his pet name is an insult unless you shared a wet-nurse.

Address and rank

Hellenorians do not, on principle, bow to men. An Archon is "Archon" or "O Archon" and then his name; a Prytanis, Epistates, Polemarch or Hieromnemon by the same rule with the local title. A Strategos is "Strategos". A tyrannos takes the style of his office as an equal rank; his own people call him by name, and the rest of the League calls him "the man in the acropolis". The Hegemon, Kleandros Nikandrides, is "Hegemon" in the synedrion and "Kleandros" to anyone who has dined with him, which is the point of dining with him. Emperor Thalorion IV is "Sebastos" (the Revered) in writing and in prayer, and nobody has needed to address him in person for ten years. An assembly is addressed as andres plus the city (andres Hellarchonioi, "men of Hellarchon"); Hellarchon's mixed Council has started adding "and women" in a tone that makes the old men wince.

Insults

"Idiotes" is a man who minds only his own business and takes no part in the city: the word means "private person" and stings about as much as "coward". "Barbaros" is anyone whose speech sounds like "bar-bar"; Hellenorians use it of Acheaorians freely and of Invictians when drunk. A "sykophantes" is a paid informer who brings lawsuits for profit; a "kolax" is a flatterer at a rich man's table. "Oar-fodder" is what Hellarchon's shipowners call the rowers whose votes keep them in power, never where the rowers can hear. "Plain-pig" is what everyone else still calls a Theban, Sacred Band or no Sacred Band. And "pitch-horn" is a slur for the Voidfolk that the Accord made a fineable offence; it is fined about once a year and said every day.

Voidfolk Names

Three names for a tiefling of the Accord: one for the register, one for the lamp, and one that has never been written down and never will be.

How names work

The register name. When the tiefling families were absorbed under the classified Voidfolk Accord, every one of them was enrolled in the Deme of the Accord under a Hellenorian name and a Hellenorian house. They chose the houses themselves and chose, with a dry sense of humour, names of night and darkness: Erebides (of the Deep Dark), Nyktidai (of Night), Skotiadai (of Shadow). The registrars wrote them down without comment. Register names follow every Hellenorian rule: Iason Erebides, Melantho Erebide, "of the Deme of the Accord" in any document. A Voidfolk who omits the deme in a contract can have the contract voided, which some Hellarchon lawyers treat as a business model.

The lamp name. On a Voidfolk child's naming-day a clay lamp is lit for it on the shelf under the painted flame and allowed to burn out. The name spoken over the lamp is a virtue name, a single Hellenorian word: Elpis (Hope), Hypomone (Endurance), Aletheia (Truth). Lamp names are used by friends and family and by Voidfolk among themselves, and are the same for either sex. Using one uninvited is presumptuous; refusing to use one after being invited is an insult.

The old name. The tiefling families came out of old pacts, and the pacts named them. Each Voidfolk has an old name, given by a grandparent in a tongue that is not Hellenorian, never written, never spoken outside the family and never told to the Truth-Flame. The Accord does not mention old names. The Truth-Flame would very much like a list.

Address and rank

A Voidfolk wants to be called citizen (polites) and will often say so. The Accord promised citizenship; for most families it is still "pending", so in law most Voidfolk sit somewhere between citizen and resident foreigner. Calling a Voidfolk a metic is technically accurate and socially a slap. Melantho Erebide, the first of the Voidfolk drawn by lot to Hellarchon's Council, is "Bouleutes" (Councillor) and answers to nothing else.

Insults

"Pitch-horn" (fineable, see above). "Accord-paper": said by Voidfolk of one of their own who has given up the old names and has a register name and nothing else. "Pending": said with a shrug, it is the cruellest joke in the Deme. "Unregistered": a tiefling from outside the Accord, from Acheaoria, the Imperium or the Farshore Realms, which Voidfolk call each other only in anger.

Acheaorian Names

A name, a father, a house and a breath: the apostrophe is where the court still sounds a vowel the plateau swallowed centuries ago.

How names work

Name and father. An Acheaorian has a personal name and is formally "son of" or "daughter of" his father: Farrokh pur-e Mehrdad, Shirin dokht-e Navaz. In speech the joining word drops and the father's name follows directly, Farrokh Mehrdad. Many names are compounds with a god or a quality in them: Mehrdad "given by the covenant", Atar-Farnbag "fire of glory", Rashnu-Vahram "the judge victorious".

The zarate. A member of a noble house adds its name: Artabazos Mihran, Mandana Nahid'zar, Roxana Surena. House names come from an ancestor, a place or a grant from a King of Kings (Suren-Pahlav, "Suren of the Parthava frontier"). Commoners have no house; they have a master, a village or a water share, and are named by them when it matters: "Bagdat of the third shaft", "Arta of the Golab looms".

The apostrophe. Court speech is old and slow, and keeps vowels the plateau dialects ate long ago. Where the plateau swallowed a vowel, court script writes the gap with a mark, and the codex's apostrophe is that mark: Qa'zshahrv'in, Shir'abad D'ar, R'eyshar. A courtier sounds the gap as a short catch of breath; a plateau herdsman runs straight through it. Old zarates write the mark in their own names (Tir'dad, Nahid'zar, Bagh'dar) to show the name is older than the swallowing. New families leave it out. The two satraps who bought Kinsman rank have recently added one each, and the old Kinsmen pronounce the catch in their names with great and visible care.

Women. Women keep their own father's name and house for life; a married woman of Mihran is still Mihran in her husband's house, which is half the reason marriages between zarates are treaties. The arashshara sign with their personal seal, not their house, and a merchant who asks an arashshara whose daughter she is has asked the wrong question.

The King's name. The King of Kings is never named in his presence and rarely named at all. He is "the Shahanshah", "the King" or, in court style, "the Magnificent". His personal name, Vishtaspa, appears on coins, inscriptions and oaths, and saying it casually in Persemenid will get you looked at by someone from the King's Eyes and Ears.

Address and rank

The Shahanshah is addressed only when he speaks first, and then as "Shahanshah" or "my King", by someone standing at the distance the court ushers mark. A satrap is "Xšaçapāvan" (Protector) in court speech, "Satrap" in the common tongue, and in letters "Protector of the Realm, the King's bandaka" (his bondsman), a title satraps value because it means no one but the King owns them. A Karanos would be "Lord of Lords", but there has not been one for five years. A Marzban is "Marzban", an azata "Azata" or "Lord of the house", a frataraka "Frataraka". The Magi are "Mobad" (a senior priest) or "Herbad" (a teaching priest), and a Magus is never called by his name alone, not even by a satrap. An arashshara is "Arashshara" and then her name, and anyone who calls her "lady" instead has demoted her.

Insults

"Without a share" (one who owns no hours of water) is the plateau's worst thing to call a free man. "Liar" is far stronger than in any other tongue, because the faith holds the Lie the root of every evil; "Lie-follower" is what the Magi call a heretic and what a satrap calls a rival he means to kill. "Your fire is out" means "your line will end". "Purchased" is what old Kinsmen call new ones. "Qanat-rat" is a city insult for a desert villager. "Eunuch" said of an intact man implies he serves the Court of Vipers, and said of a eunuch is the one thing that can make one of them lose his temper in public. "Barbarian" works in both directions: Acheaorians use the court word an-ārya, "not of the noble", for Invictians and Hellenorians alike.

Mavari Names

Father's name, clan's name, and the byname the Gate Fights gave you: the north side of Mavelon introduces itself backwards and expects you to keep up.

How names work

Name, father, clan. A Mavari has one given name and is formally his father's son or her father's daughter: Ragnwulf Ansvaldson, Hildegund Ansvaldsdottir, Gisla Thurwinsdottir. At the Thing and in the Gate Court the clan comes first: "of the Hrodnings, Ragnwulf Ansvaldson". Clans are named for a founder with -ing: the Hrodnings (Hrod's people), the Skeldings (Skeld's). A child whose father is dead or unknown may take the mother's name (Fridugundsdottir), and nobody remarks on it, because on a sea island a third of the fathers are drowned.

Name-parts. Mavari names are built from two old words, and families pass the parts down, not the whole name: Ansvald's sons are Ragnwulf and Ansgar, and a Hrodning girl will have -gund or -hild in hers. A child is never named for a living relative, because the name is thought to have room for only one; naming a son after a man still alive is a public wish for his death, and the Skeldings did it this spring.

Bynames. Everyone acquires one. They are honest and not always kind: Odo Halfhand, Wido Keelbreaker, Sunna the Loud. A byname given at the Gate Fights or in a Thing debate sticks for life; trying to shed one is the surest way to keep it.

Mixed names. Since the Gate Marriage, children of the two halves carry two names, one for each grandfather. The Reiks's grandson is Aulus to the Praetorium and Audwin to the Thing. Gate Court clerks write both, and a child's choice of which to answer to at the age of spear-taking will be read as a vote.

Address and rank

The Reiks is "Reiks" and nothing grander; the Mavari have no word for "Your Majesty" and resent being taught one. He is addressed standing, by any free spear-bearer, and the custom is to look him in the eye. The Lawspeaker is "Lawspeaker" and may interrupt anyone. A clan elder is "Eldest". A free man or woman of the Thing is "spear-bearer" in formal speech, and a Mavari crewman who calls an Invictian trierarch "Domine" is being polite to a guest, not acknowledging a lord. Invictians who want to be liked on the north side call the Reiks "Reiks", not "chieftain"; the Mavari know exactly what "chieftain" means in Invictian.

Insults

"Oar-slave" is the worst thing you can say to a Mavari: it recalls the levy the Oath abolished, and it has started more Gate Fights than drink. "Treasury-payer" is new this year: one who pays a fine to the state instead of a man-price to a family, aimed at House Sentia and at any Mavari who sides with it. "Key-turner" is a Hrodning who is too friendly with the south; "slip-burner" is what the south calls any Mavari when the arsenal has a fire. "Nithing", a man without honour, is the legal term for one the Thing has outlawed, and saying it of anyone who has not been outlawed is actionable at the Gate Court.

Deiperdene Names

A first name from anywhere and a sign over the door instead of a surname, because in the war a surname could get you killed by whichever army arrived next.

How names work

House-signs. Old families of Deiperduem take their names from the signs over their doors: the Brass Scales, the Green Lamp, the Seven Quills, the Iron Cup. A person is "Mira of the Green Lamp"; the family is "the Green Lamp"; the head of the family keeps the house the sign hangs on and is "Mira at the Green Lamp". The custom is a war habit hardened into law: a citizen standing for the Council of Thirty must use a house-sign. A family that moves house takes its sign with it, and the sign-painters' guild keeps the register.

Given names. Deiperdenes name children from all three empires and the common tongue, and since the Treaty the fashion is for treaty names, names that sound right in all three tongues and belong to none: Dara, Mira, Ari, Tavi. Older Deiperdenes have two or three given names on file and used whichever one suited the army in the square.

New signs. Incomers who settle take a sign when they buy a house. Since the peace the register has filled with signs from embassy staff, Mithril Reserve clerks and Gilded Horizon factors, and the old families sneer at signs that are only decorations (the Gilded Wheel, the Treaty Rose). A sign may not repeat one already in the register, which has made old signs valuable: a dying family's sign sells for more than its house.

Address and rank

The Arbiter is "Arbiter" and is addressed in the common tongue, never in the language of the empire that nominated them, which would imply whose they are. A member of the Council of Thirty is "Councillor" and a house-sign: "Councillor of the Iron Cup". Embassy staff are addressed by their own empire's customs inside the compounds and by Deiperdene custom outside them. Nobody bows in Deiperduem's streets; a nod is neutral, and neutrality is the city's religion.

Insults

"Three-coat" is someone who changes sides with the weather (a war word: the city kept three sets of banners). "Compound-dog" is a Deiperdene in an embassy's pay. "Bare-door" is a family with no sign: a newcomer, or one that sold its sign. And saying of a citizen that "his name was something else in the war" is the city's subtlest knife; everyone's was.

Duneforged Names

The mountain speaks the common tongue, so its lords are Duke, Marquis and Count to their faces and Dux, Marchio and Comes in the chancery, and its miners are named for the shaft they work.

How names work

Given name and house. The Duneforged Citadel names its people in the common tongue: a given name and a house or family name, in that order. Roland Caesar, Isolde Merca, Ottilde Vulkrim. Noble given names run to the old ballad names of the common tongue (Roland, Gavin, Tristan, Isolde), and the chancery Latinises them in documents: Rolandus Caesar, Gavinus, Isolda. A citizen who sees his name written in chancery Latin knows he is being taxed, sued or knighted.

Caesar and Caerthain. House Caerthain is "the Caesars", and only the Duke's own line uses Caesar as a surname: Duke Roderick Caesar, Duchess Kivia Elea Caesar, Roland, Gavin, Helena, the acknowledged Tristan Caesar and the unrecorded Scribonia Caesar. Cadet branches and the dead hero of the pass are Caerthain (Kaelen Caerthain). Using "Caesar" without the right is an offence in the citadel's law, and an Invictian visitor who jokes about the name has insulted the Duke and, the Duke's household would add, misunderstood an older word.

The great houses. Marquis houses Merca and Vulkrim and Count houses Virellarion and Zayida each have their own habit. The Merca give their children soft, old-court names (Edran, Selvane, Isolde). The Vulkrim name theirs for metals and forge-saints and give daughters Mavari-sounding names from a marriage three generations back (Ottilde, Thestun for a son). The Virellarion use long, many-syllabled names, which the alchemists say carry better in an incantation. The Zayida have given their children southern names since a founding marriage (Faris, Nadira, Idris), and nobody in the citadel finds it odd except visiting Acheaorians, who find it very odd indeed given the feud.

Shaft names. Miners take the name of the shaft or gallery they work as a surname: Merrin of the Fourth Shaft, Bel of Deepgallery. It changes when they change shafts, and a miner who keeps the same shaft-name for thirty years has earned a respect no title buys. Dwarves of Clan Ironhand keep their clan name everywhere: Haldor Ironhand, Sigrun Ironhand.

Address and rank

The Duke is "Your Grace" and is bowed to from the waist; the Duchess likewise. A Marquis or Count is "my lord Marquis", "my lord Count", or "my lady". Their children are "Lord" or "Lady" and the given name: "Lord Selvane", "Lady Ottilde". Commander Daud, the Royal Protector, is "Protector" and does not care to be called anything else. A knight is "Sir" and the given name. A Dominus Argentar is "Dominus" in the Reserve's halls and "Master" outside them. Chancery documents give every title in its Invictian form, and a noble who insists on "Dux" in conversation is either very old-fashioned or angling for the Council of Legates.

Insults

"Debtor" is an insult in a city that owes the Mithril Reserve more than any other customer. "Hollow-shaft" is a coward or an empty promise (a worked-out mine). "Tin-crown" is a minor noble who acts grand; "pass-runner" is someone who fled the Cloudspine stand, which no one living admits to being. Calling a Duneforged citizen "Invictian" is a test: the citadel is Invictian-aligned and proud of it, and also proud that it pays its soldiers on time, which it will tell you the Imperium does not.

Steppe Names

No surnames, no cities and no signatures that outlast the signer: a Malaunian is named for the tents they ride with this year and the grass where their mothers are buried.

How names work

Name and tents. The riders of the Malaunian Steppe have a personal name and an allegiance, and the allegiance is to tents, not to blood: Skilur of Amage's tents rides for whoever holds Amage's tents this year. Change band and the second half of your name changes. That is why the steppe's contracts say "with a man", never "with a nation", and why an Acheaorian clerk who writes a Malaunian's band into a treaty as if it were a family has written something the next spring will undo.

The grass. For honour and for oaths a rider names the burial ground where their mother lies: Tomyra of the Lion Grass. Grass-names do not change, and they are the nearest thing the steppe has to a surname. Holding the burial rights of a great mound-field, as Tomyra holds the Lion Grass, is holding the oaths of everyone whose mother lies there.

The dead. The dead are not named. A rider speaks of "my mother under the Lion Grass" or "the one who rode the dun mare", and the dead person's name goes out of use until a grandchild is old enough to be given it. Asking a Malaunian the name of a dead parent is grossly rude; an envoy who reads out a list of fallen chieftains at a treaty-feast will not be at the next one.

The Khagan's line. North of Thessalonika the clans of the Khagan's line keep a family name, which the rest of the steppe considers a city habit. They swear by the Sky-Father, whom the League calls Astraeus.

Address and rank

A band's leader is addressed by name and nothing else; titles are for people who cannot be recognised. The Khagan is "Khagan" and is greeted dismounted, which is the whole of the ceremony: a rider who greets the Khagan from the saddle is claiming equality, and an envoy who does so is declaring war. Elders are "Grandmother" or "Grandfather", by rank and not age. An empire's envoy is "Guest", and a guest has the rights of a guest for three days.

Insults

"Wall-dweller" (one who sleeps behind stone) covers every citizen of every empire. "Walker" is a rider who lost his horse and did not take another; "milk-spiller", one who refused or wasted fermented mare's milk offered at a tent, is about as bad as "thief". "Paper-man" is a rider who signed something that outlasted him. And "whose mother?", asked of a rider with no grass-name, means bastard, exile or worse.

The merchants who land at Mavelon's Farshore Quays and trade at Romulo's Guild Square bring their own names, and the Hall of Weights writes them down as best it can.

Each realm below has a line on how its names work and a d20 table. The clerks of Romulo spell every Farshore name in Invictian letters, and every Farshore merchant has at least one complaint about it. For the realms themselves, see the Farshore Realms part.

Family name first, then a one- or two-part given name; adults also have a courtesy name used by equals. Calling a Seric envoy by his given name is an intimacy only a parent may take. Address an envoy as "Honoured Envoy"; the Son of the Sky is never addressed, only reported to. Insult: "uncrowned" or "one who has lost the mandate", of anyone who rules badly.

Pretanna

A personal name, often with a god or a beast in it (Cuno- "hound", Bran "raven"), "son of" or "daughter of" (map, merch), and the tribe. Druids give up their tribe. Address a king or queen as "Lord" or "Lady of the (tribe)"; a druid as "Wise One", and never ask a druid to write anything down. Insult: "southern", which covers all of Asetheria.

The Feathered Courts of Ixtal

Names stacked from titles, gods and animals, written with the codex's apostrophe as a glottal catch: K'inich Yax B'alam, "Sun-Faced First Jaguar". Everyone also has a day-name from the sacred calendar of their birth, used for either sex. Address a city-king as "Holy Lord" (k'uhul ajaw). Their insults are unknown; their ships have come twice.
