Tongues of Asetheria

Three imperial languages that spent fifteen centuries shouting at each other, one common tongue that grew up in the gaps, two dead scripts nobody can fully read, and one language that is not from here at all.

In game terms the common tongue is Common. Invictian, Hellenorian and Acheaorian are each a standard language a character may learn; Mavari, Acheaorian plateau speech and the steppe tongue are regional dialects a character with the parent language can follow with difficulty (DC 12 Intelligence check for anything subtle). The Nethranan pictorial script and the Mycairos runes are written only and dead. Deep Speech is Deep Speech.

The common tongue

Who speaks it. Everyone who trades, travels or soldiers. It began as the camp pidgin of the Continental War's truce-tents, prisoner exchanges and border markets, absorbed words from all three empires and the dwarven holds, and hardened into a language. The Duneforged Citadel speaks it natively and writes its law in it, as does Deiperduem. Since the Treaty it is the language of the Treaty Road, the Caravan of the Gilded Horizon, the Mithril Reserve's ledgers and every embassy kitchen. Imperial courts consider it vulgar and conduct half their business in it.

Script. The Road Hand: twenty-four plain letters borrowed from Hellenorian shapes by Invictian quartermasters, written left to right, with Invictian numerals. Every caravan-master can read it; few imperial nobles will admit to.

UsePhraseMeaning and note
Greeting"Road and roof.""May you have a road by day and a roof by night." The reply is "And bread between."
Oath"On the Treaty and my coin."A merchant's oath since the Signing; before it, "on my neck".
Curse"Clip your silver!"May your money be debased; new, Invictian in origin, and enormously popular.
Farewell"Three roads."Go safe by whichever empire's road you take.
Haggling"Weigh it at Romulo.""I don't believe your scales."

At the table. Speak it as plain modern English with a few trade idioms. Its whole flavour is that it belongs to no one: an imperial noble who answers a party in the common tongue is being either practical or rude, and the party should be left to guess which.

Invictian

Who speaks it. The Imperium, from Aeterna's Senate to the Mavelon slips; its legions carried it everywhere, and every veteran of every army knows its drill commands. Two registers: the high speech of law, Senate and inscription, and the camp speech of the legions and the Subura, which drops endings and swears creatively. Romulo's clerks keep the strictest high speech on the continent.

Script. Square capitals for stone and seals; a quick cursive on wax tablets and papyrus that only Invictians can read and not all of them. The Assay's reports are in capitals, so they can be posted.

UsePhraseMeaning and note
Greeting"Salve." / "Ave.""Be well." Ave is for superiors and the gods; using it to an equal is sarcasm.
Oath"Per Iovem Lapidem.""By Jupiter the Stone." The most binding oath in the Imperium, sworn holding a flint.
Soldier's oath"Facturum quod imperabitur.""I will do what is ordered." The legion's sacramentum; veterans argue about who is now doing the ordering.
Curse"Di te perduint!""May the gods destroy you!" In camp speech, "Di perdant", flatly.
Proverb"Cum Iovianus redierit.""When Iovianus returns": never. Said under the breath.

At the table. Use Latin words for offices and oaths and English for everything else. A crisp, clipped delivery for officers, short sentences, verbs at the end when someone is being pompous. Have NPCs address PCs by what they are ("Medicus", "Tribune") until they learn a name.

Hellenorian

Who speaks it. The League of the Hellenes, its colonies and its trading partners; the Arcane Academy teaches and casts in it, so most wizards on the continent read it whether they like Hellenoria or not. Every city has its dialect, and they are mutually intelligible and mutually contemptuous: Thebans broaden their vowels, Corinthians speak fast and count in their heads, Delpharans answer questions with questions.

Script. The Hellenorian alphabet, twenty-four letters, which the common tongue's Road Hand borrowed and simplified. Inscriptions in old cities still run boustrophedon, back and forth like an ox ploughing.

UsePhraseMeaning and note
Greeting"Chaire." (to many: "Chairete.")"Rejoice." Used for hello and goodbye alike.
Oath"Ma ton Dia." / "Ne tēn Athēnān.""By Zeus" (strong) or "Yes, by Athena" (Hellarchon's usual). Krates swears "by the dog", which annoys the priests.
Assembly"Tis agoreuein bouletai?""Who wishes to speak?" The herald's opening at every ekklesia.
Curse"Es korakas!""To the crows!" Go to ruin, be left unburied.
Toast"Agathou daimonos.""To the good spirit." The first cup at any symposium, unmixed.

At the table. Hellenorians argue. Give their NPCs questions instead of statements, and let them enjoy disagreeing. Use Greek for offices and greetings, and have every Hellenorian name his city first when introducing himself.

Acheaorian: court speech and the plateau dialects

Who speaks it. Court speech is the language of the throne at Persemenid, the satraps' chanceries, the Magi's liturgy and every royal inscription. It is old, slow and full of vowels and honorifics; a court sentence addressed upward has at least one clause of praise before it reaches its verb. The plateau dialects are what the empire actually speaks: from Qa'zshahrv'in to Shir'abad D'ar they swallow unstressed vowels, clip the honorifics and borrow freely from subject peoples. The apostrophe in plateau place-names marks where court speech still sounds a vowel the plateau lost. A courtier and a herdsman understand each other with effort and amusement.

Script. Three, for three jobs. Wedge-script, pressed into clay with a reed, for monuments and for the ration and tax tablets the arashshara keep by the hundred thousand. The chancery hand, a flowing ink script on parchment and leather, for letters, orders and the Royal Road's dispatches. And the Magi's fire-letters, a sacred alphabet for liturgy that has a separate letter for every sound in court speech, including the catch the apostrophe marks.

UsePhraseMeaning and note
Greeting (court)"Durūd bar tu, ke Zann tu-rā roshan dārad.""Greeting upon you; may Zann keep you bright." A plateau herdsman says "Durud" and leaves it there.
Greeting (plateau)"Kh'sh-āmad.""Well come." Court speech has five syllables for it.
Oath"Ātar gawāh, vashnā Hakiyah.""The fire is witness, by the favour of Hakiyah (the Just Scales)." Sworn facing a flame; lying after it is the Lie itself.
Royal formula"Vashnā Zann, Shahanshah adam.""By the favour of Zann, I am King of Kings." Carved on every royal inscription; saying it aloud as a joke is treason.
Curse"Kārēz-at khushk bād!""May your qanat run dry!" The plateau's worst; the court equivalent is "May your fire go out."

At the table. Make court speech slow and padded: every request preceded by a compliment, every refusal disguised as praise ("Such a gift would shame my poor house to receive"). Make plateau speech quick and blunt. If a PC speaks court Acheaorian with a plateau accent, nobles will notice and adjust their opinion one rung down; a PC who speaks it with a perfect court accent will be asked who taught them.

Mavari

Who speaks it. The Mavari of Mavelon's north side, about thirty thousand people, and the south-side boys who learn its curses on the slips. It shares old words with Pretannic sea-songs, which both peoples notice and neither explains. Most Mavari also speak Invictian, which they use to Invictians and to be rude to each other.

Script. None for law: the law is held in the Lawspeaker's memory and recited at the Thing, and writing it down would make it the Imperium's. For property the Mavari cut keel-marks, angular staves on ship-shares, boundary posts and the spear-rings the Oath at the Gate was sworn on. Keel-marks record who owns what and who swore what, and nothing else.

UsePhraseMeaning and note
Greeting"Heill ok sæll.""Whole and lucky." The answer is "Ok þú" (and you).
Oath"Á baug ok geir.""On ring and spear." Sworn with a hand on a spear-ring; the Oath at the Gate was sworn this way.
Law"Með lögum skal land byggja.""With law shall the land be built." The Lawspeaker opens every Thing with it.
Curse"Marr gleypi þik!""May the sea swallow you!" Said lightly; said at a funeral, it starts a feud.
Insult"Árþræll.""Oar-slave." Do not.

At the table. Short sentences, understatement and dark jokes ("He was a little wet" of a drowned man). Mavari NPCs say less than they mean and expect the party to work out the rest.

The Nethranan pictorial script

Who used it. The dream-walkers of Nethrana, on the island of Velothis, before Eronis fell to illusion and the Third Sun. Nobody speaks Nethranan now; the spoken language is lost. The script survives on the murals of Eronis, on seven mirror-frames, on a barrow-tablet and a Tyrsan chart, and in the pact tome of Vesperine Ilaro.

Script. Pictures, not letters: an open eye, a closed door, a hand under water. The glyphs change meaning with the light, and the same lintel reads differently to each viewer. Scholars of the Three Libraries argue whether this is a property of the paint, the stone or the reader. The dream-walkers apparently wrote for a reader who was asleep.

UseGlyphsReadings (each viewer gets one)
GreetingAn open eye above a closed eye"I see you sleeping" / "Welcome, dreamer" / "Someone is watching you"
OathTwo hands holding one flame, under three suns"Sworn while the sun lasts" / "Sworn until the third sun" / "Sworn by fire, broken by light"
CurseA door with no wall around it"May you never wake" / "May you find no way out" / "Your home is gone"
WarningA mirror with a figure on the wrong side"Do not look" / "You are already inside" / "This one is not you"

At the table. Describe the glyph, never translate it, and pass each player a different reading on a slip. Let them argue. A character asleep or under a dream effect reads the "true" reading (the DM decides which, and it can change). An Intelligence (Arcana) check of DC 15 tells a reader only that their reading is one of several; comprehend languages gives a reading but not which.

The Mycairos runes

Who used them. Mycairos, the bronze-and-blood fortress kingdom of old Hellenoria, whose records describe a people descended from gods of war and fire and who dug up "the gift beneath stone". Their runes survive on fire-baked clay tablets in archive heaps, a field altar in an abandoned camp, and the hall the diggers broke into under a citadel cistern in the war's last years.

Script. Angular syllable-signs pressed and scratched into clay, with picture-signs for goods (a tripod, a chariot wheel, a bronze ingot) and numbers in strokes. Perhaps a fifth of the signs are read with confidence. Most surviving tablets are inventories, which is why scholars know the word for "bronze greave" and not the word for "god".

UseReading (scholars' best)Meaning and note
Greeting"wa-na-ka ... ke-re-te""[The] lord ... [to/from] the [gap]": the opening line of letters. Nobody knows whom it greets.
Oath"e-ne-ka ... da-ma-te ... pi-ri""For the sake of ... the house ... fire": sworn on the altar in the abandoned camp.
The phrase"o-pe-ro ... ta-pa ... ka-ta""The gift beneath stone." On six tablets in the cistern hall alone. The second sign could also be read "debt".
Curse"a-ke-ro ... to-ko""[May the] messenger ... [take your] children": on a tablet broken on purpose.

At the table. Give players a transcription with gaps in square brackets and let them fill the gaps. A character who studies at the Porticoes of Thessalonika or the Sage's Archive for a week (and 50 gp in fees) can read one tablet with a DC 18 Intelligence (History) check; on a failure they read it confidently and wrongly, and the DM should enjoy that.

Deep Speech of the rifts

Who speaks it. Nothing from this world. It comes through the rifts: faintly from Bound Rifts, loudly from Shifting Rifts. Survivors of a Shifting Rift come back marked, and some of the marked talk in it in their sleep. The cults of the Outer Gods, Maelthra, Lord of the Timeless Howl, above all, chant fragments of it they do not understand, and the Arcane Academy keeps a locked room of transcriptions and a waiting list of scholars who want to go in.

Script. None of its own. Attempts to write it in any alphabet produce strings no two scribes copy the same way. The marked sometimes scratch spirals.

UseSound (as transcribed)Meaning (as far as anyone can tell)
Greeting"Ghr'aal, ghr'aal, vesh-n'"Heard as "we see the opening". The marked say it when a rift is about to open nearby, before anyone else knows.
Oath"Ul-ithaa'gn ... ithaa'gn ... "Not an oath: the word keeps going after the speaker stops. Listeners report hearing it for hours.
Curse"Tz'kh'aar."Spoken over a sleeper, the sleeper wakes marked. Possibly a name. Possibly an address.

At the table. Never translate it. Describe how it sounds (wet, layered, as if several mouths are slightly out of time) and what it does to listeners. A creature that hears it spoken in earnest for the first time makes a DC 12 Wisdom saving throw or is frightened of the speaker until the end of its next turn. A PC who learns Deep Speech should learn words through play, one at a time, and each should be worse than the last.

Other tongues worth a line

The steppe tongue of the Malaunian riders has no script and no word for "nation"; contracts are spoken before witnesses and the witnesses are the record. Wheelwalker cant, the road-folk's secret speech, mixes plateau Acheaorian with chalk-signs left on milestones. Cellar-sign is the silent hand-language of Mavelon's Glass-Stone Cellars, where a shout can crack a sheet of volcanic glass end to end. Dwarvish of Clan Ironhand is the Mithril Reserve's vault language, and its basalt ledgers are cut in it. Pilot's tongue is the Farshore sailors' pidgin of Tyrsan, Qart-Hadethi and common words, heard on the Farshore Quays and nowhere inland.

Forms of Address and Etiquette

How to bow, salute, kneel, kiss the ground or pointedly do none of these, empire by empire, and what it costs to get it wrong.

Imperium Invicta

The salute. Soldiers and officials salute with the right arm raised forward, palm down, fingers together; a civilian greets a magistrate with a raised open hand. Soldiers salute the standard before the officer, and an officer who takes a salute meant for the eagle has insulted the legion. Veterans salute each other with the right fist to the chest, a war habit the regular army has tried and failed to stop.

The morning call. Every great Invictian receives clients at dawn: they wait in the atrium in order of rank, in a toga, and are greeted by name (a slave whispers it) and given a small dole or a promise. Missing the morning call to your patron for more than three days is a political statement. A party that wants a Dux's ear should come at dawn, in its best clothes, with a sponsor.

The table. Diners recline three to a couch, nine to a room; the host's left-hand couch is the place of honour. Wine is mixed with water; drinking it neat is a habit of barbarians and Mavari.

The empty chair. In every official hall there is an empty chair for the Imperator. You do not sit in it, put anything on it or turn your back to it. You bow your head to it on entering. Invictians who are not paying attention still do this automatically, and foreigners who do it are noticed.

Gives offenceWhyWhat it costs
Hailing anyone "Imperator"The title waits for IovianusArrest by the Vigiles; for a soldier, a charge of mutiny
Using a man's praenomen uninvitedClaims to be his family or his ownerDisadvantage on Charisma checks with him for the scene
Wearing purple-bordered cloth without rankSumptuary lawA fine of 50 gp, which nobody pays and everyone remembers
Testing a coin with your teeth in front of an officialImplies the Assay is a lieQuite right, and very rude
Turning your back on the empty chairDisrespect to IovianusEvery Invictian in the room goes cold

Hellenoria

No bowing. Free Hellenorians do not bow to men; they bow only to gods and to the dead. Greeting is a raised right hand, a clasp of right hands between equals, a kiss on the cheek among family. A Hellenorian who bows to an Archon is a slave, a foreigner or a flatterer.

Assembly manners. At an ekklesia the herald asks "Who wishes to speak?" and anyone with a vote may answer. A speaker mounts the platform and puts on a myrtle wreath, which makes his person sacred while he speaks; heckling is allowed, laying hands on him is sacrilege. Older men traditionally speak first. Foreigners may watch from the edge but may not speak unless the Assembly votes them a hearing. In Hellarchon the shipowners' factions sit together and clap together, which is technically within the rules.

The symposium. Guests recline, the first cup is unmixed "to the good spirit", and a symposiarch chosen by dice sets how strong the wine will be. Refusing to sing or speak when the myrtle branch is passed to you is surly; refusing the symposiarch's ruling is barbarous.

Suppliants. A person who clasps your knees and touches your chin is a suppliant, and refusing a suppliant is an offence against the gods. Hellenorian politicians receive several a day and have staff to deal with them.

Gives offenceWhyWhat it costs
Bowing to a magistrateTreats a citizen as a masterContempt; the magistrate's enemies will quote it
Touching a wreathed speakerSacrilegeA charge of impiety; exile or death
Naming a respectable woman aloud (Thebesieas, old Corinth)Old modestyAn insult the court notes; her kinsmen will not
Calling a Voidfolk a meticThe Accord promised citizenshipA cold room, and a note in a Voidfolk family's memory
Asking an Archon about Thalorion IV's healthNobody knows; everyone pretendsThe conversation ends; someone reports it

Acheaoria

The ladder of greeting. Equals kiss on the lips. One a little lower kisses the other's cheek. One far lower makes the full prostration, kneeling and kissing the ground. Every Acheaorian knows the rung of everyone he meets, and the greeting shows it to the whole street.

Before the King of Kings. A petitioner is led in by the hazarapat's ushers, stops at the mark, kneels and kisses the ground, and stays down until told to rise. Standing, he keeps his hands inside his sleeves, and when he speaks he holds his right hand before his mouth, so that his breath does not reach the King's fire. He does not look at the King's face; he speaks only when spoken to; and he backs out without turning. A gift is expected: the court records every gift, and the King gives one back worth more, which places the giver in his debt. Foreigners who refuse to prostrate are, in theory, refused the audience. In practice, since the Signing, envoys of the Imperium and the League are allowed a deep bow, an arrangement both sides describe as the other's concession.

Before a satrap. The same in miniature: a bow from the waist with the right hand over the heart, a kneel for a petition, a gift. A satrap who lets a guest skip the bow is either very gracious or very interested in that guest.

Hospitality. A guest is sacred for three days, and a host who harms a guest under his roof is a Lie-follower. Bread and salt offered must be accepted; water is offered first, always, because the desert taught everyone what matters.

Fire. Do not blow out a flame with your breath, spit into a fire, throw rubbish in one, or point your feet at a hearth. Magi will cover their mouths with a cloth when tending a sacred fire, and a foreigner who leans over a temple flame to see it better has polluted it.

Gives offenceWhyWhat it costs
Refusing proskynesis before the King of KingsDenies his majestyNo audience; possibly no way home
Saying the King's personal name casuallyRoyal tabooA conversation with the King's Eyes and Ears
Blowing out a lampPollutes fire with breathMagi demand purification at your expense (25 gp)
Calling an arashshara "lady"Demotes her from office to womanYour licence, if you are a merchant
Greeting an azata with the wrong rung of the ladderMis-ranks him to the streetInsight DC 12 for anyone watching to see you are a fraud or a fool
Refusing water from a hostRefuses the bond of guest and hostThe host owes you nothing, including your safety

Mavelon, Duneforged, Deiperduem and the steppe

Mavelon's north side. Stand to greet the Reiks and look him in the eye; a bow is an Invictian habit and makes a Mavari think you want something. Grip forearms, not hands. Drink when the horn comes to you, and pass it sunwise. Never offer a Mavari family silver for a death through the Imperium's treasury; the man-price goes to the kin, by hand, before witnesses. At the Gate, the custom is to touch the bronze leaves when they open, both halves together.

Duneforged. Bow from the waist to the Duke and Duchess, a short bow to a marquis or count, a nod to a knight. Kneel only in the Citadel Cathedral. The Duke's household keeps a soldier's punctuality: arrive late to an audience and it has been given to someone else. Never sit with your back to a mine-shaft lamp-shrine, and never whistle underground; the miners say the mountain answers.

Deiperduem. Nod, do not bow. Speak to the Arbiter and the Council in the common tongue. In the embassy compounds, follow the host empire's customs exactly; outside them, bowing to an envoy in the street is read as taking sides, and has been the opening move in two riots.

The steppe. Dismount before greeting the Khagan or a band leader. Do not step on a tent's threshold, which is the household's spine; step over it. Accept fermented mare's milk with the right hand and drink at least once. Never name the dead, never point at a burial mound, and never sit with your back to the hearth-fire. A guest's rights last three days; on the fourth, the host may ask what you are for.
